ADOM is the first steam game I have ever returned.   I typically read many reviews beforehand - so it's not necessary to return games.  In the case of ADOM, most of the reviews fail to mention any of the issues associated with the numerous keybindings required to play the game in an enjoyable fashion.  I didn't notice until after returning the game that most of the negative reviews were unfairly down voted for mentioning critical issues associated with poor mouse controls.
The controls are clunky and the game requires too much memorization of key bindings to play.  Most of the positive reviews posted on Steam are likely from long time players who memorized the long list of key bindings a long time ago.  For new players - this will likely be a highly unpleasant experience because of the aforementioned poor user interface and reliance on key bindings.
There are free versions of this game that you can try out before buying.  I highly recommend any new player to this game to download a free version and try out the controls first hand before purchasing on Steam.  You will easily discover if the controls bother you or not.   Like the other reviews that mention ADOM's outdated reliance keybindings and clunky controls, I expect my review to be down-voted.  I'm okay with that if it means saving other Steam users money.  The limited time listed of me playing this game is actually overstating my time spent on this game.  90% of that time was actually spent reading up on one of the many outdated keybindings required to play before deciding to uninstall the game.

One of the classics, this might be one of the finest - and most difficult - roguelike RPGs you can play. The level of detail and breadth of options are immense and it remains one of the most tense and thrilling challenges any player can look for.
The Steam edition is nicely cleaned up with a few fun additions and a new graphic tileset. There's next to no animations, but it's readable and the character sprites do change as you add/remove equipment. Overall a nice addon to the classic game. Also included is an actual (if short-lived) tutorial to help get players acquianted, but that's really just a token gesture and it doesn't offer all that much advice.
Pros:
- Excellent if you want a challenge.
- Extremely high level of replayability.
- Excellent attention to detail.
- Good variety of classes/races/playstyles.
Cons:
- Obtuse UI and keybindings can be frustrating at times.
- Learning curve like a steep cliff - prepare to die a lot!
- Graphics tileset is barely an improvement over ASCII - this game isn't a looker.
Overall I'd give it 5/7, a perfect buy.

The counter shows that I've spent 28,4h with ADOM on Steam. That is only partly true. The truth is that I've been playing this game since August, 1998. So it's basically like... 17 years. Soon my playtime will be permitted to buy alcohol and smokes. I remember the time when with my best friend we sent a postcard to the creator, Thomas Biskup, because back then ADOM was "postcard-ware" - when you wanted to thank the developer, you just had to go to the post office and send a postcard. It is worth every penny considering the game's been free for over 20 years and you can still check the free, older versions at adom.de
Now ADOM is on Steam and for ~15 euro you can experience one of the hardest, most challenging, vague (in terms of "what should I do now?") and merciless games of all time. ADOM is one of the legendary roguelike games. That means permadeath after 30hrs of game, that means all your scrolls getting soaked because you forgot to grab that damned blanket, that means drowning, because the ice you created with ice bolt just cracked and you and all your belongings are gone, that means getting burned because one of your fire resistance rings isn't blessed, that means almost crying when you see game message stating: *THUMP*. Finally that means checking every class combination and getting acquainted with ADOM Bible or some other, newer guidelike stuff, because you think that there is some magic formula, a cheat, a "best class combination -> enter google" that will allow you to "win". That if you create a trollish healer born under the Candle star sign, you will magically plow through the Caverns of Chaos and win the game.
And then, on level three of some random dungeon you stumble upon undead vault.
ADOM went through a lot during over 20 years of development - now you have graphics engine, you can choose a lot more during character creation, finally - you have a "cheat engine" so to speak, so you can try to go through the whole game without permadeath - as far as I understand, I've never tried this mode, because ADOM is in a way something that games like "Dark Souls" aspire to - you die, you learn, you die again. After a thousand deaths, you die once more, but you try again.
During the "ADOM hiatus" a lot of other games emerged - ToME, Elona, and finally - a lot of lighthearted roguelike(like)s.

The premises of Plague Inc are enjoyable - you're a pathogen with a simple wish, the eradication of all humanity. You start by infecting a patient zero on a country of your choosing, then get DNA points by several ways to upgrade your illness- tranmission by water, resistance against cold, symptoms like sneezing in order to increaser infectivity, etc.
It is certainly fun to watch humanity being more and more infected with your plague, until (in most cases) you decide to evolve it in a deadly strain.
However, there are several problems ruining the fun. If winning grants you new plagues and genes to enhance them (like increasing infectivity in arid areas), half of the plagues are too similar and thus are played accordingly : you wait until everyone is infecte, then you fuse the "bomb" to kill'em all.
Virus is funnier because it mutates like crazy and humanity will be likely to develop a cure before everyone's infected. The worm, able of thought control (like going to another country of your choice, wich is a tad bit broken) is quite fun too, the nano-virus and the bioweapon both play with humanity rushing to develop a cure.
As is stands now, there are not enough variety, strategies are often the same, plus a lack of interactivity. You wait more than anything in this game, the random events do not make this much more lively. Sure, it's only alpha, and it's to be hoped that the multiplayer will be solid, and the scenarios interesting enough.
Because, quite frankly and currently, no, 14€ is not worth it. At all. Especially not when you know that Pandemic II had the same global idea (and was a free web-browser game) and the original game costed 0,99€.
I don't particularly feel entitled as to say what price is right. But one day, I'd love to see a detailed and honest document, summing up the costs a of a mobile to PC port. Plague Inc was hugely acclaimed and sold millions upons millions of copies on mobiles- if the developer wants to extend his market on PC, why being so greedy ?
Even with all the updates promised, I'm not sure that such a price will be justified. I have my doubts about the "hyper-realistic" aspect of the simulation and watching graphs is neither my idea of fun or depth.
Not to say that the game is horrible, but overpriced. If you are interested, I'd advise the following things : buy it on a mobile or Ios if you possess one, or wait for the final version and a sale to acquire it on Steam.

I'm not sure what I could say about this game to accurately sum up how incredible the experience has been so far.
Between the PS3 version and the PC version, I've played over 600 hours of this game since its release. This is something that has to be experienced. The game has grown up a lot since its early days and with an ever-expanding range of content and regular patches, it keeps a tight balance shifting between the various roles and jobs you can take on.
I think one of my favorite aspects of this game is that it blends a few interesting elements into its MMO formula to make it a much more manageabl and satisfying experience. Micro-transactions are completely optional and are mostly for glamour items, so no Pay to Win here. The PvP element is rock solid and I haven't ever felt frustrated due to any technical issues or class imbalance.
One character can be any class at any time regardless of race or gender, and players can seamlessly switch gear sets from class to class when not engaged in combat or in a dungeon. This makes trying everything the game has to offer so much easier than in games like WoW, where your class is set once you start the game.
There are numerous options for crafting and gathering classes, and each one of them is valuable to the experience in some way. Some players even opt to play the game solely for that aspect.
The guilds, or "Free Companies" are also a nice feature. Most MMO's have something like it, but free companies fit right into the narrative of the game comfortably and offer an awesome set of new experiences, like house customization and airship manufacturing. The companies can also activate company-wide buffs that affect things like how much experience the members in the company recieve from combat, or slows down the degradation of their gear.
With the inclusion of Heavensward, Square obviously upped their game. The vanilla version of the game did have a touchy of "rushed out the door" feeling to it, but because of the disasterous first release of the game, it can be considered a master stroke on SE's part how they turned the game around. The quality in Heavensward makes me believe that they had initially fleshed out the Expansion in or around the release of 1.0, but then had all that time from 1.0's failure, ARR's release, and then the year that followed to perfect it.
They changed voice actors, added a much better fleshed out story with much more depth and characterization, and some truly inspired locations centered around the Dragonsong war between the mysterious City-State of Ishgard and the Dravanians. You can tell that Square loves this game and its users and the subscription fee is completely worth it, especially if you love MMO's AND Final Fantasy. I can't recommend this game enough. Seriously. Buy it.

Do you love subscription?
Do you love Final Fantasy?
Do you love Square Enix?
I'm assuming you said "no" to the first and "yes" to the last two, right? Normally most people are turned off by the subscription model, but I guarantee you if you are into SE and FF - subscriptions will mean almost nothing to you. This game is worth almost every penny that you put into it and it's highly enjoyable. I'll just go into it below.
Pros:
- Class system. With one character, you can play EVERY class in the game. This means you can choose the cheaper sub that restricts you to one character per server versus eight per server.
- The community in general is great. There have been a few salty people, but what game doesn't have that? It's very minimal though so don't mind it... unlike League.
- Gameplay mechanics is brilliant. It all feels very smooth and actually very fun to plan your next moves (if you like the strategy).
- Level syncing. Are you a new player and want to play with friends? Well, you can't join them for obvious reasons, but they can join you with a level sync! Their gear gets toned down to be appropriate to the dungeon/FATE level so it won't be overkill.
- End-game life is actually very enjoyable. You have many options available to you: grind for BIS gear, work on other classes, craft stuff, gather stuff or maybe even help people.
- The game provides many different ways of helping you. Dungeons get progressively harder so you can ease into the game or use the party/raid finders to assist you.
- The game patches assist those who are new to the game to speed them towards the end-game. For example, I had to restart my progress and I managed to catch up to the 24/7 players within two weeks (might be an overstatement).
- The storyline is relatively enjoyable. Sometimes a bit cliche, but the DLC provides a very enjoyable storyline.
- THE MUSIC. OH MY GOD, THE MUSIC. SQUARE ENIX GETS IT RIGHT AGAIN.
- I personally think the subscription is at a very decent price. I pay £7.69 per month for the entry sub. If you know you'll play for a long time, buy in bulk - it gets even cheaper.
- The marriage system, fairly self-explanatory.
- I'll add more pros if I can think of any.
Cons:
- The early game. It's very tedious - you usually spam two skills until 26-ish with the occasional other skill. Just hold on, man - you can survive.
- The DPS queues early on. When you play as a DPS, you would normally expect that queues are long since it's the most popular role. It does get better later on though, since DPS are needed a lot more.
- I'll add more cons if I can think of any.
If you have the money to keep a sub, play it.
If you love Final Fantasy, play it.
If you love Square Enix, play it.

Transistor is... interesting. I was sucked in by the number of potential combinations of combat abilities - and then I stuck around for the beautiful artwork and atmosphere of the game.
Transistor is an orthogonal view RPG - similar to those of the early 2000s. It's not standard, though: you don't have a party of multiple characters, and you don't have conversations with NPCs (or at least, not as such). Combat occurs in bounded areas, which you can't leave until finishing the combat - but your character can move freely within these. Abilities can be used in real time, or planned out using a "pause" kind of ability (which has to recharge after being used), making the combat more turn based and strategy focused.
There are three main things however, which really make the game shine.
First is the mystery/detective style story. The game starts with your character right in the middle of things, with very little explanation - and as the player, you spend the game trying figure out what happened and what exactly is going on. I found this to be a great storytelling technique, and very quickly got me hooked. Little snippets of information are "fed" to you through by your narrator companion; you also find various clues as you explore.
Another way of finding information is cleverly linked to the second notable thing about this game: the combat abilities.
As you progress through the game, (and level), you receive abilities called 'Functions' (a computer programming reference). Each one can be used as an active ability, set as a passive bonus, or used as an upgrade to your active Functions. This means that each new function you gain can have 3 different effects - and there are then an almost limitless number of potential combinations. The best thing about this though, is that you can freely change how you combine your Functions throughout the game. If something's not working for you, change it up. You can use one set-up to be effective against large numbers of weak monsters, and then change again for the boss battles. If you think a particular combination of Functions might be cool, fun - or even just good for a laugh - try it out, and you can always change again later. This encourages improvisation and experimentation, while also removing the pressure of making the right decisions on how to upgrade your character (which sometimes detracts in other games).
The Functions also tie in with the game's backstory. Each one is named after a character (including the one you control), and as you use the Function in different ways, more information about this character is available to read. This acts as another incentive to change around your Function combinations by slowly feeding you more of the story.
Finally, the whole atmosphere of the game really is something to experience. The character portraits and cutscene artwork are amazing, the way the protagonist hums along to the soundtrack of the game... I'm not sure what else to say - you have to see if for yourself.
Only a few complaints:
I found the combat to be a bit of a grind as I neared the end of the game (though that may just be me).
I also thought everyone's praises of the soundtrack were overrated, and left me disappointed. Ashley Barrett's vocals *are* stunning - but although the the music fits the environment of the game, it's just repetitive and mostly forgettable.
If all that leaves you wanting to know more - go play it! Why are you still reading this?
However, if that doesn't grab your attention, and you prefer your games to be a bit more standard with an overt story that starts more slowly - this one isn't for you.

It's a great game. no doubt. It has a futuristic setting which brings forth many innovative and cool design concepts. Pity the story is abit too short. Overlooking that, the storyline is great. It has a touching ending, one that hits harder than bioshock infinite's ending. It brings forth questions that we must ask ourselves - Do we have to rely on technology? And to what extend? What is the worth of life, and the consequences that follow in the name of fame? How far do we go for our loved ones?
Other than the story, the gameplay is absolutely fantastic. It allows you to customize your spells in all sorts of manner, promoting creativity and encourages people to keep grinding against the same enemies with different approaches. It also buffs the enemies as you progress further into the game, making it much more of a challenge then just a simple hack-and-slash game.
What I like most about the game is definitely the artstyle and music. It fits in perfectly, reflecting on both the initial utopiantheme and the slow descent into the dystopia which the city becomes as one approaches the end. The option to hold tab and listen to Red sing is also a gem. Her voice protrudes out from the ambient yet invigorating background music, giving even more depth to the storyline of the game, singling it out from the conventional hack-and-slash genre type of games.
Overall, it is a beautifully crafted and ingeniusly designed game. Would rate almost 10/10.
Gameplay: 9/10 (It's unique style style such as the "Turn()" ability makes it stand out from other hack-and-slash games. The enemy units are also properly balanced, posing as a proper challenge."
Visuals: 10/10 (Absolutely stunning. Art is meticulous at the proper parts and simple yet creative at other spots. The design for the enemy units<younglady, jerk, badcell etc.> as well as the transistor is refreshing new and creative.)
Concep/Storylinet: 9/10 (Very cool concept. Reveals alot about the human nature and it's instinct to be selfish. Deeper thoughts can be put into the storyline to reveal much much more about the settings and the story.)
Music: 10/10 (Beautiful. Fits into the settings perfectly. Go and listen for yourself :).)
Overall score: 9~/10
Would recommend?: Definitely

I've put over 300+ hrs and a lot of my money (for cosmetics or crates) into this game. There are soo many cool things in this game. You've got crafting, fighting, adventure, quests, houses, different playable races and much more. Let me go indepth about some things.
Leveling - It isnt like WoW, where different areas have level caps. You can pretty much go to any area (as long as you have wayshrine there or the gold to get there). The world is PVE unless you duel or go to Cyrodiil
Crafting - Crafting is like Skyrim but more (as it is an Elder Scrolls-esc game). There is Alchemy, Enchanting, Blacksmithing, Woodworking, Leatherworking/Clothworking, and Cooking (If I've missed any I apologize, i have a bad memory). You can learn ALL the crafting trees. The first few levels are quick and easy to level but I will admit, you have to grind out the last couple of levels. My blacksmithing is at 49/50 and thats on my main toon. And with all these crafting trees, you can actually create furniture.
Homes - There are two ways to buy some (not all) homes. Either Crowns (in game currency that can be bought) or Gold. I personally saved up my money, grinding out quests and stealing stuff, for my home in Grahtwood (cost about 190,000 gold). That part can be tedious and tiring but rewarding in the end. You can decorate your house with mounts, pets, and furniture you either make or find randomly through out your adventure.
Fighting - There are four main classes (Dragonknight, Nightblade, Templar, Sorcerer) I don't know much about dragonknightgs or sorcerers as I dont play them but I main a healing Templar (who can also do some damage) and a Nightblade Melee Damage Dealer. There is also Warden class that you can play if you have Morrowind. If you like bears, get morrowind lol
Races - There are 9 base races that go with the Alliances
Aldmeri Dominion: Khajiit, Bosmer, Altmer
Ebonheart Pact: Nord, Argonian, Dunmer
Daggerfall Convenant: Brenton, Redguard, Orcs
With each race, comes different bonuses to the race. Like Argonians get more from potions and can swim faster.
(Unless you have the imperial edition upgrade, you are binded to that specific alliance. With the Imperial Edition, you can be in any allliance and gain access to the Imperial race)

Overall this game is in my top list of MMOs and Games. I love playing casually though there is some competitive things like Cyrodiil Alliance Wars (which is PVP) or running to get a chest, materials, etc. Just dont be that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that steals♥♥♥♥♥♥from someone who cleared the area to get it :P

The
System - Why is the word “tutorial” in italics? Because this game does
have a tutorial. Papers, Please is a click-based game in which clients present their papers to a security checkpoint-the one you are stationed-to be cleared or denied for entry into the glorious Arstotzka. As the game progresses, various scenarios add vital components to the game’s management system.

This is where the
system kicks in: the first entrant you meet each day is usually a ‘Denied’ entrant, mainly due to that day’s clause, which teaches the player throughout the game to maintain the new ruling set by the Arstotzka command. Of course, some of these rules dissipate or change, but as new features are added or story checkpoints occur, the game instructs the player how to react to said changes with the first entrant of each day; to me, this is a masterful way to teach the player without the need to add more content for them to read.
Storytelling - Though the title is not the first to implement this style of storytelling, Papers, Please utilizes text-newspaper clippings and work noticed-to organize the ever-changing themes and rulings that occur during each day’s shift.
(and I will not say which of these are spoilers because some of these may occur and some may not)
Regardless of the scenario, the game hints the supposed rendezvous with the said individual, which may or may not occur within the next given days.
Freedom of Choice - A man, succeeding his brother in-law and wife to your security checkpoint, expresses his elation for ultimately becoming free from his previous home country and of the new life that his wife, brother in-law, and he shall have in the glorious of Arstoztka! The wife and brother in-law were accepted after no deliberation required. The husband’s passport expired the day before, and Arstoztka law prevents anyone with an expired passport, whatever the reason, from passage to the country. The man pleads for you to authorize his entry permit, but you had earned two citations from prior mistakes; one more will prevent you from earning enough to feed your family. What would you do? There are several moments in the game similar to this that obligate the player to establish a decision. Day 1, I had chosen to follow Arstozta law no matter the consequences, but found myself quoting the unchanging phrase, “What have I done?”
Overall Feel - Papers, Please is, to put it plainly, a grey title. The graphics, audio, and clients are bleakly designed to create an impression of oppression from the Arstoztka government. Even when the unnamed protagonist asked for each entrants’ paperwork-requesting their documents with the line, “Papers, please”-they do so with an ominous tone as if the phrase is ingrained as a rehearsed statement. The color palette of Papers, Please is as described: nearly colorless, with only specific objects retaining any tone of life. The clients you meet at the front gate hold a rigid design as well, seen
.
TL:DR - In this society of right and wrong, justice and devotion, pride and dignity, how you play this dismal title is completely up to you. It’s a game about questions. It’s a game about truth. It’s a game about pride in country. Papers, Please suggests a simulation fashion of action combined with the immersion of the protagonist as yourself. The game becomes less about simply doing your job, and more of who you plan to save and leave behind with the government of a questionably oppressive nation breathing down your neck, prodding you with symbols that question each action you make. This is the hunting simulator I've been wanting for years, and you can love it too, if you keep a few very important details in mind:
1. Despite its claims, this game is not really free to play, or at least, the free to play model is not great. To really enjoy it you need to invest a good $30-$40 to get some good equipment (so you don't scare every animal away immediately) and licenses (so that you can hunt any animal).
2. This is NOT an arcade-type hunting game. It actually requires you to hunt, tracking your prey and occasionally losing them. It takes time and patience. There will not be ten bucks popping out at you every five seconds. This is actually what I love about the game, but I can see how some would not take to it as easily if they were expecting something else. Besides, the world is gorgeous. Take time to walk and enjoy the sights along the way. Pro tip: After the first 150 yards or so after leaving your hunting camp, don't use the run button. It can scare the animals away. Again. you have to be able to enjoy a slower-paced game.
3. The user interface takes some getting used to. It doesn't work like your average first-person shooter, and there is not a great tutorial that teaches you everything. Most of your important items, like your weapon and deer call and such are mapped to the number keys. Watch a beginner's guide on Youtube or on the TheHunter wiki page before diving in.
If you can handle those three things, you are in for an incredible hunting simulation. The slower-pace makes the successful kill incredibly satisfying, and the online tournaments you can enter (you don't play with other people; just submit your best kills to see who scores the highest) add tons of incentive to keep playing. As I said, part of the joy of this game is just enjoying the world. I don't know how many screen shots I've taken during my time in-game. It's beautiful. Happy hunting!

It's funny how a lot games make you farm and build everything by hand these days. As if manual labour is this magical mechanic that instils intrinsic value onto game objects and resources... I mean, sure, it kinda does... sometimes... but Factorio takes a whole different approach.
This game is about automation and logistics. As you go along, you continually find ways to automate your systems until your base is basically running itself. You'll eventually reach a point where robots are doing all of the building and demolishing for you, freeing you up to work on bigger and better things.
Factorio can appear intimidating, but rest assured that you can mess with everything at your own pace. Organizing inputs/outputs and looking for ways to reduce bottlenecks is something that I find exploratory rather than puzzling.
For example, it's not about perfection or having the exact materials delivered to some factory. It's more about flow, throughput and reducing bottlenecks.
After obsessing over belt logistics, I moved on to robo-network. Eventually, I got super into trains. My train network is very modular and has cars sharing tracks, going opposite directions, and it's all setup so they play nice and never run into each other. It's a lot of fun.
It never goes on sale, but it's very satisfying to play. It's way easier to get into than how it looks. It also runs beautifully, which is amazing given how many thousands of objects you can have going at once. I would highly recommend this game. 11/10

I'm not sure what I could say about this game to accurately sum up how incredible the experience has been so far.
Between the PS3 version and the PC version, I've played over 600 hours of this game since its release. This is something that has to be experienced. The game has grown up a lot since its early days and with an ever-expanding range of content and regular patches, it keeps a tight balance shifting between the various roles and jobs you can take on.
I think one of my favorite aspects of this game is that it blends a few interesting elements into its MMO formula to make it a much more manageabl and satisfying experience. Micro-transactions are completely optional and are mostly for glamour items, so no Pay to Win here. The PvP element is rock solid and I haven't ever felt frustrated due to any technical issues or class imbalance.
One character can be any class at any time regardless of race or gender, and players can seamlessly switch gear sets from class to class when not engaged in combat or in a dungeon. This makes trying everything the game has to offer so much easier than in games like WoW, where your class is set once you start the game.
There are numerous options for crafting and gathering classes, and each one of them is valuable to the experience in some way. Some players even opt to play the game solely for that aspect.
The guilds, or "Free Companies" are also a nice feature. Most MMO's have something like it, but free companies fit right into the narrative of the game comfortably and offer an awesome set of new experiences, like house customization and airship manufacturing. The companies can also activate company-wide buffs that affect things like how much experience the members in the company recieve from combat, or slows down the degradation of their gear.
With the inclusion of Heavensward, Square obviously upped their game. The vanilla version of the game did have a touchy of "rushed out the door" feeling to it, but because of the disasterous first release of the game, it can be considered a master stroke on SE's part how they turned the game around. The quality in Heavensward makes me believe that they had initially fleshed out the Expansion in or around the release of 1.0, but then had all that time from 1.0's failure, ARR's release, and then the year that followed to perfect it.
They changed voice actors, added a much better fleshed out story with much more depth and characterization, and some truly inspired locations centered around the Dragonsong war between the mysterious City-State of Ishgard and the Dravanians. You can tell that Square loves this game and its users and the subscription fee is completely worth it, especially if you love MMO's AND Final Fantasy. I can't recommend this game enough. Seriously. Buy it.

Do you love subscription?
Do you love Final Fantasy?
Do you love Square Enix?
I'm assuming you said "no" to the first and "yes" to the last two, right? Normally most people are turned off by the subscription model, but I guarantee you if you are into SE and FF - subscriptions will mean almost nothing to you. This game is worth almost every penny that you put into it and it's highly enjoyable. I'll just go into it below.
Pros:
- Class system. With one character, you can play EVERY class in the game. This means you can choose the cheaper sub that restricts you to one character per server versus eight per server.
- The community in general is great. There have been a few salty people, but what game doesn't have that? It's very minimal though so don't mind it... unlike League.
- Gameplay mechanics is brilliant. It all feels very smooth and actually very fun to plan your next moves (if you like the strategy).
- Level syncing. Are you a new player and want to play with friends? Well, you can't join them for obvious reasons, but they can join you with a level sync! Their gear gets toned down to be appropriate to the dungeon/FATE level so it won't be overkill.
- End-game life is actually very enjoyable. You have many options available to you: grind for BIS gear, work on other classes, craft stuff, gather stuff or maybe even help people.
- The game provides many different ways of helping you. Dungeons get progressively harder so you can ease into the game or use the party/raid finders to assist you.
- The game patches assist those who are new to the game to speed them towards the end-game. For example, I had to restart my progress and I managed to catch up to the 24/7 players within two weeks (might be an overstatement).
- The storyline is relatively enjoyable. Sometimes a bit cliche, but the DLC provides a very enjoyable storyline.
- THE MUSIC. OH MY GOD, THE MUSIC. SQUARE ENIX GETS IT RIGHT AGAIN.
- I personally think the subscription is at a very decent price. I pay £7.69 per month for the entry sub. If you know you'll play for a long time, buy in bulk - it gets even cheaper.
- The marriage system, fairly self-explanatory.
- I'll add more pros if I can think of any.
Cons:
- The early game. It's very tedious - you usually spam two skills until 26-ish with the occasional other skill. Just hold on, man - you can survive.
- The DPS queues early on. When you play as a DPS, you would normally expect that queues are long since it's the most popular role. It does get better later on though, since DPS are needed a lot more.
- I'll add more cons if I can think of any.
If you have the money to keep a sub, play it.
If you love Final Fantasy, play it.
If you love Square Enix, play it.

This game was recommended to me by a friend who loves clickers, and I like clickers, too. Clickers are a type of "time management" game, a la Facebook games, where it behooves you to micromanage, but after a few, it's best to leave and come back the next day in real life.
I played Tap Tap Infinity to detox from the addictive Clicker Heroes, the game responsible for the theme of the Steam Monster Sale. Tap Tap Infinity is a lot like Clicker Heroes, as in, the game has a lot of complexity for a clicker and has many of the same Gods - expect to prestige a lot, and the clicking "spells" to cast are ususble throughout the entire game.  There is a calculator on the internet to advise on what the best way to prestige is - either through more gold or more damage, and the game soft restarts with these bonuses permanently.  There are ways of exporting your save file, but it is still possible to lose this if your computer breaks - try to keep a save file on Pastebin or something as a backup, as with Clicker Heroes.  If you do, or if you're frustrated with the game, you can always copy/paste a completed save file and grab all the achievements, if you need to detox from all this addictiveness, or get plain frustrated.
This game is not a cash grab, although there are premium gods which will increase your pace a few fold, but these gods are like 1 dollar each American to get, and there's no real reason to put more than 10 dollars in this game.  The worst clickers make it so it's several times harder to progress every 10 levels, making it so you must keep putting money into the game or bust - this is not one of those. I've played on and off for 2 years, and I've finally beaten the game. Finished, polished, has an ending to the game - 5 stars.

Hmm. Consider this a "meh" review rather than a "this sucks balls" review, but Steam has strictly binary choices for reviews, so I can't indicate that.
Tap Tap Infinity is yet another clicker game, except it's in 3D. So that's cool. Not super fancy 3D, but it's just kinda nice. Except when sometimes enemies stop rendering and you have to go to the infinity token screen to make things normal, but eh, bugs happen. That's still kinda annoying, though.
I do like the UI a lot more than other clicker games. It just feels nice and smooth. I can't really elaborate on that more, other than I do like that you can use the right and middle mouse buttons in addition to the left to click enemies, which makes spamming clicks a lot easier.
Gameplay-wise, it's kinda simplistic I guess? There doesn't seem to be much depth to it beyond the basic formula. Perhaps some would prefer that.
But I dunno. There's just not much reason for me to recommend this when other clicker games are out there, it just feels kinda... repetitive. I mean, clicker games are sorta like that by nature. But usually they'll give you some reason to actually open the game and not just blindly accumulate progress offline. Tap Tap Infinity, or so I feel, doesn't really, other than "I should probably buy some hero upgrades" every day or so.
I mean, you might as well get it if you're just looking for as many games with offline progress as possible so you can earn achievements or whatever while you're playing other games. It's free(mium), doesn't take up a huge amount of disk space, so it's like sure whatever.
It has great replayability and its a very interesting and engaging game.

I'll admit I went into this game having mixed expectations, while the reviews made me think it might be bad,  having Artifex Mundi involved (they did not fully make this game) made me hopeful. So whil I expected the worse I was hoping for the best... It was some of the worst...
First off the sound effects. Someone's job must have been to find the most soul wrenching sound clips ever. I use a high-def headset so some noises I find discomforting while on normal speakers or headphones it might be fine but I would say 9/10 sound effects in this game made my ears cringe a bit. Even transition noises between screens were bad.
The voice acting, well let's be hoest most hidden obbject games (HOGs) don't have the best voice acting. This one hits a new low. It sounds like lines just read off paper with an odd accent. I can see them wanting to make the main character having an accent but they still could have picked a better voice actor. To top that off the lines that are not in grammatically correct english are some of the lines of text that is displayed as your character speaking. The other voice actors do a slightly better job.
Plot... Okay... Usually HOGs have bad plots or typical ones but at least they usually make sense!
Hidden Object Scenes. Okay who in the world thought "Hey, you know what'd be cool to add to a hog scene Jim?" "What Larry?" "Let's add things that shift form and you can only click it when it's in the form listed on the object list!" "Wait Larry, wouldn't the shifting give away the items position anyway and just be annoying to wait for it to shift back to the correct item?" "Yea! Let's do it Jim! And make sure the shift time is at laest 5 seconds long just in case it's the last item the player is searching for it can be extra annoying!" That has got to be the most annoying feature ever thought of in for a HOG (aside from single pixel objects) Another problem with HOGs is that the items are hidden mainly with clutter and usually never anything clever.
Puzzles. If you've ever played a HOG before, you've probably already solved most of these puzzles and they were probably better designed. Often times the back arrow is too sensative and you'll back out of a puzzle, othertimes the puzzle isn't fun it's just tedious (there's a maze one that ugh... it's one of those don't touch the sides or the walls thing but with a long linear maze...).
Logic. While not always the best place for logic... HOGs USUALLY follow some logic but this game loves having you find random items in random places. I can see getting a screw driver from a tool shed... I can see getting dog food from a kitchen... I cannot see how most of these items are placed! You find a pickaxe in some case after solving a puzzle that was like a picture frame! Basically any item you need will be uncovered by solving a puzzle towards the end game, no matter how little sense it makes.
Overall this game, while not a broken game (I didn't find any glitches) it's not really worth the money or time. The plot doesn't redeem the lack of good gameplay nor does the gameplay redeem the plot. It feels like whoever made this game asked Artifex Mundi for a plot premise and their animation team and scraps from their old games. So while it makes a playable game, it is by no means a good one. If you have to pick, skip over this game and get one fully made by Artifex Mundi. Don't let the pretty art fool you, there is little substance behind it. Final verdict 4/10

Original Review, December 2015:
This was the first ever Steam game I returned; it's that bad, at least on my Mac. First, basic computer program sequences didn't work. For example, I couldn't figure out how to quit out of the game and the standard Command-Q and menu items did nothing. I eventually pulled up the "Force Quit" menu and killed the program that way (equivalent to kill -9 for Unix users). Second, the fonts and window don't scale properly, and there are about 37,000 settings for these things, none of which produce a nice, usable look and feel on fonts unless you leave the window a tiny thing on the screen. On a 2560x1440 or 1920x1080 screen it is just insanely silly. Third, the tutorial is more annoying than helpful. It randomly pops up a super-small text box that is ridiculously difficult to scroll through telling you things that are generally irrelevant at the time. Sure, it's a roguelike and so there are tons of commands, but at least list them for me in some sort of importance order on the side of the screen or something.
All in all, I've been playing Roguelikes since, literally, Rogue in the 80s and this was one of the worst experiences ever. I returned the program to Steam and downloaded the free one. I've spent a few hours with the free one and found no way around any of these problems above. If you want a truly great Roguelike to buy here on Steam, look at ToME instead. It's cheaper, easier to learn, much more beautiful, and "just works."

I don't usually write reviews, but this game is good enough to warrant writing one. I haven't played this game before it came out on steam, so I'm not really blinded by nostalgia goggles. But this game is good, only it's the toughest learning curve I've ever experienced, even harder than X-Com Long war mod. To those expecting to play something where it's possible to win as long as you play right, turn away. However for those willing to preservere through tens and eventually hundreds of character deaths this game is rewarding. It's sort of like crossing a minefield, where the signs are all in a different language, so you don't know where the mines are or what to do. And take my advice, the tutorial isn't that good, it's better to wiki everything, unless you are really really masochistic and wanna learn everything through dying.
But once you learn the tricks of the game, it's enormously fun. For example, I kept starving to death, because I didn't realize you could eat corpses and nobody minds. No karma lashbacks, and no getting sick, unless you eat something poisonous. Then I finally got past the third dungeon. That's right, I've died multiple times and still hadn't gotten past that third beginner dungeon. Then I made the mistake of wandering into a random dungeon and getting killed by a room full of giants.
Anyways the perks of this game are:
1 it's very difficult, sort of like demon souls.
2. It's a delight for people who like to imagine what the fights look like instead of seeing it. Like when I accidentally wandered into a water trap with a fluff ball in my backpack and gremlins started appearing out of nowhere. I was like "Oh, ****" and they constantly multiplied around my Monk character. Hundreds of dead gremlins later, the floor was flooded with blood and my monk had came through unscathed.
3. There are many, many, many different ways to play the game. You could be the unarmed monk,(my favorite), the untouchable wizard(too frail in melee for my tastes), or the cunning assassin(kept dying, cuz he doesn't start with heal) and much much more. Apparently there's a race that starts with the spit acid ability or something.
Oh well, this reviews getting a bit too long. In short, this is a good game for those willing to put up with how hard core it is and are willing to put up with the ridiculous key mappings.

is a beautiful little indie game by Lucas Pope, a gem that truly stands out in the ocean filled with Early Access Survival- and 8-bit "retro" adventure games. The year is 1982, and you work as an inspector at a border security checkpoint. Dozens of people flow past each day, and you must carefully examine each person's passport and then either approve or deny their application.
As days go, the game also gets progressively harder. Immigrants will be required to have more and more documents, and the payroll stays the same, yet you must also provide food and warmth for your family. Political backstabbing and tension between countries may also come into play, due to the 6-year-war between Arstotzka and Kolechia.
I really wish there were more games like this, but unfortunately both creativity and originality have become rarer as time has gone by.

Another excellent game from SuperGiant Games.
However, don't think this is another Bastion. You'll be disappointed if you do.
You play as Red: a female singer that was attacked by a secret high society group. As you go along, you'll pick up functions that can be used either as a attack, as extra effects for attack functions or as a passive. You can combine any functions you like to create unique attacks. You can also use a special key to pause the action and plan your attacks/escape. However, every function has a cost/cooldown, so you can't just go around and spam attacks.
Because of this, the game really starts to shine when you go into New Game +. Due to the learning curve, you'll only star to really appreciate it when you've unlocked many of the functions and start to understand how to best combine them.
And it's that aspect of the game that makes it stand on it's own. The massive amount of different possible combinations of attacks and passives actually makes you change your own play style. Combine that with some of the limiters, and you have a constantly changing difficulty that forces you to use almost all of the functions.
Story wise, I think it's about the same as Bastion: it has a great story that you'll fill in as the game progresses.
The visuals are amazing, as expected from SuperGiant. But what really shines and makes the game awesome is the fantastic soundtrack, made by the same artists as Bastion. I also loved that they've added a single button to make Red hum along the track that is playing. It seems something so simple but it really adds depth to Red as a character.
All in all, if you liked Bastion, isometric games, great soundtracks or challenging game play, you should definitely get this.

This game is absolutely beautiful. Although I haven't had the chance to play Bastion, it's clear that the art director and artists from Supergiant games put a lot of hardwork and thoughtfulness into their character designs and game world. The music and soundtrack is also one of my favorite things about this game, with some of the songs mixing beautiful vocals and instruments with synth-techno that really added to the environment and even certain characters (I won't spoil who though).
The combat style is definately odd, and if you're the type of person that prefers RTS games then you'll probably feel more at home than I was when I first started. Yes, it's a little hard to get used to, but at the same time the interesting variety and effects the game abilities have allow you to kind of "mix and match" your favorite ones to your keyboard/gamepad buttons, so in a way you're allowed to tailor your abilities to your playstyle. Eventually, after unlocking most of the abilities, I had gotten really used to the RTS style gameplay.
Story-wise, this game is quite vague at times. There's more emphasis on trying to piece together what happened to the main character from the beginning and the little things like function files and dialogue between the main character and the sword can tell you a lot about what's happening. I bought this came at 50% off, making it better value for the money than other reviewers. It's not up to the same standard as the other Artifex Mundi Hidden Object games, and is a bit short and uninspired. At the price I paid I think it is fair value for the money.

I enjoyed this game, although it is one of the weaker titles in Artifex Mundi's Premium Adventure Collection, all of which I have played (although this is the first I've gotten through Steam).
The graphics were  nicely detailed and skillfully drawn, not too dark.  The hidden object scenes were not too easy, but not particularly challenging -- except for some of the item listings being misleading (due to translations, I suppose).  One listing, though, I found particularly annoying.  I try to complete the hidden object scenes without any misclicks if possible, and this one had 'Flask' listed in a laboratory HOS -- the table had many flasks!  Grr.  However, I particularly liked the morphing objects in the scenes.  I didn't experience any graphic glitches during my playthrough.
Voiceovers were well done and the the music was fine.  However, I should point out that I'm happy with music as long as it doesn't distract or annoy me enough to turn it off.  This music fit well into the background for me.
The puzzles were of various difficulty, but all were somewhat on the easy side.
Two main cons I found with this game -- first, it is somewhat short, and the second is the story.  Besides the introduction, the occasional cutscene and a bit towards the end, there is very little story.  The premise was interesting, as I progressed through the different locations, I kept looking for things to find that would answer some questions about the main character's background or heighten the mystery about her mentor's death -- old films, pictures or letters, a tale from one of the characters interacted with ... something!   No real suspense or tension where I was eager to press on to find out what happens.   No real explanations really as to why certain, um, things were found at the residence.
There was certainly enough space to include more elements -- the locations had plenty of places where more content could have been added to great effect, and increase gameplay time.  In fact I was somewhat surprised at the relatively few things one had to do in each scene.
Summary:
I wanted to like this game -- it's obvious alot of work went into the development, and for a newer developer (Brave Giant Studio) it's a commendable effort.  However, in my opinion, the lacklustre story presentation offsets the technical and artistic strengths to the extent that I cannot bring myself to recommend this game.   If they come out with a sequel, I'll certainly look at it -- but only if I could try a demo first and see if the story will draw me in before I made a purchase.
Features not listed in the game description here:
- Two levels of difficulty: Casual and Expert.
- Different types of collectibles
- Morphing objects in the hidden object scenes.
- Travel Map
- Bonuses - Bonus Game, wallpapers, music, replayable cutscenes, hidden object scenes, and puzzles.

I was really excited for a new Artifex Mundi (hereafter referred to as "AM") game to arrive on Steam, but unfortunately I can't recommend this.
I love AM games and own all the others that are available on Steam, but this one is simply not up to par with what I've come to expect from the company. I noticed that it was only published by AM and was actually developed by a different company, so perhaps that's why it falls so short for me.
The story is weird, uninteresting, and doesn't make a lot of sense. In some scenes the graphics are poorly rendered and the game mechanics are glitchy. The music is repetitive and doesn't suit the atmosphere well. The puzzles are extremely easy to the point of being boring (I like relatively easy puzzles because I like to relax when I play games, but the puzzles in this game are over the top). There are typos, misspellings, and awkward use of English (I understand these games are not made by native English speakers, so I am forgiving, but this hasn't really been an issue in other AM games). To top it all off, the game is quite short; I played through both the main and bonus stories (which by the way, the bonus story was a bit weird and had little to do with the main story) in about 3 hours.
All that being said... I still mildly enjoyed playing this. It's a decent way to pass the time and is really lovely to look at. If you're a fan of this type of game, give it a go if you can get it on sale. But if you're new to the genre, try a different AM game because I don't think this one will leave a very good impression.

For me, this is a classic game that's improved by a tileset that expands the playability for new and old players alike.
This game is part of the big three formative roguelike games that set the benchmark for this type of packrat, dungeon crawling, permadeath that's so wonderfully additctive. The three consist of Angband (specifically T.O.M.E and its predecessors for me), Nethack and (of course) ADOM.
ADOM was probably the game the least like the others in terms of how everything worked. It allowed for extremes of overly complicated OR remarkably simple gameplay and has a depth far beyond any roguelike from its time and for that matter most roguelikes ever.
Once you've spent some time getting sufficiently spoiled (you kinda have to to finish the game), you'll end up chasing ultra endings and then you can pretty much kiss your free time goodbye. I'd definitely recommend this game provided you understand that there is a learning curve and you take your time to get into it.

Another excellent game from SuperGiant Games.
However, don't think this is another Bastion. You'll be disappointed if you do.
You play as Red: a female singer that was attacked by a secret high society group. As you go along, you'll pick up functions that can be used either as a attack, as extra effects for attack functions or as a passive. You can combine any functions you like to create unique attacks. You can also use a special key to pause the action and plan your attacks/escape. However, every function has a cost/cooldown, so you can't just go around and spam attacks.
Because of this, the game really starts to shine when you go into New Game +. Due to the learning curve, you'll only star to really appreciate it when you've unlocked many of the functions and start to understand how to best combine them.
And it's that aspect of the game that makes it stand on it's own. The massive amount of different possible combinations of attacks and passives actually makes you change your own play style. Combine that with some of the limiters, and you have a constantly changing difficulty that forces you to use almost all of the functions.
Story wise, I think it's about the same as Bastion: it has a great story that you'll fill in as the game progresses.
The visuals are amazing, as expected from SuperGiant. But what really shines and makes the game awesome is the fantastic soundtrack, made by the same artists as Bastion. I also loved that they've added a single button to make Red hum along the track that is playing. It seems something so simple but it really adds depth to Red as a character.
All in all, if you liked Bastion, isometric games, great soundtracks or challenging game play, you should definitely get this.

This game is absolutely beautiful. Although I haven't had the chance to play Bastion, it's clear that the art director and artists from Supergiant games put a lot of hardwork and thoughtfulness into their character designs and game world. The music and soundtrack is also one of my favorite things about this game, with some of the songs mixing beautiful vocals and instruments with synth-techno that really added to the environment and even certain characters (I won't spoil who though).
The combat style is definately odd, and if you're the type of person that prefers RTS games then you'll probably feel more at home than I was when I first started. Yes, it's a little hard to get used to, but at the same time the interesting variety and effects the game abilities have allow you to kind of "mix and match" your favorite ones to your keyboard/gamepad buttons, so in a way you're allowed to tailor your abilities to your playstyle. Eventually, after unlocking most of the abilities, I had gotten really used to the RTS style gameplay.
Story-wise, this game is quite vague at times. There's more emphasis on trying to piece together what happened to the main character from the beginning and the little things like function files and dialogue between the main character and the sword can tell you a lot about what's happening. It's certainly quite linear and does try to make it open through the artwork and character dialogue/function files, but I get a sense that we've only got a small grasp on what this world's big picture is, which is somewhat disappointing considering how interesting the characters seemed to make it and how beautiful it's depicted.
Unfortunately, this game is short. I was able to complete it within about 6 hours (and that says a lot considering how slow I am about completing games), and the boss battle at the end is.....underwhelming. It kind of just felt like I was fighting any other big tough brute monster from the game with a crapton of health tacked on.
Nonetheless though, this is still an excellent game to play with interesting characters in a breathtaking science-fiction type world. I'd definately suggest it to anyone willing to try it.

It's funny how a lot games make you farm and build everything by hand these days. As if manual labour is this magical mechanic that instils intrinsic value onto game objects and resources... I mean, sure, it kinda does... sometimes... but Factorio takes a whole different approach.
This game is about automation and logistics. As you go along, you continually find ways to automate your systems until your base is basically running itself. You'll eventually reach a point where robots are doing all of the building and demolishing for you, freeing you up to work on bigger and better things.
Factorio can appear intimidating, but rest assured that you can mess with everything at your own pace. Organizing inputs/outputs and looking for ways to reduce bottlenecks is something that I find exploratory rather than puzzling.
For example, it's not about perfection or having the exact materials delivered to some factory. It's more about flow, throughput and reducing bottlenecks.
After obsessing over belt logistics, I moved on to robo-network. Eventually, I got super into trains. My train network is very modular and has cars sharing tracks, going opposite directions, and it's all setup so they play nice and never run into each other. It's a lot of fun.
It never goes on sale, but it's very satisfying to play. It's way easier to get into than how it looks. It also runs beautifully, which is amazing given how many thousands of objects you can have going at once. I would highly recommend this game. 11/10

Factorio is probably the most insidiously infectious, mind-infesting game I have ever played. It's really hard to explain to people exactly why I love it so much: the logistics puzzles that come with scaling up your factory, unlocking the technology to create more and more complex items; the fact that the core design makes it such that the difficulty of those puzzles continues to scale up right as far as you care to push it; the rock-solid coding that gives you the freedom to scale up your factory as far as you wish-- these are all great reasons to love this game.
But what keeps me hooked is the community surrounding the game and the developers' continued dedication to polishing every element of this game. I have pumped about 170 hours into this game as of writing this review, and, per their awesome blog that gets updated every friday without fail, I know that they are going to overhaul some elements of the game along with a graphical upgrade, for free, which I expect to provide at least a couple hundred more hours of enjoyment.
Can't recommend this game highly enough.

Borderlands 2 is a game that throws you in the deep end of the pool by getting you shooting up more things than you can imagine minutes after starting the story. It is recommended to play with friends for more fun and co-operation, however playing on your own is fine as the diverse characters and the funny things they have to say keeps you entertained all the way through. The leveling system is made to keep you at the right level during the game, so after 1 or 2 levels of grinding, you will not be getting much experience to level up at all, this could be a posotive or negative depending on the way you look at it. I have heard complaints of the games art style and more specifically the outlines, however this art style gives off the same vibe as the game itself, and the game was not made to be deadly serious, with you shouting commands to your friends, it was made to be fun and interesting, and that is what the art style delivers. The skill tree varies for each character, giving lots of replay value to the game to see what combinations of skills are possible to make the most powerful class possible.
The DLC for the game hase their ups and downs in some ways. The DLC's for the first time run-through are set at specific levels, which makes it hard for you to be at the right level for each of them as they vary a bit depending on your level, but only to a limitation. You can easily go over the recommended level by playing through one DLC and end up being over-powered on the the other DLC. However, these things aside as they are only really the first time run-through that it occurs on, the DLC offers new worlds to explore and hours of more interesting storyline, witty phrases, familiar faces (and some new ones) and fun to be had.
I strongly recommend this for someone looking for hours of fun with their friends, or on their own. Anyone who is skilled and wants to make a combination of skills that work together nicely in the skill tree, or fun someone just wanting to get stuck into a game.

Papers, Please is perhaps one of the most interesting games I've ever played. It's a totally new slant on the criteria for an addicting game. Who knew that doing actual administrative work would be a catch?
In the game, you are shown to have several family members who need food, heat and also medicine. Your salary is tight and a lot of it is spent on your loved ones. This story is told only by plain text after each day's work and checkboxes that allow you to choose whether or not you want to spend money on heating and/or food for your family. It feels as though this is the aspect of the game that provides you with a motive to keep going. Not only this, but the developer has certainly drawn on our inherent nature to find enjoyment in successfully completing tasks that aren't part of our normal lives as they are too difficult or too time-consuming. There is an added frustration aspect when you fail to notice a discrepancy in the documents, which makes getting it right all the more sweeter, just like on a racing game where NOT crashing feels somehow incredibly fulfilling. It is the same case for Papers, Please.
It feels like you build your own strategy on how to complete the game successfully, which is one vital factor that the majority of popular games use to draw you in; building your own strategy and skill grants you more success than others. It’s a single player game but with its timed work clock, it makes it feel like a competitive bubble, where you’re fighting through countless immigrants to feed your family. (Yikes, I wonder how many I can process today!)
The only negative to the game is that due to the fact the game provides you with opportunities to make your own decisions on who to accept, who to help and who to deny means that there are 20 different endings to the game. Sadly, basically all but the last couple of endings warrant a failure of the game. Your inspectors will pull you up on mistakes you make and you will find yourself being quickly arrested if you’ve accidentally ♥♥♥♥ed up somewhere. I’ve played for hours and I keep getting arrested for mistakes I didn’t even know I’d made, I’ve got ending 17 so far. Although the game lets you retrace your steps and choose a workday to restart from, it means that you’re never really sure where to restart from if you mess up. The game only gives you a reason for failure, and you do not get fired for your mistakes until inspection days and official assessments; you don’t know where you messed up so you can’t know which day to go back to. This ultimately ends with giving up. If the developers simply had an indicator of which point you made the mistake, it would be far more appealing to continue playing again, even from an earlier point. Overall, highly addicting game, especially if you don’t make any mistakes. Otherwise, can be frustrating but generally a good gaming experience. You won’t regret buying it, and yes, for once, this game is worth the full price.

First of all - I usually do not write reviews but I believe this game deserves every bit of attention as it may inspire Devs to come up with a sequel in near future (at least I hope).
Let me put it this way: I pretty much hate VN and I really enjoyed this one. I also don't like eSports in general and this game made me interested in competitive Starcraft. It is truly remarkable how this simple game kept me both invested in story and relaxed at the same time. The idea was there for quite some time but until now I didn't see someone take it and make into a story of a game. Shame as this one proves that eSports make fantastic topic for "social story".
It is hard to critique this game, I mean, come on - its FREE. Devs don't have any profits from it. However as I both enjoyed it and was disappointed by some parts, I would like to offer some feedback which may lead to improvement of this one or the sequel (which of course WILL BE RELEASED SOON, RIGHT? RIGHT?!).
[Small spoilers may occur after this point]
Pros:
+ way more natural dialogues that in typical VN
+ diverse and likeable characters
+ great way to learn about competitive Starcraft
+ simple but involving story about trying to get into eSports

+ assets form Starcraft 1 (that music!)
+ nice graphic
+ nice music
+ short (for some)
+ lack of romance (for some)
+ IT'S FREE
Cons:
- lots of graphic and music assets re-use

The Room is a 3D puzzle game where a note entices you to open a number of puzzle boxes in search of an unknown element. You work your way to the core of the boxes by rotating around them, looking for items and solving small puzzles, sometimes with the help of an eye piece.
The Room is first and foremost a good puzzle game. The puzzle boxes have a number of different smaller puzzles to crack and items to find. The game also gives hints if you get stuck, you may however choose to ignore those. Also important is that I have never encountered puzzles or items whose solution or use seemed farfetched.
Furthermore, The Room is quite atmospheric. Music, sounds and the notes you find from time to time all help build the tension as the game progresses.
The negatives I would like to mention are the rather short lenght of the game and the sometimes easy difficulty of the puzzles. That being said, I have no problem recommending The Room for those fond of puzzle games.

Rogulikes; I've played pretty much all of them.  Nethack back when it was a game only played on unix servers (solaris and the like, before linux was even a thing), original rogue on a 286, angband/moria/zangband, ToME, crawl, and countless more.  Out of all the rogulikes and related games, I would rank this up there with the original nethack, and Dwarf Fortress, which is high praise indeed.
Basically, if you recognise and enjoyed any of the games above, you will love this.  If not, the nice tileset and the work which is being put into making the UI more accessible makes this an ideal entry into a genre of games which has a history going back some 35 years now.

I want monsters to be shown like the @ symbol in the the art. I want monsters displayed as shaded letters, in high definition. I want several of them, and I want them now.

I had been playing the graphically simplified version available at the original since 1998/1999.
It was one of the best ASCII roguelikes then and now, with all the new stuff it has become just THE game I am playing all the time...
But let me explain WHY do I not need any other games.
ADOM at Steam gives me the true feeling of constant growth, immersion, improvement, a shifting challenge system that changes constantly and is always just a bit less difficult than the impossible...
The graphics and sound are there - no less, no more. However, for an old ASCII fan like me, they create a nice atmosphere in a quite smart way as they are no less and no more than a formal aesthetic addition to the already complex, deep and well implemented game system.
What I do not like - actually what I HAAAAATE is the fact that I had to set the autosave backup file to 50 game turns, as - but for save scumming - I would have lost EVERY save file I had tried to recover... unfortunately, the game would often crash while trying to save the game. Some forum members say it is just a paranoidal behavior, but should I choose between frustration and safety, I definitely aim for the second one.
What I do like - nothing less and nothing more than all the features of the good old "Ancient Domains Of Mystery" from the late '90s, that is many locations, tons of stuff to find/get/steal/buy, many skills divided info combat marks, spell specialization levels, morrowind-like main skills, naturally changing mental, physical and miscellaneous attributes... Simply every game is completely different, full of surprises.
What everyone should like: every time you achieve something the game rewards it to you. Maybe it won't tell you that directly, but after a few (hundred/thousand...) deaths the world shouls start resembling a living organism that is constantly growing and modifying its contents...
This game is for the patient and strong of will ;)

Greetings fellow gamers! This is Gamer Guy (In a Suit) from the Echo Army YouTube channel! Today I am bringing you a review of indie rogue-like Ancient Domains of Mystery (ADOM). ADOM was released on November 16, 2015 on Steam by a team headed by Thomas Biskup, including: Jochen Terstiege, Zeno Rogue, Krzysztof Dycha & Lucas Dieguez.
(NOTE: This review was produced by using a key for the game that was provided by the Developer/Publisher)
Video Review:
The "Too Long, Didn't Watch" Review:
STEEP learning curve. Sky high difficulty. Permadeath. TON of replayability. Short on Graphics, Audio.
3/5 but a MUST if you're a rogue-like fan.
The "Meat & Potatoes" Review:
This has been a very difficult game for me to review. It is a solid game. I am totally getting the hang of it just fine and enjoy the genre. However, these controls are still stuck in 1994. The graphics and sound are too. But wait, there is a LOT more to this game. First, the character creation alone is immensely deep. It's really great. Oh sure, you can randomize your hero/anti-hero (yup, you can be evil. why not?), their class, race, stats. You can also choose them yourself. There are quite a few to choose from. Even better, you go through a nice little quiz (or you can randomize this too) to determine some things about your character. This makes for tons of different combos and ways to play the game. I absolutely LOVE this aspect of this game. It is straight RPG with it's abilities, talents, etc. right down to rating them by dice roll and modifier. The controls though. It takes a long time to master these controls. SO much going on all over the keyboard. I feel like some of this could be somewhat simplified, but maybe I am wrong. There really is an crazy amount of depth to this little rogue-like. Fully fleshed out tons and NPC's to be found. All in all, for your average gamer there is a lot to consume here. This is not light gaming at all. More like a Paradox game or Wargaming (a la Ageod games, etc.) there is a lot to master before being able to fully enjoy this game. As you unlock all of this though, it is very rewarding.
Avg. gamer score would rate out at a 2/5. If you take your time with this one and learn it well, or are already a fan of real rogue-likes though, you'll find this to be a 4/5. Let's split the difference and call it 3/5.
Happy Gaming!

ADOM is one of the big classical roguelikes, with 20 years of development. I had played it before the kickstarted campaign for the graphical version and had enjoyed it then, and I enjoy it now even more. It just offers a lot of depth and complexety, I can really dive into the game. The world really feels alive. I also enjoyed TOME, the other great classical roguelike, but somehow I always preferred ADOM. TOME just feels more like game, with its MMO-like skills, while ADOM has the typical quirkiness and complexety of games like nethack, just with a persistent overworld and an actual story, which for me is more immersive.
I like the music, the tilesets and the many possible options, the mouse control. The loading times are pretty much non-existent, which isn't the case for TOME for example. But it still expects much the users to use the non-intuitive outdated old keyboard-shortcuts.
ADOM is hard and unforgiving. The new ingame tutorial doesn't change that. I would recommend reading the beginners guides on the wiki and the ingame manual. It's a game for people who have a lot of patience and are prepared to die early. I contrast to most rogue-lites and also many roguelikes, such as TOME, I always grow attached to my characters, so having them die is even more painful.
Tl;dr: ADOM is still one of the best games for roguelike fans who like depth and are prepared to die a lot and I am positvely surprised of the technical overhaul. But it's still nothing for people who simply want to explore a world and don't like reading manuals.

I learned the basics of this game about 1,5 years ago and have since then been playing it fairly regularly. Haven't managed to finish one yet, but the great thing about this game is that it doesn't really matter that much. It's not about winning. It's about your character, that you'll be scared for, that you'll pray for, that you'll coddle up and train. You'll be angry at fate, god or just the rng, you'll laugh at stupid deaths, you'll get surges of adrenaline at the sight of that out-of-depth monster around the corner and be immensely relieved when you make it to the next staircase without being followed. Pride when you get out of a situation that looked completely desperate by using your wits, disbelief when you finally identify your stuff and see that you've been carrying around 2 (!!) amulets of life saving, anger at yourself when you lose that really promising character just because you didn't stop playing in time (when you noticed your eyes started itching and your vision got a bit blurry, but hey, you just couldn't leave the game at that point, no way...)
I'm really no game expert, I don't have any comparison to other roguelikes or any other computer games for that matter. But what I love about ADOM is that it's creating stories. Of course there is the ingame storyline, but it's also creating stories in your mind. Even in plain ascii mode, maybe especially there. Your heartrate goes up at the sight of a yellow & and you start hating the sight of any kind of f. You just have to admire (and love) the simplicity of that!
I'll admit that it takes some time to get into it and figure out all the commands, but that's only a small price to pay for everything this game has to offer!

A fun game, still in development (Early Access). You have to control the evolution of the Plague by spending skill points in detailed skill trees. The type of Plagues available to you get unlocked as you progress through the game, you start with only Bacteria available, you will go on to unlock Virus, Fungus, Parasite, Neurax Worm, Prion, Nano-Virus & Bio Weapon. These different Plague types will have either minor or major variations in the evolutions available to you, making for more interesting gameplay! Each game mode is unique in its own way, the different Plagues all seem to have game mechanics independant of each other.
When you beat a level you will unlock different Gene structures, which allow you to get slight boosts or powerups in your future games, these are not needed for the normal difficulty, but can make Brutal or Mega Brutal difficulty go much smoother! There will be more Gene types to come, as this is early access, I have all Gene types unlocked (25/25), but it says that I am only at 83% on Genes unlocked, so we can expect to see more in this department.
Overall the gameplay is fun & challenging. I would definitely say this is in the survival genre with a dash of world domination. If you try it out, you may enjoy it!

This game is absolutely beautiful. Although I haven't had the chance to play Bastion, it's clear that the art director and artists from Supergiant games put a lot of hardwork and thoughtfulness into their character designs and game world. The music and soundtrack is also one of my favorite things about this game, with some of the songs mixing beautiful vocals and instruments with synth-techno that really added to the environment and even certain characters (I won't spoil who though).
The combat style is definately odd, and if you're the type of person that prefers RTS games then you'll probably feel more at home than I was when I first started. Yes, it's a little hard to get used to, but at the same time the interesting variety and effects the game abilities have allow you to kind of "mix and match" your favorite ones to your keyboard/gamepad buttons, so in a way you're allowed to tailor your abilities to your playstyle. Eventually, after unlocking most of the abilities, I had gotten really used to the RTS style gameplay.
Story-wise, this game is quite vague at times. There's more emphasis on trying to piece together what happened to the main character from the beginning and the little things like function files and dialogue between the main character and the sword can tell you a lot about what's happening. It's certainly quite linear and does try to make it open through the artwork and character dialogue/function files, but I get a sense that we've only got a small grasp on what this world's big picture is, which is somewhat disappointing considering how interesting the characters seemed to make it and how beautiful it's depicted.
Unfortunately, this game is short. I was able to complete it within about 6 hours (and that says a lot considering how slow I am about completing games), and the boss battle at the end is.....underwhelming. It kind of just felt like I was fighting any other big tough brute monster from the game with a crapton of health tacked on.
Nonetheless though, this is still an excellent game to play with interesting characters in a breathtaking science-fiction type world. I'd definately suggest it to anyone willing to try it.

The gameplay is fun and engaging, and there's endless room for optimization and strategy, resulting in near-infinite replayability.
