What about these shady resistance characters? What about this guy who is clearly mentally ill trying to get home but his passport is written in crayon? You need to balance all of this with your family who rely on your wages, wages that will be cut if you get caught letting people in illegally/erroneously.
The graphics look simple, the concept looks simple, but this game will stir things inside of you. It will make you realise how much of a bureaucratic fascist or peace loving do-gooder you are. That, to me, is what games are all about. Buy it.

While some ressources are easy to obtain, for example wood, you have to find specific spots for farming things like stone, iron, clay etc. while you have no Map (not a con I'd say) this can be quite tedious sometimes. With enough ressources you can build a "crest" with which you can claim land. In this land your buildings are protected from "block decay" and other player can't trespass as easy.

The Room is an intriguing and polished puzzle game with a slightly creepy atmosphere.  The story is a little lacklustre, but that isn't what is important here.  The difficulty increases in expert fashion, it never seems cheap and the puzzles are presented in a logical way.  As you begin to unlock the secrets of your box, you can find yourself completing the game in one sitting.  That is perhaps the only problem with the game; the lack of content.  It is a very short game, with a completion time of 2-3 hours.  Obviously once you have completed it once, you will be able to fly through it a second time.  This means that the first playthrough must be savoured and should not be ruined by using any sort of walkthrough.
The Room gets most things right: graphics, difficulty, atmosphere and progression.  When it is on sale, it is well worth a purchase.  I found this puzzle box game to be highly enjoyable and worth the sale price.  It is surprisingly creepy for a game where you are just trying to unlock secrets in a box.  Ports of mobile games can be horrendous and a waste of time and money.  This is not the case with The Room, it is polished and well worth the couple of hours it will take to complete.

Imagine that you're a powerful warrior, raiding a dungeon. Enemies falling under your blows left and right, it doesn't even matter what type of beast you just encountered, they all go down just after one or two blows from your greatsword. You happily hoard treasures while mumbling something about having no real challenge. Then as you raid another of the countless rooms you suddenly see a ghost. Easy you think, you fought many of these and they are more annoying than anything. But then pops up another and another and another... a whole horde of ghosts. You fight but it's no use, each time you slay one, several others drain you with their touch. You turn to run but you cannot navigate the the tight corridors as well as these incorporeal beings. It is only a few seconds from there that you drop dead... drained till you collapse of old age.
That's one way an ADOM game goes.
In another you are a powerful mage, having no trouble burning, freezing or electrifying whatever you encounter. That is until you meet an enemy that commands even greater magical powers and easily no-sells whatever your arsenal of spells throws at it. What now? Drink a potion? Use a scroll? Run? Too late in any case. As the only tunnel leading away from the enemy already has an angry giant blocking it. Struggle or go out swinging?
And that's another way an ADOM game may go.
But perhaps you won't even be this lucky, you might be a looser who eats the first kobold, realizes his error once vomiting the contents of their stomach and then be unfortunate enough to meet a ghul, becoming paralyzed by its touch and choking on your own vomit.
Or you'll explode attempting to perform alchemy. Or you'll get bit by something poisonous and realize that without antidotes you're just on a timer to your death. Or you'll read a cursed book at a VERY bad time. Or you'll decide to stand on an obsidian altar while a particularly religious orc is in the same room. Or if you're really lucky you'll live long enough to die attempting to challenge a physical god.
In short ADOM is great for creating an emergent mini story of your own character's struggle (and likely death), offering a ton of freedom and depth, but also demanding patience, dedication and application of one's own brain to learn the game. Those who can handle it can expect a deep and rewarding experience as it is a much bigger achievement to beat superpowered bad guy when you're just a frail mortal who can be blown away at every wrong step.
Now if the game had more polish in terms of graphics and animation and a much friendlier UI I'd have no trouble to recommend it to pretty much everyone, if only for the hillarious ways one can meet their demise. This way, expect to invest a hour or two just to get the hang of the basics and then the rest of your life mastering the rest.

I have been playing this game for years and years (even before Steam release) and there are no other rogue-likes that can match the scope and complexity.  This is a must for fans of the turn-based rogue-like genra.

So after 52 hours of play I'm finally writing a review, and then giving up and moving on to something else.  There is a small list of reasons, but it comes down to the fact that the game just isn't much fun.  Perhaps that's a symptom of being 'roguelike', perhaps not.
Pros
- easy to get started, play a while and then stop.  ei no load times, no startup ads to watch, no fancy graphic splash screen
Cons
-  Vast majority of games end in you dying.  Since this is permadeath all the time invested is lost.  Period.
- Most of the things that kill young characters (hunger, traps you can't detect on doors you must go through), poisons you can't cure, monsters that one-hit-kill and who are also faster than you are) you have no possibility of avoiding.  The game doesn't attempt to balance things, it mostly just rolls RNG's and eventually you die.
- Your character rarely knows anything about the equipment/potion/buffs.  You could die with a potion of healing in your possession and have no possibility of finding out.
- Even if you choose a class that allows you to see cursed/uncursed status, the game has undetectable cursed items to saddle your character with usless sh*t.
- Game does a very poor job at allowing balanced characters.
- Too many things completely invulnerable to player attacks/spells, and very little chance to determine what could be effective against them before you die.
- If you need something (food particularly, healing, a decent weapon, an identify scroll) you will never find it.  If you don't need it, the stuff drops like rain.  And of course this lack is going to kill you.
Pretty much the game is more of a fancy RNG, rather that someting that is fun.   Some will find this fun, most people will find it frustrating and unrewarding.  And the fact that it kills you repeatedly without any possibilty of not dying makes it more fruitless.

Even though I knew upfront that I would never go for the microtransactions, the free-to-play aspect of this game got me to try it, and what I could play I actually enjoyed.  The quality isn't all that impressive, but the tracking gameplay isn't boring and the shooting mechanics seem fair, at least.  The problem is that the paywall is completely solid, and there is an extremely limited amount of content that isn't locked behind it.
I strongly dislike microtransaction based pricing models, but hypothetically I might have given it a try if the pricing was reasonable.  It is not.  If the developers had elected to sell the game as a traditional standalone purchase (like they did with their related title, theHunter Primal), with a reasonable in-game unlock system, I would have probably bought and played quite a bit of it.  As it stands, I will probably never touch the game again.

But couldn't shoot them.. oh well right? I decide to try to go for moose instead "Also allowed to hunt" so I choose a differen't region, find moose tracks, follow them forever it feels like, till I find a tree stand thing. I sit in it for quite a while calling for whitetail and watching for moose. Nothing again, so I start walking and following the moose track even further, I finally find the moose. Line up my shot with my Nosler, direct hit in the heart... I get a message saying I used the wrong gun. So I decide to just quit and ask a few people that have also played what they think if it, see if maybe im just impatient or something which I realy don't think I am considering everyone I talked to said "It's pretty boring, you basically walk around pointlessly finding animals you can't hunt, or finding nothing at all." So I come to the conclusion.. If you like realalistic hunting games, this is a great game... but you need to have a bit of money to spend on the membership, lisence, guns, well basically you need to buy everything to enjoy this game. If not don't waste your time. Aside from the money, you need to be willing to walk through the bush for quite a while and don't expect to anything for a while. So be sure to have plenty of time on your hands.
All in all, I'd rather go buy a gun and a hunting lisence and do this all for real. This game would be suited for those who can't hunt because they are too young, or had the hunting lisence revoked or something. I give it a recommendation still though.. but the rating.. 3/10

The Room is an intriguing and polished puzzle game with a slightly creepy atmosphere.  The story is a little lacklustre, but that isn't what is important here.  The difficulty increases in expert fashion, it never seems cheap and the puzzles are presented in a logical way.  As you begin to unlock the secrets of your box, you can find yourself completing the game in one sitting.  That is perhaps the only problem with the game; the lack of content.  It is a very short game, with a completion time of 2-3 hours.  Obviously once you have completed it once, you will be able to fly through it a second time.  This means that the first playthrough must be savoured and should not be ruined by using any sort of walkthrough.
The Room gets most things right: graphics, difficulty, atmosphere and progression.  When it is on sale, it is well worth a purchase.  I found this puzzle box game to be highly enjoyable and worth the sale price.  It is surprisingly creepy for a game where you are just trying to unlock secrets in a box.  Ports of mobile games can be horrendous and a waste of time and money.  This is not the case with The Room, it is polished and well worth the couple of hours it will take to complete.

ADOM is very much a old school style rougue-like. You can tell because even the tutorial doesn't hold much back, instead providing simple instructions. Hell, even the second monster in the tutorial can completely destroy you if you don't play your cards right.
If you're not into the hardcore first-dungeon-you-enter-is-full-of-blinding-traps-and-pit-deal-with-it-punk style dungeon crawler then don't bother with ADOM. If you want to get into rougue-likes then I'd recomend a free dungeon crawler like Stone Soup's Crawl or a more jokesy game like Dungeons of Dreadmore. If you take to to those then congradulations! You might have what it takes to handle ADOM.
Either way, ADOM is a great delve into a world of fantasy, fighting, drunken fools and a never ending stream of death.

First things first: Be prepared! ADOM is a demanding and difficult game with permadeath coming at you around every corner. Several secret handshakes that you just got to learn about the hard way. And it's not even really fair at all times. Also you will be consulting a wiki often.
However,
The sense of reward in this game is unparalleled. When you kill that Ancient Chaos Wyrm with one tremendous blow from your Vanquisher, getting revenge for those five other promising characters who died to him. Or when you finally get that one race/class/sign combo running properly that you've been trying for ages.
There is a lot of death in this game no doubt, but the huge variety you can have with character creation added to the general randomness of the game makes every adventure significantly different. The replay value of this game is immense. Dying means that you get to try something new once again!
As you start out, you might be spending as much time reading a wiki as you are playing. That's okay, there are no real spoilers in this game. Knowing everything beforehand does not really affect your experience in any negative way. And there is a fun sense of mystique; even after years of play you'll be learning new things.
The steam edition packs this classic of a game in a neat and functional package. Definitely worth the price when it comes to amount of gameplay. Also worth it for the veterans. Though if you are very particular to ascii graphics (though you can play this version in ascii aswell), you might not find enough new features as of yet.
Definitely one of the better games ever made!

I posted a review within hours of release. For some reason it isn't on here, so I'm trying again.
This game is to roguelikes what Baldur's Gate is to CRPGs. After playing for over ten years, I can safely say that this is one of the best games I've ever played. The reason for this is it's strict dedication to its core mechanic -- you, dying.
One of the best descriptions I've ever heard of game mechanics was concerning Dark Souls, in that (paraphrased) "this is a game that is fair to the player -- always FAIR -- and the difficulty does not surprise you if you pay attention."
ADOM is like this. Sort of. Instead of there being ways to see what's ahead and then killing you a la Dark Souls, ADOM's core mechanic isn't actually dying. That's the means to teaching you. You will suffer legitimate losses of equipment, stats, companions, or everything you have in a gripping, slow or numbing, painless death. Then, you are expected - required - to learn from that experience in your next character.
This shows in everything that the game does. RPG classes in 99% of RPGs are meaningless. In ADOM, some are similar to eachother, but every class has at least one unique quality to them that will change the entirety of the game. Races are the same, with each having a sort of opposite, such as the Mist Elves and Trolls; M.Elves have unstoppable magical capabilities and dodging, but Trolls have towering health WITH regeneration (the MOST coveted skill in the game) and can massacre just about anything (can I just say Troll weaponsmith w/sword of sharpness? Yes, I CAN say that!) (... right before I died).
I've been playing off and on, but the adventures have been memorable. I was introduced to the game by scumming and knew too little to understand that this was NOT as the game was designed. Once I found the ADOM Guidebook online, I started playing rogue (with a little experimentation). My first winning playthrough was a Human Fighter, Phaeton; he ran into a vault of Greater Molochs. It took me HOURS to kill just one, but once I did, my level rocketed and I was able to kill each one easier until my 100 Courage could take on 2-3 at a time, hitting lvl50 in no time. The Balors at the end nearly killed me, but I desperately used a scroll of familiar summoning and hit the jackpot -- a Greater Flame Elemental killed literally everything but me on the entire floor. I just followed it around and picked through the carnage. My second playthrough was a Wizard, Gafgarion, that died in the duel with Nuurag-Vaarn. When 1.2.0 was released, I dove in head first with a LOT of attempts, but finally got a High Elven Paladin, Matthias, and for the first time I got Justifier. For those who don't know, this may be one of the best non-minmax occurrences in the game. I edited my sprite to epic proportions, turning Justifier into the Master Sword from Zelda, and mopped through every dungeon. You think such imbalance isn't fun after while... until your save loads a JSON error and corrupts, thereby losing everything.
Now that I'm done rambling, here's what makes this Steam version special. You can remove all of what I just talked about. However, that's not such a bad thing. What the Steam release signifies is a willingness to accept new players. The depth and complexity of content in ADOM is such that I probably haven't seen half of it. And it's probably only going to get bigger. Therefore, it makes sense to have ways to let players explore it. There's still tons wrong with it, as one review brought up the online-only functionality. This doesn't really bother me. Unless he's travelling in the bush (doubtful), turn on hotspot on your phone for 5 mins. The act of getting ADOM on Steam in a saleable format was probably a Herculean task, and so I expect errors. Any aspersions against customer sales disrespect are fallacious and made by people who have clearly never perused the forums or seen comments made by Thomas Biskup. Since Morrowind modding, I have never seen such a dedicated community of collaborative effort.
It has never been a better age to get into roguelikes, and this game is one of the best. If you've been poisoned against rogues by the more recent entries in the genre, give a classic a try and see what made them great to begin with.

Tiny Barbarian is good in a crowded field of great games. If you've already had your fill of Shovel Knight and want something crunchier, or Rabi Ribi and want something less crunchy, Tiny Barbarian is certainly a decent buy.
The opening is strong, a cold open straight into a doomed survival match with the barbarian battling hordes of goblins (This doubles as your survival mode minigame.) and once you lose there, you get to start the real game and realize you probably killed more dudes in that minigame than you will in the main game.
Which is good, as you probably died in that minigame from a combination of cheesy hitboxes unbefitting of a fighting focuses game.
Tiny Barbarian is a platformer. And it's good at that, don't let me dissuade you. Most of the fun is strutting across pixel terrain and hopping up and down things to get through. The game is divided into 4 episodes roughly an hour long each, less if you're good. You could certainly get that down to 30-40 minutes and it goes straight into the action from start to finish. Run, jump, slice, even go up against some nasty bosses. Lives are infinite and checkpoints are at the start of the room, but unlike most infinite life platformers, you have a pretty generous health bar and can usually find health hidden in cracked wall blocks as the game goes on. (You are expected to be able to do these in one life, after all.) The only save points are after bosses though, so be careful. Tiny Barbarian is quick and easy to play but it does not want to let you go very easily. It is quite tough, but it does not feel punitive.
The first episode puts you against a snake cult wizard, straight out of Conan, and each episode beyond that ramps up the difficulty and adds new mechanics. You're riding bees pretty soon into episode 2 and then episodes 3 and 4 go really off the wall. The second half of episode 4 is absolutely nuts. The episodes themselves are certainly the right length to be replayed and the game breezy enough to make it worth considering, but you don't have much to aim for. A better time, a better score, maybe collectibles (I don't see why anyone would bother. I don't think they give anything but a cheevo and a lot of them require some serious wall humping, wrecking the pacing of the game.), maybe the coveted no death run? But the polish isn't quite up to a replayable shump level of arcade quality. Sure, the music is really nice and the graphics do the job without being irritating and the levels have a lot of variety, but it just does not quite reach the mark of greatness. And this is a tough thing to say; a game that doesn't do much wrong but you can't really say why it's not at A+ level...
Downsides, the only level select you get is at the episode level, with a continue only checkpoint at various bosses. If you want to replay a chunk of the game, you gotta go through the whole episode to get there. Second, it is close to greatness, but it does not reach it in a way that some of the competition has. Shovel Knight and Rabi Ribi stand well above Tiny Barbarian. Khimera, I would say is a better play too and that's free (Not to say Khimera doesn't have a boat load of issues TB does not, but the charm shines through there.). Once you're through this, Tiny Barbarian stands proud above games like Gunvolt and Volgarr and easily deserves your time if you're hungry for another platformer.

Tiny Barbarian DX is an action platformer that is easy to pick up, but extremely hard to master. The presentation is awesome, the sound is even better and the controls are tight. You just need two buttons and a d-pad, which makes it ideal to play with a SNES (or NES) style controller. The episodic nature means that you can finish one episode and then take a break before you continue. The episodes are varied and all have their own gimmicks like mounts, swapping between fore- and background or shooter stages. There's also a local Co-Op mode now. But I have to warn you, the game is not for players who are easily frustrated. If you love action platformers and are up for a challenge, then this game is for you.
The first episode is a pleasure to play. Beginners will be able to finish it in 40 to 60 minutes and after that there is a lot of replayability if you want to find all secrets or go for a speedrun. Episode 2 released a year later with more than double the length of the first episode. After three years of no updates, in which the game was picked up by Nicalis as a publisher, we finally got the full game. Episode 3 and 4 are both good, with lots of variety and even more challenge. They are both easily as long as episode 2 and especially episode 4 offers so much content and variety that it could pass as a standalone game. Episode 4 is hard, and not just retro "Nintendo hard", but even harder. Especially the bosses are extremely difficult to master, and I bet that many players will have to try again and again until they get lucky. One thing that I found odd about this episode was the beginning. The other episodes all had some kind of opening that kicked off the action, but the final episode just begins with no introduction.
Overall I liked the first episode the most. It has the least difficulty spikes and is the most fun to replay. There's a remake of the old freeware version thrown in as a bonus, which is also pretty fun to play.
The original price of this game was $10, but after Nicalis picked it up it was bumped to $30 to match the price of the physical release on Switch. I'm against price parity between digital games and physical releases, which offer much more value and can be resold. So out of principle I don't recommend picking this up for $30. But I fully recommend this game once it goes on sale for under $20.

I rate the game Papers Please 4/5. Good.
If you can get past this game's terrible graphics and ugly colors it's actually pretty fun considering this is essentially a game that revolves around following bureaucratic procedures, comparing codes and other information between different simulated pieces of paper, doing other simulated paperwork and stamping people's simulated passports (and doing all this as quickly as possible and learning how that usually isn't fast enough).
The game has a good, detailed story mode plot and can end with any one of 20 different possible endings. This game (and its plot) appears to be heavily influenced by George Orwell but is also influenced heavily (as George Orwell was also heavily influenced) by Soviet Russia and its various border states. This game (which starts simple but becomes increasingly complex) is also often funny but in a very dry and tragic manner. For added replayability it also has two difficulty modes (one mode causes your character to be paid adequately while the other difficulty mode gives you inadequate pay). The amount of money you make affects your family who must be kept warm and be fed and if they are not, will suffer and die (in a sort of oregon trail style menu which says how poorly they are doing).
Ultimately, this is a desktop game which can be quickly opened and closed like a round of solitaire which tests your gameplay ethics in a situation which is, to say the least, full of ethical uncertainty and injustice. The biggest downside to this game is that it can get boring pretty fast (the ugly colors, the ugly graphics the 1 piece of music the game has, the paper-shuffling gameplay all contribute to this) requiring a break from it now and then. This is still a good game if played for short durations and a nice reminder of how bad it can be (even (if not especially) if you really try hard to be upstanding citizen) in a soviet-fascist styled nation-state. And it has dry humor. Don't forget the dry humor because that's a whole lot of what makes this game as good as it is. That and the really cheap price. No bugs.

Dwayne Douglas Johnson (born May 2, 1972), also known by his ring name The Rock, is an American and Canadian actor, producer and semi-retired professional wrestler, signed with WWE. Johnson was a college football player for the University of Miami, winning a national championship on the 1991 Miami Hurricanes football team. He returned to wrestling part-time for WWE from 2011 to 2013 and continues to make sporadic non-wrestling appearances for the company. As of November 2015, he has had seventeen championship reigns in WWE, including ten as a world champion, winning the WWF/E Championship eight times and the WCW/World Championship twice. Sometimes, after playing a lot of competitive multiplayer games, you just have to step back and enjoy something much more authentic like Transistor. This game allowed me to really appreciate a story based single-player game as I was drowned in a breathtaking world with its own unique atmosphere and gameplay.
During my first few minutes in to the game, I instantly recognized the amount of work Super Giant Games put into Transistor's presentation. The visual aspect of the game consists of beautiful hand drawn art, a vibrant colour scheme, smooth animation, and excellent character design. The auditory aspect is also just as outstanding as the visuals; the soundtracks consists of a mix of haunting guitar rifts and electronic music which captures the mood of the empty and haunting city of Cloudbank, and the voices and sound effects are also on par with this.
The gameplay is also unique and makes the game more strategic compared to Super Giant's previous game, Bastion. The turn system allows you to plan your attacks, but there's also a mix of mechanical play with this, such as having to decide the best times to switch to turn mode or real time. I also really enjoyed how the functions worked (which are the skills), as there are thousands of possible combinations as you can use, since you can either use the function as an active, a passive, or you can stack the function on another function to add a unique property. I also liked how they added limiters in the game to make the game much more challenging in a unique way that rewards the player.

This game is an absolutely excellent follow-up to Bastion, being made by the same dev studio. However, this game is an altogether different beast than Bastion: It has a fascinating noir style, an engaging story, and an incredibly inventive gameplay system that forces you to think on your toes and mix up your strategy, while also coming up with all kinds of said strategies. This is also the only game I have found that does the whole mute protagonist thing that other games have done before (BioShock, Half-Life, Portal, Mirror's Edge, etc), yet actually characterizes said silent protagonist and make them a character, rather than just a blank slate. I would recommend this game to really anyone, as it's just a really good game.

It's alright, though I'd recommend going with the free trial they have on their site before purchasing.  There are limits on the trial version but it should be enough of a taste to determine whether you'd like this game or not. Crafting is nice but I made the error of taking up too many skills which has led to a serious space issue.  You won't be able to use the market (sell to other players) until completing the level 17 storyline quest, that's also when you get additional storage in the form of retainers (125 slots each, 2 free retainers).
They've got great ideas going on, but again, space is turning out to be a major issue.  You'll be given 100 spaces for everything except armor and crafting clothing - those go into a separate storage area.  The problem is 100 spaces goes quickly when you're able to collect high quality crafting items in addition to regular quality.
Say you're working on cotton.  You'll collect cotton bolls and you'll likely end up with high quality (HQ) and regular.  That's 2 spaces.  Then you have to craft that into Yarn.  Again, HQ and regular.  That's 4 spaces.  That yarn gets made into cloth.  HQ and regular.  6 spaces.  You use Both yarn and cloth in recipes so you don't get to reclaim space by using up the yarn.  A few recipes require the raw material, yarn and cloth so don't bet on using up all the raw materials to reclaim space.
Hemp comes before cotton.  So you'll have 6 spaces taken up by hemp because you can't trade on the market, yet, nor will you have your retainers.  You won't want to vendor the hemp HQ items because they sell decently to players, so that's at least 3 spaces you're using to hold on to that hemp.  9 spaces for Weaving.  Ahhh, but that's not all!  You don't get away that easily.  Some recipes require additional items like leather or beast sinew.
So, until at least level 17 you're going to be juggling space.  At level 25 you can get your two free retainers.  A retainer stores 125 items and acts as your liaison for trading on the market board as well as being a gopher.  There is housing available at level 50, but that's still a ways off and if you wait until level 17 or 25 to start crafting you're going to be playing a game of catch up.
Gameplay isn't bad in a group.  Solo is slow at the lower levels I was still not able to one-shot a level 2 mob at level 20.  That's because gear is limited at the lower levels and there aren't many stats to be had to boost your character.  It doesn't detract from gameplay or make questing difficult, but when you need all that leather that falls from lvl 1 & 2 mobs it's going to take a while to collect what you need due to cool downs on skills and the lack of being able to one-shot minor mobs.  FATEs are a good way to gain that leather fast because you're usually hitting the same mob as other folks, making the kills go faster.
All-in-all we're enjoying the game, but tweaks would certainly be appreciated.
Oh, and the gold spam is out of control.  However, you can set your status to Busy.  This blocks (everyone) from sending you tells so no gold spam.  It also blocks Free Company (guild) invites, which players like to spam you with.

'You find yourself in the bowels of a dank dungeon, your robes burned to ashes, bleeding from your wounds.  The dread beast that inflicted the wounds upon you lies smoldering before you, the last of your power expended upon its ruin.  Through the doorway that led you to this chamber, you hear a thunderous 'HARUMPH'.  This can only mean ruin.  You frantically search your belongings, desperate for salvation.  You pray to your God, but the ground quakes at your request, a stern denial from your patron deity.  A tremendous stomping grows nearer, and you fear that your time is short.  Sweat pouring down your bleeding face, you find a Wand of Digging in your pack, intact but depleted of charges, alongside your Wand of Door Creation.  Like a man gone mad, you plunge the Wand of Digging into your only potion of Booze, and cry out when the wand glows once more.  You fire it behind you, creating a vast tunnel wherein you dash for safety.  You zap your Wand of Door creation behind you, and with your faintly regained power Magically Lock the summoned door.  You run down your new corridor, seeking escape, only to find another dead end.  The impossibly heavy steps of the impending creature grow close now, as you huddle in the corner of your shelter.  The steps cease, you hold your breath in sheer terror, silently attempting to gather yourself in meditation and regain power.  An explosion of splinters erupts from the other side of your corridor, and the many eyed horror that approaches from the gloom freezes you in your place.  You think of Terinyo as the horror steps toward you, you think of the home you left behind.  Your fear gives way to darkness, the darkness to silence; Ancardia's greatest hope extinguished like a torch in the rain.'
You die.  You survive.  You learn. ADOM is a game that offers you a canvas upon which to design your own adventure.  Are you a hero?  A villain?  Do you aspire to seal the forces of Chaos away, or reign over it a mad God for eternity?  Are you a simple farmer, far from home?  A gambler, seeking the highest stakes casino in all the world?  Call it a roguelike, call it a fantasy role playing sandbox, call it a sadistic RNG exercise, ADOM is all that and far more.  No experience is perfect, games crash, characters are lost.  ADOM is mysterious, and you may puzzle at the Scroll of Dark Predictions in your inventory, or the Tract of Chaos you see on the ground.  You may wander to the Tower of Eternal Flames, and enter without caution.  You die.  You survive.  You learn.  ADOM is a game of mystery, a game of skill, a game of chance.  Distinct from its peers, beloved by its fanbase, and better than ever here on Steam.  Don't fear the learning curve, if you've whiled away hours exploring Morrowind, Baldur's Gate, Fallout, this game may be the gateway to a genre you've never given a thought to before, as it was for me.

Tiny Barbarian is an episodic 2D platformer, and you might think that means it's four parts of the same story, but no, it's actually four separate adventures, which means you're basically getting four games in one. And for $30, that means you're paying less than $10 per episode, and that's not a bad deal at all!
It's a simple game to pick up and play, but it's intensely difficult to master. You've got two buttons, one for attacking and one for jumping. You can do cool combos depending on how you move while attacking, but there's no need to go over a long combo list or anything. Everything will come naturally to you as you play. The controls are pretty tight, too. It's one of those games where if you die, you have only yourself to blame. And believe me, you will die and die and die. I wouldn't be surprised if I died over 300 times. Despite this, at no point have I felt like the game was impossibly hard. You make mistakes, you learn from them, you practice and get good, and then you feel legitimately cool. It's the kind of game where playing skillfully is its own reward, because it just FEELS good.
The game's episodic nature, along with its graphical style, are a nod to MS-DOS games from the 90s, which were also often episodic. And as someone who's been PC gaming since around that time, I absolutely LOVE this stylistic choice. More games should have an MS-DOS aesthetic. And speaking of style, the game simply oozes it. There's just so much personality and attention to detail. There isn't a single word of spoken dialogue, but you can tell just from the hero's movements what kind of person he might be. Same with his lady-friend and even a lot of the enemies. There are tons of games out there that serve as love letters to the olden days of gaming, but a lot of them either limit themselves because of that, or they break their own rules and try to be something they're not. Tiny Barbarian gets it just right, however, by having the game look like a genuine 90s game, but still taking advantage of modern technology to bring a refreshing new experience to the table. And that is super cool.
There are a few flaws, however. The first is that the camera doesn't always scroll far enough for you to see what's up ahead. Vertical segments in particular suffer from this, due to the lack of a "look up/down" button. There are many parts in the game where you take leaps of faith, or where you need to dodge enemies coming from above but can't see their trajectory.
In addition, while I say you have only yourself to blame if you die, an exception can be made for the bosses, many of which have attacks that are sometimes unavoidable. Episode 1 and 2's bosses are fine in this regard, and episode 3's bosses are bearable, but it seems like most of episode 4's bosses can only be beaten through sheer dumb luck, especially the final boss.
Overall, this is a simple, but solid game. It does what it does, and what it does is pretty great. And with four episodes, you get plenty of bang for your buck. I admit the first three episodes are fairly short for a $30 game, but that last episode more than makes up for it. Bottom line, if you're a fan of action games and retro 2D platformers and you're looking for a new, exciting game that's easy to play but hard to master, then look no further.

So I played one of the earlier Smugglers games (Smugglers 2) that I somehow ended up with on my first pc around the mid 2000's. I loved the exploration and trading elements of what was essentially a text based game even though I was a slack-jawed pre-adolescent cretin. Now a 20-something, slack-jawed cretin, I noticed this game on sale during a weekend sale and my nostalgic fondness got the better of me.
The original experience is largely intact in regards to trading and piracy. Yes, you can live out those fantasies of being a merchant king jumping from system to sytem, buying low and selling high. Alternatively, if that's not your thing you can engage in piracy against other would-be merchant kings and steal their wares, though as the saying goes "live by the sword, die by the sword."
Over the course of a 15 hour game, I managed to carve out a decent set of systems where I had money and influence as a merchant king, though sadly I lost my saves and couldn't achieve my vision of galactic economic dominance. Though eventually even such lofty ambitious lose their lustre disappointly quickly as gameplay becomes almost formulaic.
Smugglers 5 definitely has some glaring flaws. Lack of a narrative hurts more than it helps in the modern era, strategic inconsistencies in gameplay and the fact that the game has largely been superceeded in the genre by other titles. There is some depth to this game, but it becomes a little bit of a grind at times.
But if you're one of the nostalgia suckers like me who played the original games or have a thing for text-based space exploration/trading games and Smugglers 5 is on sale, I'd definitely suggest picking it up.

I rate the game Papers Please 4/5. Good.
If you can get past this game's terrible graphics and ugly colors it's actually pretty fun considering this is essentially a game that revolves around following bureaucratic procedures, comparing codes and other information between different simulated pieces of paper, doing other simulated paperwork and stamping people's simulated passports (and doing all this as quickly as possible and learning how that usually isn't fast enough).
The game has a good, detailed story mode plot and can end with any one of 20 different possible endings. This game (and its plot) appears to be heavily influenced by George Orwell but is also influenced heavily (as George Orwell was also heavily influenced) by Soviet Russia and its various border states. This game (which starts simple but becomes increasingly complex) is also often funny but in a very dry and tragic manner. For added replayability it also has two difficulty modes (one mode causes your character to be paid adequately while the other difficulty mode gives you inadequate pay). The amount of money you make affects your family who must be kept warm and be fed and if they are not, will suffer and die (in a sort of oregon trail style menu which says how poorly they are doing).
Ultimately, this is a desktop game which can be quickly opened and closed like a round of solitaire which tests your gameplay ethics in a situation which is, to say the least, full of ethical uncertainty and injustice. The biggest downside to this game is that it can get boring pretty fast (the ugly colors, the ugly graphics the 1 piece of music the game has, the paper-shuffling gameplay all contribute to this) requiring a break from it now and then. This is still a good game if played for short durations and a nice reminder of how bad it can be (even (if not especially) if you really try hard to be upstanding citizen) in a soviet-fascist styled nation-state. And it has dry humor. Don't forget the dry humor because that's a whole lot of what makes this game as good as it is. That and the really cheap price. No bugs.

Such a hard game to review...on one hand it can be strangely fun, but on the other hand many aspects come across so poorly you wonder if they were conscience design choices and even if they were, WTF!?
Playing as a border crossing guard, you are given money for the number of people that are permitted to into the country and docked pay for those you allow in that should be turned away. At the end of the day you go home to your family who slowly freezes, starves, and gets ill as the game progresses. The intent is, do your job well enough and you can keep your family (mostly) alive and eventually move them out of the country. Don't, and you fail in a variety of different ways.
Possessing extremely simple graphics, sound, FX, and story means this game must stand heavily on gameplay elements. To that end, "Papers, Please" revolves around its simple "point and click" interface, forcing the player to review stacks of constantly changing "papers" to determine whether the person trying to gain admittance to your border crossing booth is permitted entry or not. If this sounds boring, it isn't...at least at first. For the first 30 minutes or so the game is a fun "spot the thing that doesn't belong game" with a few characters that liven up the experience (the guy trying to come into the country with a hand drawn passport was priceless).
The problem comes as they ramp up the difficulty. Rules for admittance change on a daily basis in response to regional activities and new control schemes are introduced along with them. It starts by first introducing new documents to look over and quickly gets into full body searches, interrogations, etc. However, many of these new mechanics are barely mentioned and even less so demonstrated. On one hand (speaking as a person whose worked in bureaucratic agencies for too long now) this accurately portrays how most top level directives are given and thus realistically uses gameplay to mimic real life...on the other hand its frustrating as hell. And just when you start to think you get a handle on the new items to look for they throw in a random thing like person gender being wrong, expiration date, etc that make you feel like an absolute moron for not catching the mistake. And mistakes you will make...and be caught for every single violation. This does create a palpable sense of anger at "the man" and feelings of hopelessness as you and your family suffer the results of your ineptitude, but in the end made me wonder if they can always catch my screw ups, why can't they just screen the border themselves?!
In the end, the game has an interesting premise and does well in conveying some aspects of life, but I have to seriously question if I consider this "fun". To those looking for and/or good at "spotting the thing that is wrong" this game is definately for you. Otherwise, I'd say pass.

This review was written as a comparison of the free flash game Pandemic 2 as compared to Plague Inc.:
Alright, I went back and played through Pandemic 2 on Realism to get a better understanding of your arguments, or complaints (as it somewhat seems).
Right off the bat let me state, I am not saying that Plague Inc. does not share a lot of similarities with Pandemic 2.  Considering that the developer himself has stated that this game is inspired heavily from Pandemic 2.
1) The interface is different.  Granted, again, there are similarities in the interface, and given enough time and patience, Crazy Monkey Games would probably create a better interface for their game, but it hasn't happened yet.
Specifically the interface is cleaner, and makes more sense (IMHO).  When it comes to navigating and looking for specific information, Plague Inc. does a much better job at displaying the information and making it easier to understand (especially if you are a new player).  Not only that, but you can actually see the effects of certain abilities taking affect in Plague Inc. (specifically livestock, bird, mosquito, and blood transmission), if you took the time to actually look at the numbers after selecting certain abilities.  The math and numbers are there, whereas in Pandemic 2 it seems to just add a dice-roll (bad explanation I know) to the amount of infected persons.  It seems as though Plague Inc. is upfront on what exactly certain abilities will do, if you take the time to analyze it.
2) Different disease types, and better playability of existing disease types.  Again, we have 3 disease types taken from Pandemic 2 (Bacteria, Virus, and Parasite).  Pandemic 2's disease types almost all felt the same, with minor modifications in certain areas (whether it be evolution, infection rate, or noticability).
While adding several completely new (at least compared to Pandemic 2) disease types, the existing disease types felt much more fleshed out as a whole.  The way that they mutate, spread, and travel is all different for each disease type.  Each disease actually feels unique.
3) The world map is "more" realistic.  The way the countries were seperated in Pandemic 2 was not the best.  It was rather unrealistic the way that certain countries were lumped together, seeing as wealthier countries were being combined with poorer countries, and also less technologically advanced countries being combined with the more technologically advanced (not being mean, but there is a reason we use the term "3rd world countries").  An example being grouping Morocco in with the rest of North Africa.  In that group, there are 3 different world economies; 3rd world countries, Countries that are members of the European Union, and 2nd World Countries.
In Plague Inc., The dev has done a better job of isolating the countries based on their certain abilities.  Specifically, wealtheir, more technologically advanced countries are harder to infect based upon the abilities you have given your disease.  Whereas starting in a poorer country is much easier, seeing as the spread of disease would be much easier based upon the living conditions found there.
4)  Random events.  Pandemic 2 did have some random events that happen throughout the game, and they consist of flooding, drought, or storms.  They really don't affect much other than a slight change in the dice-roll when it comes to infections.
Events in Plague Inc. are much more varied, and can help and hinder the spread of your disease.  Seeing certain events pop-up (specifically events such as "Festival of Love", "Olympic Mystery", "Icure", etc.) requires the player to change their plans and react to an ever changing world.  It adds a deeper strategy element to the game (again IMHO).
5) Your disease is not immediately noticed.  In Pandemic 2, you are in a race against time to spread your disease as fast as you possibly can before the world randomly decides to work up a vaccine to wipe your disease out.  From the get-go, your disease is known to exist, and is being watched.
In Plague Inc., your disease is not known to exist from the start.  By using strategy, you can keep it that way for a decent amount of time (unless you play on higher difficulties, but that requires another type of strategy).  Again, a certain event will eventually cause your disease to be noticed, but the event is more realistic and has an explanation.
4)  The game is visually different.  If someone were to comper the two games side-by-side, as Supplysidejesus did in the one thread (here:
, you can clearly see the difference in quality.  A lot of work was put into the game engine running the game, and everything was built from the ground up.
Pandemic 2 was done in flash.  Programming a game in flash is no easy task, and I think the graphics were a necessary choice based upon the type of game they were going for, and the amount of info they wanted to display at a given time.  More of an necessity rather than aesthetic choice.
I may edit this post later to add more, but at this point I am too tired of typing.
tl;dr-  Pandemic 2 is a good game (not great, but fun).  Plague Inc. is a much more visually appealing, strategy-oriented, easier to navigate and find information, fleshed out game.  Both games are good in their own right, but (IMHO) Plague Inc. comes out as being a better game.
To answer his question if someone would confuse the 2 games (Pandemic 2 and Plague Inc.), yes they would.  But if somebody saw Plague compared to Pandemic, I would believe they would choose Plague (IMHO).

First off, I'm not a fanboy.  This is the first time I've played ADOM, but not the first roguelike I've played.  I've heard about ADOM for a long time but never played it.  I heard it was coming to Steam, so I thought I would give it a try.  So far, it seems very good.  There are a lot of options, things like your character's backstory are very well done.  I have to say, I really enjoy the tileset.  To me it's nicer than Tome's tileset.  Tome's tileset is almost too detailed to sit well with a roguelike, it kind of gets into the "uncanny valley" territory.  ADOM's tileset is HD, yet stylistically better.  The details are smooth and well done, but it avoids the mistake of trying to put too much detail into a tile.
If you like games like Caves of Qud, Tome, or roguelikes in general, this is a great game and you will enjoy it.  The devs seem very eager to improve the game and listen to their community.
The only complaint I have is there are a lot of strange key combinations that maybe would be better off in a menu (like if you push esc).  It's not bad by any means, but the UI could use a bit of streamlining.  Key combinations (like CTRL+nm) are just really archaic and not really acceptable in this day and age.  Other than that minor complaint, it's a damn fun game and I recommend it to roguelike fans.

It's a me, Factorio!
Start a base. Cut down enough trees to make an environmentalist cry. Fuel stone furnaces. Smelt iron. Pollute the atmosphere. Enrage the wildlife. Build weapons. Murder wildlife. Upgrade machinery. Wildlife upgrades. Upgrade weaponry. Murder upgraded wildlife. Automate machines. Wildlife upgrades. Upgrade weapons again. Use upgraded murderous boomstick of rage to butcher upgraded wildlife. Get angry. Build Tank. Use blood of the wildlife to grease the tank's fresh treads. Plan comes to fruition to build rocket.  Why build a rocket? World domination!
In all seriousness, this is one great game, however, there is a word of caution.  This game is meant for those who like to build things, explore, and automate machinery.  The absolute gem of this game comes from the intricacies you learn the more you play.  As you play, you can learn how to automate switching stations to send raw materials to other areas.  If one area beings to run low, the automated system will shift resources, if you program it right.  My only gripe comes from the enemies being just an annoyance vs. a real threat once you get to later stages in the game.  Laser defense systems are near impossible to with and make you an unstoppable killing machine.  It would be nice to see some underground enemy attacks to keep the player on their toes.
One thing I will say is that the devs behind the game are a definite A plus in my book in terms of content updates, upgrades, and keeping their playerbase informed about material coming down the pipe.  They're far, far better than some of the supposed AAA companies out there trying to pump out games non-stop like a fast-food joint shoving greasy concoctions down their customer's throats.
Pros:
*Intricate system that lets you program a lot (I mean A LOT) of stuff to automate your little factory setup
*Devs keep the playerbase updated on what is happening
*Game feels unique and fesh compared to other items out there right now
*I can build a dang choo-choo! I like a choo-choo that can run down my enemies!
*It doesn't feel tedious when expanding your base or starting another base then connecting them
*Can build an army of robot minions to do your bidding
Cons:
*Enemies feel pointless towards late-game stages in sandbox mode
*Game still neds some spit and polish in some areas (minor gripe)
*You don't require additional pylons

Look, I'm torn.  I wanna give this game a positive review.  It does a lot of great things.  However, in the end, it stops becoming satisfying.  The difference between 2000 and 23,890,756 damage is minimal because the whole numbers feeling scales into unrealistic, nonrepresentative miniatures such as 23k, 23AB, 23EF, etc.  Once you unlock every fighter, the game becomes dull and uninteresting and you start to realize just how pedantic and one-note it is.
If you like clickers, definitely download this.  I got it for free a long while back.  However, it is a clicker, which means scalable damage.  All you face is a steep uphill climb with no sense of satisfaction or reward.  At least the grind in SRPGs like Disgaea or other games allow you to dominate as an unstoppable badass.  Since there is a continuous challenge, with little payoff and no major change to the main portion of the game (increase fighters' power to increase their auto damage, or increase your click damage so you do more damage) it becomes another stale clicker clone.  I admit some of the bonuses that could arise as a result of the Infinity Coins are intriguing, but ultimately you would be resetting your progress so that you can play through the game and get to where you are again faster.  Since this hardly changes the outcome or the gameplay, it's ultimately meaningless again.
For a clicker, however, the graphics are great, the animations are bright and the character design is very cute.  Even the reskinned monsters are acceptable and seeing the new levels is satisfying.  Compared to other clickers, I would highly recommend this one, even if the lore doesn't necessarily reach high levels of insanity.
As a game, however, it suffers from being a clicker.  I would love to see the resources put into a game like this from a company like this used to make a more traditional role playing game.
Do I recommend: yes, with the proviso that it's a clicker.  No, if you're looking for a real game with actual gameplay.

I'll give Tiny Barbarian credit for one thing, it has one of the best openings of any platformer around. Right when you start, the game pans up to a desperate mountaintop siege, you versus an endless horde of slavering monsters. The game proper starts when you inevitably die, but it's a great sort of free-form tutorial and a lot of fun on its own. It might also be the one truly unique part of the game, but that doesn't make it any less enjoyable on the whole.
Tiny Barbarian is a retro platformer that poses you as a Conan-looking fellow about the size of a Broforce character (flexing and all!) against many stages of monsters and traps. In your quest to vanquish evil and rescue your comely companion, you'll master a host of sword slashes and combos that can juggle your opponents in hilarious fashion. You can also hang from and climb vines and chains, and vault up ledges you can't quite clear. The controls are tight and the challenges the stages present give you some creative workouts with them.
As a platformer, it hits all the right notes without being too terribly hard. You get a life bar of about seven hits before you go down, and death just puts you back at the start of the immediate area. There are two chapters to tackle, the first being a straightforward romp through deserts and caves to take on an evil warlord, and the second being a fantastic journey through jungles and on the backs of bees to save your beau. There's a jump in difficulty between the two that I didn't find particularly welcoming, but nothing that really turned me off of the game.
The only factor that should give anyone pause at the moment is the state of its future content. Tiny Barbarian was slated to get two more episodes to round it out but they were promised years ago, with not even teaser images to keep hope alive. However, the game has just last year been picked up by Nicalis who is intent on releasing the full experience sometime in the near future. In anticipation of that the price has gone up, so that at least lends credence to the idea it'll be finished eventually. But that also means you're paying a premium for content that isn't there and has been promised for longer than some games have lived in Early Access.
I'm sure you know by now I don't normally factor pricing into my reviews but this is a pretty unique situation. All you're getting right now is about two hours of quality retro platforming, priced up for something at least twice as dense. Don't expect any big unlocks or secrets, just jumping and hacking away. It occupies a nice space between the likes of Volgarr and Shovel Knight, more accessible than the former and simpler than the latter. Assuming it gets finished with enough content to round out its jarring price hike, Tiny Barbarian should be a good bit of hack 'n' slash fun.

Call of Juarez: Gunslinger is my first game in the franchise and really surprised me, although at the same time disappointed me a bit.
The game is all about the story, the game itself is about as linear as it can get and heavily relies on the story. But the question is, how is the story?
The answer to that, is great. While your character tells the story in the background to people in a bar, you'll play and do whatever he says. Meaning if he makes a mistake and says: wait no, that's not how it went, you restart as well. This in combination with the great voice acting makes the game basically feels like listening to a story but you're the one playing it! And the story is really wel written and breathes the western theme. The scenery in combination with all of the small details makes this an immersive game for sure. And it would be even more immersive, if it was not for the waves of hundreds and hundreds of enemy's. I mean, the game is great and all but all you're doing besides listening to the story is shooting waves of enemy's. And they just keep coming and coming. This get's really repetitive after a while and the more I came towards the end of the game the happier I was the game isn't all that long. However, the game is pretty unique. Not a whole lot of games use this way of story telling and make it work as good as Call of Juarez does.
Gunplay is really satisfying and although there's only a small amount of guns, this personally didn't bother me at all. While playing you gain XP and are able to upgrade weapons and get new perks. The scenery is great, and you'll come across some fun and great looking locations. Keep that in mind together with some great western/country music, and you have Call of Juarez: Gunslinger. The game has a decent replay value, completing the game once unlocks some new and harder modes.
Now would I recommend it? Well it really depends if you like these types of games. The great shooting mechanics in combination with the cool cowboy duals made it a really enjoyable experience. But these type of games really need to fit you. If you have no idea if you like these types of games, buy it. The experience is well worth it.

This will be a review separated by categories.
You probably know by now that this is an old west shooting game, so bear that in mind, please.
***Controls***
The aiming mecanism feels quite solid, although, in Duels, it sort of loosens up a LOT. Perhaps it's how it's meant to be, heck if I know what Ubi was thinking.
I have a multi-DPi mouse that changes on the fly with a button and boy, did I use that feature! Close quarters combat really needs a higher sensitivity and a quick firing and reloading gun. I found the combination of Quick-Shooter revolver and a Rifle to be the best match, provided you get the added ammo for the rifle first thing, 'cuz you're gonna run out easily.
***Sound***
The sound effects in general are pretty good. Wood breaking sounds just like it. Bullets whoosh by you constantly. Firearms firing could be more of a loud "BANG!" instead of a mild pop, but it's ok, since most people would not enjoy that for prolonged gameplay. The music sounds authentic and period-correct, making the experience quite enjoyable and relatively immersing.
***Physics***
Physics in a western game? Yeah! And a pretty good one at that!
You shoot flimsy stuff, it breaks apart and flies away! How cooler could it be? You shove your head into some fabric, it floats around. You kill a dude standing next to an edge, he'll fall down and ragdoll. Major points here, fellas. It all feels quite nice and, quite simply, "right" the way it is and behaves.
***Graphics***
Graphical quality here is also very good. You do get some Borderlands effect, with silhouettes drawn in bold black, but the textures and lighting are of high quality.
Sun glare is there and works nicely. Objects, even when up close, don't look washed up at all. I never saw too noticeable pop-ins either, so it loads the scenario a bit further in every direction. The animations are all pretty well done and don't look broken at all in any situation.
***General quest mecanics***
You got your usual "go there and do this" kind of progression, but the maps make you feel like you're sort of "going somewhere". It follows with the story in quite a satisfying fashion.
The whole revenge deal does get a tiny bit old by the time you're about to finish the game, but gets the job done.
The nuggets of truth are absolutely enjoyable for fans of factual history (not game related, real life related!). I used to read them thoroughly at pick-up until late in the game, when i sort of got lazy and left them for later.
At the end of the game, you get a choice to make and i'll play it through again to see how the other ending happens.
===CONCLUSION===
I'm quite hesitant to give it maximum score, because there is room for improvement, but I can't really point out any serious flaws, and, I wouldn't be fair if I deducted any points from it for minor stuff. So, yeah, my first maximum grade.

The early game in ADOM constantly asks you to make risk vs reward decisions. Whether to stand and fight, or run away and heal. Whether to kick down a door and risk activating a trap, or come back later with a key. Whether to risk delving one level deeper, or travel to a safer location. Making the wrong call will often lead to an early death, but negotiate these issues and your character will be set up for the challenges that follow.
For newcomers to the game, I advise choosing a stong melee character (e.g. an orc fighter), and start in the tutorial dungeon to get used to the basics of moving around and hitting things with swords. This is what you'll be doing for the majority of the time, regardless of class. You can then let the complexities of the other mechanics seep in over time.
I used to play a lot of the ASCII version, but not so much recently. I'm already impressed with the new graphical tileset and other features which are in this version, and the game underneath is still the exciting combination of exploration and danger it always was.
If anything, this game is worth it just for the laughs.

I'm so happy ADOM is on Steam with nice graphics and sound effects! It's a great roguelike with many quests, large world map with many types of dungeons and  large variety of classes and races. There is a lot of small details that make your character seem like a real person - aging is very amusing, you lose appearance points and strength but gain wisdom :) Your moral or immoral actions directly affect how the enviornment reacts to you (certain quests unavailable, monsters hostile). Finding desired loot is difficult, thus good items are more meaningful. I absolutely love the magic system (as opposed to other roguelikes such as Stone Soup) - you learn spells through books which you don't have to carry around (you cast them from your memory for a limited number of times e.g. 700- which can be increased with other books), the spells get better as you use them. Finally the game has a lot of secrets :) I highly recommend purchasing it.

A very basic visual novel with decent visuals and simple but good storyline. It's a VN that's mostly reading and little gameplay. Don't expect meaningful choices. It's pretty mediocre as a VN but is somewhat special because it deals with a topic not used so much (esports/SC2) rather than generic school life.
After recently playing Telltale's Walking Dead I can't help but feel how unsatisfying this storyline is. There is no branching, no twists, just conversation options that either don't matter or immediately lead to a game over. I don't expect the same quality but was hoping for at least a little depth. I doubt they'll continue developing this but at the very least it would've been nice to have multiple people to recruit (and see changes based on who you recruit).
You can choose gender for the main character but (as they say) it only affects character appearance and every once in a while dialogue is added (that has no impact on the game). The SC2 ingame pictures were a very nice (and necessary) addition to help show the action moments. They also threw in a random fanservice hot springs pic in the extras which was unnecessary but I think many people will enjoy and expect from a VN.
They have a Day[9] do a quick skit and glossary that helps a little but I do think you need previous knowledge to really enjoy and understand everything that goes on in the VN. It's also very useful to know the basics of SC2 which are glossed over in the VN (unit names/purposes, building names/purposes, basic strategies). Otherwise it could be hard to follow the actual SC2 action. One example line: "My hellions make a beeline for his natural expansion's worker line". I'd recommend watching Day[9]'s old introductory videos (not the extra skit) if you don't know at least that much.
It also helps a lot to know common shortcuts of visual novel games because it doesn't mention anything in-game (like R-click for menu/back, ctrl/tab for skip, mouse scroll up for chat log and more). You can find out a lot by pressing random keys on your keyboard and hoping for the best (that it doesn't exit out/quickload and ruin your progress).

This "game" is an interesting concept with lots of nostalgia wrapped within it. It's not really that much of a game. It's more of a short interactive experience. The premise is that you are a person using AOL Instant Messenger who has a friend named Emily that you talk to throughout the game. The game spans the years 2002-2006 as the characters go through the senior year of highschool all the way to the senior year of college. You get to choose a screen name and a buddy icon for your character and there are some nice little nostalgic references with the buddy icons and the profiles of your friends having cringey song lyrics and stuff in them. To be honest though, the game itself is really something you would play once and never touch again. There are no alternate endings or interesting branching paths from your dialogue choices. No matter what you choose the game always ends the same. This is a good thing because it really helps with the message of the game, but unfortunately it also kills any replayability. There can also be also a disconnect between the player and your character. Some of the dialogue choices I found were not something I would say. I understand the message of the game being that people grow apart and relationships change over time, but I guess I'm just not into the whole young drama thing as entertainment. But hey, it's free. I would recommend giving it a try. You might find something worthwhile and relatable about it since the premise can get pretty close to home with people that have been in similar relationships.

Alright then...
Right off the bat, you may believe that this game is just another pixel art indie game with no sense of style or substance. Well unfortunately, after spending about 2 hours playing this game, I can safely say that this game is 100% accurate to the barbarian lifestyle and a DAMN fine Run-And-Slash platformer.
The overall presentation is immediately charming, with the first chapter starting off with a well implemented homage to Conan. From there, the game plays like a combination of golden axe and a low-fi rayman origins. You run, jump, attack, climb ledges (by the way, go into options, into config, turn on "AUTO GRAB" and thank me later), ride huge cats, get killed by rolling snakes. Y'know, the basics of any barbarian lifestyle.
The game itself can be described as taking inspiration from classic arcade games like the aformentioned golden axe whilst implementing its own unique style to make it interesting. However, this game can be rather unwieldly at times, with one poor jump sending into instant death (VERY common in chapter 2), or setting you so far back in progression that you'd might as well kill yourself to start the screen again.
The main aspects of this game that hooked me were the cute graphics, superb music and the simplicity of the controls when they weren't freaking out and getting me killed by gorillas and snake wizards.
If I were forced to grade this game, I'd give it a 6.5/10. Nothing groundbreaking and the controls freak a little occasionally, but it succeeds in producing a satisfying experience with charming visuals and decent challenge that won't deter Noobs and Vets alike.
P.S. The Manual (Check the library page) comes with a comic and an enemy and control breakdown. Nostalgia achieved.

Tiny Barbarian DX is a very good game, but not quite a great one. Admittedly, only two episodes have been made available at the time of writing, but having played them to near completion I think I have a pretty good feel for how the rest of it is going to go as well.
As a gaming experience, Tiny Barbarian doesn't put a foot wrong. The controls are simple to learn, a combo move keeps things interesting, and if you really want to you can flex your muscles in the middle of a life-or-death fight. The monsters are distinctive and challenging. The graphics and music design are pure retro 8-bit goodness (barring a couple of small anachronisms, like the floating Z's of the sleeping Barbarian). The checkpoints provide a way around the outdated lives system without taking away the sense of challenge or urgency, at least if you're aiming for a fast run or a no-death run.
The thing is, there's a difference between a great game and a game that doesn't make any mistakes. For all the skill and care that went into the game and its presentation, the whole experience still feels inescapably...familiar. You aren't really going to see anything here that you wouldn't have in some other 8-bit platformer, or platformer in general. There's no real experimentation, no high concept, nothing more than a token attempt at narrative, and the Conan-inspired aesthetic is there as window dressing rather than as a means of informing gameplay. These things may change with subsequent episodes, but personally I don't really see the developer deviating from a structure which has served the project well so far.
None of this is to say that Tiny Barbarian is a bad game - and I do recommend this game, because as an exercise in legitimate challenge it really is worth your time. It just feels light, even unnecessary - a throwback in an era which has already moved on. Braid has more interesting gameplay; Redder has more atmosphere; Fez looks better; Super Meat Boy is more exciting. This wouldn't be a fair comparison if Tiny Barbarian really were a retro game, but it isn't - it's an imitation of retro games, and ultimately it doesn't feel like anything more than an imitation.

I've been playing a lot of these types of games lately and they can take some time to start becoming fun. This game took about 2 weeks to start picking up speed. This forces you to lose all your stats but makes you stronger on the next attempt.
To play this game, don't stare at it! Set it up the best you can (use "Chompy" or better) and then close the game and let it run on its own. The next time you run it you will see all the progress since you last played.
If you like this game, you might also like "Clicker Heroes," "Time Clickers" and "AdVenture Capitalist." Happy gaming!
