TL;DR
It's Drug Wars in space with worse graphics a bizarre 4X twist and tons of random errors and crashes that should probably only be bought on sale by people who have made thirty or more mortgage payments and think vector graphics are just a bit too intense.
This is a really great turn based strategy game with some truly annoying issues and no autosave feature so you can confidently do a bunch of things and then lose it all with a random black screen.  Also if you click a greyed out button you will literally get a popup error message from windows, and sometimes you get one for no reason.  Sometimes it crashes for no reason too.  Sometimes you get caught up in battles you can't win or avoid for no reason.  Sometimes you will upgrade your ship and totally regret the decision because it will for no reason make the game impossibly hard.
You will literally have all these problems and more.  Many more.  The tutorial is kind of a joke and prepares you for nothing that happens.  You will make poor upgrade choices based on no information whatsoever.  You will do all this, and it will be surprisingly enjoyable because the game is cheap.
You'll keep playing, learning, and crashing the game.  Mostly crashing, but some of the other stuff too.  The graphics can be boiled down into this sentence: "It's two jpeg images set on a black background with one of two basic overlay effects on them and no concern for consistency or integrity of the images themselves or the overlays actually.  In fact if you were to tell me the entire game was random images with random overlays I'd accuse you of trying to cover for the devs for the flaws in the overall game."
You may be wondering, why such a scathing review if I claim to like the game?  Well let me explain something to you.
Now friends, in a simpler time of computing when games could fit on a floppy disk and still be entertaining... this still wouldn't be a stand-out game in any sense of the term.  But the type of game that this tries to be was a popular one, low graphical content, simplistic, tier-based strategy... done one turn at a time.  If you remember the old Windows turn based strategy that was known by many names, the most common of which was "drug wars" you'll fall into and understand the strategy of this game immediately.  If you liked that game you'll even find enjoyment in this game.  Better yet, it doesn't have words on the screen like "Heroin" and "Crack" so you can casually shrug it off to friends without explaining that you really don't need an intervention.  Honestly it was one weekend in Malibu.
So should you buy this game?  Here's the definitive list that Buzzfeed hasn't yet syndicated into an interactive facebook quiz:
Yes:
-You like turn based strategy.
-You don't like special effects.
-You've heard of and possibly seen live either "The Mighty Mighty Bosstones" or "Seal"
-You have played many Alpha games and understand that not every game (even one this simple) can be well polished (or even finshed).
-You played "Drug Wars" on a Compaq laptop with under 256MB RAM and always thought it should have more of a Space 4X feel to it with none of the baggage.
-You think vector graphics are way too advanced.
-You've ever apologized for an EA (and I mean Electronic Arts) title.
No:
-You never played either Doom or Wolfenstine 3D.
-You were/are under the age of consent as of the turn of the millenium.
-Call of Duty is a game you have played more than once in the last year, twice if you were forced on a holiday with younger children who beat you mercilessly.
-You think games should actually be finished before they are published.
-You have something better to play.
-It's selling for more than $2.50, and you are at a point financially where $2.50 is the amount of money you can shrug off on a bad investment without becoming bitter.

I recommend this game with reservations.  On sale it's dirt cheap, so you probably won't feel ripped off, but it's definitely an odd game not meant for everyone.
On the positive end, if you enjoy those sorts of turn-based open-world games where you just do your own thing, this can be a lot of fun.  If you like action, run now.
What you see in the screenshots is mostly what you see the whole game.  This game has very little by way of simulation, and almost everything that is calculated is either randomly spawned on the spot or hidden away with very little player interaction.  How's the war going? WHO KNOWS! It doesn't seem to change anything so far as what ships are travelling the not-sea-lanes.
There's also a frustrating lack of clarity in many tasks you need to accomplish.  If you accept non-government missions, there is no mission review for you, so I hope you wrote down what you're supposed to do, and screw you if you put the game down for a while, there's no reminders of if you even took that mission on at all.  Much of the game revolves around being part of factions, and if you start out as an independent trader or smuggler, there's a large chunk of the game barred from your access until you join one... and joining one is frustratingly vague.  Apparently, it's a
, but everyone berates you for not doing something you haven't been given an opportunity to do... and for that matter, getting the person berating you for not joining the war effort
that chance, and this is
.
Incidentally, this guy is the governor (always a male) that lets you marry his daughter and have kids if you bribe him enough... regardless of your own gender.  Odd that the game even has an option to play female characters then, or is it that in the far future, everyone's bisexual, and IPS cells make lesbian pregnancies routine?
The game's combat is also crippled by its 1-on-1 nature.  You're at the extreme end supposed to be a fleet commander on a battleship leading a whole fleet into battle against another fleet... and this is represented with 1-on-1 battles where "reinforcements" are additional damage done to the opposing lead ship at the end of every third turn.   This game begs for a tactical grid map.
Beyond that, combat is performed with a pseudo-card game.  Your basic attacks are always present and can be used as frequently as you have AP for them, but you get a hand of action cards that refill at the start of the turn.  These can do things like evasive maneuvers that decrease enemy accuracy or increase your own to scramble enemy computers or harden your own against similar attacks, or "Luck" cards that discard your hand so you can draw a new one. (Which bizarrely costs you AP, as well, making them sometimes more punishment than help, as while they're supposed to let you discard useless cards, THEY are useless cards, themselves, and you can often wind up using a luck card to discard other luck cards...)
When you level up, (experience is obtained through absolutely everything, even standard trades,) you get a message telling you that if you keep on levelling up, you will eventually get a
up, which is the real level up.  (Like everything else, they don't tell you how long you have to keep doing this to get the actual rank up, so the experience bar is a lie.) When you
up, you get a new skill, which gradually lets you fill out a skill tree, and also can potentially give you a new card to use in combat.  You have no particular control over your "deck" beyond this, however, and each new skill is a new card in the deck that you can't remove.  Passive skills aren't deck cards, however, so they are more "safe" to take as a path up the skill tree.
Classes basically exist to deny specific game features to the player until they have played each class (from a new game) to get a high enough rank to reach the end of the skill tree, where only then are you allowed to buy property.  Fleet Officers and Bounty Hunters get a fleet command ability that lets them buy battleships and lead fleets, traders get to buy factories, smugglers buy pirate stations, and pirates can buy pirate stations and found pirate empires.  It's more than a little annoying, as, even if you do want to focus on one path, you generally are far more than rich enough to buy a factory if you are a trader before you have the "skill" to be a factory owner, which is an arbitrary roadblock that forces you to keep shuttling goods around for far too long.
Trading basically just involves buying low and selling high, but involves whether or not you can tell what prices something sells for is utterly random - you have as good a chance of knowing the price of engines on the other side of the galaxy as you do the sector you just left.  That said, war tends to make things easier: Sectors at war just plain double the prices they pay for everything, making profits large enough to pay for your freighter take only a couple trips and a minute or two of your time.  It's so much more profitable than anything else that anything else is a waste of time, in terms of optimization, but it's also rather dull to just keep running the same routes over and over.
There are other things available, like talking to governors, talking in bars, exploring planets, and other ships in the sector, but they're generally so invisible that you have to go out of your way to remember to hunt them down.  There should be more variety in the average game day than just having these things be the random distractions from the all-important freight hauling where you have zero human interaction.
In terms of plot, this game names all its sectors things like "New Ireland" or "New Germany" or "New Italy", but the story is unabashedly Amero-centric.  It straight-up tells you in the manual that the game is meant to be The American Revolution and American Civil War.  So, the story basically goes that the Federation (or Empire, as it's called anytime it's supposed to be the bad guy, because empires are bad, 'mmmkay?) passed some "tyrannical" laws, so some of the colonies started a rebellion after having a Tea Party. (Subtle!) What were these tyrannical laws, you might ask?  A prohibition on slavery, of course, since the economy of the rebel colonies are based upon slavery.  (No mention of race, though, that part's whitewashed out in more ways than one.)  Needless to say, this kind of undermines the whole rebel unifying cry of "freedom", or how "tyrannical" it is to demand freedom for others, but hey, I guess I can give points for capturing some of the moral hypocrisy of it all.  Anyway, the Federation is still portrayed as evil because they also burn Savanna - I mean, perform orbital bombardments, although EVERY faction commits similar war crimes willy-nilly, which raises the question of how the economy springs back to normal after half its population and its entire industrial base were incinerated.
In any event, there's two other factions besides the Federated States of American Imperial Union and the Colonial Confederacy: There's the Trade Coalition, which seems to have no particular backstory or role in this at all, aside from being a place for supposedly neutral merchants, although the AI that controls them is no less aggressive in trying to conquer everyone else.  Considering their European colony names, I guess they're supposed to be Dutch traders or something.  Then, there's the Syndicate, which is basically the "LOL, we're totally evil!" pirate faction, although they're surprisingly hostile to smuggling rum,
for no good reason.  They're given planets like Barbados, which implies they're the Carrbiean pirate nations, but also have New Moscow as their capital, because Haiti isn't threatening enough on its own, if you want real villains, you need them to be Russian!

At first, the game seems incredibly complex. There are many ships, faction politics, a trade mechanic with a black market aspect, tons of skills and abilities, and a large map.
After a couple hours of playing, you'll realize that everything that looked good is actually poorly executed.
The combat plays out pretty much the same every time regardless of your ship and skills (which are badly balanced). You have almost no control over the combat. Everything feels very random and there is no strategy apart from picking the best skill out of the random pile of them that the game gives you every turn. Not that any of this matters. There are a few mid-level ships that are undeniably better than everything else. After a little experimenting, you’ll have a ship that can’t lose unless the random number generator has something against you.
The faction politics are almost pointless. You only need to get friendly with the factions if you want amnesty for committing crimes. You won’t be committing any crimes unless you have a combat oriented ship. If you have a tough ship, you generally don't need amnesty. It's a self-defeating cycle of uselessness.
The trade system could not be more boring. You go to a system that sells something cheap. Buy it, fly to somewhere where it is expensive, sell it, rinse, and repeat until you can afford a ship with a bigger cargo hull. Then you get the exciting experience of doing exactly what you were doing before but in larger quantities. The black market is the exact same, except you might have to a do a little more fighting.
The skill tree is incredibly frustrating as it forces you to buy a number of useless skills before you can get to the good ones. The useless skills will then fill up your queue during combat with abilities that you will likely never use and make your life harder. No, you can't disable abilities that you have already unlocked.
Apart from the differing commodity prices, there is no real difference between the systems. The factions constantly fight, pirates are everywhere except for the starting areas, and random piles of money float through space, making it far more profitable to aimlessly bounce around between planets than to actually play the game.
The most frustrating aspect of the game by far is the class system. At the start of a campaign, you have to choose a faction and a player class. The classes determine the skills that you can pick. Only certain classes can unlock the skill to buy a business while others can do things like invade systems. The class system only exists to force you into multiple playthroughs and extend playtime in order to see all of the content. The irony here is that there isn't much content to begin with.
TL;DR: You’ll have more fun with a free flash game. Don’t buy this unless you hate yourself.

For starters, I'd like to menstion I have 15 years and god-knows-how-many-hours total in all the different iterations of ADoM, so my Steam time definitely isnt accurate.
Ahh, ADoM. Its what most roguelikes aspire to be. Its a *Hack, as opposed to ToME, which is an *Angband. ADoM is the grandchild of Rogue, and the great granddaddy of all those f'n games out there that seem to think "roguelike" means "permadeath with random generation". Nope. THIS is what a godd*** roguelike is. If you like the genre, you probably already have a copy, one of the free ones. Why buy it on Steam when you can get Version 60 for free? To support Thomas and his team to keep adding to it, cleaning up bugs, making more options. I did. Its totally worth it for any die hard fan. It has full tiles, done really well. But it also has the capability for the old school ASCII that was all that existed until just a couple years ago. Its deep, its awesome, its everything a Roguelike should be. Processing immigrants at the border of a Soviet-like nation doesn't sound like riveting gameplay material, but 'Papers, Please' makes it work on every level. After receiving your new posting as the Inspection Officer of Arstotzka, you take your place in a small, dingy booth and call the first person of the day to the desk. Each 'level' of the game is a new day, and your salary each day is based on how many people you (successfully) process. With rent, food and heating to pay for each day, and four family members to look after, processing as many immigrants as possible is of the utmost importance, but becomes more difficult in the wake of civil unrest, terrorist attacks and diplomatic emergencies. Each of these brings about changes to the admittance protocol - new documents are required, all with new information to be correlated with the person's statements and passport. This also affords moral decisions - if someone comes through in an attempt to escape unjust persecution or even murder in their homeland, but lacks the correct paperwork, will you still let them through?
9/10.
Glory to Arstotzka.

Wow and I thought my job was bad! You play as a paper checker at a border crossing. As you progress along the requirements that the different citizens must have get more complex. I enjoyed helping the little people who really needed to get through (and in one cased really did NOT want to get through). Or getting hit on my strippers, that was a nice chuckle.
9/10

This is probably the most underwelming thing i've ever purchased, and that includes some incomplete and unplayable early access games. Papers, Please was so completely outside of my comprehension that I had to write my first review about it just to get closure.
The gameplay consists of looking at a picture and making sure all the numbers & letters on it match up to some other numbers & letters distributed around your screen and filed away in leaflets that you must flip through to find the correct page. Essentialy this is the worlds least interesting and most frustrating 'spot the difference' game. It is tedius, cumbersome, and unengaging. Which is what I expected, to a degree.
My ability to track every detail of small grainy images is apparently lackin,g because after the first game day it took me a minumum of 2 minutes per passport to comb for all the minutia, and I still had a failure rate of 1/3. Once it cited me for an incorrect photograph, and I honestly had not noticed a discrepancy between the two pictures despite comparing the two; I had thought they were similar enough having the same face, hair, and beard, but apparently not.
I played half an hour before I could bear no more, my levels of irritating and impatience. It was over a year before I gave it another try, inspired by all the praise I had read. My experience was no better than the first, and I cannot see myself trying again ever.
When I began I cut off all food and heat expenses, since the game offered no incentive to keep them on. Processing the amount of documents necessary to maintain those expenses is beyond my capabilities, so letting my "family" die would be the optimal choice from a gamey perspective. From a story perspective, if you can call it that, the game gave me no reason to care about them: just letters on a form, after all. They didn't even have names.
The game punished me for my apathy when the game suddenly ended on the forth day. Apparently the family dying causes instant loss. Since I am not capable of playing the game quickly enough to pay for their expenses, this is as far as I progressed and as far as I coupld ever potentialy progress in this game.
But that is the gameplay. As I understand it the real reason this game gets praise is for its story, art and atmosphere, apparently. After playing the game, I am legitamately questioning whether all this praise is some kind of elaborate joke, as far fetched as that sounds: the coordination required would be astounding.
The story in full as I experienced it is, you are a man who checks immigrant's paperwork. You have 4 family members. the job gets harder every day. I kept waiting for some kind of twist or element that would explain the hype, suddenly make it engaging, or at the very least make me feel someing, or care even slightly, but in never came. If it comes later in the game, I am both unwilling and incapable of reaching that point.
Occasionaly the immigrants say things or beg to be let in, etc. but seeing as there is no apparent gameplay benefit or narrative pay-off to be had basing your decisions on anything but whether or not you earn a citation, I quickly tuned them out.
As for the atmosphere and art, there are some grey pixels, some black pixels, and I think even some white pixels. The intro and failure screen has red and orange pixels. There may have been some blue pixels but I cannot confirm or deny this.
So as should be clear at this point, did not enjoy this game. The gameplay is unbearable but I could have forgiven this if there was at least something outside of the gameplay to experience. I personally play games more for their story, characters, narrative and world anyway, but there are almost none of those things in Papers, Please, and I am given no reason to care about what little there is.

Above all I am left confused. If all the things that the game is praised for barely exist, and the other elements are addmitted to be terrible even by the fans, where does the praise come from? I found no redeeming qualites in this game whatsover and am completely baffled that most players did. What am I missing? What have I overlooked that explains why people liked this? I am genuinely baffled.

Prologue: Once again, it's time for me to review an online game, AKA an MMORPG. This one is the next part (Or prequel) of not only The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim, but all others which came before it. So, without further ado, I hereby present my review for The Elder Scrolls Online-A game where each player can select his or her own race and wander about his or her own path...
Gameplay-Impressive, dynamic, and with much variety, fantasy fans are sure to find something nifty or interesting to do in The Elder Scrolls Online...Set in the Second Era of Tamriel, players can learn many interesting skills or do many things to earn them precious experience, including but not limited to: Going on a quest (Or two, or three, or four), purchasing a home (Or two or...), purchasing and learning to ride a horse, learning one (Or two) of several crafting skills, and much more besides. Gaining levels is mainly done by completing one or more quest chains, but can also be gained by slaying monsters or even simply by discovering new places across Tamriel. And since this is a mostly open-world-game, you can always encounter other players around you. And at least 90% of the time, those players are friend and willing to help you. This is not a free game however, so players must be prepared to purchase a copy in order to play. In addition to this, however, they can purchase a horse or a house for as little as $15. This isn't quite bad at all! Gameplay Score-8 out of 10.
Items-Lots to use, consume, and equip! While their descriptions are not always vivid, most of the items are helpful in some way or another. If not, one can always try selling them. Be aware, however, selling items isn't always easy. Tamriel is a very remote place, after all, so don't be expecting to find a place like a buying/selling exchange where all players go to buy or sell their items. Items Score-7 out of 10.
Weapons-Yesh, there are powerful weapons one can find in this game. And like many good games, there are a plethora of melee, missile, and magic weapons to make use of. In addition to this, the weapons are not limited by Class. However, there aren't just '50 levels' to gain-Even after Level 50, one continues to level up. And even reaching Level 50 is no easy task. Therefore, if one decides to purchase a stronger weapon than one already has, then he or she must be careful to avoid purchasing something above their current level. Plus, unlike the Armor (Which we'll be getting to shortly), the weapons never break down; they can be used forever! Weapons Score-7 out of 10.
Ammo-Surprisingly enough, none of the missile weapons (As far as I know) use any kind of ammo. So you don't have to concern yourself with running out of it during a battle. The only thing you have to worry about is how much Mana or Stamina you have remaining. And by the way, these two (Along with your Health) automatically replenish over time. Ammo Score-10 out of 10.
Armor-Of course, there is powerful armor to be had here. One only has to know just where to find it. And like the weapons, there are 3 main types of armor: Light, Medium, and Heavy. These can be combined in a mix/match-up style or one can wear all of a certain thickness of armor. Be aware, however, the armor does wear down over time. I didn't give it a chance to break down completely, though. Yes, it can be repaired using any one of several kinds of repair kits. These can be bought or found across Tamriel. Plus, each armor type has its own skill set, which you can spend your skill points in order to improve your armor's ability to protect you better in combat. As if this wasn't interesting enough, you can buy or obtain materials to upgrade your armor's overall quality (From white onto green, then blue and so on). Doing so makes it stronger overall. Armor Score-7 out of 10.
Plot-If you've never played an Elder Scrolls game in your life, and ESO is your very first adventure in Tamriel, well then...Be prepared for a massive story, which will fully immerse you, no matter what your chosen race and/or class are. Plus, even creating your character will give you something to look forward to once he or she makes their entrance into the world. I won't give out any spoilers, but know the plot runs deep and has many surprising twists and turns. Plot Score-8 out of 10.
Characters-Throughout my 165 plus hours of playing this game, I found all of the characters to be likable or dislikable in some way...But I say this in a good way! This is especially true of Razum-dar, one jolly good fellow Khajiit who saves your neck. After all, a game with dull characters or those who are to powerful for their own good is like an old rusty sword or dagger. On one hand, it'll be to dull to be of use in a battle. But by the same token, you may cut yourself on it if it's to powerful to start with...As in one Sliske. Yeah, Jagex...I'm talking about you! Characters Score-10 out of 10.
Sound-Definitely good enough to listen to, but keeping your graphics at a low to moderate level actually improves the quality of your sound! Give it a try if you don't believe me. Then, be sure to see if you can pinpoint certain vital sounds during a critical moment...Sound Score-8 out of 10.
Music-Since I haven't given the music here a fair chance, I can't give it a score. However, judging by what I heard of the music so far, I'd say it's mediocre at best in a melancholy sense. As this was the case with a lot of games I've played, I've come to generally turn the music down, but other people may agree or disagree with me. At any rate, I don't have a score for it just yet. Music Score-N/A.
Graphics-Even at a lower level, the graphics are surprisingly nice to gaze upon. They rival even some games including The Lord of the Rings Online and Arche Age. It may take a moment or two for them to render properly, but even on medium level, they render faster even than the graphics would in say...Second Life. And even their graphics aren't quite as pretty. Besides this, the only drawback is not being able to see into or out of buildings. Graphics Score-9 out of 10.
Final Score-As you can probably guesh, The Elder Scrolls Online-Tamriel Unlimited is more than just a great game; it's downright amazing! And even though some aspects of it are much harder than they need to be (Such as picking locks or 'dancing' in the heat of battle with a monster), if you just ask the developers for help, they WILL help you. I am dead serious. Only today, I was actually given several items from a very friendly female associate. So, if you're still not convinced as to whether to buy this game, then this will hopefully seal the deal. It sure did for me, and also gives this game an extra point...Something I feel it well-deserves. The only 3 things this game needs for a perfect score are...1: Make the skills and levels a little easier to gain. 2: Make monsters a little easier to defeat. And 3: Make trading and making money a little easier, although directly interacting with players in this regard (As well as other methods of doing so noted above) really does make the online aspect of this game shine. Kudos to you, ZeniMax! Final Score-9 out of 10.

The graphics and soundtrack are also top notch, some tracks being so good I noticed my feet tapping against the floor. :)
If there's some critique, it would be the grabbing system, BUT fortunately you can put it to automatic via options. And I really recommend it. Don't worry: It won't make the game easy, it just corrects one thing, that's a flaw in this game (IMO).

And like I always say: quality over quantity, and in this case it really once again is true.
Oh, and I really recommend gamepad or arcade stick for this one.

Already in early access I'm absolutely enjoying this game.
Since I've always liked games similar to this like Pandemic 1 & 2 it's hard for me not to love this game too.
It has a simple mix of laid back strategy, chance and punny humor.
The gameplay starts off by of popping little bubbles, as if it was on a phone, (it originally was), in hope to give you enough points to make some effects on your plague, varying from symptoms to transmissions and "research complexity"... And then you wait (speed time up) and hope you don't get your plague detected before you've spread out at least a little, as your ultimate goal is to end humanity by killing everyone.
Of course this comes with variations of diseases and parasites which changes the play style, each with their own advantages or disadvantages which may prove challenging.
The addition of pretty graphics are alright, yet it does not enhance the gameplay.
The music and atmosphere is sweet and generally just fits with the theme without being uncomfortable.
Overall it's pretty solid, but could still use some improvements which seems to be worked on.
I'll list a few things I did not like from the time I did this recommendation:
Low variation of symptoms: Many diseases and parasites has the same "symptom tree" with the exception of the new Neurax Worm which is unique and absolutely brilliant. Amazing to play with, not so much the others as it is mainly too similar and dull.
In-infectible countries: You may be playing the game, having infected the entire world with only one tiny island with closed borders and ports, yet it becomes completely impossible for you to infect the country with most plagues once this happens, immediately deciding that you won't be able to win. Even though, logically it would still be possible for the disease to be carried there, regardless of border control.
Common geography: I've noticed a few countries have been fairly detailed in some areas but a bit too vague in other areas by calling them after the biggest country, then overlap the smaller neighboring countries, Yet it would have been more appropriate, for instance "the balkan states" which is absolutely correct, not too vague and not too detailed. While you see Germany overlap five different countries. Instead better naming would had been Southern Europe, Central Europe, Southern Europe, Eastern Europe, Northern Europe, Scandinavia, Britain, Balkan States (even though technically still Eastern europe), etc.
The pricing: Having to pay 30% more in Europe and only half price in Russia doesn't seem all that fair. If the pricing had a smaller percentage difference, maybe it would be more attractive globally.
Still.. It's a fair game which I consider worth the money in contrast to its entertainment value.

Don't let the fact that it's an MMO fool you. There's a proper Final Fantasy plotline sandwiched in between all the MMO trappings, and the main story quests can be played mostly solo if you're antisocial. From a technical standpoint the game runs really well. It's not as demanding on resources as you might think for a game as pretty as this game can be (If you're not sure it'll run well hunt down the latest benchmark utility they put out with the Heavensward expansion,) and even on the lowest settings it still looks really nice. The game's core new gameplay conceit is that you can switch classes and jobs just by swapping equipment. This works well, and some skills are even transferrable between classes which can give you a leg up. Crafting and gathering are their own classes as well, and the process of crafting high-level items can be exhilirating or heartbreaking. If you're a fan of MMO's, then there's a lot to like here. If you're a Final Fantasy fan, then there's a lot to like here. There's just a lot to like all around.

Though there is a great level of complexity and depth to this game, and replayability, a lot of the game is based highly around text.  The learning curve requires a lot of reading, and even character creation requires a lot of reading.   Everything you do requires reading basically.  The combat system is pretty basic and simple, despite a proclaimed deep tactical system in the description.  The controls are overly complex to the point of being unnecessarily complex and having different unique key strokes and key combinations for everything you can do, to the point where you barely remember how to navigate your inventory.
I could see this game being enriching and deep if you are into a lot of reading, a big learning curve, using primarily keyboard commands for everything, and a lot of figuring everything out for yourself or reading tons of help menus.  It's not that I am opposed to text-based RPGs, it is just not what was advertised, and I was expecting a lot more action-packed adventure.

ADOM was the defining game of my childhood. Biskup's little project established the framework for so many of my preferences in gaming and game design for years to come. While my tastes have since drifted, there was an *immense* and overwhelming feeling of nostalgia opening up this remastering for the first time. My hand still intuitively knew all of the hundred-odd keybindings necessary to really play the game effectively. This, I knew immediately, was something that I was going to rack up an embarrassing number of hours on.
Or, I would, at least, if it were more stable. An hours worth of attempts at play lost me several characters due to crashes. That part is definitely new. While I think everyone should give ADOM a spin, I recommend giving it a little while after launch to sort out its issues.

Been happily following this game and I'm so glad to see it finally reach to Steam. Coming from someone who's been playing Nethack and Roguelikes since I've started PC gaming, this game is a wonderful treasure. I've known friends to lose entire summers to this game back in 1998/1999 and so many more hours poring over notebook pages of stats and abilities and trying to come up with THE BEST character combination.
Pros:
+GUI. No more ASCII. If you come from the old-school, you remember how much time was taken up by trying to remember every monster in the ASCII alphabet. Be all the "purist" you want but not everyone likes remembering each monster type and name by a symbol and color.
+Characters and monster sprites change according to what's equipped. Sure! Leave that suit of Chainmail on the floor for that Goblin to pick up...see what happens...
+A significantly more detailed FAQ and instruction booklet and questionnaire. Praise be to Kormak!
+Tutorial added. Never played a roguelike in your life? TOO BAD! We'll explain it to you!
Cons:
--Oh the crashes. The crashes. The CRASHES. Somewhere in this game's code is a terrible memory leak that causes the game to go from running to utterly unstable at random and there is something punch-a-baby-rabbit-to-death infuriating at losing 2-3 hours work without a Save and Resume OR saving, game crashes mid-save and coming back to find your savefile and your backup file gone. Hope the devs fix this at some point.

Processing immigrants at the border of a Soviet-like nation doesn't sound like riveting gameplay material, but 'Papers, Please' makes it work on every level. After receiving your new posting as the Inspection Officer of Arstotzka, you take your place in a small, dingy booth and call the first person of the day to the desk. Each 'level' of the game is a new day, and your salary each day is based on how many people you (successfully) process. With rent, food and heating to pay for each day, and four family members to look after, processing as many immigrants as possible is of the utmost importance, but becomes more difficult in the wake of civil unrest, terrorist attacks and diplomatic emergencies. Each of these brings about changes to the admittance protocol - new documents are required, all with new information to be correlated with the person's statements and passport. This also affords moral decisions - if someone comes through in an attempt to escape unjust persecution or even murder in their homeland, but lacks the correct paperwork, will you still let them through?
9/10.
Glory to Arstotzka.

This is probably the most underwelming thing i've ever purchased, and that includes some incomplete and unplayable early access games. Papers, Please was so completely outside of my comprehension that I had to write my first review about it just to get closure.
The gameplay consists of looking at a picture and making sure all the numbers & letters on it match up to some other numbers & letters distributed around your screen and filed away in leaflets that you must flip through to find the correct page. Essentialy this is the worlds least interesting and most frustrating 'spot the difference' game. It is tedius, cumbersome, and unengaging. Which is what I expected, to a degree.
My ability to track every detail of small grainy images is apparently lackin,g because after the first game day it took me a minumum of 2 minutes per passport to comb for all the minutia, and I still had a failure rate of 1/3. Once it cited me for an incorrect photograph, and I honestly had not noticed a discrepancy between the two pictures despite comparing the two; I had thought they were similar enough having the same face, hair, and beard, but apparently not.
I played half an hour before I could bear no more, my levels of irritating and impatience. It was over a year before I gave it another try, inspired by all the praise I had read. My experience was no better than the first, and I cannot see myself trying again ever.
When I began I cut off all food and heat expenses, since the game offered no incentive to keep them on. Processing the amount of documents necessary to maintain those expenses is beyond my capabilities, so letting my "family" die would be the optimal choice from a gamey perspective. From a story perspective, if you can call it that, the game gave me no reason to care about them: just letters on a form, after all. They didn't even have names.
The game punished me for my apathy when the game suddenly ended on the forth day. Apparently the family dying causes instant loss. Since I am not capable of playing the game quickly enough to pay for their expenses, this is as far as I progressed and as far as I coupld ever potentialy progress in this game.
But that is the gameplay. As I understand it the real reason this game gets praise is for its story, art and atmosphere, apparently. After playing the game, I am legitamately questioning whether all this praise is some kind of elaborate joke, as far fetched as that sounds: the coordination required would be astounding.
The story in full as I experienced it is, you are a man who checks immigrant's paperwork. You have 4 family members. the job gets harder every day. I kept waiting for some kind of twist or element that would explain the hype, suddenly make it engaging, or at the very least make me feel someing, or care even slightly, but in never came. If it comes later in the game, I am both unwilling and incapable of reaching that point.
Occasionaly the immigrants say things or beg to be let in, etc. but seeing as there is no apparent gameplay benefit or narrative pay-off to be had basing your decisions on anything but whether or not you earn a citation, I quickly tuned them out.
As for the atmosphere and art, there are some grey pixels, some black pixels, and I think even some white pixels. The intro and failure screen has red and orange pixels. There may have been some blue pixels but I cannot confirm or deny this.
So as should be clear at this point, did not enjoy this game. The gameplay is unbearable but I could have forgiven this if there was at least something outside of the gameplay to experience. I personally play games more for their story, characters, narrative and world anyway, but there are almost none of those things in Papers, Please, and I am given no reason to care about what little there is.

Above all I am left confused. If all the things that the game is praised for barely exist, and the other elements are addmitted to be terrible even by the fans, where does the praise come from? I found no redeeming qualites in this game whatsover and am completely baffled that most players did. What am I missing? What have I overlooked that explains why people liked this? I am genuinely baffled.

It's a real shame that I have to not recommend this considering that it's got a great first episode and has solid game play, good music and graphics. At the time of writting this, there are only 2 episodes out and because of how different they are from each other, I will review them separately.
Episode 1:
The game begins with a very familiar and simple play style, small weak enemies come in low numbers and attempt to hit you. You can make quick work of them though. As you progress through the level, more difficult enemies are added and more challenging environments are present. There is even a few areas where you get to ride a beast like thing, it's pretty fun. Numerous well designed boss fights are included. Although it really starts to ramp up the difficulty at the later areas of the level, the game never feels unfair and with frequent checkpoints and 6 hits for a life bar, the difficulty is just right. More of this would be excellent. The final boss in this episode is pretty tough but reasonable enough. Although this episode is short, it's great and it got me really excited for more episodes. It really did impress me. If I had to give it a score, I'd give it a 9/10
Episode 2:
And than suddenly the game does a complete 180, changing everything about the design that made the first episode so good. At first, it's a slow paced platformer with very few enemies. In fact there aren't many enemies at all in this episode, at least ones that give points and are stationed through the level. As you progress through this level, you will face more difficult platforming sections, most of which will either send you to the beginning via vertical drops or instantly kill you through large areas of pitfalls.
This episode also features riding an animal, this time it's a bee. This creature does not like to cooperate though. If you fall off, it will fly around you avoiding you as much as possible, though it stays roughly in the same area that you lost it. This can make it a huge pain just trying to progress through those areas as one hit will send you flying off the bee. Later on you have to use the bee in automatic screen scrolling sections where flight is mandatory. It's a mini bullet hell out of no where and the short range attack and instant kill from falling off the edge of the scrolling screen makes it infuriating. Oh and I forgot to mention that despite some bees being somewhat friendly, all the others will try to kill you and they spawn infinitely at the sides of the screen while you try to fly tightly crowded areas of spikes.
The only other main enemy in this level are apes, these guys are very annoying. When in high numbers, these pests can cause a lot of trouble. They jump around the room and throw what I hope to be rocks at you. These rocks are high speed and perfectly accurate, if thrown while you are in mid-air, they are almost guarenteed to hit. There is also a giant ape boss, which is very difficult. Ironically enough, it captures a blonde and throws barrels at you. Sound familiar? It should. A reference to one of the most iconic and classic games of all time, Donkey Kong. Only this is no easy breeze jumping over simple barrel trajectories. These barrels bounce all over the place with high speed and they're the same size as the player. Incredibly challenging and will take you many tries to overcome, if you have the patience.
After all that the level is still not complete, well over an hour now and you still have to keep going. The last sections I played were consistently frustrating. The auto scrolling of the screen which moved way too fast for me to keep up, killed me mercilessly. Not to mention the huge number of projectiles that fly at you. There is a lot of grabbing vines and ceilings reminiscent of some Shinobi levels, only the grabbing controls don't work all that well here. I died at least 30% of the time from the character refusing to grab a ledge or vine only to fall to my death. All of this combined created an experience that was punishing and sadistic. I'd have to enjoy the pain to finish this level. I did not.
Conclusion:
So to conclude these reviews, I'd say that the game has great potential. The first episode being a shining example of great game design, while the second episode takes all the worse elements of older platformers and throws them all at you at the same time. This leaves me very conflicted as to what I should rate the game as a whole. I also cannot understand the massive shift in design here. The first episode featured almost no instant death or pitfalls, while the second episode is full of it. The game goes from fun and fair to brutal and painful in a flash. It's a true shame to see yet another retro throw-back desperate to relive the "glory" days of punishing quarter-devouring arcade games instead of improving on any of it.
In the end I do not recommend this game as I can't see the next episodes going in a better direction. Odds are they'll continue trying to make it harder and more brutal as they release the other episodes. It's not really worth the time and frustration for the average gamer. This is only for true hardcore platformer fans.

I really am in two minds about this game.
On the one hand I really want to like it and it's not like there isn't much on offer here. The game has an appealing aesthetic, lots of indie charme, surprisingly fresh level design, varied enemies and locales, multiple moves, combos, an old-school soundtrack - take your pick! I even backed this game on Kickstarter.
On the other hand I have not walked away that frustrated from a playsession with a platformer in a really long time. So what's wrong? That's not so easy to pin down.
Just for perspective: I have been playing platformers for half my life now (so in the realm of fifteen years and counting - yes I'm old, I know) and consider myself to be fairly able at it. Of recent fame, I finished Cave Story, Guacamelee and Shovel Knight. All these games contain more than their share of challenging platforming and boss fights, but have I ever felt that frustrated playing them? No.
So: What wrong? Well first off the timimg of the controls and the game as a whole (as in how "tight" and responsive the controls are and whether a given level plays out deterministically in terms of when does which enemy fire etc.) seem to be really wonky. I cannot count the number of times I have taken cheap hits or deaths because some button press did not register or the "pattern" of the level just did not play out the same way this single time.
Secondly, as good as the overall level design is, it sometimes suffers from the chosen aesthetic. Foreground and Background sometimes merge too much to support the amount of twitch apparently required. It also often takes the one step that makes a fun challenge into a more frustrating ordeal. Ample amounts of spikes at the bottom of an already challenging platforming section with enemy involvement (and wonky controls) are an example of this. It also sometimes feels like there is exactly one thing too much going on on the screen to be able to figure out the "rythm" or pattern of the level that is usually required to master it. I don't have the feeling this is possible in this game (especially given the wonky timing mentioned above). Might be that's not the kind of platformer gameplay envisioned by the devs, that's fair. But for me that is the heart of every good platformer: There can be a good amount of twitch, but if you really figure out a level, beating should not require big amounts of it.
So can I recommend it? If it comes down to the most important question, namely whether I enjoyed playing the game, I guess the answer is "No" for the above reasons - as much as it hurts me, especially after having backed this on Kickstarter. I am not looking forward to playing the game again, although I likely will to finish it at some time.
There is much good in the game, but given how frustrating it is to me, I cannot recommend it.

Short but exciting shooter game. The story is told in a unique way through an unreliable narrator, which in some places causes parts of the level to suddenly change in drastic ways.
The gunplay is satisfying, and while the choice of weaponry is fairly standard, each weapon feels powerful and good at slinging lead, and also specialised to a certain playstyle. I recommend switching weapons out during gameplay for the best overall experience. Virtually every level involves a quickdraw minigame at the end, which I feel is a nice way to wrap up an explosive chapter in the story.
There's a simple progression system of exchanging skill points for perks, and earning said skill points is based on getting kill streaks, headshots, and other flashy displays of marksmanship and combat prowess.
In all, the game is fun and doesn't take itself seriously, and you get to step in the shoes of a badass hellbent on revenge.

Is logistics your thing? Fancy spending an evening trouble shooting bottlenecks in your production chain? This game is made by Supergiant, the company that made Bastion. I expected similar quality with this game but it's not even close.
First of all, the naration is awful. Yes, it's the same voice actor but he doesn't do anywhere near as good a job as in Bastion. He delivers lines without any passion and just doesn't have the same charm. Plus, you can barely hear him because he is really quiet even on max volume.
In Bastion he explains what's going on, gives you the background information of the story, and tells the story gradually as you play it. It was really fun to learn about the lore and listen to him tell the story. And the best part was, you get to actually play the game while doing it. In this way there is a perfect blend of action and storytelling.
All of this is missing in Transistor. The narrator just makes a bunch of dumb general comments that barely have anything to do with what's going on. He doesn't give you any background information about the setting, explain the lore, or tell the story. You just wander around in a city, feeling confused without even the most basic context or narrative. I've played for several hours and have no clue what's going on. When you take away the story, really all you have is a bunch of combat. Which wouldn't be too bad by itself, except for the fact that the combat sucks.
The main problem is that the combat is not only WAY too hard, but also severely flawed. Your character is etremely weak and can die in about two seconds from enemy fire. You can mitigate this by using the turn feature. Basically, you can pause the game and issue orders to your character. When you unpause, she carries the orders out while all the other enemies are frozen. It's not as broken as it sounds. When your turn is over, every single one of your abilities is on cooldown until turn recharges, meaning that you can't use them. Which means you are defenseless after using your turn. So basically the game is use your turn so you can actually kill stuff, and then run away and try not to die for 5 seconds. This is a lot harder than it sounds and is also just boring to do.
In addition, when you kill an enemy a battery pops out. You have to run to it pick it up in 5 seconds or the enemy respawns with FULL HEALTH. On top of this, it's even shielded from damage and you have to damage the shield to be able to pick it up. When you use up your turn to kill an enemy, you oftentimes cannot break the shield on the battery because you can't attack yet, and so the enemy respawns with full health.
It wouldn't be so bad if there were actually a difficulty slider. Or like in Bastion, you can do challange areas to gain upgrades if you're having a hard time. Instead, the challenge rooms give music tracks as a reward. Seriously?
So essentially it's a game with no story and ridiculously hard/flawed gameplay.
I expected the soundtrack to be amazing like in Bastion, but again this game doesn't deliver. The soundtrack isn't very unique, it sounds like generic video game music. And you don't get to hear it anyway because the music turns off when using your turn feature. What a bummer.
Oh and this game doesn't have a start menu or anything. Literally, the most basic feature in video games is missing.
The only reedming feature could be the graphics I guess. The enviorments are absolutely beautiful, just like Bastion. However, a game needs to provide solid gameplay and a story and can't get by with just fancy visuals. That's why they're called "games". If you want good art, go to a museum or watch a movie.
There is also only about 5 hours of gameplay. It took me that long to beat it. But even then, the game time was artificially inflated because of difficulty. It would probably be like 3 or 4 hours if you are skilled at action games.
TL/DR: No story, bad narration, flawed/ridiculously hard gameplay, lack of features, poor soundtrack.

A beautiful game with a unique art style and influences, and a painstaking amount of effort and creativity put into its maps, classes, and bizarre host of monsters. It sells its visuals almost purely on the quality of the storybook-esque hand drawn art, mixing sprites and 3D models seamlessly in a fixed perspective, building a visual style all its own without chasing photorealism.
The music is also an absolute triumph, with a quality soundtrack more than a hundred songs broad. Every environment has not only its own leitmotif, but its own *playlist* of motifs, 3-5 tracks long.
The minute to minute gameplay is satisfying and reasonably deep, with big active skill lists, short cooldowns, and manually aimed attacks eschewing the target-based systems of past MMO's like Ragnarok. The greater gameplay loop is fairly set in stone, however, without too much extra to do beyond the crazy storyline, dungeons, GvG, seasonal events, and daily queued activities.
ToS's class system is an interesting proposition for anyone interested in building both unique and well-optimized characters, and offers a lot of freedom to do unusual things, though for its incredible breadth it pays in being unevenly balanced. Still, what can one really expect when classes exist whose entire set of skills is solely magical wood-carving, kabbalah, or falconry?
But honestly? Here's the real reason I play Tree of Savior: it's made by developers who care.
Not about you; not personally. Other reviews will back me there: IMC is a Korean company, and the language and distance barrier is real. But they're unlike any other developer I've ever known, Korean or otherwise: they legitimately care about what it is they're doing, beyond the point of obligation, and have the power to see it done.
ToS is long past its initial surge of popularity, but it sees frequent and regular updates in every aspect - UI, core systems, classes, areas, dungeons, graphics, sound. Every few months there's something new, and something old has been refined to work a little better. IMC blunders often, at times almost comically naive or misguided in its intentions (yet never malicious) - but it self-examines, adapts, and corrects itself in ways I'd never thought plausible. It does something I've never seen before in a professional dev studio: it takes fault and then it actually fixes what's wrong.
This is a developer who envisioned a classic paywall MMO, asked the world what it wanted, rolled out a F2P beta instead which granted earlier access in increments to supporters who paid more, and within a week retooled everything to a simple formula of "any donation = early access" in response to the (fully justified) displeasure of its players. This is a developer who nearly a year into release undertook a complete rebalancing of every skill, class, and weapon to address balance and playability concerns. These are the people who keep a running, up-to-date blog on their official site that talks honestly about issues in its core design and the studio's plans for fixing them.
There's no profit in this; ToS itself may not even be a particularly profitable endeavor in 2017, though I sincerely hope it's at least holding steady. But they keep at it, because it's the game they want to make. Because it's their pride and joy, and they care about it more than anyone.
If you've little interest in slow progression or classic eastern MMO sensibilities, or come bringing very specific expectations from grinders like RO, you may want to give ToS a pass. It's its own thing, rooted in the genre's history but not defined by it. But if you're in the mood for a work of art, enjoy gonzo class mechanics no triple-A designer would dare attempt, or are just looking for an interesting game with a the most earnest, naively innocent, and hardworking developers in the business, give Tree of Savior a shot.
I guarantee you won't do better.

I played this game because I was in love with Ragnarok Online years ago. I've played a good many hours and have a character pretty high level.
First, This is not ragnarok. You will be mixing and matching classes (sometimes ones that are stupidly terrible at what you want them to do). You will also be aiming for the highest damage possible (even as a tank) because overkill experience is the only way to level.
Second, the maps are buggy. And I don't mean "ooh I got to an area I wasn't supposed to" buggy. I mean "I can't cross this bridge that is required to advance the plot" buggy. That and monsters will spontaneously teleport.
Third, grindtastic is pretty applicable here. After my second job change, I just couldn't read these terrible quests/story anymore. I then moved on to trying to get higher level and skipping the quests. When you do that, you have your standard "World of Warcraft" quests to run but they aren't efficient. Most efficient way is just to overkill mobs.
So I leave you with this. If you liked the grind of Ragnarok Online but not the role restricting nature of the classes, you'll probably like Tree of Savior. If you've moved on from having 15 hours a day to mindlessly play the same game and only have 2 or so hours because you now have a life, it's probably not for you.

I will start with the con (just one) in this game: The learning curve / keybindings are tough on this. You need to be patient and learn/ list lots of commands on the keyboard.
I first played ADOM around 2003-2004. We had a crappy computer which couldn't handle many games at all, but my brother had ADOM on it. I tested it and was instantly hooked: So much to explore, so hard! Only one life? The merciless roguelike system where the game is permanently over when you die made me curious.
The added graphics are quite nice addition to the game and I imagine it's easier for new players to get into the game. I use only the keyboard controls for the game, as it is much faster (and I've played it for years so it comes natural). I recommend tackling the keyboard commands if you want faster gameplay.
There are so many ways you can be good (or bad) at this game. The game has been around for decades so it is well-balanced, but also still very challenging. I haven't still finished this game without "cheating", that is what was known as save scumming, where you copy the save file in case you die and continue game from there. I died just once to a stupid mistake which I don't remember anymore, but it still annoys me, even after multiple years. I'm fully determined to finish ADOM in the near future...
In a nutshell, the reasons I enjoy playing ADOM:
- Challenging enough
- Addictive - you'll probably end up screaming like a maniac for dying, swear you had enough ADOM for a week, only to find yourself trying a new character 10 minutes later
- Variable - Dozens, if not hundreds of ways to play the game (race, class combinations + different endings, quests to pursue, places to visit)
- Unpredictable - You might get mighty lucky early in the game, or really unlucky (dying to a random stone block trap early on for example), or both at the same, or neither. Just like life!
- Bang for your buck - If you end up liking this game, you will probably enjoy it for years - I estimate that I have played more than 1000 hours pre-steam
If you decide to buy the game: Don't totally spoil yourself reading guides beforehand - just go to places, explore them and read late-game guides only if you get stuck to some place. Trust me, you will enjoy the exploration more on your own.

Running over the course of History with a giant boulder
It has be admired that someone came up with a simple concept of pushing a bolder down a hill and making it into stragety game. In this terry gilliam inspired world you are sisyphus the once banished king of ephyra who was doomed to all eternity to push a boulder hill only to do that exact same thing for the rest of eternity. But one day ol'sisy got the idea to instead use that boulder to escape his prison and from there go on journey through history to challenge famous figures in history against there giant boulders. People such as Vlad the impaler, Napoleon, and... a goat, okay sure why not.
The whole game is about getting your boulder down the hill to smash against the enemy gate to literally crush the opposition into a fine pancake and move onto your next challenge. The courses are usually filled with normal obstacles like houses and people, traversing the enviroment for the fastest speed is the name of the game. But when you face off against your opponent they will set up more dangerous obstacles, such as defense towers, catapults, and elephants. All that will chip away at the layers of your rock decreasing its impact and sending it back to the top of the hill for a second go.
But while your jumping and cereaning, the enemy will use there own boulder against your fort. You learn by your enemy that you have to create obstacles to stop the enemy boulder. The key being to find spechific spot that will slow down the deadly or just halt it all together. Its an interesing air of stragety and travesel that isn't seen very often in tower defense games.
The boulder fantastically designed, its starts off slowly and requires a lot momentum to leave an impact in the enemy door. Those few seconds of falling off a cliff or being stunted by an elephant will cost you time and force to win the match. There are also varietes of the boulder, such as the spike boulder and the fire boulder, that will give you some extra fire power on getting past enemies. And getting past enemies is not that hard as the enemy boulder doesn't seem to know how to properly get around obstacles but a well time jump will get you over nearly anything.
There are also boss battle in this strangely enough. Where you have to just aim for the right spot and ram into the bosses weak point to win. There pretty interesting from a design aspect but the gameplay around them amount to little then waiting for the right moment to strike, not really implementing much in way of stragety.
Rock of ages is fascinating look into a tower defense game. It has funny visuals, responsive controls, and never really gets to hard in the way of gameplay. It may not be the longest game but if you have a passing interest in running over queen elizabeth, well this is the game for you... ya weirdo.

So you want to play a MOBA.  Well.  I enjoy this game, but there are so many flaws that I think it is damaging to my mental health.  There are a variety of gamemodes to choose from, though many are left unattended to with several issues.  I think a big part of this is having to few players for each game mode, and match making just can seem really poor trying to work around this.  The game really requires team coordination on higher levels, so solo queuers beware, as you will be matched up against team of 3 to 5 for a large chunk of the time.  The gameplay is some what smooth, though constantly changing with avoidable balance issues.  I really wish patches would be larger or more frequent, but there is no doubt with enough practice, a player can make any god preform well.  The games have varying paces so patience and awareness are needed, or the game will be incredibly frustrating.  The game requires a lot of time.

I am pleasantly surprised at how much I enjoy this game as I did not have really high expectations coming from Dota 2.  Smite is a really good mix of being easy to pick up for really casual or new players, while also being really difficult to master.  New content is constantly added to the game and patches are implimented every two weeks to help keep things fresh.  I would also say this game is really free-to-play friendly - There are a lot of microtransactions (as expected for a free-to-play game); however, most of this stuff is cosmetic and does not impact gameplay at all.  You can unlock characters at a really fast rate just by simply playing the game.  There are a lot of different game modes, which somewhat makes this unique amongst other games in the MOBA genre.
There are so many more positives things about this game, but I want to touch on a few negatives as well:
*  The servers are somewhat of a problem.  This has gotten better (for me personally, at least) over the last year, but there are still times where the servers will create in-game lag or the servers will be down.  I know Hi-Rez isn't some massive company like Valve or Blizzard, but more consistent server preformance would be greatly appreciated.
*  This complaint is more for veteran players than it would be for a newer player.  As I mentioned above, new patches are introduced every two weeks, yet the balance in this game is mediocre.  Newly introduced Gods are oftentimes over-powered at launch and it takes entirely too long to buff/nerf certain Gods that really need it.  Taking too long to buff/nerf Gods might seem strange because the game is patched so often, but because patches are so frequent it lessens the impact each one has.  Compare this to a game like Dota 2, that may have a massive game changing patch and not have another major patch for another three months.  In Smite, a character that is really strong and dominating the meta might get nerfed 3-4 consecutive patches.... each nerf being a minor nerf.  Now all 4 nerfs combined are strong, but that takes 8 weeks!... Just nerf or buff a God fully the first time and if adjustments need to be made, do so in the next patch.
*  This might be my biggest complaint about this game - No in-game voice chat.  There are third party chat services you can use:  Curse (actually integrated into the game's software), Discord, Team Speak, etc, but I don't like using any of that stuff.  It blows my mind that a game in a genre that is so team work focused does not have in-game voice chat.  Apparently this is the norm for some other games in this genre (Heroes of the Storm, for example), but I think the exclusion of voice chat really lacks foresight.  The main reason it is not in the game is because of toxicity, but this is poor reasoning.  This game NEEDS in-game voice chat and I am happy to report that it is getting it.  Back in January it was announced Smite will have in-game voice chat, we are now currently in August and still no word of it.  I have played this game for well over a year now and this is a feature that will greatly enhance the game.... whenever it comes.
Outside of those issues the game is really fun.  I would highly recommend trying it out.  Out of the 80+ Gods currently in the game, I am sure there are several you will immediately recognize and that also enhances the fun for a lot of people.

If you like to buy low and sell high. Then you like to play trading games like I do. I picked this game up after spending a few minutes with the demo. Since I have played close to 12 hours. The majority of that was playing the free trader. What I have found is the trade system is extremely weak. Once you spend a while in your starting system. As a free trader you start off in a fighter craft unable to warp out of said system. Profit comes slowly and the first warp ready corvette cost over 100 thousand credits. During this stage of the game profit per unit is anywhere from single digits to a 100 credits. However after you get a corvette and explore for a little while. You will find that certain systems produce Antimatter, Diamonds, and Super Ore. These systems are where you spend most of your time after wards. Buying those items and running to the closes invaded system. Where you can sell Antimatter for 1000 to 2000 profit per unit 600 or more for diamonds, and 150-200 profit for super ore. This allows for extremely easy progression and quite easily shows what this game lacks.
The main thing the game truly lacks is an assortment of ships. There are 4 classes fighters, corvettes, destroyers, and cruisers. Besides a few faction or class based starting, capital ships there are 2 or 3 options per level. With one per level with a decent cargo hold, as a trader I would have hope for more options. At the highest level ship you will have around a 2000 thousand unit cargo hold.
It isn't to small if all you do is trade. However as you level up you get the option of owning companies. Sadly it is utterly simplistic to my knowledge there is only two branches. Synthetics factories which can be upgraded to produce robotics then engines. This requires super ore and is the only other factory branch that I know of. Super ore factories can be upgraded to produce diamonds and antimatter. This branch of industries require robotics.
I would like to set up a production chain. Where I can produce super ore to ship to my robotic factories, then ship my robotics to an antimatter factory. There is no other way for you to ship your produced goods automatically. You are limited to automatic purchasing those required units in system or galaxy wide. This of course increases the cost of the factory. You can also automatically sell at a loss of 50 percent. You can of course ship the stuff to and from yourself. However this causes the final product antimatter to simply stock up while you resupply the other factories. After you stock them up enough to give you some time you will find you have already produced thousands of antimatter. Or in my case 10 thousand antimatter so as you can see a ship with cargo capacity of around 2k will make a killing with all that antimatter. However I have a stockpile of antimatter growing by the week. Once you tack on travel time to and from contested systems. Which can take months your stockpile has grown, and the robotics and super ore factories are in need of supervision. In the end it is just easier to automate the robotic and antimatter factories and closing the super ore one. They will operate making you a little profit unless the system is under attack. Where as if it had been flushed out and you could ship produced goods to and from systems automatically. And had access to capital sized freighters you could simply set around all day making billions.
So while the trading is fun it is short lived and the trader end game of companies is shallow at best. I would still consider this game worth the price of admission.

I very much want to like this game. It has everything I want - sandbox game-play, customizable spaceship, turn-based strategy, the ability to create your own empire and take over the universe, etc. It sets itself up as a sci-fi, turn-based version of Sid Meier's Pirates. Sadly, it falls short of all of these expectations.
Yes, you do get to customize your ship somewhat, and you can board/capture other ships so you can take on bigger and badder stuff (which equates to more loot). In practice, you find yourself breezing through the lower-tier ships and quickly gaining a cruiser (through capture or purchase). In order to hit the late-game content, you need a battleship, but you can only get one by successfully boarding one. Since you're outgunned and outmanned, it is a difficult process, and not a fun one.
Combat is already tedious (your guns miss more than half of the time, and most of your special abilities aren't available when you want them, so they're practically pointless). In order to board a ship, you need to drop their shields to less than 25% (not terribly hard, even against the Battleships), but then you also have to hit the enemy with an EMP (again, this seems like it hits  less than half the time), and THEN you have to successfully attempt to board. Both of these have to be in your skill lineup at the same time, and they both have to be successful. This means you could be sitting around for several turns getting pummeled, just in the hopes that you might be able to board. And then you have to hope that your crew is good enough to successfully overtake their ship - which is also far more random than you'd like.
So, you've successfully captured a Battleship so you can start taking over systems and winning wars? Now the real tedium begins. You really have very little control and spend all your time fighting the same enemy ships over and over again until the game decides you've done enough to tip the battle in your favor. (It seems your allies can't win wars without you.) So you move from system to system repeating the same process, (then back-tracking to formerly controlled systems that keep getting attacked or rebelling), until you've managed to grind away enough of your life and sanity and the game tells you that you've won the war.
When that happens, you feel a sense of relief that the game is finally over and you can stop playing.

In my opinion this is a more character-driven (and way less hectic) version of FTL and in some ways is very much the intergalactic version of Sid Meier's Pirates. For those who don't mind a turn-based and strategic/creative thought combat system I highly recommend this. Happy pirate-raiding along the trade lanes you rapscallion space dogs!

This is easily the best MMO I've played in years. The graphics are beautiful, the character creation is very in-depth, and it actually feels like you're involved in the combat instead of just sitting there tapping buttons until you fall asleep. The crafting system is unique and fun (albeit frustrating sometimes), too. If you get bored of questing, dungeoning, and crafting, you can go play games and race chocobos at the Golden Saucer, if you're so inclined. You'll never run out of things to do in this game.
And if you're a roleplayer like me, Balmung has a huge and varied roleplay community--you're more than likely to find what you're looking for, no matter what your RP style is.
The only thing I don't like about the game is the character creation restrictions. If a server is overpopulated, you can't make a new character on it, and have to wait until the populated is a bit lower, which is usually really early in the morning (if you're in America). This is a huge problem on Balmumg, which really stinks if you're looking for an RP server. Other than that, though, this game is great and totally worth the $15 a month.

I had to think hard about whether or not I wanted to recommend this game or not. Its one of those "two-and-a-half to three stars' moments.
Now I have to explain that I'm one of those people who were playing ADOM since early-days. I spent countless hours and spent dozens on dozens of characters to their eventual deaths. And that is something you have to get used to in this game. Your characters die. When they die, they're gone for good. Shiny gear. Nifty abilities. Everything. Gone. The only thing you'll have to remember them by is their entry on your personal high score board reminding you that your best character died on level 5 of some hole in the field because he/she died of the black plague because you ate a kobold corpse on the ground.
I'm resisting the urge to ramble on and on here. ADOM really is a good game! Its wonderfully complex yet simple in its premise. There is no real story involved. 'Go and fight Chaos'. They drop you on the world and wish you good luck. The overworld is always the same. And the dungeons you dive into are always random. But this time, instead of the ASCII characters representing yourself, enemies, and items on the ground, you have a nifty little graphical representation. And in the 'old' game, you had to memorize a LOT of hotkeys, as combinations of letters with alt/shift/ctrl were what you had to press to perform actions and bring up menus.
But that's the rub. The GUI (that's Graphical User Inferface), in my opinion, is about 75% of what you're buying here. Yes, there are a few different modes you can play in. Yes, you can now play by using the mouse and right-clicking to bring up a menu of things you can do instead of remembering its keystroke to make it more forgiving for newbies learning how to get around - though the game itself can still be brutal. But when you get down to brass tacks, you're buying cosmetics.
That's why I wavered on the tumbs up and tumbs down. I love ADOM. It's a relic from junior high through college for me. But are you willing to drop more than $10 for what adds up to little more than polish? I did, for the nostaliga. But it might be a touch stiff for others when they could have gotten the original ADOM for free in the past.
Pinacle of rogue gaming. Own at your peril! You've been warned.

My four brothers and I have been playing ADOM since about 2000. We have dedicated uncountable hours to this game, improving our talents/skill choices, learning which monsters are dangerous (nearly all of them in their own way, even as food!), how to not starve to death, how to infer properties of unidentified items, how to make your deity happy (very useful), to always eat ogre and blink dog corpses, and that you should never attempt any alchemy as an amateur no matter how innocent appearing (not even mixing water and carrot juice).
Yet not once have any of us beat the game. Some of us have gotten close a couple times, but no cigar.  Unlike the vast majority of all games, beating this game without scum saving is truly a respectable achievement and the journey itself will yield many super-intense close calls.
Despite the difficulty, we still play it and always come back to it. The ADOM world has so much depth, playing the game is really like exploring a new world.
ADOM is probably one of the best RPGs in existence. If you can look past the simple graphics and turn based play, this game will yield many, many hours of fun.
