This is a very detailed review of the game, it will discuss the different functions within it.
Crafting System:
There is a large crafting system in Reign of Kings, to unlock more recipes you have to upgrade certain stations.
Being King:
When your king you can set taxes for everyone to pay on the server. You have access to the best sword in the game and the kings crown.
Crest System:
The crest system is where you can conquer land for your guild. There are 3 types of crests(leather, iron and steel), each one conquers larger amounts of land, you can upgrade them.
Building system:
The building system is very flexible, you can create a variety of different structures with it. The building system uses blocks, but this is what makes it flexible as you can create huge structures. There are 9 different block types, cobblestone, reinforced wood iron and stone blocks cannot be broken by melee weapons, so I encourage you to use these blocks for your buildings. Do you want to create a small home to live in or a huge fortress? The choice is yours.
Siege:
To siege you need to gather lots of materials. You have to craft a siegeworks before any siege weapons can be crafted. Siege weapons include the Ballista and Trebuchet.
Capture:
You can capture other players with a rope or shackles. The rope can be broken out of by a sharp stone and the shackles with a lockpick. You can put captured players in cages or use torture devices on them.
Overall rating:
8.0/10

The Room is a puzzle game with a focus and atmosphere that is outright missing in most other similar games in the genre but would feel right at home in a creepy horror or possibly supernatural mystery game. The intricate designs and wonderful yet subtle music only adds to the gameplay where you, as the player, can immerse yourself in trying out various solutions, knocking on wooden panels, feeling brass filigreed overlays, and rotating slightly oily steel gears to figure out the puzzle boxes you encounter.
The additional gimmick of the Lens adds a very different, almost creepy, vibe where you are peering into another world, one not quite visible to the stunted human senses and needing aid to see what is really there. The overall game is somewhat short and ripe for expansion. The puzzles are lengthy and can be obscure but you're left with an accomplished feeling (turn off the hints!) and a genuine curiousity to see the wonders that are in the next Room. Thankfully there is little frustration for the patient and the solutions aren't unfair - just concealed.
Wholeheartedly recommended for any puzzler and for those who want a nice layer of spooky atmosphere to compliment it.

Initial Disclaimer:  I own both the mobile version (Plague Inc) and this version.  Most elements of this review apply to both versions.
Summary:  Plague Inc: Evolved and its mobile counterpart are both great games - when they want to cooperate.  Plague Inc: Evolved has a cleaner, easier to use interface and a few extra features on Plague Inc, but they're essentially the same game.  If you have one, you're not missing out on anything groundbreaking by not having the other.  The biggest problems with the game are its randomness and lack of strategy.
Details:  The game features a unique premise (wipe out all of humanity), functional graphics, and various addictive modes of play that keep me coming back time and time again.  Each plague you can use plays a little differently, though the basic strategy for success with all of them is basically the same.  My biggest complaint with the game is that later on, you get fewer and fewer bubbles to pop (other than cure bubbles), so if you didn't set yourself up properly from the very beginning, you are doomed to fail and all you can do is watch as you are eradicated.
The game's random element makes choosing a difficulty setting almost moot.  This can make the game incredibly frustrating when you play on Casual and just want a quick, easy game.  Infecting everyone on the planet works pretty smoothly, but once you've done that, the influx of DNA points usually slows to a crawl - you no longer get red bubbles because everyone is already infected (which makes sense), but curiously, you also rarely get orange bubbles, and when you do, they're frequently worth much less than they used to be (usually only 1 pt).  At the same time, costs for all changes skyrocket, making those hyper-infrequent 1 pt orange bubbles essentially worthless when you still need 22 pts to buy the next symptom or ability.  This can very quickly leaves you in a situation where you can see that you're losing (humanity is creating a cure faster than you can kill them), but can't do a single thing about it.  On the other hand, you might be given a huge influx of points during play that means that you can easily afford all the symptoms you need later on in the game, which makes the game easy.  It kind of sucks feeling that your fate is completely beholden to some random number generator within the game's code.
The game has multiple plague types, as I mentioned before, and they play a bit differently.  The virus, for example, mutates (develops symptoms) wildly.  On the other hand, the fungus doesn't spread across countries as quickly.  Despite the differences, there's really only one way to win - build up a couple abilities and transmissions while de-evolving any symptoms you get until you've infected everyone (making sure to stay undetected at the same time), then buy a whole bunch of lethal symptoms all at once.  If you're given enough DNA points through the course of the game to buy all the necessary lethal symptoms, you will win.  If you aren't, you will lose.  It's as simple as that.

And if you're a roleplayer like me, Balmung has a huge and varied roleplay community--you're more than likely to find what you're looking for, no matter what your RP style is.
The only thing I don't like about the game is the character creation restrictions. This game is made by Supergiant, the company that made Bastion. I expected similar quality with this game but it's not even close.
First of all, the naration is awful. Yes, it's the same voice actor but he doesn't do anywhere near as good a job as in Bastion. He delivers lines without any passion and just doesn't have the same charm. Plus, you can barely hear him because he is really quiet even on max volume.
In Bastion he explains what's going on, gives you the background information of the story, and tells the story gradually as you play it. It was really fun to learn about the lore and listen to him tell the story. And the best part was, you get to actually play the game while doing it. In this way there is a perfect blend of action and storytelling.
All of this is missing in Transistor. The narrator just makes a bunch of dumb general comments that barely have anything to do with what's going on. He doesn't give you any background information about the setting, explain the lore, or tell the story. You just wander around in a city, feeling confused without even the most basic context or narrative. I've played for several hours and have no clue what's going on. When you take away the story, really all you have is a bunch of combat. Which wouldn't be too bad by itself, except for the fact that the combat sucks.
The main problem is that the combat is not only WAY too hard, but also severely flawed. Your character is etremely weak and can die in about two seconds from enemy fire. You can mitigate this by using the turn feature. Basically, you can pause the game and issue orders to your character. When you unpause, she carries the orders out while all the other enemies are frozen. It's not as broken as it sounds. When your turn is over, every single one of your abilities is on cooldown until turn recharges, meaning that you can't use them. Which means you are defenseless after using your turn. So basically the game is use your turn so you can actually kill stuff, and then run away and try not to die for 5 seconds. This is a lot harder than it sounds and is also just boring to do.
In addition, when you kill an enemy a battery pops out. You have to run to it pick it up in 5 seconds or the enemy respawns with FULL HEALTH. On top of this, it's even shielded from damage and you have to damage the shield to be able to pick it up. When you use up your turn to kill an enemy, you oftentimes cannot break the shield on the battery because you can't attack yet, and so the enemy respawns with full health.
It wouldn't be so bad if there were actually a difficulty slider. Or like in Bastion, you can do challange areas to gain upgrades if you're having a hard time. Instead, the challenge rooms give music tracks as a reward. Seriously?
So essentially it's a game with no story and ridiculously hard/flawed gameplay.
I expected the soundtrack to be amazing like in Bastion, but again this game doesn't deliver. The soundtrack isn't very unique, it sounds like generic video game music. And you don't get to hear it anyway because the music turns off when using your turn feature. What a bummer.
Oh and this game doesn't have a start menu or anything. Literally, the most basic feature in video games is missing.
The only reedming feature could be the graphics I guess. The enviorments are absolutely beautiful, just like Bastion. However, a game needs to provide solid gameplay and a story and can't get by with just fancy visuals. That's why they're called "games". If you want good art, go to a museum or watch a movie.
There is also only about 5 hours of gameplay. It took me that long to beat it. But even then, the game time was artificially inflated because of difficulty. It would probably be like 3 or 4 hours if you are skilled at action games.
TL/DR: No story, bad narration, flawed/ridiculously hard gameplay, lack of features, poor soundtrack.

Tiny Barbarian is a game that some might rail against for being short, but for me, it's the whole package.  The music is glorious, the gameplay simple and addictive, and the pixel art graphics are very fun and surprisingly expressive, much like an early 80s arcade or NES game.  I backed this on kickstarter because I liked the original Tiny Barbarian and this game made me smile.  It's long enough to give you what you want, each episode being about an hour to an hour and a half, but not so long it over stays its welcome.  And I love the Conan the Barbarian parody going on here, which is very much underused in modern gaming.  I absolutely adore Tiny Barbarian and the creator is promising four episodes, none of which will cost after the initial purchase.  Two are out right now and they are a blast to play through.  I heartily recommend this game.

This is a good mix of challenging gameplay, classic platforming, well-scripted boss fights, and stands as a loving homage to the Barbaric bash-'em-ups of old. Only now as I type this has the second episode been released - it's been worth the wait, as I'm enjoying it so far and it flows on nicely from the challenges of the first. Some good humour mixed with fun chiptune-style music and pixellated graphics that actually look the part - nothing seems messy or out of place from a game that could have barely scraped through on a Master System. Controls are quite tight, though you might feel a bit cheated when Tiny doesn't grab a ledge while he's right next to it. Recommended if you like a decent challenge and cracking good value!
It's fun and all but wait till the all the episodes are out for it until then I cannot recommend it.

Somewhere in a desert wasteland, a tiny barbarian hangs crudely nailed to a tree. He contemplates the shifting of the sands, the hungry gleam in vultures' eyes, and the sweet brutal revenge he must take. Break free in as dramatic a way as possible! Your adventure begins!
Within 15 seconds of playing, you'll have savaged the local wildlife, defiled ancient ruins, and most likely♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off about a dozen evil warlocks just by being alive. A few steps later you'll already be discovering secrets as you bash through cracking rocks to uncover coins, gems, and... meat! Collect treasure for score, and replenish health by eating strange meats you find hidden in crevices, or even just laying on the ground! Fearsome barbarians eat whatever they want!
Battle wizards and their beastly minions! Punch rocks until they turn into diamonds! Hack away at vicious armored soldiers intent on slaying you and taking away your totally sweet loincloth! Discover wondrous and deadly ancient mechanisms! Tame ferocious beasts! Flex your guns and pecs indiscriminately! Dangle from chains 1-handed like a true badass! Handle explosives with little to no care whatsoever! Dodge snake-based traps, the most fiendish kind of traps known to man! Experience love, lust, and loss! Followed by triumph! Possibly followed by even more lust, the most important emotion!
All this excitement (And more! So much more!...eventually!) is packed into an experience just under 2 hours long, with 3 more adventures (episodes) to follow once they're finished and released by the developer. All future episodes will be available to you for free by buying this game (Episode 1), with the second coming very soon as of the time of this review (and I use the term "review" loosely!).
If you can't wait that long because you're an impatient prick or have Restless Gamer-Finger Syndrome, this game includes an endless Horde Mode that strands you atop of a pyramid and pits you against an endless army of goblins, skeleton archers, and trolls! (Or possibly very large hairy barbarians, I can't tell, but they bleed all the same!) You might rage at the constant potshots the archers take, I find myself losing most of my health to them, but YMMV.
Enemy variety is alright, we'll probably see different enemies in the upcoming episodes. I'm more annoyed that there aren't that many enemies hanging out in the main game's levels. However, the ones that are there are strategically placed for a challenge, and Horde Mode has all the mobbing you could want.
Enough combat moves are available to keep you alive, but face it, all you really need is that badass Elbow Drop! Snake getting grabby? Elbow Drop! Need to deflect a barrage of arrows? Elbow Drop! Vulture trying to eat you? ELBOW DROP IT OUT OF THE SKYYYY!!!
The other moves are your basic slash attack, a useful 3-hit combo that sends enemies flying, an overhead swing useful for crowd control and deflecting arrows, and a midair spinning attack that multihits (I find it hard to pull off, the timing is weird). Check the Steam Community Discussion page for more info on the attacks. The main game is easy enough to play through with just the basic attack and occasional 3-hit combo, the extra moves are more for Horde Mode survival.
What else, what else... oh right, buy this game! The music fits the bill, the levels are well designed so they aren't monotonous, secrets aren't terribly hard to find thanks to the level design "hinting" at them, boss fights are entertaining, there are nekkid ladies, and that's about it. It's a simple and fun game that I'm sure is far from simple and fun to make, so throw your money at the developer so he can crank out those other Episodes.

Knowing nothing about Starcraft or eSports (in its current form, at least), getting into this was still really easy. There was a slight bit of novelty starting out, but from there, everything about it was really intriguing and built in a way to keep you reading.
The story is written by someone who definitely sounds like they know what they're talking about, in terms of culture and gaming. This can result in it being a bit hard to grasp at times, but there's still a lot of genuine writing and emotion, and not just someone writing about video games because they think it's "cool" or "hip". The characters as well are written in a sincere way, not coming off as caricatures or stereotypes, but as actual human beings.  There's nuance and layering to them.
The way the story paces itself is also done in a smart manner. There's not too much dumping of exposition and action, yet you don't stall in the story for too long as well. It's a great way to get you accompanied with the setting, the characters, and the playing field as well. And, as an aside and small bonus, you can pick whether you play as a male or female protaganist, which doesn't change the story much (and if it does, it's not too noticeable).
Which is another good thing about this game! Occasionally, you get to play in some mock Starcraft 2 battles,  Rather than actually controlling the battles yourself, you're given action trees to decide which way the story goes and how the characters react. What help is that these options are rarely designed to make you super awesome or unbeatable; they're how a player who's in a bit too over their heads would think and react. The game and story, then, doesn't require you to be a hardcore fan of SC2 or eSports to really get it. You can start right out of the gate and still feel connected with everything.
There are a couple drawbacks though. The first one only really applies if you don't know much about the subject matter going in beforehand like I did. The dialog and jargon around the game can be confusing, and you'll likely not know what's going on because of it. The game tries to combat this by giving you a glossary when opening the menu, and updating it with terms bolded in-game whenever you encounter them. It still doesn't help too much though, as I had to google some of it in order to really pick up on it. The game tries to combat this by giving you a tutorial video accessible when you first start the game, or on the extras menu. It's voice-acted which... which makes it really cringeworthy at times. It got annoying enough to where I quit out of it early because I didn't think I'd make it through. And finally, while the game has some nice music at times, at others... it sounds too stock-music-esque and a touch unfitting to really sell itself.
Still, this doesn't detract from the game majorly. At heart, the story is a simple one; someone who wants to make the most of their talent and is willing to risk their finances and reputation to pursue it, even in a field where fame and longevity is uncertain. Make no mistake; though the game can be a bit silly at times, it doesn't treat its subject matter in a non-serious way, and that gives the game a much-needed breath of fresh air that most visual novels recently can't give you. Also, it's free and has low requirements, so any competent computer should be able to run it.

Having just completed this, I decided to pop a quick review on Steam just so anyone considering purchasing this can get a flavour of what to expect from the game.  As with all game reviews, please note that this is based on my own experience and is therefore subjective - I quite enjoy puzzle games, if you don't, you may not like this game.
You play as a silent protagonist, responding to a letter from a friend who has gone missing.  Their behaviour has been increasingly erratic and secretive and you fear for their well-being, so upon arrival at their home you start to search for them, a search which leads you to the attic room with a small puzzle box in the centre of it.
That's the basic set-up.  There is no exploration, everything takes place with a focus on the puzzle box as it is the key to finding out what has happened to your friend and it is entirely mouse controlled.   You manipulate different parts of the box using the mouse and this gradually unlocks to become something that is visually surprisingly impressive - graphically the game is no slouch, despite being able to run on a modest XP setup, when put on my AMD Black/720 graphics card set up and cranked up it looks superb.  Sharp, detailed and with wonderfful animations.
Sound is good, with a nice soundtrack, but I found it could be repetitive particularly when interspersed with sound-effects.  It does change slightly over the course of the game and the overall quality of music is high.  You do have the option to turn volume completely off and to window the game by altering the resolution using the options menu in-game or from the start menu, so you can stream music or video  whilst you play if the in-game sound isn't your thing (or there's something else you want to watch).
Now to the main problems of the game, and these are two-fold: the length of the game is short and the puzzles vary wildly in difficulty.  This is compounded further by some of them having slightly off controls or moments when an animation is repeated even though it isn't necessary.  Moments like this feel like they've been left in as a result of padding to help fill out a very short game (I've finished it twice in 5 hours) or are the result of poor programming decisions.  Later in the game some puzzles were understandly much more difficult but a few felt VERY easy and almost out of place in comparison to where I was in the game.  The difficulty curve affects the game length as you can whizz through the easier puzzles once you've got the mindset for it and are used to the games logic.
The promise of further installments in the series, either as sequels or as DLC are something that I am looking forward to and I fully recommend buying this if you are a fan of puzzle games.  If you want to test the water and are curious and a fan of a bit of Lovecraftian horror then you may also find a lot to like in this highly-polished, challenging but short entry to the puzzle genre.

I'm a huge fan of the Wild West genre, and for that reason, Call of Juarez is one of my favorite series of all time. The first two games (I will persistently ignore that a third one exists) were fantastic at recreating the atmosphere of the wild west, including the music, the environments (cities, small villages, and uncolonized wilderness), and most importantly, the action. The feel and speed of the guns felt authentic, and brought a lot of freshness to the FPS genre that it so frequently lacks. The first two games perfected the formula, and I was incredibly excited to hear Gunslinger's announcment.
It's really good. It's not quite the full package as the first COJ games, but because it's cheaper, it doesn't have to be. While the first games included lengthy campaigns and multiplayer, this one only includes a short (4 hr) campaign. But it's a ton of fun - the graphics, atmosphere, and sound of the untamed west not only return, but they've evolved with the technology of today. It's a gorgeous game, and the guns feel just as unique as they've always felt. Additionally, the campaign is made very fun and fresh with it's narrator-flashback theme: the entire game has you replaying memories of an old and kind of intoxicated narroator, and his inability to remember exact details or his constant exaggeration of certain events translates in a very hilarious and unique way into the game environment. You'll have to play the demo to get a taste of what I mean when I say it's a really fun twist on the tired "you're playing through flashbacks" cliche. It's a great game that's a must-have for anyone who enjoyed the first two COJ games, for anyone who enjoys the Wild West genre, and for anyone whose looking at a change-in-pace for FPS games.
Setbacks: Short Campaign, No Multiplayer, And the last hour of the game kind of overstayed its welcome, as the formula was getting a little old. Unlike the prior games, they've completely stripped any stealth and platforming mechanics, so there's a little less variety in the gameplay area. No puzzles, just shootouts in a variety of environments and situations (train robbery, indian ambushes, etc.). There's only 6 guns, which is a major setback from previous games and definitely contributes to the feeling of reptetiveness as the game progresses. It never completely overstayed its welcome, but it definitely got close as the game concluded at the 4 hour mark.
Final Rating: 7/10. Very much worth the money, but not revoluationary

This game has potential, clearly some effort has gone into it, but sadly it feels unfinished, unpolished and unloved.
Along similar lines to FTL (Faster Than Light) and SPAZ (Space Pirates And Zombies) with nods to classics such as Elite it's a good concept. Fly a spaceship around, trading, killing and / or completing missions to earn cash to buy better spaceships and equipment to complete harder tasks. You can start as a member of one of four factions and then choose a profession. Once your character is promoted (levels up) you can choose a skill to purchase which effects your options, (primarily in regards to combat). There are options to purchase pirate bases, take over areas of space etc... But at it's core it's just a couple of simple mechanics over and over again. If you havent played FTL or SPAZ and are considering buying this, then absolutely do NOT buy this, buy one of those instead, they are far more polished and feel like finished products. With all the typos, clunky UI design, jarring save system, lack of useful tooltips (which can sometimes be confusing to make sense of), Smugglers 5 quickly becomes a lesson in frustration. It's a shame, it has enough individuallity that it could have been a real hit, but for some reason it seems the developer abandoned it rather than give it the love it needed to succeed.

I'm a longtime MMO veteran. I have dumped countless hours into WoW, LOTRO, Warhammer, SWTOR, GW2, Allods, etc etc etc over the years.
FFXIV is hands-down the best MMO on the market atm and well worth every penny. The game starts off very slow with an ungodly boring story but really takes off around the early 40s. The game gets pretty good sized content updates every 2-3 months adding 3-4 hours of main storyline, 1-2 dungeons, a new raid, a new "primal" boss fight, new gear/crafting recipies and some other side quests/experimental content. There is plenty to do to keep you around for a long time.
Every single class (even the crafters and gatherers!) has a full storyline in addition to the main overall story. The crafting and gathering systems also have unique mechanics and go well beyond the standard "right click to gather" system seen in countless other MMOs. The game also grants you bonus XP for your lower leveled combat classes.
The community for the most part is very helpful and welcoming. It is not hard to find a guild or people to group with. However, if you wish, this game is also enjoyable and playable "solo" as any required group content can be completed via a group finder.
I would absolutely recommend FFXIV to any fan of traditional tab-target MMORPGs, 2005-2009 era WoW players, fans of Final Fantasy and really anyone just looking for a solid RPG experience.

In developement since 1994, and by reading over its history, I can say it has come a long way. This title can certainly hold its own right up  there with the best of modern games. Some may have you believe a single person (Thomas Biskup) built this, but as is stated in the credits, the end product is the result of thousands of peoples hard work and ideas.
Sure, there is a certain trade-off between user interface, graphics, and learning curve that pays out with a giant world with metric tons of gameplay and fun.
+Timeless game that has been shaped over 20 years, which is reflected by system complexity that goes unmatched in modern games.
+The ability to seemlessly (simply push F10) switch between classic ASCII and tiles.
+Tiles and music are beautifully done.
+Many modes that are all well recieved. In example, Crowd mode alters the difficulty of your game by how many Steam friends you have that play
. This is fresh and certainly encourages community.
+++Highscores leaderboards!
+++Ghosts of your fallen Steam friends show up in your game lol.
+Both keyboard and mouse support. I find the control scheme very intuitive. The updated user interface is very nice IMO.
+In-depth tutorial.
+Great community.
+Super active developement.
-Yeah there is a steep learning curve, but that only applies to people that are new to roguelikes. Get through it, or simply realize these types of games are not your cup of tea.
It amazes me how this classic has evolved over time and can still outcompete modern titles.

I *love* this game. I've been playing for almost 20 years and I'm still not bored of it. Massively recommended classic roguelike, now with prettified graphics and sound.
HOWEVER, you should be aware of a few things before you buy:
- Turn-based (Roguelike)
- Steep learning curve, including Permadeath (Roguelike)
- Tile graphics covering up an ASCII system (Roguelike)
- Somewhat archaic control system (but the best amongst the classic Roguelikes IMO, with decent inventory control)
- Awkward to play without a numpad - especially if you don't have an actual mouse. Not recommended for any but the biggest laptop keyboards.
- Just in case it wasn't really obvious, this is very much a thinking gamer's game. It has ZERO twitch.
And probably the worst point:
- Many new releases thusfar have included a fatal crash bug... although these are generally fixed in about 24 hours.
BUT...
If you're willing to persevere through this, you've got a game of almost unparalleled depth and enjoyment. SO much to learn, SO many different viable strategies, SO many different character builds, and SO much tension and excitement in a turn-based game.
TWENTY. YEARS.
Not bored.

I found it extremely difficult to get past the southern dungeon on my way past the map.
All dungeon maps are always rectangular in nature, vary very little; granted they seem to be using a random seed of some kind, but after 3-4 times it gets stale.  There are torches on the wall, other than that, there is no decor.  Character animations are limited and are only left face and right face.  Also when I equip certain equipment like the helm it is barely visible or not visible at all.
There is no soundtrack, the ambience sound is almost non-existent.  Occasionally I hear the drop of into a puddle in a dungeon.  Again, the atmosphere of the game feels incomplete.
There are TONS of games similar to this, Gauntlet $19.99 (when not on sale, 2015 game)
) is a popular game my friends play that has a multiplayer aspect, which this game does not have.  Also Hammerwatch $9.99 (not on sale) which does exist, unlike what the Dev has said and exists here on Steam:

I roll this toon, spec into two handed weapons, and I go into the trial dungeon, first door is locked, I can only kick it down, in the process of kicking the door down my huge club is broke, lol wtf ok.  So basically your skill that you used to get the 2hed item is worthless and now you have to punch guys.
Overall sound effects are stale, limited, and lackluster, and could be improved dramatically.
If you are going to bring back a game from 1995 update date, improve it a ton.  Check out Divinity Original Sin
, a game which was just enhanced w/ over 90+ hours of gameplay and fully AAA voiced acted.
Spell casters feel bulky and there is not hotkey menu like modern games have (again you are paying for a 1995 1st addition D&D type game).  I have to constantly hit he escape menu to break away from the immersion of the game to open a spellbook.  After some casting of the spells they are "forgotton" (no tutorial on this at all btw, to explain this to first time players of ADOM like myself), and I have to relearn them.  Which means you have to worry about carrying 100 stone tombs everywhere you go.  This is a problem if you play a gnome mage (which I tried out), and tried carrying around 5 tombs plus heavy rations.

Tiny Barbarian DX is hands down one of the best retro platformers you can grab your hands on right now. Everything about it is just fantastic, albiet an extremly short experience.
- Levels never feel unfair, and check points are frequent enought that you won't feel cheated by death.
- Jumping on platforms and slashing your sword feels tight. Chaining kills is satisfying as hell.
- Boss fights require you to be patient and figure out how to use their attack against them.
- The game's visuals are gorgeous, with multiple scrolling backgrounds with beautiful pixel art.
- Horde mode to keep you occpied if the campaign gets too rough
- AND ONE OF THE BEST CHIP TUNE SOUND TRACKS EVER TO HAVE GRACED VIDEO GAMES; THUMPIN ALONG AS YOU FIGHT YOUR WAY THROUGH THE GAME. SERIOUSLY JUST LISTEN TO IT:
- If you buy the game right now you only get 1 out of the 4 episdoes. The rest are included with the purchase but their release dates are all TBA.
- Some of the vehicle levels are a bit tedious cause your GIANT CAT controls a bit floaty. But I guess that's part of the challenge. It's not impossible though, just take your time.
- While the jumping is very responsive, grabbing on to ledges sometimes was hit and miss as i fell 1/4 of the time. This is a VERY MINOR complaint.
- AGAIN TOO DAMN SHORT. I NEED MY TINY BARBARIAN FIX YO.
Ultimately while not a complete experience (yet), this game is definately worth the price it's asking for admission. Episode 1 will take around 1-2 hours to beat, but you can replay it to get achievements and find secrets. You can also play the Horde mode to keep busy.
Tiny Barbarian DX episode 1: 9/10

Not a Starcraft player. Hell, my last serious RTS was Age of Empires 2, and that in of itself should normally make a specialized VN like this outside of my place to play, much less review. But hell, I gave it a try when it claimed I could make due without knowledge, and it did not lie. So if the only thing keeping you on the fence is whether you'll understand anything, relax. The game has a glossary, for crying out loud.
Where else to rank it... Well, I'll be as blunt as I can be. It's a free Renpy VN, after all.
Gameplay boils down to your typical faire of making choices at select points, as you might imagine. You can play as either a male or female lead, but it makes little difference. Still, props for the option even existing. My point is gameplay isn't the main focus here... Though I do hope to see innovation in anything going forward.
Visuals are smooth, nice, and right where they need to be. Likewise on the sound, everything from silky smooth tones to alt rock, everything blends pretty damn well in setting the scene right where it needs to be for the player. The game also shifts to something different just enough times to keep the player surprised without becoming expected, which I applaud.
Story and characters are compelling in their own way, too. Even without knowing squat about SC personalities, I was more than amused by the faces shown here. Even if half the fun was figuring out the archetypes early on, and watching how they'd be played out. Speaking of, game's clean. Save for a tame extra scene, there is no fanservice or anything of the sort, much less romance to worry about, so don't expect that. I will say I enjoyed what bonding scenes we did get, and caught myself questioning what relationships other characters had before I showed up... A mark of good narrative delivery in my eyes, considering I actually was interested.
Three things of note. First, no auto/skip functionality, so prepare to experience SC for yourself... When you feel like you need 300 APM just to get anywhere. (See? Wouldn't have known that before this game. Ahem.) This is swiftly dealt with by the second note, that the game is... Relatively easy to get the good ending on. It's no Sakura Spirit, there are numerous choices and -presumably- bad endings, but ah... I didn't get one. Yeah, somehow I got what could only be classified as a good/true ending on my first run, blind. No guides, just two google searches to find out what the hell Protoss even played like (and learning they were expensive as hell) and another to look up a term. All I did was play smart with basic logic from what the game showed me, and things played out flawlessly. So either I'm a natural SC2 player in the making, or the game's rather easy to complete unless you're a bonehead with this sort of thing. Third and finally, I was outright disappointed the ending I got, well... Ended so soon. It's a short game. But.
That is actually a good thing, I suppose. For as many minor (and they are minor) gripes as I have, they are tremendously outweighed by the positives the game provides. Hell, I'm listening to the credits song on repeat because it's just that good wrapping things up. The game's short, the game's small, but it's free and packed with personality and warmth. Let me put this in no uncertain terms, okay?
SC2VN is a short experience, but it's one I don't regret taking in the slightest, and actively want more of.

Starcraft II: Visual Novel is definitely an interesting tale of a game. I can say first and foremost that it achieves what it set out to do; inform people about just how rough the eSports scene can be. Before anyone get's scared by this game being too heavy about eSports or Starcraft, don't be. It has an excellent glossary to help you with terms being used. As well as a cute, voice acted intro by Day[9] (a popular Streamer & Starcraft II commentator.) On the other hand, if you're a big Starcraft eSports fan, then you'll instantly recognize some players & personalities which are homages to other popular figures from the eSports scene. As well as some call backs to old strategies that were once viable in the competitive scene. Unfortunately this game doesn't have any branching paths, and choice isn't too much of a factor with a very short story. Simply talking and listening to your team's advice can get you the "good" ending without having any real prior knowledge of Starcraft. This game is also built on Ren'Py so you can litterally run it on just about anything.
Pros:
* Solid Story
* Excellent Glossary for Terms
* Enjoyable and well written characters
* Great intro movie for players unfamiliar with Starcraft
Cons
* Very short, 2 hours at most.
* No Branching pathes (just success or fail states.)
Other Thoughts
* Not fully voice acted
* Gender choice available but not terribly relevant to the story.

Call of Juarez Gunslinger is a western themed FPS with a story-driven campaign and, arcade and dueling modes.  You take on the role of Silas Greaves a cowboy turned bounty hunter who must take on an assortment of robbers, thieves and legendery outlaws in order to track down and kill the gang responsible for murdering your brothers.
A deeply immersive story links together fourteen campaign levels, with high production value cutscenes, writing and voice-over dialogue.  Gameplay consists of running through linear but detailed levels, shooting enemies as they come into view inbetween hiding behind cover.  The higher your score the quicker your level rises, the faster skills can be chosen from three styles of gunslinger.  The more enemies killed, the more slow-mo time is generated, best used when outnumbered or outgunned.  Difficult duels that rely on focus and fast reflexes take place at the end of some levels, against one or two infamous outlaws.  Together with accuracy these same skills are needed for the arcade and dueling modes, with take out chunks of the campaign to replayed again but with a twist.
+ Amazingly written & voiced, authentic western story.
+ Superb graphic novel-style cutscenes and shaded in-game graphics.
+ Well-suited western/country style audio & soundtrack.
+ Good amount of varied locations and enemies.
+ Three skill trees: rifleman, pistolero and shotgunner; one for each style of play to specialize your gunplay.
+ Great use of shooting-based QTEs/slow-mo mechanic to help you during the hardest firefights.  The more you kill the more you can slow time.
+ Uplay 'not' required.
+ Not an easy game to beat on harder difficulties.
+ A few areas have gatling guns! :)
- Duels can be a very frustrating experience.  Until you get to grips with the mechanics.
- Arcade mode is essentially a rip-off of the levels from the campaign played like you would have an arcade game, a few decades ago.  Fun but a derivation of the campaign levels.
- 100% completion will require several playthroughs (two to three) and multiple sessions for arcade and dueling mode.
- Small and linear level design.
- Not an easy game to beat on harder difficulties.
* All modes are singleplayer only.  Good for some.  Not so for others.  Depends where your preferences lie.
* Nice use of flashbacks to retell story allows for some levels to be partly replayed in a different manner.
* Campaign of fourteen missions are fairly similar in terms of gameplay, even if locations are graphically varied.
* Heavy on spoken narration.  Can be skipped.  Mostly.
* Multiple playthroughs needed (at least 2 for some achievements.)  Good if you enjoy the game.  Not so much if you were only planning one playthrough.
* Basic enemy AI provides decent enemy behaviour which becomes predictable however.
* Enemy spawns are almost identical every-time you restart a section.
Call of Juarez Gunslinger is worthy of being called a AAA title.  Having beaten the campaign on Hard and True West difficulties from my point of view the game's campaign is excellent.  A good size, with a good amount of variation and layouts.  Indeed everything about the game is stylish.  Top draw.  With high production values, amazing story, colourful visuals and outstanding voice and audio.  Together these elements provide as good a western experience as you will discover on PC.  One I found to be highly immersive.  I particularly loved the wonderful soundrack.  So if you're a secret redneck/hillbilly like me, youll probably also enjoy it.
Gameplay is fast, fluid and well-paced and the clever use of storytelling, fairly varied level design [given their linearity] works well with the three distinct skill-trees and authetic era weapons.  While QTEs/slow-mo shooting mechanics are helpful to inexperienced players adding another dimension to gunplay, keep the experience interesting.  To the point that it should be an FPS that everyone plays.  At least once.
However its not all plain sailing.  Ive found it difficult to put a finger on why exactly so many gamers give up on this game. I did the first time I tried it.  I imagine that some players just  lose interest in playing. Maybe it is the linear nature of levels, the low technology level of weapons, the dated setting, or just the nature of gunplay.  Im not sure but there is something here that stops some gamers from getting the most out of this gem.
I guess some players may just feel that the true nature of gameplay is slow and plodding.  Maybe despite the initial easy learning curve, players find the difficulty ramps too fast.  If players don't get used to the game's slow-mo mechanics, learn when to make good use of cover, then they will die alot and frequently.  And then there are the Hard and True West difficulties which will really need an investment of time and practice.  The hardest levels require maxed out skills, good knowledge of the map and gameplay mechanics but above all else, fast and accurate reflexes.  Duels against known outlaws can also be a frustrating experience. Until the mechanics are understood.  Even with tutorials this is not a trivial thing and will take alot of repeated tries until the whole dynamic suddenly clicks.
The Arcade and Duel modes are good enough to be tried at least a few times.  Yet looking at my friends list most give up after playing a few levels.  The arcade mode is essentially a rip-off of the levels from the campaign with the aim to get the the highest kill chain possible without missing one.  These also have a separate smaller skill-tree for each gun-slinging style, so if you don't like repeated play to level up again then you wont like this mode.  Duel mode comprises of fifteen stand-offs between the player and bosses from the campaign.  Where the ultimate goal is to beat every one without drawing first - easier said than done.  A word on achievements.  The game possesses more difficult than easy ones. Definitely one of the harder games to complete.  So if you're planning to complete the game I would suggest you know what you're in for.
Despite these negatives I would whole-heartly recommend the game to gamers who are after an FPS with a western ambience.  For what it is, its excellent.  Just be aware that you and this game just may not click, which would be a shame and a waste if you do happen to get it.  If you're still unsure then wait for a hefty sale and get it then.  However if you have the tenacity, patience and reflexes to get the most out of this game, I dare say you will not regret it one bit.

A fun little time waster. My biggest problem with Clicker Heroes was that it took
to get to Dread Knights than everything that came before them. I felt the curve there was unfair. I also didn't like how you had to choose between Ancients, and if you happened to get four you didn't want to choose from, then tough luck. Gilding heroes in Clicker Heroes is also random - it's possible to get a useless hero upgraded, and then you have to expend resources to fix it.
Tap Tap Infinity is very similar to Clicker Heroes, except it fixes those aspects of the game. There are 21 heroes to hire and upgrade, and they're all available very quickly. There are 4 Guardians with 4 skills each, and you always have access to all of them as long as you have enough infinity tokens to pay for the next level. There's even some semblance of a plot, to explain why the level design loops every 100 levels, and why the heroes are willing to fight for you. You can also upgrade your spells, which I don't remember whether you could in Clicker Heroes - I got too frustrated with the progression curve in that game to keep up with it. And when it comes to upgrading your heroes, you get to choose which ones to upgrade when.
Basically, this game is Clicker Heroes but trimmed down to exclude some of the fat, and improve on some of the weak points. It's streamlined. And it has 3d graphics. If you're looking for an idle game to pop in on when you have some time to kill, this is a good option.

It’s been a pretty solid year for side scrollers on the PC front this year so far; we’ve seen Dust, Ducktales HD, D&D Chronicles, Volgarr… it’s just been a good year!  And yet in comes Tiny Barbarian DX like it ain’t no thing.  While I can’t promise you will like Tiny Barbarian DX more than the other games that’ve come out this year, I can tell you I had a blast, and continue to have a blast.  This is the good news.
The bad news is it’s not finished.  Not yet.  You can buy this on Steam for ten dollars, but a lot of people will get miffed when they “finish” the game in a bit over an hour for their first run-through and say “That’s it?” because at current count, the game is missing three more chapters.  If you want the rest of the game, you have to wait.  It’s being released on a “when it’s done” basis.  Updates will be pushed out through Steam when available (and the main man has already published a patch that fixed an issue with leader boards), but until then, you’re stuck with what you’ve got, which includes an hour-ish long Episode 1 and an Endless Horde minigame.
With that out of the way, let’s take a look at the game itself.  The graphics are simplistic and stylized; too many colors to be a Nintendo game, but it’s definitely got a retro feel to it.  It runs at about sixty frames per second, and animation is fluid. The textures used for bricks tend to get old pretty fast (whereas, for instance, I didn’t really get that feeling when I was playing Fez), but enemy and character presentation is definitely solid.  Background details range from okay to “Oh, there were background details?”  You’ll find often you’re too busy focusing on the action to pay attention to the little stuff.
Which is pretty telling about the game.  The controls are a snap, and responsive.  I was able to play with both keyboard and 360 Wireless game pad flawlessly.  One button jumps, the other attacks.  Holding up near a ledge will boost you up.  You stop pressing a direction, he stops moving.  Once you learn how your attack combos manipulate your movement speed when jumping, you’ll know when to stop and when to go… when to press an attack and when to hang back a second and wait for another time frame.  That’s good, because this game can get somewhat demanding as far as game mechanic mastery is concerned.  Timing on spell returns is fairly precise, and progressing through waves of enemies means you need to be paying attention with both hands on the controller unless you want to faceplant into the spikes below.  Luckily, even this isn’t an instant death.  The game is very forgiving, and has many checkpoints in each stage, and dying resets your health to full.  There are no lives; you play until you win, or quit.  I’ve done both.
You play as the titular Tiny Barbarian, and you progress through five stages, defeating enemies and boss encounters in order to beat up a mage, save a girl and escape her prison.  No writing awards here; just tried-and-tired damsel-in-distress male power fantasy sexist piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥patch job.  As this game borrows heavily from themes presented by the likes of Conan the Barbarian and Korgoth, I wouldn’t have it any other way.  It’s supposed to be a romp through better times where you didn’t need a “why”, you just needed a direction (right) and a weapon to kill things with.  It works just fine.  Sometimes I did find combos not executing as planned (two short swings followed by a short swing instead of the three-hit combo) but I just chalked that up to personal fail.  It didn’t happen often enough to care.
The music, as I have masturbated over in the past frequently, is fantastic.  I think I like it better out of context, but there are a few spots in the game where it matches up very well with the action.  Jeff Ball did very good work here.  Can’t wait to hear what the next chapters sound like, assuming he stays on board for them.  My ONLY complaint with the soundtrack is a half-compliment; this game has a theme which can be heard in several tracks.  It adds a continuity rarely ever heard in games these days, but at the same time it can become grating during your eighteenth death in the same stage.  The songs that depart from the thematic progression tend to stand out more impressively in the end.
So I guess whether you buy this game is a matter of taste.  Clocking in at about an hour, this game can be speed-run at under thirty minutes.  That would take several playthroughs, but it’s possible.  Most of the play time in this game comes from the achievements, and leader board progression, which if you’re playing this game offline won’t matter very much at all.  Is an hour something you would pay ten dollars for?
When I compare it to my Turtles in Time purchase back in the day ($60 for 25 minutes), it doesn’t seem bad at all.  The achievements are compelling, the game is challenging and was clearly designed with multiple playthroughs in mind, as there are plenty of hidden items and stashes you won’t find all of even on your third run-through.  At the end of the game, you are scored based on completion time, deaths and hidden gems found, so for once the scores in a game *aren’t* completely arbitrary if you enjoy seeing your name up on the leader board.
It’s an hour game, with at least three chapters being worked on in the future.  And it’s fun.  And the music is great.  I have no problems recommending this to someone who still enjoys some Nintendo time and doesn’t mind a challenge.  Tiny Barbarian DX is worthy, and it’s incomplete.

Initially I liked this game quite a bit. I'm a sucker for space exploration games and I really like building up my ship as I progressed through the game. The interface is a bit of a mess however. Some buttons launch in game popups like you'd expect while others launch sperarate executables which overlay your game. It looks like they set out making a browser game, but at some point decided to do something different.
I had quite a bit of fun early on in the game, but it didn't take long until I ran into a staggering lack of content. The big ships they talk about in the menus are actually not in the game. Carriers and other large ships which the game says you need to have your own fleet can't be bought as far as I can tell. So you get to a point where you can't really progress any further.
The starmap is very limited. I don't see why there couldn't be many, many more star systems and different types of planets. The amount of weapons and ship upgrades are also very limited and are mostly the same across all ships. There is virtually no point in trading past the first hour or so of the game. The combat system is ok, but gets extremely repetitive. There doesn't seem to be an endgame of any kind. There are even menu items not in use and place holder text which calls this an early access game. I could go on, but the point should be clear.
What makes it even worse is that as you try to close the game the developer advertises an expansion for the game which can only be bought through their website. Which apparantly is a standalone game with a lot of the missing features this game looks like it was supposed to have. They even have additional DLC on top of that thing. I looked at their website and if you try to buy the game they add on all the previous games in the series without asking, try to push DLC and have some sort of "download premium" service which lets you download the game whenever you want for extra cash. These are practices I thought we had put behind us years ago.
To sum it up: Stay away from this one. It is an unfinished buggy mess and not the latest version of this game. The developer are using some rather dishonest tactics to push this game on you despite it being an inferor version of a probably equally buggy mess.

This is the first MMO that I've played, since I started playing World of Warcraft back in 2006, that I will play instead of WoW. As of this review, my highest character is 36, so I have not reached end game as of yet. I do own the Heavensward expansion, and both collector's editions.
Let me begin by saying that, as a wee lad, one of my first loves was the original Final Fantasy for the 8-bit NES. My younger brother hated me because, well, there was only one save per cartridge, so he didn't get to play. Sorry, bro. If I was a better big brother I would have let you play instead... but I wasn't. Anyways, back to the review.
The job system is amazing -- who needs alts when you can do so much with only one character! The graphics are beautiful, character models are jaw-droppingly gorgeous, monsters are creatively done and true to the series, the sound is wonderful, the questing is ... well it's questing. Dungeons are straight forward (so far) and interesting enough. Combat is more than spam action buttons; you have to watch your environment and not stand in mob attacks (a glowing area will appear on the ground where an attack is about to land). Active help in game tells you everything you need to know about whatever it is that you're doing. You can choose to play with a gamepad or using keyboard/mouse.
The interface layout is customizable, and very easy to set up. Getting my graphics to a good place took a bit of tweaking, and there is no mouseover-help for what the graphics settings do, so some 3rd party web site reading was necessary in order to optimize my graphics. And that only took a little bit of effort.
I think the only thing I do not like is that you need to play through the story line quests in order to unlock things, such as riding mounts and the market (auction house), so the concept of leveling in dungeons may not apply here. Oh, and if you're an altoholic like me, it is IMPOSSIBLE to mail items between your characters; they need to quest long enough to unlock the market, and then you can buy/sell items from/to them, so yeah that sucks.
Most importantly, there are no "Horde vs Alliance" factions in the game; in my experience so far, players are actually friendly and help each other out. I have yet to sense any sort of hostility from anyone in any way. Random groups in dungeons weren't elitist jerks, and people helped out. I've only tanked dungeons (rolled a gladiator to start) and I've caused a wipe or two by over-pulling or not noticing a patrol, and there was never name calling or griefing or cursing or anything negative. People just res'd and started over, and offered actual constructive advice.
TL;DR:
Pros:
* beautiful graphics, lovely sound, some voice acting
* interesting storyline with some memorable characters
* in-game help welcomes MMO nubs and pros alike
* combat and questing move quickly enough so it doesn't feel like a grind
* repeatable FATES and Levemetes (stuff happens in the environment periodically, or you can choose stuff to do)
* crafting and gathering play as their own class; you are not a lancer going fishing, you change to a fisher
* (in my experience) friendly and welcoming community
Cons:
* must play through story line to unlock key things, such as mounts, market, retainers (think bank space), etc.
* storyline is only worth reading once; if you do play an alt you will break your mouse button trying to skip dialogs
* it is a subscription game, so a monthly fee is required
That's all, thanks for reading! If you're on the fence, download the demo, though I read somewhere (I could be wrong) that if you buy the game, you need to reinstall (the demo does not become the full game if purchased).

This game is all about style, but that's not to say there's no substance. The story line unfolds bit by bit, giving you a slowburn view into the life of the main character Red, and her home Cloudbank. Most of the plot is told by the narration of Transistor, the USB like weapon that you weild throughout the game and unlocked by using your Funtion() abilities during combat. The narration gives depth to an otherwise fairly straightforward storyline, as you feel the lamenting of Transistor as you learn more about his fate. This gradual unlocking, however, can mean that there are certain things which are not 100% clear, and there are a lot of unanswered questions, but this I think plays into the games styling.
Gameplay wise the Turn() system for the fight mechanics are easy to use, but as you can combine your abilities into combos there is enough that you won't get bored easily as you try to find the optimum strategy. For me however, this was a game about style and storyline, not gameplay.
All in all, a brilliant game that will stay with you long after you play it. Buying the soundtrack only with it is a must.

Hah. How to review ADOM? Well, it's one of the Great Few, an actual roguelike (not roguelikelike or light or anything) that helped define the genre. ADOM's strongest points are a mix of a persistent plot with procedurally generated elements, and a much deeper lore than its kin.
Once again the ultimate evil raises its ugly head and only a single hero can defeat it because fate says so. That hero is you. Or, will be you. Eventually you will defeat evil. But before that, you will die. A lot. And then again, and then some more. And you'll probably love every single death because you learned something, or had the chance to try out a new trick, or just had a brief moment of clarity how something COULD be done, only you didn't do it.
ADOM "Steam" is a pretty huge package. While the original game can be played for free, this version comes with a nice set of "deluxe" options and, seriously, this is a game that has been around for ages. I played it for ages. I think it's fair that at some point someone gets a bit of my money for the entertainment I had, because this is a game made for old dogs like me. A perfect throwback to my teen years, not pimped out until it's no longer the game I learned to love but with a nice, sensible lick of paint and a sleek interface. And I can still have it all in ASCII if I want.
There's just no way not to recommend this game.
If you already know it, you want to buy it for the same reasons I did: For nostalgia, for running the dungeons again, for feeling the thrill of a fight where each move matters, for smiling at the fact that your Steam Playtime can never, ever, match the hours you already sunk into this monster.
If you never heard of ADOM, you want to try it out because it is a nicely structured, engrossing game that polishes some concepts of the genre to a silky sheen. You'll appreciate the interface, which is readable but doesn't get in your way, you'll start out small and then you'll be hooked.
All this said, it's still a roguelike. As in, one of the games that took care we HAVE roguelikes. There are many things here that are part of the genre but not to everyone's taste- a fairly rocky early game, permadeath, TONS of ways to die yeat another stupid death, and an omnipresent element of randomness that can, and will, screw you up big time at least once per run. ADOM doesn't pull any punches and you need to be aware of that, this is not a recent rogue-light, this is bedrock. If you are just curious what the craze is all about, you may want to try the free version, just to see how it sits with you.
Because like most old roguelikes, ADOM is a game that rewards patience, planning, developing strategies and preparing for the worst- while still allowing players to improvise and come out of a tight spot with some sweet experience and a new trick in their book.
15 Euros can buy you more recent, visually impressive, or (to be honest) more streamlined games after all, but ADOM takes time to master, and beating it once is nothing, considering the endless replayability the genre itself has to offer.
Happy dungeon-dwelling, spell-singing and corpse-cursing!

I've been waiting years for a way to pay the author for creating ADOM, which I view as the finest procedurally driven RPG ever created.
ADOM is a game in the tradition of rogue, hack, and nethack. To describe it as "hard" would be both true and misleading: It's actually very easy to play and very easy to make a lot of progress, but actually winning is a delicate and unlikely affair. Dying is practically inevitable and although in the "Deluxe" version it's possible to turn off perma-death it's certainly not in the spirit of the game to do so. I can't even begin to enumerate the number of games I've played but I've saved well over a hundred memorials to "notable" dead characters on this computer alone. I have only approached the approximate half-way point twice, I have never come close to winning... and still I play, because what keeps me coming back is the variety and the challenge.
This is not a game you will win in a weekend, or a month, or a year, but you will enjoy every session (right up to the moment you die). I encourage you, dear reader, to cough up the meager sum that is asked here for this gem and immerse yourself in a wonderful game in which the developer has truly Thought Of Everything. If mud splashes on your face it blinds you until you wipe it away. If it's dark or you're illiterate you can't read books or scrolls; if you're deaf you can't hear what NPCs say to you, but the wail of a banshee will also not affect you. Sometimes kicking things breaks them, sometimes it just hurts your leg. You can eat the raw corpse of a hurthling but it will taste better and sustain you longer if you cook it first.  The texture and depth is incredible and, thanks to randomly generated elements, your choice of race, class and winning strategy it's never quite the same twice.
For new players I recommend three things: Patience, determination, and to avoid standing directly in front of doors when opening them. Your reward: endless fun.

is a casual idle/clicker game, very similar to a certain other Steam game,
(CH). Now why would a gamer like me with several thousand games (some of which might actually be good) waste time to play this? For achievements of course.
Now that my lousy motivation is out of the way, let's get dirty with the details. Being a clicker game the gameplay itself isn't very complex. A monster appears on the screen. Clicking it will damage it. Once it gets enough damage it dies and bleeds gold, with which you can buy upgrades and train your heroes to be able to beat higher, more difficult monster waves.
becomes distinct from other similar games by having a story. It's very basic though. Some monsters have appeared and the world is in danger, so you have to beat them up. A catch is that beating monsters will "bring them to their senses" and then you can hire them to fight for you.
It's also 3D: what a time to be alive, huh? Models are fine but not exceptional. Some of them looks rather ridiculous but that's likely a personal preference and you really shouldn't make fun of stupid-looking monsters because that might hurt their feelings.
I disliked the sound effects that I found to be too sharp and having too many high notes. Music is fun though, but since its loop is not terribly long, I found myself muting the game 99% of the time.
Typically in clicker games there's a restart mechanism. This one is no exception: after a while you can go
You'll be doing that a lot, since it gives you Infinity tokens that are used to buy permanent upgrades to e.g. gold farming and damage your heroes and clicks make. They also grant a fixed bonus to your DPS (damage per second).
But wait, there's more! Killing monsters and beating waves grants you experience, that increases your rank that directly affects all damage you make and also unlocks active skills.
Skills are a bit different from other clicker games on Steam, which is fun.
is probably the best of them, allowing you to skip through several hundreds of waves by only killing boss monsters (usually every 5 waves). Since there is no skill to increase the DPS over a single run (no equivalent of
from CH), deep runs are less useful (which is good: I find them boring). But grind is real, so you can also upgrade the skills with Infinity tokens.
Finally, Infinity tokens can be used to
, which resets the rank. Ascension roughly doubles the DPS in the long run.
Your heroes also get kind of experience tokens (i.e. Valor tokens), which are used with the in-game currency, gems, to upgrade the heroes.
The grind, while not infinite, is still great if you are going for all the achievements.
Fortunately one can play
in many ways. Both casual playing of couple of minutes and long sessions are supported. Once you close the game it will progress through the waves until it reaches a spot where it no longer can beat the boss wave.
You can in effect return once in a while to use the skill combos. Still, it's slightly faster to proceed and you can get farther into the waves when playing actively, since click damage outdoes the idle damage. You could even play hybrid, only succumbing to clicking when it becomes too slow to progress by idling.
Game is generous with idling: you could click one moment and after just a few seconds the idle mode starts again, and of the skills only Clickstorm (which grants a constant, frantic clicking of monsters) breaks the idle mode.
Conveniently, there's a direct link to Wiki from the game so the optimizing players find their thing easily.
Finally, while the game doesn't have Steam cloud saves, it does support cloud saving through their own servers. I suppose this makes it compatible with the mobile version as well (also hence the name has
instead of
).
For myself it took over 9 months to beat the game achievement-wise, recorded as 350 hours on Steam. I could still struggle to reach the final wave 5000 but I'm good, thank you very much.
A paying player could probably cut a few tens or hundreds of hours out of that, since one of the achievements directly depends on the in-game purchasable gems. Thankfully, even a non-paying player can grind them out and even succeed before doing the last of the super-grindy ascension cheevos.
It's not a terribly good game, but it's not bad either. I would recommend
for a busy person who doesn't have that much time for gaming but who also likes to hunt achievements. It's also nice to play a few minutes between more occupying games since it doesn't require too much dedication.

The game is playable and has some interesting freedoms. for example regardless of your chosen class you can become pretty much completely different type of character. sorcerer-tank anyone? But I have few criticisms for sure.
Irritants resulting in possible brain damage and loss of IQ:
1. The world (nature+architecture) is bland and boring. Art direction is quite non-existent.  Someone mentioned it was due to 3D engine used but nonetheless game of its magnitude should find ways around obstacles.
2. The crafting stations and the whole process is slow unintuitive and underwhelming to say the least. Half built town with crappy tables where everyone is standing in rain and mud 24/7. Nothing makes sense on its own, you need good few hours of reading before you start playing a game. Bank is like a shed with one chest where everyone keeps their entire loot...talk about lack of imagination
3. User Interface and Experience for questing is horrible! The markers chosen for quests identifiers on a map are absolute garbage from UX designer standpoint. Tracking quests is like a quest on it's own. you'll spend half of your attention figuring out what quest you're on and what to do next. Feels like research every time. Quest progression or completion has no visual feedback whatsoever, you have to manually check quest window to figure out if quest is done. Witcher 3 is the prime example of how to do quests right and how to mark them and give completion feedback without being another wow clone.
4. Spell casting visuals feels like I'm using discount spells. Nothing visually compelling.
5. If nobody is helping you as a beginner, you WILL struggle like hell just to figure out simple stuff.
Why I'm recommending this game ?
1. Chill factor, you can be a lizard or lion or panther or a hot chick or muscly Nord with giant axe. Run around at your pace.
2. Mobs scale down to individual players, meaning you can party with hi level and mob will be scaled to you personally.
3. Variety of spells and skills is great. You can be anyone. you can tank as sorcerer and heal as tank.
4. You can port to your guild and or party member anywhere on map.
5. you can be an outlaw attacking guards or friendly target in towns.
So quality of life 5/10

As a female player I feel this game isn't very female-friendly. The female characters are plain ugly, manly, with manly animations(the male chars are ok). The female armor isn't feminine either... I have crowns in my pocket but there's very little in the crown store that looks appealing and I already own it. Fighting, crafting, exploring all these are fun, but I think many women like beauty too. At least I do. That doesn't mean I'm asking for metal bikinis or princess dresses, don't get me wrong. But I find myself looking around at other players and I can't tell the gender of their characters under that armor. The manly animations don't help either. Having a gentle mage in cloth robe, with a flower in her hair run like a primitive brute chasing a mammoth...
That being said, the game is fun and it got me quite addicted. You will get frustrated when you see that exploring isn't encouraged, but forced! You have to travel on foot, or horse from one point to another, until you unlock teleport shrines. Your horse is very slow(you run faster than your horse) and it takes REAL TIME months to train it to be faster. Not even mention 385388 mobs that will aggro on you from miles away and slow down your travels, it gets annoying pretty quickly. You'll also encounter MANY rocks and mountains you have to go around because there's no way to climb them, that will slow down your traveling speed even more, so you need a lot of patience and time.
The world is beautiful! You have day and night, weather, and zones with different climate/seasons so if you like exploring, this game is for you! Not even mention you'll find mats for crafting, treasures, secret places, secret tombs, solo dungeons, public dungeons, cool mobs, and very interesting quests in your travels.
The lore is very rich and the quests are amazing. I found myself laughing and even crying(some have very sad stories) while doing these quests, they have depth and are very entertaining. Also love seeing my impact into the world; completing quests in certain areas will change the world for you, making hostile mobs neutral, happy villagers, extinguished fires, and even more but I don't want to spoil it.
Another strong point is that this game has nothing gender/race locked, you can be any combo of gender, race and class you want. And that's really cool.

"Tiny Barbarian DX" is just a good old-fashioned platform jumping beat-em-up, extremely (and deliberately) reminiscent of old classics of the genre like Castlevania or the original Prince of Persia, with deceptively simple but painstakingly polished gameplay and presentation. The controls consist of four directions, jump and attack; the only power-up is health. The graphics are pixelated, the sound effects minimal and the music pure chiptunes. The difficulty is unforgiving.
AND THERE IS NOTHING WRONG WITH THAT.
(Fair warning, there are also Goshdarn Bats. Endless streams of them, flying on those predictable yet somehow UTTERLY DECEPTIVE sine curve paths any old school gamer knows and HATES HATES HATES WE HATE THEM KILL THEM AAAAAAAALLLLLLLL!!!!!!!!!! Ahem.)
It does get frustratingly hard at points - the bats, OMG THE BATS!!! - but the challenge is always a genuine matter of skill rather than the game just being a jerk, always beatable with a little more practice and becoming just a little more badass than before. Personally, I find myself getting stuck quite regularly but every time I take a break and come back I seem to get another checkpoint further. That's real old school game design, right there. It builds character!
Thank Crom for unlimited continues.
Now, it may be that you don't care for old fashioned platforming goodness. In which case screw you, I just elbow dropped an eagle!

Tiny Barbarian DX is a 2D action-platformer that was recently greenlit on Steam. You control the Conan-esque main character in his quest to…save a princess, I think? Hang on and let me back things up for a minute, this game just finished kicking my♥♥♥♥♥and I need a minute to regroup my thoughts.
Tiny Barbarian DX doesn’t mess around. This is a retro style game, and it’s “NES hard”. Many games currently give you a “death count” while playing or upon completion (Angry Vdeo Game Nerd Adventures, Rogue Legacy, and Stealth ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Deluxe are three fine examples), and I died 35 times in the hour and 15 minutes it took me to get through the first chapter. Some of these deaths can be really frustrating and unfair, but luckily the game has auto-checkpoints every few screens. This isn’t “I Wanna Be the Guy”-tough, but it’s still pretty difficult.
When you begin the game, there are no tutorials whatsoever. Unlike a game like “They Bleed Pixels” which has a fairly robust tutorial system, Tiny Barbarian DX throws you to the wolves. You know you can attack and jump, and pressing them in combinations with each other and with the D-pad does stuff, but…I still can’t figure out how I did a jumping spin attack. To be honest, the first time I started playing, I didn’t even know the game had started yet. Before you even get a title screen, you’re thrust into the action. A group of baddies are climbing up a mountain, all the while the camera is scrolling up to show you standing at its peak.
PROTIP: This is where you start taking control.
You’re now in a king of the hill type showdown, facing off against a never-ending horde of increasingly difficult opponents. After you’re eventually defeated (or if you just jump off the mountain), the game will begin proper. You have a choice between “Adventure Mode” (the main game), or “vs. the Horde” (essentially the same as the intro). Going into Adventure Mode you’ll notice that there are 4 chapters, although only the first one, “The Serpent Lord”, is available to play. The other three are not attained by unlocking them. They are still currently being worked on, and will be free upon completion for anyone who already bought the game.
The music is chiptune-tastic. When you get frustrated by all the constant death, the music is there to keep you pumped and ready for action. A good example of this is my favorite track, “Rebirth”, which plays while you’re ascending a tower in a rudimentary elevator. I probably died in this section more than any other (the Serpent Lord battle being a close second), and it wasn’t so I could keep listening to the music. The soundtrack is available on Bandcamp, and is definitely worth a listen.
If you want a fun, challenging game that’s low on story to the point of forgettable, high on action, and makes you feel like a badass for being able to get through it, check out Tiny Barbarian DX. And when you have gotten through it, just know that there are 3 more chapters to challenge you at some point in the future.
