I have to say, this is one of my favorite premises for a visual novel ever.
I wasn't really into starcraft personally; I've played for a bit and I know the basics, but my RTS of choice was always Company of Heroes. As great as it is, is too beholden to an attempt to maintain historical accuracy to become an esport. But, I love the esports community; I'm engrossed specificlly in the Smash circuit, doing locals and following the exploits of legends like Mango, Hungrybox, and Mew2King. In those regards, I can easily relate to the culture of the scenerio, while also exposing differences in how certain comptitive circuits.
For a free game, this is actully pretty damn good. I love the art style, and the designs of the characters are really distinctive and good-looking (I especially like female Mach and Jett's designs). The characterization is a little one-dimensional, but then again the game is short and free; they only have so much time they can focus on. The music is ok; didn't really like the credits song to be perfectly honest, but the other songs combine electronic beats that mirror the Starcraft soundtrack almost perfectly.
I also loved the Day9 cameo and how Jett was basiclly a genderswapped IdrA (definitly my favorite character in the story by far). I knew enough about starcraft to appreciate those. The extra scene also shows how much love the developers have for the series, pointing out many other nuances that completely went over my head.
My biggest problem, is that the game feels, and I quote what I told a friend, "more railroaded than transport tycoon". There's no branching paths, no romance, nothing that really involves meaningful player interaction in the visual novel. Even the starcraft playing segments is a binary "win-fail" choice, leaving the player to have very little agency in the story as a whole. Yes, I know this a debut, free game, but it really kills any interest in replaying in the game. There's so little choices, there's only two bad ends that I even know of, near the beggining of the game!
In all, this is a solid effort and I think most elements of what makes a good visual novel is there. Before playing, I probably wouldn't have bought it if I had to pay for it, but afterwards I'd be more than glad to have the option of supporting the developers. If the hinted at sequel happens, I really hope that the game becomes more interactive. Let the player specialize in strategies, make matches actually engaging, manage relationships, or even offer a zerg/protoss route if all things fail, SOMETHING which allows the player to influence the game.
If you're on the fence, I reccomend giving this a shot. It's free after all!

In SC2VN you play as Mach - a male or female (yes you get to choose the gender at start) Terran player who has a grandmaster status in the online ladder, but lost the qualifiers to VSL (I believe it to be ESL). So he/she goes to Seoul, Korea, to try vs some of the best and learn. And then it begins....
Let's take a look at the good about this novel, and the bad. I will do my best to leave any spoilers out. I will, however, say that I've played through this novel twice before it came to steam - its existence was well known to SC2 fans well in advance and many wanted to try it out - as it was kickstarted and the author made it clear that it will be free for all (SC pun intended).
The Good:
1. A valid representation of the international Stacraft scene.
2. Good writing and pleasant pictures to look at.
3. The writer obtained permission from Blizzard to use the Terran Starcraft + Brood War music, which I really love.
4. Any fan of Starcraft will easily recognize that the fake player and team names actually have real ones behind them, often with a single letter or so swap. If I am not mistaken (as I watch SC2 matches only leisurely and for fun), VSL is ESL, Enoch is Epoch, Jett is probably IdrA, Accel should be Flash, etc.
5. You get to play matches, and even have choices how to proceed, which will determine its outcome.
6. Over 2 hours of "gameplay".
7. It's FREE!!!
The BAD:
1. Some strategies used on the screenshots are clearly outdated.
2. There could have been more choices during the matches.
3. Some gameplay representations are not close to the reality (even in my meager knowledge from watching ESL games and other streams).
4. I was hoping for a more in-depth, action ending, but it is serviceable and fits the story well.
There is absolutely no reason why you shouldn't download and play this free visual novel. It's nice, it's well written, and it portrays the Starcraft universe both in-game and outside of the game really well with all the trash talkers, nice guys, events, and so on. It is nice short experience that in my opinion, one shouldn't deny oneself. Download it, read through it and have fun :) And... maybe read through it again, like I am doing now... for the third time...

Between playing on the PS3 and now on PC, I can say without a doubt that Final Fantasy XIV: A Realm Reborn is one of the best games in th entire Final Fantasy franchise. With an engaging story, plenty of quests and activities to take part in, and an addictive and fun combat system, the game definitely lives up to its status as a numbered FF game.
However, as an MMO it adds the wrinkle of playing with others to the normal FF format. While not the first MMO in the revered JRPG franchise, this one is definitely a worthy successor to Final Fantasy XI. With its rough start far behind it, the game doubles as an in-depth MMO and a great entry point for players new to the genre.
The convenient Duty Finder easily allows players to group up for dungeon runs and major boss battles, and the wealth of tutorials allows everyone to gradually learn the ins and outs of the genre and start playing with those far more experienced.
Add in the development team's desire to make the game the best it can be, and Square has a winner that goes above and beyond what anyone expected after the original release of XIV 1.0. Free story updates (new storyline quests to follow) and new content coming consistently, and balances and fixes coming frequently, the team definitely works hard to keep the player base satisfied; something that makes the monthly subscription well worth it.
So, if you don't mind paying a monthly subscription and are a fan of the Final Fantasy series then FFXIV:ARR is a game that I would recommend without a question. Even if you're not a Final Fantasy fan, there's a lot to like in this game. I highly recommend FFXIV:ARR and hope to see you out there in Eorzea.

So I thought I should change my review a bit. This gave have changed a lot since I first started playing it in 2013. Today we have received two expansions so far - Heavensward and Stormblood - Stormblood we got this summer 2017.
You get lots of content for your money, including a good and helpful community. You may feel it start of slow, but everything change as you gain higher levels. Something I find great, is the option to level multiple jobs at only one character. No need to make 5 alts just to focus on one specific thing. A lot changed during our latest expansion and the game is now more friendly to new players. It no longer force you to do a lot of extra work to reach your full potential. This could be a good time to catch up.
This game got a monthly fee. You will need to pay for each month you wish to play. It got a cash shop mostly selling old event items and some mounts (mounts does not have speedbuff) + extra stash. Recently they added an item that will let you skip the story up to a certain point and a instant leveling option up to lvl 60 (limited how many you can buy). This is meant to be bought for returning players and I would not recommend buying it if you are new. Everything you buy is because you wanted it. You are not forced by the game to spend money.
The game is target-based. You may think it will be a slow game, but amazingly it is not. In my opinion it can be rather too fast. Do not fear the global cooldown, you will learn to respect it well.
Personal experience
I have spent some hours on this game. This will be my 3rd time reaching endgame as they increased the level cap two times - 50 -> 60 -> 70. I enjoy endgame the most, since it is a good time to find out what you like to do. Are you a crafter by heart? You prefer gathering maybe? Or perhaps you are a fighter. You can do whatever you like. If you want to go hardcore, be ready for a bit of grinding - but fully enjoyable. In a way, everything pays off in the end one way or another. I have made some great friends. You can easily get into a Free Company even as a lvl 1. Something bad about this game? Should have some more snuggly emotes for your dear one... And mentors are not always as kind as you may think.
And yes, Bahamut is in the game.
And the bad review, do not let them scare you. The price is now even for us all.

The Good:
Amazing artwork from Maggi and stunning music from Soundtemp!! This game brings a Ragnarok vibe while still having an ambience of it's own genre. The maps are a delight to explore and there are so many quests available in game that it is a great pastime for the people that enjoy playing at one's own pace.
The Bad (Oh noes!):
While the complexity of the game brings a more in depth RPG experience, the lack of information or misleading in game tooltips brings a general sense of confusion about game mechanics. Outside sources of information are mostly outdated and many people in game spreads unintentionally wrong knowledge about the game. Drama usually follows when players dispute over in game mechanics with opposite infos. This becomes a problem after investing many hours into a character that has locked stats, skills and ranks. It's possible to reset them but you are limited with 1-2 free resets per  ***account***   with in game items or else you have to spend in real life money for the resets, which are not cheap by the way! Also the game company do intense class balancing from time to time while rarely giving out the resets needed. It feels like the game is still in beta after so many months and almost each update patches break the functionality of the game. When skills get bugged after updates, you can expect them to provide fixes after...  -MONTHS!- leaving some characters near the state of uselessness if it involves core skills. Again, they wont give out resets if they break your character.
The game also has a channel system which brings out different instances of the same maps. It's possible to sell services like enchants, buffs, repairs and etc with characters that you need to invest a lot of time without the new account events that fasten up leveling. The bad in this is the channel crashes. Each time the channel crashes, you need to set up your shop again. Not only that, some maps are broken and unintentionally doesn't allow you to set up your shop. It has been like that for months without any fix. You can also expect the channels to crash at least once a day.
The list of unfixed bugs and server problems is very long, and not only that, you can also expect to have very poor customer service if you need help from the company. Their support system works with a -ticket system- that usually takes a lot of time to get replied by the support team and that is... if you get replied! Also most of the time, if they answer you, you'll get replied with someone that either doesn't understand your query by lack of English comprehension skills or by someone that will reply you with how they are sorry but can't do anything to help you!
If this wasn't enough, you are limited to 2-3 entries a day per character for the dungeons. One of the problems here lies with the games instability. It happens quite often that the game crashes or that the server disconnects you while still consuming your entries. This becomes much worst when you buy boosting leveling items with real life money that gets completely wasted.
Also, this game suffers from bots and sadly many of them still remains rampant after weeks and months of reporting them in game. If you really want to get them banned, you need to take screenshots or record videos and post them in the forums to get the attention of the GMs. But no matter how much time you spend to get them banned, they will make new accounts and keep coming back. You might also feel in the end that there isn't a single employee actively searching for bots in the game and that you are actually doing their job, for free.
Speaking of which, very long awaited and needed content update also gets delayed in part because the company doesn't hire a translator to bring the content in English. Well who does the translation you might ask? Yes, you read right, the community does the translation from Korean to English without a pay. Take a moment to let this sink in. The level of greediness of this company is a phenomenon itself. Not only they are asking for absurd amounts of money; -for example 20$ for a premium haircut or near 20$ for resetting one of your character’s stats-, they don't bother to pay a professional translator or ask one of the employees to do it. This in itself, tells a lot about this company stance towards it's player base in the international version of Tree of Savior.
At this time, near December 2017, you will also find that the population of the game is very low which results sometimes in very long queue times for dungeons at peak hours and surely very long waiting time off peak hours. The fact is, a lot of players got tired of the mismanagement and lack of content of the game. There isn't really an end game except for doing "Earth Tower", which rewards you with the current best gear but takes a lot of time and dedication. For example, getting the end game weapon takes months of playing and for this reason, it is very rare in each server. Well -was- rare. The company decided to reward 12 of these weapons per server from a bugged pvp event which many players abused. Despite near 9 players out of 10 players asking the company to not give these items because of exploits, cheats, hacks and bug abuse, the company completely ignored it's player base and decided to also disgrace the dedicated players who spend -months- of precious time for getting these items. Even thought some honest players won, this resulted in rewarding mostly the people abusing bugs and hackers which I personally encountered and saw laughing and being mean to players in chat! This also created a more profound division within the community and if you find the players being generally tense and toxic, it is no wonder! The company keeps frustrating it's player base and sends you a message as a gamer that your life time is of poor value for them.
And the list continues!! Like bad optimisation of the game (while WoW, GW2 for example run at max settings with constant 60 fps, ToS doesn’t run at more than 30 fps at average settings outside of crowded areas) and so on!

-NO for the rest! And this is why I took the time to make this review; to help you make a more informed decision and think if this kind of game will leave you with a bad taste in your mouth in the end if you intend to invest your precious time and money or get serious in any way about this game. The first RPG I've played, and one I still come back to every now and then. I've been excited ever since the crowdfunding campaing, and been singing praises of this game ever since. It's brutal, hard and random, yes, but such is the nature of TRUE rogue-likes.
Deluxe version gives you the options to lower the difficulty for more casual of players, so they can get enjoyment out of this game as well. Even giving you option to properly save your game, unlike the normal mode, where your game save is tied to your characters life, once character dies, it's gone. This is something not available in the free version. More on that later.
But the true meat of this game comes from flexibility of the combat... You have your basic Melee, Ranged and Magic attacks, but you also can use Mindcraft, companions, special race/class abilities and alchemy to name a few varied methods of dealing damage. But you can in turn take damage from ridiculous stuff among others, and get killed in many, many ways, including getting crushed by dungeon, whipping yourself to death, getting sacrificed to one of many gods, having too much stuff in your inventory and my personal favorite: Getting eaten by grue. Also, you can get killed before you even move (or take your first step) with certain race/class combinations on certain day.
There are plenty of static elements in game that stay same from game to game, but majority of the dungeons are randomly generated, keeping you on your toes every time. No two games are the same, which makes this game highly replayable.
Deluxe version of ADOM is not only worth your money, but as it gets more features, which will keep coming until the Creator of this game feels this game is complete (and moves onto the Sequel) makes this game truly worthwhile. But if you are not certain of getting the Deluxe version yet, you can always download the Free version of this game from ADOM homepage, and try it out as much you want. The base game is the same regardless, but There are bunch of nifty features that will not be in the free versions ever. But if you so desire, you can run the newest free version of this game on your Amiga or old MS-Dos computers. That's how old-school this game is.

- Point based Character creation has been Added to the game, which allows more customization.
- You can now also Choose your starting Starsign, unlike previously
- Majority of Bugs Fixed (Basically, unless you applied to the beta, which you can do if you so desire, you shouldn't encounter any bugs)
//Coming Features
- Animations
- Volcano (A new dungeon, that is completely different from other places currently in game)
- More Quests

It's a decent little game to pass the time, considering the price. While I wouldn't exactly call it an outstanding game by any stretch of the imagination, I would firmly place it in the category of: 'If you have 10 bucks to spare, some time to kill, and like strategy games with a sprinkling of story and RPG thrown in, why not?'.
It comes with a quick little tutorial to help you get started, which is nice. However I would still strongly recommend either reading or glancing through the simple manual as well, because there may be things that are of interest to you that you'd want to do and have no real idea about otherwise. Such as starting your own faction. That however is something that will take several hours and much dedication.
There are 4 factions that you can join and level up with, however if you don't join any you can go about doing what you want (minus missions) and still level up as a civilian. If you eventually join your ranking will carry over to your new faction, so at least you don't lose anything.
It's no surprise that virtually everything in the game revolves around money. The only things that don't are your own individual skills depending on which profession you choose - however note that it can take quite a while to level up and get new skills, so for some people the game might get a bit tedious, or even monotonous. You need to 'level up' 3 times before you get new skills - and some pretty big skills are on opposite ends of entire skill trees that require you to have prerequisites. So expect a lot of grinding.
If you're someone who likes games based upon their graphics - my suggestion is to move along. There won't be anything new or fancy here, and if you have a really high resolution you're going to be doing a fair amount of squinting. Otherwise you can make it full screen and squint again as everything gets stretched out. If you see something once in the game, you'll see it a thousand times.
Same for the sounds. The music will tend to cut out at various random intervals, but strangely enough I really only noticed it when it suddenly stopped. Otherwise it was fairly forgettable. Much the same for the sound effects.
There are a few instances of flavor text missing, usually in the 'quotes' area stating that this is an early access version even though it isn't. Also, if you're the one who tends to shudder every time you come across misspelled words or bad grammar in a game, then prepare to shudder a few times. Thankfully most of it is fine, but you'll notice a few spots here and there - and plenty of walls of text. Though considering the resolution I'm not really surprised.
All-in-all it's a fun little game to pass the time, or if you have that space rpg urge. It's 'just one more turn!' addicting for the first hour or two until you get the routine down. You might get to switch it up when you learn a new skill or get a new ship, or get a battle with a random event - but otherwise nothing major happens for the first large chunk of the game.
With enough dedication you can eventually reach the higher ranks and unlock more activities, but you'll have to be able to slog through a fair bit of early grinding, -especially- if you choose the civilian route.
My final score for this is a fairly decent but not great 6.5/10. It will keep you entertained for a while and will be worth it to those who are willing to put the time into it - assuming you can put up with old-fashioned graphics and sounds for quite a few hours.
For the rest of you who can't do that, I'd recommend waiting to see if it goes on sale later. At 10 USD it's still an iffy buy, but if it ever goes to 7 or less, I'd say grab it.

All in all I would highly recommend this game to anyone from MMO veterans to people who enjoy Elder scrolls or anyone really looking for a time sink with a decent progression system.

I want you to imagine the following... Six designers and a programmer sit around a table discussing what game they are going to make next. One suggests let's make a puzzle game and then the next one suggests 'yes and let's make it all about the occult and worshipping demons'. Welcome to fireproof games which can be found here...
and more importantly 'the room' game.
Over two million people have played this and most probably won't even understand what the story was all about even after finishing it as the references are only sly.
The story is that as an old understanding friend you receive a letter from someone we only know as A.S. who is a member of an alchemy group called 'the circle'. This group does not approve of A.S's fascination of trying to control the fifth element known as 'the null' basically because it has no bearing in the pursuit of gold. Regardless of this A.S continues solo and finds a way of creating a mechanism which contains the null which he obtained 'through sacrifice' even going to the further extent of creating an eyepiece from it through a distilling process. The null therefore seems to be the human soul. A.S goal is to summon the prince of demons known as Satan (ashtoreth) and interrogate him. However A.S finds himself trapped in another dimension after opening up a doorway which harbours this demon.
So how does he then go on to create a complicated series of Yosegi safes to keep his null controlling mechanism from the hands of the general public is never quite explained. Maybe after it is dormant for a while the safe locks itself back up?
Either way your completely clueless to this back story and will be for quite some time. All you know is that your standing in a attic with a big box.
Why fire proof games thought this was a good story is beyond me. Do they really think the occult/seance is harmless?
The Yosegi puzzles are really good and there is about 4-5 hrs of gameplay here trying to work out how to get in the thing. The different mechanics of the box does play out nicely with hd graphics. There is great satisfaction in working out the puzzles alone without the hint box which accompanies you throughout the whole duration of the game.
Thumbs up in concept, gameplay, graphics and sound.
Thumbs down with story.

Rock of Ages is a strange tower defense game of some sort: in every match you will spend your time between making a huge rock slide towards your enemy door, in order to damage it, in a platform, third person fashion, and examining the battlefield from an aerial view, to set up defenses (towers, animals, explosives, ...) against the enemy rock.
In truth, the main appeal of Rock of Ages is its art style: a Monty Pythonesque adventure taking place in different time periods (Ancient Greece, the Medieval Age, Italian Renaissance, Baroque, XIXth Century), with plenty of artistic references and a catchy soundtrack.
Gameplay-wise, you can choose between a singleplayer campaign and a multiplayer experience. The AI for the first trips more than once, but it can be challenging nevertheless (more specifically, your enemy will be far less elastic than you in dodging obstacles and defenses, and later elephants will stagger his/her rock ad infinitum). Aside from the campaign, you have a challenge mode too.
I suggest you Rock of Ages if you are going to enjoy the artistic, pop-culture and history references, or you just enjoy a rather good indie game

This game is old school but is not too difficult.  I bought it once for myself and then again for my brother who shared the same love of snes and nes games.  It fits right into that kind of collection.  It's difficult and forgiving at the same time.  If you die you can start back at the intro to the screen you are in but the work to get through the screen may hold you up and if you want to not die at all then you will have to bring your A game.  There is a good variety of enemies, mechanics and methods to take them down.  I absolutely loved this game and think more developers should try and hone their games to the level this one was.
Oh one last thing, this game doesn't have a tutorial but it teaches through example.  To cite one example, there is a platform with a guy on it below you.  You jump and elbow drop the guy to kill him and break the block under him, discovering that blocks can be broken.  This kind of learning is missing from many games these days and replaced with tutorials.  I was very impressed with how natural it all felt and the level of exemplary game design.

ADOM is the definitive rogue-like experience. If you're a fan of rogue-likes, you've probably played ADOM already. However, this is the first of the classic rogue-likes to make its way into Steam and a wide new audience. People who are interested in rogue-like themes and the so called rogue-lite games might find a lot to like here.
As a rogue-like, ADOM is a turn-based RPG. This means that every time you take an action, all of the other characters in the game do so as well, including enemies. In a sense, it's not really turn-based as all the movement happens at once, meaning you never have to wait for the enemy's movement. Combat is a simple matter at ground level but gets more complex as the game progresses. In its most basic form, you are simply "running" into enemies. This causes you to attack them and they will attack back at you and so on. However, you can influence this combat in many ways. This includes switching your tactics to gain better to-hit chance and damage at the expense of defenses (can be used flexibly and in different ways depending on the situation), casting spells, drinking potions, zapping wands, reading scrolls, firing missiles, using skills and maneuvering around the dungeon to name a few. Trash mobs you can simply run into and destroy with ease, but whenever you encounter a new and unknown, potentially strong monster, you might want to slow down the pace and consider what gear you have to help you. And remember the number one rule of rogue-likes: always have an escape plan in mind!
ADOM is absolutely brutal. Rogue-lite games often mention how they are extremely difficult and will require multiple tries before you beat them. These games also tend to be relatively short, 1-2 hour experiences in various genres from fps to platformers. ADOM on the other hand is a purebred rogue-like through and through; a successful game is likely to take 15+ hours and the hundreds of failures you will suffer on the way will add even more hours on top of that. Now I happen to think this is a strength; there is immense amounts of replayability in the game due to a variety of races and classes you can play as, in addition to a huge amount of procedural generation when it comes to monsters you encounter, loot you find and dungeon layouts you will explore. And once you beat the game normally, guess what! There's several Ultra Endings to attempt as well! These endings are insanely hard to pull off, require EVEN more tries than the normal one and are virtually impossible without some outside information sources.
ADOM's strength in relation to other rogue-likes lies in its structured nature: Terinyo is always in the same place as well as the main dungeons of the game. There are quests that you will undertake in a logical order and once you learn your way around the early game, it is possible to form a strategy. This is absolutely key; where many rogue-likes hinge purely on RNG to get you going, ADOM actually has a very deep strategy layer to its gameplay. The other notable selling point in relation to other rogue-likes is the skill system; every race and class has a set of skills they start off with, and these skills can be improved as you advance in levels. This gives leveling a more meaningful feeling compared to some other rogue-likes where you simply gain more health and magic points.
Now this review could go on forever, but hopefully I've given you some insight into whether or not ADOM is something you might be into. Personally, I love this game. I have beaten it three times the normal way and once I've achieved the Avatar of Order ending. I've played this game over the course of 15 years, two development cycles and who knows how many hours. It is truly something special.
Lastly, some meta-advice:
-Do not play the game in softcore mode! Permadeath is an integral part of the rogue-like experience and you will hate ADOM if you don't have permadeath on. A character is very likely to die; you have to learn to deal with it. The entire premise of the game is that you roll hundreds of characters until finally one of them sticks and gets farther into the game than the others. If you keep struggling with a character who was never even meant to survive the experience will be miserable. Not to mention you will never have that feeling of utter disaster when your best character dies at the final level. Or on the way back after winning the game. And all of those losses will build up to the final success; when you finally, after all that heartbreak, beat the game and leave Drakalor Chain, you look back at the time you've spent and go: "♥♥♥♥ yes, I actually did it. I beat this son of a ♥♥♥♥♥ of a game. Hell yes."
-Don't be afraid to look up stuff on the wiki: ADOM is a massive game and very cryptic in some areas. However, I would suggest avoiding making a habit out of this. Explore the game freely; you're going to die so many times anyway so what's the point of completely spoiling yourself? But once you get a promising character rolling, you might want to check up on the effects of eating this specific monster's corpse, or how dangerous exactly that Gorgon is ;)
-Give the ASCII version a try! The tilesets are very nicely done and the bare-bones ASCII style might seem clunky and unintuitive at first. But you'd be surprised at the advantages it has. For example, you will easily identify new enemies: a small "g" is always going to be a goblin-like small humanoid, an uppercase "D" is always going to be a dragon or dragon-like huge lizard like drake and so on. Very clear and handy compared to the tilesets imo. Not to mention the ASCII graphics are just so damn charming!

Ancient Domains of Mystery... what a name. Truth be told, of all games I have played on my PC in the last 15 years, ADOM has surely been the one I keep returning to most often. And if there's anything that hasn't changed since the first time is that, whenever I do start up a new character, I can hardly keep myself off the game until the character dies... or until I win. Today the game is officially released on Steam, and the least I can do to repay ADOM and its team for hundreds upon hundreds of hours of fun is to review it.
So, what is ADOM about? It's a fantasy-themed roguelike RPG where you create a character of your liking, choosing from a roster of several races and professions, and embark upon a journey to find out what is it that's plaguing a remote mountain chain. Most of the elements are pretty easy to grasp now that we have mouse control, graphics, and even some rudimentary animation, but should you spend some more time with the game, you'll certainly realize the complexity and level of detail that manifest themselves in almost every aspect of the game (well, except the dialogues—this isn't Planescape: Torment for sure) and this tends to hook everyone who spends more than a couple hours with it. It's not often that you play something for years and keep learning something new and relearning old things with every playthrough. Most of the in-game situations have lots of different possible solutions, which is something that large expensive AAA-titles have all but forgone these days. This game certainly rewards intelligent, thoughtful play—which in no way dimishes its ability to pump adrenaline in certain situations.
As far as roguelikes go, ADOM is definitely more on the traditional RPG side: the world isn't as sandbox-ish as something like Dwarf Fortress, there are a lot of fixed elements and reasonably fleshed-out quests; a typical ascension (the roguelike lingo for completing the ultimate quest and leaving the game) takes from a full day if you're just rushing everything to something closer to a week—even for experienced players. Virtually all the development decisions with regards to its content are also made by the same person, Thomas Biskup—the ageless director and Creator of ADOM. Obviously, there are some disadvantages to this approach, which served to be the main reason the game has at one point spent a decade in neglect, but this man's creativity and burning passion for hardcore RPGs, the fantasy, and the adventure, is what's taken it here—after more than 20 years since its inception. So when Thomas started a crowdsourcing campaign in 2012 to make massive updates to ADOM, I was among the people who contributed without a second thought. Getting ADOM here on Steam, which is almost unthinkable for a genre so niche and seemingly impenetrable, is a huge success. No-one thought this would be possible before the campaign ended. All of the funds that were raised were put to good use, and the backers recognize the main reason behind it: to give the development a strong push, not to make money out of a free product (more on this below).
If you've never played roguelikes, or have no experience with turn-based RPGs in particular, ADOM in its current form is definitely a good place to start. It's definitely a slow burner, and it might seem a little unforgiving at first, but don't discard it if your character keeps getting killed in the first 10 minutes. Try different approaches to the same problem, play to your character's strengths, take the easy ways and pay attention to many generous cues—all of this will be rewarded. At some point you might even decide to turn the graphical interface off and continue playing with good old ASCII—you'd be surprised how immersive can gameplay get if you let your imagination paint the picture. It works just like a good book. Although the monster designs are definitely sweet, and they make the game seem more like a Spiderweb Software RPGs—another dear favorites of mine.
Those of you who have already tried ADOM many years ago and are wondering what is different about it these days are in luck: virtually every aspect of the game has seen improvements—often drastic ones! Difficulty curve is a lot less spiky now, most of the infamous exploits are fixed or toned down to sane levels, and there's quite a bit of new content to dabble in if you feel like it (none is shoved down your throat, mind—TB recognizes the game is long as is)—both semi-fixed and completely random. Even if you keep playing without graphics, I encourage you to leave the in-game music on: it fits the game quite well and definitely enhances the roguelike experience.
So, to sum up, if you enjoy some or most of:
...ADOM just might be your top pick. It has its problems, but they're relatively minor and ultimately dwarfed by the good stuff.
Let me conclude by saying this. Those of us who have been playing ADOM for years upon years don't do it because of nostalgia—we never did.
. How many games you know have seen their authors grow into successful businessmen and yet
keep working hard upon improving and polishing a piece of creative effort they have started back in their college years? This game is an honest-to-god result of so much love, thought, and craft, that you'd be hard-pressed to find anything that compares. We play ADOM because we feel this. We play it because it's
. And by the way: if you don't want the fancy and convenient stuff in the Steam version of the game, the classic, fully-hardcore version of ADOM with the same fully up-to-date quests, mechanics, and content has been, and will always remain,
on the
. This speaks of honesty and love more than anything else I could think of. Support it while you can!
So, would I recommend ADOM? Well now, why

Many games these days boast to have vast open worlds, open-ended gameplay and endless replayability - ADOM actually delivers.
- Background -
I first played ADOM in 2003. I've since spent hundreds of hours exploring the mysterious Drakalor Chain. ADOM is one of my all-time favourite games, and certainly the only game originally released in the 90's that I don't play for nostalgia - but because it is still fresh.
ADOM is an RPG in the true sense of the word: it does not impose restrictions on you. The problem I have with most RPGs these days is how they limit the player's actions. The choice between good and evil is often in fact the choice between the good and evil dialogue option. ADOM is different in that you can actually do whatever you want, be anyone you want to be. And doing whatever you want actually means something in ADOM, since the game has a ridiculously large amount of content. Really, it does.
- Gameplay -
In ADOM, first you'll create your character. Your character will be given a starsign that will have some effect on him/her. After that you'll choose your race, profession, talents etc. from a ton of options. These choises will guide you as you start your journey, but won't limit you as (or if) you progress.
As the game begins, you enter Drakalor Chain, a troubled valley with many mysteries to explore. From then on it's all up to you. Go to the nearest village and interact with the townsfolk or find your own path. Battle fierce beasts, learn incredible spells, rob stores, fight for money, make friends, embark on quests, search for artifacts, brew deadly poisons, control minds, barter items, cook food, worship your gods, play instruments, raise the dead, clean your ears...
And of course you'll die. You'll be drowned, burnt and crushed to death. You'll die of hunger and sickness and bloodloss. You'll accidentally kill yourself conducting dangerous magical experiments. You'll die as you are sacrificed to strange and terrible gods. You'll die and return. And maybe, just maybe you'll one day defeat the powers that plague Drakalor Chain. I never did, yet, but I'll keep on trying.
See you in the Caverns of Chaos!

The Room is a three-dimensional puzzle game. The game has a minimal story, in which the player is told by letters of a mysterious box in a room in a house; as the player solves the puzzles around the box, more notes from the same author - one who previously had solved the mystery of the box - are found, describing the box's use of an ethereal material called "Null", as well as showing the author slowly descending into madness.
On starting the game, the player is presented with the first of four puzzle boxes. The first box is offered as a tutorial to the game's controls, which demonstrate how to move around the box and interact with features of the box. The player has a small inventory for items like keys found in compartments in the box. A key inventory element is a special lens that, in-game, allows the player to see things made from the Null element that compose parts of the box. The lens can generally be equipped at any time to see these secrets, often requiring the player to manipulate the view to align secrets into a coherent symbol. The goal is to fully unlock each puzzle box, extracting a smaller but more complicated box within it.
The Room is great. The puzzles are both challenging and discoverable, and you’ll milk at least three hours of fun gameplay from the app. The graphics and sound are top-notch. If you prize replayability over those other factors, however, note that it’s limited; once you’ve completed The Room, it’s unlikely you’ll want to go through the entire game again. But you’ll probably get a kick out of introducing the game to someone else and watching them work their way through it.

I liked FF14: ARR up until the expansion.
I've played a lot of MMOS (I think at least 30 now) and there are certain things I look for, and really enjoy an MMO having. It doesn't have to, but it gets a big plus in my book if it does. One having interesting and complicated enough mechanics that when you actually finish a boss for the first time, or a dungeon run, it feels like an achievement; that you had to work for it, but it was worth it. The second is having the ability to have different playstyles; the ability to tune your characters closer to how you want to play. The third is an engaging, interesting, and above all USEFUL crafting system.
FF14 had 2 of the three; there's no skill trees at all, and not really any way to modify your gear; there's BiS and that's about it. You can do vanity gear over it though, so at least you can look different then every other player the same level as you. Still, the mechanics were awesome, I loved the music and a lot of the themes of the dungeon, and actually LOOKED FORWARD to gathering and crafting, because people LIKED getting HQ gear and useful items later.
The world was engaging to look around. The story was... well... decent for an FF game (I don't care for FF games in general myself, I played this because I liked it as an MMO). There was always plenty to do, plenty to collect, plenty to save for, etc.
That changed with the expansion. First off, the new maps are a horrid PAIN to get around. They made them HUGE with the intent that "It'll look cool when you fly around" and obviously did not give a damn about people who had to hoof it, trying to unlock flying.
Oh yeah, you have to hit random nodes and do random quests on the map (including main quest and side quest stuff) to be able to fly. PER NEW MAP. So by the time you unlock flying, you're probably going to be done with wanting to be ON the map.
The mechanics are pretty much mostly just ripped from other previous dungeons. One of the first new ones, Sohm Al, we recognized very easily as a 'weenie T6'. And to me, the music was just really boring...
As for the crafting part...
Apparently Yoshi P (one of the main developers, if not THE main one) has basically stated he hates the fact that crafters figured out how to make things better then dungeon drops. Oh, sorry that the ENTIRE WEEK one might put into making the HQ accesory and the MILLIONS of gil that you might dump into boosting it up to make it SLIGHTLY better bothers you SO MUCH that you basically made ALL crafting completely worthless.
Okay, there's pretty much three reasons to craft in games: To make items a cheaper way then just buying them, to make items you actually want to use, and to make unique items you can't get anywhere else.
Since quests just THROW high quality gear at players now, and there's NO POSSIBLE way to get the same TIER as dungeon drops, the only item adventurers would really use is food, and there's not really a market for seliing (level 55 gil for 500 gil on the marketboard!). And the only 'unique' items that are remotely worth making are vanity gear, housing items, and stuff for your mounts. Which makes the HUNDREDS of hours both in gathering and crafting completely not worth it, since almost all the housing items aren't that expensive.
There's a lot of other things to mention, but basically I felt they ruined the two main reasons I was playing this in the first place. They MIGHT fix it, but I've already been soured on the idea.
When I started playing, I wasn't really that into it. Now, 400 hours later, I'm finally done with the main story (including Heavensward and A TON of Sidequests) and I don't regret any of it.

Overall, I've had a good experience with FFXIV. While certain aspects of it show it's relatively young age as an MMO, Square Enix has been doing a good job figuring out how to improve things. Right now, I'd say the only thing Warcraft has on FFXIV is a much longer head start, but it doesn't look like FFXIV will be bowing out any time soon. The graphics are lovely, the quests make you feel like you're actually contributing to something, there are plenty of non-combat options (numerous collecting/crafting professions, player/guild housing, gambling at the Golden Saucer, and more), engaging dungeons, raids, and trials (after lvl35 things start ramping up), and oodles of options for customizing your character.

From what I had heard of Papers, Please, I was expecting a very unique game, but also something that was very limited in terms of gameplay and variety. Boy, I was wrong!
So, everyone must have heard about the general premise by now. The whole moral conundrum between the people you decide to pass, despite of their document's validity, is a very important aspect. However, there are several different "storylines" that you come across. And that's where some of the big decisions come into play, as you try to balance family and principle. There are several ways you can play this game, each character you encounter encorporating a different trait of your play style.
I felt genuinely bad with some of the decisions I made. And genuinely good as well! And it's not all that common for a game to make me pause and think about what I'm about to do.
There are some really memorable moments and characters. Overall, you should stick with your decisions, as you definitely feel the repercussions of most of them. Use your better judgement and do good for Arstotzka!
Replayability is certainly there, although I doubt I'll ever do it. I'm quite satisfied with the experience I got out of the game, honestly.
However, there are lots of ways where you can choose different! The campaign should remain largely the same, though, regarding the "filler" moments. Of course, those are necessary for the game to have meaning! I support that, it just hinders replayability, if you deem that necessary.
Definitely give this one a go!

Game: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2
Original Release Date: 12 Nov, 2009
Date of Review: 05 September, 2015
Update Febuary 2016: VAC has now been made useless, where VAC bans do not prevent people from playing.
The Good:
- No overcomplications, no future/exo stuff.
- Special Ops is kinda decent, and the campaign is alright.
- Most guns are fairly balanced.
- Config files not encrypted.
- Fairly well optimised and decent graphics (by 2009/2010 standards) if you put them up to "Extra".
The Bad:
- VAC REMOVED, cheaters roam free with no punishments.
- Abandoned by developers, no bug fixes/patches.
- P2P Networking, no dedicated servers (Unlike every previous CoD), therefore more hackers then any other CoD.
- No included DLC, even though the game has been out since 2009, so small community split even futher.
- The start of Infinity Ward hating PC gamers.
- No mod support (Unlike every previous CoD).
- No map editing support (Unlike every previous CoD).
- Locked 65 FOV (Unlike every previous CoD).
- No developer console access (Unlike every previous CoD).
- Have to edit config files to customise commands like max FPS.
- High cost, few sales. £37.99 for the game and all DLC, 6 years after release.
- Literally a killstreak that ends the match.

Hello everyone!
So after about 150 hours in the game I decided to write my very first Steam review. I want to mention that I have not yet experienced the "engame" of the game. I've been leveling a few classes (as in every MMO i try out lots of different classes before actually leveling one to max-level.
So far I played White Mage, Paladin and Ninja.





So far the game really impressed me. I played a few MMOs before but the style and gameplay of Final Fantasy XIV really drew me in. I recommend you at the very least try out the free trial.

Square Enix goes above and beyond to make this a great title among MMOs. Every aspect of the game is really nice to look at, beautiful scenery to appreciate while running around and a lot of flair to every action made by the characters. The story is deep and engaging with a good level of charm to keep things amusing, as is standard with the final fantasy series as a whole. There is a whole lot more strategy to crafting as well, with a system that makes it much more interactive than clicking a button and waiting for 20 things to be done at once (which you can still choose to do to streamline the process if you're not concerned with a loss in experience or a higher failure rate). With the ability to swap between all the classes in the game at any time on the same character, you'll never even need to create more than one to experience everything, there are even specialised story quests for each class for you to enjoy. Whether you're leveling all your classes to the cap level, crafting up a storm and making money, destroying false gods to deck out your gear or just making your house look nice, you'll never run out of things to do either. All in all, probably the best MMO I've had the pleasure of experiencing, I highly look forward to the next update and I can't see myself stopping any time soon. Give it a go, it's definately worth the price even if you only play it for the first month.
If you didn't want to read all that then here's the short version: This game is better than any other MMO I've played, you should buy it.

This is a case study on interactive storytelling and moral choice in videogames, but it's not hollow. The personal stories and grim setting are built around the core of a solid (if unusual) game mechanic: stamping passports. Of course, when you play it you'll soon come to understand there's more to it than that. The challenge comes from struggling to keep on top of all the ever-increasing, bureaucratically mandated steps you have take to stamp each passport, but the game never feels grindy or unfair. Throw in a branching storyline and lots of surprises, and you have a truly classic game.

One of the best puzzle games I've encountered on Steam so far. The Room involves solving puzzles based around complex machinery and contraptions, requiring the player to explore both visual (through an eyepiece) and functional aspects of a variety of puzzle boxes. Each level is a box, and you have to scour every inch of them in order to get all the pieces to fit together and reveal the next level. Coupled with extremely polished and realistic graphics that are accurate to the point of tiny details, this game is enjoyable to play as well as explore. And half the time I don't even know what I'm doing :D

I'm sorry to say that even really wanting to like this game it has plummetted on my want to play list. Reasons? The short version is, unbalanced and lazy design.
Building a character is complicated and largely ineffective, as the difficulty of the game is based on your level. That makes critters like mudcrabs insanely tough yet unsatisfying to crush at level 40. Leveling up before returning to a tough quest where you got stuck getting killed every single time by the end boss will help just a little bit. Fights tend to get harder due to lag even on recommended hardware, it looks like the mega server architecture is flawed. You need to read up on main quests beforehand to avoid getting stuck with ineffective selections - selections that you cannot change nor abandon and restart. This gives a truly dated feel. Limited character deletes and massive attention to in-game purchases all add to the impression that it is built as income generating (for the creator) time sink (for you).
Redeeming features? Nostalgia about earlier Elder Scroll games. Some nice landscaping and extensive exploration. Moderately interesting quests.
But it all gets old mighty fast if after that next patch all you seem to be able to do is die, lose money on gear repairs, and slower and slower leveling up, and a growing sense of deja vu because the next town is so much like the last.
Only recommended for the truly dedicated MMO and/or Elder Scroll afficiados. But do know that it is NOT a Bethesda Softworks product and this becomes very noticable after a while.

I don't often see single-player games this generous for such a low price. It took me over ten hours to finish the game, but the generosity isn't only in game length: the game might not look like much on the screenshots, but the amount of details is really cool! Close-ups of the characters' face, mini-games and small cutscenes galore, and it adds a lot to the game's atmosphere.
I also really liked the story, the ending, and the overall atmosphere of camaraderie that transpires through all the interactions you have with the other characters. You'd think a point-and-click adventure game about martial arts would be mostly about fighting, but it ends up being mostly about helping out.
Definitely recommended if you like point-and-click adventure games and are looking for something rather epic in scope while still being relatively character-driven.

I bought this game for its quirky, scratchy fountain pen style, unsuspecting that it was one of the best adventure games on Steam.  Most adventure heroes are trolls, right?  We accept it.  We
it.  We revel in their devilry as they pull the wool (doubtless fashioned out of polyester shag ripped from a derelict van) over countless eyes and make a general wreck of their environments.  Wouldn't it be nice, though, to play a point-in-click in which the protagonist strives to take the high road at all times, and is far more likely to meet an insult with a bemused shrug rather than a sarcastic comeback?
In this island-hopping Wu-Xia fantasy, your character, whom you name yourself, is a martial arts prodigy after the Shaw Brothers tradition; he can learn a whole new fighting stance, or even a difficult poison-dispelling technique, in a matter of hours.  However, rather than breaking face for most of his quest -- the object of which is to find a vanished martial arts legend who holds the key to preventing war on the mainland -- he spends the majority of his time
conflict, patching strained relations, making lives better.  He fights when he must, but never to the death.  If he inflicts damage out of necessity, he strives to repair it.  While holding the importance of his great task firmly in his mind, he always manages to remember the sanctity of all the individual lives, great and small, that intersect his path.  And the supporting characters in this game!  There's so many of them, all so weird, yet true-to-life -- everywhere you look, Cloak and Dagger has put to skillful use that golden combination of outre and relatable.
The puzzles in this game are fairly easy, but difficulty doesn't always equal fun.
is all about the journey, and for a mere seven bucks, you get one heck of a long, wild, and thought-provoking one.  Highly recommended!

A charming, funny, genre-bending point-and-click adventure. The plot and puzzles work well together and the pacing rarely wavers. The RPG elements are light enough to not be distracting, and works in context a lot better than many adventure games with combat (Escape from Monkey Island, Dreamfall, etc). As far as I can tell there are no big glitches and, despite its jagged artwork (which I really like, actually), is a lot more polished than most indie games out there. Reasonably priced too. Definitely worth checking out!

Despite the low price this is a polished full length game with an epic story, lots of puzzles, RPG elements and some mini games. Everything about this game feels polished. The bold art style, the fine character animations, the straightforward GUI, the excellent music and sound effects.
And above all, the atmosphere. Every island you visit has its own distinct character. While the story starts light-hearted and slow, with every new island you visit it gets more tense and serious, always with the right amount of humor that is never distracting from the darker tone in the late game. In terms if atmosphere Legend of Hand does everything right and is one of the best games I've played this year.
The puzzles are more on the easy side, but have a lot of variation to them - I only got stuck twice because I overlooked an entrance. Most of the mini games were very nice, with very few exceptions where it wasn't clear what to.
So yeah, if you like adventure games with RPG elements, go buy and play this game! It's well worth the money and for its length and the amount of polish it might as well cost twice as much.

A fun, quirky point & click adventure game with an oddball style.  The game is surprisingly long, and generally just the right degree of difficulty.  The music fits the general aesthetic, with a casual feel to it while still being surprisingly catchy in places.
Point & click purists should be warned that the game does contain several different minigames atypical of the genre.  The most obvious is the "combat" system, which is really more of a puzzle interface than an action sequence.  For this, actions are turn-based, not timed, and progression is usually either straightforward or linked to spotting clues or solving puzzles elsewhere.  Most other mini-games are action-lite and just add some quirky fun to the gameplay.  There is one sequence, however, that point & click purists are unliklely to enjoy, involving precisely timed clicks to parry objects thrown at you.  Fortunately, you can skip this puzzle if you find you're having trouble with it.
All in all, a surprisingly long, casual, fun time.  Go for it!

Hello everyone!
So after about 150 hours in the game I decided to write my very first Steam review. I want to mention that I have not yet experienced the "engame" of the game. I've been leveling a few classes (as in every MMO i try out lots of different classes before actually leveling one to max-level.
So far I played White Mage, Paladin and Ninja.





So far the game really impressed me. I played a few MMOs before but the style and gameplay of Final Fantasy XIV really drew me in. I recommend you at the very least try out the free trial.

Square Enix goes above and beyond to make this a great title among MMOs. Every aspect of the game is really nice to look at, beautiful scenery to appreciate while running around and a lot of flair to every action made by the characters. The story is deep and engaging with a good level of charm to keep things amusing, as is standard with the final fantasy series as a whole. There is a whole lot more strategy to crafting as well, with a system that makes it much more interactive than clicking a button and waiting for 20 things to be done at once (which you can still choose to do to streamline the process if you're not concerned with a loss in experience or a higher failure rate). With the ability to swap between all the classes in the game at any time on the same character, you'll never even need to create more than one to experience everything, there are even specialised story quests for each class for you to enjoy. Whether you're leveling all your classes to the cap level, crafting up a storm and making money, destroying false gods to deck out your gear or just making your house look nice, you'll never run out of things to do either. All in all, probably the best MMO I've had the pleasure of experiencing, I highly look forward to the next update and I can't see myself stopping any time soon. Give it a go, it's definately worth the price even if you only play it for the first month.
If you didn't want to read all that then here's the short version: This game is better than any other MMO I've played, you should buy it.

I feel like most of the negative reviews for the game come from people who expect it to be free; understandably, given that it is, in fact, listed as "free". The full reality is that this is a game that works like an old-timey MMORPG - you pay a fee to be able to enjoy it in full. The free version allows you to, well, demo it, mostly, though if what you want is to roam around a ginormous, gorgeous map with a rifle in hand and shoot some stuff, I feel like you might be satisfied with what you get anyway.
Personally, I don't mind paying 10 bucks to enjoy a full version of what appears to be a perfectly functional, engaging multiplayer game. I used to pay that amount for a single month, but maybe that's just me being old. Having checked out the microtransactions as well, the prices really aren't too obscene (when accessed via Steam, anyway - the official page offers less savings, for whichever odd reason), and you can pretty much do without buying any of that, especially if you do end up getting a membership access which automatically grants you a set of clothes to get you through the tougher maps. The core system's in place, the environments are incredible, and the animals are believable and natural. Shooting, whether you prefer that to be with a bullet, an arrow or a digital camera, all seems to be in order too.
That said, this isn't a shooting gallery. It's more in the line of a walking simulator, or a "crouching through the forest" simulator, so expect to do a fair bit of that. For me, that adds to the experience; for someone else, that's a gamebreaking flaw. But if you're an Old Person like I am and maybe enjoyed the Deer Hunters from the past, which also involved a lot of waiting.... waiting....... walking...... and..... waiting...... you'll definitely enjoy this one, too. And frankly, after testing it out, I'm prepared to say that this game is worth a full total of 40-50 bucks on all grounds that I usually judge my games by (content, playability, replay value, graphics), which so happens to be about the amount I expect to be paying for it in the long run.

F2P is a Demo-Mode only. Solid hunting game with detailed hunting grounds, cheap MMO-like payment model, rare but large actual content updates but loads of optional microtransaction material.
The F2P content contains the license to hunt Whitetail Deer, Pheasant and three kinds of Rabbit only. As of the latest major Patch you now get a shotgun for free as well, so the grindwall for hunting the rabbits and pheasant is gone. One ingame currency "GMS" can be obtained by doing missions like "Track a Mule Deer", "Harvest a Mule Deer", "Spot a Whitetail Deer". Its a pretty useless currency though.
The payment model lets you pay per month in order to get a license for all animals, so think of it as a "cheap MMO-type payment". However in contrast to MMOs, actual content updates to be played by you as a license holder appear only a few times a year. On the other hand these updates usually contain a new hunting reserve with new animals, so they offer quite some content.
There are a lot of weekly minor updates with new guns, clothes and other equipment not really needed for playing the game though.
In my opinion thehunter is a well-made hunting simulator with decent animal behavior and very well made highly detailed hunting reserves.
The negative points I want to mention are random fps-drops in certain areas of the map which many players seem to encounter, "old animals" seem a bit lacking in texture quality compared to the new ones as well as "old reserves" are not as diverse and different from each other as the more recent ones. Some reserves are considered lackluster by a majority of the playerbase due to "recycling" of animals, e.g. the Australia reserve only contains the kangaroo as a specifically australian animal.
Some content patches in the past caused problems for players to connect in multiplayer games.
If there is no sale going I can not recommend buying a membership via the Ingame Store at all.
Instead, I highly recommend to get the DVD Version of 2013 for ~10 € which is a far better deal.
Basically this DVD Version comes with everything you need in contrast to the ingame-store sets. Even if you want to extend your membership, the DVDs offer much more.
For some animals, callers are quite handy, so you might want to plan another ~10€ for callers. For fox and coyote I think the "Jackrabbit caller" is essential, for the rest of the callers you dont own it is really dependant on your playstyle.
The same goes for any more "advanced" hunting clothing.
To summarize, I think buying a DVD-Version which offers a fair deal, if you can not get the 2013 Version you will need ~5€ for a decent big-game hunting rifle, depending on the ongoing sales.
Important:
Do not buy any of the starter packs unless the largest one gets a hefty discount on Steam, because the other ones will leave you with the lack of a big-game rifle as well and are lackluster in value proposition compared to buying any DVD Version.
One thing that should be mentioned here is goose and duck hunting. Though you can find those animals without any special equipment, you will need this equipment should you want to hunt birds in large scale.
Since geese and ducks require dummies and a special hunting setup you need ~15 €, depending on the current sales for a goose or a duck setup, so these act as "DLCs".
Most of the "Cabelas" Hunting  games are just mass animals shooters, the "Cabelas Big Game Hunter Pro Hunts" is not bad though, just simplified mechanics.
If you enjoy the detailed landscape and the "slow" gameplay, you might want to look into "Fishing Planet". This one actual is true F2P, but comes with a high grindwall.

Reign of Kings has a simple plot and that is gather, craft, storm the King's castle, execute the king and finally claim the throne. The concept is bad, but could be better if they actually tried. Not much thought process in terms of gameplay and execution.
Reign of Kings has been released for going on a year now and in its current state is still an Early Access title. My 1 hour playtime is more than enough to see how Codehatch works. Yes, let's not forget the amateur development team is Codehatch. Remember when they release Starforge unfinished and abandoned Starforge afterwards? I still remember. Codehatch made me realize that I don't need to be so trusting with Early Access titles, and I thank them for being nothing but scam artists. You might ask, "Then why are you here buying another one of their games?" - Well, this game is dirt cheap, so dirt cheap it is worth $4 or less on certain websites, not $19. Still trying to think of reasons why Reign of Kings is $19 when this game is worth no more than $6~$9 in its current state. Not sure who would pay full price for Reign of Kings in the first place, not me!
My first impressions when first logging in is my character (camera) uncontrollably started spinning. I'm sitting here like, "what?". So I searched to see if anyone else had the same issue and they did. Apparently having a controller plugged in will cause this and you have to unplug it for it to stop. Ultimately that is no solution if you didn't want to unplug your controller.
After I had to be forced to unplug my controller, I joined the same server with my friend. We were farming and all of a sudden some laggy chinese guy on a US server started coming after us fully geared. He killed us both. After that incident he started camping, killed my friend again whilst I'm avoiding him. Don't forget we're new with no gear. Afterwards my friend gets stuck, and with no way in becoming unstuck he had to be forced offline and we haven't played since then.
During that time I found out that gathering, you start off with a crappy axe to gather wood (and other resources), but gathering other things is basically running around pressing the pick-up action button. Items like clay, wood and other certain resources have to be gathered with a tool (I never tried unarmed). Crafting is just a big scroll menu with categories and there's no search bar in the said crafting menu (if there is I missed it).
I honestly never got to try the "fun stuff" since we could never get that far. We'd either be killed by a higher tier player and camped, become stuck with no way in getting unstuck (unless we were killed) or we cannot find certain resources because they are very scarce for some reason. Yes, we could go on servers with 0 players, but what's the point? It is a multiplayer game and a pretty dead one.
Reign of Kings probably had potential when they were very actively developing it or when it first announced. It appears this game had a nice spotlight on it at the start where everyone had "fun" in it, but those days are over. The game's current state is awful, especially when they had plenty of time to make it better than it is; not much content, gathering, crafting and combat are VERY simple and safe, servers are almost always empty or very low populated, and it feels, yet again that Codehatch released their own game too soon since Reign of Kings should still be in Early Access.
2/10.
It might appear that I'm very aggressive, but Codehatch has always been a disappointment. They are such a disappointment, I'd rather write a positive review about No Man's Sky and praise Hello Games. Avoid Codehatch in the future.

I can highly recommend this game. For those who are already familiar with the mobile version:
All additional content is or will be included but has to be unlocked during play. The visual presentation was adjusted for the PC and looks way better. The world map looks beautiful, and the country pages now include a textual description and camera surveillance. You get much more stats about how your plague is performing, and as a bonus, you can save and load your game at any time. Other gaming modes like speed run and campaigns will be added, but those seem to be added to the mobile version as well.
For those new to the game:
You get a quick to play, casual strategy game with an interesting theme and excellent visual presentation. On first glance, it may seem repetitive to just having to add perks until all humanity is wiped out. But the different plague types and random events require different strategies. It's quite rewarding when you succeed with your plague on the harder difficulty levels. As an additional challenge you can try to get the over 50 achievements, some of those are very interesting and require additional thought.
Pricing and Early Access:
I won't discuss the price as it is a personal choice of how much one wants to pay for a game. But compared to many other mobile ports, this one stands out because it was adjusted to PC standards and not just copied over. Also, for an early access game, it is quite stable and the basic gameplay is already there. I did not encounter any bugs, there are of course some very minor issues.
Summary:
If you are on the edge, and the price is ok, then buy it without any doubt. If it seems too expensive, then at least get and try the mobile version. There will be a steam sale eventually ;-)

State of Extinction is developed and published by Stone Pixel Games LLC. Since it’s their first Steam project and within Early Access stage to boot, I shall consider this a preview rather than fully fledged review. Alas, I shall judge it by the same standard I use, in regards to my reviewed video games.

Fetch quests. This is the phrase which seems to describe the vast majority of time you shall spend in State of Extinction. Even if I am a history buff, I can accept some…artistic liberties undertaken by those which try to make history more digestible for the masses. History has little to do with truth, since it is always manipulated by those which control power under its many forms. And yet fiction it is not. The game I’m analyzing today? It brings together both hominids and dinosaurs within the same time frame. Dinosaurs existed during Mesozoic Era (250 to 65 million years ago) while hominids (early humans) did not evolve from primates until about 3 million years ago. The latest stages of evolution, Homo sapiens and Homo neanderthalensis not appearing until about 200,000 years ago. I mentioned those two since even within this game, the “valley of Neander” is referenced by some of the NPCs, yet it is debatable how closely did these subspecies interact.
History lesson’s over though. State of Extinction at first glance seems like a generic role playing game and since it’s still in Early Access, I guess I’ve seen less than half of what it promises to show upon the full release. I could only select one of the three tribes available when you start a new game. The Tribe of the Wolf. Not much to spoil regarding the story or characters since it plays all too familiar. A coming-of-age tale, perhaps used also as an allegory to the human evolution at that early stage. You are a warrior which must learn to adapt to your surroundings, craft weaponry and tools and even barter from time to time for basic resources. But you can forage plenty by yourself while you’re out fulfilling another repetitive fetch quest. You will eventually prove your worth to the tribe elders and “level up” through Intellect Points that function like classic experience gain in most RPGs. I couldn’t really say you’re becoming overpowered too fast since at the very start of the game you’ll be mostly running away from threats, rather than facing them head on. Basically, if you get attacked by not one but two dire wolves or bears at the same time, you’re better off reloading a save before they certainly maul you into a tasty snack. I think we can rephrase that as “unbalanced difficulty”.
Ideas were fine, but the way they are implemented is not helped in any way by the rather limited selection of audiovisual assets. Yes, even the sounds are repetitive and “character dialogues” are little more than a few growls that are somehow subtitled into coherence. Fully 3D environment but the Store Page official screenshots do not really reflect what you’re playing. A barely functioning control scheme doesn’t improve the situation either. Keyboard is there, supported but rarely used since you can get by, simply using the mouse.
+ Interesting setting and characters, even if not historically accurate
+ Shows potential once it leaves Early Access
+ Steam Achievements.
- Simplistic and occasionally unresponsive control scheme
- Overpriced
- Repetitve gameplay and sounds
- No Steam Trading Cards
I didn’t expect State of Extinction to be as polished as Far Cry Primal (obvious budget differences) but I did wish it would have been less phantasmagoric and dreary at the same time. If someone who takes a fringe interest in this prehistoric period got so bored by it, I cannot fathom what someone who’s completely clueless about early humans, might consider of this title. Just another fairy tale? Unacceptable.

State of Extinction. What can I say? I had high hopes for this game. While they weren't shattered, they have reached levels as obtainable as the max flying height of penguins, (spoiler alert: penguins dont fly).
First, let me just say, that I can overlook a lot of bugs/issues that come with any alpha/beta game that is released regardless of its closed/open state.
Havins said that, be aware that, like many alphas, betas, and even final releases, State of extinction does mave many bugs/issues. Clicking issues, which this game is very dependant upon mouse clicks, less keyboard imput, definitely exist.
The mini-map for me is a very big issue. Its a static map, but many times, while I am heading in, what I believe to be northeasterly direction, the mini-map shows me heading somewhere completely different. I could be more forgiving of this if the directions it said were opposite of where I could see myself going, unfortunately it didnt even seem that way. There is not even an indicator on the mini-map giving you a clue as to which way the mini-map believes is north. The good news is, the landscape doesnt change, so there is an option to turn off the mini-map, which I recommend given its current awful state.
Graphics look like they were pulled from a freeware/shareware database. Forgivable, I suppose. But given how much more advanced we have become technologically since the 90's, I expected more/better. So to me, it seems lazy to go with half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥graphics.
While I can forgive lack-luster graphics and some bugs and/or issues, For me story line needs to be not just compelling, but strong. Initially, the storyline is compelling, but as you progress, you find a lot of filler, that doesnt really seem to lead to a better story so far.
The dialogue is the worst for me. Every audible dialogue is, "blah blah blah, bblah bla, blah, blah, bla". Seriously, the audio provided is some one mumbling, and not even kind of english. It is deliberately not intended to be comprehensible. They didnt even have the decency to try to make a pretend primitive language and have voice actors do their jobs. While this may have been done to save money, it almost completely destroys any chance for immersion.
The written dialogue isn't a whole lot better. Its almost as if they hired a screenwritter to write how primitive people would have talked, and he looked at native american tribes, and studied that half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and then wrote with that limited knowledge. Sometimes its hard to even understand what they are trying to say because of the cryptic way they try to write. I fear that this will create a lot of issues with younger players who see what potential the game does have.
My last issue is with the quest log. Its very frustrating to be told, "You need to go make something. To do that, you will need to get this and that. So you leave the game for whatever reason. You come back later, dont recall what you needed to gather, so you open you questlog, and bam! It tells you you need to make this item, but not what you need to gather.  At his time, and I dont know if this is planned to be included later or not, there is no way to remove a quest and restart it. See the potential issues?
I personally couldn't recommend anyone purchase this game at this time.
I will come back and play this game in a year, after there have been hopefully 10-15 updates to fix many of the issues, and, again hopefully, they will have used some of the money obtained by early backers to actually improve and fix the game from its current state.
