Early Access Watcher Public Service Announcement
Game: State of Extinction
Update Version: Initial Release (November 29, 2016)
Disclosure: This game copy was bought by the reviewer.
Gameplay Footage:
Before I get into this, I want to give a shout out to the musical score used for the game. It isn't the best in the world, but I found it to be quite fitting.
This game managed to peak my interest by the unique setting, but I also discovered the mechanics of the game seem to follow in the primitive footsteps of Early Man. Following a decent, if not a bit frustrating first hour, problems began to arise that made trying to progress past chapter three a living nightmare. Trying to interact with characters and items can require three to five clicks to either activate the conversation or to pick up the items. This is once you manage to get close enough to them.
Quests have an issue of updating properly, which was fixed as soon as I returned to the main menu and returned to the save. Enemies also have a strange issue of attacking you even if they are dead. The best example comes from the Mystic Wolf (killed to acquire its' pelt) remained targetable when I tried to grab the pelt and still did damage when I moved closer to grab the pelt (which took eight clicks). Bears also have the same issue, including the Great Bear needed for a special story quest that produced a terrible audio bug upon its' death. Regardless of where I went, the high pitch growling continued for a good ten minutes before I decided to just restart again. When I went back to kill him again (it respawned following my completion of the quest which I assume is intended) and did the same thing, except it ended after a minute or two.
Prior to this, I managed to get stuck behind a NPC after talking to him about making a spear for a specific reason. I talked to him in an accessible space, only to then be teleported behind him once the conversation was complete. This happened twice and thankfully didn't on the third attempt. I somehow managed to get stuck between two rocks. The rocks disappear later as the story progresses, but at the time they were positioned to block access to another area.
I am going to continue attempting to press forward with this title, but as of right now the combat feels unresponsive at times, glitches really impede patience, interacting is a major pain and the main interface is awkward.
This has been a EAW PSA.

Let me just say, that State of Extinction is a newly launched Early Access game, and is currently available on Steam. What I talk about now could and In my opinion will definitely change in time. That is why I write Journal entries, to kind of document it. Please enjoy the impression.
ss1‘ State of Extinction ‘ is an early access  game by Stone Pixel Games. SoE is also an isometric, survival type of game and was released on November 29th, 2016. Games like these usually take on first person point of views, so it’s refreshing to see a company try something new. For this Journal entry, my playtime was a little over an hour. In SoE you still search for materials, explore, and craft items like it’s peers. But here, here you do it all the while traversing a lush green forest/jungle themed area. So pretty much there isn’t too much of a difference, except it’s caveman-esque period.
At the start you are given a choice of three different classes, Instinct, Intuition, and Intelligence. The ‘Instinct’ class is the strong ‘Warrior’ type, ‘Intuition’ an Assassin type that can set traps, and last ‘Intelligence’, the Sorcerer. I chose the Instinct class, but I didn’t play long enough to get a grasp on what he could do. When you are choosing your class, you can also set a mode that gives you just one life, and if you die, your character is deleted. Diablo fans rejoice.
State of Extinction
The story starts out with a Bible tone that quickly gives way to a story about the coming of age. You and your rival Kaar, are to take a test to pass into manhood. During the tutorial phase you learn of the test, and meet Kaar’s instructor, who teaches all kinds of great survival lessons. Again, I only played an hour of the game so I didn’t get much farther than that.
Once in the game you are put through a lengthy tutorial that was actually fun to play, unlike most games where you are just dying just to pass it get. You will learn the basics to survive, first thing is getting a weapon in your hands by collecting a branch, and crafting it. Learning to craft an actual useful weapon you can use comes later as does learning how to heal.
That’s my first experience of playing ‘State of Extinction‘ Overall it was a fun one. In my next Journal Entry I’ll write more about of the story, music, graphics, and of course most importantly in my opinion, GAME PLAY.
3/5

Tap Tap Infinity is an incremental clicker/idle game.
Click to deal damage to enemies. Earn gold. Spend that gold on upgrades to your click damage. Purchase automatic damage over time, and upgrade that. Unlock special skills and use them to defeat enemies faster, or earn more gold per kill, and invest that gold into more upgrades so you can kill faster and get more gold to invest so you can kill faster and get more gold to invest so you can kill faster and get more gold to invest so you can kill faster and get more gold to invest so you can kill faster and get more gold to invest so you can kill faster and get more gold to invest...
Yep. It's one of these types of games. There's a prestige system that gives you a special currency that you can use to purchase various powerups that do a lot of things, such as decreasing skill cooldowns, increase gold dropped, increase dps.
To many people, this type of game seems boring. To those people, I'd suggest peeking at a few games like this to see what the appeal is. It's basically a distillation of most game genres that have some form of upgrade system, such as obtaining better gear or gaining levels and powerful perks.
Personally, I like these types of games. They satisfy that reward center in the brain. It's a perfect example of the Skinner Box.

On the odd occasion when people ask me "
", I'll often answer with Factorio. It is one of the best examples to give as a counterpoint to "early access doesn't work". It is addictive to the point of me wanting to call this review "Cracktorio" instead.
When I get asked that, I respond with another question: "*Have you played modded Minecraft?*" Minecraft mods change that game massively, especially with tech mods. It changes from an explore/dig/build game into an automation game. If people have played modded Minecraft, then I'll continue with
Factorio takes that automation urge, and refines it to a point. You're dropped into a near-empty world, gather some wood, coal, iron, and copper, and craft things. Place down a burner drill, feed it some of the coal you mined, and it'll do the mining for you. Craft a few more of those, craft some belts to carry the mined resources to some furnaces you've set up, and use inserters to put the resources in. Great, you've automated smelting!
All this coal consumption is getting tedious, time to look into electricity. Before long, you've got some boilers hooked up to steam engines, producing power to run fancy electric inserters. However, you're still crafting things in your hand. It takes time, time you could spend setting up more mining and furnaces.
Time for some research. Plop down some labs, make some science packs, pop them in the labs, give them power, and before you know it you have an assembler chain that is producing all of the green circuit boards you'll ever need,
.
---
I won't go into more detail than this. The first playthough of Factorio should always be done alone, without getting advice from others. You learn why when playing it.
Right at the top of this, I said that Factorio is an example of Early Access done right.
Every Friday, the developers make a new
(FFF) post. These aren't short "we're still workign on the game" posts, either. As of writing this, the latest one,
, goes into the optimizations they were making that week.
is about redesigning the rails to prevent weird overlapping. This communication, combined with their activity on the official forums and other forums, is essential.
It's not just developer updates that make this a success, it's game updates too. Who knew that people liked playing games? Updates to Factorio come whenever they are ready. They contain bug fixes from reports given on the forums. They contain things talked about in the FFFs. Every once in a while, they contain surprises that weren't talked about.
Bugs in this game, apart from Biters and Spitters, are rare. I, in my *many* hours of play, have only encountered one bug that affected gameplay. It was that switching hotbars would crash the server if playing multiplayer. It was fixed in the next couple of days when a bug fixing update came out. That's the kind of actions all game developers should take, Early Access or not.
[h2]Pros[/h2]
* Engaging
* Polished gameplay

[h2]Neutral[/h2]
* Not going to go on sale
* Some like this, because it will stay the same price because it won't go on sale a day after they buy it.
* Some don't like it because $20 is too much for them right now.
[h2]Cons[/h2]
* Self-control
* You'll need it, otherwise you may not sleep tonight.

This is a hidden object puzzle game. Most gameplay consists of rotating an object in the center of the screen to locate a secret button or compartment which unlocks the next secret and allows you to proceed. I know some people love hidden object games, but others may be turned off by the fact that the entire game consists of searching for something you can click on.
The game's biggest weakness is its mouse controls. Clicking and dragging the mouse across the entire screen is normally not enough to completely rotate an object, so you'll often be dragging the mouse back and forth across your desk several times to see the other side of something. Clicking is unresponsive since it ignores mouse input every time it animates anything... and it animates everything.
As I suggested in the above dialogue, the objects themselves are a bit ridiculous and don't really make any kind of real-world sense. The key to this sort of puzzle game would normally be in trying to figure out what a mysterious object was used for and drawing logical conclusions about its function. However, when the objects themselves would serve no internally-consistent purpose, the game reduces to randomly prodding the object until the next puzzle activates.
The good graphics and atmosphere don't make up for the poor puzzle design and controls.

Thoust hast cometh across the 7th wonder of the known world! Ok, seriously, you can turn your character into the child of the hunchback of notre dom and Grendel and become the king by sitting on the throne after getting to the castle first and building layers of walls across the sword bridge without killing a single person, or any current kings. I played this with a group and we took the character creation reletively seriously. The game is somewhat remeniscent of minecraft but with better graphics, no advanced circuitry and musical instruments. Play this game, make a long horn and walk up to someone. Once you advance far enough to make stone castles and full plate armor, you can then start kidnapping people. Once this is achieved, you can throw them in the stocks and whip them repeatedly while your fellow noble knights dance naked around him and smash on drums like someone having a seizure.
The great thing about this game is that in order to break into a stone structure, you actually have to build a trebuchet and skillfully aim boulders to take down walls. To this day, I only have fold memories of the game and the community, while sometimes strange and a bit overly kinky, has always been welcoming and fun.

Well, Modern Warfare 2 is maybe one of the best opus in the COD series.

Why this is one of the only CoD games that truly deserve your time and money: For the first time in the Call of Duty series, the infamous veteran mode is actually a fair challenge. Enemy placement is rational, said enemies are no longer just aimbots with brain damage, and they no longer endlessly respawn. The visuals (at least for the time) are impressive. Especially the character models.
There are some great over the top moments to experience during the campaign. You'll fly over a mountain on a snow mobile, chase the enemy down the rapids in a speedboat, and of course; listen to Prisoner 627's suicide run speech towards the end of the game. An awesome bit of sillyness.
Whilst not dragging the game down too much, the multi-player side is, unfortunately, a different story. Unlike CoD4, there are no dedicated servers, so matches suffer from bad lag spikes, and good luck finding anyone playing outside of team deathmatch and free for all. Spec Ops is the better option. This mode allows you to play an alternative version of select single player missions from both Modern Warfare, and Modern Warfare 2. Either solo or with a friend. My personal favourite is Hidden. A co-op version of the Chernobyl mission from CoD4.
This is the last Call of Duty title (with the exception of maybe Black Ops 2) that actually tried to evolve the franchise above the level of an interactive movie. Definitely gets my recommendation.

I enjoyed Clicker Heroes. I put a few months into the game. As of posting this, I have every achievement in the game (and on steam) except for 3400 and 3600. I'm on my final run, just passing 3260. I expect to be done with this game completely very soon. What clicker game will I play next?
Tap Tap Infinity is definitely my choice. When I saw that Clicker Heroes was nearing its end for me, I downloaded Tap Tap Infinity, Time Clickers, and Crusaders of the Lost Idols all on the same night. Each of my clicker games had its own quadrant on my screen (best night of my life if you ask me). This kept going on for maybe a day, then I closed down CotLI. I'll get back to it in the future, but it's too slow paced for my liking.
Time Clickers and Tap Tap Infinity were the 2 remaining. After browsing and considering every achievement, every upgrade, and every aspect of the game in general, I decided to stick with Tap Tap Infinity. Clicker Heroes got stale after 97% of the achievements, Crusaders of the Lost Idols is too slow, and Time Clickers is just too damn massive. Thousands and thousands of time cube upgrades. Weapon cubes weren't even near my horizon.
Tap Tap Infinity has just the right amount of content, a well-balanced fairness to it regarding gems especially, and you progress pretty quickly, which is ideal for an incremental game. Also praise the left/right mouse clicking!
If you've played Cookie Clicker, AdVenture Capitalist, or Clicker Heroes and you enjoyed it at least a little bit, try this one out. If you like it, great! If you don't, you lose nothing.
If you like idle clicker games, this is a decent one to waste some time on.

As someone who couldn't check on the game as often as it would really require to "maximize" my progress, it was still fairly forgiving and updated often enough in the 4~5 months it took to clear this game completely.  It ran through quite a few upgrades since the time I started the game including the addition of Soul Links, which was very helpful.
The cash shop in the game is very fair and not required at all (outside of wanting to support the developer) for idling in this game - though it definitely speeds up your playthrough.  For those who are trying to complete all the achievements, a few of them are tedious and require micro managing the idle game (namely the 3,000 gifts clicked on achievement) which is why the game took as long as it did for me to complete fully (this and my inefficient use of spells as well).
Featuring 5,000 levels with many repeating sprites that steadily grow bigger, there are a few one time only boss monsters that are a bit satisfying to clear.  Plenty of ways to upgrade and branch out though the priorities are pretty straightforward now with the inclusion of Soul Links, which should always be aimed for first in order to gain more Soul Gems (the paid for currency) to speed up things.
On a platform where more and more options out there now that the genre is increasingly becoming more saturating... it's a solid idle game that can stand up on it's own.

I've played some clickers up to this moment, and I can admit, Tap Tap Infinity is not the most original, or breath-catching of them. In fact, I even agree with the point that it looks so much like "Cliker Heroes" title. Only better.
Let's just say about clickers in general: they are little games with tendency to keep on going, like, forever. The good side of those games, as I see it, is that you can leave the clicker game going, and even close the game window, and yet it will be playing - for you. All clicker games are about numbers - you starting with 1 coin, then, after 1 hour, you're operating millions, then you learning about googoles... and bigger numbers. At some point, I bet, the Graham number can be achieved through some clicker game...
So! As I thought when first started some clickers, the process is easy enough - you start the game, making first moves (clicks), and then you go to your business, and the game running itself forward, making some achievements with numbers on its way. Funny thing, but only Tap Tap Infinity was good enough in that. All other clickers after some point getting more and more deserving for your time, to the point where you'll be mindlessly clicking the mouse all day long. All - but not Tap Tap Infinity! Yeah, despite the name. Getting controversial here...
With some latest addons, it become one of the most fanciest clickers I've met. It is more stable, and more fair than "Clicker Heroes", where you just can't beat the latest levels normally. All big numbers are messed up in your precious "Clicker Heroes", dear fans, and I really can't even feel sorrow for you, if you still climbing to the upper levels, but not able to achieve them!
Okay, let's summarise: Tap Tap Infinity is your standard clicker game, one of those which I actually can recommend to play if you're wandering what's it is all about. Although if you want all 100 achievements, be prepared to spend dozens of hours on that (I was playing offline mostly, so don't think it is as fast as 14 hours to beat the game). And, besides time, which is still more precious than all those clicker games, to start with... If you still want to try a piece, don't play it with your best mouse (the one which is worth more than 10$). Clicker games are made for killing touchscreens and mouses, keep that in mind.
My mark will be 6/10. Almost a normal game, and free-ware! But really, better play something more mind-catching.

F2P is a Demo-Mode only. Solid hunting game with detailed hunting grounds, cheap MMO-like payment model, rare but large actual content updates but loads of optional microtransaction material.
The F2P content contains the license to hunt Whitetail Deer, Pheasant and three kinds of Rabbit only. As of the latest major Patch you now get a shotgun for free as well, so the grindwall for hunting the rabbits and pheasant is gone. One ingame currency "GMS" can be obtained by doing missions like "Track a Mule Deer", "Harvest a Mule Deer", "Spot a Whitetail Deer". Its a pretty useless currency though.
The payment model lets you pay per month in order to get a license for all animals, so think of it as a "cheap MMO-type payment". However in contrast to MMOs, actual content updates to be played by you as a license holder appear only a few times a year. On the other hand these updates usually contain a new hunting reserve with new animals, so they offer quite some content.
There are a lot of weekly minor updates with new guns, clothes and other equipment not really needed for playing the game though.
In my opinion thehunter is a well-made hunting simulator with decent animal behavior and very well made highly detailed hunting reserves.
The negative points I want to mention are random fps-drops in certain areas of the map which many players seem to encounter, "old animals" seem a bit lacking in texture quality compared to the new ones as well as "old reserves" are not as diverse and different from each other as the more recent ones. Some reserves are considered lackluster by a majority of the playerbase due to "recycling" of animals, e.g. the Australia reserve only contains the kangaroo as a specifically australian animal.
Some content patches in the past caused problems for players to connect in multiplayer games.
If there is no sale going I can not recommend buying a membership via the Ingame Store at all.
Instead, I highly recommend to get the DVD Version of 2013 for ~10 € which is a far better deal.
Basically this DVD Version comes with everything you need in contrast to the ingame-store sets. Even if you want to extend your membership, the DVDs offer much more.
For some animals, callers are quite handy, so you might want to plan another ~10€ for callers. For fox and coyote I think the "Jackrabbit caller" is essential, for the rest of the callers you dont own it is really dependant on your playstyle.
The same goes for any more "advanced" hunting clothing.
To summarize, I think buying a DVD-Version which offers a fair deal, if you can not get the 2013 Version you will need ~5€ for a decent big-game hunting rifle, depending on the ongoing sales.
Important:
Do not buy any of the starter packs unless the largest one gets a hefty discount on Steam, because the other ones will leave you with the lack of a big-game rifle as well and are lackluster in value proposition compared to buying any DVD Version.
One thing that should be mentioned here is goose and duck hunting. Though you can find those animals without any special equipment, you will need this equipment should you want to hunt birds in large scale.
Since geese and ducks require dummies and a special hunting setup you need ~15 €, depending on the current sales for a goose or a duck setup, so these act as "DLCs".
Most of the "Cabelas" Hunting  games are just mass animals shooters, the "Cabelas Big Game Hunter Pro Hunts" is not bad though, just simplified mechanics.
If you enjoy the detailed landscape and the "slow" gameplay, you might want to look into "Fishing Planet". This one actual is true F2P, but comes with a high grindwall.

Great game, not too challenging, a great plot and excellent artwork. This game is based off of Edgar Allan Poe's Gold Bug, though it does take its liberties, understandable since the original story is pretty short. LeGrand is a character in the original story; there is a Newfoundland dog in the original story; in the original story, the protaganist finds Captain Kidd's treasure buried under a tree with the help of an encrypted parchment - the message of which is the exact same as the one in the game. There is where the similarities end. The creator of this game took great liberties to thicken the plot of this rather plain story, and we are much obliged to him (or her) for that. Also, Poe fans like myself know that Dupin, the detective who is your partner in the game, is the legendary French detective Poe created for Murders in the Rue Morgue, so very cleverly done by the creator of this game to combine two Poe classics into one. This game is fun to play, although I wish the puzzles were more difficult, as they are quite easy in this game compared to other point-and-click games I've played. Overall, an enjoyable game.

If you enjoyed Ragnarok, go right ahead. If you enjoy grindy, combat-focused games, and are willing to endure a few server problems here and there, go right ahead too.
It's okay. I've heard that people that play for the time that I've played (8.7 hours so far) and actually know what they're doing (and I assume also have friends) can get somewhere around level 100 or so. I only got to level 58, but the experience was okay. I'm a lone noob, I don't mind.
I got a single incredibly broken moment after being frozen by an enemy. After the freeze time ran out, my character was still stuck. I had to wait for my pet to finish the remaining foes and then go back to the character selection screen so that I may continue playing normally.
This being my second day playing, I can say the South American server is mediocre. Not bad, not good, just mediocre. Today was the only day I experienced a few spikes of extreme lag, with my character suddenly appearing meters away from where she was, and everything I had done in the past seconds just being nullified. Most of the time the server functions properly. Only had one time when I got disconnected during a transition between screens. The main town lags a lot,
. No crashes whatsoever. There were no game-breaking bugs either. Almost everything I experienced is functioning properly.
The story is bad, just plain bad. I thought it wasn't going for a “THE CHOSEN ONE” trope until it got to a certain point where it did. You are the player, and you are the only Savior. That is, until you notice you're surrounded by hundreds of other Saviors in the main city. Whatever, we're used to this. Even if it didn't have this trope, though, it's just a terrible story. The world they built isn't as colorful and vibrant as Ragnarok's, but it gets the job done. I'd love if they took more influence from the Mana series instead of relying so heavily on Ragnarok.
Gameplay-wise, it's grindy. The majority of quests are some variation on “kill monsters to get this item”. Then you use the items you got on altars, wells, ponds, whatever... a mini-boss appears (I assume those are mini-bosses, as they are so easy to kill and so ubiquitous; there's a boss every five minutes or so), you kill it, you finish the quest. You go back and receive your reward, then move to a different area. Few quests are a bit more creative. There was this quest where I had to dress as a demon, fool other demons into going to an altar, and break their souls. That's the most creative one off the top of my head so far.
The game can be confusing. They barely even teach you the controls at the start, so I had to find out for myself that they were going for a QWERTY/ASDFGH/ZXC kind of thing. Being used to MMOs like ArcheAge, I was a tad bit confused at first. It's not bad, it works fine, it's just that I actually had to go to the settings to find out that Z is a normal attack, and ASD... are for skills. I wasn't able to understand the color scheme for quest markers on the map yet, and sometimes quest markers just don't show up, a weird (albeit rare) glitch.
The characters are cute. I went for a Peltasta, and I was glad at first that the costume for them is quite cute. But the female version has a skirt that raises up to the goddamn sky when you walk in certain directions, revealing the character's panties. Of course, you're not forced to use the class costume, so I just went back to using the standard swordswoman one. Customization at the start is very poor. You cannot choose your character's skin tone, eye color, and not even their hair color. Colored lenses can be bought, but they don't make much of a difference. Hairstyles come with a set color that you have to change with a dye later in the game. Each dye can be acquired in a completely different manner; or you can buy them, I guess. But at least giving players a few color choices at the start would be nicer, in my opinion.
Don't expect this game to have any major weight towards other areas that aren't PvE or PvP related. The markets are extremely simple, the economy is extremely simple and centralized, and there's little reason in seeking classes that aren't combat-focused in some way. As expected, this game is all about the combat. Even the social features are quite toned down. For an instance, you need to be of a class specific to the Swordsman tree (Templar) to be the leader of your own guild. I don't know who had that idea, but I think it's bad in many ways.

Well, Modern Warfare 2 is maybe one of the best opus in the COD series.
A very well written scenario, full of action and a graphic engine that ensures a good standard for its age.
Even in 2015, it's still fun to play.
Can't tell for the Multiplayer part, as I don't play online.
The Spec Ops mission are very nice as well, though sometimes very challenging especially if soloing them (Echo missions are mission impossible type...).
Overall, a very good modern FPS, focusing on the arcade part rather than the pure simulation like Arma series.

Why this is one of the only CoD games that truly deserve your time and money: For the first time in the Call of Duty series, the infamous veteran mode is actually a fair challenge. Enemy placement is rational, said enemies are no longer just aimbots with brain damage, and they no longer endlessly respawn. The visuals (at least for the time) are impressive. Especially the character models.
There are some great over the top moments to experience during the campaign. You'll fly over a mountain on a snow mobile, chase the enemy down the rapids in a speedboat, and of course; listen to Prisoner 627's suicide run speech towards the end of the game. An awesome bit of sillyness.
Whilst not dragging the game down too much, the multi-player side is, unfortunately, a different story. Unlike CoD4, there are no dedicated servers, so matches suffer from bad lag spikes, and good luck finding anyone playing outside of team deathmatch and free for all. Spec Ops is the better option. This mode allows you to play an alternative version of select single player missions from both Modern Warfare, and Modern Warfare 2. Either solo or with a friend. My personal favourite is Hidden. A co-op version of the Chernobyl mission from CoD4.
This is the last Call of Duty title (with the exception of maybe Black Ops 2) that actually tried to evolve the franchise above the level of an interactive movie. Definitely gets my recommendation.

Aside from visuals, this game is not significantly different from any other "idle" game you've seen before. Kill things, level up, unlock people to fight for you, eventually reset the whole thing and start over endlessly.  Upgrades are there, but like all of these idle games they're either going to take you weeks to get anywhere significant, or you're going to end up paying for them. I can't even call this a "pay to win" model because you never actually win. The game goes on forever.  So this and most other idle games become a test of your patience.  Are you willing to wait several hours or several days for that next tantalizing upgrade, or will the game convince you to spend your hard-earned cash?
I suppose it's good enough to kill a random few minutes here and there, so long as you don't get too invested in it.  That said, there's really not much in the way of gameplay.  You click things. You're never in any danger and there's no real risk. You just sit there and click things.  All of these games eventually get boring because you're just rehashing the same thing over and over again. It wouldn't be so bad if they weren't all so similar.

If you like Clicking, you like this game.
If you don't like clicking, you don't like this game.

It seems like a lot of comments don't understand this type of game.
I've played quite a few, mostly browser based instead of on Steam.
It's really not the kind of genre with new exciting things. It's an idling game.
You buy things and upgrade things in order to buy better things and better upgrades. There really isn't anything deeper than that. It's the kind of thing I play while rewatching stuff on netflix, or listening to music and podcasts. I tend to multitask online, not a good thing while listening to podcasts. Reading something and listening to people talk, and trying to pay equal attention to both... well, it doesn't work. And that's why I like this type of game. It's a fun thing to focus on.
I played Clicker Heroes first. I was excited to see this kind of game on Steam and it was much better than the browser based ones. Then when checking free games I saw they were adding even more! That was awesome!
So I started Tap Tap Infinity and instantly liked it more. The graphics, designs, menus.
I have 3 hours on Clicker Heroes, and over 100 on this. I can't really see either as being bad, but I prefered Tap Tap Infinity. It's not the type of genre where you should fully play through every game. You click things to get money to buy things to get more money to buy better things to make even more money to buy even... Well hopefully you see how the pattern goes.
I like Tap Tap Infinity. I like that these types of things are on Steam now. It gives me the added bonus of getting achievements. This definitely isn't a genre for everyone though. If it is, just find a game you like and stick with it. Have it as something on the background. Idling games are.. well, to idle.

Gotta say, I was very sceptical about this game at first, what with it not coming from Todd Howards amazing team in Bethesda Game Studios. But I gave it a try, and while their are definatly things that can still be improved upon, the core gameplay is very fun and engaging.  A particular high point for the game, for me at least, is the monster designs. Some of the model assets, for example the Mace of Molag Bal, are used from the team over at Bethesda, which is kinda disapointing. Yet the monster models are unique for the most part, and the ones that are being introduced for the first time are just awesome. The harvester is one of my favorite models. The crafting is unique, and actually has features that could be implemented in the original games, since the style of craft is something that has kinda always been lacking in previous titles. Getting into the game I was not pleased in seeing classes, as these games are notorius for being pretty open rpg's. That being said the class system in the game does not nessecarily break the old style, changes it sure. But as I started playing I realized that the class you pick really only decides your first 3 skill trees, and many many many more skill trees are available and not restricted by class. I feel like the team that worked on this section of the game did a farely well job in bringing balanced and fun skills into the game while giving the player the urge to replay as a different class. All the while mainting a good rpg element that doesn't break according to your class, in some cases it amplifies it actually. The gambling boxs can be quite bad at times, but there is a system that makes it so that if you lose enough times and still dont get what you want, you can turn the things you didnt want into an alterantive gem that you can then save up to get what you wanted out of the crates. Definatly a wallet emptier unless you get real lucky. Sadly I joined after a certain costume stopped being available so I do hope that, while it was advertised as limited time, it will soon be brought back as either a crate option.(Which I will dread having to go through that experiance) Or as people in various forms point out, will be brought back as a motif style, which would be less painful to deal with. The costume I speak of is of course the only morrowind inspired daedric armor in the game, the Telvanni Master Wizard costume. Mind you that I am a Redoran through and through, but that costume just looks so sick I hope the add it to my collection some day. If you made it through this review and are still not sure if you want to buy it or not I would recommend you give it a try. It is definatly fun to play and the quests for each zone are intriguing to say the least. If you still are unsure perhaps you could wait till a free week rolls by and give it a try then.

So, I finally decided to pick up Elder Scrolls Online this sale, since its been on my radar for a while, but due to some Steam review complaints about content and performance, was skeptical at first.
At first, I was a little confused by the initial download size (66GB in a single download... yeah, my poor internet took the whole DAY to download it :( ), but when I launched it, was very impressed with the performance. I am currently playing on a laptop with an i7-5500U, 8GB of RAM, and 1 TB HDD, with Intel HD Graphics 5500, and I can run it on Medium settings really smoothly. Granted, the CPU isn't that old, but is definitely not meant to run meaty games.
The content was also something I am very impressed with. I love the amount of quests available to you from the start, the fact that you level relatively quickly (am already level 8 with only a few quests really completed and with only 2 days of owning the game). You can acquire very powerful gear really quickly imo, and the dedication to lore detail is really nice.
All in all, I say Ill give it a solid 9/10, and its a purchase I definitely don't regret! So if you are on the fence with this one, I highly suggest you give it a shot! :)

TL;DR - (The first game I played on my Xbox 360 so slightly biased). The best singleplayer and coop in a cod game to date. When the game did have innovation and not trying to ♥♥♥♥ your wallets.
Performance - As you could expect good. Solid 60 fps and looks great. Nothing more to say it will run on a lot different setups.
Graphics - Good even now. Textures in places are weak which considering its linear they could do a better job of hiding.... It’s got a more of a realistic look with a whole colour palette to choose from than what other games in the franchise use; MW3 grey colour palette and Black Op 2 orange colour palette). Why they don’t vary colours is beyond me but at least this game does not.
Gameplay - Good. Guns actually have recoil, good punch through and feel military grade. Movement is also quite slick. Equipment as well as a selection of combat scenarios that vary up. Stealth sections are instant fail sections (for the most part) and if you’re good enough you can get through them loud. Less hand holding in this game. Feels more open and free though the odd corridor does loom over you from time to time but that’s expected.
Replayability - From the campaign there are some missions that you will want to play again as they were unique (Enemy Of My Enemy), just plain awesome (Cliff hanger) or just ♥♥♥♥ed up (No Russian). Spec Ops also has a range of mission modes to cater to different playstyles and different challenges. Get to Echo set of missions to know what I mean. And best of all try to collect 69 stars.
Conclusion - If you can’t tell this game is great for a reason. Cod at its peak when it was not rushed, lacked innovation and climbing over each other to take more money from you. Multiplayer is filled with hackers which is ♥♥♥♥ but singleplayer and spec ops make up for this and are worth for a great purchase.

I've been disappointed by "standard formula" MMOs (hotbar full of skills, AoEs, DPS, Raids, etc etc) for years, for a number of reasons. I pop into one every now and again, but always end up dropping it quickly. This game changed that trend.
First things first: it's adorable; there are a lot of aesthetic choices pointing toward cuteness and away from compulsory heterosexual sexuality or Generic Badassery. (there's plenty of each of those too, but options definitely exist!) Again and again I get the feeling that the designers of the game actually thought about the fact that women would want to play. As a result, there seem to be more women playing this game than I've encountered in other MMOs. Probably as a result of that, the community is, on the whole, less toxic than many other MMOs. There are still plenty of jerks, sure, but the ratio is a bit better.
And It's a nostalgia-fest. Fans of the Final Fantasy series in general will find a LOT to love here. Moogles everywhere! Your own personal chocobo, with dyeable feathers! A dude named Cid! Magitek armor that plays the FFVI overworld theme when you ride it! Materia, chocobo racing, the gold saucer! It has a great many lovely callbacks and easter eggs throughout, and yet still manages to feel distinctly like its own game. This is the Final Fantasy game you've been wanting to play for years.
And, honestly rating a distant third for me: the gameplay is really solid. The game design team here has learned from the mistakes of the MMO industry. Nearly everything is well-polished, and the whole experience hits the effort vs reward tradeoff really well. The dungeons get gradually more mechanics-driven and interesting, so that the learning curve feels just right. It's not perfect; there are definitely examples of poor game design. There are repetitive/predictable side quests and occasional game mechanics that aren't well explained. But it really feels like the best offering the genre has given us to date.

Plague Inc: Evolved is the port that cramped iPhone users have been waiting for, featuring all of the latest updates from the App version and has been well executed for the wider PC audience.
Although it's obvious that little has changed between platforms, because even on the PC this game will boil down to 'Click the bubbles to get points --> spend points on upgrades --> win'. Hopefully in the ongoing steam updates this game will branch out into new areas more suited for PC gaming, which it is more than capable of doing. There is little going on here in terms of a plot, because of its iPhone roots but again we can hope this will be addressed.
Having said all this, this game is incredibly addictive and although the £11.99 price tag is quite steep (as with most Early Access titles), you'll soon forget what was spent as you'll keep going until the game has been played, start to everything unlocked.
Essentially, you play as some mystery overview character who can freely create diseases, whether they be based on bacteria, viruses, parasites, etc. etc. and you can freely infect 1 person anywhere on the planet, following that it's your job to evolve the disease by spending "DNA Points" to help infect more and more people across the globe until you've managed to wipe out the human race.
Yes, you heard me right. It's not enough to infect everyone on the planet with some incurable nonsense like the common cold, but the game is truly won when you've evolved your pathogen of choice to have some pretty horrific symptoms and attempt to wipe out the entire human population.
There are various difficulty levels but regardless of which you choose, trying to achieve your goal is a challenge. This game bills itself as a "hyper realistic simulation" of what would actually happen which means you have to think of and respond to various scenarios, these range from fairly obvious (some countries having better healthcare than others) to more complex (the Olympic Games means alot of people being gathered together in one place, ideal place to spread the disease). These little variants and the specific characteristics of the pathogens gives this seemingly simple platform alot of variation which will keep you coming back to finish it and check out the new updates.
All in all, a good game, limited by the fact it's a mobile port, but will hopefully evolve into something more suited for PC gamers.

Rock of Ages is an interesting riff on the typical strategy game. Your goal is to get your boulder to the enemies gate and crash it down. But before you control your boulder, you and your opponent are given time to set up defenses like catapults (which damage boulders) or Elephants (which can push your boulder off the map). When the set-up time expires, you can control your boulder and try to dodge your enemies defenses to get to their gate. The singleplayer campaign is split with about 90% of these "break the opponents gate" maps and about 10% boss battles, which really don't work as well. The game also has a 2 player VS mode, as well as a race mode where you try to get to a goal as fast as you can. The game also has a cool Monty Python animation style in its cutscenes, and it has some oddball visual humor as well. It works well in Single Player, and the AI is pretty fair, but if you want to get some more legs out of the game it's worth it to play the VS mode with a friend.

Emily is Away is a visual novel game developed by a single developer, Kyle Seeley. The game was released for free in November 2015 and uses the popular visual novel game engine, Ren’Py.
The game takes place in a classic MSN chat window, with your friend, Emily. Gameplay is very simple. You are offered a selection of responses as to what you type to Emily and she will respond accordingly. This is done in such a way that you actually have type out on your keyboard (you can also type out complete garbage and the game will still type out your response.) I wish I could type as fast as you do in this game…especially back in those days.
There isn’t much to say about the graphics, you are simply just sat in front of a Windows XP computer and your UI is the computer screen. It is clean and easy to navigate outside of the chat window.  You can check out other character’s MSN profiles, and see their good ol song lyrics that they have on there…but sadly you cannot communicate with them. I would of personally liked to have seen that as a feature, especially with the other characters which are key to the plot.
Emily is Away has a story which is somewhat interesting, if anyone has ever had some sort of “one that got away” relationship with someone, this may strike a familiar tale with you. Personally I found it to be somewhat cringy in the way it plays out and the character Emily, comes across as someone who I wouldn’t want to associate with, but I given that  it gave me such strong feelings towards her, it means it is a well fleshed out character though. The story can be a little frustrating at times, since you only have three dialogue options at each interval, your feelings can not always be portrayed in the manner in which you want them to, which funnels your responses into three categories, one being pleasant, secondly being an on the fence response, or finally a blunt/unkind response, mainly you have one of these generic choices to make. The story does have a few elements that can change each time you play it, I played it through about six times and always saw something a bit different every time.  Without wanting to spoil too much, there is only one effective ending to the game, the way you get there can differ, but the outcome is always the same.
The audio in Emily is Away has very satisfying sound effects, the key strokes from typing come from that glorious sound of a mechanical keyboard, to Windows XP bootup/shutdown theme. There is no sound track, but you could always load up some Coldplay and get in the zone of your inner teenager from 2000 if you wanted….
A single play through the story will take you roughly 15-20minutes, the game is split into six chapters spread out over six years. This is a short game, but given that it has a couple of different storylines you can explore via different options and choices, you can easily get about ninty minutes play out this if you wanted.
Technically Emily is Away is problem free. Obviously you are going to be wanting to play on a keyboard given that it is set in a chat client, and the game can run on a potato if you wanted it to.
To sum up, now the game is Free to play, I can recommend people try it out, it’s a short enough game that you aren’t really going to miss those twenty minutes if you don’t enjoy it.  Visual novel fans will definitely enjoy it, and like I said above, a certain group of people will certainly want to check it out if they have ever found themselves on the wrong side of the friendzone.

Borderlands 2 is an outstanding game, I highly recommend getting the Game of The Year Edition.
Short:
Amazing CO-OP/Solo (up to 4 players) game with a good story, enjoyable gameplay and satisfying loot. Get this game if you like the shootie-shoots.
Not-as-short:
The game supplies a good amount of comedy and well written main story / side story to go with it. I still enjoy playing through it, and will keep enjoying myself playing it with many different friends.
The gameplay itself, depending on the character that you have chosen, is amazingly satisfying and has three skill trees that you spend your skill points in. The skill trees will change how your character plays and feels.
There are many types of randomly generated weapons (To an extend) that you can gain from killing bandits, monsters and/or robots. Like many RPG-like games the game gives out different quality weapons, ranging from a common (white) gun to legendary (orange) weapons. The legendary weapons will have special/unique attributes to them, making them rare but  very useful in combat.
The difficulty depends on how long and/or much you play it for. If you beat the game once and want more you can replay the story and fight stronger, different named/sometimes skinned, enemies for better loot.
There are three main difficulties. Normal Vault Hunter Mode (1st playthrough), True Vault Hunter Mode (2nd playthrough) and Ultimate Vault Hunter Mode (3rd playthrough). The last of the three has "Overpowered" Modifiers as well, that goes up to 8.
All the DLCs that you can purchase are pretty good and worth the money, but you can always wait for them to go on sale.
There is not a lot of character customization, but you can gain more skins and headpieces. As you do not make your OWN character but rather play a character from the story itself, I feel it has more than enough customization as it is.

Unexpectedly fun,
gameplay and in a lesser degree the story, is the final installment (currently) of the franchise. Having been disappointed with Call of Juarez®: The Cartel and even though it diverged from the first two games, I started Gunslinger with very little expectations but it turned out to be a quite fun experience.
The game is an FPS with a western theme. That means sixshooters, dynamite, duels, the whole shebang. It is interesting to note that this particular niche has not been explored fully in my opinion and it's actually kinda refreshing for an FPS game to try and bring this theme to life. Admittedly you're partially limited to history with regards to available weaponry and various game mechanics however Gunslinger manages to keep you entertained for as long as it lasts. You can only carry up to 2 weapons, choosing between 2 types of revolvers, 2 shotguns and 2 rifles along with dynamite. You can dual wield your pistols but that's just about it. Truth be told, you don't need a whole arsenal of weapons for this game. It would be nice sure but I also think it would kinda chip away from the overall spirit and narrative.
You'll be aiming your weapons on your foes, inspired and loosely based on famous outlaws of the 19th century American west. There's a few interesting environment to visit, from train robberies to lumber mills to town and swamps. Enemies will shoot at you and your mission of course is to kill them before they gun you down. There's a concentration meter which fills up as you get kills and acts essentially as a
mechanic. Getting kills also fills up a combo meter which grants extra experience which you can use to unlock certain passives and improved weapons to take down all those lawbreakers.
Then there's the whole duel mechanic which although was interesting it was also a little bit annoying to use. You have basically your focus and draw speed and you need to have both quite high in order to win a duel. Using it requires a little bit of ambidexterity and you can get a dishonorable kill if you fire before your duel partner does but it doesn't really matter in the overall scheme of the game. Dueling made for some awkward times and could definitely use some polish if the developers want to use it in a prospective sequel/spin-off/other franchise.
The game is strictly linear and by that is the most linear game I've ever played if that makes any sense. What I mean by that is the game will actively warn you when you deviate from the 'proper' path of the story. That means even
terrain you're not supposed to be on then you'll
killed. It kinda kills and break any sort of immersion of the game, to see your character die because you touched a body of water and frankly I don't see the reason for such a feature to be included in this game in the first place. The linearity of this game and the its short duration is otherwise countered by a new game plus mode and some collectibles to be found but for me I wasn't particularly interested in those things.
There are few quick time events which allow you to escape death or make for some awesome killing montages but fortunately they're spread out and do not define the game. If anything they made the game a little bit more interesting when they occurred.
The story is your typical western, badass guy out for revenge, filled with all kinds of cliches and tropes but fun nonetheless. It doesn't take itself too seriously, there's some nice features into the narrative like the world building in front of your eyes due to your characters being an unreliable narrator and changing his recount of the story as he goes through. There's a decent comedic value and it makes for a good plot device in the overall spirit of the game.
I'd say that Gunslinger is the best game in the franchise, it was really entertaining and fun to playthrough and despite its relative short length of ~5 hours, you'll be definitely enjoy if you're fan of the series or you want to explore the western FPS theme.

So far Reign of Kings has proven to be a very enjoyable survival/ building game set in a medieval world. I think it has been reviewed harshly by the community and while some of the criticism might be deserved, that does not mean it is a bad game. At the five-dollar (Canadian currency) price range that I bought it at, it was more than a bargain but even at $21.99 it's still worth the price.
The mechanic of becoming King by claiming the ancient throne is very interesting for those who are ambitions and like PVP and the ability to raise taxes on their subjects (other players.)
I believe one of the reasons Reign of Kings has been ill received by the community is because of the player base which is sometimes described as "toxic." There are a lot of completely inappropriate comments made and without any form of monitoring system that I have seen so far. Also, after I crashed at one point, I was told that it was because a player somehow crashed the server. This only happened to me once and since then I switched servers.
Unfortunately, another problem with the game is some of its bugs. I haven't encountered many but one was game breaking for me, until I had to switch servers: Every couple of minutes I kept "magically" spawning in a cage no matter what I did or where I went. This glitch would have made it impossible for me to play if there were no other servers.
Overall, despite its community and glitches, both of which I was able to get overcome, Reign of Kings is a decent game worth a try if you like games of the survival/building genre such as Rust.

Considering that I just bought it for $7.50 and it was made almost entirely by five people, this was a surprisingly kick♥♥♥♥♥game.
This game is not a well polished AAA title. There are six enemy types plus five bosses. The level design is simplistic and highly linear, and the game pace is set by road blocks that open after defeating a pre-determined number of enemy waves. Finishing a playthrough on Normal difficult took me less than three hours, and it's pretty clearly intended to played on a controller.
What this game does deliver is frantic, feel good hack n' slash action, and every time the pace relents a moment for a cut scene, you'll realize your fingers hurt from your white-knuckle grip on your controller. The English subtitles deliver charming doses of Engrish, the story is delightfully nonsensical, and the protagonist's fighting animations are glorious. And it's all set to an infectiously enthusiastic soundtrack.
This game plays like a low-budget weeby version of Lollipop Chainsaw, and I loved every moment of that.

SMITE is a fantastic game that takes the MOBA genre into a 3rd-person perspective; allowing me to implement the aiming, timing and skills I've gained from playing other games, like shooters, but with a stronger emphasis on strategy and team building-- making the combat fast and highly addictive.
Compared with League of Legends and Dota 2, it relies less on builds and the minions/creeps, but without removing those elements of strategy either. Rather than losing an integral part of what makes other MOBAs enjoyable and meaty, it replaces them with what gives games like first-person and third-person shooters depth. It panders to and compliments a different style, giving a different experience but in a familiar format.
Minions aren't as relevant late game as they are in Dota, but it feels right. You're playing the role of a god, and by the time you're at end-game, you have bigger threats to worry about-- other gods. It's satisfying to build a tank that 5 enemy gods and a tower, all at once, can't easily kill. It feels great to have your team expect you to clutch, but succumb to the pressure and miss all your shots. I love saving a teammate at the last possible moment by landing a perfectly aimed and timed kiss from Aphrodite, which stun locks the enemy.
It's about timing, weaving in and out of battle, aim and speed. Team fights are intense and replicate the rush you'd expect from a competitive shooter, all while respecting the governing outline of a MOBA. That makes SMITE a truly unique experience.
Most people who claim SMITE "sucks", play LoL or Dota. They see other games within the same genre as direct competition to the game they love. They don't care about enjoying games for what they offer; they compare and contrast simply to feel like they’re part of a team—for the sake of ego. It’s as though they themselves had a hand in the game development; they're very, very proud.
Most of them like to say SMITE’s not as deep. I argue the opposite. I feel where it lets go in micromanaging, it substitutes with a skill-oriented, high speed combat experience. It has depth and develops a skillset absent from other MOBAs. So it comes down to misunderstanding the skills necessary in SMITE.
I've been playing SMITE for probably a year now. I should have at least 300 hours, perhaps more. I wish my friends would play with me, but most of them have 'standards' and strongly draw the line after LoL. They’re better than Smite, and If I want to play with them, I’m going to have to play their favorite MOBA.
It would enhance my experience to play with them on SMITE, but even without a single friend, this game has kept my attention and I'll continue to play it.
Moreover, SMITE is constantly evolving. New skins, new gods, new maps, redesigns, new items, nerfs, buffs, new UI, etc. In the short amount of time I've played the game, I've seen many drastic changes. If you tried Smite years ago, it’s a promise that this SMITE is a completely different game today-- by this time next year, it'll have drastically changed again. All these changes are enhancements and true refinements to the game. It continues to get better and better, and HiRez listens to the players.
SMITE literally looks different graphically and the devs aren't scared to try some pretty wacky♥♥♥♥♥♥to make things more fun but balanced.
Free to play; pay to look cool. Smite's become one of my favorite games of all time.　
Note: I play LoL, Dota and Heroes of The Storm as well.

I play a lot of MMOs. Well I used to. I like MMOs. FFXIV I picked up on recommendation of a friend, played it for a month or so and stopped. I mostly stopped because said friend said he'd play with me but never did, so fu'ck him.
Pros:
- Race, class customization is pretty good
- FF universe, always a plus for me
- If you like the DPS/Healer/Tank thing it has that

- The "random" events are really good ways of leveling and are super fun IMO; reduces the feeling of a "grind"

- Some pretty unique quests not usually found in MMOs; fetch quests usually are very small (fetch 3, 5, 7, rather than 10, 20, 30)
- An attempt to lower the dungeon queues by giving rewards to players who play dungeons they've cleared previously.
- Catgirls are playable

Cons:
- WoW clone, which means you target a mob and hit buttons. I really don't like that kind of gameplay tbh.
- Gotta buy the game and its expansion, then pay for Subs after the first month. IMO not worth the price. It was fun, but not THAT fun.

- I suspect the end-game gear grind is ridiculous, but I never actually reached it so who knows.
- A lot of reskins/recolours for mobs.
- Solo play kinda sucks (MMO, so duh)
Not really sure what the end-game is, just running raid dungeons and PvP I guess?

You know, for the longest time I wanted to have an Elder Scrolls game that I can play online with other people, and this is not it.
ESO: Tamriel unlimited is the furthest thing from what makes Elder Scrolls great. Instead of interesting dialogue that shows off the diversity of the NPCs and builds on the lore, you basically have a bunch of voice actors throwing around lines that sound like they're playing a medieval version of GTA. Instead of having a well polished, expansive world that you can easily lose yourself with while exploring, you have a barren wasteland that has a few points of interest dotted in between the empty void. Instead of having a fun questline, you're given missions that consist mostly of 'Follow the marker and activate/kill/collect the thing, then get rewarded with an item that will help you activate/kill/collect the thing later'. Instead of having everything available to you at the start of the game, I have to go through a paywall to play as an Imperial or get a horse.
Maybe my opinion is devalued from having only played an hour, but if your first impression is this bad I think that should speak for itself. From the short amount of time I've spent with ESO, I've come to the conclusion that Zenimax now just likes getting high off of the smell of their own farts when it comes to the Elder Scrolls. Rather than capitalizing on everything that makes Elder scrolls great, instead they focus on making lazily designed cash-grab games knowing that people will buy it because of the legacy that The Elder Scrolls has. Save your money and go play literally anything else.

This game has really stepped itself up.  I have played several different MMORPGs, but ESO by far is the one I've consistantly returned to.  The first thing is that this is a game with something for both the solo player and the group player.  There are intricate and fully voiced storylines to follow, and most challenges can be overcome on your own if you play smart.  But, there are sufficient challenges which are more fun to do with groups and many public dungeons and public missions.  You can be doing a quest and suddenly meet up with other players who aren't on the quest, but exploring or something...and help you out.  I also love the environment and their choice in character design and clothing designs.  Nothing that's too risque (of which many MMOs are known for) and most of the gear looks quite practical.  In addition, I love the freedom in classes.  It doesn't come close to Ryzom where you can even build your own individual skills and actions...but for a modern MMO it has the most freedom.  What I mean is that you don't have to be an archer  OR a healer...i'll just explain by describing my character.  My character in particular is a healer (blending "classic" cleric style heals and animist style ones where plants and whatnot are summoned), with a a sword and knife offensive combo, and then a few archery tricks to boot...and I also have summoning capabilities for a combat pet.  I can switch between two loadouts automatically (so I switch between my restoration staff or my knife-and-shield) which also swaps the skill inventories.  I then keep a bow in case I need to employ my archer skills, too.  I also dig the combat...it's realtime in a weighted (ala monster hunter) first or third person (depending on what you set).  Finally, I just love the community...they are not so toxic and extremely helpful and quick to respond when someone needs a hand.  They even set up groups for some of the tougher bosses.  So, all in all...I'm a happy customer.  And you don't even need to spend money to be "useful".  Up to now, I've just been using money purely for cosmetics and for my first mount (which is extremely helpful considering how big the world is).

Let me just start off by stating that I’m giving a positive rating because I think TheHunter is a decent game, but despite this I’m going to get pretty negative in this review, mostly because it’s essentially one very long complaint of a problem that I think is crippling to the game. I’m also not going to summarize how the core game works at all, so if you’re looking for a review of that then this probably won’t help much.
As you can probably already see from the Steam reviews, there’s been a lot of controversy about Thehunter’s Free 2 Play model. I never had much experience with this, as I started out paying for membership, but the controversy eventually led Expansive Worlds to revise their model to a slightly less intrusive one, but asides from the confirmation that is was indeed a pretty bad model I think that maybe a lot of the negative reviews are undeserved.
In general I think that periodical charges are perfectly reasonable in a game which offers continuous updates and new content, and TheHunter is one of the better hunting games in a video game genre otherwise marred by some pretty embarrassing design standards. It should be pretty clear from my playtime here on Steam that I like it. Despite a visible need for polish in terms of the games UI design and how the game conveys important information, as well as a pretty♥♥♥♥♥♥decision to make everything including the launcher fully dependant on Expansive Worlds’ servers (which means that when there’s problems on their end you can’t play the game at all, not even singleplayer, and sometimes a host can lose connection to her or his own game). However, the main problem that I’ve chosen to write about in this review stems from how the ingame store operates.
For all means and purposes, TheHunter is a stealth game where the primary goal is to kill animals. In a stealth game about killing things, what are some of the general design elements that are the most crucial to providing variety and thereby prolonged engagement, i.e. fun, to the experience? Well, having different environments to play in and having different ways to kill things.
If you pay for membership, (or if you use in-game currency to buy permissions for hunting different animals) you’re provided with the rudimentary means to hunt all animals within all 10 different reserves, and the environments of the different reserves do impact the difficulty of the game and the way you have to play in order to hunt efficiently, so in that case the game fulfills the first of those requirements.
There’s also a large variety of different weapons to use and different equipment to use, and they all impact the way you can hunt significantly. Some weapons are silent, some weapons are light, some weapons are powerful and heavy, and you can get hunting blinds, bait, camouflage clothing, dogs, bows, and all other sorts of cool stuff to hunt animals in different ways,
-BUT ALL OF THAT COSTS MONEY.-
Like most Free 2 Play multiplayer games with microtransactions, there’s two kinds of currency, gm$, earned by completing missions ingame, and em$, earned by paying for it with real money. What is different and ironically worse than the microtransactions of most other Free 2 Play multiplayer games is that the stuff which can actually be bought with gm$ is currently limited to only the absolutely most pitifully uninteresting consumables that the game has to offer;
You cannot buy weapons with gm$. You cannot buy tents or hunting blinds with gm$. You cannot buy bait barrels, which are required to use bait, with gm$. You cannot buy dogs with gm$. You cannot buy clothing with gm$. You cannot buy scopes with gm$.
Essentially, any digital items which are permanently added to your character, or which actually do something significant to the gameplay requires payments in addition to your membership subscription, which to me is much more significant assery than the notorious former Free 2 Play structure. The concept of having to buy ingame equipment in order to have fun in a game that you’re already supporting through periodical charges is ludicrous.
TheHunters main equivalent of points in its semi-competitive community high-score system is HunterScore, which is rewarded for getting ingame milestone achievements, like “25 Mule Deer harvests” or “100 .243 bolt action rifle harvests”. There is a maximum limit to the HunterScore which can be achieved, but since getting there requires killing animals with all weapons in the game, including those which cost money, it effectively acts as a Pay 2 Win structure if you really want to spend the ridiculous amount of time it requires to actually compete with the top players.
The problems of the cost structure are slightly alleviated by the retail packages, which in some areas are actually way cheaper and offer more value than just buying membership online. With my first retail package I felt that I was getting significantly more value for my money than the 14.99€ “Wayfarer” starter package I bought on Steam, and this led me to later buy a couple of other packages from a german website in order to get some more new equipment and some added membership time. This time it was far less of a satisfying purchase, though, partly because it was less cheap and partly because only the membership and the single “special edition” weapon I got from the packages was actually useful to me. Most equipment offered in the retail packages is the same as every other retail package, save for usually one “exclusive” premium item, usually a weapon.
You can stack multiple pieces of the same equipment in TheHunter, but it seems like an oversight much more than anything else, because you can’t actually do anything with spare pieces of equipment. There’s no trading system, you can’t sell them for a bit of money, and there’s no point of having two of the same gun with you on a hunt since you’re limited to the same amount of ammunition as when you’re carrying one anyways. If anything they do make navigating your inventory more tedious, because you’ll eventually see, like, 6 .243 bolt action rifles and 6 12 gauge single shot shotguns because you’ve activated 5 different packages which all contained roughly the same guns and because there isn’t even any option to discard them. In fact, with one of the recent updates the 12 gauge single shot shotgun is now the only weapon in the store which costs 0 em$, so just for ♥♥♥♥♥ and giggles I bought 100 and now my ingame inventory is cluttered with them.
Anyways, now that I got the retail packages from Germany and activated them, I haven’t really ended up feeling like I made a good purchase. Instead, I really feel like a gullible idiot, and probably rightfully so. It’s mostly this feeling which is the reason as to why I’m writing this review in the first place. The weapons in TheHunter are only digital trinkets after all, and I don’t think it’s right to spend money on digital trinkets like this in the first place. I don’t understand the need for it either, if it was possible to at least also buy weapons for gm$ in addition to em$, it would provide a major incentive for players to keep playing the game, and since membership requires a subscription already, then what’s the problem?
Shouldn’t the membership subscriptions be paying for the maintenance and content updates of the game so that these seemingly kind of greedy and seemingly unnecessary micro transactions wouldn’t be needed? What’s the point of having two separate payment systems operating in the same game?
I like the game, but looking at the store really just makes me annoyed. After the tremendous amount of negative reviews following the former Free 2 Play model, though, they did revise it in the end. Maybe one of the next priorities could be revising the payment system?

Plague Inc: Evolved is the port that cramped iPhone users have been waiting for, featuring all of the latest updates from the App version and has been well executed for the wider PC audience.
Although it's obvious that little has changed between platforms, because even on the PC this game will boil down to 'Click the bubbles to get points --> spend points on upgrades --> win'. Hopefully in the ongoing steam updates this game will branch out into new areas more suited for PC gaming, which it is more than capable of doing. There is little going on here in terms of a plot, because of its iPhone roots but again we can hope this will be addressed.
Having said all this, this game is incredibly addictive and although the £11.99 price tag is quite steep (as with most Early Access titles), you'll soon forget what was spent as you'll keep going until the game has been played, start to everything unlocked.
Essentially, you play as some mystery overview character who can freely create diseases, whether they be based on bacteria, viruses, parasites, etc. etc. and you can freely infect 1 person anywhere on the planet, following that it's your job to evolve the disease by spending "DNA Points" to help infect more and more people across the globe until you've managed to wipe out the human race.
Yes, you heard me right. It's not enough to infect everyone on the planet with some incurable nonsense like the common cold, but the game is truly won when you've evolved your pathogen of choice to have some pretty horrific symptoms and attempt to wipe out the entire human population.
There are various difficulty levels but regardless of which you choose, trying to achieve your goal is a challenge. This game bills itself as a "hyper realistic simulation" of what would actually happen which means you have to think of and respond to various scenarios, these range from fairly obvious (some countries having better healthcare than others) to more complex (the Olympic Games means alot of people being gathered together in one place, ideal place to spread the disease). These little variants and the specific characteristics of the pathogens gives this seemingly simple platform alot of variation which will keep you coming back to finish it and check out the new updates.
All in all, a good game, limited by the fact it's a mobile port, but will hopefully evolve into something more suited for PC gamers.

It makes you care. You care about doing well at your job because all the money you make goes to keeping your family alive, and if you don't do well you get penalized for it. Easily makes one of my top five games ever played. Yet another top quality game from Supergiant Games, who continue to be one of the most reluctant game developers on the market.(They never intended to make more than one title, and at the time of this writing, still may only have made two.)
The story is thought provoking, and the vague and organic nature of telling through gameplay rather than cutscenes and the sort does a lot more for the game than against it. The superb intergration of music and gameplay is welcoming. The combat system as a whole is inventive - In some ways superior to Bastion, in some ways inferior. Complexity and exploration of a system is better than stagnation, and on the whole I had more fun with it than Bastion's, though I must say that it's a tad unfair to take this review as a put down of Bastion - The two games are so close to each other in overall quality and design that the comparison was bound to happen, and even though Transistor wins out from the two, I have little illusions that Bastion would make a top ten list of mine somewhere too.
Ultimately, I feel Transistor is the title to go for because it pushes what it can do with ashley barrett's voice, humming, and singing in this game more than it did with Bastion, and as utterly superb as Darren Korb's composing is, he's just that much better with a singer good enough to back him up, and as the game intergrates her singing into combat, taking your 'Turns' (She'll hum to the soundtrack.) And giving her more sung songs, it soon starts to feel like Bastion falls short not through lack of quality, but because Transistor simply gave as many talents as possible more stage time. It also feels as if the artistic developers from the first game have expanded their quality further again - The zones feel as if they're rendered with greater clarity and vision than the first, and the skyline seems as if it shows depth a little better than some of the fortresses and multi-tiered plantlife zones of Bastion, which sometimes felt a little flat or disorienting.
If I had to give Transistor flaws, it's that the story requires thought, and isn't willing to compromise at all - Reading the setup to the game and watching the trailer does fill in a few gaps, and part of me just wishes the game did start with a more confirming step so that it had a solid foundation to build the plot on, and that losing a function usually means reloading a save, especially if you're built for combing attacks with each other. It's not as tight in these areas as Bastion, and this leads to swings in gameplay because of it. Still, both games remain memorable, and I think I've got more hours of the soundtrack played on my computer than the game itself.

One being fungus, it seems silly that it's got such a limitation on it's ability to transmit itself without spending points.  You're basically using that ability to wait for the fungus to not be infecting hard to infect areas to use it.

Sure, you might be killing off doctors, but just because there are only , say a billion humans left, that doesn't mean they can't cure the disease any slower just because there are fewer humans left.
Other then that, it's really a indepth cool way of learning how diseases can work.

"Factorio is a game in which you build and maintain factories."
What a simple way to describe a game that is so absorbing that it can suck you in for hours and it only seems like minutes...
Factorio, while is it still in Early Access at this point, is one hell of a game, and one of those rare gems that show how Early Access REALLY should be done!
You start off chopping wood, like in far too many games these days, but almost everything else from then onwards you can automate with machines! The real trick is getting the resources from the mineral patches to the processing machines and then onto the actual component building machines efficiently and constantly.
No matter what you do, there always seems to be something more you could possibly optimise, speed up or outright change for a better/faster result.
There are a lot of YouTuber's who run Factorio campaigns, that would be my best suggestion to see what the game is like and get a feel for it.
I would suggest either Arumba or Steejo depending on if you prefer non-swearing or swearing commentary respectively ;-)
An incredibly fun game to play by yourself or with your friends.
