I play a lot of MMOs. Well I used to. I like MMOs. FFXIV I picked up on recommendation of a friend, played it for a month or so and stopped. I mostly stopped because said friend said he'd play with me but never did, so fu'ck him.
Pros:
- Race, class customization is pretty good
- FF universe, always a plus for me
- If you like the DPS/Healer/Tank thing it has that
- Big world to explore
- The "random" events are really good ways of leveling and are super fun IMO; reduces the feeling of a "grind"
- I'm going to put "the story is good" here, but I didn't actually pay attention to it so...
- Some pretty unique quests not usually found in MMOs; fetch quests usually are very small (fetch 3, 5, 7, rather than 10, 20, 30)
- An attempt to lower the dungeon queues by giving rewards to players who play dungeons they've cleared previously.
- Catgirls are playable
- No P2W. Can't believe I have to list that as a pro. There's a subscription though (duh).
Cons:
- WoW clone, which means you target a mob and hit buttons. I really don't like that kind of gameplay tbh.
- Gotta buy the game and its expansion, then pay for Subs after the first month. IMO not worth the price. It was fun, but not THAT fun.
- Gear progression is weak while leveling. Very weak.
- Dungeon Qs are hella long for DPS classes. 30+ mins for some of the lesser ones.
- I suspect the end-game gear grind is ridiculous, but I never actually reached it so who knows.
- A lot of reskins/recolours for mobs.
- Solo play kinda sucks (MMO, so duh)
Not really sure what the end-game is, just running raid dungeons and PvP I guess?
Overall, recommended if you don't mind the initial paywall. I could see myself playing this for many many months if I had people IRL to play with, which I don't.

, my unluckiest playthrough of a game yet.
There are no less than four playable characters whose stories all intertwine with each other to the point where I often mistook who I was playing:
I've played the first game,
, and I've convinced myself that director, Ragnar Tørnquist, started development on this game to resemble the first; a top-down, traditional point and click styled adventure game, only to see and play
- a game that was released one year prior to this - and experience a sudden burst of inspiration to completely change the direction of
to the detriment of its developers and its gameplay.
is a mishmash of incomplete ideas executed poorly, from forced stealth and combat to illogical puzzles and half-hearted vocal delivery.
This is one of the buggiest games I've ever played where little planning was put into its puzzles. Many of the voices during cutscenes were filled with stuttering and static, some stealth segments where my character could hide behind objects caused them to enter an animation loop that required reloading the game, sometimes I couldn't walk up staircases or
without getting stuck. There was one puzzle early in the game that required Zoë to play a series of notes in the correct order, the only issue there was that I had killed the creatures that hummed these notes in an earlier scene. Once combat has begun there is no way to escape so I was forced to murder these aliens not knowing how vital they would be to a future puzzle. The creatures were not replenished with additional patrolling aliens like I would expect in any other game. During a later chapter with April, taking place in the same area, these creatures will retreat rather than face me and will replenish and resume their patrolling routes. That's some extremely poor and inconsistent game design and it's not an isolated instance.
is a magnificent example of why developers should stick to what they know and what they do best rather than trying to emulate what's popular at the time. I feel deep remorse for fans who played this game at its time of release and had to wait a decade to find out what happened to the two dozen cliffhangers and unresolved plotlines that were left wide open.

2. Good story, with voice acting and amazing cutscenes.
3. Lot's of low level and high level dungeons. From 4 party to  raid dungeons(8-24 party size).
4. You have access to so many different classes when you start and once you hit lvl 10 you can change class to any of the available classes including the crafting and gathering classes.
5. Crafting is very nice and useful, Its more than just clicking what you want to make and making it you actually have a crafting skill bar. Gathering is the same way.
6. You have your own gear inventory so if you have outleveled some gear you can still keep the old gear for other lower level classes you would like to level.
7. Most everything has to be earned and or awarded in game, including mounts. So you can't just get really nice gear by paying real money in a cash shop.
8. PVP arena's. There is no open world pvp or pvp servers. I prefer it that way.
9. Great community.
10. Free companies(guilds). You can build a "guild hall" and decorate it. You can build different things for it as well. There is also player housing.
11. The gold saucer casino offers a wide variety of different mini games and prizes. Daily and weekly draws. There is a collectable card game that is pretty neat, and chocobo racing.
12. You can have a grand company chocobo mount, and use it in battle as a companion as well. It gains its own skills and can be equiped.
There are many many more things in ff14 to see, do, experience. So i recommend you try it out for yourself.
Con's
1. There are some annoying gold sellers that pop up on chat every once in a while. Mostly i just blacklist them.
2. The expansion jobs could use some buffs.

The biggest problem with this game is that it's more of an interactive movie than a game. It feels like they wrote a big script, and then sat down and asked themselves "which parts of this script can we let the player act out?", and built the game out of that. The result is incredibly shallow gameplay that feels like going through the motions of the plot in between cut scenes. You will frequently find yourself in situations where there isn't much to do other than head straight to the objective with not much getting in your way, and no real way to fail (either because there's no challange, or because the challange is trivial). They try to spice things up a little bit with some puzzles and some fight sequences and exploration, but it's all really really basic. The fighting mechanics are as barebones as they can be, with no room for any sophistication. The puzzles are simple and not interesting, and there isn't really much to explore.
Strangely enough, the above shortcomings do not necessarily mean a bad game. Everything I said above can also be said about the typical Telltale game, and those are pretty awesome. But there are some key differences between the two.
First of all, a key element of Telltale games is that they let you steer the story in the direction of your choice, which as it turns out is fairly engaging. Telltale games makes up for their limited mechanics that don't allow you to express yourself through action, by allowing you to express yourself through meaningful decisions. In Dreamfall there's only one storyline for you to go through, which make the limited interactivity all the more hollow. Not only will you not be able to express yourself through action, you also can't express yourself through decision, so what's the point of playing? To experience the story? Well, here's another key difference between Dreamfall and Telltale games: Telltale games have good stories.
WARNING: minor spoilers ahead.
I don't want to trash Dreamfall's writing too much, because it has some nice parts, and it certainly tries really hard to be good, but it also tries to do too much and ends up not fully satisfying on either one of its literary fronts. The original game had a satisfying core: we discover that there are two cool worlds, and now we get to explore them and along the way- save them, and it was a joy because both worlds had a lot of charm to them. With Dreamfall we once again have a story arc about the interplay between the two worlds, but then there's also a political story in Arcadia, and a loss of faith story of some random generic Arcadian warrior, and a corporate conspiracy story in Stark, which includes a tragic story of a test subject, a lover in peril, and some family related twists, and April from the original game also has her own arc. So there's a lot of stuff going on, and none of it is particularly original. There isn't anything that takes any of the plot lines from "yet another version of an idea we've seen before" and elevates them to something with at least a pinch of novelty. Even the twin worlds seem to have lost their charm. Arcadia feels like a generic fantasy setting, and Stark, well... there are much better examples of futuristic cities in other games and moves.
Finally, after you slog through all the in-between-cutscenes segments of the game and the mediocre writing, the game abruptly ends, with many loose threads remaining. It's almost as if they just ran out of time or budget and had to call it quits.
I'm a big fan of the original game, and to me this isn't the sequel it deserved. It's a mediocre game with a story that seem to be the result of literary feature creep, which doesn't deliver the same quality and expands the game in some really unnecessary directions (of all the things we wanted to do when we finished the original, playing as a generic Arcadian warrior caught between a political rock and hard place just wasn't one of them).

This is the 2nd game in the Longest Journey trilogy, and it's best summed up by the opening lines in the 3rd game. "They say every story has a beginning and an end. That isn't always the case. Some stories simply... stop."
This game was light and fun with a good story, and lovable characters. These days, it's pretty unusual for me to get as emotionally involved in a game as I did with this. But then when the game ended with most mysteries and conflicts unresolved, it was just heartbreaking.
There's quite a few intersecting plotlines in this game. The web is being corrupted by Static. The protagonist sees visions of a young girl begging for help. A reporter boyfriend has disappeared. An evil coporation is making a power grab, while an internal powerstruggle is being waged. Then in a parellel world, a girl is fighting a revolution, a religious zealot is having a crisis of faith, an holy empire is building a tower to the sky on the site of an unknown magical power, while a hidden cult seems to be pulling strings of a mysterious conspiracy from the shadows. Through it all, the destinies of our heroes Zoe, April and Kian are woven, and all against a backdrop of a mystical realm of dreams which faces an unknown threat.
Sounds awesome right? Seriously, it is. These are all expertly woven together.
Except then when things are most exciting, Zoe goes into a coma, and the game ends. Two of the plots I mentioned above are resolved. The rest are just abandoned. It's the most frustrating ending of any game I've played since the soul-reaver series, or perhaps the LOST tv series.
So there's a third game, but honestly it doesn't pick up where this one leaves off. It kind of goes off in a new direction (it's not made by the developers who did the first two). The characters are significantly different, and some of the plot elements from the 1st and 2nd games just kind of are swept aside. But that's a criticism of the 3rd game, not this one (and honestly, i haven't finished the 3rd, so it might eventually resolve everything).
The game does have some technical problems, mostly resolving around bad control. There's a combat system with is clunky as hell, some of the long-distance controls are bad, there's a sneaking mechanic that is good at times, but very poor in one specific part of the game, and camera angles in caves are terrible. Honestly though, the storytelling is so good, those are all forgivable.
So I'm giving this game the thumbs down because, while it's incredible storytelling, it leaves so much unfinished. I haven't gotten far into the 3rd, but it seems so different that it doesn't really feel like it's part of the same story, leaving this story unresolved.
Voice acting is terrible, controls are janky, and Zoë can be frustratingly dumb sometimes...... however despite all of this, the story is compelling enough to make this a game I can recommend.

I finally finished Transistor by Supergiant Games, the team behind the wonderful Bastion. The music was sublime ,which is no surprise when Darren Korb is involved, and the world was beautiful. Like in Bastion, the protagonist is the silent type(though for good reason) and most of the story is given and narrated by your companion. The gameplay is a mix of hack'n'slash and turn based strategy and was quite a unique experience for me. If you liked Bastion I highly recommend you pick Transistor up (In fact, the Steam summer sale is going on right now and I imagine it will be discounted soon).
Music, animation, art direction and gameplay. Everything in this game is absolutely beautiful. The game truly shines in it's Recursion (New Game Plus) mode.

Wonderfully stylized, engaging story, and a great soundtrack. The turn-based combat mechanics are a nice change, although they also feel clunky and a little button-mashy at times. Still, well worth the 5-10 hours that it will take you to zip through the story (more for the completionists, of course).
A WORK OF ART THATS NEEDS TO BE EXERIENCED.

Easily makes one of my top five games ever played. Yet another top quality game from Supergiant Games, who continue to be one of the most reluctant game developers on the market.(They never intended to make more than one title, and at the time of this writing, still may only have made two.)
The story is thought provoking, and the vague and organic nature of telling through gameplay rather than cutscenes and the sort does a lot more for the game than against it. The superb intergration of music and gameplay is welcoming. The combat system as a whole is inventive - In some ways superior to Bastion, in some ways inferior. Complexity and exploration of a system is better than stagnation, and on the whole I had more fun with it than Bastion's, though I must say that it's a tad unfair to take this review as a put down of Bastion - The two games are so close to each other in overall quality and design that the comparison was bound to happen, and even though Transistor wins out from the two, I have little illusions that Bastion would make a top ten list of mine somewhere too.
Ultimately, I feel Transistor is the title to go for because it pushes what it can do with ashley barrett's voice, humming, and singing in this game more than it did with Bastion, and as utterly superb as Darren Korb's composing is, he's just that much better with a singer good enough to back him up, and as the game intergrates her singing into combat, taking your 'Turns' (She'll hum to the soundtrack.) And giving her more sung songs, it soon starts to feel like Bastion falls short not through lack of quality, but because Transistor simply gave as many talents as possible more stage time. It also feels as if the artistic developers from the first game have expanded their quality further again - The zones feel as if they're rendered with greater clarity and vision than the first, and the skyline seems as if it shows depth a little better than some of the fortresses and multi-tiered plantlife zones of Bastion, which sometimes felt a little flat or disorienting.
If I had to give Transistor flaws, it's that the story requires thought, and isn't willing to compromise at all - Reading the setup to the game and watching the trailer does fill in a few gaps, and part of me just wishes the game did start with a more confirming step so that it had a solid foundation to build the plot on, and that losing a function usually means reloading a save, especially if you're built for combing attacks with each other. It's not as tight in these areas as Bastion, and this leads to swings in gameplay because of it. Still, both games remain memorable, and I think I've got more hours of the soundtrack played on my computer than the game itself.

Borderlands 2 is an outstanding game, I highly recommend getting the Game of The Year Edition.
Short:
Amazing CO-OP/Solo (up to 4 players) game with a good story, enjoyable gameplay and satisfying loot. Get this game if you like the shootie-shoots.
Not-as-short:
The game supplies a good amount of comedy and well written main story / side story to go with it. I still enjoy playing through it, and will keep enjoying myself playing it with many different friends.
The gameplay itself, depending on the character that you have chosen, is amazingly satisfying and has three skill trees that you spend your skill points in. The skill trees will change how your character plays and feels.
There are many types of randomly generated weapons (To an extend) that you can gain from killing bandits, monsters and/or robots. Like many RPG-like games the game gives out different quality weapons, ranging from a common (white) gun to legendary (orange) weapons. The legendary weapons will have special/unique attributes to them, making them rare but  very useful in combat.
The difficulty depends on how long and/or much you play it for. If you beat the game once and want more you can replay the story and fight stronger, different named/sometimes skinned, enemies for better loot.
There are three main difficulties. Normal Vault Hunter Mode (1st playthrough), True Vault Hunter Mode (2nd playthrough) and Ultimate Vault Hunter Mode (3rd playthrough). The last of the three has "Overpowered" Modifiers as well, that goes up to 8.
All the DLCs that you can purchase are pretty good and worth the money, but you can always wait for them to go on sale.
There is not a lot of character customization, but you can gain more skins and headpieces. As you do not make your OWN character but rather play a character from the story itself, I feel it has more than enough customization as it is.
Rpg fps makers should take this game as a veeeeeery good example

PREPARATION
To make baked soda: Spread a half-cup of baking soda on a foil-lined sheet pan. Pop it in a 250°F oven or toaster oven for 1 hour. Store extra baked soda in a jar with a lid indefinitely.
Put the warm water in a large mixing bowl. Dissolve 4 teaspoons of the baked soda in it, then add the cold water. Add the flour, stirring and mixing to form a crumbly, pebbly alliance—not exactly a nice dough.
Turn that crumbly dough out onto a work surface. Knead it together, working the dough for 5 full minutes. (It will be a tougher sparring partner than any flour dough you’ve ever tried to make.) Wrap the dough in plastic and let it rest at room temperature for 20 minutes, then knead for another 5 minutes. (You will curse and sweat.) Rewrap the dough and put it in the fridge for at least 1 hour.
Divide the dough into five or six portions. Roll each portion out using a pasta machine (Italian-made is fine). Progress through the thickness settings one by one. The final thickness of the noodles is up to you, as is the width and shape into which you cut them. I like taking the dough to the second-thinnest setting, then either finely hand-cutting them or cutting them through the finer of the two cutters that came with my machine. Keep the noodles well floured to prevent them from sticking.
Cook the noodles in a deep pot with plenty of water. Noodles cut on the thinnest setting will only need two and a half or three minutes to cook. Check the noodles regularly while they’re cooking; if they stick together, rinse them under cold water immediately after straining them from the pot to stop the cooking and rinse off any excess starch.

The Room is strickly a puzzle solving game and it is superb. Your character enters a room with a mysteriouz puzzle box and on it a note from a friend. You read the note then you are on your way to puzzle solving galore.
The puzzles in this game have an extremely wide variety. While some of the puzzles can be fairly difficult, there are hints that, while they are helpful, do not directly give you the answers you are looking for. These can be disable for veteran puzzle solvers of course. You could easily get stuck on a puzzle without the hints, but with them you will likely not spend more than 10 minutes on any given puzzle. Your progression will be saved after each puzzle you complete, as opposed to after each chapter. This is excellent because it makes diving in to solve the next piece of the puzzle that much more conveniant.
You will be doing everything from searching for keys to hunting for clues on which square to turn which direction.
The room is unique in that the entire game takes place at the box and by hunting, you are just searching in, on and around the box for said keys and clues. Each time you unlock one puzzle you can expect there to be another one come out of it, each one bringing you closer to the mystery inside the box.
One of the best features in The Room is the sound effects. Everytime you hear the turning of a key, the snap of a puzzle piece you just insterted or the ever so satisfying click of a new part of the box being revealed you will feel truly immersed in the experience. These little noises are the song of progression.
You can expect to complete The Room in around 3 hours depending on your skill at puzzle solving. I did encounter one bug near the end of the game but thankfully there was a solution on the Steam forums already so I was able to move quickly past it. The game was extremely satisfying and I am glad to have experienced it. If you enjoy puzzles, this is a must play.

is a great little Indie game which doesn't take up much disk space and is actually very fun to play just to pass the time. The play style is almost casual, but there is also a story mode that can become quite difficult.
My first impression of the game was mixed. I couldn't choose decisively if it was a good game or just decent game. I knew it had potential though and I did enjoy playing it. On the surface,
may seem like an odd East-Berlin Checkpoint Guard Simulator, with pixel-styled graphics and nothing much more to do than stamp passports and analyze them. It seemed like it might be just one of those repetitive games that's fun to play every now and again...then I gave it a chance. Now, I must say that I do enjoy playing this game very much.
As the story mode progresses, you'll begin to understand your role, equipment, and use of analytical skills more thoroughly. In addition to your job, at the end of the day when you collect your pay you must take care of your family by using a simple budget system of Rent, Food, and Medicine. If you cannot take care of your 4 family members (i.e they stay Cold, Sick, Hungry) they will die. Once you get a week or more into the story, this is when the real fun begins. Crazy things begin to happen at your checkpoint. From terrorist attacks to people trying to sneak in drugs to women whose passport says they're male (and they aren't lying). When it all started to get crazy, I decided that this game is not as simple as I first thought. It's a great game and it deserves a play from any Indie game fan.
- A 'Story Mode' in addition to an 'Endless' Mode (Unlockable)
- Doesn't take up much space on any computer (About 40 mb)
- Interesting Pixel-style artwork
- Incidents that happen randomly or according to the story
- Use a range of given tools to perform interrogations (if necessary). These tools include a strip-search camera, discrepancy detectors, and the ever handy Newspaper & Rule Book.
- Use the little money you make to keep your house heated and your family fed. If not, they'll starve and/or die. This is a fairly difficult objective considering your pay.
- Addictive play
- Fun story mode which will keep you wondering what the next day might bring.
- 20 different possible endings
- Some events in story mode will repeat themselves, but it helps to make to game flow along
- The graphics were a turn off at first, but you get used to the style
- There are only about 3 or 4 different sounds to represent the language (sounds like a mumbled mash of German and Russian). One of these sounds is "Papers" grumbled by your character.
- A
learning curve (which will dissapear after playing through the story mode for a few days)
-
happens to be a really fun Indie jewel. There are various tools you use as a customs officer to help you identify or interrogate people whose documents, IDs, papers, etc. don't match. There's nothing much more I can add besides what I've written. I can safely recommend this game to people who are open minded, love indie games, or just like break from the usual high-graphic, PC melting games of the now.

Sequel to 1999's
, Dreamfall is an adventure game with a number of curious features. It deviates from the traditional point & click style of its predecessor, opting instead for something in between 3rd person action game and puzzle-solving adventure game.  Some aspects worked out well, others not so much.
Still the story, which is what Adventure games are for (IMHO.)  It's not
as The Longest Journey's story, but it's a worthy sequel.  The game has you switching back and forth between 3 different playable characters; April Ryan, Zoe Castillo and Kian Alvane.  They also get creative when these characters inevitably start crossing paths with each other.  One particularly clever sequence has two of them bump into each other on the street, resulting in a conversation where you get to choose dialogue options for both characters in turn.  You walk into the sequence controlling one character and then walk away from it controlling the other.  I found that amusing.
The controls.  Believe it or not, I actually played through the entire game using keyboard and mouse, and trust me when I say, these controls are every bit as confusing and awkward as other reviewers make them sound.  I got used to them in time, but they definitely ARE NOT intuitive.  You may want to use a game pad instead, if it's an option for you.
Apart from the actual controls, the game also includes some mechanics that really have no place in an Adventure game in the first place.  They work poorly and feel like an afterthought during design - thankfully, they're easy enough to work around once you get used to them.  Combat, for example.  There are two kinds of fights you get into; ones you're
and ones you're
In the former kind, you just spam attack buttons and the enemy AI barely reacts, let alone fights back.  The latter, you'll be killed (or almost killed) in one shot and do next to no damage yourself.  You're
, and it should generally be obvious as to how.  Honestly, they should've just left combat out or made these sequences cut-scenes instead.
Hard to say.  Depends on how important the story is compared to the actual game play in your opinion.  I like the game because it continues the story and setting of one of my favourite Point & Click games ever, so I can overlook the trash controls.  Your mileage may vary.
If you played and enjoyed The Longest Journey, this is a worthy sequel.  Just be aware that it ends on a cliffhanger, so you may want to check out the third game, too (it does wrap everything up!)

You learn more about the Dark people and finally see their city, learn more about Brian Westhouse,
, we learn about what happened to April and her friends from Venice, etc. That stuff alone makes playing this game worth it, the abundance of world adding information.
I did love Zoe as the new main character but after playing the first game I'm a bit more attached to April. I am thankful that through Zoe we do see more of Stark (Our world) Russia, Japan, even an updated version of Marcuria & Venice. I will say like most people have already the combat is terrible but not broken or hard to pull off. The music and voice acting once again is great, so happy to see returning cast members. The change from the first game's graphics to this (I played this game right after beating the first) is honestly unbelievable, so many old places from the first game updated, they did a great job with transitioning noticeable details for those looking.
I could go on talking at lengths about how great an addition this game is to the series but its best to just dive in and play it for yourself.

Worthwhile game for people who like fast response based action games (Devil May Cry, Ninja Gaiden, Bayonetta). I will be mainly critiquing mechanics and design in the review--it may come off as negative given the amount of things I will be nitpicking but I think this game is very close to being excellent so I wanted to take the time to be specific about things. As it seems they may still patch things, I will mention this review is as of Sept 4, 2017
About the camera, reading the other reviews it seems like a lot of issues had been resolved prior to me playing the game, but there's a few more points to potentially improve. An option for a farther camera would be helpful--I often found myself getting hit from offscreen by the fast dashing attack that claw enemies have.
This situation is very common due to what I expect is the typical encounter strategy of running around baiting suicide robots, then hunting down ranged enemies before engaging in the meat of the melee combat. Ironically, this approach to begin with is to minimize the chance of getting attacked from offscreen. This strategy is further supported by the fact that the ranged enemies have much lower health than other enemies and the sprinting attack will prioritize ranged enemies over everyone else nearby. A potential fix to this problem of strategic variety would be more enemy types and/or more actions within each enemy type.
To further expand upon the sprinting attack, it is a quick dash attack towards an enemy that is initiated by a light attack during sprinting. The interesting thing about this move is its auto-locking function which targets an enemy in range for you automatically, making it essential for hunting ranged enemies (as previously mentioned) but also as a gap closer for bosses, which I will go into further detail below.
Enemies are not aware of the Y-axis and will initiate attack attempts if you're hovering over them, making the downward falling slash risky as you can end up attacking into a move you can't see that has a more favorable hitbox. Additionally in the few encounters that happen on multiple floors, melee enemies are incapable of chasing you and ranged enemies can only attempt to shoot you.
Dodging has a bit of a long vulnerability time. While it's important to punish defensive indiscriminate dodge chaining, it also limits the offensive potential of the player. This is most notable in the variant of claw enemies that will block most attacks. In the tutorial you are taught to guard crush them with heavy attacks, but as this guard crush also pushes them back, they often end up out of range and using a dodge as a gap closer is too slow as they re-gaurd while you're still in dodge recovery. Getting close and using a strong attack chain is usable but as there are no combo options from a strong attack initiator and strong attacks within higher level combo chain that start with light attacks often fail to crush means this can be a boring approach. The actual approach i found best to use on these enemies was to sprint away at a small distance then use the sprinting attack to quickly close to perfect distance before they can bring their guard up and enable a full combo chain. One solution to the dodge recovery issue is either allow for limited chaining whereupon a long recovery will be incurred after a certain number of dodges (Bayonetta) or simply prevent dodge-to-dodge chaining but allow dodge into attacks freely.
The ranking system is based simply upon amount of HP remaining at the end of the encounter, with all hp being refilled after an encounter. Given that there is a way to self-heal 30% by using all your SP for a full screen attack, this is generally the best way to use SP as your ranking affects the amount of points you get to buy moves with per encounter (unless of course you are having no problem with hp at all). As far as I can tell the ranking system is something like 85+% hp remaining full 1000 points, with anything under being scaled to your health (e.g. 72% hp remaining gets you 720 points) and an overall rank at the end of a level. If you consistently get 80+% you can easily buy all the actions before the end of the game, which is a plus for me as these games are all about having options.
The boss battles are probably the low point of the game for me. You can almost never complete any of the better combos, with the bosses dodging out at the transition point, with some of the later bosses dodging even out of the basic light attack combo. Additionally, bosses' "safe" strike times are fairly strict, meaning even if you do a perfect dodge/perfect block into a counter they won't be staggered and usually end up hitting you on follow up attacks anyway--you absolutely have to wait for the right time to attack. Combine this with bosses having very little wait time between attacks and it could be pretty frustrating until you figure out the general pattern most of them share. With only a couple of exceptions, this results in the correct strategy for every boss being sprinting in a circle around them until they use one of their slow (usually ranged) attacks whereupon you immediately use the sprinting attack to close in, using a light combo before backing off and repeating. However, as a saving grace boss health bars are reasonable and once you get the pattern it does not take too long to finish one. This is a shame as I generally prefer the more agile character-vs-character fights in these types of games (think Vergil in DMC3, Angelo and Dante in DMC4) when they are made correctly.
Some final nitpicks, these mostly are minor issues that just go away with getting used to the particulars of the game:
Your striking range and coverage always seems shorter than it should be, I found myself constantly misestimating how safe i was in the middle of or initiating an attack chain, especially from the claw enemies.
The dodge distance is a bit too far, with dodging past an enemy to hit them from behind often overshooting resulting in a whiff. Dodge distance being shortened wouldn't be a problem as there are plenty of invincibility frames in the dodge. Air dash should be lengthened however. Alternatively weapon range could be increased as mentioned above and dodge length left alone.
Non-sprint walk speed seems a bit on the slow side. Sprinting is fine as is though it could also be sped up without much detriment if a similar move speed bump was granted to enemies so they couldn't be completely dusted.
Control customization would also be nice
As quick comments about non-gameplay aspects the game:
- Story and cutscenes are like an abridged cliche anime. I won't hold this against it as I know how expensive cutscenes are to make and how small a team this is. Taking the effort at all to contextualize things is a net plus considering the circumstances for me.
- The game is very short, taking under 3-4 hours to complete once, though these types of games are generally highly replayable due to the inherent appeal of its gameplay. There's additionally a challenge mode.
- Character models look decent, costume design is definitely anime-style, with the face models for the female characters looking very similar to some of the dead or alive characters.
- Gameplay animations generally look great, with nice looking FX work going with a lot of moves.
- Environment models don't look as good as the characters but the gap isn't distracting
- Music is surprisingly catchy though there's only a few tracks. Given that the game is fairly short, the latter isn't a problem
As much as I nitpick, I want to again clarify that for fans of the genre I think it is worth playing, especially at sale prices. The responsiveness of the system is inherently satisfying to play and is something I very rarely see done correctly outside of Platinum-developed/originated games, even at AAA budgets.

"The Initial" is your typical 3d hack-n-slash/action type of game that is similar to ninja gaiden / devil may cry / bayonetta series.
At the start, players will be given a choice between 2 beautiful female heroines who look different but have the same skills.
There is little backstory, where an evil corporation is trying to take over the world and using replicated(clone) girls for battles. Surprisingly, it has some cut-scenes with decent voice acting.
The learning curve is easy, as players are guided with a tutorial at the start, the main gameplay is all about fighting and running around clearing "zones".
Each "zone" will consist of a range of enemies and unique bosses. There is also an added feature of obtaining coins after clearing each "zone", allowing players to unlock more fighting moves.
+++ The Good +++
1) Fantastic 3D character models, very nicely done.
2) Decent voice acting during cut-scenes.
3) Easy learning curve, lots of action.
4) Gameplay, fight scenes are amazingly fluid.
5) The music is fast paced, and fits well with the gameplay.
6) There is support for controllers and key-mappings in settings.
7) There is character progression with unlockable combos/abilities.
8) Developers are active and open to suggestions/feedback.
--- The Bad ---
1) Even though character models are beautiful, the expressions are poor, feels "wooden" at times.
2) Limited replayability, once the game is completed, starting a new game becomes repetitive.
3) There is a lack of content, could have more enemies / unlockables / costumes / moves / secrets / levels.
4) The backstory could be improved further, players get thrust into the action too quickly.
5) Translation could be improved further, you do get minor grammar mistakes or awkward sentence structures. However, this is NOT game-breaking, do take note the developer's main language is not english, so please bear with them.
To conclude, "The Initial" is a fun action-packed game, with beautiful graphics and fluid combat mechanics.
Even though there are some minor translation issues and lack of content/backstory, I believe both casual players and hardcore hack-n-slash fans will still enjoy this title.
Final Score : 8.5 / 10

Shrouded in the suspense and mystery of the mystical and unknown, this first-person puzzler is sure to be every puzzle-lover's cup of tea. Unlock puzzle boxes within puzzle boxes as you delve deeper into the dark and mysterious depths of The Room. Seek to uncover the bizarre truth behind your adventure as you spin dials, unlock stuff, push buttons, unlock stuff, refract light, and unlock stuff.
The game's music, while not so much music as backround noise, is very atmospheric. The story is revealed mostly through a series of cryptic notes left behind by the mysterious researcher guiding you through the game. The puzzles themselves are (at least for me) oftentimes quite difficult; but they nearly always have an answer that, when discovered, will leave you slapping your forehead and yelling "Oh, duh!" And although the play-time is fairly short and does not possess any real replay value, I feel that the length was appropriate for a puzzler and the price was more than fair.
I highly recommend The Room to anyone who likes puzzles and a healthy dose of mystery and magic. Can't wait for the sequal to come to PC.

Man, I'd really love to love ToS. I loved Ragnarok Online and everyone assumed this will be a good successor. I actually _bought_ this game to play earlier than release. My hours are off, I don't know if it was because this game wasn't on Steam back then or something else.
Graphically this game is cool, it looks beautiful. The combat system is fine and fun. The classes are great, it has a deep class system, many different skills, good teamplay between classes. This would be an awesome MMO.
But let me put together the downsides that make this game unplayable for me:
1. It lags. Graphically and network-lag. I tried it on release. I tried it one year after. I tried it the day writing this review. The servers are unstable and lag really hard, I get random disconnects or e.g. my skill keys I just set up randomly reset, my position randomly resets. I get graphic lags with a PC that can handle most current AAA-games on ultra-graphics.
2. The controls are really bad. Put on mouse and keyboard, you're stuck with keys that are not localized and just feel klunky to use. Yes, you can set it up, and even then it feels klunky, but I expect this game to bring somewhat intuitive controls right from the start. Controller is easier to play with, but you can't set controller keys up and dialogs or the UI in general are not supported, which means you still have to use the keyboard/mouse to read item descriptions, put your stats and skills, pick a quest reward etc.
3. It crashes. It is unstable. You constantly have random crashes, even when just walking around. How can anyone write such an unstable engine and release it while taking money from people, it's beyond me.
Man, you already have a cash shop and grab money from innocent little kids, stop ♥♥♥♥ing around and finally put some work into this. If you actually want to make money with it, that is.

Call of Juarez: Gunslinger is an exciting albeit short adventure, and it's arguably the best game in the Call of Juarez series. Gunslinger's gameplay starts off slowly and methodically. Fortunately, as you accumulate upgrades, the intensity of the gunplay increases.
Although the game is great, it isn't perfect. The biggest 'flaws' I found with this game were the boss battles and duels. The boss fights aren't particularly challenging, but the bosses are massive bullet sponges (at least on Hard difficulty and True West). Also, the duels are frustrating, to say the least. The game expects you to focus on multiple things at once during a duel. To duel, you need to control your hand (speed), the crosshair (focus) and watch your opponent's hand. The worst part about dueling is the HUD. It tells you your speed on the left side of the screen, your focus on the right side and you need to pay attention to your opponent's hand, which is roughly in the middle. You should expect to go cross-eyed a few times before you get used to it.

This review is based on a full Normal difficulty playthrough and 1 and a half hour of Very Hard.
The game itself has gone through a few revisions since I beat it and all for the best. On normal mode I feel it's a good action game. You start out with a simple moveset like you do for most action games and buy combos and abilities. These can range from "Buy XXXYYYXXXX" or "Press X to attack back after right timing." You get coins to buy these skills after beating areas in a game. There are a few small variety of area scenery and enemies. It's enough for a game that takes about three hours to beat. The bosses seem to be well thought out as it can be a matter of trial and error before you figure out the pattern needed to beat them.
Now for what I care about most. The combat is much better than most action games you would find on Steam. You have the ability to cancel your animations, but not at all times. The defensive options are a simple dodge and block at the beginning. Eventually you can unlock the ability to parry and dodge with a follow-up attack. The parry is an instant kill, but only kills one enemy even if you're surrounded. However, attacking back with the dodge affects everybody within proximity of the attack, but it won't kill. One other ability is to intercept the enemy with your own attack, but with the start-up on moves you would need to know they're about to attack to use this. There's no indication of when they will other than their own start-up too.
Your offensive options are a few simple combos, but are usually interrupted easily unless you launch the character. It seems like the character will only hit everybody in some instances. Each combo serves a function and is used for things like trapping characters in furious sword swipes and allowing you to move. Another combo allows you to blow all of your enemies away. There are finishers in the game when an enemy is red, but you have to be neutral to use it for some reason. Movement from character to character is done well. There is a dash button and it's utilized during combat to instantly teleport you to the enemy you want to attack. The game equips you with a gun to put an enemy into stagger state. You are also able to charge your regular attack to deal a lot of damage to a single enemy on screen or charge until you're red to kill every enemy on screen. One of the abilities you buy allows you to instantly go into red state. Unfortunately going into this stance is near impossible in Very Hard. Your last attack is an attack that kills everything on the screen instantly and refills your life gauge. The former two require resources from the bar below your life that you slowly build up. You can build it up faster with finishers, a parry follow-up, and apparently intercepting an attack. Since the bar only serves as a function for these two things I didn't feel it needed to be mentioned immediately.
The game is a joy to play on Normal and is a real challenge on Very Hard. I feel some of the challenge on Very Hard comes from being unable to utilize all of the tools given to me, though. I cannot intercept, I am given no time to charge an attack, I get hit at certain points in combos too easily, and I can't recommend playing on Very Hard because of these flaws. I find myself making it through areas by press attack a few times, dashing to the next enemy, pressing attack a few times again, and repeating. Sometimes I will use parry and dodge, but it's usually too suffocating or there's an environmental hazard.
I recommend the game because I had a lot of fun on Normal and most people probably won't touch Very Hard. This review is based mostly on the game's mechanics and Very Hard difficulty.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.
Eat.

I'm not a huge puzzle game fan but the reason I loved this game was that the deeper you go into solving the puzzle box the further you step into this well wrought gentelmen's occult atmosphere. You are in fact following in the footsteps of a friend or colleague who has disappeared. Hidden in the box is a treasure that is also the answer.
The puzzle stages themselves require some mystical paraphernalia and solving them can invoke some mild paranormal drama that makes the stages feel satisfying. It is this gently sinking immersion that pulled me in and made me a fan.
The puzzles themselves involve checking over the beautifully crafted box itself for hidden mechanisms and codes that require concentration and deduction but are thankfully not frustrating. The graphics are beautiful and intricate so this type of exploration is a welcome part of the experience. The controls and camera viewpoints work well which is essential for this kind of investigative mystery. Optional clue flags pop up to help guide you if you want to click on them.
It is clear that the game is crafted to take you on a (relatively short) journey of discovery rather than present a series of difficult brain-teasers. In this vein, the puzzles are really just invitations to look deeper through a glass darkly, so to speak. This game is absolutely worth a look.

Dreamfall: The Longest Journey loosely continues the story of The Longest Journey while featuring a new main character and new plot elements. I really liked revisiting places from The Longest Journey and seeing those characters from the first game again.
The gameplay hasn't fundamentally changed, apart from switching from Point-and-click to a more direct approach via third-person. However, puzzles are not what they used to be, and while I found all of them intuitive and easy to come by, especially compared to more traditional adventures, they where a tad too easy in my view and too sparsely placed. They felt more like being there for the sake of it, than actually meaningful gameplay.
The story is where the game shines a little brighter. I found the characters, both recurring from the previous game and new ones, engaging and fun most of the time. The story itself kept me fascinated for the most part, apart from the section right to the end maybe. It has some pacing issues and some character's developments I found questionable. It felt kinda rushed in certain parts, wasting a lot of potential. Its a pity it is set up to be followed by a sequel, resulting in many threads of the story being left unconnected and a huge cliffhanger at the end, which wasn't the case for The Longest Journey.
As for the tech, the game originally came out in 2006, and it certainly looks the part. Voice acting is good most of the time. Some Voices however sound uninspired and lack motivation. Sound and music design didn't particularly stand out but also weren't noticably bad.
In the end, this game is more like typical walking simulators, focused on telling a story while giving some hints of gameplay, instead of being a full on adventure. Compared to Longest Journey and Dreamfall Chapters, this is, in my view, easily the weakest of the series. Still, it kept me going till late at night with an engaging story.
Having the benefit of all 3 games available when I played it, I can't really imagine what a let down the cliffhanger and loose threads of this game were at the time of its release. But in the present state, I can recommend the game, especially if you want to have the full story package.

Sequel to one of the best and most thrilling games I've ever played, The Longest Journey, is yet another example of great gaming experience. Interesting, original, mysterious and even surprising story, great characters with different personalities, many diverse locations to explore, some very nice puzzles and this time around even stealth and combat mechanics. Are you ready to continue your longest journey?

Rating: 6/10
Overview: Third Person Adventure
The Good:
+An interesting story that takes place 10 years after the events from the first game. The story is filled with interesting locations and people. Its really cool re-visiting areas from the first game in a fully 3D environment and discovering what happened to some of my favorite characters.
The Average:
+/- Camera control could use a bit more work
The Bad:
- The “puzzles” if you can even call them that is either fetch quests that have you running from one end of the map to the other or some variety of stealth
- Stealth feels out of place, clunky and simply not fun
- Combat is also an element of the game and feels like it was implemented last minute. The animations feel stiff and attacks have no weight or feeling to them.
Conclusion:
This is a massive….MASSIVE step back from the Longest Journey. While the first game was an instant classic and still amazing to this day, this game was already out dated even when it was released. This game was made at a time when no publisher would even consider making an exclusive point and click adventure for the pc so the developers had to go after the console demographic instead. Thus we now have fully 3D levels with simplistic puzzles, terrible stealth and combat.
This game has been my favorite since I've been a kid, and replay it now has in no way changed my opinion about the game.

Dreamfall is the 2nd game on the series and its following the footsteps of the original game that was a huge success in Adventure Point & Click genre. Obviously when industry started to move towards 3D lot of these type of games become unpopular or they had to adapt and go 3D themselves, to put it bluntly was rather rocky ride, dreamfall aint exception this.
They entered new elements such as combat and stealth, which to be fair could've been lot worse and used more in the game, but thankfully werent. For its time it does have decent scenery and terrain that looks impressive and is faithful to the original game, while i personally think the 2D art is more cooler, it did good job of re-doing certain scenes from the old game.
Sounds & Music are good in Dreamfall and story ain't half bad either, its just it ends up with cliffhanger which pretty much forces you to buy Dreamfall chapters as well. The new characters introduced like Zoe weren't as appealing as April Ryan, but did do their part telling at least interesting plot even tho i think zoe was bit lackluster main character.
Overall the game is great, 15h of fun for ~20$ isn't bad price at all, it has controller support too. Playing original game isn't required but i recommend due to lot of cool cameos and people coming back from first game.

"Factorio is a game in which you build and maintain factories."
What a simple way to describe a game that is so absorbing that it can suck you in for hours and it only seems like minutes...
Factorio, while is it still in Early Access at this point, is one hell of a game, and one of those rare gems that show how Early Access REALLY should be done!
You start off chopping wood, like in far too many games these days, but almost everything else from then onwards you can automate with machines! The real trick is getting the resources from the mineral patches to the processing machines and then onto the actual component building machines efficiently and constantly.
No matter what you do, there always seems to be something more you could possibly optimise, speed up or outright change for a better/faster result.
There are a lot of YouTuber's who run Factorio campaigns, that would be my best suggestion to see what the game is like and get a feel for it.
I would suggest either Arumba or Steejo depending on if you prefer non-swearing or swearing commentary respectively ;-)
An incredibly fun game to play by yourself or with your friends.

After the introduction of several characters (among them the young Dwight D. Eisenhower) and nips of his beer, Silas shares his bounty hunter stories and that's where the narrator, Silas, put us in.
You play as the young Silas Greaves and piece by piece you will find the reason(s) why he became a bounty hunter.
During his vengeful travel through the wild west he encountered several villains who came across his way and vice versa. Interestingly you will come toe to toe with some of the popular villains such as the Dalton Brothers, The Doc or Jesse James who were well known across the wild west and yes, like a real cowboy, you will face them in a gunslinger duels.
The narration is kind of unique on its own due to the interaction by his audience such as questioning his stories (did he get attacked by Apaches or got attacked in Apache STYLE?) or "what-if-else" when he entered
or
. It shakes off the seriousness and tension within the narration which can be sometimes really funny when he tries to go back where he stopped or even tries correct himself like watching a movie via video cassette and you try to go back- and forward through the story *lol*. The comicish graphic and the comicish screen borders, which reminds very much about Borderlands 2, gives the whole narration a nice touch which I find it pretty good!
During the storyline you will earn skill points to upgrade (which are divided into three seperate trees or 'revolver drums') your character which i find it is a good motivation in a long run.
Your investment will also pay off by the changed look of the guns which I find really cool.
I guess the quote "God created man, Samuel Colt made them equal" holds up to it *lol*.
Speaking of revolver drums, the shooting mechanics in this game are really satisfying, especially once you lay your hands on
. It has been kept pretty simple which means there are no 'bullet drops' or anything related to it but you will notice the guns lose its effectiveness due to the range thus the damage per bullet.

Wow! I'm not sure where to begin. Though I guess I should start by saying that I LOVED it.
But it's not perfect.
The art-style and enviorment are absolutley beautiful. Especially at first. After a while, I think you sort of get used to it all though, and it CAN get a bit same-y. But at no point do I think the art detoriates. Gorgeous from start to finish.
Same with the music. However, I sort of felt that there wasn't enough of the most beautiful parts of the soundtrack. Though I think it's good if the soundtrack leaves you wanting more.
I'm just a sucker for cyberpunk and sci-fi, so the clean futuristic look and the use of computer terms throughout the game just made me smile throughout.
Okay, so the two biggest parts of the game are probably the gameplay and the story (at least to me). I'm going to start with the gameplay, because I loved that part more:
Awesome. Just awesome. I like hack-and-slash, and I love puzzle and strategy games. I feel like Transitor is a wonderful mix of both. Every ability (or "function") can be used it about three different ways: As a stand-alone attack, as a upgrade (attack-modifier), or passive ability. There are many fun combinations to discover, and though many may feel the game was too easy, I actually felt it was a nice little challenge. There is real-time combat and pre-planned combat, and knowing when to use which was always a hassle for me. But the switch between fast and slow combat always made things interesting to me. I don't really want to get too deep into it (mostly because people already have), but I think if the idea of customizing and planning sounds good to you, then you'll like the gameplay.
My one problem with the game is the story. It isn't bad. It isn't bad at all. The main character is likeable, and so is the narrator for the most part (though I'm sure some people might get annoyed at his constand talking). The world is awesome. The characters all seem pretty awesome for the most part. It's just the way it was told. I saw someone say that this game is, at its core, a love story. And that's true. If you treat it as such, then there's nothing wrong with it. I just wish I didn't have the be confused about everything that was going on, about the world, about the city, about the enemies, and the Transistor and all that. I only know now how cool the world is because I read about it after beating the game. I wish more of the city of Cloudbank was prevelant, and I wish things had been better explained throughout my play through. Admittedly, I didn't go out of my way to find out, but I think most people will be confused the first time around.
Is it better than Bastion? To me, yes, and it's a bit annoying that it has to be compared to Bastion, but they are very similar. I wonder how it would have rated had Transistor came first?
I haven't played Recursion mode yet, but so far, it's one of my favourite games in a long while.

-The characters themselves are also gorgeous in the sense that they are heavily stylized and have unique looks
-Female protagonist (yes, that's a plus. I'm not a believer in forcing gender quotas in games, but it's nice to see women characters in the spotlight. Too bad she's a silent protagonist.)
Cons:
-I bascially had to force myself to come back to this game months after playing it for only a few hours.
-The characters didn't grip me nearly as much as the environment. This made the ending not mean much to me.
-Although the combat system is unique, when not using Turn(), you're essentially just running around waiting for the Turn() bar to fill back up. (or maybe I'm just not good at combat! :P)
Overall, in the wake of games that seem to just be clones of each other and reboots, it's nice to see a game actually try something rather different like this game did with its combat system. Although I wasn't exactly thrilled by it, I still enjoyed it. I may even go back to it. With all its flaws, I still recommend it.

So far I really enjoy this game. I picked it up on the Black Friday sale and no regrets (yet?).  I've played WoW for years and am finally feeling kinda bored with it and FF14 just isn't exciting enough for me to play continuously.
Decided to check out ESO. The battle system is fun, fights can be a challenge, it's cool that you can go about anywhere and do which part of the story when you want and it's not really linear.
Crafting is kinda fun as well. Seems like resrouce gathering is a bit more ogranic due to not just finding a ton of one thing in one area. I do believe there's addons to help but I guess I prefer the challenge of finding it on my own.
Races are a tad limited IMO just like Skyrim. You can be human, elf, cat, or lizard...not super exciting so I chose khajiit.
Making different builds to jsut use while leveling is fun and not something I'd been able to really experience in WoW since BC era when you could really use any weapon on any class.
The cash shop is ok. It seems pretty 1:1 for $ to Crowns. Dye pot sets are 1 set (3 colors predetermined to dye certain parts of your outfit) for about .50 to $1? (I belive that's what it was?) Mounts are as cheap as 700 crowns ($6.99) up to over $15. There's a few costume options, some hair styles, tattoos, emotes, furnished housing, bag space upgrades and some other stuff. I don't know if I really saw any truly P2W elements, I know there's a starter pack that awards you some XP scrolls, but that's about all I saw.
It is buy to play, with sub options, I chose to sub for the benefits of getting 1500 crowns per month (similar to dropping $15 anyways) and you get a crafting bag which allows to free up a substantial amount in your 60 slot default bag space.
Grahpics are pretty nice and runs super smooth on my pc, the occasional load time in larger cities but I think that has to do with the server, not my pc or internet. I have a 2013 or 2014 hp with upgraded graphics (nvidia 960) and larger power supply. That's it. Runs smooth.
Im bad at reviews but that's my take away. The community for NA server that I have seen is a lot more mature, less racist and all around nicer than my recent WoW experiences as well, which is really cool. I guess if you like Skyrim and previous ES games, then this would be worth checking out.

I played through the first level of this and decided I'd write a review on that and update it later as I play. The Initial is a hack and slash game about a girl in a skirt with one warmer missing, though that's not important. I've seen some comments say that the main girl looks like Marie Rose from DOA, I'd comment more on that, but I have no idea who that is. I will say that the game isn't localized as well as it could be. It's never really to the point that I can't understand what's supposed to be going on, but some of the dialog is a little confusing. Story seems to have taken a bit of back seat to gameplay, which is fine by me. Something about being able to create robot clones of people to fight others? It's a decent set up to just let you run around and fight in, which is probably the highlight of the game.
Combat is pretty smooth and is animated well. I don't see many Hack and slash games made these days that interest me, so when I saw this one, I had to jump on it and at least try it out. You have light and heavy attacks and can alternate between them to make combos. All of the combos are not available right off the bat, as you fight you gain points to unlock combos. It's a nice little progression system and you can buy combos at any time in the pause menu. One complaint is that there isn't any lock-on. Well, there's kind of a soft lock-on, but I would have liked a dedicated button to lock-on to an enemy. Combat isn't really as in-depth as something made by Platinum Games, but it's also clear they didn't have as much money and honestly did a great job with what they could.
Graphics are nice, if a little plain. The game looks good for it's price point, but I don't think it will blow anyone away. Character design is little wierd, but that might just be because it seems anime inspired and I don't watch a lot of anime. The character models themselves are good and detailed, I just don't really get the strange clothing choices. I think one of the most important things to note it that the developers seems to be listening to the reviews and updating the game constantly, which is very nice. Especially compared to something like NieR: Automata which hasn't been updated in like ever.
All in all, I like what I've seen so far and will be playing through to the end.
Edit: Now that I've beat the game, I'll update the review. It's a fairly short game at around 2 1/2 hours to beat, but I can see myself playing through it again once or twice to unlock skills and play on a higher difficulty. What I wrote above stays mostly true throughout the game. Localization could definitely use some work, but I still got the story. Boss fights were a little difficult, but once you get the idea of how each boss operates, it's not too hard. Updates are still being relased that make the game combat flow better and it really shows how much the developers are listeing and want to make the game better. I hope the game does well and that the developers can get more of a budget for the next game they make. I'll be keeping an eye on them to see what else they do.

It is difficult to review Dreamfall: The Longest Journey in 2017, eleven years after its original release. One must apply the historical principle of charity and examine Dreamfall squarely in the context of its time, to overlook the dated visuals, frequent backtracking and a couple questionable jokes and decisions. After the success of Telltale, Life is Strange and many Indie hits, it is easy to forget that, a mere 10 years ago, the adventure game genre—for all intents and purposes—was considered dead. But just like it was for Mark Twain and Rock music, reports of its death have been greatly exaggerated.
Originally, Funcom launched Dreamfall on both Windows and Xbox. This was a Funcom before Age of Conan and before The Secret World. It seems that the Norwegian company was trying to appeal to a different demographic than The Longest Journey and traditional point-and-click adventure games, courting mainstream appeal. This would explain the game's gamepad-centric control scheme, not to mention the awkward and unnecessary combat system. Things did not quite work out for Funcom: in 2006, sales of original Xbox titles were in decline, losing ground to popular new Xbox 360 games such as Gears of War. The PC version of Dreamfall did marginally better but it is telling that it took a decade (and more importantly, pledges of over 20,000 fans) for Ragnar Tornquist to revisit the world of The Longest Journey.
But what of the game, you ask? Well, as I mentioned earlier, there are no certainties here. It is impossible not to respect or appreciate the scope and ambition of Dreamfall: The Longuest Journey but it is not an easy game to like. The control scheme takes some time to get used to and the aforementioned combat is laughable. More importantly, the game lacks a minimap, which makes the constant backtracking tedious. While none of the puzzles are difficult, Dreamfall has an annoying habit of offering only the vaguest directions towards the next plot-point, which occasionally results in the player wandering aimlessly among the labyrinthine streets of Mercuria. Then again, none of the puzzles make use of the infamous 'adventure game logic' of 90s LucasArts games.
The single biggest problem with Dreamfall has actually little to do with the game. It is likely that Funcom fully expected to release a sequel within a couple of years, addessing the half-dozen or so cliffhangers that the ending provides. Unfortunately this wasn't the case, and yet reviewing Dreamfall: The Longest Journey after the release of Dreamfall Chapters has been made a lot easier. In short, yes, I definitely recommend this game but not without reservations. This title did not age gracefully but was ambitious for its time and so full of heart. It is certainly worth playing either as a relic of mid-2000s games or as a prequel for Dreamfall Chapters.

I absolutely loved the first game so I was super excited to play this. It was almost be inevitable that this was going to be in the shadow of the original but it is a still a great game.
I was initially unimpressed. I generally hate using a gamepad rather than a mouse but here after fiddling around with the settings for a bit I just couldn’t get the mouse controls to feel right at all and had to switch to a controller.
The other thing that put me off at the start was Zoë’s voice acting, I know the character is supposed to be overwhelmed by ennui but she was just so emotionless to me that it always sounded like someone just reading off the script that it kept breaking the immersion. This was particularly disappointing as one of the things that was so good about the original was the quality of the voice acting.
Another misstep from the first game is the introduction of stealth and combat. I kind of get the feeling that someone in the production of this game was adamant that point and click games were not popular any more and that they had to include some kind of combat.  It really could have benefited from some more intricate puzzles.
The one thing that is an improvement is the graphics are a world apart as in you can actually see what is going on.
The key thing that made the original so good was the story and the story here is a worthy successor. It revisits various locations and characters from the original but does not feel like it is retreading the same ground. The conclusion is not quite as satisfying at the original as it leaves a few too many unanswered questions.
So if you like the first game then you will enjoy this but just not quite as much.

4) Most innovative Skill: BossRush! You skill the normal waves and jist do Boss waves for a limited amount of time, and can therefore skip a huge amount of levels to again reach those levels where you now might be stron enough... makes full runbs much faster and less grindy, great invention!

6) Mystery gift... every 30min, you get a short window where you can click 1 of 3 gifts... can be Gold, Valorpoints, Infinity Tokens or (very rarely) Gems
+ Nice achievements make it worthwhile to continue and get stronger.
Therefore, 9/10. Would have been perfect without the Gems, which are too rare, and which are too much of a cash grab (can be bough for real money)

I came right off playing the original Dark Souls into this game, and the difference in quality is staggering and dissapointing. The game drops you into Drangleic with no explanation of why you're here or what exactly it is you're doing. So far I have yet to really figure either of those things out, and looking at other reviews, it doesn't look like I will.  Aesthetically, Drangleic is very pretty, but they changed the previously very cool Hollow design into something that looks like a cop out to make them more like Ye Olde Video Game Zombies, and the player walking animation looks like you're hobbling around trying not to♥♥♥♥♥♥yourself. Combat is significantly harder than in the original, but unlike the original, the difficulty doesn't seem implemented in a fair manner.  The renewable healing method is so slow it makes healing in combat nearly impossible, and the new healing crystals are so limited you run out of viable ways to heal pretty quickly.  The fact that your health bar drops slightly each death and can only be raised again with an expensive and limited consumable just exacerbates this.  There were also several points I had my shield up but took full damage anyway.  I don't know if that was a bug or a feature, because I did find a disheartening amount of bugs (at least, I sure hope I wasn't intended to talk to NPCs through building walls).  Overall, I'd say skip this game if you want to play a proper Dark Souls game. If you just want a difficult game to hack and slash through, this might be for you.

World of Goo is a simple yet innovative Puzzle-based game where you help colonies of Goo Balls find their purpose in the universe.
Each puzzle involves using the Goo Balls to create structures and reach a pipe.
Each Goo Ball species has its own unique abilities and each puzzle has its own theme.
The player wins when when a certain number of Goo Balls go through the pipe.
In addition, each puzzle also has an OCD bonus that require the player to complete the puzzle within a certain number of moves, an allotted time, or by collecting extra Goo Balls.
Since this game is so simplistic, there's nothing really "wrong" to say about it.
The only issue I had was that it could've been longer or more fleshed out.
I was also disappointed with the Tower of Goo minigame, which you can play by collecting extra Goo Balls, since all it gives you are bragging rights for building the tallest Tower of Goo.
The story itself is... interesting, to say the least since it has no basic structure.
There IS a story, which centers around the Goo Balls trying to destroy the World of Goo Corporation after it conquers the world by using them as ingredients for commercial products.
Of course, you wouldn't know that from playing the game since there are no main characters.
Aside from the Goo Balls, which are so cute when they wake up, there are ten characters the player encounters throughout the game.
However, only two progress the storyline while the rest are exclusive to certain puzzles.
The first is the Sign Painter who gives advice for each puzzle and narrates the story.
The second is MOM who is a mysterious entity that the player eventually meets in Chapter 4.
It's definitely a fun game to play, especially since the Goo Balls cameo in several other games.
Of course, if you're looking for a story or some form of immersion, you won't find it here.
World of Goo is one of those games where you play for the sake of playing.

While "Rock of Ages" tries to be a strange combo of "Marble Madness" and a tower defense game, the tower defense portions of the game are a bit half baked. The game basically consists of two players building defenses along a track to prevent the other from breaking down their castle doors with player controlled boulders. While this sounds good in theory, in practice the defenses are mostly so weak that PvP games usually just boil down to whoever can rush to hit the other player's door 3 times first, rendering placement of defenses mostly moot.
However, I still had fun with "Rock of Ages" mainly because its "Marble Madness" portions play so well.  Barreling down a path as a boulder, avoiding obstacles, collecting keys, and crushing everything else in your wake never gets old. Plus, the single player campaign (a humorous tour through history with an incredibly well realized Terry Gilliam-esque aesthetic) is one of the most amusing and creative things I played all last year.

Rock of Ages is a fun game with a quirky style and sense of humor. You play as Sisyphus, rolling boulders down various levels to break an enemy gate, while your opponents (a series of historical figures) are simultaneously trying to do the same to you. Rolling the stone is only half of the equation, though. In between rolls, you also have to set up defenses to hinder your opponent's progress towards your gate. It's an interesting mashup of genres. Aside from the gameplay, there is one other cool thing about the game - the cutscenes. Between levels, you are treated to very odd (but really funny) paper-cutout interludes starring the aforementioned historical figures. The scenes are reminiscent of Terry Gilliam's work from Monty Python, and are very enjoyable. All in all, this is a pretty fun game that works best in small doses (it tends to get a bit repetitive if playing for extended durations). The music is great too! I definitely say give it a shot if you're up for something different.
