Yes, please! Paper, Please is surpsingly simple and equally as addicting. You spend your days in Arstotzka reviewing legal documentation at the boarder's check point. The game really requires you to inspect as many people as possible all whilst paying close attention to detail. You are attempting to support your family on this job so any mistakes, or simply not turning out as many people as possible, can result in poor wages or possibly worse. Perpare yourself to be presented with some tough choices. I love a game that allows you to empathize and take risks by doing so. Overall I highly recommend this game.

Papers, Please is a puzzle, simulation game focused on the emotional task of working as an immigration officers, deciding who you let in and who you deny entry of. The game is based in a fictional country called Arstotzka.
The game play focuses around the work life of an immigration inspect at a boarder checkpoint. Players will inspect documents and using a selection of different tools to work out whether the papers meet all of the criteria to warrant access to crossing the boarder. When you do find a problem with the paper work presented to you, there is also the option to interrogate the applicant, which may result in the need for further information such as a full body scan or finger printers.  Once you have worked out all of the paper work and questions being asked, you have to make a choice whether to Accept or deny entry, and then call the next person in line. Only then are you told any mistakes that you have made in the form of a warning slip.
On top of wading your way through all the paper work, you also have a time limit for the day in which you have to process as many applicants as possible.  At the end of each working shift, you will earn money based on how many people have been processed, bribes collected, as well as deductions for any penalties you accrued.  Then you must decided how to spend this money with your families budget, spending it on rent, food, heat and other necessities such as medicine or upgrades to your working environment.
Paper, Please has a very prominent sound track, which starts as a slow marching rhythm made by bass to represent flow of entrants in the line of applicants and how tired and depressed they are. Although the technical side of the music is basic, it is probably one of the most memorable soundtracks you will hear from a game.
The game is only as difficult as you make it; if you pay attention to every little detail, you shouldn't fail. Only if you missing key bits of information or just not paying attention in general will your warnings pile up, and you will start to get less and less money, which results in your bills not being paid, which then results in having to start all over.
The game took me a little over twenty hours to complete one run, there is just a huge amount of content to go through, although some of the applicants are scripted such as terrorists or smugglers, along with plot characters, a lot of the others are randomly generated which means no run should ever be the same.
Technically, I had no issues what so ever. It's a very technically simple game which can be played in Windows mode without problems either.
Papers, Please will certainly not be for everybody, but if you want to try something different from the regular shooting and spell casting games we are drowning in today, pick this up. I got over twenty hours of game play out of this awesome £6,99 title.

The minds behind Bastion, Supergiant Games ,are back with their newest game: Transistor.
If you've played Bastion before, you can clearly see that this is indeed, the same people making a different game.
I played this game a few months back, and i still find myself making questions about this game. It's just... Too much to handle.
The world of the game is quite opposite from Bastion. As Bastion features this beautiful, broken world , Transistor gives us this utopian perfect world that on the surface seems absolutely troublefree.
As i quite obviously foreshadowed in the previous sentence, Cloudbank (the so-called
perfect city) has it's flaws.
The storyline of this game borrows one thing from Bastion; the game just throws you in the world and gives you a vague hint of the story  and let's you figure it all on your own. The game starts with the Camerata trying to assassinate the main character, Red with their weapon, the Transistor. (roll credits please). Emphasis on the word "attempt" and instead of Red dying, a another character, a nameless man gets killed and stuck in the Transistor.
The Story itself features the revenge for the said assassination attempt and the story reveals more than one side to the motive on the attempt.
A one more thing about the story; prepare to get sad. Whereas Bastion relies pretty hard on the "everything is going to be fine" attitude on the matters at hand, Transistor does the opposite.
Go figure what that means.
The game is very heavily driven on aesthetic side of things and on the absolutely gorgeous soundtrack, that i'll tell you more about in the next part of this review. I purely bought this game on the impulse of seeing this game on the Steam Marketplace (on a sale if i recall right) and i instantly fell in love with the games visual side. After the installation and first try of the game, i instantly fell for the audio side of this game.
Darren Korb (the composer/producer) who worked on Bastion's Original Soundtrack is also back in this one, except two things have changed. The game features a beautiful female vocalist (Ashley Barrett) and instead of Bastion's brighter, cheerier major-sounding tracks, the tracks are clearly very much darker, sadder minor sounds.
I personally find myself having the Transistor
soundtrack constantly on loop and i highly recommend you to do the same. But after the finishing the game of course, since the OST's vocals are
more or less connected to the storyline.
The mechanics of the game are quite refreshing, the game features this "pause the game and plan your next move" mechanic that is quite... different from
what i've before used in my quite lengthy gaming journey. The game has quite good controller support, but the aiming on the controller isn't that
fine tuned and it usually required me to aim on the mouse. And that sometimes made my game glitch.
The game really enjoys the contrast between a few things.
The main character, Red is a singer without a voice and the man trapped inside transistor is a man without a body.
9.5/10 Buy it, Love it , Cry a little bit.
Who am i kidding , cry a river.

It is a game which, from the very beginning, provides just enough guidance without overwhelming with too much information. Controlling the game is simple and the unique mix of real-time action RPG and turn-based tactical RPG is very satisfying to master. The story is not told directly -- rather, it is presented over time by voice-over as you play, through subtle interactions between characters, and through clues in the world. No long-winded tutorials are necessary to get started, with a very simple introduction getting the player up and running in less than five minutes.
There are some minor complaints I could raise, such as the lack of much exploration (the game is quite linear) or optional content (what optional missions are available are interesting but fairly simple). With the design being as solid as it is, however, I struggle to name how these weak points could be improved without weakening other points.
Overall, I highly recommend this game. It's a perfect example of what can be done with design focused on the player's enjoyment, not on creating a spectacle. There are many options available for varying styles of play, there is easily-adjusted difficulty which should challenge even the most extreme of players, there is replay value with a very difficult New Game+ option, and most of all, the story is absolutely amazing.
I could go on, but this is simply a game which must be experienced, not described.

Elder Scrolls Online, is a good game and, in my opinion, a nice take on the elder scrolls series as a whole.
Being set around the 2E 582, ESO is the earliest game in the time line being set before all 5 predecesors, you play as the prophesised souless one who is destined to stop Molag Bal's invasion of Tamriel.
The game features a good combat systems with a good skill tree system having different paths for race, class, weapon types, armour types, world based, guild based, and more.
It's a nice looking game with varying environments depending on where you were on Tamriel/Summerset Isles.
The banking system is essentially an improved version of the storage system used in other elder scrolls games, and allows you to store money and items inside, as well as giving you access to all crafting materials inside at any crafting station.
Although I do have some issues with it.
the first thing that lept out at me was the fact that the Imperial race (one which i commonly use for the first playthrough of games in the series) is locked behind a paywall if you didnt get the imperial edition of the game.
another thing was that one of the major expansions ESO: Morrowind is also locked behind a paywall (while this is not uncommon, it's one of the few games i have seen which have DLC/Expansions asking for £30 to play)
And the final thing I'm going to mention here is the cost of crowns (premium currency) vs. what you can get for themif you want a large furnished house (only purchasable with crowns) from what i have seen it can be from 7500 to 12500 crowns (or £48.97 (7500 crowns)) for a single house, i understand that it would be expensive to use the premium currency to buy things rather than spending the time to grind up the gold to buy the unfunished version. but it just seems wrong for a single house to be valued higher than a full DLC/Expansion.
over all, while i do reccomend ESO, i cannot reccomend crown purchases untill value for money has been increased

I think it is quite odd that I have never played another Call of Juarez game. Even when everyone I knew was playing "Bound in Blood", I just never wanted to play one. However, after playing the Demo for this at my Friends house, I was quite interested to see where it would go. After playing this, I am now quite interested in playing the others.
The story is quite fun. You play as Silas Greaves, a drunken old Bounty Hunter who has stopped at a bar to tell his tale to those who are interested. You play through the stories as he tells them, going through ridiculous memories of hunting down some of the most famous figures of the Western Era. Jesse James, Dalton Brothers, Butch Cassidy, Wild Bill Hickok and More. It’s quite funny hearing the listeners explain what books and history has told them as opposed to what Silas went through. The game also changes depending on the story, so if you hit a dead end sometimes the Silas will add a new detail to his story and your surroundings will change too.
The gameplay feels good to. All the guns have that great thing about them where it actually feels like they have a kick to them and that they are doing damage. There is a slow-motion mode where it highlights all the nearby enemies (a Red Dead Redemption Dead Eye kind of deal) that can really help out when you are swarmed with enemies to kill. This doesn’t feel overpowered luckily as it doesn't last very long at takes a while to recharge, meaning you don't just end up running around spamming this feature and not actually fighting normally. The duals also add a nice change of pace to each of the levels. Going from guns blazing insane shootouts to tense and precise one on one duals works well and provides a good contrast of gameplay. I do wish there was a bit of a better health system. The screen just turning redder as you get hurt is alright but it can make it difficult to judge how much health you have. This means that sometimes you risk running in to situations thinking you can survive only to be killed in one shot. I know this problem isn't just limited to this game, but it is annoying none the less.
The Graphics are alright. There wasn't really anything that stood out to me or stuck in my mind. It has the shell shaded Borderlands look to it which works but doesn't add to or take away from the experience. The colours are quite vibrant and stand out, a look that I like. I wish there where nicer set pieces to this game. You play in some cool areas, such as the caves when fighting the Indians, but nothing really jaw dropping which is a shame as I think this game could easily have them due to the great setting and the lovely colours. I also would have liked to have a bit more control over some of the graphics options. The FOV feels way too low. If you could just put the FOV up a bit, it would feel and look a whole lot better.
I did enjoy this game enough to get every achievement on it. It has just enough gameplay to feel like you are getting your money’s worth without absolutely flooding you with content. The story is long enough that you can get into and enjoy it without it dragging on and overstaying its welcome. I would recommend this game even if you haven’t played any of the other ones; And It’s nice to see that fans of the series are saying that this is a great addition to the franchise.

What appears to be a simple game with primitive graphics and tedious repetitive tasks unveils to be a one-of-a-kind unforgettable experience not a single triple A title has managed and probably will never manage to provide.
The simplicity in graphics turns out to be just right for the grim, monotonous setting of the game, where the present is not bright and the future is not promising to be any better.
The necessity to follow every instruction to the letter. As the government becomes more and more paranoid and constantly implements new rules as they're meant to fix the mistakes it has made, the difficulty increases - for you, the mere paper worker.
Combined with the fact you're being paid accordingly with the amount of papers you've processed, it turns out that you cannot process them as quickly as when you got this position. A single detail is missed, and you're fined. You've got to make a choice between analyzing papers carefully and giving up on your earnings and trying to get through them quickly risking to miss on a little detail.
Later on, it turns out that you cannot even put a little piece of decoration in your office, a little display of humanity in yourself. A swift reminder that you aren't a human - you're a human unit, a worker supposed to operate at a machine level efficiency, no matter the difficulty.
The longer you play, the more tension there is - and no way less morbid one than the one against the final boss of the level/the game. The longer you play, the more questions there are to ask and to answer to yourself. The longer you play, the further your work style shapes who you become closer to the end.
No surprise there are 20 endings - the game, being simple in graphics and context, not moving you any further than but one location, provides a pretty wide range of moral choices, work styles, opportunities for a better future, and overall psychological development of your character. You aren't the same since you've occupied this post. Who will you turn out as?

I've played this game for about 3 days now, and it's absolutely amazing. Please note these are my own personal opinions on the game, and I still have a large majority of the game to uncover.
Pros
-Breathtaking graphics.
-Skill animations.
-Roleplaying.
-Replayability.
-Story.
-Inventory
-Sountrack
-Armor/Mounts
Graphics - Absolutely wonderful, especially for what is coming up to be a 5 year old game.
Skill animations - Nice, fluid, look awesome; very eye appealing.
Roleplaying - A large of roleplaying can be had in this game, especially with the requirement of a Forename and a Surname.
Replayability - Literally 20+ classes you can all level up on one character and switch between, really awesome idea that works amazingly.
Story - Super in-depth, and really worth-while taking your time on your first playthrough to explore the world.
Inventory - Literally THE best inventory system I've ever seen in any game. Seperate inventories (literally 20+ slots) for every armor piece, then another 100 for junk/misc, and ANOTHER for quest items.
Soundtrack - Beautiful sountrack from Square Enix, as is to be expected.
Armor/Mounts - THE best plate armor I've ever seen, weapon designs make sense, along with some armor. Mounts look cool as ♥♥♥♥ as well. Great amount of custimization.
Cons
-Global Skillcooldown
-Confusing at first
-Map system
-Teleportation is a bit odd
-Learning curve
-Voiceovers
-Tab targeting
Skillcooldowns - After every cast, whether instant or a 2-3 sec. cast time, you have a set amount of time before you are able to do another action. Feels a bit awkward at first, and still does right now, but something I disliked.
Confusion - Game throws you in, no ♥♥♥♥s given, and it can be a bit overwhelming, take things one at a time and it'll get good.
Map system - Feels clunky to use, hard to tell where some locations (i.e. exits, towns, quests) are.
Teleportation - Teleporting feels like it should be done at "Aetheryte Crystals" allowing you to go anywhere, but they limit you to zones. Teleportation is done as a skill and costs money, just feels weird and unexplainable.
Learning Curve - Big learning curve, but once you get over it, it's very rewarding.
Voiceovers - Some of the most random cutscenes have voice overs, and ones that feel detrimental to the storyline have none. Just feels weird at times; inconsistent.
Tab targeting - Tab targeting SHOULD (in my opinion) be the closest monster towards you, and it isn't. I don't understand the mechanics and it can cause unnecessary aggro on monsters due to misclicks.
TL;DR - Great game with a bit of a hard learning curve. Worthwhile in the end.

I'm not an MMO player, but I love FInal Fantasy. And that's what drew me to play this game after hearing that the story and music were the best in the FF series in a decade. Having beaten the story up to the end of Heavensward, I can confirm that is true. Although the gameplay is classic MMO, the atmosphere, music and story all bring back memories of the Final Fantasy series.
The story will have multiple twists and turns and will keep you wanting to know what happens next. The Heavensward expansion is especially good with this imo. To note though, because it is an MMO, there ARE portions of the main story questline that are filled with filler quests and fetch quests. They definitely felt dull, and feel like Square just put them in to increase the amount of "content" in the main story when they didn't need to. Again, the Heavensward expansion did not have that. The main culprit is the post-ARR, patch 2.1-2.4 content.
The game has some of best FF music in awhile, enough to make me seriously want the soundtrack. There are a lot of memorable area/city music and battle/boss themes. The world and areas are another strength. There are many varied locations in the world, and some beautiful scenes. The lore is extensive, and I can't wait till they open up even more of the world. There is so much left unexplored in the world and story (that will most likely be explored in future content).
In terms of end game content, the constant updates gives you enough things to do throughout even if it is possible to "binge" through all of it fairly quickly. Raids are fun and challenging.
In terms of an MMO game, there isn't too much innovation, but FFXIV:ARR executes everything really well and hence its status as the foremost MMO rival to WoW.

In this game, you ARE that organization, making the perfect organism to wipe out human life on the planet and selecting Case Zero, before a cure can be synthesized.  My first bacteria took just over three years to kill everyone, whereas my virus took just over a year...kinda freaky.  As it is still in its initial build, there are several menu options not yet available, but there is still plenty of fun to be had in the Main Game.  It'll be interesting to see how they develop their multi-player aspect; P1 creates the disease while P2 tries to find it and cure it, or, P1 and P2 BOTH create a disease and whoever wipes out more wins?

When old bounty hunter Silas Greaves stumbles into a saloon and finds some folks willing to listen to his stories, we take his role and flash back to his adventures.
Like the times he rode with Billy the Kid, or when he won the praise of Injun magic men, or that shootout he had with Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid....
Gunslinger’s action is a lot of fun, and its gunplay is extremely satisfying. Enemy AI is intelligent and aggressive enough to keep things interesting.
You earn greater amounts of experience points for headshots, for shooting enemies while they are running away, or by discovering the so-called 'nugget' collectibles.
Kills also fill a 'concentration' gauge, which can be used to momentarily slow time.
While 'concentrating', you're even able to pick out incoming enemy bullets, strafing out of their trajectory. Meanwhile, 'sense of death' gives you a 50/50 chance of survival when your character is riddled with bullets and ready to expire.
Apart from its story-driven campaign and its two separate endings there are two other modes.
One mode is Arcade Mode, where the idea is to kill as many enemies as you can as quickly as you can to generate a high score. The other is based on the dueling.
I highly recommend this game.

This game is a love hate relationship.  The gameplay can be extremely fun at times and extremely infuriating the next.
This game basically hates casual gamers and makes no point of hiding it.  And I'm not even talking about the difficulty curve.  The game literally has features that serve no other purpose than to target casual gamers and make their SPECIFIC experience more infuriating.  So a skilled player who experiences these features probably won't even notice anything.  Only people who die a lot more at a boss will find their game getting harder.
There are four major differences between Dark Souls 1 and 2.  Each of them sucks for varying reasons.
1) Every time you die, a bit of your max health will be taken away until eventually you are at 50% health.  You can then use a human effigy to restore your max health (not that they tell you anywhere in the game about this).  This is a feature that targets casual players.  Skilled players will probably have dozens of human effigies by the time they need them and won't even care about their health bar.  A casual player on the other hand will eventually run out and be forced to play the game at half health eventually.
2)PVP is now mandatory UNLESS you unhook your internet either through Steam or unplugging your ethernet cable.  Even then you'll get invaded by NPCs.  But in the ladder case, they won't match you against some monstrous speedrunner who knows the game by heart and has perfected his PVP strats.  The only reason From Software forces you to do this is because they wanna keep PVP alive for as long as possible.  This is basically them hanging the PVE gamers in favor of the PVP gamers.
3)They decided that the boss fights didn't have enough RNG in the last Dark Souls game.  Now half the bosses are a group fight.  Some of them are ridiculously easy, some of them are ridiculously hard.  Multiple bosses didn't make the game more fun, they actually took the fun out of it since there's nothing you can do half the times you get hit.  You just have to keep trying until you win.
4)If you kill the same enemy over and over again, he'll stop respawning after 15 kills.  This is another feature targetting casual gamers as they'll initially feel like the game is making fun of them for dieing so much.  It also prevents grinding enemies that drop human effigies should you run out.  It also limits grinding souls should you want to level a bit before challenging a difficult boss.  None of which will affect a truly skilled player.
Also, various other players have already mentioned this, but anyone who bought this game with the DLC is basically getting screwed because From Software has basically mandated that if you want ALL the NEW Dark Souls 2 content, then buyers of the original game no longer qualify.  People who play this version of the game will literally have less enemies in a smaller variety to fight.  UNLESS you rebuy the whole game which they've relabelled as "Scholarship of the first sin"
Another annoying thing is the alternate weapon slots.  Did you know that even though you aren't using the weapons in the two extra slots, they still add weight to your character?  I beat half the game before realizing this stupidity... Another tidbit they didn't tell you is that 70% weight capacity allows for the fastest rolling and running.  I'd been playing at 73% without knowing either of those pieces of information.  So now I'm faster and I have heavier armor on...
My final criticism of the game is that half of the bosses are just plain uninspired...  There are a few great bosses, but the vast majority of them seem to be just boring or stupid.  Even some of the cooler concepts they had fell flat because of the terrible implmentation.  Several bosses just felt like rehashes of old bosses.

Don't listen to anyone who tells you it isn't worth it. I'm in about knee deep (20 hours or so offline, blind, and alone) and Dark Souls II has been nothing but fun to play. Albeit the designs of the bosses don't seem to be quite as amazing as before (as far as the first six I have beaten are concerned), and certain mechanics are a bit annoying (the increasing curse with each death --  in its defense it does serve to raise the stakes of each attempt at a boss) but all in all, it is still 100% a Souls game, and that is good enough for me.
Even the most basic looking bosses give you that rush of adrenaline, that stiffening of the spine, and that ultimate feeling of satisfaction and exuberance (or vengeful despair) you come to expect in the Dark Souls experience. It is, as I have been told, the most Japanese of the series, which is in no wise a bad thing -- it just... feels different. Slightly less immersive than Dark Souls, quite a bit more than Skyrim (imho), and more worth it now than ever, since the DLCs are a package deal. If the first one is the golden standard (10), then Dark Souls II is at least an 8/10, which is a helluva lot of praise considering the boots it had to fill. Try it for yourself and form your own opinions about it. Don't let mine or anyone else's tell you what to think about it, just trust me, because I'm always right ;)
Cheers, and praise the sun!

Though certainly the most flawed game in the series (including Bloodborne), it's still definitely fun.
DS2's main problem lies with the fact that Hidetaka Miyazaki was not involved with this game, and it shows (he was busy with the magnificent Bloodborne at the time). Most boss fights feel enourmously lackluster and often are over so quickly you haven't got time to really comprehend what the boss is all about (looking at you, Dragon Rider). The game feels like an imitation, rather than a true "Souls" game. The game also lacks a certain level of polish that one might have come to expect from these games, such as boss fight music ending ubruptly upon killing the boss.
This, however, is not to say that the game is bad (though I would strongly suggest getting a fix for the controller deadzones). The world is extensive and many of the zones in the game make a refreshing change to the usual dark and depressing areas from the other games in the series. The relative ease of the game also makes for a refreshing change from Dark Souls 1 in particular, with certain zones feeling more like a field trip rather than a gruling gauntlet.
Overall, though certainly not a perfect game (such as DS1, DS3 and BB), Dark Souls 2 is a perfectly enjoyable experience despite it's flaws. I'd definitely say that this is the version to get, though, as SotFS has some issues regarding weapon durability and questionable choices in regards to making the game "harder".

What appears to be a simple game with primitive graphics and tedious repetitive tasks unveils to be a one-of-a-kind unforgettable experience not a single triple A title has managed and probably will never manage to provide.
The simplicity in graphics turns out to be just right for the grim, monotonous setting of the game, where the present is not bright and the future is not promising to be any better.
The necessity to follow every instruction to the letter. As the government becomes more and more paranoid and constantly implements new rules as they're meant to fix the mistakes it has made, the difficulty increases - for you, the mere paper worker.
Combined with the fact you're being paid accordingly with the amount of papers you've processed, it turns out that you cannot process them as quickly as when you got this position. A single detail is missed, and you're fined. You've got to make a choice between analyzing papers carefully and giving up on your earnings and trying to get through them quickly risking to miss on a little detail.
Later on, it turns out that you cannot even put a little piece of decoration in your office, a little display of humanity in yourself. A swift reminder that you aren't a human - you're a human unit, a worker supposed to operate at a machine level efficiency, no matter the difficulty.
The longer you play, the more tension there is - and no way less morbid one than the one against the final boss of the level/the game. The longer you play, the more questions there are to ask and to answer to yourself. The longer you play, the further your work style shapes who you become closer to the end.
No surprise there are 20 endings - the game, being simple in graphics and context, not moving you any further than but one location, provides a pretty wide range of moral choices, work styles, opportunities for a better future, and overall psychological development of your character. You aren't the same since you've occupied this post. Who will you turn out as?

Papers Please is a point-and-click simulation in where the player uses investigative skills in looking at papers. The gameplay is monotonous, dull, and repetitive, thus truly simulating the work of a border immigrations officer. If the papers are inaccurate you decline, if papers are accurate you accept. The player receives money based on performance to pay for amenities at home, then the next day begins.
The nation’s immigrations policy changes, and so do the people you service; the stories are told from the glimpses of a small border entry. You, the player, the insignificant being of the grand scheme of things, play a cog in the clockwork that this game has created. Your seemingly insignificant choices influence the multiple families and organizations through a simple choice between red or green stamp.

This game is not for everyone. It is not grossly fun, flamboyant, or explosive. But I recommend it for those seeking something more than just a cheesy dramatization or a shooter.

Interesting twist on the "End of the World by virus/plague/disease/etc" genre.  In games like Resident Evil, you (typically) fight against a big organization (Umbrella) who released a disaster. In this game, you ARE that organization, making the perfect organism to wipe out human life on the planet and selecting Case Zero, before a cure can be synthesized.  My first bacteria took just over three years to kill everyone, whereas my virus took just over a year...kinda freaky.  As it is still in its initial build, there are several menu options not yet available, but there is still plenty of fun to be had in the Main Game.  It'll be interesting to see how they develop their multi-player aspect; P1 creates the disease while P2 tries to find it and cure it, or, P1 and P2 BOTH create a disease and whoever wipes out more wins?

If you came here looking for a review, you're in the wrong place. If you came here looking for a blueberry muffin recipe you're in the right place however, So without further a do.
1 1/2 cups all-purpose flour
3/4 cup white sugar
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 teaspoons baking powder
1/3 cup vegetable oil
1 egg
1/3 cup milk
1 cup fresh blueberries
1/2 cup white sugar
1/3 cup all-purpose flour
1/4 cup butter cubed
1 1/2 teaspoons ground cinnamon
Prep 15 m
Cook 25 m
Ready In 40 m
Preheat oven to 400 degrees F (200 degrees C). Grease muffin cups or line with muffin liners.
Combine 1 1/2 cups flour, 3/4 cup sugar, salt and baking powder. Place vegetable oil into a 1 cup measuring cup; add the egg and enough milk to fill the cup. Mix this with flour mixture. Fold in blueberries. Fill muffin cups right to the top, and sprinkle with crumb topping mixture.
To Make Crumb Topping: Mix together 1/2 cup sugar, 1/3 cup flour, 1/4 cup butter, and 1 1/2 teaspoons cinnamon. Mix with fork, and sprinkle over muffins before baking.
Bake for 20 to 25 minutes in the preheated oven, or until done.

This is a great puzzle indie game, though the price has a mixed opinion for me. If you haven't played it, then yes, I'd recomended it, that is if you like puzzle games. But if you've already played it on the Wii, IOS/Android, or the Switch, then I'd be hesitant to recomend it. As a puzzle game, it's an original concept. It's difficulty is perfect in my opinion (i like difficult puzzle games soo yeah). However, it's annoying that you can't change the audio settings period, and you can only change resolution in the files, or else it will be 800x600, which looks terrible on most monitors. Also, this game looks blurry as hell above 1080p, so don't even try 1440p, 4K, or even 8K for the people who are that rich. Though 1080p does look okay, so it shouldn't be too big of an issue.
However, in my opinion, the gameplay is extermely enjoyable and original, and still holds up great in 2017. However, the annoying way you set up options, takes away points from this otherwise great game.
So this game gets a 7.5/10. And yes, I do recommend it. But only if you've haven't played it yet.

World of Goo is a strange sort of puzzle game. Its gameplay mechanics are based on structural physics, involving lots of little balls of Goo that you can use in different ways.
Everything about this game is well made. To me, perhaps the most accomplished of all is the developers' theme of combatting a corporate soullessness with tiny cogs of construction, in the form of the Goo. The minimalist story brings a smile and gives gamers a critical eye on consumerism while maintaining a light and fun gameplay.
Also, props to the music.
If you like puzzlers and haven't played this game, you should really try it out.

You'll want to go inside The Room. The puzzles and challenges presented by the safe therein offer several hours of entertaining gameplay.
The Room is a fascinating game. You’re in a room with a well-locked safe, and your goal is to get that safe open. The game makes the story more detailed than that, but The Room’s storyline is its least interesting aspect. The fun comes from the hours of puzzles and challenges required to break open the safe, coupled with the game’s delightfully creepy ambience.
There’s a lot to like about The Room. The first thing you’ll notice is that ambience mentioned earlier: The game’s graphics are excellently drawn; the faux three-dimensional room—and the safe it contains—look great, and are fun to explore. And the soundtrack and sound effects set a mood not quite of fear, but something entertainingly off-putting about the experience: Why is this safe so intricately locked up? What the heck is it protecting?
(Okay, when the creepy whispers start in Chapter 3, yeah, it’s a little scary.)
All that excellent mood setting and imagery wouldn’t amount to much were it not for the intuitive gameplay. You’ll need to navigate around the room to unearth discoveries—oh, this table leg can also unscrew to reveal a hidden key, and this seemingly plain panel masks a tappable portion to access another section, and tapping these buttons in the right order will open a secret drawer.
Get into gear: You'll need to twist dials, push buttons, turn keys, and find all sorts of hidden compartments to finish The Room.
As I mentioned at the outset, there is a story behind why you’re digging through The Room and the safe it contains, but that’s the boring part. The fun is the journey: figuring out how to solve the increasingly intricate puzzles in the game.
If the Room aren’t fanciful enough for you, the game adds a further element of magic with an eyepiece you discover early on. From time to time, you’ll need to put the eyepiece back on to discover otherwise hidden imagery necessary to solve certain puzzles. That element adds a nice dimension to the gameplay.
Hidden in plain sight: Secrets, knobs, and buttons will hide all over the place in The Room.
Where The Room excels is in layering its puzzles upon further puzzles. When you find a key, you might also need to rotate pieces of that key to make it fit in the keyhole you discover. As you place cogs into a gear system, you might need to reposition some to get further along. And when you discover items that you can add to your inventory, you might in turn need to examine your own inventory to uncover the secrets those items hide.
If The Room has a weakness, it’s the controls. I found them fussy and occasionally frustrating. You can double-tap to zoom in, but only pinch to zoom out, and sometimes getting those zoom gestures recognized in either direction takes multiple tries. Since zooming is an integral part of playing the game, that can get a smidgen tiresome. But the truth is, you—like me—probably won’t care. The game and its puzzles are so engaging that you’ll look past the intermittently annoying controls to get back to the intricately crafted puzzles.
Bottom line
The Room is great. The puzzles are both challenging and discoverable, and you’ll milk at least three hours of fun gameplay from the game. The graphics and sound are top-notch. If you prize replayability over those other factors, however, note that it’s limited; once you’ve completed The Room, it’s unlikely you’ll want to go through the entire game again. But you’ll probably get a kick out of introducing the game to someone else and watching them work their way through it.
The Room
Pros
Excellent ambience, sound, and graphics
Brilliantly crafted puzzles
Three or more solid hours of addictive gameplay
Cons
Occasionally fussy controls ( you—like me—probably won’t care )

One of the best and most entertaining puzzle games I've played. I found the puzzles were exactly as challenging as I would have liked them to be; some thought required, but no pesky pixel hunting or cheap tricks.
If you ever get stuck on something, clues are unlocked based on the time you spend stuck on a specific part of the puzzle. I admit to using them in three or four places where I was beginning to feel confounded, and found they helped guide me immensely without giving me any information I didn't already have or telling me what to do (e.g. "I think I've seen that pattern before", "What else is this shape?", that sort of thing).
I would love for it to be longer, or for there to be a sequel (which I understand is planned?), but for the low price and high quality of the puzzles, graphics and atmosphere, nothing else even comes close. I definitely recommend it.

This is an excellent game for those who like to make their own fun, especially in creative ways. The game gives you a wide array of destructive weaponry to use, (most of it explosive in nature), and it's up to you to innovate, if you're so inclined.
Basically, you could either blow up every chaos object away with an RPG and find yourself bored in a couple hours, or you could try mixing things up.
For example, you could strap some jet propelled sticky mines to the back of a car, drive the car towards the object, eject yourself from the vehicle, activate the explosives, and watch the rocket propelled vehicle plow into whatever you were aiming at and detonate.
The gameplay is repetitive in nature, but makes up for it with a beautiful landscape to explore, a great sense of scale, numerous abilities and upgrades to use, and fluid gameplay. The wingsuit is tough to use at first, but once you get it down, flying becomes exhilirating and enjoyable.
Also, this game was plagued at launch with horrendous AMD card issues, and I'm not sure if those are fixed or not. It's possible that they are, so I'd look into it, I just don't know.

I got to talking to a friend one day about games with great stories. My mate then brought up Call of Juarez Gunslinger and I was instantly slightly repulsed because of what I'd heard about another game in the series, Call of Juarez The Cartel. He reassured me that this game was great in terms of story and gameplay and then gave me a spare key he had laying around for it and told me to play it. So, here I am now, writing this review shortly after completing it.
Overall the sound was very average. Nothing really to call home about, but it wasn't bad. The music used was good, but not memorable, the sound effects sounded as they should, and the voice acting overall was very good though some characters felt a little bland due to sounding very generic. This all said it was fine and didn't take away or add too much to the experience, which is fine in my opinion since other aspect of this game are much stronger.
I'm an absolute sucker for cell shading and this game pulls it off really well. It gave everything that slightly comic/hand drawn look which was very nice to look at all the way through the game. The game had many great environments for you to traverse, from small towns to lush bushland and all of them are bursting with character. This makes getting immersed in the game early on quite easy and allows you to really power through the chapters of this game.
The gunplay in this game is arcadey and I love it. It always felt so rewarding to play and get better since the flashier your kills are and the longer the chain you get, the more points you get. Seeing that counter go up and up and up, oh it's just so satisfying. It gets even better though since it tells you the kind of kill you got when you do it, so you end up living for the moments you get that piercing long shot headshot for 200 odd points.
And now for the reason why I was told to play this game; the story. You can judge by the score I've given the story that it does not disappoint at all, and let me tell you why. The first thing that this game does really well is narrative delivery. The way the story is fed to us is through a bunch of stories that the protagonist Silas tells to some folks in a saloon. Because it's told like this, it can take lots of liberties when telling the story and not break the immersion. It also means that the story feels more natural, more real. You'll find while the story is being told that the world is being built around you and that as details change, the world also changes. Now the story itself I wasn't actually particularly fussed about. I sometimes found it hard to follow and a bit silly, but that added to the charm the story has as one through word of mouth. So even though I ended up not really catching a good portion of the story until I was near the end of the game, I was drawn in by the delivery which was charming till the very end.
Call of Juarez Gunslinger is an absolutely brilliant game that I can recommend to anyone. The story delivery, the gameplay, and the visuals all add up to make this a very worthwhile experience, even though it is very short. So pick it up, and buckle up for a great gaming experience.

Paper's Please is one of those rare games that you don't really even consider to be that amazing or even enjoyable at first glance. However, once you put in your first hour into the game, you begin to realize the big picture.
In Paper's Please, you enter the job as an immigration inspector and you have to regulate who enters the country of Arstotzka and who doesn't, all while trying to barely earn enough money to keep your family alive. This may sound stupidly boring but the game begins to question you as a person as you make choices on whether or not to help the people how enter your booth. Do you choose to help out a married couple by letting both the husband and wife into the country, despite the fact that if you let the wife in with her inaccurate documentation, you will receive a citation, causing you to possibly lose money, the money that you now need to buy your ill son the medicine he needs to get better? That's one example of a choice your going to have to make. This game, of course, has you checking the documentation of those who wish to enter Arstotzka.  The process itself starts off simple, but more layers get added to the inspection process as time passes while you play. This requires you to think fast, as only if you correctly approve or deny any visitors will you actually receive the money that you need to keep you family alive. If you incorrectly approve or deny, you'll receive a citation noting the mistakes you made along with how much money you are being penalized with as you rush to make enough money to last until tomorrow before the clock strikes six and you are done with your work for the day.
If you are someone who would enjoy or finds interest in a game where you have to think fast, but without all of the typical action sequences you would get in something like you would see in something like counter strike or would like to play a game that will bring out your inner morals, then I highly recommend you pick this up as I'm sure you'll enjoy the games complex nature and 20 different endings. Glory to the 'New' Arstotzka.

I normally never write reviews, but this game was a little special enough for me that I wanted to.
The story starts out confusing and it remains confusing throughout, but I think that's part of its beauty.  It can turn people off though, as it did me a little in the beginning.  Or, as time goes on, it could grow on you, as it did on me.   I say give it some time to sink in, though I know that this game won't be for everyone.
You're thrown into the world of Cloudbank and Red's story--and because you are, part of the gameplay is piecing it together as much as it is about getting to the end.  The music gives you as much answers as its characters do, and the little words here and there tell you so much about the world you're drawn into.  Or so little that every time you read something new, the world recreates itself for you.  I personally like that we have to figure it out and even to an extent, put our own meaning to what's going on.  I've re-thought the ending so many times now that I've finished the game and I realize that's part of what makes this game so special.
At its heart, this game is a beautiful, gorgeous story about a voiceless girl and a bodiless sword caught up in a city falling apart.  Though the game doesn't go heavily into who the characters of Cloudbank are, you get the chance to see glimpses of who they are to piece them together, both within the narrative plot and within the character notes from the Transistor (the sword).  The game is detailed with one of the best utilized soundtracks to be incorporated into its storytelling and gameplay.  The RPG elements of fighting with planned strategy is done uniquely too, as far as I've experienced (I have not played Bastion yet, but I've heard the gameplay of Transistor is an expanded version of Bastion's).  The game is as fun as it is immersive.
What really sells this game though, for me at least, is its art and music.  There is something so charming about its whole presentation atop the gameplay that I wouldn't be surprised to see myself coming back to this game again and again.  Not many games immerse you in the way you get to with Red.  How many protagonists do you have that can hum at will while you're walking down a street?  It's quite special.
To call this game a spiritual successor to Bastion would be acurate, but a disservice. This game is more polished, more engaging, and more compelling. Exceeded all my expectations.

I can't recommend this game enough. A top-down action game with innovations where it counts, Transistor will quickly find itself on your "finished games" shelf. One of my favorite parts of the gameplay is how every attack also functions as an upgrade to either you or your active abilities. Couple that with the stratigic "Turn()" phase and the hectic times when your Turn() is on cooldown, and you have a combat system that makes you want to find more things to smash up.
And of course, I can't review something without taking it's storytelling into account. The storyline seems to go the normal rout of "there's X ammount of badguys, and I must fight and defeat them all in order to win!" Though, I don't want to spoil it for you, I will say that there are a few twists. Most of your lore comes from reading the OVA consoles, or by listening to the narrations of your plucky sidekick sword. I do feel that the story, when you think back on it after finishing, is sort of shallow. The big explainations you feel you'd find at the end don't all show face.
Overall, love this game. Play it with the game music on rather than your own. 9/10. Can't wait for the new game plus!

Even if I had a good time with this game I will focus more on it's negatives rather than it's positives. The reason that I am doing this is because the game looks like a wasted opportunity. The graphics and the design are beautiful. So are the abilities of the heroine and the music. But I really felt that there could be so much more in this game.
Story: The story is serviceable but it could be much better.The narrator really talks too much sometimes and he puts too much effort in sounding "cool". To be honest the most of the narration is gibberish which is made to look so cool because they make the gamer wondering what is going on. At any case it is not a horrible story, so 7/10
Choice: In an RPG choice is always an important element. But here, no, forget it. The game is extremely linear. Even the encounters are in an almost pre-arranged order.
Battles: The battles are for me the real missed opportunity. The types of enemies are limited, and sometimes tha challenge is to encounter just a big number. The mixed turned based system could work if someone could use all the abilities in the real time. But if one uses the turned based system then he cannot use offensive abilities for the time in which the turn based control is charging. Everything else though if you dont mind the grind you can buy in the Market in game for in game currency.
The main lure of this game for me is the artstyle as well as the music, it pleases my ears. Take what i said about any other MMO because if you have friends here then it will be fun comparing builds and what not with them. It the same everywhere, if you have friends then the game will stay fun for a while.
As for the P2W thing, having 4 characters maxed out with the highest rank (8 atm) with different builds, I can say that P2W is not an issue with this game, I've wrecked plenty of people who had better items than me mostly because of how I built my character. If you honestly want to play this for PvP then research because a good build in this game will out damage any P2W character, 3 out of my 4 characters can vouch for that, each being 1 of the 4 base classes. Take advantage of certain events and you can lvl up quickly in this game. Those that complain about the AFK problem are just people that cant be patient to grind slowly. Lvling up in this game is not hard, and usually there are 3 places where the AFK problem but in all honestly its not really worth it.
Take what i say with a grain of salt, i am a simple man with simple pleasures, i am not claiming to be someone knowlegeable of games but again, as someone with over 1800+ hours, 10 characters all around 200, with 4 of them being PvP focused, I know a few things about this game. This game is not that hard, if your willing to do trial and error then you will get by, and if you have a friend to play with this will be enjoyable. Dont come in here expecting it to be really easy though, until at least lvl 100, gear wont matter but after wards you better be ready to grind because if not you character will seem very lack luster.

As a Christmas present from my brother, I could easily assume that: a) he bought it because he thought I'd like it, b) wanted to buy me the game to see if it was good enough for him to buy or c) was a game he thought HE would like so that automatically meant I would like it for some reason; therefore, I initially wondered if I'd even enjoy "Rock of Ages".
Well, I DO like it. In fact, I love it!
The principle is simple: Roll a giant boulder down a hill and break down your opponent's barricade before they do the same thing to you. It also has a convenient 'skee-ball' mode.
While optimally enjoyed in short bursts of play, "Rock of Ages" can be surprisingly intense. The "Monty Python" style of humor keeps the simplistic gameplay from getting too stale or boring and the graphics are not only clever but implemented very well. The storyline is entertaining and even gives you a bit of a contrived history lesson.
You'll get plenty of LOL's playing this one. It's a gem of a time-waster.

This is the best MOBA there is.  All, and I mean ALL purchasable in-game content is strictly cosmetic, there is nothing you can buy with real money in this game that will give you an advantage over "free to play" players.  The only thing you can buy is the "God pack" that unlocks all playable characters, but you start with enough players to get a feel for the game, and every single one of them is unlockable with the in-game (free) currency you earn by playing and logging in every day.
There is excellent variety in playable game modes and all of the characters are truly unique, which makes for a very large number of viable group compositions.  Yes, there are a couple "meta" group comps like in any other game, but the best part is there are enough options and so many characters to counter them as long as you are skilled enough. A short action game full of excitement and good storytelling.
The main hook of the game is that you're playing a retelling of the story, meaning that it can be false or it can be rewritten during gameplay. A neat concept, but it's mostly let down with the lack of use of the actual mechanic. Yeah, some ladders appear and some trees pop up, but that's about it. They could've done way more.
The story itself is pretty neat. The voice acting's pretty over the top for the protagonist, but overall it's fitting and good. If you're a fan of the history of the Wild West, in specific the criminals of the Wild West, then you'll love this, since you'll be dealing with them.
The gunplay's hit and miss. Killing enemies feels good, but at the same time there's a lack of blood and gratuity, which would've fit this game perfectly. The length of the game could get some children ♥♥♥♥♥ing, but I doubt that a reasonable adult would have time to play a 20 hour game. This game is 4 hours yet it's 4 hours of pure quality. I prefer 4 hours of quality to 16 hours of♥♥♥♥♥♥and 4 hours of quality ratio.

Gunslinger is the pinnacle of the Call of Juarez franchise through its ability to get enough things right and nothing glaringly wrong. But, in the grand scheme of FPS's with a story, there isn't enough here to call it truly amazing. It might be one of the best Ol' West shooters on PC because of how small of a niche it is, but the game is  a great bite-sized shooter (around 5 hours on normal campaign) at an awesome price - sale or otherwise. If you're a western nut, this won't disappoint.
Was pretty straight forward in terms of the content, but what made it interesting was how it was told - as a matter-of-fact story by the narrator and protagonist after the fact who is recounting his tales of woe against the baddest outlaws of the Western 1880s. And it's all done at a bar, infront of an active audience. Many take his word for it, but there are moments that are also set in a way where you don't quite trust the narrator. The way they were able to construct the narrator as unreliable through what was written and how
was highly innovative. Unfortunately, the actual content felt stale - you didn't feel for the main characters in the same way in other games, and it just felt like you went from level to level just to duel and kill someone important to get information on how to kill another person in another area. The game also does a great job of nailing the historical accuracy around some of the key figures of this time through finding collectables labeled as "Nuggets of Truth". History nuts, eat your heart out.
It's quite nice. There's an upgrade system that finally works around your playstyle, but the shooting and duelling hasn't changed much since Bound in Blood. They got rid of the cover system which I liked so much in Bound, but I did enjoy the variety of enemies and quick time events. I also really enjoyed how the game made the best use of their environments through clever enemy spawns. The combo-making and levelling up system complimented the concentration system nicely, as well. But what really got me was the lack of truly memorable sets and levels. They all felt mostly the same, despite giving off the feeling that you were a supposed Western world traveler. But they made zones distinct enough with their smaller budget for it not to feel dreadful. But you'll find yourself in moments where sets look pretty cookie-cutter.
They just nailed the grittiness through the cell-shaded style. Like XIII meets the Red Dead franchise, who was coincidentally having lunch with Borderlands 2. Model detailing makes everyone look like innovative McCree reskins, but I'm okay with that. But when it came to the babbling brooks and canyon vistas, I caught myself thinking about hitting F12 a few times. I think that this was the only time in the series that art was worth mentioning - it did really feel inspired. I had no real issues running the game from a graphics standpoint.
Fairly generic. It wasn't bad, but not memorable. The tracks got a bit repetitive, and the music began to sound the same. I just switched it off.
I think that I convinced myself after writing this that it's a better game than I thought. I forgot how great the visuals were, and it helped slog alone the mediocre story and gameplay. I guess that pulls it up to good or at least a few notches above the average FPS. In the smaller field of PC Western games, it's at the front of the pack. So if the screenshots catch your eye and you're dying for a decent Western shooter, this is it. You'll feel like you stole it when it goes on sale.

How about the plot? There's no lack of originality. Right from the beginning I had plenty of questions, and eagerly sought out more information about the world and... situation. The game ended, though, before I really got any answers, and there just isn't enough time to get to know the characters.
All in all, then, an ambitious effort from what is clearly a very talented team, but one that just falls short of the mark.

I really loved Bastion, so I came into this game with high hopes. Unfortunately, I don't think it was nearly as good. The story wasn't particularly relatable, which might have been due to the heavy sci-fi nature of the game world. It's never really made clear to us if Red and the whopping 8 other people she comes into contact with are living in a computer simulation or not, and as for the fate of the greater world at large, well, you never actually see any other people around, so it seems like all is pretty much lost from the get-go. All that's left to invest you in the game, then, is the relationship between Red and the Transistor. Unfortunately, this relationship, while probably meant to be touching and impassioned, has very little support in terms of either backstory or character development throughout the game itself. This is exacerbated by the fact that Red, for (cough) 'story' reasons, is herself mostly mute. All that's left, then, is the excellent voice acting of Logan Cunningham, which, while grainy and evocative as it was in Bastion, is not enough to carry the relationship by itself.
All that being said, however, I still think this is a fairly good game in its own right, and if it weren't for the comparisons to Bastion, I think I would care about all those problems a good deal less. Play this if you enjoy action RPGs, with interesting worlds, unique art direction, and, of course, great music. Just don't expect to be too involved in the story emotionally.

It's a great "Filler" MMO.  Either in a lull between expansions for higher quality titles, or between content patches, however it has so many problems that the developers won't or cant any longer address that make it hard to recommend as someone's primary MMO if combat is the focus of your play.  If you enjoy the entire scope of things from story, questing, content and crafting, that could sway the decision for this to be your go-to MMO title.
Positives:
•	Fantastic storytelling, and interesting characters.
•	Unparalleled crafting system.
•	Stable economy.
•	Tons of relevant content.
•	Visually fantastic with great effects.
•	Great community.
•	Fun dungeons, raids, and public events.
Negatives:
•	Poorly engineered combat system.  The long global cooldown, while it drags out combat and makes it feel less exciting, that isn’t really the big issue.  Animation cooldown, animation delay, animation lock all make combat incredibly unreliable and inconsistent.  Also because of the issues with animation locking out abilities, it can completely break macros since the game has no queue system with macro-activated abilities.
•	Pet system has terrible AI.
•	Companion system still doesn’t allow you to queue for Duty Finder
•	Inability to leave/return to an instance.
•	Inability to replace a member in a pre-made group in an instanced environment.
•	Terrible UI designs that can easily be addressed by UI Mods, which were planned to be implemented over two years ago.  A lot of layered and counter-intuitive menu systems, as well as tons of unnecessary information.
•	Map is terrible.  You can actually drag the map, out of the map bounding window, and completely lose it, or at the least make it much more difficult to navigate it and find information quickly.  Also elements of the map UI appear/disappear based on scale, making it hard to find a comfortable zoom level and still retain information.
•	Inventory system is clunky, and there was a sorting system implemented but it’s not apparent or intuitive.
•	Tons of “Features” intended to hinder RMT, which actually just make life harder for legit players (kind of like DRM).  You can’t add a friend while they are offline.  You can’t send mail to people who aren’t friends, 1mil gil limit for trade and mail.
•	Infuriatingly large amount of limitations on actions with the UI.  Lots of UI windows lock you out of performing any actions that use the UI.  For example being in certain windows will prevent you from being able to accept a group or linkshell invite.  Opening vendor, retainer, chocobo stables, etc., will close all other open windows.  No “Repair Everything” option in menders, you need to scroll through several nested menu options to repair ALL of your gear.  Several interfaces prevent you from moving items in your inventory. This particular list is nearly inexhaustible.
•	No on the fly hotkeying.  Restricted to only 6 horizontal hotbars and 4 vertical.  Can’t alternate horizontal/vertical per hotbar.
•	Can’t communicate with people while in an instance, can’t even open your free company window while in an instance.
•	Horrible free company interface.  Can’t sort party, can’t make player notes.  There is a note system, but only editable by the player themselves… if you give them permission to edit it… which is incredibly stupid.  Very clunky permissions and hierarchy system.  Incredibly limited company chest space.
•	There are tons of limitations with just about every system from housing to aethernet, that developers have acknowledged but just don’t care about.
All in all, there are tons of issues that really fall into quality of life issues, that they have simply stopped working on even after acknowleding the tons of people on the forums who complain about things.  In their favor they have fixed an asinine number of grievances since launch... which makes you wonder how things are comparatively now to then (although still leagues better than 1.0).
So many issues holding this game back from really drawing in the population, numbers and money that titles like World of Warcraft is bringing in, and all of them are things they just refuse to fix.  It's like they don't want to make any more money than they already are.
I do sincerely think everyone should give the game a chance.  I just think that everyone who does should keep an open mind to finding better alternatives when they present themselves.

Final Fantasy 14: A Realm Reborn is a new version of the original game, just called Final Fantasy 14 Online, which came to be considered a complete failure. The title, available for PS3 and PC, did not disappoint in his recovery and has met the expectations of fans.
Realm Reborn is a very appropriate name for the game, as he was redone from scratch and this is already felt in its first minutes. Not just the game system, but also its history, characters and operation. Even those who were at advanced levels in the previous version here returning from scratch, entirely renovated.
And so resumes the story of Eorzea, where goes the adventure. Entitled to reset characters and a new mythology, the player gradually gets involved in the action and drama lived by this world. Arriving with his hero in a city, out of nowhere, it needs to give their all to be recognized as someone of value.
The character creation system is well done and complete. Even in the PS3, with commands totally focused on the joystick, it is possible to find and not get lost in the confusing menus. The game does not disappoint in this initial step and is quite complete in everything from races options the initial classes, through appearance setting.
The introduction also fulfills its role well, with a story narrated in the third person and scenes breathtaking, setting the stage for what the player must face over the next few hours - and they are many. As a true MMORPG, Final Fantasy 14: A Realm Reborn has a lot of content.
As in any game genre, the evolution of the characters is due to the missions to be accomplished and advanced levels. Here the experience levels are back (remember they are gone in Final Fantasy 13?), Then the progression is natural. At each level, new skills and more news are unlocked, but there are some surprises.
The first is the possibility of moving level with each class available in the game and others that can be enabled. Unlike other online RPGs, it is not necessary to create several characters to test other classes of heroes. OKAY..you see..about a week or so ago, I came back from work and sat down onto my computer chair. I started to scroll through my library to see what i was in the mood for. I opened one game, played it for about 5 minutes then immediately closed out of it. Found another game, i made it to the title screen then remembered how bored I will probably get. Needed something new.
SO for starters, I had bought this game about a year or so ago, I dont remember exactly when BUT i do know it has been sitting in my library, not installed, for a long time. I guess there was a deal or something that was the reason why i mainly bought it. I remember discussing with my friends one day that i bought it and they totally took a dump on it. SO i think that was the reason why i let it sit in my library untouched. Was discouraged! LMAO
LONG STORY SHORT: Sat down - rumaged through library - got super bored - decided what the heck*shrug* bought it anyways - installed it after a long unknown length of time sitting in my library - played it - was super satisfied.
REVIEW: I absolutely enjoy this game. I have a few reasons why!!
-For one: THE COMMUNITY - As soon as i logged in, a Free Company (or guilds/clans in other games) has invited me to join them. They were super friendly and talkative. Helped out with every question i had. I didnt find the same kindness just inside the Free Company but everywhere else as well!! For example: I normally judge my jumps down cliffs pretty well to survive it in this game(LMAO) but one instance i totally died. So i sent out a SHOUT to the area to see if anyone could revive me. Almost instantly about 5 or 6 players answered my newbish cries!! -  10/10!!
-THE CHARACTER CREATION -  I'll make this one short but i have to say i like the character creation a lot. Maybe not as detailed as some MMOs but still detailed and Square Enix did a good job. - 9/10!!
-THE CLASSES AND JOBS!!! - OMGOSH, I love this part of the game. There is wide selection of classes divided up into certain categories. To just name a few and to be brief as possible: You have the Disciples of War, which are the basic combat classes. You have the Disciples of Magic, self explanatory. You have the Disciples of Hand, which are your basic manufacturing classes such as an Amourer or Blacksmith all the way to a Culinarian(the cooking class)(much more to list though). Then you have the Disciples of Land which basically gather/harvest materials for the DOHs!! WHAT I LOVE MOST THOUGH are the JOBS. When you reach a certain point you are able to have job which requires you to be leveled in two certain classes. For example, the class i started out with was the Pugilist(use their fists basically). Later at level 30 i became a MONK which required me to be level 15 in lancer. Theres a lot more detailed stuff to discuss about classes and jobs but thats why guides exist!
BUT WHAT I LOVE MORE THAN WHAT I SAID I LOVED THE MOST..is..you LITERALLY...LITERALLY can use every class and level every class in the game on JUST ONE character. BUT its probably better to focus on your initial class early on.
!!!!!10/10!!!!!!
*and time to speed up things up as i am getting a little tired of typing:
-THE DISCIPLES OF HAND: Creating items is extremely interactive as you actively make the item yourself for a chance to make a high quality version of the regular. - 10/10!!
-MANY QUESTS!! - Important game mechanics begin to unlock in the game as you progress the main storyline quests and side quests.
-ALWAYS SOMETHING TO LOOK FORWARD TOWARDS: as mentioned previously mechanics as well other things begin to unlock the more you progress though the game. Through my eyes i think there is plenty of content! -  10/10!!
-LEVEL CAP IS 60: though it is a true statement BUT each class has its own level progression.
-FANTASTIC SOUNDTRACK: Ahhh yes, as i am venturing through dangerous lands, i am constantly reminded of old fond memories of the older Final Fantasy games. I get goosebumps sometimes. - 10/10!
-VOICE OVERS: Meh... =\ I think it could be better and more frequent. BUT it should do. - 6ish7ish/10!!!!
-CROSS PLATFORM!!! Love the fact that i am playing with a variety of players from different platforms like the PS4!
-AOE FROM BADDIES!! I think its a little finicky but maybe i am lagging...couldnt tell yuh to be precise - 6/10!
-SERVERS!! To choose a server is little different compared to some MMOs but they are full or highly populated often. For some it is bad but others seem to like it. I LIKE IT!! 10/10!
!!!!!!!!!THE END!!!!!!!!!!!!!!
THAT IS ALL!!...for now... as i am still playing and havent made it to the end game yet.

As I said in a review of one of the other Dreamfall games, I was feeling nostalgic after moving and so unboxed my original XBox.  While doing so, I found this game unplayed and still in its shrink wrap with all my other games.  I knew absolutely nothing about it whatsoever except that it had a pretty girl in a pink tank top on the cover (maybe that's why I originally bought it, lol).  But I was surprised at the quality and immersiveness of this game right from the start.  The details of the scenery are completely believable.  You have the ancient city of Casablanca with it's original arcitecture and wooden and stone benches along side high-tech computer terminals and holographic billboards.  You have sleek ultra-modern glass cars driving along narrow stone roadways, and modern skyscrapers off in the distance.   Exactly how things will probably be in such places.  One thing I must point out is that I actually played this game on the original Xbox.  I just recently bought this game on Steam as part of a package because, after finishing it, I wanted to play the prequel "The Longest Journey" and the sequel "Dreamfall Chapters."  One minor gripe I have with the Steam version of this game (which I actually didn't play very long because I played it to the end on the Xbox version) was that the mouse was inverted left to right, which made it nearly impossible to control.  There was no option to invert the left-right movement of the mouse.  It did the same thing with my Logitech USB gamepad, the left-right movement was reversed with no way to invert it.  When, oh when, will developers learn that it is absolutely necessary to provide "invert" options on EVERY control axis?!?!  Otherwise, this is arguably the best of the three games, though I really liked how Marcuria was an open-world city in the first couple of chapters of Dreamfall Chapters.

Sequel to the Longest Journey, a game I strongly recommend.  If you played that, play this too for more of the world you've likely come to love.
Pros:
-Story, if you aren't here for story then you really shouldn't be playing this game at all.
-None of the bizzare puzzles and even more outlandish solutions that plagued the first game of the series.
-There are still some puzzle elements, but not really a focus of the game.
-The already well established setting of the first game is built upon here in the sequel, and you really start to get a feel for this world as a whole.
-More characters with more interesting motivations and personalities.
-The humor is still there and still great
Neutral:
-Not really a ton of gameplay, mostly walking and talking with a few fights, puzzles, and other segments sprinkled in on occasion, which isn't a negative for me, but opinions may vary.
-This game is way shorter than The Longest Journey, and way shorter than the sequel Dreamfall:Chapters as well.
-Combat is pretty garbage, I didn't care, but maybe you might, just know going into this one that they focued more on story than gameplay.
-The graphics are good enough that it isn't distracting.
Overall, if you love story focused games, play The Longest Journey, then play this and the sequel.

Prepare for a journey of self discovery through distant lands and fantasy wrapped science fiction flavoured worlds.
Dreamfall: The Longest Journey is primarily an adventure game following the story of one Zoë Castillo and taking place in multiple different and diverse environments. Futuristic sunny and warm Casablanca, downtrodden rainy Venetian canal ridden streets of Newport, snowy medieval steam punk infused Marcuria and even hidden damp tree house based Swamp City. The characters that fill these worlds are also all interesting and unique. As the game relies on plot to drive the player forward, I will not mention anything about it but it does its job very well. The story is interesting and full of well designed characters and locations. The lore is presented in easy to swallow chunks and allows room for interpretation while still feeling solid and believable. This is a must as much of the game relies on walking and interacting with objects. There are some light environmental puzzles that slow down your progress through the story and break the monotony of walking or pushing through the story too quickly. Though it did feel like there could have been more of them as the gameplay is very shallow mostly consisting of walking and talking to characters. There are some fight sequences but it is evident the developers did not invest much time into them as they feel very wonky.
Technically speaking, the game has no larger problems. Mouse and Keyboard controls are not the best but can be tweaked to your liking – I found the gamepad works best. Graphics are acceptable for a 10 year old game and the high colour vibrant art style means time has been kind to it. 1080p works fine with no frame drops on modern machines. Voice work is all very well done and the soundtrack is nothing less than wonderful.

All in all, then, an ambitious effort from what is clearly a very talented team, but one that just falls short of the mark.

I really loved Bastion, so I came into this game with high hopes. Unfortunately, I don't think it was nearly as good. The story wasn't particularly relatable, which might have been due to the heavy sci-fi nature of the game world. It's never really made clear to us if Red and the whopping 8 other people she comes into contact with are living in a computer simulation or not, and as for the fate of the greater world at large, well, you never actually see any other people around, so it seems like all is pretty much lost from the get-go. All that's left to invest you in the game, then, is the relationship between Red and the Transistor. Unfortunately, this relationship, while probably meant to be touching and impassioned, has very little support in terms of either backstory or character development throughout the game itself. This is exacerbated by the fact that Red, for (cough) 'story' reasons, is herself mostly mute. All that's left, then, is the excellent voice acting of Logan Cunningham, which, while grainy and evocative as it was in Bastion, is not enough to carry the relationship by itself.
All that being said, however, I still think this is a fairly good game in its own right, and if it weren't for the comparisons to Bastion, I think I would care about all those problems a good deal less. Play this if you enjoy action RPGs, with interesting worlds, unique art direction, and, of course, great music. Just don't expect to be too involved in the story emotionally.

You are just some person working a menial job, even at first it seems a little tedious (See below for a more positive note.) but you have a family to support and this is your day job. I work full time so an emulation of tedium isn't so appealing at first, why would I want to enter that World again?
