Every decision you make will effect the ending and there are many endings. Do you stay loyal or do you rebel? Do you turn a cheek to help your family for own needs or be strict and let your family suffer? That five credit fine for a twenty credit bribe could make a lot of difference.
I know this game has been out for some time, has won a lot of awards and is most likely out of a lot of people's memories. But I'm writing this review for anyone sitting on the fence. Buy it! Even at full price, you won't regret it! The tedium and increased difficulty is overshadowed by an intricate multipathed storyline which will just cloud your judgement at every turn. There's some secrets to discover too.
Even if you try to be the nice guy, there's parts of it where you just want to be a♥♥♥♥♥♥the next time. This is one game with a lot of options and outcomes for your actions and each playthrough will never be the same.
Note: The main game play is never actually tedious, it's just a fun challenge which increases the difficulty with each day. Once you've got the hang of how it works the first few days are a gold mine. The best experiences are found in exploring the decisions you have made and exploring different options each time afterwards.
I have nothing negative to say about this game. I'm just glad it exist's and will thrust it upon any person who is looking for something to play.

Papers, Please or Red Tape of a Red State
I enjoyed this game and I certainly got my money's worth. It is executed brilliantly and the music, sound, scripted events and design are great. The bleak tone of a red state is presented well and should appeal to a child of the 80s who remembers the closing decade of the Cold War.
However most gamers in general may not enjoy the relentless bureaucracy; let me explain. Each in-game "day" normally lasts 12 hours (about 10 real minutes) and your income depends on how many entrants you process (too many mistakes penalizes your income). In theory this is a good risk/reward balance and keeps things moving. In practice it gets pretty grueling.
If you don't have an eye and attention span for detail this game won't be very appealing. If you've ever worked a desk job it will feel very much like real-life work. On my second playthrough (achievement hunting) I actually found myself checking the in-game clock to see if my shift was almost over. That's when I realized I couldn't give this game a thumbs up to the general public in good conscious.
Lastly I do recommend this game to achievement hunters. It's not difficult, extremely inexpensive on sale and easy enough to get to 100% in <10 hours.
Glory to Arstotzka, glory to relentless bureaucracy!

Imagine you’re living under a communist regime, in the early 80s, and working at a border checkpoint where you verify the credentials of people wishing to enter the country. The ministry for which you work passes down various orders and new requirements for entry-approval. Your workload increases with each new edict. The amount of information you’re required to verify borders on the absurd. Make more than a couple mistakes and your wages are penalized (and it’s very easy to make mistakes). It becomes increasingly harder to provide for your family because your salary is docked to depletion. And because it’s so hard to earn money legally, bribes and trafficking start to look attractive.
I’ve just described the game Papers, Please to you. You’re thinking, “that sounds incredibly boring. Stressful, even.” Yet, somehow, I found it be one of the most fun gaming experiences I’ve had in recent memory (and I’m not alone).
At its most basic, the game works like this: Person enters your booth. You inspect their credentials (passports, permits, etc.). You either approve or deny them entry. They leave. The next person enters. Repeat.
There are, of course, other gameplay and story elements littered throughout, but that’s the gist.
It’s set in the fictional country of Arstotzka, just after a war with neighboring country Kolechia. The major city that sits on this border, Grestin, has been divided for some time, and the border is finally open once more. It’s your job to inspect those seeking entry.
The design of the game screen is deceptively elegant. Your workstation manages to be both streamlined and inefficient. I found myself, at times, intensely frustrated that I couldn’t move people through faster. And that somehow added to the enjoyment. The recognition of that frustration intensifies the feeling that you’re some lowly border clerk being asked to do a job that no one could do well.
And when you do get the hang of that workstation, you can make it sing. I learned to immediately place documents where I needed them, readying my cursor for a printout of some supplemental material or other, developing a workflow that would identify elements that were easily verified before moving on to the items that were buried deeper in the documents. It was incredibly rewarding once you could get people flying through that booth.
And no matter which way you choose to play the game, it’s fun. When you adhere completely to the rules, denying entry often, ignoring pleas from the destitute and hard-luck cases there’s a (sick?) satisfaction in keeping Arstotzka “safe.” On the flip side when you do all you can to help those in need, often sacrificing your job and livelihood, the game becomes even more fun and rewarding.
The art is suitably grim and lo-fi, complementing the dystopic nature of Arstotzka perfectly. Everyone is unattractive and sad. The design of the documents feels authentic and plays a key role in identifying forgeries and the like.
The absolute best part of the game is the sound design. Every little mechanical click, punch, and stamp is weirdly satisfying. The strange gibberish used in place of dialog feels impersonal and emotionless (as it should). It greatly enhances the gameplay experience.
Papers, Please is self-described as a dystopic document thriller. And it totally makes good on that promise.

•	Pet system has terrible AI.
•	Companion system still doesn’t allow you to queue for Duty Finder
•	Inability to leave/return to an instance.
•	Inability to replace a member in a pre-made group in an instanced environment.
•	Terrible UI designs that can easily be addressed by UI Mods, which were planned to be implemented over two years ago.  A lot of layered and counter-intuitive menu systems, as well as tons of unnecessary information.
•	Map is terrible.  You can actually drag the map, out of the map bounding window, and completely lose it, or at the least make it much more difficult to navigate it and find information quickly.  Also elements of the map UI appear/disappear based on scale, making it hard to find a comfortable zoom level and still retain information.
•	Inventory system is clunky, and there was a sorting system implemented but it’s not apparent or intuitive.
•	Tons of “Features” intended to hinder RMT, which actually just make life harder for legit players (kind of like DRM).  You can’t add a friend while they are offline.  You can’t send mail to people who aren’t friends, 1mil gil limit for trade and mail.
•	Infuriatingly large amount of limitations on actions with the UI.  Lots of UI windows lock you out of performing any actions that use the UI.  For example being in certain windows will prevent you from being able to accept a group or linkshell invite.  Opening vendor, retainer, chocobo stables, etc., will close all other open windows.  No “Repair Everything” option in menders, you need to scroll through several nested menu options to repair ALL of your gear.  Several interfaces prevent you from moving items in your inventory. This particular list is nearly inexhaustible.
•	No on the fly hotkeying.  Restricted to only 6 horizontal hotbars and 4 vertical.  Can’t alternate horizontal/vertical per hotbar.
•	Can’t communicate with people while in an instance, can’t even open your free company window while in an instance.
•	Horrible free company interface.  Can’t sort party, can’t make player notes.  There is a note system, but only editable by the player themselves… if you give them permission to edit it… which is incredibly stupid.  Very clunky permissions and hierarchy system.  Incredibly limited company chest space.
•	There are tons of limitations with just about every system from housing to aethernet, that developers have acknowledged but just don’t care about.
All in all, there are tons of issues that really fall into quality of life issues, that they have simply stopped working on even after acknowleding the tons of people on the forums who complain about things.  In their favor they have fixed an asinine number of grievances since launch... which makes you wonder how things are comparatively now to then (although still leagues better than 1.0).
So many issues holding this game back from really drawing in the population, numbers and money that titles like World of Warcraft is bringing in, and all of them are things they just refuse to fix.  It's like they don't want to make any more money than they already are.
I do sincerely think everyone should give the game a chance.  I just think that everyone who does should keep an open mind to finding better alternatives when they present themselves.

Final Fantasy 14: A Realm Reborn is a new version of the original game, just called Final Fantasy 14 Online, which came to be considered a complete failure. The title, available for PS3 and PC, did not disappoint in his recovery and has met the expectations of fans.
Realm Reborn is a very appropriate name for the game, as he was redone from scratch and this is already felt in its first minutes. Not just the game system, but also its history, characters and operation. Even those who were at advanced levels in the previous version here returning from scratch, entirely renovated.
And so resumes the story of Eorzea, where goes the adventure. Entitled to reset characters and a new mythology, the player gradually gets involved in the action and drama lived by this world. Arriving with his hero in a city, out of nowhere, it needs to give their all to be recognized as someone of value.
The character creation system is well done and complete. Even in the PS3, with commands totally focused on the joystick, it is possible to find and not get lost in the confusing menus. The game does not disappoint in this initial step and is quite complete in everything from races options the initial classes, through appearance setting.
The introduction also fulfills its role well, with a story narrated in the third person and scenes breathtaking, setting the stage for what the player must face over the next few hours - and they are many. As a true MMORPG, Final Fantasy 14: A Realm Reborn has a lot of content.
As in any game genre, the evolution of the characters is due to the missions to be accomplished and advanced levels. Here the experience levels are back (remember they are gone in Final Fantasy 13?), Then the progression is natural. At each level, new skills and more news are unlocked, but there are some surprises.
The first is the possibility of moving level with each class available in the game and others that can be enabled. Unlike other online RPGs, it is not necessary to create several characters to test other classes of heroes. Here you can simply decide that tired of being warrior and changing careers, becoming mage or archer. Of course, this will reset the level that chosen profession, but the former remains.
This kind of change only adds personality of A Realm Reborn, striving to be a MMORPG different from the others, even though some follow successful trends - such as own missions. Fortunately the class system works very well, recalling the classic Final Fantasy Tactics at times - after all, many professions require various levels in others and so on, just as you learned in PlayStation 1.
In fact, much in the Realm Reborn seems to have been inspired by previous games in the series. Elements ranging from the class system up to some spells, elements, materials and so on. Overall, the game risks trying to please enough who is long-time fan, although it can be availed by those who favor recently.
We will not lie, the gameplay of Final Fantasy 14: A Realm Reborn fit like a glove to the game. Everything is very well fitted both on the PC, as the PS3. Play on either platform is a rewarding experience, which is even more impressive for console users.
It is worth mentioning that everything works well in DualShock 3 control, and even the PC version is fully compatible with an Xbox 360 control plugged into the computer. Commands are natural, menus can be easily accessed and attacks are activated easily, quickly and accurately, as a struggle requires.
This type of adaptation is played master of Square Enix, since the game can be availed on both platforms with just one account. Unfortunately you have to buy it twice, once on the PC and one on the PS3, to play with them, but later the first month tuition - $ 15 every 30 days - goes for both platforms simultaneously. A nice plus.
In addition, all the characters, friends list and historical are saved in both the PC and the PS3, the online server of the producer. This happens because the game is exclusively online, of course, but there is an advantage in this.
A Realm Reborn has decent graphics to be called a legitimate representative of the Final Fantasy saga. With the right effects jaw-dropping, neat monsters and spells with many special elements, the game does not make ugly, despite the PS3 version lose a little - just a little - the title on the PC.
Another point that stands out are the very cities. Some, at first, are very small, but then it changes exponentially. The player soon stumbles upon megacities, stuffed characters, either other players or the computer, but what matters here is the visual. A quick Internet search reveals, for those who do not have the game, as he is really beautiful in their environment, something that is difficult in a MMO, in many cases.

OKAY..you see..about a week or so ago, I came back from work and sat down onto my computer chair. I started to scroll through my library to see what i was in the mood for. I opened one game, played it for about 5 minutes then immediately closed out of it. Found another game, i made it to the title screen then remembered how bored I will probably get. Needed something new.
SO for starters, I had bought this game about a year or so ago, I dont remember exactly when BUT i do know it has been sitting in my library, not installed, for a long time. I guess there was a deal or something that was the reason why i mainly bought it. I remember discussing with my friends one day that i bought it and they totally took a dump on it. SO i think that was the reason why i let it sit in my library untouched. Was discouraged! LMAO
LONG STORY SHORT: Sat down - rumaged through library - got super bored - decided what the heck*shrug* bought it anyways - installed it after a long unknown length of time sitting in my library - played it - was super satisfied.
REVIEW: I absolutely enjoy this game. I have a few reasons why!!
-For one: THE COMMUNITY - As soon as i logged in, a Free Company (or guilds/clans in other games) has invited me to join them. They were super friendly and talkative. Helped out with every question i had. I didnt find the same kindness just inside the Free Company but everywhere else as well!! For example: I normally judge my jumps down cliffs pretty well to survive it in this game(LMAO) but one instance i totally died. So i sent out a SHOUT to the area to see if anyone could revive me. Almost instantly about 5 or 6 players answered my newbish cries!! -  10/10!!
-THE CHARACTER CREATION -  I'll make this one short but i have to say i like the character creation a lot. Maybe not as detailed as some MMOs but still detailed and Square Enix did a good job. - 9/10!!
-THE CLASSES AND JOBS!!! - OMGOSH, I love this part of the game. There is wide selection of classes divided up into certain categories. To just name a few and to be brief as possible: You have the Disciples of War, which are the basic combat classes. You have the Disciples of Magic, self explanatory. You have the Disciples of Hand, which are your basic manufacturing classes such as an Amourer or Blacksmith all the way to a Culinarian(the cooking class)(much more to list though). Then you have the Disciples of Land which basically gather/harvest materials for the DOHs!! WHAT I LOVE MOST THOUGH are the JOBS. When you reach a certain point you are able to have job which requires you to be leveled in two certain classes. For example, the class i started out with was the Pugilist(use their fists basically). Later at level 30 i became a MONK which required me to be level 15 in lancer. Theres a lot more detailed stuff to discuss about classes and jobs but thats why guides exist!
BUT WHAT I LOVE MORE THAN WHAT I SAID I LOVED THE MOST..is..you LITERALLY...LITERALLY can use every class and level every class in the game on JUST ONE character. BUT its probably better to focus on your initial class early on.
!!!!!10/10!!!!!!
*and time to speed up things up as i am getting a little tired of typing:
-THE DISCIPLES OF HAND: Creating items is extremely interactive as you actively make the item yourself for a chance to make a high quality version of the regular. - 10/10!!
-MANY QUESTS!! - Important game mechanics begin to unlock in the game as you progress the main storyline quests and side quests.
-ALWAYS SOMETHING TO LOOK FORWARD TOWARDS: as mentioned previously mechanics as well other things begin to unlock the more you progress though the game. Through my eyes i think there is plenty of content! -  10/10!!
-LEVEL CAP IS 60: though it is a true statement BUT each class has its own level progression.
-FANTASTIC SOUNDTRACK: Ahhh yes, as i am venturing through dangerous lands, i am constantly reminded of old fond memories of the older Final Fantasy games. I get goosebumps sometimes. - 10/10!
-VOICE OVERS: Meh... =\ I think it could be better and more frequent. BUT it should do. - 6ish7ish/10!!!!
-CROSS PLATFORM!!! Love the fact that i am playing with a variety of players from different platforms like the PS4!
-AOE FROM BADDIES!! I think its a little finicky but maybe i am lagging...couldnt tell yuh to be precise - 6/10!
-SERVERS!! To choose a server is little different compared to some MMOs but they are full or highly populated often. For some it is bad but others seem to like it. I LIKE IT!! 10/10!
!!!!!!!!!THE END!!!!!!!!!!!!!!
THAT IS ALL!!...for now... as i am still playing and havent made it to the end game yet.

I usually like to play a game for several hours (or finish it) before I write a review, but in the case of ToS I felt I could make an exception. After an hour of play it seemed like I was experiencing all the game had to offer but still I kept going. Not much changed as I continued, it was the same old thing: killing mobs, leveling, killing mobs, leveling... Let me just say that the game does have an awesome art style, the sole thing going for it. It is fantastic to look at and what initially drew me in, but the positives end there.
Your senses are saturated while playing, I think it's a ploy to try and distract you from the lack of anything worthwhile in this game. From the moment you login you are distracted by several scantily-clad women with big chests for no apparent reason. Coins fly everywhere when you kill a mob, little buttons and character menus abound, the class system promises a multitude of possibilities and combinations, and the world map is massive. All these things are presented well and then countered by fundamentally flawed execution. All those coins you pick up don't mean much, this game is pretty grindy. All those menus contain very little interesting information, some of it I was wondering why it was even there. All those classes have only four abilities each that look boring when used and do very similar things, and the map is a buggy mess when trying to navigate it. It crashed on several occasions while playing and some of the English translations were awkward as well.
Don't fall for this stuff people, this is just another run of the mill eastern MMORPG that we are seeing everywhere now. It looks good on the surface but there is nothing substantial here. It isn't worth your time and if you're looking for a satisfying game to play you should really just find something else.

So I actually have mixed feelings about this game, but as a stand alone game aside from the rest of the series it has to be my least favorite one. To recap, you are continuing from the Longest Journey series of the heroine April Ryan and her adventures in Arcadia and "Stark". The game has you starting off as Zoe Castillo from Casablanca  who seeks to help her ex-boyfriend Reza with a story he was working on. Things happen, and you end up as Zoe going to Arcadia where many of the original characters are at. For those unaware, this series has a sequel after this one as Dreamfall: Chapters.
The storyline is still good. You can actually watch this game like a movie and its really enthralling. I really loved the Longest Journey, but given the gap in development of course I expected a different type of gameplay. This game certainly has a bit more action, however, there are some frustrating elements. For example, there are many times in this game where you have to do some stealthy movements where the slightest wrong move will cause you to lose. It reminds me of Hitman, which I actually liked, but going into this game I wanted to relax and enjoy the story. I have two set modes when I'm playing games, high adrenaline for action games, and mellow enjoyment for point and click games like this. There's also one particular part in the game where you're in a cave and I had to watch a YouTube video to prevent myself from rage quitting. Based on the comments on YouTube a lot of people got frustrated with the game at this point. There are some minor bugs, but don't thankfully haven't prevented me from completing the game. The bugs are usually problems in getting to certain parts where the character seems to be stuck on an invisible wall. If you play around with the resolution sometimes that fixes the problem.
That being said, I am now playing Dreamfall: Chapters. I haven't completed it yet, but it seems to really fix a lot of complaints people had with this game. It really makes up for the previous game, and I recommend continuing on with the series. If you're like me you might just like to complete all the games for the sake of completing series, and I understand that. Its not completely unbearable so if you must do play it!
Tl;dr Nice story, irritating gameplay. Play Dreamfall: Chapters because it makes up for this one.

This entire series has been amazing and definitely worth looking into. When I first found that it was available for PC and it was on steam I was so excited I bought it right away, yet didn't play it. Instead I looked into it's predecessor "The Longest Journey".
The game is ten times more satisfying if you have previous knowledge or experience playing the first game "The Longest Journey" in April Ryan's point of view. I couldn't be bothered actually playing the first game myself since I have a hard time
getting into games with really low graphics, so Instead I watched an entire playthrough of the first game no commentary before starting the second one. I am super glad I did, since they referenced several things from the first game and acknowledged characters that I could actually recognize, it was just so satisfying to be able to recognize them.
The only thing I didn't like about the game was the lack of consequence or choice effect in the game, whether you chose to do one thing or not didn't effect anything in the story. The most difference it did was effect one aspect of gameplay to make something harder or difficult, like silently disarming a guard or attacking them full on, going the long way around, or taking a short cut. The only differences were dialogue, and even then, most of the dialogue was mandatory to read anyways leaving little to none replayability.
At the same time, I liked that there was lack of choices I know I'm contradicting myself... It was telling you a story in the way they visioned it instead of you putting your own input to it. I loved it, to it's very end.
I also got super excited hearing the news of the third installment Dreamfall Chapters, and knowing that the choices DO actually effect storyline and have tons of replayability.
10/10 Definitely worth playing, Highly recommend playing or watching a playthrough of the first game beforehand though.

The action keeps you on your toes, never knowing where the next attack is going to come from or what it might be. I constantly find myself anxious about whether there's an unexpected boss battle around the corner and what weapons I'm going to use to kill it, also what loot I might get after killing it. The art style and shaders are also something to behold, with that cartoonish, comic-like outline of the characters but realistic lighting and texturing, it really is a unique and beautiful game.
Just amazing 10/10 game.

While the original Borderlands scratches a nostalgic itch, and the Pre-Sequel is a fun bit of extra content, Borderlands 2 is the penultimate Borderlands experience.  Combining a lore-rich world with a cast of amusing characters, a passable story, good leveling systems, and an excellent co-op mode, Borderlands 2 manages to be a fun RPG and a satisfying shooter without ever overstaying it's welcome.  While you can stop after the story ends, the amount of post-game content, DLC, and NG+ options are likely to keep players coming back for days, months, or years to come.
I look forward to sinking more time into the PC port, and eagerly anticipate Borderlands 3.

-Open InstallerData, Disk1, InstData then open the zip file Resource1.
-Open $IA_PROJECT_DIR$, then open src_path and finally locate Launcher folder.
-Drag Launcher folder to the desktop
-Locate your Steam Library folder, steamapps, common, Zenimax Online folder.

Yet another step forward in the genre.  Yes, there are things in common with Clicker Heroes, but, guess what, a LARGE portion of Clicker Heroes was based on Cookie Clicker.  That's how games work.  Tap Tap Infinity, despite not having the best name ever, is an improvement on Clicker Heroes in many ways.  The main thing that is better in CH is that you can look at the ancient (guardians here) list while the game is running.  Also, in TTI you may hit a point where a paid currency is required to advance in one aspect, but I've not hit that yet.  I personally prefer the enemies in CH, but that's a soley a stylistic choice.  On the other hand, In TTI, you can actually advance, including clearing bosses, and receiving their respective loot, while offline.  The gifts are more powerful and varied here, but, because of this they are less common and you have to actually notice them.  There are quite a few mechanics, spells, and ancients different.  The rank system is solely TTI (YOU level up, as well as your heroes).  Graphics are better (obviously).  The grid display is a VAST improvement.
TL;DR  If you think they're the same game, you've not played much of either.  If you like the genre, you'll VERY likely like TTI.  It's an actual step forward from CH, IMO, unlike all the other recent ones that feel more like side-steps.

This analogy is probably going to get lost on 99% of users here, but I feel like it'll be helpful for the 1% that does: back in 4th or 5th grade, we did something called the Bridge Project where we had to play this bridge building game as a sort of engineering exercise. Basically, you had to create a stable bridge while trying to balance costs.
World of Goo is essentially a puzzle game version of that. Here, you use sticky goo balls to create structures that get you to each level's end goal (a pipe that sucks up unused goos). The main obstacle here is physics, as you need to keep your structures from toppling over. There's a sort of built in comedy to watching all the ways your creations just topple in on themselves. And conversely, there's a huge sense of satisfaction when you actually complete a puzzle. It's not just that you've figured out an answer; you've used your ingenuity to build a unique solution.
The controls are unfortunately a bit of a hindrance here. It's often difficult to grab a goo without the cursor selecting one near it instead. This can lead to some frustrating moments where you accidentally destroy an entire level's work with one tug. Some of the game's more satirical humor doesn't quite work either. There's an anti-corporation theme throughout the story, but it's not really cohesive or well delivered enough to work. It comes off as being snarky without any real bite (I've never played Little Inferno, but from what I understand, that satire is built into the mechanics. Here, it's just sort of superimposed onto a puzzle game).
Those gripes aside, World of Goo's mix of construction and puzzles is still incredibly unique all these years later. It's an essential game for fans of the genre.

Combat to me is great. I have never played a tab-target mmo before, so the entire system was new to me. I came from a somewhat action-combat oriented MMO, but I find myself really enjoying the combat here. However, in the beginning levels, it is a little lackluster. You don't have as many abilities open to you though, so obviously you're gonna be restricted to your basic 1-2 combo over and over (sometimes even less depending on the class).
Aside from just talking about combat in itself, there are an array of dungeons and trials to do. 4-man, 8-man, 24-man parties all there. There are roughly around 90 (I'm including all the different difficultly levels plus counting floors/turns as their own) dungeons/trials/raids so far. Some trials have a normal, hard, and extreme version, and some dungeons have a hard version as well (although the hard versions are completely different from the normal version, so it's a whole new dungeon in itself. Nice move SE /proudofyouthx). The mechanics for a lot of these are super fun to me, although a bit daunting when you first start out. Some say it's like memorizing a dance with how crazy some fights get. I dig them, though. A lot. I find myself replaying a lot of the dungeons/trials just because the fight is amazing, not to farm gear or whatnot (
)
The dungeon/trail/raid private instances aren't just it though. There's still plenty going on in the open world, like FATEs and Hunts. Tons of people party up for those, granted you are in a pretty populated server.
Okay. If you haven't heard already, the music in the game is pretty stellar. Go on any FFXIV boss fight youtube video and people will be raving about how sweet the music is. And it's true. The music, especially for the boss fights, gets you SO pumped (
). It's the kind of music where you hear it as the battle starts and you're just like 'Awww man.♥♥♥♥♥♥s gonna be
'.
But it's not just the boss fights (although those are what get the most attention). Just about anywhere you go has some nice music playing. And I actually notice it (!!). I say this because there's some music that blends in with the atmosphere, like in most movies/games/commercials/etc., which is great (and perfect for most scenarios), but then there's the music that jumps out at you. That just compells you to look it up on the internet later. And that's the kind of music that I dig. And FFXIV has plenty of that. The soundtrack for the Heavensward expansion couldn't come out any faster. I crave it.
So aside from the aforementioned lackluster combat in the beginning of the game, I figured I should put the couple of things that aren't so nice about FFXIV.

I didn't go into any detail about what makes this game great.
Graphics - 9/10 - It's stylized, but limited due to it being darn-near impossible to mod the game. The highest settings are beautiful, and fulfill the needs of the gamer.
Gameplay - 8/10 - There are certain glitches that ruin moments in the game. If you use the Siren's power against certain bosses the game can freeze, or the boss will just float away. Other than that the controls are responsive and enjoyable without an oversaturization of combos or a crazy learning curve.
THE LOOT - 10/10 - The road to getting the perfect version of your favorite gun is long and difficult. There are ways to "increase" your chances of rare loot, but the best way is to learn what sidequests do what to each of the bosses that drop their own special weapons.
The Story - 9/10 - Same repetition of style as a lot of RPG's. The difference with Borderlands 2 is the level of silliness in the storyline, and how it was integrated throughout the missions. The story initiated a level of seriousness still; however, there was so much playfullness on top that it didn't seem to take itself too seriously.
The Coop - 8/10 - It becomes too easy too quickly. We found ourselves walking through the low minions on our way to the sometimes overpowered boss fights. It was fun fighting over loot, though.
Overall Impression - 10/10
I am a believer in the thought that everyone has their perfect game. Mine is Borderlands 2. The issues I have with it are on the surface. There are references to things I love throughout, and more well-written moments than I ever thought necessary for a game. A nearly limitless number of ways to kill things. So many guns. So much fun.
I own this game on three platforms, have about ten characters, and have played every DLC at least a dozen times... I enjoy this game very very very much. Play it.

This western-themed FPS provides a decent story, quality soundtrack and a rather short campaign. Actual shooting part is reasonably satisfying, but is somewhat hamstrung by its sheer repetitiveness - there are very few weapon types and only a handful of enemy types. This monotony is broken up with a bullet-time mechanic, narrative tricks, scoring system, character skill progression and an emphasis on combos, which is further helped by how good the shooting feels. The campaign itself is short - it took me about 6 hours and I certainly took my time. Considering the campaign's replayability and a couple arcade modes, I'd say the value is good.
The game is also well optimized and is a competent PC port, requiring very little tinkering to run properly.
That said, the dueling system is irredeemably atrocious - it's floaty, unresponsive, feels unfair and random. Its only saving grace is that duels usually only take a couple of minutes to beat. Also, boss fights are pretty bland - only thing that sets bosses apart from regular enemies is a beefy health pool.

I have played this game for more than 1000 hours, just not through steam. The game is beautiful and probably the best hunting simulator you'll come across for a very long time. Some new players won't enjoy it because they don't realize that the game is not meant to be played as COD or Battlefield, and you'll have a hard time getting alot of harvests if you sprint around with your rifle when trying to find animals.
The biggest problem for new players though, is the awful payment model. You need to buy membership or licenses to be able to hunt all the animals, which costs real money. You also have to buy in-game currency to buy new weapons through the store, which is the only way you'll to be able to take ethical shots on all species. You can buy membership packages (bundles) which comes with discounted weapons and equipment, but it won't take long before you wish you had more callers, camos, tents, weapons, you name it, even if you bought the 1year membership bundle. There are alot of items in the game, and pretty much all of it will cost you real money, aswell as being somewhat expensive compared to most other F2P games.
All this taken into consideration, I still love the game, simply because I feel the gameplay is worth the money you need to spend on it to enjoy it. If you are looking for a good hunting simulator, this is your game, but you will have to be willing to spend quite a bit of money on it to be able to enjoy it to it's full potential. If you are just looking for a F2P time-waster, then this game is very likely not something you want to spend much time on.

Transistor was an beautiful game with amazing soundtrack. The game mechanics were pretty interesting (I haven't played Bastion yet, so the controls and combat system were pretty new to me). Here's a quick little list of my likes and dislikes for the game.
Liked:
+ Beautiful art and very atmospheric. A great part of the gameplay for me was discovering all the beautiful scenery. Let's just say I took a whole bunch of screenshots...
+ Amazing soundtrack - yes, I know, everyone says this, but it's very true. Darren Korb did an amazing job composing an enchanting and futuristic-piano pop, jazzy, yet hauntingly beautiful soundtrack, and Ashley Barrett (the voice of Red) has the voice of a goddess, even when she's just humming.
+ Interesting storyline. Although you only get the story in pieces, once you put together all the parts of the story, you get a very intriguing plot (no twists or turns or anything though), but nonetheless, still enjoyable in a romantic way.
+ The voice acting. Can I just say I love Logan Cunningham's voice? Whoo, man. And Ashley Barret's singing is perfect. [Logan Cunningham voices the narrator].
+ Skill system. I really liked that you could mix and match all skills, enhancing via the slots. It made for a more interesting gameplay, plus (for the achievements), I had to figure out a lot of ways to use all the skills in the best way, which was a pretty good challenge.
Dislikes:
- Lack of utilization of the amazing soundtrack. Like others have said, the game has an amazing soundtrack but in-game, you don't get to hear much of the great music except during some boss battles. I wish more of the music was played while you traveled around.
- Restricted movement. By "restriction," I mean that you are unable to go back to areas you've passed so if you miss any secret areas or items in the game, you aren't able to get it.  Kind of just a personal preference thing for me, but I like being able to go back and forth between areas of a map because I'm very meticulous about checking everything, every little crook or nanny before radvancing in the story.
- Hard to level up. Because of the restricted movement, the chances to "level up" are limited as well because you aren't able to go back and keep fighting spawned enemies or things like that.
Systems:
* Semi turn-based combat system. The game possesses four key skill slots that can be executed real time. However, the Transistor has the ability to "pause" time in which you can plan your next couple of moves. These "pauses" in time are called "Turns ()" in the game.
* Variety of skills and enhancements. A slot system allows for the mixing and matching of different skills. Each skill can used to enhance another skill or provide a benefit in overall combat.

* Limited Saves (no slots/files). By limited saves, I mean that you can't save on files. The game has specific points where you can save, and I'd say those save points are pretty well spread-out. Just remember to save often, and the game also automatically saves when you enter different areas. "Saving" will be indicated by a gold triangle in the lower right hand corner of your screen.
* Enemy upgrades. As you progress through the story, the enemies gain more skills, "leveling up" in the game.
* Limiters. For more challenging gameplay, you can equip "limiters" on yourself. Like doubling the chance of your enemies spawning more enemies, limiting your skill set, etc. In turn, you gain more bonuses for leveling up.
Okay, that's all I can really think up right now (because it's 2am on a weekday and y am i even up adfla;sdfk).
Also, although I bought this game at full price, you should probably wait for a sale to buy this game. I mean it's a great game and all, but not as much storyline as I'd have liked, and for me, not enough to warrant buying this game at full price.

The play style took a little bit to get used to, but once you understand it it's intuitive.  The story and atmosphere had me hooked.  It's fairly short, 6-7 hours, but I could definitely see myself playing it again soon.

Transistor offers superb and original game mechanics, an atmospheric journey through an eerily digitalised futuristic city, excellent replayability options and fantastic storytelling. It's definitely one of my favorite games. Edit: Still a favorite, all this time later.

(Alright, time to give this review an overhaul now that I've officially given this game 1000 hours of my life. Just gonna add in some extra tidbits here and there.)
FFXIV has easily become my favorite MMO.
. And it's weird, because I just sort of downloaded it like, (shrug) yeah, I'll check it out, why not. But then after a while, I realized, 'Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ I'm having
much fun.' The thing is, I've never viewed Final Fantasy as an MMO sort of game. It was always the main console games for me (FFVII, FFVIII, FFIX, etc.). So FFXIV, and FFXI for that matter, was never something I even looked at or took interest in. But hey, now I'm a full-fledged passenger aboard the FF MMO hype train.
I really don't even know where to start with this review. A part of me just wants to go EVERYTHING IS AWESOME THIS IS AWESOME AND THAT IS AWESOME AND IT'S ALL SPECTACTULAR. A+ review. I don't really think I'll be able to cover everything I want to, but I'm gonna take a shot at (some of) it:
Whenever I think MMO, I think, half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥basic story. And that's fine, because it's all about the gameplay and getting the gear and doing the dungeons and getting your rake so you can go farming. And whenever I think Final Fantasy, I think, five-star story that will leave you with great memories for years and years to come.
FFXIV actually has a good story to it. And I got pumped for it when I saw that opening cutscene, a scene that I still watch over and over from time to time. Now, the story isn't out of this world, but I did enjoy it a lot. Everything built up to make the end boss much more satisfying. And there were cutscenes. Tons of cutscenes. So many. Which can be good or bad depending on the person obviously. I appreciated it, and it did immerse me into the story more.
Edit: And now that I have gotten much farther in the story and, again, have spent 1000 hours of my life with it, I can say now that I absolutely love the story in this game. I mean, the story was good in 2.X (and got real ♥♥♥♥ing crazy around 2.55), but with Heavensward (3.0), I just sort of realized how much I love these characters, I love the story that's going on, and
. I HAVE CRIED
TEARS MULTIPLE TIMES. I have gotten angry, I have been shocked, I have felt many emotions through the course of this game. Other games I'm like cool, cool, cool, let's get on to the fighting. Here, I will shush the ♥♥♥♥ out of anyone who won't let me finish my cutscene. Like a good mini-movie ayyyyy.
In the manner of my kobold friends, this game is gorgeous, stunning, beautiful! I mean really, I'm not even sure how to phrase how much I appreciate the graphics in this game. I think I was killing this buffalo type creature the other day, and the sun was rising (Yes, there is a weather/day/night cycle system. Yeah, it's awesome.), and you know when the sun is shining in someone's eyes and you can see just how pretty their eye color is? Yeah, well I thought this buffalo looked sweet as ♥♥♥♥ in the sunlight. So that, but transfer it to every single zone and x100 because I can view the zones during night/day/dusk/dawn/etc. Also, the newest zones for the 3.0 expac are gorgeous, except now I can just stare at all the beauty while
and listening to the banging music and ijustlovethisgame. And I still don't think I expressed how much everything pierces my soul. I can't guys, just. Max settings 4 lyf suck ittttt~~~~
Combat to me is great. I have never played a tab-target mmo before, so the entire system was new to me. I came from a somewhat action-combat oriented MMO, but I find myself really enjoying the combat here. However, in the beginning levels, it is a little lackluster. You don't have as many abilities open to you though, so obviously you're gonna be restricted to your basic 1-2 combo over and over (sometimes even less depending on the class).
Aside from just talking about combat in itself, there are an array of dungeons and trials to do. 4-man, 8-man, 24-man parties all there. There are roughly around 90 (I'm including all the different difficultly levels plus counting floors/turns as their own) dungeons/trials/raids so far. Some trials have a normal, hard, and extreme version, and some dungeons have a hard version as well (although the hard versions are completely different from the normal version, so it's a whole new dungeon in itself. Nice move SE /proudofyouthx). The mechanics for a lot of these are super fun to me, although a bit daunting when you first start out. Some say it's like memorizing a dance with how crazy some fights get. I dig them, though. A lot. I find myself replaying a lot of the dungeons/trials just because the fight is amazing, not to farm gear or whatnot (
)
The dungeon/trail/raid private instances aren't just it though. There's still plenty going on in the open world, like FATEs and Hunts. Tons of people party up for those, granted you are in a pretty populated server.
Okay. If you haven't heard already, the music in the game is pretty stellar. Go on any FFXIV boss fight youtube video and people will be raving about how sweet the music is. And it's true. The music, especially for the boss fights, gets you SO pumped (
). It's the kind of music where you hear it as the battle starts and you're just like 'Awww man.♥♥♥♥♥♥s gonna be
'.
But it's not just the boss fights (although those are what get the most attention). Just about anywhere you go has some nice music playing. And I actually notice it (!!). I say this because there's some music that blends in with the atmosphere, like in most movies/games/commercials/etc., which is great (and perfect for most scenarios), but then there's the music that jumps out at you. That just compells you to look it up on the internet later. And that's the kind of music that I dig. And FFXIV has plenty of that. The soundtrack for the Heavensward expansion couldn't come out any faster. I crave it.
So aside from the aforementioned lackluster combat in the beginning of the game, I figured I should put the couple of things that aren't so nice about FFXIV.
I still left out a lot of the tidbits that I just absolutely love about the game, but alas, this
short review will have to suffice. I surprisingly ended up loving this game, and you should check it out if it sounds like something you're even remotely interested in. I love it lots. Square Enix and Final Fantasy have (again) taken my soul hostage and I'm ok with that.

JC2 was. and still is, one of my favorite games of all time. I waited until just recently to get JC3 on sale for $8 to finally try out the sequel- and I couldnt have been more dissapointed.
Things I liked:
New wingsuit/grappling abilities, helped to make the already great movement system even better
Updated graphics
That's about it.
Things I disliked:
Driving controls are not fixed- if anything, they are even worse than the last game where they were atleast serviceable. Unlike every other game where Space is the default handbrake, in here it is the button that makes you exit the car, making for extremely frustrating situations. Cars are extremely floaty, and there is little incentive to driving when you have so many other methods of travel.
Flying controls are absolutely broken; you cannot turn around in less than about 30 seconds of full-mousepad length swipes of the mouse.
The camera for all vehicles in the game (expect for boats, oddly enough) are absolutely broken and often snap you into looking directly ahead of you.
While the graphics are updated, the landscape is a massive dissapointment compared to Panau. There are less biomes, and each area feels extremely desolate and unpopulated. also, the lighting in JC2 is (I feel) far superior to this game's.
The towns feel extremely copy and pasted, as each look identical and have the exact same chaos items to destroy. Same goes for most of the military areas- with a few exceptions, most are extremely identical and have the exact same chaos items to destroy.
There is no difficulty selector in this game, which is puzling as the difficulty seems to change on the fly- at one second, enemies will stare at you for 30 seconds without doing anything, and other times, they will be able to hit you with every pistol shot as you are flying 100 yards away from them at 100+ mph. It makes no sense how drastically different the AI will react.
There is far less weapon and vehicle variety in this game- including the loss of the dual weilding system in JC2.
The challenge system locks away abilities that you had in the previous game (EX: zoom-in aim) and makes you perform boring and meaningless challenges to unlock them. All the interesting upgrades you can get are also locked away far down the challenge list. It seems like an attempt to artificially lengthen the game/increase content by forcing the player to do these challenges.
The dialogue and story in this game are laughably bad. It almost feels like that was the kind of tone they were going for- an intentionally badly-written story- but if that was the intention, it was done very poorly. There are often odd pauses in dialogue, and many of the Medici radio broadcasts (which were actually very entertaining) are cut off by boring settlement announcements or other dialogues. Even Rico has had a massive voice change, and his little quips and jokes are often hit-or-miss. New characters have almost no background or character development to make them at all interesting to the story. Gone is the 3-faction system, and you are only working against one very poorly written villian. The missions were very unappealing, and lacked the variety and surprise that JC2 missions offered. The game is also much, much shorter (even with the AGL's in the form of challeneges) overall, and only includes one bossfight at the very end, and is the most simple and uninteresting bossfight I've played in years.
The game is a clear console port, as the menus all handle very clunkily and dont even allow you to use the escape key to exit most. It is also full of bugs, including one gamebreaking bug that will not allow you to complete a mission about 3/4 of the way through the story- this bug is not rare, either: any PC gamer that uses the "precision aiming" upgrade will experience this bug.
I would complain about fast travel in this game, but it is actually a plus- because Medici is so barren and uninteresting, and most vehicles handle so abhorrently, I feel no desire to actually traverse and landscape, and instead opt to use the new fast travel system.
There are dozens of more complaints that I could go on to talk about, but I will refrain from doing so. This game is not even worth the $8 sale asking price. If you do not own any Just Cause games, ignore this game and buy the second.

At a low price (like the sale) it may be worth it for the quick foray to complete the story, but as a whole unless you love MMO's in general and the grind that comes with it, i wouldn't recommend.
One of the reasons i enjoy Oblivion and Skyrim is because the worlds are beautiful to experience, (or atleast on release in Oblivions case), however due to the type of game it is, you lose beauty in favor of performance and so visually your almost going back to Oblivion's now empty looking landscape.
--
Now the grind, now unless you just skip everything and run through too the finish line to then grind it later, you'll otherwise end up with a full storage within the first 2-3 dungeons, which is a nightmare if you like to plan and prep for future forays, upgrades and levels.
You'll be left wondering how rare is some of this stuff, non of which you would really want to find out it's rare as hell and you got a lucky find, nor would you want to spend hours grinding it later, so you collect as you actually "play"... but that brings you back round to a tiny backpack & bank space... with each 10 point upgrade the cost doubles.. to the point you find yourself contemplating the subscription so you can get the extra crafting bag to store all your ingredients in.
Like many games these days, that item hogging part of your inventory that you just want rid of, you wish you had kept by the time your half way through the game, which again is another kick in the♥♥♥♥♥♥when it comes to storage.
--
The crates & crowns, unless you plan on spending more in the game than you actually spend on the game itself, i would just put them to the back of your mind.. some of that stuff looks mighty nice, but for what? the cost of another game or double?
The question is, is all that really worth it? i mean yeah people work to make this kind of stuff, but the majority being cosmetics they probably add up far more than if the cosmetic was a DLC available for purchase on steam, but when translated to crowns it doesn't look like a whole lot.
Ontop of that some of these things ar elimited to the season they are introduced in, so once that season is up it will no longer be available, again forcing the hand of those who may try to work up to getting it, to instead make a quick purchase of crowns in order to get it before it disappears.
But even then, it isn't that simple, as most of these items are purchased with "crown gems" which from what i gathered are gained when you purchase "crates" with your "crowns". So it ends up being a gamble for how many of these "crown gems" you can actually get and could mean the purchase of what? 8 crates or more? and these things are like 400 crowns each... and just look at the price of the Crowns on the steam page..
Intruth people will spend far more than it's worth to get this gear, now it's their choice, but at the end of the day they will refuse to accept that it makes it much worse for everyone else, as their willingness to purchase virtual items only gives Developers and the Publishers more inclination to introduce such systems within the games they make, many, many of which are far from worth the purchase price. This especially for a virtual item that will become redudent when you no longer wish to play the game, or when the servers are eventually shutdown as the cost will outweigh the income earned one day.
--

Browsing the "most helpful" reviews I mostly saw people who hadn't even spent two hours playing this game, called it a Clicker Heroes ripoff and quit, thus they might not have realized a lot of the differences.  Allow me to set things straight.
I want to clear up one thing up first though:
Yes, the game IS very similar to Clicker Heroes.  But in my opinion, it's an improvement to the formula that CH was composed of.
Mystery Gifts
Clicker Heroes has these little objects that randomly pop up on the screen that always gives you gold and occasionally a ruby.  In TTI these mystery gifts randomly pop up after you defeat an enemy, but they don't always give you gold.  They may give you gold,  or they could give you infinity tokens or valor points instead.
Infinity Tokens
They ARE almost identical to Hero Souls.  You can only obtain them the very first time you clear a boss stage on a run, and they act as a currency that doubles as 10% dps per IT.  However you get them much earlier (I think stage 30 is the earliest), and after you've discovered them, you may find them in mystery boxes as well.
Upgrades
For the most part, they are the same... except (and this wins me over), YOU HAVE ALL OF THEM UNLOCKED.  There is no accepting whatever is available to you, or spending hero souls hoping for better options.
Valor Points
I suppose you could look at them as Infinity Tokens that only work for specific heroes.  If you must compare to clicker heroes, then it's a form of gilding for a hero, and after you collect so many for a specific hero you may upgrade the hero so that their skills and dps are higher.  (edit:  Finally found enough VP to start upgrading some of my heroes.  Apparently each upgrade after the first costs Gems as well as VP)
Infinity Gems
Took me a while to find one of these.  The premium currency, though like CH Rubies, you can find these during normal gameplay.  Though these are found through "super-boss" rare drops instead of the mystery gifts (or perhaps "as well as" but not for sure)

I never thought I'd recommend an engineering game for the story, but here we are.
World of Goo owes a lot to how well it executes on its aesthetic. The intrepid soundtrack coupled with a narrative that promises answers just over the next ridge contextualizes this game as one of exploration and discovery instead of just construction and puzzle solving. The goo balls themselves are simple but surprisingly lovable, and the mysterious Sign Painter brilliantly combines context, hints, and humor making these necessities of function into friends that are joining you for a journey into the unknown. It really is fascinating how the tone these elements create makes for a totally different game than what it appears to be mechanically.
Ironically, the 'living building materials' gimmick that gives this game so much personality is also its most obnoxious quality. Once the goo balls make contact with a structure and awaken, they never stop moving. They constantly pulse around the structure both changing its weight distribution and making the selection of an individual goo ball difficult. This becomes a real problem as the goo balls become more diverse in nature, and timing becomes more of an issue due to the need for increasingly unstable structures. Introducing a 'whistle' mechanic in the second of the five chapters seems to have been done to solve this as it draws the goo balls to wherever you're clicking. But, in my experience, it only sped up their movement with a slight preference towards the vicinity of the whistling. The ability to pause and select a ball would have solved this issue, however it also would have taken away from the 'grand adventure' atmosphere that makes World of Goo the joy it is.
So I suppose it's best to accept the frustration caused by their incessant fidgeting as a quirk of rather than a flaw, even if that does make the OCD extra challenges even more insanity-inducing than they would be without it.

TL:DR An adventure game with a great setting and interesting story. Its terrible (but thankfully infrequent) combat sections and poor voice acting lets it down slightly.
Full Version:
The Dreamfall universe is a very interesting one. You've got Stark, which is basically our world but more futuristic, and Arcadia,a sort of fantasy world with magic, with both worlds seperate and still sort of linked. A small few people have the ability to travel between both. You start off playing as Zoe Castillo, who is the games main character and a resident of Stark. As the story progresses you get to play as April Ryan, the main character of this games predecessor The Longest Journey, and Kian, a sort of holy warrior. The story and the duel settings in particular are interesting and are what kept me invested in the game. The gameplay is mainly of the traditional adventure game sort with a lot of dialogue and cutscenes as well as a  (thankfully) little bit of combat which is poorly executed and doesnt fit with the rest of the game.
However its the story that is the main selling point here. Its also worth mentioning that playing the Longest Journey or at least reading a synopsis of that games story is advisable as some of the lore and characters might be a bit confusing and the game sometimes assumes you have this knowledge.
Good points:
- The games settings of  futuristic Stark and fantasy Arcadia are great and the relationship and lore between them is interesting enough to keep you wanting more.
- The story is quite good which is important for this type of game and having April and Kians sections is a welcome break from the dull Zoe.
Bad points:
- the voice acting is pretty terrible for some characters. Theres one minor female character with an exotic accent that sounds like they kidnapped the voice actress from the airport and forced her to dothe lines at gunpoint. The dialogue was also a bit glitchy at times as every now and again the dialogue would skip.
-the combat it a steaming pile of crap. You have a light attack, heavy attack and a block button. But its like trying to control a an arthritis riddled person to fight agaisnt another person with arthritis who happens to be severely ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Thankfully though these combat segements arent very frequent and are easy enough. They just add nothing to the game.

LINUX GAMERS : The game is short. (But hey, SouthPark Stick of Truth takes as long but was 60$) But, if you really get into the game atmosphere (and you will) and you take time to read the characters background and all the lore, you'll have one of the best immersive game there is. The story was so good, that, once I finished it I did it again. I think this is my first Steam review and I'm happy it is for Transistor. 10/10 would buy again.

As far as MMOs go, ESO is unique. You really don't have to play with others - but you can, and that's the beauty of it. Want to quest alone? There's a trove of content you can take on and excel at. Meanwhile, if you want to do all of the quests with a friend, you can also do that. But questing isn't where this game ends, and that's where ESO is special for me.
PvE content is stacked. You can do dungeons, which can take up to 4 players (but if you really want, you can solo these or two-man them). There are a variety to choose from, and they all drop unique weapon and armor sets. There are also two difficulties (normal and vet), where vet gets exponentially harder. Most of the vanilla dungeons are pretty easy, some will challenge you on vet - and as a low level character all of them will challenge you. The DLC dungeons are designed to break you though. Even after over a thousand hours, I've not completed a few of them. Specifically Horns of the Reach.
Trials are for up to 12 people, and they are designed with a challenge in mind. Like dungeons, they'll require you to learn mechanics and work together with others in your group. I've completed all the trials on normal, but vet is another monster entirely - and it's great.
The part I like about ESO the most is that I feel as if it pushes me, and that there is a skill wall for the harder content. No one likes a game where you can basically god-mode through the entire thing... and ESO does well to make you work to beat end-game content.  PvE content is exciting and sometimes time consuming. You'll spend hours in some of these longer dungeons, and you'll feel as if you really worked for it.
PvP content is crazy. Once you think you're a badass and have mastered PvE content, you take a walk into Cyrodiil and you get your♥♥♥♥♥♥pushed in. Once again, ESO raises the bar for end-game content. Massive groups of players all in a huge battleground simulator, taking over keeps, defending landmarks, and it all being open world. After some time and effort though, anyone can PvP successfully.
CONS: This game is buggy, sometimes a bit ugly, and it certainly has performance issues when you're in a group of 40+ people in one place. The crown store is not a pay-to-win concept, and there ARE freebies, but some of the content is indeed behind a paywall of DLC. I also recommend paying for ESO+, as the craftbag is necessary for not wanting to kill yourself for having a full inventory.
PROS: Game exhibits all of your favorite things about Skyrim, Oblivion, etc... The world is set before all of these events have taken place, but you get to see familiar spots in their infancy. The game will continue to push you, and you will NEVER run out of content. It is also relatively easy to make money in the game, so long as you loot early and often + join a trade guild (of which there are plenty). Game is compatible on PC with a controller, if you really want that Elder Scrolls feel. Graphics are beautiful and the world feels very much alive. Populations are high in-game, but it also does a nice job of making it not feel crowded.
As someone who came from TF2, it's nice to play a game where the devs seem to care and update it frequently.

Supergiant Games may not make long video games like other Indie groups or even the big studios, but they have clearly adopted the mantra of quality not quantity when it comes to their games.  Fans of BASTION will find themselves falling in love with Transistor.  Your mission as Red is to save the city of Cloudbank from destruction with the help of a weapon called the Transistor.  The gameplay doesn't pull any punches with its easy to learn, difficult to master style and can keep even a skilled strategist busy for quite some time.
As expected from Supergiant Games, the visuals, music and artwork are breathtaking and suit the mood and theme of the game perfectly.  It will definitely be worth a second playthrough if you're still trying to figure out what's going on like I am.
Buy this game.  You won't be disappointed with its Steampunk feel and general loveliness.

It was raining when I decided it was time to write this review. Frigid drops fell against the window outside, no moon out this night. I knew what I was doing, and it wasn't hard to tell this was a great game. My cat purred away steadily on my lap while the clock ticked away the minutes against my wall. It was warm inside, away from the darkness of this cold, cold night.
What was their left to say about this game, having played all the way though. These words had probably been said by a thousand other reviewers. My xbox controller still rested firmly in the grip of my hands, but it was time to start typing.
A romance. High tech but still bound by the conventions of film noir. It had evoked memories in me of better times and places. By the end I felt sadness, but jubilent in my own success. Red wouldn't let me go that easy it seemed, there was a new game plus, a whole new set of challenges. Despite all the joy and tragedy that had just unfolded, our heroic heroine didn't want to stop just yet.
Another time lady. I set my xbox controller aside, wiping away a tear. It was time to part with this game. Maybe I'll be back some day, I just don't know.

Just finished this gem, and I will definetly need more time to let the ending 'sink in'. - Probably come back and take more time for this review.
But I need to write something down, and tbh I normally only spent time on writing book reviews. In fact, this game took me by surprise. I experienced something we do call a sophisticated walking simulator these days - a game with unrelevant gameplay mechanics. Fortunatelly it had parts which required to move in stealth - or let find a more sophisticated way to describe it - required to stay 'undetected'.  So, if you want some envolved gameplay mechanics, you wont find any. As a matter of factly, I strongly suggest to play this game with a controller (does it work with the steam controller, TBH i dont care - it worked wonderfully with an old XBOX 360 controller -  had just  to remap 1 button) as I couldnt cope with the Mouse and Keyboard controls. The puzzles were easy - the combat was just awful. (There are alternative solutions to avoid most combat in the game).
So if not for the gameplay, why do play it at all? For the storytelling and the story, and If you have not played "The Longest Journey - Funcom 1999" yet - play this rather classical point and click adventure first. In fact do it now. You will miss some meta-story elements which actually made Dreamfall - and its last chapters a blast for me. Oh, and besides that, handful characters and many locations from the first game had a comeback in Dreamfall.
And no, no synopsis and summary will do it - trust me on that. Some parts need time to sink in.
Futhermore - the writing is superb and rather mature compared to other games out there. The voice acting is outstanding. Within the first chapters I'd say - TLJ 1999 had the better voice acting. But after finishing the game. my opinion changed drastically. I would say its different. I missed the sarcasm and humor of the first game. But some of it came back in Chapter 8 (with certain characters). And i am sure Ragnar Tornquist had his reasons to keep the theme a bit darker/serious.
Be warned - the ending is not for the faint of heart and the weak of mind. And there is a reason why so many people wanted a continuation in "Dreamfall Chapters" (3rd game in the series)
Do your choices matter - some minor choices and decisions made in the chapters will have some minor impact on the story, but will not change the outcome or the plot on the meta level (unlike LiS or TWD Season 1)
Graphics: so this game was made in 2006 - I recently googled some of the 2006 Titles - back then this game was top notch - and I'd say, Dreamfall still looks acceptable today - it was rather awkward, because some the settings are astounding. You will travel between so many locations - and it will be impossible for you to guess what will come up next. The Characters are very well made - top notch lip-sync - eye movement etc. but the great character-art will feel awkward compared to these days facial animations - rather like blunt doll faces.
On a different level - compare this to KOTOR 2 - which was made in 2005, KOTOR 2 just looks awful compared to Dreamfall.
Dreamfall runs with all modern 16:9/16:10 resolutions.
Sound: Great support for all kinds of Soundchips from back in the day, Dolby 7:1 worked fine. The Soundtrack is amazing. Everything here from modern lounge music to non synth classical tracks played by a real symphonic orchestra.
Will I like this game?
If you rather lack in patience - do not like long dialogues. Dislike games with mediocre gameplay mechanics: better stay away
If you need to feed your hunger for a unpredictalbe story written by of IMHO best writers in the gaming industry (Ragnar Tornquist). Want some outstanding voice acting -  go for it.
Is it better than "The Longest Journey"? Its different in many aspects. IMHO the pacing was better, but TLJ requires a lot more discipline to play, Especially if not using a walkthrough. (which is way more rewarding) Storywise - until chapter 8 I'd say TLJ any day, but after finishing the 2nd half of the game - I started to like both games for different reasons. If you have played and enjoyed TLJ (1999) - I'd say go for a playthrough of Dreamfall.
One final Warning - as already stated: the Ending is not everyones cup of tea - There are cliffhangers. As IMHO the story itself was mostly resolved - but the mystic metaplot kept my mind spinning (in a good way). Luckily Dreamfall Chapters are almost finished.

I recommend this to anyone that likes a good story, because that certainly is this game strongest point. You don't have to play the first game in the series, but you will get more out of the references, returning characters, and world in general if you have played the first and gotten to know Arcadia before this game.
The controls are... a bit annoying at first, both combat and sneaking are really bad. But luckily you get used to it after awhile, so it doesn't drag the experience down too much.
The game has a variety of characters, most of them interesting and/or fun. As for our two leading ladies, Zoe and April. They are just so cute, and they both have both adorable and funny moments (which I appreciate) in the middle of this dramatic journey. They are also both flawed in their own ways, but their cuteness and capabilities outshine that, so it more adds to the complexity of them.
As for the third playable character, Kian... Here is a character that seems to be defined entirely by his gender in this story. He is about as interesting as that sword he loves waving around, which is to say not at all. He is strong, tough, manly, honorable. And all his flaws come from him being too manly, too tough, too selfrighteous and confident. None of his parts really added anything good to the story or the experience for me.
The music is mostly great. I say mostly because a few times it is really distracting
The best part of this game is the story and the emotions of the characters. And while there are times when it isn't perfect, it mostly nails it. When it needs to feel serious and dark, it does. When it tries to be cute, it gets super cute and makes me just want to hug and cuddle the leads, even if those girls are more capable and bigger badasses than I will ever be. And when it tries to be funny it is. And when it wants the story to be tragic and sad, it pulls it off pretty well as well.
So yeah, if you can suffer through the controls, the combat and stealth sections of the game in particular, there is a great story here for you.

Hi all, pzratnog here. December 18th was the day I found this game. I had just lost my save file in clicker heros. I can't even begin to describe how lucky I was that that happened since losing my save is what brought me to tap tap infinity. Initially, I was pleasantly surprised by two factors in TTI - namely the cloud save and an active, polite, responsive developer. Players starting the game now benefit from dozens of features the game did not have when I started: spells, ascensions and ranks, valor point upgrades,grid mode for easy buying, multilevel buying, presents, and so many more. All or most of these features were added at least in part due to community feedback. The dev, ScaryBee, is truly fantastic about that kind of stuff. New features constantly are rolling out to keep the experience fresh. I've been playing 7 months now, been through the game 3 times, coded an optimizer (find it on the wiki), had a superboss named after me, and am still in love with this game mostly because of how great the dev is. Give it a go, and if you like incrimentals, I can almost guarantee this will quickly become one of your favorites!

It's funny to read reviews from people who have barely played the game calling it a knock-off. Fragsworth actually defended this game on Reddit when someone called it a clone. The differences become more apparent the longer you play, so give the game a chance if you are into the clicker/incremental genres. The Spells, Guardian powers, currencies etc. all function differently here than in Clicker Heroes and there are other unique features as well, with more constantly being added.
I've played the game since December on the web version and am currently on my second playthrough (reached the final level and hard reset in June). I even had the privilege to be made a boss in the game because of my contributions to the game's wiki. As I see it, TTI has numerous advantages over Clicker Heroes et al.:
Long after I gave up on CH and Adcap, I'm still here playing TTI and I am really excited to see how the game continues to develop. If you're into the genre or interested in getting into the genre, give this game a chance!
