Don't let my time fool you. I have sunk hundreds of hours into this game. You can playing it without the Steam Client open or even on.
This game is great.
If you are not at all familer with FFXIV, the 1.0 release sucked. It was horrible. Combat was a chore and stupidly slow. Dungeons were a waste of time. Raids, heh nope. Crafting, usually the best way to make money in any MMO, imo, required so much time to do get anything done. Honestly it was a waste of time and money.
Then Square had Bahamut blow up the world.
After a few months, 2.0 A Realm Reborn came out.... and it was a complete 180.
My personal favorite part of this game is the Job/Class System.
Basically one character can be everything. You wanta start as a Puglist? done. Don't like that? try a Lancer, or be a Arcanist, or maybe a Warrior.
Then the game pulls a FF1 and upgrades your class with Soul Stones. Puglists become Monks, Lancers turn into Kain-err I mean Dragoons, ect.
Combat has been reworked into something that feels more active for a MMO.  While it's still hotkey based, you have to move around a hell of a lot more often, and constantly be aware of where the enemy is facing, because if your a Melee class you can get bonus damage, and otherwise the enemy can launch AoEs that can hit like a truck.
Dungeons and Raids are actually fun now.
So thats a start.
While I feel the game is stingy with loot and gil in dungeons, Raids like most MMOs are where it all is at in terms of fun.
The game has a dungeon finder like system to fill gaps in your party or put you with randoms, but it actually tries to encourage good play between randoms with the player commendation system, which can lead to some pretty neat rewards for those who try and play well with others.
Raids are great. Boss design in my opinion is fantastic with every movment of your character needing to be precise to avoid some pretty horrible debuffs, one hit kills, ect. You actually have to pay attention. OMG.
Also, there are Trials in which you fight aganist classic Final Fantasy summons (in this game called Primals) and everyone is great and a spectical to watch if you have a computer to handle it.
One note for fans of Final Fantasy in general.
The references are piled high. If you have played a lot of the older games you will be drowned with little nods to some games (like Project METEOR) and some huge love letter to others (LIKE ALL OF CRYSTAL TOWER)
Srs thou. The final boss of Crystal tower is so great. I've never seen FF3 get so much love.
Also this has a plot that's not half bad.
It makes sense sometimes.
The small amount of voice acting there is boils down to basic standard fair for like english anime dubs. It ain't bad. but I've cringed so many times. You will be reading a lot more text boxes then listening to them.
It also resolves it's story archs, and gives some closure. *Stares very hard at WoW*
A few problems exist.
One I have is still the crafting system. It bores me to tears. For many hours it's not worth it, and it's expensive if you don't know where to get the parts. It's time consuming until you can get it done automaticly. Even then you might not want to do it auto because you can't have HQ parts which makes things more worth selling.
Questing sucks. While going into a dungeon is cool, EVERYTHING ELSE FEELS THE SAME. Go here, kill something, find something, mine something. There is very little in questing variety. AND YOU HAVE TO DO THE MAIN QUESTS TO GET TO EXPANSION CONTENT. The main questline is long and tidious just fyi. so unless your very invested in the story you will be bored unless you got a guild to chat with or friends over skype. It feels like a slog to me.
Also, Sub models suck. But what ever, It's worth it if you have a lot of free time, but if you're a normal human who can't spend 15 hours a day on a game, I wouldn't recommend this.
Otherwise I love this game.
And wholeheartly recommend this game to other people who have stupid amounts of free time.
(Srsly thou the Bahamut fight is worth playing for. It's just great)

I'm a fan of The Longest Journey, but unfortunately I can't recommend this sequel. If you really want to play it, reason being you want to see how the story continues, be prepared for boring and clunky gameplay.
The game can be broken up into a few categories: dialog/cutscenes (story), exploration, fetch quests, "stealth" gameplay, and combat. The story is solid, and the exploration is just ok. Everything else is flat out bad. The "stealth" gameplay doesn't fit and it's cumbersome. The combat makes Morrowind's combat look like the pinnacle of game design. The fetch quests are just repetitive and pad the amount of time it takes to complete the game.
If all you want is to see the story continuation, I'd recommend another avenue like watching cutscenes on youtube and reading the story on a wiki page. If you do choose to play this one just know that it'll feel like work.

As much as I enjoy playing this time to time, there are a few reasons why you shouldn't get into it. That's all up to you to decide however.
First, the good:
1. Fairly adult playerbase, I guess mainly because most are the original players from the day.
2. I haven't played Campaign in many years, in fact since I completed it, about 5 years ago, but I remember it was pretty good.
3. Fastpaced multiplayer action.
4. This game doesn't attempt at stealing all your freetime like some other games do, it's fun, but not addictive.
5. This works on Mac, I am not sure if other CoDs don't, but one of my friends recently bought this because it was Mac compatible.
Now the bad:
1. Hackers. It wasn't always nearly as bad as it is now. I am not sure how it works exactly, but InfinityWards seems to not have updated their anticheat system for a few years now and just about any lobby is permiated with a hacker as a result.
2. Unbalanced weapons. I'd guesstimate that 65% of all players use UMP, which is a clear sign your game isn't very well balanced. Some things like reloading on the Intervention has clearly been artificially slowed down, to balance stats out I guess, but still, it's not pretty and it stands out a country mile.
3. It's bloody expensive! I mean, this is 2015 we are living here and this came out in 2009 and it costs 20 USD, which isn't far off what it was at time of its release, I am thinking 7-10 USD maybe? I know it's CoD and CoDs must be expensive by law, but still... If you are going to have a 6 year old game still available for purchase, maybe make it more appealing by offering it at a lower price?
4. Playerbase is small, as You would expect, you'd have to work out the hours when most people come on, otherwise tough luck getting into a SnD when there's like one lobby hosted in the world.

Not quite like Bastion like everyone told me it would be, but still just as good in its own way. Also the sound track is totally worth the 10 bucks. 10/10 would play again.

Transistor maintains the poetic beauty you expect from Supergiant Games. The shared DNA from Bastion is obvious in the music, the narration, and the self-induced apocalypse that has shattered the game's world.  But you shouldn't take this to mean that this is a sequel to Bastion. It is completely separate, and stands entirely on its own.
So, can it stand on its own? Well, mostly.  The game feels shorter than Bastion, and yet it has consumed more time -- about 8 hours in a straight playthrough. I think a part of that is the enforced linearity of the game. Once you leave an area, there's no coming back. There appear to be paths in the game, but on a single play-though, I can't tell if I missed anything in them. There's also no overworld map and no home base, which would serve to give you an idea of where you are in the story. Consequently, when the ending happens, it comes as a surprise, and not necessarily a pleasant one.
The health and resourcing part of the game isn't immediately obvious, and it took most of the game before I finally understood what actions refilled my health. I still haven't figured out what causes the 'overload' to steal weapons from me, although I finally can tell which one is on the block. The end result is a resource anxiety that feels so terribly unfair:  if you get beat up by an emeny, the game takes away your weapons, so that it is even more difficult when the next enemy appears!
But... you know, at the end of the game, I think that was part of the experience... I made it through okay, and in the end, the game made me feel something.
Sure, you should buy this, because it is inexpensive and beautiful, but if you're waffling between the two, I think Bastion is a better game.

The art and the music in this game are fantastic. There are plenty of customization options for combat, which will make me sound odd when I say that combat is slow, sometimes tedious, but never particularly exciting or difficult. Supergiant clearly tried to innovate, but I'm not a fan of what they came up with. I'm sure it appeals to those who thought bastion's combat was too twitchy.
For me, the story was one big melodramatic flop. The antagonists are not developed much during gameplay so it's difficult to get much satisfaction from your victories. Tension is missing, mostly because some themes present in Bastion get carried over, and its hard to get excited over cookies you've already eaten. Red ends up less of a hero in this story, and more a victim of a tragedy she wrote for herself.
Nevertheless, the game is fairly short, so its worth a quick run through for the art and music alone.

Transistor is a game like no other. Although it only lasts for 5 hours for a single playthrough, every second of the game was something to be celebrated. Much like Bastion before it, Supergiant's Transistor is truly  exemplary, and perhaps one of the strongest arguments for games as art. Not only are the visuals stunning, the music haunting and gorgeous, and the storyline engrossing, but the characters are some of the strongest I've seen in any form of media to date. Transistor is not the story of Cloudbank, The Process, or the Camerata, Transistor is a story about Red and The Transistor. Their relationship is the driving force behind the game, and even with a deliberately silent protagonist, Supergiant manage to create a more fleshed out character than any I've seen in years. The gameplay is not the reason that you should play the game, although it can hold its own any day of the week. Playing Transistor is an experience like no other. To any on the fence about this game, I can only say that it will be well worth your time.

Story: The story continues 10 years after The Longest Journey. Like the original, the voice acting was strong and most of the old cast showed up in this game. However, that's where the similarities stop. The story becomes convoluted and confusing and introduces more questions than it answers. Even the ending was a cliffhanger that left a lot to be explained.
Gameplay, in comparison to the first game, involved a lot of walking... a lot of it... and had attempts to weave stealth and combat into the gameplay. Unfortunately, despite the addition of these additional elements, neither combat nor stealth felt polished to a point where it made meaningful impact.
Environments: The limited 3D graphical engine used also didn't do the game much justice. Although it meant the world could be explored in an RPG manner, it also meant that the world was void of on-screen assets resulting in a very plain world.
Music: I thought the choice of a romantic (theme) song was terribly wrong. Unlike other games where similar music invoked strong emotions, Dreamfall's two romantic interests didn't communicate their romantic tension very well in game. I think it may also be due to the game engine's lack of facial movement when talking.
6/10. I was actually pretty disappointed overall.

PROS: Good story compared to most games, interesting use of aboriginal folklore, pretty and unique environments
CONS: Frustrating camera controls, awkward fighting mechanics, somewhat awkward animations
OVERALL SCORE: 7.5/10
Dreamfall: The Longest Journey is, as you might guess, the sequel to The Longest Journey. In it, we follow a new protagonist, Zoe Castillo, as she attempts to track down her ex-boyfriend Reza. We also catch up with April Ryan, who has become jaded after the events of The Longest Journey, and Kian Alvane, a member of the Azadi who is brought to Marcuria in an attempt to destroy April and everything she stands for.
Story-wise, the game was quite impressive. We get multiple perspectives throughout the game, which was a nice was to gain knowledge that might have been harder to obtain if we'd been stuck with Zoe. There is a strong mythos a dreaming, as Zoe is a dreamer - she can use her dreams to move between worlds. The idea of the dreaming and dreamtime was pretty clearly inspired by Aboriginal mythology on dreaming and the creation of the universe. The mythology itself is fascinating in its own right, and very underused in writing so Dreamfall gets some major points for utilizing it. The story itself had lots of twists and turns, many of which I did not see coming (especially the ending of the game).
The gameplay mechanics left much to be desired, though. There are a small handful of combat scenes that involve spamming the left mouse button and they mostly only serve to be annoying. They don't regularly appear so I have to wonder why the appeared in the game at all. The camera was also pretty awkward at time, especially during the numerous stealth scenes. However, it wasn't so bad that the game couldn't be finished.
Overall, I would say Dreamfall is worth playing, especially if you are already invested in the series from playing The Longest Journey. The story and the mythos are enough to make the game worth it.

I honestly enjoyed the absolute hell out of RoK when my two close friends persuaded me to buy it on sale for, at the time, $5.00. The survival aspect of constantly scavenging for food, water, and materials such as flax from their respective bushes, wood from trees, and stone from rocks on the ground to create your first armor and tools was what intrigued me to continue playing. Meeting players of various temperaments as a noob was to be expected, so dying from one stroke of a steel sword while completely naked wasn't that big of a deal. However, after me and my two friends finally settled on our first base hovering over water in Crownland in an offical server, we soon started to realize the core problem with this game.
The problem wasn't the constantly encountered bugs, lag, fluctuating ping, or even that we were just plain bad at the game. It was the hackers. Our hovering-over-water wooden base was completely overrun by three raiders with wood armor, javelins, and spears. We were in, mind you, full iron gear. All three of us were killed, and no matter how many sword swings, iron javelins, or steel crossbow bolts met our foes, they barely flinched. They had also entered our base because one of us accidentally let them in while trying to escape to safety, so our beds and chests were griefed and destroyed.
Honestly, since we were pretty new to the game (especially myself), we thought we were terrible at the combat and that's why we had lost. Well, before we had all died while we had iron gear, all three of us died from a full steel equipped player on the nearby beach. I think I recall him watching us yelling how pathetic we were over voice chat as we were completely slaughtered by pieces of wood.
Well, the three of us attempted making a strong cobblestone base on a supposedly better community server. We were met with multiple issues with players killing us with underpowered gear, despite the fact we were in full steel and hit them more times than they hit us back. One player, I recall, killed me with an iron spear in two hits to the chest, despite the fact I clearly hit them in the head with a steel great sword THREE times. The player had killed me on sight, which is against the server rules, so I personally talked with one of the admins about it. He could not find that the player ever existed on the server, and said he could usual find players even if they were logged out. I never received what I had back.
Finally, to end this unbearably long review, us three made another strong cobblestone base on a different offical server than the first, and there was a player that had gone by the name Sweet Sugar Lips (if you ever read this review, I hope you've found a better life). She (the player's character in-game was female, so I will address them as such) is probably the one player that ruined the game for all three of us. She killed us literally tens of times with by standing on top of our cobblestone base and waiting for us to pop out and attempt to kill her. She only bandaged herself ONCE throughout the entire process (of which lasted for about a whole hour), and finally brought a friend. She and her friend went to the iron barred entrance of our base, was roped by her friend, and glitched into our base. You can probaby assumed what would happen afterwards. This is, of course, not to mention the many other times she has instantly killed us and resulted in our loss of steel gear to an iron battleaxe and wooden javelins.
For the sake of length (screw that at this point), I only mention the significant moments where a seamingly beautiful and potential-filled game completely and utterly crushed our dreams of creating a large castle and even getting CLOSE to properly and fairly raiding other players. Sure, maybe none of the experiences I mentioned had to do with hackers at all and we really DO just suck at the game. But honestly, the developers have done nothing significant to this game since it was in early access, and the ability to hack this unpolished turd is becoming easier every week.
I wish I could check the "received this product for free box" so it would be easier to forget I spent five dollars on a hackfest. Thanks for reading my second review :D

gameplay is pretty straight foward. only problem is that unless you're using a controller. the controls can be tedious to go through. the game can be quite criptic on whats going. and you'll be lost most of the time as to where you need to go.  you got 8 classes to choose from and ech of them come with their own set of stats and loadouts. you also have the choice to choose your starter gift aswell.
The most important thing to keep notice on is your stamina bar. this thing depletes on everything you're doing. from swinging your weapon or using your bow to sprinting, blocking and rolling. is always best to play it safe while going up aginst an enemy as you're gonna be constantly ambushed and damaged by them. luckily all hope isnt lost yet. you do have a Estus Flask wich serves as a free health potion. should the flask get emptied out theres usually life gems for ya as an alternetive. although limited they can come in handy for those intense moments were using a flask would be too risky since using it forces the player to stand absolutly still.
Bonfires in general serves as your typical safe zone. resting refills your health aswell as your flask, cures any status elements and refreshes your item abilities. only bad part is everytime you revisit one all the enemies respawn. I've also heard that bonfires let you level up your stats in the first Dark souls game. unfortanetly that feature have moved to a certain character in your sanctuary called "Majula" wich means that whenever you feel the need to level up your character you have to travel back in order to do so.
Speaking of stats. holy crap theres alot to take in here. you got your left handed stats, right handed stats and your main stats. and lets not forget theres even stats for the amount of gear your character can wear.
It may seem like alot of things to read through but do not worry since most of those numbers are easy to go through
(I mean look at this! You have already read through most of this reveiw lol)
Should certain stats seem too confusing theres a button that explains ech stat for you and what their function is. you have tons of weapons and armor that you can find throughout your journy. ech comming with their own weight. having too much weight on your character and you'll walk around slower then the main protagenist from Fallout and it'll even drain your stamina much quicker.
Since we talked about stats and level lets bring out the main currency in this game, souls. You get souls from anything you kill. bosses themselves even have special souls wich gives you a high amounts of currency.
When you visit Majula theres either a blacksmith, merchant or the herold aka the lady that lets you level up. theres also a cat (yes this is a thing...) who sells you special items, like a ring that helps you connect to people easier if you worship the same god.
Oh yeah, theres multiplayer in this game. most of the time you're not exacly gonna see anybody.
But from time to time you'll witness ghosts of other players. theres sometimes even layed out messages from them that either gives you good advice, or just random and sometimes bad advice. theres even bloodstains that lets you witness othe player's deaths, giving you insight of what could have happend in the area you're in.
You can however summon a player into Your world by using one of the glowing signs found on the ground. the summoned player becomes a Phantom when entering your world and its up to them to help you find and defeat the boss. You can also become one by laying out a sign aswell using a Soapstone. This can sometimes become a bit complicated should you and your friend decide to do a coop playthrough together. since the connectivity requires one another to have a certain amount of collected souls shown in their stats.
Buuuuuut besides all of that hows the Combat? well the combat itself is pretty alright. a bit repeatitive, I say this since I find myself mostly just cyrcling around the enemies until they stop or finish attacking. a somewhat simple but certain times, challanging thing to do while facing off multiple enemies at once.
Most enemies dont exacly change their behavier some may have a few tricks up their sleeves but other then that often they will just charge at the player most of the time, attack a few times and then stop. giving the player the time to strike. dosnt sound much but just the idea that one wrong move can cost you half if not most of your health is just nervewrecking.
But if the enemies werent challenging enough for you then wait til you get to one of the bosses. Holy ♥♥♥♥ing♥♥♥♥♥♥ these bosses man! They dont mess around. even the second boss screwed me over multiple times as I had to waste several human effigies and souls just to beat him. its gonna feel unfair, you will get angry yes, but the feeling after beating one of them is O-so-satisfying! and it gives off the feel of wanting to face off the next boss suprisingly.
PROS
Rich lore, great enemy and character design. beautiful enviroments to go through. pretty good boss battles. lets you build your character however you want.
CONS
Repeatitive combat. certain moments can feel unfair and unforgivable. comparing the levels to Dark souls 1. not that many veriaties to look foward to. game can be very vague on what to do and where to go.
I'd say Dark souls in general is really good. its pretty much the third person game of ghost n goblins. or the Cuphead of difficulty :P

A game that traverses the outlaw legend of the old west, through the story of its lead character, Silas Greaves.
Off the bat I will say its a good game, it has everything you may possibly want for a quick and entertaining experience.
The graphics are very nice, in style somewhat reminiscent of Borderlands, but better. The scenery from the old west countryside is gorgeous & the towns are well made and feel authentic.
The variety of guns is limited and the different models seem to make very little difference.
There is also limited variety as far as enemies go, Cowboys and in a few cases Indians, plus all the unique characters you will meet (and have to kill) - as in all the known outlaws of the old west.
Unfortunately variety is the least of the problem here as it seems like there is zero AI involved in these enemies... (all of them follow the same patterns, either they just hide and shoot - in timed intervals, or they just stand there and shoot - ok one or two types just move forward towards you... but there doesn't seem to be even the attempt at variation of behavior).
There is a slight RPG element in that you gain levels where you can unlock various skills. While a nice idea, it is so basic, I honestly feel it makes no difference, regardless which abilities you choose (this might be more important at higher dificulty levels).
Still.. the rpg junkie in me enjoys leveling up, so I liked the concept, just don't expect much from it.
My biggest beef is the linearity of the game, it seems impossible to stray from the one and only path of the game. With the exception of deciding whether to use the left or right tunnel, there is very little choice (and mind you both tunnels always lead to the same place).
You get no choice where and whom to pursue and you have very few options regarding how you do it. In a couple of occasions you can choose your approach to a building but thats as far as it gets.
Apart from the scenery change, most stages consist of the same motif, you move till you are ambushed by a few enemies, you kill them and move on the next ambush and so on, although there are some very nice touches that connect the story in between such encounters.
As far as combat goes its fun, a lot of shooting, plenty of ammo, non stop head shots, blood splattering... what more could you ask for.
The narrative can become long and boring at times, but on the other hand it keeps the game together.
Each chapter is a stage you have to go through (in linear fashion), some stages are very short and some are simply short, but none would even qualify as medium sized.
Still... the game is fun...
I played it at normal difficulty and it was kind of not challenging at all (with the exception of a few boss fights - and I am not sure even if those would qualify as challenging).
So, do I recommend the game ? Sure do, because even with all its faults, it is a darn fun game. I played through it and had fun, no regrets for wasting a few hours of my life whatsoever. However I doubt I will ever revisit it , even at a higher difficulty mode because I don't think it has something to offer me.
Depending on the time you have available, expect to spend a day or two in it, having fun and living the legend!!! Just dont expect something more from the game... I was actually hoping for much more (given all the positive reviews and press) and even though I was disappointed in that sense, the game was still fun.

This is a reluctant, perhaps backhanded, recommendation, no scratch that. I don't recommend this game, UNLESS you really enjoyed The Longest Journey's plot/world. I'm not really going into the plot, visuals, voice acting, except to say I really wasn't taken with them so much. As a continuation of The Longest Journey, it is definitely satisfying to revisit the world and check in with the various characters from the original, but this is in spite of the rest of the game.
First, there's combat, and it's bad. It's awkward as hell, it plays sort of like a bad minigame from Final Fantasy or something.  Basically it tries to be Rock Paper Scissors with very silly looking animations: fast attacks beat strong attacks, strong attacks beat blocks, blocks beat fast attacks, and circling beats. Enemies only ever approach one at a time, and the whole thing just comes off as a stupid, tedious affair. Not really difficult to deal with, but there was no reason to include it, or implement in the way they did. It takes away much more than it adds.
Next there are stealth sections, and they're also pretty terrible. Your character has a 'stealth mode' for movement, which is frustratingly slow. It's not required on every stealth section, but the game doesn't do all that much to indicate to you when you need it and when you don't. Patrols and security are very simple, and these sections are once again pretty tedious. I don't really feel like they added anything much to the game, and the world would be better off if they were handled more like point and click puzzles where once a solution is found you don't have to continue sighing and playing around whatever issue.
Then there are the item puzzles, which weren't all bad, but lots of obnoxious back tracking which just wastes time(really missing the ability to skip time from the first one). A couple also weren't very intuitive and of course there's the song cave puzzle which gives no hints whatsoever basically forcing you to bruteforce a 4 point permutation (or look it up because who can be asked). Basically every other puzzle in the game is: use your phone on X, use the one item other than your phone you have in your inventory, talk to that person again. I never really felt challenged, but I was a bit annoyed. Seriously, I've played first person shooters with harder puzzles.
And, guess what? The plot ends on a cliffhanger. Very disappointing. Conversation options don't really seem to matter either, that's kinda okay I can understand not wanting to bother with branching story, but the choice doesn't matter if the outcome is the same.
If they refined the above sections this game could've been like Beyond Good and Evil, well maybe it could've been. Everything about this game just felt like a half-hearted attempt, and I'd give it a half-hearted recommendation except that's really not a recommendation is it?

cheap makeshift ways to gain the ability of having ranged without having to farm too much at the cost of not dealing a great amount of damage.
just some small examples of things that could have a large impact on both immersion and gameplay.
only balancing can decide how good it would actually be.

The Room is a pure puzzle game.  The game was originally released for tablet, but was ported to the PC with superior graphics.  The Room has players work through a hundred or so thought-provoking puzzles surrounding a series of puzzle-boxes, vaguely reminiscent of the Hellraiser movie series. The game is not of the horror genre, but does produce a slightly unnerving and eerie atmosphere.
Unlike most puzzle games, The Room has very few, if any, puzzles that are unintuitive.  Progression is based almost entirely on one's attention to detail.  A full play-through will bring about 5 hours of entertainment.  Full-price on steam at $5, it is worth purchase for puzzle-fans, and definitely worth it for under $2.50 on steam sale.  It notable that The Room 2 is available on tablet, but has not been ported to the PC.  Apparently it will be ported if PC sales of The Room are sufficient.

To put summarize that part, the story, art, and music all are engaging and beautiful enough in their own right.
The atmosphere works well with the combat system, which can switch between a meter based planning stage, or a top down point and shoot. Both work and you will probably find yourself using both. It really creates just a wonderful pace with the encounter based combat. As well as damage penalties and how those pertain to changing play style it is really well put together in terms of design choices.
As far as difficulty, you could struggle to recover from mistakes time to time, but if you think things through it is pretty easy to deal with most of the time. However, if you want more of a challenge the game gives you the option to turn on difficulty increasers, that do things such as make enemies have a better chance to revive after you kill them or have certain enemies doubled in an encounter, or the classic hit twice as hard. This is aviable before you even need to make a New Game+ (which is an option) and gives you an experience boost.
All in all, I think it is a beautifully designed game in terms gameplay and enviroment, and the two dont feel very seperate. The only critizism I could give it would be calling it too short but I think I am very happy with the length, as I never once felt bored, or needing to grind. The pacing from start to end was fantastic and I am not sure if a longer game could've kept that.

When I played, it was easy to lose myself in the game's world.

Also, make absolutely sure your system meets the recommended settings. It was unplayably laggy on my system which barely met the minimum, so I had to wait for the Mac version.
But it was well worth the wait. Pick up the soundtrack, too if you can. No fade-outs. Lovely.

Reign of Kings is an interesting game. One I'll never forget, for sure. Any time I'm playing... really any other game, I always arrive at a similar thought about a feature in this game that no other game that I'VE played seems to have.
Captives/Prisoners.
Obviously it's never enjoyable to be hogtied by a nude man weilding a lasso and then thrown in a cage only to be forgotten until you die and rot in a crude prison... But it is enjoyable and satisfying beyond belief when there's that one far-too-annoying player or group that we have ALL seen at one time or another that you finally get the opportunity to tie them up and keep them around as ornaments on your property for all to see that may travel by.
A word from the wise... always keep at least one sharpened rock in your "oriface slot".
That being said, the PvP is difficult to cope with sometimes. Sometimes the game can't seem to track your hits or even keep up with all the movement of battle. Momentary hang-ups, misses that went through the body, misplaced hit tracking, etc. All things to expect from every fight. The most frequent being the 1 or 2 second "pause" in combat. You can still swing for the person but it's as if the server has stopped tracking everything and time has stopped around you, then it returns to normal and retracks all of the hits during the "pause" and instantly kills someone.
Frustrating when you're dealing with someone weilding the King's sword.
All in all, I'd give this game... a 6 out of 10.
If you want the most bang for your buck on this game, buy it on sale like I and my friends did. It's a good game that brought lots of fun and laughs to us but you'd get the most out of it by spending a little less than what they are charging.

I may only have played 51 hours but I feel like I can make at least a small review on how I feel about the game so far.

It does however offer a large and well built world with a large amount of stuff to do.  I play it along side eve online and it's been keeping me more then entertained and in the early levels doesn't take to much concentration so that I can't also pay attention to farming eve. ( It also plays well with other games running, and snaps nicely to one side something a lot of games don't even program in).
It runs well, so far the only issues I've had are loading screens that don't end. But just reset and it fixes it.  It jumps sometimes with frames if I'm using more then a single game at once but it tend to hover around 30-40fps if I am, if not I get 90+ at 2k resolutions ultra on a 980m.
Gameplay seems fun and varied between the classes, and the elder scrolls world offers a large variety of enemies npc's to   fight. Being elder scrolls things are instantly recognizable from the previous games in the series. It's nice to join an MMO where you kind of all ready know the lore, and background to the regions in the game. And being as the games got cosole versions, it comes with a rather decent controller mode that works almost as good as the mouse and keyboard and is sorely lacking in a lot of MMO's.
Being as I'm still in the early game content, it's not a full review. I'll come back to the review at a later date when I've gotten at least one character at the games highest level. So far the oly gripe I have about this game is how much it throws its Crown store and it's Microtransaction currency crowns in your face every chance they get. For a pay to play game, with a subscription model for those who want an improved experience/more content the random number generater microtransactions seem overly greedy and IMO lessons the experience and trully makes the world seem like nothing more then a theme park.  Breaking the overall immersion.
It's kind of a disapointment to see them go the way of the randomized loot box/card system junk, and a secondary in game currency you have to pay real world money to obtain, that mobile games have made so prevelent. I don't play mobile games due to their horrible designs based around their stupid monitization skeem. And to see it in a game I had to actually pay for makes me think twice about purchasing future titles by this developer.  Or any developer that thinks their game needs a lootbox/cardpack system to monitize. It's boring, preditory and far too many games do it and I'm sick of seeing it.

A very stylish Sci-Fi Noire-ish game about a strange and somewhat utopian city, "Cloudbank", falling to an epidemic/invasion of some kind, "The Process". The protagonist, a famous musician of the city called "Red", vanishes after one of her stage acts and finds herself right in the middle of the city's demise. The game drops you into a scene with Red pulling a tool resembling an oversized sword from someone's body, which is accompanying and talking to her and which narrates many of her actions and compensates for the city having "taken" Red's voice, who herself is mostly silent. With this tool, the "Transistor", you fight your way through the declining urban environment to the source of this epidemic trying to save the city.
The game is short, but very impressive. The art design feels special and there is some pretty cool music. Cloudbank is a rather mysterious city/town, the game isn't straightforward with what world, place or time you are exactly finding yourself in. The "traces" of former certain city inhabitants absorbed by the Transistor to power your abilites while handling it in combat (fitting to their stories and roles within the city) give you hints to events predating Red's disappearance and are interesting to read - but overall the game loves leaving you in a wondering position for many parts, which (in a good, engrossing way) mystifies the whole experience and leaves room for own interpretations, possibly even for pre-/sequels or novels or other things that would build on the strong lore pieces which are there (I believe I have noticed this in the devs previous title "Bastion" to some degree too, but to my knowledge it was never worked out further, whether that is good or bad I'm not sure).
Like "Bastion" this is a rather "soft" strategy action RPG in the way that you need to fight with some brains but not by being confused by millions of units and possible actions. You engage enemies with selective combat options organized at check-/savepoints, either in real-time or by utilizing a limited time-stopping/slowing planning feature. There are minor leveling elements and rather trivial but curious choices planted selectively throughout the city circling around some of its former daily routines and design questions (voting on things was popular among Cloudbank's citizens, it seems). Apparently, as a neat gimmick, the choices and a few other stats of the playerbase (like the kill count for each enemy type) are woven into this (or the game at least made me believe so). Maybe this could have been something to expend more, as it is effectively working into Cloudbank's digital and scientific ambience. You see the city through various stages of decline but without the levels building themselves up just before you (which I found somewhat irritating in Bastion), and without the "hit and run" concept of Bastion where you would often have a sanctuary to return to and select new levels to start from. This makes your journey feel a bit more like a real series of events rather than a level clearing maze, the city more persistent and you to be "actually there (as much as that is possible in this mysterious world). The narrator doesn't feel as annoying as the one in Bastion sometimes does, but maybe too distant - or even lethargic - at times. But this could be the idea of his role within the story. In general I was thankful to have him as my - or Red's - companion. However I would have loved to hear Red being properly voiced too I think. I'm not exactly the biggest fan of this "silent protagonist" concept. Here it feels rather fitting though as the whole game is strange in a good kind of way, and it allows some certain love of detail to shine more for example when Red is answering to news feeds and polls on public terminals and correcting her own sentences while being in the middle of typing them to the point where she may even give up hope for the city herself - a subtle but strong way of projecting the protagonist's emotions despite her voicelessness.
There is a little sandbox-like place in which you can practice combat and take part in some challenges. It's not as big as in Bastion, but I don't think it needs to be as it would probably only distract from the main experience. A new game will retain your level and abilites and ramp up the strength of the enemies accordingly. There are modifiers too - "limiters" - to make your enemies stronger and you level up faster, for an added challenge to whoever seeks it. That aside there doesn't seem any significant replay value, whether there are multiple endings I don't know yet. But the initial experience is an engaging and memoreable one, the game feels bold, thoughtful and determined and it's just impressive to see an apparent great vision turned so seemingly smoothly and confidently into a finished product that would very well deserve to be called a work of art.

► Game: Call of Juarez: Gunslinger
► Genre: Western, FPS, Action, Fast-paced
► Developer/Released: Techland/2013
► Rating: ■ ■ ■ ■ ■ ■ ■ ■ □ □ 8/10
▲ Pros:
- Great/funny plot that is told in a 'old-novel' style and that is worth paying attention as the game develops.
- Brings real characters and facts from the past.
- Well-designed enviroments, keeps you very immerse into the Old West world, bringing a lot of heat from the 'bang-bang' era.
- Very solid/easy gun handling and shooting, with some pratcie you'll beat every bad guy in a fast-paced way.
- Smooth graphics and soundtrack consistent with the western theme.
▼ Cons:
- Story could be a bit longer, besides the lack of weapons.
From the same team that made Dead Island & Dying Light, Call of Juarez: Gunslinger came as a notable kind of shooter that emerges you into the 'bang-bang' world and to fulfill that duty, brings many elements such as known characters from the past, e.g. Billy the Kid, Jessie James. It also has great soundtrack, history facts and curiosities concerning costumes and traditions from the old west.
You begin as Silas Greaves, a bounty hunter in a journey of revenge on those who hurted him in the past. His story is told in a 'old-novel' style, with images instead of the usual animated cutscenes, which makes it very interesting and unique. The game mechanics are very solid, gun handling and shooting works fine, and the AI isn't going to make you sweat hard, but I guess it's on purpose, since you wouldn't be able to take out as many bandits single handed in a realistic plot. In my opinion thats one of the things that makes this game good, the feeling of walking through the streets and saloons, pulling the trigger at anything that moves.
Like almost all games from these days, it has a ranking system that gives you points for leveling and let you spend them in many upgrades, focusing on three skill trees: Trapper (Shotguns), Ranger (Rifles) and Gunslinger (Revolvers). The game also has two game modes besides Story: Arcade and Duel. Both are worth playing after you finish the main story.

TLDR: I recommend and not recommend at the same time, see below.
After playing TLJ, it is clear that Dreamfall is a different game that "follows" the storyline of the former. I am quoting "follow" because the events take place 10 years after. However, the game feels very different both in gameplay and story, so I think it should be viewed as a standalone game.
Gameplay wise, it is fully 3D with heavy reliance on conversations. Not many puzzles that challenge your mind at all. Inventory is reduced to a minimum and normally you keep forward just by walking your way to your objectives (some running forth and back too). The game features stealth and combat, which is made in a poor fashion. Stealth mechanics are kind of ok, but forces you to press a key (def. key control) all the time, instead of just toggle stealth with a key. Probably one of the reasons playing this game with a keyboard can be punishing. Combat is just terrible, you just smash the button and attack. Luckily there isn't many combat. I can understand why they decided to put it in game, but the implementation really is terrible.
In terms of story, it is really complex, cryptic and creepy at times (character design, especially the faces contribute to that level of "creepyness"). Travelling through the two worlds, I found Stark to be more fun and interesting than Arcadia (this also happened to me for TLJ). After finishing the game you end up with hundreds of questions. The game story isn't closed and this can be frustrating.
Therefore, I can only recommend playing this game if you plan on playing Dreamfall: Chapters and you are interested in the story of these worlds (and wait for a sale ofc). If you liked TLJ only for the amazing point and click adventure game it was, you will be disappointed with Dreamfall.

This might have been okay for it's time, but the story was a bit boring most of the time or it wasn't immersive enough, and there was a lot of tedious running back and forth. Still good to know the story if you plan on playing Chapters, which is a much better experience.

Dreamfall: The Longest Journey (the sequel to The Longest Journey) is an adventure/puzzle/sort-of-actiony story-based game that tells the tale of two worlds colliding. The characters are interesting, the dialogue is well written and well acted, the graphics are good, and the UI has been completely overhauled - a huge improvement on the previous game in all ways.  It does expect the player to be familiar with terms and characters fromt he previous game, but I only played about halfway through the previous game and I wasn't too lost.
Dreamfall is the good kind of sequel: one that transcends the original and builds off its ideas without remaining shackled to old UI, graphics, and voice-acting. The only problem I have with the game is that combat is poorly implemented, clunky, and either too easy or too difficult, depending on the fight. Luckily, the combat sections are short and few, so that's not a dealbreaker.
If you've already played The Longest Journey, I heartily reccomend Dreamfall. If you don't want to deal with the previous game, you might want to read a quick summary first.
A strong example of the "Second Episode Syndrome" - but still a wonderful example of the genre.

The good: I found the puzzles a bit easier than in The Longest Journey (maybe that was just exposure though). I really liked the story - on par with The Longest Journey. The main character is great, and it is a fun game to play. Overall, I would highly recommend it, especially if you like games with lots of cool female characters and ones that are highly story driven.

Everything you may hear about this game is true.
Yes, it's buggy.
Yes, it has some bad or lazy translations.
Yes, it has tons of bots that sometimes annoy you when trying to farm.
Yes, it has tons of grinding.
But I haven't had as much fun in a long time.
This game features a complex class system, allowing 4 main classes to branch out into almost 70 classes to customize your playstyle. It encourages making alts to explore all these classes and provides the tools for it.
Cash shop focuses on cosmetics, consumables like EXP tomes and megaphones (you still get free premium currency that caps at 5 but regenerates overtime, so you can always buy megaphones and talk in server chat without having to pay) and some gacha items that bring new costumes, potions, materials, pets and other stuff into the game, all of which are nice to have but not necessary, so it's not P2W in any sense.
Quests can be a little generic but it has great storyline for those interested in storytelling. You aren't forced to do them but doing so grants you some nifty bonuses and starting gear for each step of leveling.
PVP can be done through open-world duels, arena matches 3v3, 5v5 and open-world GvG. But having 60+ classes makes it hard to balance perfectly, so there will always be dominant classes (classes with tier 2 CC or higher dominate).
Events are added in maintenance periods and they last for 1-2 weeks. Some of these are new gacha items or daily events that award you costumes or helpful consumables, including enchant scrolls and EXP boosts.
Despite having a bad reputation for the way problems were handled in the past, I think this game has started to pick up, fixing and improving an ever-changing game.

Rock of Ages is a mix between racing Super Monkey Ball-style down a track to break your opponent's gate, and tower defense to set up defenses to prevent your opponent from doing the same.
It's a very whimsical game, with cutscenes reminiscent of Monty Python and a presentation to match. It's got a great charm and even if you don't like history too much, it will bring a smile to your face.
The gameplay is actually pretty simple, but executed well. Although the rolling is kind of stiff, the boulder doesn't feel out of your control (unless you hit an explosive barrel or get shot by a catapult), and has a good sense of speed. The defense phase (while waiting for a new boulder to be prepped) is alright but it feels somewhat arbitrary, since it's difficult to tell how well your defenses are working.
Overall, this game has style, and the gameplay is pretty enjoyable. It's quite cheap and worth checking out!

If Marble Madness were made by Monty Python, this would be the delightful result.
It may look like a goofy indie game - and let's be clear, it absolutely is - but that by no means makes Rock of Ages a bad game. There's action, strategy, comedy and a bombastic classical soundtrack that brilliantly complements the zany nature of the game.
Rolling a giant rock around breaking physics objects could not be more satisfying.

First of all, let me state this: World of Goo is a classic among indie games. 2D BOY, the studio responsible for its creation, has crafted something incredibly imaginative, fascinatingly fun and spectacularly simplistic back in 2008. World of Goo is, simply put, one of the most unique and enjoyable experiences one can have. The gameplay is easy-to-learn yet utterly adictive. (And for all the completionists out there, you'll be pleasantly surprised to discover that the achievements are rather hard to obtain.) The game's design is eternally elegant, the graphics are glorious and – what surprised me even more – the story is staggeringly thoughtful, drawing numerous parallels  between our world and, you guessed it, the world of goo. If you reflect on what is being said (or rather being written by the "Sign Painter") it is positively possible that the game will leave you in a state of peculiar wonder. That, and many other of its aspects only further prove one very important thing: that World of Goo has aged incredibly well.
TO SUM UP: Whether you like games that force you to think a bit while playing them or whether you'd just like to experience an undying classic of independent gaming, World of Goo is the right place to go. So do not hesitate for a second. Just buy it.

Call of Juarez Gunslinger is a fun western/cowboy themed arcade style game. This is the first western/cowboy type game I've played and I enjoyed it quite a bit. It has a distinct visual style in that the game looks like a painting more than computer generated graphics. It's quite scenic. There were times when I just stopped to admire the view.
Since it's set in the old west, the type of guns available is limited. You get a rifle, 3 different types of revolvers, and shotguns and that's it. This is not a bad thing though. The gunplay feels quite good. I mostly stuck with the rifle as it was my favorite. It has quite a bit of recoil so you need to be careful while aiming because if you miss, you lose a lot of time. You can't spray and pray like in modern shooters. Again, it's not a bad thing. Since there are no scopes to help you aim, lending a headshot feels really satisfying.
The main story isn't continuous and so your guns and ammo aren't carried forward to your next mission. Basically the entire game is flashback. The protagonist is telling his stories of derring do in a bar and you get to play those stories. There are three types of gameplay modes: first is the main story. 2nd is arcade where you have to carry out certain tasks such as get from point A to point B and killing anyone you encounter or to survive waves of enemies. The third one is my least favorite - duels. You have to keep the mouse cursor pointed at your enemy to increase concentration and then when the time is right, shoot. It has very little to do with FPS.
My only criticism is that the game is too short. I finished the story in about 7 hours and I played it in a leisurely fashion, taking my time to explore.
Overall it's a good game and I recommend it, especially if you like western/cowboy style games.

My parents came to America from Cuba as children back in the 1960's, so we talk about Communism a lot. One particular story my mom brings up is how she had a brand new story book that my grandfather bought her to read as entertainment on the long plane ride and a watch to keep as a memento of her country she was now abandoning. The customs official confiscated both FOR THE REVOLUTION!!! and let them leave with only one suitcase each. It was weird playing that jerk for this game, but my family said the atmosphere was correct. They were just confused how this is a game about people going IN to a Communist country instead of breaking down the door to get OUT! Enough personal stuff, to the game itself.
Positive:
-Suprising amount of choice in the game. Are you a corrupt official taking bribes from criminals and terrorists? Are you a noble patriot helping refugees and resistance fighters? Or are you souless automaton only following regulations?
-Good replay value with lots of endings except they can be boiled down to just being variations of Three major endings.
-The game is hard in a good way. Gets your brain working overdrive as you have check every tiny detail of multiple documents in only 10 seconds.
-The atmosphere of oppression is well made with dark depressing colors and communist iconagraphy.
Negative:
-The story is a little thin, but I think they squeezed out as much as they could given the game's structure.
-Some people might be turned off by the graphics, but its reasonable given the price range.

This game is way more fun than it should be. Players take on the role of an immigration worker, checking passports and other paperwork at the border of a fictional country called Arstotzka. Your job is to make sure their paperwork is in order, and either let them pass into Arstotzka or turn them away. While this may sound like a simple, boring concept, it quickly becomes quite difficult, and the story kept me intrigued enough to keep playing long after it should have gotten boring. Players must balance duty with morality, while trying to bring in enough money to take care of the worker's starving, sick and cold family. Terrorists strike, family members die, and all along the way you must perform your job or risk being terminated. The simplistic 8-bit style graphics are not distracting: actually, they seem to add to the dreary, mundane atmosphere, allowing you to more fully immerse yourself in the dystopian world. There is a bit of comic relief (GLORY TO COBRASTAN!!!) but even with the minor comic relief, this game is dark and depressing in the most perfect way. It really makes the player think about society and political problems in a communist state, bringing up deep questions about humanity under the guise of a simple game. Definitely a must-play.

you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if you're looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

RECOMMENDED - If you like total puzzle games.
The Room has 5 chapters, each with a tonne of small puzzles to figure out. None are particularly difficult; focused more on looking around the subject (an intricate box, basically).
I only completed the first two chapters, due to the whole game up to that point being centered around the same subject matter. There was no real story and while the puzzles were quite fun, there were far too many little fiddly 'puzzles' in each sector of each chapter for it to hold my attention. I didn't know where the game was going or what the point of it all is.
If there were 3 chapters, or if each chapter didn't have quite as many puzzles in, I feel the game would still hold the same value but have presented itself more efficiently. At the end of the day it's only going to take a couple of hours to work through anyway, what does it matter if it loses 20 minutes of the more pointless puzzles.
However I recommend this game because the general quality is high, the puzzles on the whole are interesting but not too challenging and some of the mechanisms are very intricate. If you're interested in this type of game then I'm sure you'll have a blast.

The Room is a clever observational puzzle game with creepy atmosphere and detailed visuals. It's satisfying to put all the pieces together, but frustrating when you miss something that you know must be right in front of you...

TL;DR: Do you want a mindless games that will help you to unload all the stress you have accumulate during the day. Just buy this game, you will have quite of bit of fun with a simple and straight game that don’t requires you to think at all.
Are you looking for a game that will keep you occupied with a deep story and an amazing system? Don’t buy this game at all.
Tip: Even if the game has got a lot of positive reviews don’t buy it at full price, is not worth it at all.
So…we all know that alcohol usually helps to be honest and sincere and speak straight about facts that REALLY HAPPENED indeed. That’s what this game is all about: a guy simply destroyed by pain, revenge and indeed his whisky jar. That’s why I recommend you before playing to fill your desk with bottle of beers, vodka or your favorite alcohol to drink while you are playing so you can actually REALLY IMMERSE yourself into gameplay.
Even if this game has got a story mode it’s just a simple point-shoot-reload arcade game. Yes you can move around the map and find some lore here and there (collectables) but that’s all. There are no enigmas, no keys to find, no hard objectives to do to go on with the story.
The fun is indeed guaranteed not only from the gameplay itself but mostly from the narration; it is very funny and it is probably the best thing in this game. You will be the narrator of your own story, as I mentioned before, a man that is looking to have his revenge and he’s willing to kill an army to satisfy this.
With every boss you will find the game will give you a “taste” of what the old west was….DUELS…and this is another good and fun thing about this game. You will have to focus on your enemy (by aim at him) and be fast (by keeping your hand near your gun) to win.
There isn’t a big choice of weapons but who doesn’t love to have double pistols or double shotguns?
During the game you can earn XP points that you can use to unlock particular abilities but again, nothing of really special. Some of them are just satisfying….a lot (like the ones that makes you multiply the dynamite….for more BOOM BOOM BOOM effects)
There are other two modes in this game:
Arcade: 10 maps where you have to simply kill everyone (quite boring after a while….the enemies will always spawn in the same areas and do always the same stuff….but…yeah its arcade mode)
Duel: 15 Duels to win and you have only 5 lives
This game is really missing a multiplayer mode or at least a Co-Op mode. This could help the game to be more fun and actually to stay alive a bit more after you have finished it. But like this in 20/25 hours you could be able to finish the game at 100% and that’s all…it really doesn’t have any replayability value.
Overall:
Graphics: 8/10
Sounds: 8/10
Longevity: 7/10
Fun/Gameplay: 9/10

Call of Juarez: Gunslinger is a great game. Go buy it!
Not convinced yet? Stick along, I'll promise to keep it short :)
In a time where wild west games are a dime a dozen, this one takes the cake.
You take on the role of a bounty hunter named Silas Greaves (voiced by John Sygan), a very likable character. On his quest you'll meet tons of historical old west figures, like Billy the Kid for instance. He tells his story and you play it.
Though not all portrayed historically accurate, the game gives its own twist to it which makes it refreshing, though sometimes this can lead to some odd happenings. You'll know what I mean when you get there.
For the most part the story is pretty good.
The voiceacting is pretty good. Silas definitely takes the cake, but some of the side characters are pretty memorable, too.
Levels are linear, which is a bit of a downside. There are some instakill sections and invisible walls aswell. There are collectibles in each level that tell the real story of the old west though I found these are pretty much copy pastes from Wikipedia.
The graphics are very nice and despite that the game runs well on lower end systems. They went with a very stylized look which I love. The cutscene work is awesome for the most part, though near the end it seems they are much less detailed.
The outdoor areas and skyboxes look stunning.
The game/gunplay is your typical FPS, with regenerating health and quicktime events. The guns don't sound all that meaty and lots of the weapons have animation errors, but this is a minor problem. The gameplay overall is very fluid.
The game consists of episodes, with each episode ending in a bossfight. This can either be a duel or a regular "tanky boss in arena" fight. Both have their problems and you will probably die a lot fighting the bosses on your first run, which kinda sucks.
Overall the game is short, around 6-7 hours, but for the price you get enough bang for your buck. Besides the story you also have a duels mode in which you can duel all the bosses from the game. Next to that there is also the arcade mode, in which you have to score as many points as possible. Both the duels and arcade will yield a few good hours of fun.
The soundtrack is awesome. it has this western metal theme and it when playing under the action it fits right in.
That wraps up my review for Call of Juarez: Gunslinger. I can recommend this game to both western and FPS fans. Go buy it, you won't regret it!

There was a variety of gods to choose from and wasnt to hard to grind for them, or you could get all and all future gods for 30 bucks, which isnt as much as other games *cough* league.
Fast forward a few years and now you have new smite, released on smite. This game feels much like league now in updates, changing almost all the items completely, map, and many other things. Pros

>It's constantly updated, they keep up with the graphics, updating gods, and keeping it nice and clean, and also balancing the game.
>The game for the most part is quite balanced, still a few gods there and there, but its not a mess.
Cons.

Played since beta and am diamond 5 to diamond 2 in ranked conquest since season 2.  Therefor this review is biased from a ranked players perspective.
HIGH SKILL CAP
If you're looking to dedicate alot of time and crush other players then this game has that to offer.  Skilled players are rewarded and it feels good outplaying the opposing team.  Mechanically gifted players will definately thrive here.  The macro game is important, but ultimately when both teams are tied, the team with the best mechanical skill will usually come out on top.
COMMUNITY
It's a moba.  You know what to expect from other players.  Other than the usual f*ckboys and trolls that litter all mobas. the community is pretty great.  Smite playerbase is small compared to in competitors so you'll occasionally queue into the same people if you play enough.  HiRez is also very strict with behavior in games, you will be banned if you consistenly get reported, afk, harass, or just overall f*ckboyness.
GODS (heroes)
There are currently around 80+ gods available for purchase right now.  With new gods revealed every 4 weeks approximately.  Gods are divided into 1 of 5 archetypes; Warrior, Guardian, Assassin, Mage, or Hunter.  Gods are incredibly varied from one another allowing for a ton of different strategies and team comps.  There are only about few gods that are unplayable in high level ranked due their kits just not being able to compete.  But more importantly there are no gods that feel unstoppable or/and unfair.  Great balance overall.
Great game.  HiRez studio definately hit it out of the park and striving for a better and better game.

It's pretty fun, nothing groundbreaking in the MMORPG genra but definetly a very good entry into it that's worth checking out.
The negative reviews the game has is mostly due to two things,due to the large 80GB size and the fact a lot of people who got ESO never played an MMO before and thought this was just Skyrim but online.
Now onto the review :
The most note worthy thing that sets it apart from most MMORPGs is the fact the combat is rather active, there's dodge rolling with iframes,blocking,timing certain spells to stun someone, it requires you to actually aim to a certain degree and attack on your own [no auto attack], the movement feels good and responsive due to the emphasis of actually having to do more then just spam hotkeys like in a lot of MMORPGs,HP and Mana regenerate so it's more about managing what spells to use and not spaming too much during a fight [since during combat it regenerates far slower, thought there's potions you can use],there's also a decent stealth mechanic where you can rob merchants by pickpocketing or lockpicking their chest and to a degree you can stealth some parts of a quest. Overall, i think they really did a great job with the combat in this game.
Visualy it looks pretty good for an MMORPG and has some really nice facial animations, frame rate depands on the area if i'm around a place with a ton of players like a capital city then it's usually holding around 45-60fps while everywhere else it hits 100 on max visuals but view distance set to 60/100.
[i5 4670k 4.0 Ghz, RX 580 8GB, 16GB DDR3 RAM]
The world you get to explore can in some areas feel a tad empty, thought in most cases it feels populated with a decent/good amount of things to do and discover, it's a bit of weaker point of the game however it's still better then some other MMORPGs but it does get overshadowed by like Guild Wars 2's exploration and public events.
Quests so far from the time i spent have felt pretty fun to do, some of em' are the usual generic MMORPGs quests just with some actuall more proper voice acted story behind them but most quests have felt like something along the lines you'd get in an Elder Scrolls game, it's a very mixed bag of standard Elder Scrolly quests with MMO quests, you can tell on which ones they put more effort in [the ones that feel more like Elder Scrolly] and which ones they kinda half-a*sed and just exist to fill in the gaps by just being "Kill X amount and collect Y". A few quests even offer choices which can change the ending of a quest or even some of the objectives in it which is nice. Sadly the 'public' events are rather lackluster, before ESO i played GW2 for a few months when it launched some years ago and that game probably still has the best public events in MMORPGs that actually offered some really good loot reward and crazy fun fights to participate in, in ESO calling them events would maybe be a bit too kindly really, there's so few and they're just really kinda meh with the content they offer.
Dungeons are your standard MMORPG thing, you go through a dungeon with a 4 player group, each picks what their job is "Healer,Tank,DPS" via the dungeon finder and then you just clear rooms filled with tons of adds and a couple of beefy bosses that have unique mechanics, especially DLC bosses which are pretty interesting to fight. There's story elements in them with characters talking and even some scripted stuff happening but don't expect randoms to stick around listening to how the story unfolds, you'll have to group up with friends if you wish to experience that better if you care about story content. The vanila dungeons are not all that difficult however be carefull venturing into the DLC ones since those can kick your a** really hard when you're new and yes there are raids [Trials] which support 12 players.
There's no global player market, instead all you can do is trade gear you got from a dungeon with the three other people you were grouped with or join player made trading guilds which often ask of you to do things for the guild [like sell 20k at least] to keep your stay which just feels kind of a hassle to be able to sell gear drops or materials you don't need, ESO should've simply had a global player market where you put stuff on sale and or buy. You can join regular guilds but trading via them is of course not as nearly as effective as they often have next to no traders around.
Classes in the game don't fully dictate what role you'll have, they give you three categories that have spells specifically tied to them but you if you wanna, you can be a sorcerer who uses melee weapons, it's not really the smartest combo but the game allows you to do stuff like that, kinda well like in a regular Elder Scrolls,it lets you mish mash all sorts of combinations and doesn't tie the player down to one bog standard role, you're free to be whatever it is but of course there's certain combos which are simply the smarter choice to go with. You can be a plate wearing magic wielding sorcerer with a bow, it'll probably be fine enough for regular questing but don't be surprised if you try to do some of the more difficult activaties and have people looking confused at you as to what you're doing since you won't be very effective in the group.
PVP is something i never had any interest much in MMORPGs, bearly ever spent time PVPing in WOW, Guild Wars 2 or any other MMORPG i played since i usually don't find that aspect all that enjoyable in those games so i can't comment on the PVP in ESO all that much, however a lot of people say ESO PVP is pretty well done. I did try it  with a guild i joined and it simply isn't for me, just not a fan of how PVP works in MMORPGs, with your pve characters being kinda useless in them and it requires you to pretty much make a seperate PVP focused character by following a guide/meta build.
There are microtransactions which sucks but it was the way for em' to remove the monthly sub that was required to play it before when it launched, a monthly sub still exists but it is not required to play, the monthly sub gives you crowns to spend in the microtransaction store, a 10% XP boost, more bag space,a VERY usefull crafting bag for materials and all of the current DLCs to play [not expansions, just the smaller DLCs], the microtransactions are almost cosmetic only, some stuff can give you special healing potions that are better or a short buff to your HP,mana and stamina but it's nothing too crazy and almost all of it really is just cosmetics.
RNG drops could use some slight fine tuning, perhaps increase the chances to drop gear we don't have yet, often makes me wish more that the game had a simple global trade market to make selling unwanted mats and gear easy. However the actual loot you get is pretty well done, some sets offer some interesting gameplay styles or weird new elements which you can build upon.
The game overall feels like a good combo of Elder Scrolls and an MMORPG, i and probably many others would've liked if it pushed even more towards Elder Scrolls elements but it has enough of em' to warrant the Elder Scrolls name. It's often pretty cheap during sales, i got it for 9.99 and later on even bought the DLC packs, i even got a month of ESO+ for some of the benefits since i'm now finding myself playing the game every day for a somewhat unhealthy amount of hours, how long this new lil' addiction will last for me i don't know.
There are some MMORPGs out there that do things kinda better but ESO is still a fantastic choice , it has the best combat of any MMORPG imo,but i do wish they expand more upon public events and explorationr, thankfully regular questing is done pretty well with only some feeling like mmo style filler and dungeons are well made. I happily recommend giving it a shot during a sale, might be the next MMO that'll suck you in, it sure got me.

PRO'S:
- Very Good and Dynamic PVP Mode (One of the best features in the game)
- Hundreds of Hours of PVE content in Base Game (Not Including DLC, Which add even more Content)
- Very Good Graphics for an MMO with post processing effects (Godrays, ambient Occlusion, etc)
- No Subscription Required
- Very Good Character Creation system, highly detailed
- No Class is weaker or stronger, they all have pro's and con's that balance them out
- Classes do not restrict gameplay as in most other MMO's, if you are Dragon Knight (AKA the Warrior/Tank) You can play the game with a Magic Staff and Robes. Play the way you want to play
- The crafting system isn't to much of a grind to level up and they are all equally fun to use
CON'S:
- The game is litered with Microtransactions and Loot Boxes. As a catch for the no subscription required model. Though they are mostly cosmetic, if you are into those things prepare to empty your wallets for that sweet Robe and Bear Mount
- Players who pay subscription get many benefits that can turn the tide in PVP, as every month they get free crowns (the in game currency used to buy DLC and Microtransactions) and can buy poisons and potions exclusive to the "Crown Store". This gives them a huge advantage in 1v1 PVP or even 1v2 PVP Combat.
- The DLC pricing is to much for most players to afford. The way it works is:
Dungeon DLC = $15 (2 - 3 hours of content)
New Zone DLC = $20 - $25 (20 hours of Content)
Chapters (AKA Full on Expansion Packs) = $40 - $50 (30 Hours of Content)
This system is very overpriced for the content you recieve especially compared to World of Warcraft where Dungeon DLC is released more often and is a free update. And Expansion Packs are only $20 - $30 instead.
Overall I had a great time with this Game and recommend it to any MMO lover. But the DLC is way overpriced and I think it should be much cheaper, and Dungeon DLC should be like WOW and just be free. And those buffs and debuffs in the crown store need to be removed.
