So, this game is amazing. I can't recommend it enough, and I urge everyone who is interested in PVE-focused MMO's to try it out. They even have a free trial, so it costs nothing if you don't like it (even though I bet you will like it). To address the complaints of having a monthly expansion: any games of this size and structure require some sort of reliable income to keep the game running. Servers are expensive, and they are constantly adding new content (dungeons, quests, etc.) through free updates to the game.
Pros:
- Beautiful environment and world
- Amazing music
- Being able to be any class/job on the same character, with no need to create multiple
- Fluid, fun combat
- Great story
- Lots of options for customization through character creation, gear, and glamours/dyes
- Options to play solo or join a Free Company (guild)
- Ability to build a house and customize it
- Can train your mount to fight with you, and customize it
- Large variety of very different environments and enemies
- A seemingly endless end game (lots of content)
- Ability to level various crafting skills, and rely on the land and your craft to create various gear
- Epic fights and dungeons
Cons:
- They like to schedule maintenance for times when I'm staying up much later than I should be playing this
- Can be a bit difficult to figure out the map and directions at first
- Lack of voice acting can make cutscenes boring at times, but the story is still great
- PvP is very flat, which they intend to address soon
- Too many lalafells - IGN

It was hard for me to determine whether I want to recommend this or not and I think if I wasn't curious about
(which I haven't played yet) and I still had some goodwill left over from
, I probably wouldn't have.
If you play this game right after the first one, brace yourself for disappointment.
The voice acting of almost all characters (except those who were in the first game's cast) is amateurish - which would be more tolerable if the main character, Zoe, wasn't among the bad crowd. Combine that with the character being less convincing and A LOT less likable than
's April and an overall much weaker premise for the game, and you have a lead character that's just dull.
Speaking of which, April Ryan is back... and
is a complete ♥♥♥♥♥. Her voice acting and reasoning is still more solid than Zoe's but she's too weak the carry the story on her own and, as I said, Zoe is more of a hindrance to that than anything. The story itself is okay but far from mind-blowing. It's quite obvious that the people responsible for it wanted to take it in a "different direction" (as some self-proclaimed 'visionaries' tend to do) and failed miserably to recreate that sense of purpose the first game gave you, even when faced with more overwhelming odds.
The combat system... Well, let's make it quick: It's painfully bad and its
saving grace is that there's only few instances where you actually have to fight. A few more of them and all the goodwill in the world couldn't have convinced me to recommend this game. Yes, it's that terrible - among the worst I've ever seen in a game I actually wanted to play.
As for the camera and controls, they're clunky at best but you can get used to them enough to not be hindered by them. When it comes to the adventure gameplay, well, it's not in the same league as its predecessor or any other adventure game, really, but if you're playing this game, you're probably here for the continuation of the story from
, and for that, it's okay...ish. What is not, however, is the unbearable sneaking system. You are annoyingly slow, the areas are large, you have no idea when they'll see/notice you or not... Again, it's only tolerable because there isn't too much of it.
The graphics have improved from the first game... and yet they haven't. The first game had pretty (if dated), well designed maps and backgrounds. This game has 3D environments that are large and empty. Yes, the graphical quality has increased, especially the character models, but they've lost that spark, that soul somewhere along the way.
The music somewhat makes up for that. Actually, it may very well be the one thing I have very little to complain about. It's fantastic, a few vocal tracks aside that push the "romantic" or "sad" over the edge... It's like the one in charge of these scenes had William Shattner compose them.
Overall, the game gives the impression of being half-cooked: A couple of ideas thrown together without giving them a critical once-over, half-hearted execution, unconvincing design and voice-acting, a story just one step shy of being boring (and a few more steps away from being actually interesting)... In a word: A filler - something to push out the door until somebody could come up with something better. Which is weird, since they apparently had six years between this game and the first one. You'd think that'd enough to make a better game.
The cameos and returns of characters from the first game are convincing but, overall, the writers were a little too quickly to discard ideas, characters and motives from
and they didn't have the skill to turn a good story-driven adventure into a fresh action adventure of similar quality.
Now that I read my review again, the only reason I'm still giving this game a recommendation is because I want to know if
can make up for it.
If you're coming from the first game and want to know what happens, pick this up on a sale. That is the ONLY circumstance under which you should buy this game. Otherwise, go and find something better.

Some may argue that DreamFall is a classic, like the game that came before it. If it wasn't for the fact that it was released in 2007 it could have been. It is only fair to compare games from the same year which were focussed on a strong narrative and see how Dreamfall compares. So lets take a few choice picks: Bioshock, Half-Life 2: Ep2 and Mass Effect.
Stand Dreamfall side by side with these games and you'll see the problem. A strong narrative can be achieved in 3 distinct ways, The story itself can either be engaging with various twists, turns and intrigue. Or the presentation of the story itself can really be entertaining even if the story itself is simple. Or finally, a game has both a great storyline and presentation. HL2:Ep2 was a simple storyline which was well presented, Bioshock had an engaging storyline which had mediocre presentation and Mass Effect had both an amazing storyline and amazing presentation.
Dreamfall however, has none of these.
** MINOR SPOILERS AHEAD **
The general plotline surrounds Zoe, an art student who is sinking into depression over her tedious life. Drop into the mix a sudden disappearence of her ex-lover and the story is away. Or at least, it manages a clumbsy take-off. The presentation of the story is done at a snails pace with it dragging out some very mundane 'secrets' which frankly you'd not be very keen to uncover. Around part-way through it drops an utterly pointless appearence by 'generic-broody-anti-hero' type known as Kian the Apostle and a cameo appearence of the previous games' April Ryan. The storyline around these two is both tedious and has absolutely no connection to the main plot except for the seemingly mysterious message driving Zoe forwards leading to the envitable encounter with April. The game spends an extended amount of time suggesting a great deal of links between the various parts of the tale but ultimately leaves you with unsatisfying loose ends. The ending itself is a slap in the face and feels like the last half of the game and story was completely pointless, it actually feels like the ending belongs in the middle of the storyline but the developers squandered that part by focussing on the resistance movement headed by Raven in Arcadia.
I genuinelly had to force myself to keep playing through this game as the storyline became so bland and lifeless after the 5th chapter that I actually stopped playing for months. Occasionally I'd dip back in with the hopes that things would improve. Just as things got interesting I came to the realization that I'd actually reached the end of the game.
While there seems to be Dreamfall chapters around now, you may be wondering - Would playing Dreamfall: Longest Journey actually give me greater appreciation of the storyline? The answer is no, because there is so little here that you are not missing a thing. Playing the original Longest Journey would be beneficial however.
Oh and yeah, 7 hours on record. That is how long the game takes from start to finish. The fact I took months to complete it shows how tedious it was because in theory someone could finish everything in a weekend.

This feels like watching a random guy in Youtube, watching some other random people playing a game in observer mode.
Above anything else I could say about this game, there’s this huge feeling that not only you don’t have any impact on the game (I don’t even mean making choices), as the characters you follow pretty much watch things happen for the whole 18 hours of gameplay.
I loved the first The Longest Journey, but this sequel only shows something remotely interesting when it refers to the first. Everything in the story is shallow and blunt, in special the characters.
You play three different characters in order of appearance:
Zoe Castillo: Cute Spanish girl that you want to like, but simply can’t. All she does is walk around and complain about her lack of interest on things. You do get to play detective with here, but at the end it’s only so you learn about the story. You cannot even make the smallest decisions, like not kissing that blond guy that never appears again.
April Ryan: I love April from the first game she is fun, curious, driven and bold. In this game, a plank with a sad face on it could very well substitute her. She nags the whole time and gets about nothing done. Of course other characters mention she has not been herself, but even if that’s supposed to be the reason she could at least be someone with some depth.
Kian Alvane: The perfect action hero archetype. It’s not too difficult to excuse him for his apparently shallow personality, since it’s pretty much a given to action hero’s archetypes. There’s one thing though you do not forgive from them, not taking action. As “the girls”, he’s another execrator to everything.
Blunt characters, no decision you make matter, a story clearly created to be only the hook for the sequence that only 9 years later they are managing to pull together, a tiny world, more loading screens than any other game I can remember… this is a disaster.
I’m not sure that you could find many worst sequels, but if you forget the original game, this is playable. Not a good buy in any case.

I beta tested this game way back before public release. I downloaded the massive thing, got in and ran around for awhile and thought, this is boring.
This time I thought I'd give it another go because they've had all this time to add to it. Well, I downloaded the extra massively bloated thing, got in and ran around for a few hours more this time, and my thoughts are still the same, this is boring.
Here's why I'm giving this game another thumbs down:
-The world is bland. It's not like the Skyrim single player game we all love. It's a much less detailed, much less atmospheric environment.
-Your character isn't the highly detailed, physics based, almost human character that it is in Skyrim. In this game it almost feels like its apart from the rest of the world. It glides around, all jumpy, like they made the environemnt with one program, then made the character with another. It just doesn't feel like your character fits.
-Endless, mindless quests. It never seems to get out of tutorial phase. It's just one "run here and get this item, then run here and light this torch, then run here and talk to this NPC....blah blah blah". I don't think I've read any of the dialogue. Just click through the crap till you get the next stupid objective.
-They say fighting is "visceral". But really, all that means is you have to keep the crosshairs on your target. "Visceral" just means theres no target locking. Which is just dumb, and not fun. It's bland combat without target lock, that's it. If that's "visceral", then I don't like visceral.
-Skill trees are bland. It's nothing like the complex, logical skills trees you see in Guild Wars 2 or World of Warcraft. These are just; level up and put a point in this skill line or that skill line. Then hotkey new skill and press button when in combat. Theres no strategy to it. No planning out combos to make you style unique.
-Wierd character class/race combos. Nothing seems to be the "right" character. They all just seem weird.
If there was one major deathnail for this game, I'd have to say it's the never ending, mind numbing tutorial-esque quests. They're just stupid and boring.
What a disappointment and an upsetting, boring game.

Played since beta and am diamond 5 to diamond 2 in ranked conquest since season 2.  Therefor this review is biased from a ranked players perspective.
HIGH SKILL CAP
If you're looking to dedicate alot of time and crush other players then this game has that to offer.  Skilled players are rewarded and it feels good outplaying the opposing team.  Mechanically gifted players will definately thrive here.  The macro game is important, but ultimately when both teams are tied, the team with the best mechanical skill will usually come out on top.
COMMUNITY
It's a moba.  You know what to expect from other players.  Other than the usual f*ckboys and trolls that litter all mobas. the community is pretty great.  Smite playerbase is small compared to in competitors so you'll occasionally queue into the same people if you play enough.  HiRez is also very strict with behavior in games, you will be banned if you consistenly get reported, afk, harass, or just overall f*ckboyness.
GODS (heroes)
There are currently around 80+ gods available for purchase right now.  With new gods revealed every 4 weeks approximately.  Gods are divided into 1 of 5 archetypes; Warrior, Guardian, Assassin, Mage, or Hunter.  Gods are incredibly varied from one another allowing for a ton of different strategies and team comps.  There are only about few gods that are unplayable in high level ranked due their kits just not being able to compete.  But more importantly there are no gods that feel unstoppable or/and unfair.  Great balance overall.
Great game.  HiRez studio definately hit it out of the park and striving for a better and better game.

This game proved to be more tedious than fun. As an immigration Inspector, the premise of the game is to check prospective emigrants' paperwork for defects and inconsistencies. As the game goes on, you are charged with enforcing ever-more complicated rules. The chief problem is that the entire game is done under extreme time pressure--you have a set amount of time each "game day" to process as many applications as possible.
You earn money when you correctly process an application, and get penalized when you incorrectly admit or deny someone. At the end of each game day, you must pay a set of expenses to keep your family alive and healthy (ex., rent, food, heat, etc.). If you ever run out of money, you automatically lose the game. But as the game goes on and the rules you must enforce become more and more complex, the game grows ever more tedious. Trying to process as many applications as I could without making mistakes, without wasting undue time, etc., made Papers, Please more stressful than fun to play. I couldn't appreciate the (admittedly, often creative) content, because I was CONSTANTLY under the pressure of an unforgiving clock. At least it only cost me $10.

- Options to play solo or join a Free Company (guild)
- Ability to build a house and customize it
- Can train your mount to fight with you, and customize it
- Large variety of very different environments and enemies
- A seemingly endless end game (lots of content)
- Ability to level various crafting skills, and rely on the land and your craft to create various gear
- Epic fights and dungeons
Cons:
- They like to schedule maintenance for times when I'm staying up much later than I should be playing this

I am generally not a fan of MMOs, but, as you can see from my playtime, this is definitely my exception.
I really enjoy that a lot of the content is able to be played solo or with my spouse, and that I really only have to group up for the group dungeons, delves, and world bosses. I also really appreciate the community and that a simple request for help in zone chat is almost always immediately answered by kind players who are willing to jump into the fray and help me defeat the tougher content. There's no expectation to stay grouped up, and I'm allowed to explore and enjoy the content at my own pace, which is extremely appreciated.
Originally, I was not a fan of the One Tamriel update, as my character suddenly seemed a whole lot squishier and content got a whole lot harder as it scaled up, but since returning to playing after a few months, it seems as though the kinks have been ironed out and all seems well now. I now really love the update and that I can explore the entire world whenever I want, as well as complete whatever quests around Tamriel that I feel like taking on. I also really enjoy that there are transportation options to visit anywhere and everywhere through boats and caravans.
The landscapes are beautiful and exploration is one of my favorite things to do in the game. It's a huge game in terms of required disk space, but I think it's completely worth it!
It'a not exactly Skyrim online, but it's pretty close and there's so much to do and see. It's also thankfully not a pay-to-win game, with most items from the Crown Store being things you can either get in game with gold, just cosmetic, or just small boosts (yay crown scrolls!). There are lots of giveaways, usually, to get extra perks here and there. Their subscription model is also very worth it without being unfair to non-subscribers or giving a huge advantage to paying players.
It's also a nice change of pace that dying does not have a major consequence, like loss of exp. Instead, if you die, your equipment will need to be repaired, but it's usually a nominal fee (my highest so far was 542 gold after embarrassingly dying a few times in a row and jumping off a cliff into the void to see what would happen) or using a repair kit (usually pretty cheap from any merchant). The only other consequence is that you will be teleported and resurrected at a wayshrine if you do not have a charged soul gem (also easy and cheap to obtain in game) or a skill that will let you resurrect without a gem. It's a very forgiving system.
So far the only thing I am not very impressed with is the player housing. I do love that it is individually instanced, as I am so used to games being a first-come-first-serve with housing and leaving most players without. However, I wish the houses were actually useful, especially for the prices in gold/crowns to own some of them (the free places are a nice touch, though!). Right now, I have collected all the free homes, but they're really only good for a free teleport when I need to be in the area, but don't have a wayshrine to conveniently use. Otherwise, apparently the houses are really only good for crafting tables (these seem expensive to own, but I'm assuming there's another way to get them) or for training dummies to check your dps/skills. There's no storage provided and a lot of the furniture (other than some seats, lighting, dummies, and crafting tables) are decorative only with no interactions available. It's basically like playing with a doll house, in that you can decorate it and look at it, and that's about it. I was hoping for something more like Skyrim's homesteads, where I could have a little bit of extra storage and some weapons/armor on display. Unfortunately, as it stands, I will probably not buy any of the houses (they're like 45,000+ gold, with some being in the millions. or like 3000+ crowns...), until there's some sort of point in having a home outside of the freebies. It definitely has potential to be expanded upon and made useful.
Otherwise, I fully recommend this game, and I also recommend the subscription, if you can afford to try it. It's worth it for the craft bag (unlimited crafting supply storage without filling your inventory) and extra storage (double bank space), but the additional perks of 1500 crowns, 10% extra experience points (not a huge boost, but still helps and is still fair), and access to all DLC content is amazing. I used to be very careful with looting because my inventory would fill up so much with provisioning supplies, as well as avoided most harvesting and mining, but now I can run around all of Tamriel and grab as much crafting stuff as I want without consequence! It will all be mine! MWAHAH! Ahem... anyway, yes, crafting bag is a wonderful perk. It also costs less for the monthly subscription than it would for me to just buy 1500 crowns, so that's nice. I feel like I'm more than getting my money's worth for everything they've tossed in, and I'm super excited to explore all the DLC content now that it's a more affordable option than buying each one outright.
If you're looking for an MMO that does not constantly pressure you to have a huge group of people to play with at all times, this is a great choice. There is tons of solo content, and players are always willing to help out with anything that you need a group for or are struggling with. Of course, if you do want a huge group of people, the game allows for that playstyle as well, and there are plenty of guilds to join (you can join 5 guilds account-wide).

I tried. I really did try.
Dreamfall and its predessor, The Longest Journey, are often praised by adventure game fans, and I like adventure games, but I just cannot find anything to like about either of these. In Dreamfall's case, the adventure/puzzle component has been stripped down to a bare minimum and combat and stealth has been put in to make up for it. The trouble is, it doesn't do any of these things well, so by trying to appeal to "everybody", it becomes decidely mediocre at everything.
This isn't purely down to the game's age, as even fans of the game recognised these shortcomings at its release, but still praised its story. Well, after 7 hours, I can't share those sentiments either. The "twin worlds" idea of "technology" and "magic" is a naive concept at best (what do you think stoves, spinning wheels and doors ARE if not technology?), fate and destiny and conspiracies and ancient civilizations are potentially great sources to mine for a story but I found nothing new or interesting about any of it, at least not by the half-way point. The voice acting is terrible by today's lofty standards, which I accept is an unfair criticism of a relatively low-budget game, but the end result is something that comes across as amateur.
I've sat through worse games, and to call it terrible would be doing it a disservice, but the shoddy stealth/combat bits comined with a fiddly camera have broken this particular camel's back and I cannot summon the will to continue.
On the plus side, I had no problems getting the game running properly this time, which was nice.

Before I played this game, if someone had told me that I would find comparing and evaluating paperwork to be at all enjoyable I would have called them a liar and a couple other names to boot.  After having played Papers, Please though, I have to admit that - at least in this game - paperwork can be fun.
It doesn't seem like such a difficult concept at first: receive documentation from person, examine documentation (and sometimes the person) for any discrepancies, approve and deny as appropriate.  Like many things though, what is explained simply is not so easy to do.  While the game starts off with one document you need to examine, before long you're looking at as many as 5 pieces of paperwork for any one person, each which must be examined for consistency within itself AND compared to all other documentation.  It could be overwhelming, but the difficulty curve of Papers, Please is ramped up perfectly, neither too fast nor too slow.  By the time you're faced with this wall of documentation you're prepared... mostly.
I know, I know, what I've described sounds like a harrowing experience.  Yes, it can be tense at times, but for some reason it's also rather fun.  The precise reason why escapes me in part, but a good deal of the enjoyment comes simply from the challenge of trying to figure out when someone is attempting to slip something past you, potentially for nefarious reasons even.  Every forged document, stolen identity, or smuggled bit of explosives you find is a satisfying emotional payoff, a virtual pat on the back for having stopped someone up to no good.
Truthfully though, what makes Papers, Please an enjoyable experience isn't so much the gameplay as the story.  Not that the gameplay isn't solid, but much of the appeal would be meaningless without the personal drama that comes across on any given day of it.  Love, death, loss, joy, sadness, humor, all come across in the small conversations and interactions the player character has with the various people he encounters. Mindlessly approving or denying paperwork all day is somewhat trivial, but what if your decision to approve or deny a passport could make the difference between a family being reunited and one being torn apart?  Between true love and tragic loss? What if it could shape the very future of the country you serve?  All of these things come up as part of the plot of Papers, Please, and there's no right or wrong answer to each.  Your actions have consequences, and for better or worse you can see them out.
Bluntly put, Papers, Please is a perfect example of how decent plot and unique gameplay can combine to form something greater than the sum of each.  Examined separately, the plot of Papers, Please is a bit derivative, while the gameplay is mostly unique rather than truly gripping.  Combined as expertly as they are, however, leads to a final result that is both highly enjoyable and very memorable.

This is one of my favorite games.
You will start out very similar to Minecraft, chopping down trees, harvesting coal, stone, and iron, but then it takes a turn. Soon you will have drills mining all of your ores for you, and you will also use conveyor belts to pull the ores over to your smelting area which smelts all of the ores without you having to lift a finger. Then all you have to do is pick up the products and craft them into other useful items.
Later on, however, you will probably get tired of crafting those items, so you will make assembly machines to craft your items for you so you just have to walk up to the chest and say "THANKS" and you get the items easy peasy. Then you can spend your time doing better things like expanding your base or automating the production of other things.
Further on than that, however, you will probably get tired of walking over to a chest to pick up the items that are being crafted automatically. So you will set up a logistics system to have flying robots grab the products for you and bring them to you. Then all you have to do is walk around and set down your products wherever you want them to be in order to fulfil your wishes.
Down the line, however, you may get tired of having to walk around and place items down, or having to build the same system again when you have already perfected the design. So you make construction bots that will place down items for you and you don't even have to walk up to the pace of where to put the items, and you will copy blueprints of your best-designed systems so that if you need more of them you can just tell your robots that you want another set up and they will set it all up for you.
Overall, this is a very well made game. I have only encountered one bug in my whole experience and it was patched out pretty quickly. The community is helpful and the possibilities of what you can do in this game are vast. There is always something to do and the multiplayer in this game is just as fun. I have played a lot of games in my life and this one is designed better than most of them.

"The answers you seek are inside this box; along with something else. Something they said could never be built. It is the only one in existence, and it is the key to incomprehensible power." The note you read sits on top of a large, ornate safe, along with a smaller box that contains an eyepiece without which the note claims you will be "as blind as the rest". It warns you that the stakes are high and that the safe was constructed to keep this incomprehensible power away from lesser minds. There's only one thing left for you to do: put on the eyepiece and open the box.
Except this safe isn't easy to crack. There are dials to spin and knobs to turn and pieces missing. The whole thing is designed with puzzles in mind, providing you with a pleasantly interactive challenge to surpass in order to unlock the safe's mysterious contents. The eyepiece allows you to see once hidden drawings and symbols, which often provide important clues on how to solve certain puzzles. There are hidden compartments and switches to flip (or not to flip) and buttons disguised as decorations. And once you open up the safe? Well, let's just say there's more than one box to open.
The puzzles in the Room are well-balanced and exciting, with each one being easy enough to solve that it doesn't frustrate you. Puzzles are often interconnected, with the completion of one puzzle unlocking an item that makes the solution to another puzzle accessible. As the game progresses, the puzzles become more involved and intricate. The design of each box is intriguing and, as the environment around you changes with the game's progression, the experience slowly becomes something far more surreal and fantastic than the dusty attic you start in.
Overall, the Room is a short game that will pique your interest and encourage your curiosity. It isn't a game that will force an extreme intellectual challenge on you, but it will require some logical thinking and a few of the puzzles will make you scratch your head for a minute or two. The plot is vague enough to entice you without becoming hard to understand. The Room's shining glory is, without a doubt, its slow escalation from the ordinary to the extraordinary and its wonderfully beautiful atmosphere and handsome puzzle design. Very enjoyable and definitely worth a thumbs up!

Just Cause 3 seems to use a different game engine from JC2 (and has a different development team as well apparently) which might explain why there's some optimisation issues here and there. The issue has more to do with memory available so if you have at least above 8 GB RAM, you should play it just fine. Otherwise, might be a problem for others. I myself never had I problem, and in fact, the game ran so well I could max out most settings on my mid-end video card.
Graphics are really different from JC2 and had me yucking out the first time but it wasnt long before I started embracing it.  Once I did, that's when I became engrossed with the game. The world of Medici is phoneomenal and leaves you for a lasting first impression. The lands are vast and open, and the flowery and greenery is just so awesome to look at.
Like JC2, you will spend most of your liberating settlements across the island while doing main missions. And you're pretty much...forced to, if you want to unlock main missions. I love how the devs continue to force players to become completionists...
One big step up however is that game now makes it much easier for you to complete settlements this time round, by actually highlighting to you the exact locations of chaos objects and collectibles. This really saved me the hassle from looking high and low for the objects and I probably would have taken twice as long to complete this game otherwise.
Although Michael Bay set pieces are still the main advertised point of Just Cause, I always found the world more fascinating, and the main reason for every purchase.
The world of JC3 takes place in Medici, another fictional lalaland, but this time, it's alot more grounded in reality than the ridiculous fantasical place that was JC2's Panau. As such, it was quite a disappointment there was no longer any desert/snow/jungle biomes at all once but the same time, made Medici all the more believable in scope and design. From the lush flower fields, to flat greenlands and dense forests, Medici is a really rich and beautiful island to explore. There's also a large snowy mountain that reaches up to the peak of the world, an archipelago of islands and wide areas of construction sites which serves for the country's mining grounds.
For settlements however, you shouldn't expect much but the same most copy-paste buildings and structures from previous games but it was not something I was too bothered by when too busy exploring the otherwise incredibly huge world.
Another great addition to my exploration was the wingsuit, which you can use in combination with your existing grapple and physics-defying parachute. The wingsuit, if I dare say, is by far the BEST THING THAT HAS EVER HAPPENED IN A GAME EVER.
I honeslty just bought this game for the wingsuit, and I have no regrets.
It's just so f***ing brilliant. It's clear how much effort the devs have put into the design and mechanics of the wingsuit, which made traversing the lands, air and seas so easy, seamless and very very enjoyable. It's not easy to control at first, and many who can't simply stop using it or don't use it often or JUST AREN'T USING IT RIGHT; a shame in that they're missing out on the sheer awesomeness of it. You can pretty much fly forever, do amazing stunts and zip like superman with the wingsuit.
Another last highlight I should point out is the introduction of challenges in JC3. This is an expansion from the simple races in JC2 and can range from driving a ticking time bomb, collecting bavarium stones using a magnet, races and just blowing s*** up. It's ironic given how easy the game might seem on the surface, most of the challenges are by no means easy. Gear upgrades are all tied to challenges so players who don't complete the challenges won't get much upgrades, a controversial decision by the devs some hate. Initially skeptical about it, I've soon come to love how they made it as such.
After all, why should you get upgrades if you can't prove you're qualified for 'em? Challenges like races arent hard, once you get the right vehicles and boosters available, although others like the wingsuit challenge might pose some difficulty to people.
Overall, JC3 is a fine sequel to an already solid game. If you're only into action shooting and blowing things up, JC3's repetive nature might not be for you.
But if you're just looking for the best, greatest-looking and largest effin' sandbox open world ever made, you should pick this game up right away. And just as a disclaimer, the first two islands the main missions brings you to can get pretty repetitive, but once you get to the northern island, trust me, the world is SO much more different.
Of all the open world games I've played, none has given me this much freedom to explore than JC3 does.

That not withstanding, however, this was a lovely adventure game, an easy winner for any fans of the original game and any of the adventure P&C surge of the 90s, though this game in of itself veers from its P&C origins. A good story which becomes excellent primarily in its final act, writer/director Ragnar Tørnquist once again serves up thoughtful, charismatic and well-written characters whom- with the exception of main character Zoe- are generally voice-acted very well. This game will definately appeal to any looking for a new venture into story-driven, fantasy games, whilst I would recommend those who consider the mechanical aspect vital to give this a miss, as the limited camera scope and movement mechanics will likely have you tearing your hair out!

This game was a chore to play through. For fans of either point and click or action genres, this game is a boring slog that does not reward your patience.
Controls are obviously set up with consoles in mind, leaving the PC controls extremely awkward.
The combat system is pointless and seemed like an afterthought.
Stealth is either boring or frustrating due to the awkward controls.
Puzzles are significantly oversimplified and very unsatisfying.
The game is told in the perspective of three different characters and while this is not always a bad thing, it was poorly executed in this game, ruining what immersion there could have been.
The voice acting for the playable characters isn't bad, but other characters will often stop mid sentence because the game needs to change the page on the subtitles.
If you haven't played the first game (The Longest Journey) you may find yourself scratching your head at some parts.
The ending was not an ending. There are more unresolved plotlines by the end than at any other point during the game.
There are a few bugs that cost you some time.
The music was nice, the story was fairly interesting, and the graphics were a marginal improvement over the original (but it should be seeing as though it came out 6 years after.) They did a good job recreating a couple areas from the first game.

I went into this game expecting nothing considering it's a free to play game, but I was surprised at how much I enjoyed it. In an age where every game is trying to push the boundaries on what good graphics are, this game's simpler type of graphics reminded me of a time where I'd spend hours playing Final Fantasy Tactics, although it's nothing at all like that game.
There is quite a bit of grinding if you want to play that way and get the best in slot gear for your level, but you level up so quickly that it's almost made redundant, by the time you have the best gear for your build you're already a high enough level to start having to grind for the next set.
Speaking of leveling, it's very easy to level in this game I've played 23 hours as of writing this review and I'm already pushing level 80.
One downside is that even though there is a myriad of classes to build towards, it is very easy to mess up your build and become sub-optimal, or just outright useless. There are ways to reset your skill points, but it's exclusively in the cash shop with no way to get it for free to play players. That being said, there are a ton of build guides out there for your viewing pleasure that are constantly being updated, just make sure you read them carefully.
All in all I'm enjoying my time in Tree of Savior, best of all if you like going solo, you're not forced to party up at any point unless you want to run dungeons, which from what I've seen so far, are optional.
I'd give it a 7/10. Not the best MMO I've played, but far from the worst.

Hey wait a minute there! I haven't even started the game yet! And there's 24h left of this "free play opportunity!" And you want a "review"?
Hand me the full game and I promise to deliver a full-blown 50-word review. Maybe even 100.

It isn't fun.
Don't mince words with any junk about how it made you cry. Don't waste your time singing the praises of a video game because of its art or its music or (god help you) its story.
The movement is slow and clunky. Pretty much every attack option leaves you wide open to enemy fire (your enemies suffer no such restrictions, of course).
The idea is that you're going to freeze time and belt out a series of attacks, but every time you do that it stops being an action RPG and becomes a plain old RPG. After freezing time, you can only attack out of Turn with the aid of upgrades (for individual moves), so your choices are to be effective in combat or to be involved in the combat, basically.
There's some genuinely cool ideas. No one's going to deny that. Combining all your moves to give them cool side-effects is really nifty, the setting is fascinating (and ties directly into the gameplay) and there's real merit to blending strategy with action like this. But it all sort of falls flat on its face with how uninvolved it is.
All Transistor needed was a couple more mobile attacks, the sort of thing you can use on the move or that doesn't slow you down massively, and a dodge roll.♥♥♥♥♥♥that gives you REAL options when you don't want to use Turn.
It put in a flourish and a sing-song button instead.
Make of that what you will.

Before I played this game, if someone had told me that I would find comparing and evaluating paperwork to be at all enjoyable I would have called them a liar and a couple other names to boot.  After having played Papers, Please though, I have to admit that - at least in this game - paperwork can be fun.
It doesn't seem like such a difficult concept at first: receive documentation from person, examine documentation (and sometimes the person) for any discrepancies, approve and deny as appropriate.  Like many things though, what is explained simply is not so easy to do.  While the game starts off with one document you need to examine, before long you're looking at as many as 5 pieces of paperwork for any one person, each which must be examined for consistency within itself AND compared to all other documentation.  It could be overwhelming, but the difficulty curve of Papers, Please is ramped up perfectly, neither too fast nor too slow.  By the time you're faced with this wall of documentation you're prepared... mostly.
I know, I know, what I've described sounds like a harrowing experience.  Yes, it can be tense at times, but for some reason it's also rather fun.  The precise reason why escapes me in part, but a good deal of the enjoyment comes simply from the challenge of trying to figure out when someone is attempting to slip something past you, potentially for nefarious reasons even.  Every forged document, stolen identity, or smuggled bit of explosives you find is a satisfying emotional payoff, a virtual pat on the back for having stopped someone up to no good.
Truthfully though, what makes Papers, Please an enjoyable experience isn't so much the gameplay as the story.  Not that the gameplay isn't solid, but much of the appeal would be meaningless without the personal drama that comes across on any given day of it.  Love, death, loss, joy, sadness, humor, all come across in the small conversations and interactions the player character has with the various people he encounters. Mindlessly approving or denying paperwork all day is somewhat trivial, but what if your decision to approve or deny a passport could make the difference between a family being reunited and one being torn apart?  Between true love and tragic loss? What if it could shape the very future of the country you serve?  All of these things come up as part of the plot of Papers, Please, and there's no right or wrong answer to each.  Your actions have consequences, and for better or worse you can see them out.
Bluntly put, Papers, Please is a perfect example of how decent plot and unique gameplay can combine to form something greater than the sum of each.  Examined separately, the plot of Papers, Please is a bit derivative, while the gameplay is mostly unique rather than truly gripping.  Combined as expertly as they are, however, leads to a final result that is both highly enjoyable and very memorable.

This is not a game you have "fun" with. It's a very bleak tale about the nature and abuse of power, the burden of knowledge, and above all, hope. The gameplay, which escalates throughout the story into more and more of an intellectual challenge, is a vehicle for the game to toy with your emotions. The choices you make have a wide range. Should I arrest the old woman for having false information on her passport? If I do, I will get a bonus that may well mean affording medicine for my wife. But then again, the old woman is hardly responsible for what is likely a typo made by an immigration officer as fallible as you. Should I listen to the mysterious revolutionaries? On one hand, they may bring about a better world; on the other, I may well end up under arrest along with my innocent family. Should I accept the bribe from the man who claims to be just smuggling harmless medicine for a friend? These are the kind of choices that I would impulsively make, knowing I had to process more people to make enough money, and then ponder over for the next fifteen minutes, turning the moral dilemna over in my head. You rarely win in this game, and that's the point.

Dreamfall is the sequel to "The Longest Journey" and I had just finished that game before playing this one (bought it as a game pack). TLJ and Dreamfall both have breathtaking storylines. I felt that this game was a lot more enriching for having just played TLJ.
There are many differences though. For instance, TLJ was more heavily focused on problem solving and interaction with NPCs. This game was very different gameplay wise, including a heavy focus on stealth puzzles, this boring minigame where you match up symbols (it was fine the first time, but after the 5th time of doing it, it was old hat), and a combat system which was not very well executed.
I also had huge problems with the camera and movement when I first started. I recommend this game be played on a gamepad if at all possible as it did not react well to my mouse and for some reason the camera movements were inverted.
But I am a player who plays games for their story, and this one had a fantastic storyline, although you are left with many questions at the end. I couldn't imagine having played this game 8 years ago when it came out and then having to wait until now with Dreamfall Chapters to finally get answers to those questions.
If you play for story, I recommend this game, (but play TLJ first; its graphics are definitely dated, but it's story is timeless).

A *nice* casual adventure, almost terminally marred by an atrocious interface.
Sigh. Dreamfall: The Longest Journey has an engaging story, narrated nicely. It's more of an interactive novel than a real adventure, and quite linear. But the characters and story are well developed, and you actually care about what is going on. The puzzles are simple to solve so even a casual gamer can enjoy playing the game. The graphics are nothing to write home about (this is a rather old game), but this game is defined by the story, not the graphics, and I rather enjoy that.
The big drawback is that this game was obviously originally developd for a console, and the PC version inherits one of the most atrocious, braindead and next-to-unusable control schemes I've had the misfortune to have foised on me. During porting, the developers did, kinda-sorta-way, include mouse support, but it always gets in the way of camera control. Movement *also* forcs camera control - in exceedingly stupid ways - and the result is an interface that makes it neigh on impossible to navigate your character. I've sat and screamed in frustration at the screen because something as simple as turning left and looking at something specific (required to trigger interaction) becomes a cumbersome, dragged-out affair that can take a minute. Now imagine using the interface-that-hates-you for combat that is (luckily) used sparingly, and you have a recipe for desaster. It took me a while to clue in to the fact that you must never, ever, touch the mouse if you engage in combat, or you'll invariably end up with the camera showing you a wall, and your opponent killing you solwly.
However, if you can overlook the dubest, most unrewarding and relentlessly hostile control scheme that you only need to navigate the whole game, this game is actually fun. The story *is* nice. This is a really, really engaging casual adventure. The puzzles are solvable, and most situations allow for multiple solutions. Since combat is something to avoid (crummy control), it even makes it feel like an accomplishment to get out of a situation by sneaking (which unfortunately *also* requires fine control), or some quite humorous dialogue.
It's a great journey - but it's made the 'longest journey' only because of the silly way you have to control the actor.
tldr; - good story, atrocious controls, sum: above board.

Dreamfall is a heavy storyline game.  This is good if you're like me and like games that have a great storyline.  There's also heavy dialogue throughout the game.  This may be a good thing depending on what you like.  If you're not into story-based games you may not want to play it.  If you skip dialogues you'll miss the story and may not know what to do next.  It's not
dialogue.  There's more exploring and adventure than anything.  This game has a mix of sci-fi futuristic and medieval environments.  This game has a feel of Tomb Raider on how the adventure gets exciting.  If you're a fan of story-based games you must play this.
I also have to gripes about this game too, not real bad but must be said.  The game is a little old so the graphics are dated but still good for the game.  If you're like me and play it with a Xbox controller you need to take the time to adjust the controller settings.  If you don't you'll be pulling your hair out. The mouse, oh I hate the mouse in this game. Even when playing with a controller the mouse arrow never goes away so you have to drag it to the corner.  But
: do not drag the mouse into the lower right corner of the screen.  Windows has that feature "show desktop" and for some reason the game doesn't ignore it.  If you drag your mouse to that corner the framerate will suffer greatly!  Keep the mouse out of the lower right corner!  I thought my game was broken but it was that little glitch that messes it up.  Finally, the fighting.  There's a few places where combat takes place.  Normally I'd welcome it but this game isn't easy to fight with.  The controls are stiff and unless you practice in the dojo level (at the beginning of the game) you'll fight bad.  The game is mostly moving around and getting from A to B and the fight scenes aren't big and very few.  It's just annoying.  Otherwise it's still worth playing.  It has a great story and I can't wait to play the sequel.

There were several times i wanted to throw my computer out the window playing this. It's a follow-up to a pretty decent adventure game, and this really is an adventure game too, but with an identity crisis. It uses a god-awful third-person perspective, without being point-and-click, so the camera constantly ends up in stupid places and you can't really enjoy the beautiful environments as much as you would in first-person. To add insult to injury there are some incredibly out-of-place combat and stealth scenes, all of which cause insta-death if you press the wrong button. And yet... the world of The Longest Journey is a rich and beautiful one. The fantasy half isn't my cup of tea, but the sci-fi half is great, and the ending is extremely compelling. All the pain of the earlier parts of the game go away when the story truly unfolds. The denouement does go on a little long - i wish they had ended at a particularly poignant fade-out (you'll understand when you get there), but it's still got a real emotional impact and some very cool ideas.

This game feels too much like a chore. Now, don't get me wrong, I like it when games are hard and challenge me. But Dark Souls II takes it way too far. I don't want to sound like a whiny little kid in this review, but I'm afraid there is no other way to put it: This game is too hard. This is my first Souls game, and quite frankly I don't know why anyone would want to put in enough time and effort into any of the games in the series, which I heard are just as hard. Really quickly, like right when I got to the Forest of Fallen Giants, I simply wasn't having any fun. I was forcing myself to log on and play for a couple hours just so I could make the tiniest bit of progress until it got to the point where I asked myself "Why am I still playing this?"
When all is said and done, this is a really well made game. I can tell that the devs put a lot of work into it, (even though I haven't really seen much of the game). The fighting mechanics are definitely my favorite of any fantasy game, but the game is so hard it's off putting, especially when you have to face multiple enemies at once. Oh, and this game likes to throw hordes at you, so you have to inch your way slowly closer to the enemies to draw them out one at a time, which is very tedious, but sometimes that's unavoidable.
So yeah, if you've never played a Souls game before, and you feel like punishing yourself, this is the way to go!

A dark and brutal 3rd person fighting game. It's kind of a combat simulation from a chess masters perspective. Yes combat is about speed and precision, however it's also about the moves, where, when and how. Every button press can matter in the right battle, blocking, dodging and rolling are probably more important than attacking when it comes to your skill set. You can master melee and ranged weapons as well as magic abilities. Like many RPGs you choose a 'class' and then level up and spend points to increase stats. higher level weapons are more dependent on stats, so it's important to know what you want to do and how you're going to master your character before you take actions. While the game doesn't have a direct question system or a real map, you don't usually feel too lost, though you can end up going places before you should and running into some creatures that can destroy you instantly. In dark souls though death is not a maybe, it's certain, dying is just a part of the game. Did I mention it's dark? There is a story, but it's so convoluted the makers even held a competition to see who could piece together the most coherent story from what they had put together in all 3 games. There is DLC for this, but don't buy it stand alone, instead buy DS2: Scholar of the First Sin. It's DS2 with all the DLC and is cheaper than buying the game and then the DLC. Scholar also alters the original game in some minor ways, it moves some enemies, adds others. Again, like a chess board, enemies are hand placed, nothing is randomly generated here, everything you see, fight and kill was intended. Dark Souls is Merciless, but fair. It can be a little wonky on pacing, the hardest bosses in the game for me were in the middle, the final boss was actually pretty easy compared to the rest. In most cases though the bosses, while trying, aren't the most difficult part. Typically there are some areas that simply getting from one side to the other is the greatest part of the challenge, fighting one vigilant enemy after another wears you down and typically will kill you far more often than bosses. Then the levels themselves, the world you travel through, has handfuls of hidden goods and items, most of which are placed in perilous ways that will kill you multiple times before you manage to get to them and pick them up. Everything here is meant to kill you, and most of it will. This is Dark Souls, Prepare to Die.
This version of the the game is for the most part obsolete. Go pick up Scholar of The First Sin: the same amazing game, all of its DLCs, more bonus content, and a new final boss!

I'm gonna be frank - Magic DotP 2012's awesomeness above the other Magic games was blown out of proportion. I kept reading how this version was supposed to be better than the rest, but after really playing it out for hours in comparison with the 2013 and 2014 version, I realized the fact that its unlocking gameplay is kinda clunky and just frankly exhausting, whereas with 2013 and 2014, all you need to do to unlock the "good cards" is simply typing in the promo codes. Simple.
Now, I realize that a lot of people appreciate the kind of feeling where you put in a lot of hard work just to earn a single card-unlock every 30 minutes or so in a battle you might very well lose and waste your time anyway. Not me. I don't personally recommend this because I don't like this type of slow grind in video games, so if you like that, knock yourself out and ignore my recommendation. Me, I would rather have everything unlocked in the beginning so that I could have fun experimenting with a full deck at my convenience and test out what damage I could do.
The UI compared to the other versions of Magic is acceptable. Being an older model of the game, it's of course a bit uglier than the newer ones, but it's nowhere cringey enough for me to complain. Besides, it's just superficial aesthetics compared to the aforementioned real problems in the core of the game.
The campaign is short without the expansion, and only a little longer with it. Since the multiplayer is pretty much dead at this point, there's little to the game experience after you beat the campaign, though playing as archenemy (only when you buy the expansion) has its kicks at times (and I do mean "at times", because despite the unfair advantage an archenemy has, playing against three opponents is actually far more challenging than I expected).
One thing I want to be clear about the unlocking gameplay - I don't mind having to unlock a single deck one boss battle at a time. What I couldn't stand is unlocking a single card one battle at a time, which is a really big waste of time. In other words, unlocking the decks of bosses as I battle them can be rewarding, but unlocking one card at a time is a big grind. So there's pros and cons with this kind of unlocking.
I'm gonna keep playing the 2012 version, but I'll probably get bored of it soon enough and return to the much more flexible 2014 version.

While Magic 2012 can be fun and outshines later versions where bugs and microtransactions completely ruin the experience, it's not without its own share of frustrations.  Freedom to deckbuild and manually tap lands is sorely inadequate, and the game pretty much expects you to jump through a paywall to unlock the rest of its content, which is unacceptable after already paying $20.  These dealbreakers make getting started a waste of time.

Long Review version:
This is a solid example of how a First Person Shooter game doesn't need to be "military shooter" to be good. In fact, with the oversaturation of the genre nowadays, this game looks better and stands out throughout the years for it's own gameplay mechanic. Here below is my breakdown of Pros and Cons regarding this game:
Pros:
+ [COMEDY] Humour is spot-on, every quips Silas said during his storytelling and paired with the reaction of people who heard his story makes comedy gold
+ [STORY] despite some parts that has questionable validity due to its comedic nature, the story is, in a whole, is surprisingly good
+ [SOUNDTRACK] The soundtrack is strongly atmospheric which makes you feel like you're brought back into the wild west era, every sound of harmonica and country-style guitar is a pleasant hear
+[GAMEPLAY] second strongest after its comedy. The weapon set is appropriate, and while it's small in variety, it makes up for having its own functionality. Also the skill set is varied to create different playstyles
+[ADDITIONAL CONTENT] Duel Mode. 'nuff said
+[REPLAYABILITY] this game has plenty of replay values including Arcade a.k.a High Score mode, and also the one I mentioned above, the Duel. people may find duel the more interesting of the two due to it's unique mechanic in itself. Also some new difficulty level will unlock after finishing the game
Cons:
- [STORY IS SHORT] It has potential to be expanded upon, but for what it's worth, it's a great time
- [COLOR PALETTE] Graphics and color tones are actually its strongest point, and biggest flaw, at least for me personally. While the semi-shading style is quite good, it sometimes difficult to distinguish the enemy from the background, what with its brown and yellow saturated tone
Conclusion: Should you buy this?
For me personally, yes. And also I bought this on winter sale, which is one of the better deals I have. Definitely recommended. But if you happen to found this game not during sale, i still encourage you to buy it on full price, if you're not a cheap♥♥♥♥♥guy. It worth its full price

This is a game that stuck with me and told a grim yet realistic story. While the graphics aren't spectacular and it's not the high intense gameplay you can get from other games, this is a game that took a mundane job and made it into a political commentary. I was skeptical initially thinking that a paper pushing game would be easy and I'd get bored of it. In reality, it was the opposite. The game's difficulty progressed with the story line, or in other words, the levels of bureaucracy and trying not to get too many citations. It gets harder when you have to deal with terrorists and providing for your family. The historical backdrop of East and West Germany (ofc in fictional terms) made it even more realistic and moving. This game  impacted me and it is a true masterpiece.
Of course, it is not flawless, at times it can feel a bit repetitive and while you can have many endings (20 in fact), it's hard to replay it immediately (better wait a few months to try it again).
In short, if you'd like a break from an FPS and try to be an immigration inspector then this game is for you.

I'm very, VERY disappointed.
This game is a sequel to "The Longest Journey", a point-and-click adventure released in 1999.
I bought both games one year ago, and finally got some spare time, enough to play them both.
TLJ was simply beautiful. It had good puzzles (and a couple of difficult ones); I instantly fell in love with the world, the characters and the story.
Then I started playing Dreamfall.
You can clearly tell this game was born in an age when classic point-and-click adventures were dead, and the developers started using different mechanics for them (Grim Fandango comes to mind, but that was actually a wonderful game). Also, Dreamfall was developed in a period when consoles were the main target. This combination caused a long string of very bad design decisions that affect the game negatively.
Here are some aspects of the game I'd like to talk about.
As soon as the first cutscene ended, I noticed a certain difficulty in interacting with the game. The controls are AWFUL. So awkward and counterintuitive. It is clearly designed with controllers in mind, so I said "Hey, I'll just use my Xbox360 Wireless Controller". But it didn't even work. And if you're planning to use one and you somehow manage to make it work, you still need some third party software to bind the triggers to keyboard keys because they won't work otherwise. So, after 30 minutes of googling and tweaking of input options, I ended up playing the game with keyboard and mouse.
Oh, the pain we must endure. This is supposed to be a game about exploration, about searching the environment for clues and items to solve puzzles (I'll talk about "puzzles" later). The way the camera is implemented makes it so frustrating to even look around in smaller rooms. It just gets in the way. Not that there's a lot to look at, anyways. Gone are the descriptions of places, objects and such. There's so much less. And it's written so poorly.
Nonexistant, basically. You have a couple of minigames that you will need to play 5-6 times during the entire span of the game (the hacking one, and the lockpicking one). They're both extremely easy.
There's never been a single moment where I was stuck in this game. The puzzles, which should constitute a good portion of the gameplay, are instead few and boring. The inventory space is very limited, but it's not a problem, since I don't think I ever held more than 5 items at the same time (counting your mobile phone and a lockpick that you always have with you, so that makes it 3). With some characters, you even play big portions of the game without any item whatsoever. At some point, you feel like the game consists only of walking, talking to people, and watching cutscenes. 10-12 hours of cutscenes.
So, puzzles are not a big thing in this one. They instead decided to dilute the gameplay with...
Seriously, this is the sequel to a point-and-click. It's mainly story-driven. so, WHY ON STARK did the designers think that STEALTH and COMBAT sections were a good idea, I honestly cannot fathom.
Stealth sections are EVIL. Note to all devs: DO NOT put stealth "missions" in ANY kind of game that does not make stealth its primary mechanic. It's frustrating and boring at the same time, and it just has no point whatsoever. You get caught, you have to redo the section. Now combine this with awful camera and controls. Oh, the FUN!
Oh, and the combat. Dull, buggy and boring to death. I honestly don't know why they put combat in this. Luckily you don't get to fight a lot, but still... it's like Serious Sam with crosswords in it. It breaks the flow. Badly.
You will control 3 characters throughout the game:
She's the "main" character of the game, and gets the most screentime. Some people disliked her, but I actually liked her since the beginning.
He should play the role of the "Zelous assassin that will slowly come to question the dubious actions of his religious order". But he gets at most 20-30 minutes of screen time during the whole game, provided you don't get lost (which is quite hard in this game). They don't give you enough time and depth to actually see his transformation, or to actually care about him in general. Could have easily been an NPC.
By the Balance, girl.
You suck so much in this game. What a sad, sad person you've become. I loved you in TLJ, you were fantastic. Now you're an empty, self-loathing shell.
So this game has its flaws, I got it. And I forced myself to play it, because I loved the first TLJ and I really liked the story of Dreamfall. And you get to rivisit some of TLJ locations, and assist to events that you knew happened if you played TLJ. And I think this is just awesome.
So I pushed on. And I played avidly despite the awful gameplay because, well, the story is all this game has to offer, and it's actually pretty good.
And when the story is at its peak, it all abruptly ends with the BIGGEST, most cruel cliffhanger ever done. It just ends.
They managed to close a single arc about an insignificant "The Ring Girl" character that you don't really care about during the whole game. And they leave 10-15 threads not just open, but brutally cut. Including the ones about the 3 main characters, whose fate is unknown. Hell, the fate of the WORLDS is unknown. This enraged me to no ends. I played the whole game just to see the ending, and I got NOTHING out of it. It's like they ran out of money and they had to cut this short. And by "cut" I mean "just leave it this way and maybe we'll make a sequel in 8 years where we'll (hopefully) fix this mess".
I ragequit as soon as the credits began rolling.
So, TL;DR.
Awkward controls and camera management; it's impossible to enjoy the scenery. Then again, you won't be able to analyze half of the things you should be able to in a game like this. Terrible inventory system, but it's not such a big deal since the game has very few puzzles in the first place, and they are all boringly easy. Frustrating stealth sections and dull, boring combat sections, mechanics which were hastily developed and don't belong to this genre anyways. Some great characters but some terrible ones as well. Great story, but AWFUL, rage-inducing incomplete ending with huge cliffhanger.
As much as it pains me to say so,
spend money on this game. It's a 12 hours long, frustrating, and incomplete cutscene.
If you loved the first TLJ like me, wait until the last of the Dreamfall: Chapters is released, so that you can at least get a complete story out of it.

Dreamfall: The Longest Journey is a fantastic narrative-driven adventure game. I started the series because I saw the trailers for Dreamfall Chapters and wanted to get caught up on the story. I played it immediately after finishing The Longest Journey (which I reviewed
), so it was interesting to compare the two.
Dreamfall definitely holds up better than TLJ from a technical standpoint. Being able to play at 1080p and 120Hz was a breath of fresh air, and the graphics are clean and recognizable. They've also thankfully foregone the most egregious uses of classic 90’s adventure game tropes (combining an object with every other object, pixel hunting, etc.). Unfortunately in its place they put some pretty mundane combat and stealth sections, but those sections are mercifully brief and infrequent.
The story is where this series really shines, and Dreamfall definitely delivers. I don’t want to go into too many specifics, but it was very interesting and thought-provoking to say the least. As always I was very satisfied with the writing, though I felt the voice acting wasn’t as strong as The Longest Journey. It was also kinda creepy how everybody’s bodies are
stationary while talking – only their mouths move, which is slightly unsettling.
All in all I still greatly enjoyed it – though I would definitely recommend playing The Longest Journey first so you can get all the references and callbacks, plus you get to be amazed at seeing familiar places recreated in FULL THREE DEEEE. If you enjoy narrative-driven games I highly recommend it.

TL:DR  This is the worst SoulsBorne game in the series.
Cons:
Poor targetting system  You will randomly attack behind you instead of the enemy in front of you.  Spells and arrows from enemies will track you harder than they did in Dark Souls 1.  Enemies will also glitch and attack behind them to avoid getting hit by you.
Hit boxes are off, either by being shorter than the weapon or being longer than the weapon.
Enemies can hold their attacks and glide across the ground like they are ice skating, while also being able to quick attack so far their isn't an animation.  Some enemies can even double fire their bows.
The world is inconsistant, you will arrive in a new area that doesn't match up.  IE the Earthen Peak elevator that leads up to a lava filled ravine inside mountains, when you were miles away from any mountains.  Going from Majula to Heide's Tower of Flame their are sewer grates that should be present on the outside of the building but their is none.  No Man's Warf should be submerged in water, but it isn't.  You can see the Lost Bastille from No Man's Warf, but when at Heide's Tower of Flame Lost Bastille is no where in site.
Static sky boxes in every zone.
Soul memory - used to put your into a teir of collected total of souls, and you will only be match up with people around your tier level instead of the old coop/pvp mechanic.
Many of the textures look reused over and over, which makes the poor textures stand out more.
Dodging was tied to a stat Adaptability, at start you have so little iframes that rolling was about useless.  This was compounded by your armor benefiting from this stat as well.  Like a peice of armors b/c of looks, too bad it has an E rating so you will dodge worse. =/
Most of the levels are just rectangle boxes with little decor leading to another rectangle.
THE BIGGEST CON This game was release twice, which are incompatiable with each other.  If you own the Scholar of the First Sin edition, you can not play with your friends on Dark Souls II.  You can not transfer your saves over as well.
Bonfire Ascetics, allows you to reset an area but kind of like a NG+ version.  Will respawn bosses if used at correct bonfires, but the reason this is a negative, it allows experienced players to get NG+ items sooner, giving them an even greater advantage in PVP by twinking.
Healing Gems - same problem as in Demon's Souls, near infinite healing items.
Killing "trash" enemies in the zone 10 times will make them no longer respawn.  Making the game more grindy feeling and allowing you to just kill the same enemies over and over so you can just walk through empty rectangles to the boss.
Pros:
Depletion of Stamina made your attacks weaker and staminia recovery slower. (death to R1 spammers)
Added a lot more spells (miracles, pyromancy, sorceries, and the new Hexes), and casters were vaiable in pvp.
Powerstance weapons made for fun mix/match of weapons.
More options on which route to go first at the beginning of the game, but each of those paths are very very linear.
Lots, and lots, and lots of various armors to pick from.
NG+ adds more normal enemies into the zones, with addtional red phantom enemy variants sprinkled about as well.  Some of which are one time spawns, but adds a bit of caution to playing NG+ and not just beelining it to the boss b/c you remember the zone.
NG+ adds new items in areas and better versions of items, bosses will also drop new items as well.
I know this review is coming in very late, but to keep people from buying the worst version of DS2, it is needed.  If you are looking to pick this game up, go get the Scholar version (it comes with the 3 DLC), unless your friends has this version as well, then enjoy trying to make the best of it.

The archaic, paywall-enthusiast archenemy of good PC incarnations of Magic.
It demands your attention, freezing the (single-player) action if you tab: part of a programme of digital CCGs preceding Hearthstone's (et al.) self-awareness of themselves as background pastimes. If you want to play multiplayer Magic and you know the rules, use Tabletop Simulator and a variety of deck importation tools. You won't be beholden to a rules-lawyering external justice, and so doing you can play a larger variety of formats. Hell, you can even watch adult videos or browse magical subreddits with your friends in nigh real-time.
If you don't know the rules (and need a digital hand to jerk you along), or if you want some single-player campaign experience, the current iteration of Magic Duels (since 2016, or thereabouts) has much of the same gameplay with a hypothetical eternally-expansive card pool. You stand to sink way more money in the modern Duels title, but your potential return on investment drastically outstrips 2012. Going to avoid discussing Magic Online beyond claims that it's deprecated and has such an invested playerbase and virtual economy that it'd be hard to change/redeem/bring salvation to it now.
I recommend you buy Tabletop Simulator instead.

Absolutely Fantastic game. It's got creative and satisfying mechanics, a lovely soundtrack, and a really engaging story. The Hybrid action/turn-based combat is executed so well. Transistor is definitely the best game I've played all year.

Story: 5/5
The storytelling to Transistor is told through the interactions between Red, the mute singer protagonist, and her weapon possessed by her lover as well as various messages on computers you find throughout the 5-hour campaign. Plenty of blanks are left for you to fill, and the ending, although a bit confusing, is extremely open to interpretation.
Visual: 5/5
The game looks like a painting that is gradually losing its colors. At the beginning everything is colorful and brushed with bright colors but as the game progresses colors become darker and by the end there is almost no bright color. This beautiful take on artstyle really adds to the mood of the story and its themes. The city of Cloudbank is a beautiful piece of art that you will want to learn about and explore.
Sound: 5/5
The soundtrack for this game is amazing, especially the songs with lyrics. Every song felt perfectly attached to the mood of what was going on in the story at the time of whatever exploring or fighting being done at the time. The voice acting is brilliant, especially the voice of Red's lover. Sound effects for your attacks and enemy attacks fit perfectly.
Gameplay: 4/5
The combat system takes a while to get used to due to a lack of handholding, but after the learning curve it's one-of-a-kind. Abilities are obtained that can be used to experiment with various combinations of equipping some abilities to others or using them as passive effects. At death instead of returning to the last check point immediately an ability is lost until 2 checkpoints later and health is restored to max, forcing you to use the abilities you have left in new innovative ways. Time can be slowed down to make strategic decisions on what abilities to use. Limiters can be used to add challenge to the game while allowing you to level up faster.
Replayability: N/A
Will edit after I replay the game on its "new game plus" that allows replay with past unlocked abilities.
Verdict:
Transistor is an experience I have never had with any other game I have ever played. You will grow to care about the main characters, Cloudbank, and its inhabitants. The presentation value is extremely high with beautiful visuals, amazing sound design, and fantastic storytelling. The gameplay has a learning curve and can take getting used to, but once it clicks it's extremely addicting. Transistor is proof that video games can be art. If Transistor is on sale, you owe it to yourself to buy it.

Stanley Parable + McCree = Call of Juarez Gunslinger

Long Review version:
This is a solid example of how a First Person Shooter game doesn't need to be "military shooter" to be good. In fact, with the oversaturation of the genre nowadays, this game looks better and stands out throughout the years for it's own gameplay mechanic. Here below is my breakdown of Pros and Cons regarding this game:
Pros:
+ [COMEDY] Humour is spot-on, every quips Silas said during his storytelling and paired with the reaction of people who heard his story makes comedy gold
+ [STORY] despite some parts that has questionable validity due to its comedic nature, the story is, in a whole, is surprisingly good
+ [SOUNDTRACK] The soundtrack is strongly atmospheric which makes you feel like you're brought back into the wild west era, every sound of harmonica and country-style guitar is a pleasant hear
+[GAMEPLAY] second strongest after its comedy. The weapon set is appropriate, and while it's small in variety, it makes up for having its own functionality. Also the skill set is varied to create different playstyles

What a beautiful puzzle game!  The graphics really are amazing.  I never expected such intricate details and textures in a "simple puzzle game"!  The objects just look real with the shadows, reflections, and wood grain, etc.
Puzzle-wise the game also delivers.  The puzzles are numerous, unique and logical.  None of the "random connections" of some "point-n-click" animated puzzle games.  Whenever I completed a puzzle that stumped me for awhile (with only a few hints from the in-game system) I always looked back and thought to myself "how'd I miss that" or "I should have gotten that" and never once did I have a "What? That makes no sense!" reaction.  Great puzzles that are sometimes challenging, but certainly doable.
The only two minor "negatives" that can really be said is 1) it's short, which leaves you wanting more of this amazing world, and 2) it's not replayable -- but that's the nature of this type of puzzle game and I accept that.  So those aren't really negatives.  However, even though I wasn't that interested or care for the mystical story-line, it also didn't interrupt or detract from the puzzles or the beautiful environment at all.
Despite being on the short side, it's an absolutely fabulous puzzler not to be missed!  10 out of 10.
