Borderland 2 is one of the best games that I have found so far. It is a game that can challenge you for the most part mainly at the ends of each world. If you like a shooter game then I highly recommend you try this baby on for size. I don't about you but I like to shoot things!

A very RPG-ish shooter based on the Unreal 3 engine. There's a lot of content, and it's high quality. The world is quite open and the maps are well made. There's many, many hours of play available (especially with the DLC, which is worth it).
The combat is reasonable but not outstanding. The AI aren't terribly bright, but they're not terrible.
Story:
The story is OK. Kinda inconsistent in places, linear in others, but mostly reasonable. Lots of annoying and/or offputting characters, though. However, the main DLCs are mostly better than the game IMHO. Especially Dragon Keep - although that's probably a personal preference. Scarlett's Pirate is 2nd.
Script:
Funny in places, although some of the humor needs to be flushed down one of the thousands of toilets it probably came from (Perhaps some level designers mistook them for rocks??!). I also got a bit bored with the sadistic violence fetish that permeates a lot of the game (far more than most shooters, which is saying something).
Difficulty:
As with many RPGs, the difficulty is controlled by you choosing where to go based on level difference. If you want it easy, do all the side quests. Unfortunately, if you want a hard game you have to skip lots of it. There are additional "difficulty" modes (True Vault Hunter, Ultimate Vault Hunter), but they require completing the game first and starting at higher level, which doesn't solve the problem. IMHO it really needs a difficulty setting or slider right from the start.
Misc:
Suffers a bit from console-itis - saves are crude (just checkpoints plus gear/quests), UI feels geared for console and it has a few minor console-ish UI bugs.
IMHO it could do with a few more interesting mechanics or a more complex gear and skill system, again I'm blaming console-itis.
Overall, a good game to kill many hours in, just remember that you control the difficulty by where you go. And get the GOTY for the DLC.

This is a beautiful, immersive and meticulously detailed game, the amazing gameplay of which will reel in franchise fans and newcomers alike. While Final Fantasy XIV is unlike its single player predecessors, the lore recognizeable by the long time FF fans creates a story with depth and character interactions generally forgotton by MMO creators.
As such, the attention to detail regarding idiosyncracies of certain characters is conveyed through their speech, and this attention to detail extends to the environment as well. Small things that one would barely notice can be found in the game, such as the pattern of shadow created by light shining through a grate, as well as that shadow adjusting alongside the in game time of day; the stitching on armors and clothing, right down to the shadows created by them on the player; and many more details that add to the game's wonderful environment.
Within this environment is gameplay that is executed uniquely, and superbly. Skills operate in a style familiar to MMO players, with a relatively short global cooldown, and individual skill cooldowns which vary depending on the strength and usefulness of the skill. Combat utilizes a TP, similar to a stamina system, while magic utilizes the classic MP. Some magic skills of which rely on a casting time, which occurs at the same time as the global cooldown, making casting fluent yet balanced. Skills can be clicked, hotkeyed, setup through user macros, and so forth. The combat truly appeals to every style of play, as well as every player through its broad range of classic Final Fantasy jobs that players can quest as.
The questing is reminiscent of other MMOs, and yet the game approaches these concepts in ways that makes them less of a grind than they could be. Rather than the traditional, "Kill 50 of this monster," or ,"Gather 30 of this material," the quests bring these numbers down to 5s and 3s, which allows the player to take the time to actually understand WHY they are doing what they are doing.
Furthermore, many players will actually be ABLE to do what they want to be doing, for the game has been optimized wonderfully. Areas are divided by loading zones, but the transition between these is so fluent and quick that it took me this long to even remember they were there. With easy to use presets such as "High end PC" or "Low end laptop," adjusting settings is user friendly. If you would like to adjust things yourself, there is of course an option for custom settings.
Yet what truly sold me on the game, what I believe to be the greatest of its qualities, is the job change system. Many MMOs have you make one character, choose one class or destiny for them, and that's that. You're either forced to pay for some sort of reset, make a new character, completely start over or combinations of the above. NOT in Final Fantasy XIV. By simply equipping a new weapon, your stats, gear, abilities, everything switches to the role that weapon relates to, and you can head back to lower level areas to train yourself anew. This is done WITHOUT losing any of your previous progress. In fact certain jobs can use abilities learned from other classes, and often need to in order to reach their full potential. The best part is that no mistakes can be made with this system. There is no "woops, you didn't train your warrior class so your strength is too low," there is some minor ability point allocation, but this is done easily and can easily be reversed. A single character can serve you for every adventure, and as such, the character creation allows you to bring that perfect character to life.
One truly could spend a few hours just in the character creator, detailing everything from the muscularity of your character, to their eye color, to the color of the tips of their hair vs the rest of their hair, etcetera, etcetera. There are four basic races each with two deviations in appeance to begin with, and the next perk that comes along is that you don't have to worry about "which race has the best looking armor." Armor is purely based on class, scales based on size, and doesn't vary from race to race, only between genders. There exists a range of emotions to emulate via these characters in game, if roleplay at all interests you, and the community has considerably less..."game challenged" players than other MMOs.
Worth every cent of the subscription fee, Final Fantasy XIV is a game whose developers LISTEN to their community (see the 2.1 Patch) and who truly care about their game. The friendly community, and the freedom and beauty offered by the environment will leave you wondering why you didn't play this game all along.

I originally played ESO in 2014 when it was first released, and at the time did not find it all that appealing. To be fair, I was expecting a "Skyrim Online" experience (urealistic, I know) and still very into a couple of other games so I quit playing after only a short while.
Fast forward to earlier this year when I decided to pick it back up again. Boy howdy, was I pleasantly surprised!!! In the past 3 years, ESO has really found its stride and grown into itself. One Tamriel gave it the quality-of-life change it needed (and that every MMO needs, honestly) which is level scaling. No longer are you confined to play in certain zones at certain levels; the entire world is now wide open to you, beginning at level 1! This means that every zone is frequented by players of all levels, and anybody is available to quickly get together to defeat world bosses, daedric anchors, and public dungeons. It also means you can zone into a dungeon with players of any level between 10 and 690, and you no longer have to wait until you're caught up with your friends/guild mates, or swap around alts, in order to group up and enjoy content together. You can quest with your friends in any zone and don't have to worry about anybody leveling too quickly or too slowly. Just group up and enjoy the game together!
I happily played through that open world for a good while, until I decided I liked the game well enough to purchase the Imperial Edition. Because I wanted a mount, and I definitely wanted to re-create my Imperial from Skyrim who had been one of my favorite characters in that game.
This led to me jumping into the subscription shortly afterwards, because I wanted to experience Dark Brotherhood and Thieves Guild without actually purchasing the DLC. Instead I figured "for $15 you can try everything and see if you even like it, before you buy it." The difference was immediate, and remarkable. My bags magically emptied themselves of crafting materials (unlimited crafting bag, hooray!), and my bank space doubled. I quickly deleted a couple of "mule alts" I had created for storage, and instead started creating a couple of more "live" characters to actualy play and enjoy the game with and experiment with different race/class combinations.
In July I was already deeply invested into the game and into my characters, and had joined some active trading guilds. So a few weeks after Morrowind was released, I bought it without hesitation and immediately created a Warden (who is one of my favorite characters, still), and began my journey through Vvardenfell. I never did really play TES Morrowind, so there was no nostalgia factor involved, but I did enjoy the zone and the quests and the storylines immensely.
I have 7 characters that I play all the time, and am in 5 guilds that I enjoy a whole lot. The ESO community is extremely friendly and supportive, especially people in active guilds (please don't judge the maturity of the ESO players based on zone chat; that's not where most of us can be found).

This is a beautiful, immersive and meticulously detailed game, the amazing gameplay of which will reel in franchise fans and newcomers alike. While Final Fantasy XIV is unlike its single player predecessors, the lore recognizeable by the long time FF fans creates a story with depth and character interactions generally forgotton by MMO creators.
As such, the attention to detail regarding idiosyncracies of certain characters is conveyed through their speech, and this attention to detail extends to the environment as well. Small things that one would barely notice can be found in the game, such as the pattern of shadow created by light shining through a grate, as well as that shadow adjusting alongside the in game time of day; the stitching on armors and clothing, right down to the shadows created by them on the player; and many more details that add to the game's wonderful environment.
Within this environment is gameplay that is executed uniquely, and superbly. Skills operate in a style familiar to MMO players, with a relatively short global cooldown, and individual skill cooldowns which vary depending on the strength and usefulness of the skill. Combat utilizes a TP, similar to a stamina system, while magic utilizes the classic MP. Some magic skills of which rely on a casting time, which occurs at the same time as the global cooldown, making casting fluent yet balanced. Skills can be clicked, hotkeyed, setup through user macros, and so forth. The combat truly appeals to every style of play, as well as every player through its broad range of classic Final Fantasy jobs that players can quest as.
The questing is reminiscent of other MMOs, and yet the game approaches these concepts in ways that makes them less of a grind than they could be. Rather than the traditional, "Kill 50 of this monster," or ,"Gather 30 of this material," the quests bring these numbers down to 5s and 3s, which allows the player to take the time to actually understand WHY they are doing what they are doing.
Furthermore, many players will actually be ABLE to do what they want to be doing, for the game has been optimized wonderfully. Areas are divided by loading zones, but the transition between these is so fluent and quick that it took me this long to even remember they were there. With easy to use presets such as "High end PC" or "Low end laptop," adjusting settings is user friendly. If you would like to adjust things yourself, there is of course an option for custom settings.
Yet what truly sold me on the game, what I believe to be the greatest of its qualities, is the job change system. Many MMOs have you make one character, choose one class or destiny for them, and that's that. You're either forced to pay for some sort of reset, make a new character, completely start over or combinations of the above. NOT in Final Fantasy XIV. By simply equipping a new weapon, your stats, gear, abilities, everything switches to the role that weapon relates to, and you can head back to lower level areas to train yourself anew. This is done WITHOUT losing any of your previous progress. In fact certain jobs can use abilities learned from other classes, and often need to in order to reach their full potential. The best part is that no mistakes can be made with this system. There is no "woops, you didn't train your warrior class so your strength is too low," there is some minor ability point allocation, but this is done easily and can easily be reversed. A single character can serve you for every adventure, and as such, the character creation allows you to bring that perfect character to life.
One truly could spend a few hours just in the character creator, detailing everything from the muscularity of your character, to their eye color, to the color of the tips of their hair vs the rest of their hair, etcetera, etcetera. There are four basic races each with two deviations in appeance to begin with, and the next perk that comes along is that you don't have to worry about "which race has the best looking armor." Armor is purely based on class, scales based on size, and doesn't vary from race to race, only between genders. There exists a range of emotions to emulate via these characters in game, if roleplay at all interests you, and the community has considerably less..."game challenged" players than other MMOs.
Worth every cent of the subscription fee, Final Fantasy XIV is a game whose developers LISTEN to their community (see the 2.1 Patch) and who truly care about their game. The friendly community, and the freedom and beauty offered by the environment will leave you wondering why you didn't play this game all along.

If you played TLJ (The Longest Journey) then you'll like the story of this game, but quickly realize how big of a change there was in gameplay mechanics of this sequel. As a very big fan of the original, I have to admit, at the start off this game, with the different controls and lackluster main character, I was thinking I wouldn't be a fan of this one and in turn, would end up being disappointed or would avoid the 3rd game, Dreamfall: Chapters- this ended up not being the case. The story is a 3rd person adventure/puzzle (WSAD/arrow key movement, not Point & Click) with minimal fighting and frequent puzzles. The puzzles aren't terribly challenging and only 1 part of the game has you do a lot of back & forth "fetching". You swap between 3 roles or characters in the game with the main character being a new girl, Zoe. Chat can be fast forwarded with the space bar, game is saveable at any idle time (non-conversation/cut scene), and, sadly, the game does not allow full screen windowed, which is something I enjoy in many games due to my dual monitor set up.
Pros
-Game is now realized in a full 3D environment. Graphically much better than TLJ.
-Main character, Zoe, grows and changes from when introduced to the end of the game. I really appreciated this as I initially was very uninterested in her.
-Story developed nicely. It was slow in the start and middle as it built up. The last couple hours of the game I felt very attached and well immersed.
-Puzzles weren't bad and most were easily solved without external assistance. I do want to call out I always use a guide in point & click games because, honestly, I just don't have the time for all the trial and error and I really do enjoy the stories of these games.
-Once you figure out the controls, the WSAD keys, Space Bar, and Tab can control your inventory, action wheel, and every other in game action needed- very easy to play from a laid back position.
Cons
-Movement and camera control gave me motion sickness during the game, especially at the start as I adjusted sensitivity and tried multiple configurations to find the "sweet spot". Eventually I gave up and primarily used the movement turn keys to control the camera turn.
-The combat was dumb. Controls were clunky and fighting was unneeded. This was during the time where game devs were trying new features and hitting as many check boxes as possible.
-Main character was kinda pathetic in the introduction and start of the game. I really felt she started to hit her stride when she arrived at Japan.
-Focus mode was mostly pointless and forgotten the majority of the game. A couple puzzles required it, otherwise it didn't do too much.
-1 Part of the game had you go fetch quest items, back and forth, twice. I really missed the ability the double click the edge of the map to instantly move- something found in other Point & Click Adventure games (Deponia trilogy & TLJ, for example).
TL;DR/Bottom line: Get the original, The Longest Journey, and this game, the sequel, Dreamfall: The Longest Journey, as soon as you can afford it. I highly recommend them both and they go on sale together for $6.24 at the lowest. The 3rd game, Dreamfall: Chapters released 2 days ago (10.21.2014) and is, at the time of this writing, receiving very positive reviews.

I recently played through both The Longest Journey and Dreamfall again. TLJ is a masterpiece in storytelling and has some of the most well written characters in any game. Dreamfall is the sequel to TLJ and it follows a new protagonist and has a new plot but it all takes place in Stark and Arcadia again.
Now, I need to make this perfectly clear: TLJ is a classic point-and-click adventure. Dreamfall is not. Dreamfall is a third-person action/adventure game. This sets the game apart quite a bit; they are not the same type of game.
The lore is definetly the main part of both games and it's amazing. The two worlds, Stark and Arcadia, has a lot of wonderfull characters and creatures that you encounter. Dreamfall continues the story of April Ryan as well but the game is mainly about Zoë, the new protagonist. You get to meet some of the people and characters that helped April in the first game and quite a few new ones. For the sake of the lore, Dreamfall does bring a lot to the table but it's a whole new game that tries to introduce quite a lot of new features and action elements; for good and bad.
Let me elaborate. First of all; it's in 3D and not 2D any more. You no longer point-and-click but you control Zoë with the WASD-keys. To find/view/interact things or people of interest you have to walk up to them and press a button. You also have a targeting function where you can view or interact with things from a distance. They have also added a fighting mecanic in Dreamfall in instances where you have to fight. This makes this game a whole new plattform and moves from classic adventure to fore action than adventure.
Needless to say, this upset a lot of fans of the original game and to me it comes across as it's trying to hard to bring a modern design into the genre. It still works but it's quite annoying at times when you get stuck in camera angles and what not.
But this game (weird controls or not) is still a great game thanks to the mentioned lore, amazing story and well written characters so I can only recommend it. I still recommend that play TLJ before this game; not only for the lore but because it's one of the greatest games ever made. Dreamfall is like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child of TLJ but you need to look past the quirky controls and experience the ride.

TLDR: Magnificent story, mildly annoying controls & combat, great voice acting and dialogue, moderately fun but sparse mini-games. If you can get past the controls/combat and enjoy a good story, play it.
Dreamfall: the Longest Journey is not a direct sequel to the original Longest Journey (apparently that is planned for later release after Dreamfall Chapters) but is set in the same world(s) ten years after the events in Longest Journey and involves some of the same characters. The main protagonist, Zoe Castillo, is a new character, but you'll also be able to play as characters from the original game. It's also a departure from the original in that it's not a point-and-click adventure game - instead the developers tried to use a 3rd-person over the shoulder perspective and threw in some combat and stealth sequences to break up the story. However, even the developers admit that these added sequences are not very fun but thankfully there are relatively few of them in the game.
The 3rd-person over the shoulder controls are not very well done and it will take you a little while of fiddling with the settings to get them to a playable point. There is very little tutorial (if it can be called that) or direction given to the player on how to play but the controls are fairly simple so this doesn't seem to impact gameplay in a negative way. The UI is incredibly minimalist to the point that you don't even see it unless you're in a fight (health bars) or you open up your inventory. There are far fewer items used in this game and you will instead be talking to people a lot more.
The conversation system displays a series of one-word dialogue choices which when moused-over, are elaborated on by the controlled character at the time giving you a good sense of what the character will say if that choice is selected. The choices often indicate a direction that the conversation should follow (aggressive, friendly, tell the truth, etc.) rather than a specific sentence or phrase. My one problem with the conversation system is that the option to exit several conversations (Thank you) was also used as a non-exiting conversation branch, so I would recommend always mousing over the options before selecting to make sure that you don't miss a branch. I particularly enjoyed the conversations with Crow and being able to see and control the conversation between two opposing sides.
The story itself is fantastic and will send you on several twists and turns through the game world, and getting to see the game from different perspectives. It's all set on an Earth split into two - the futuristic/cyberpunk "normal" world (Stark) being the science half, and a fantasy-themed world (Arcadia) the magic half. I won't go into the story so as not to spoil it, but you get to adventure in both worlds and examine the relationships between them. The dialogue was also very engaging - usually thought-provoking and even sometimes laugh-out-loud funny.
At some points there are mini-games to hack or unlock things. They are fairly simple but fun and do not interrupt the story much if at all. The same cannot be said, sadly, for the combat and stealth sections, but again there thankfully aren't very many of them - or at least not many of them that will be hard/annoying. The stealth usually involves clicking on objects to hide and using your stealth walk (right CTRL). There were only one or two points in the game where I had trouble getting through the stealth, but the game seems to always autosave when you get to one so you thankfully don't have to replay too many cut scenes if you fail. In longer stealth sequences (the catacombs come to mind) I recommend saving and saving often whenever you're in a "safe" spot so you don't have to re-sneak all the way back. For the combat sequences you'll never really get stuck, as once you figure out how to beat the very simple AI you'll never lose a fight again. Hint: characters always block after you hit them, and you happen to have an attack that always passes through a block... you're welcome!
Overall, I think the Metacritic score (75%) is almost spot-on, but for me personally I absolutely loved this game despite its flaws. If you enjoyed the first game and want more of the same style of story, or if you enjoy great story-telling in general, definitely play this game. If you haven't played the first game and enjoy point-and-click adventure games though, I'd really recommend playing the original Longest Journey first. It isn't required to play Dreamfall strictly speaking, but you will enjoy Dreamfall a lot more if you do and the references in Dreamfall about the original will open up the storylines from the Longest Journey that you would otherwise miss.

Dreamfall: The Longest Journey was entertaining to play, but it didn't hold a candle to The Longest Journey. The whole game made me wish for less tacked-on combat and stealth and more of the point-and-click puzzle solving that made TLJ a great game. The few puzzles it did feature weren't much of a challenge and didn't require much logical thinking to solve.
Still, the voice acting, environments, and entertaining characters made this game worth playing. I loved seeing all of the familiar faces as well as some interesting new characters. Despite being released in 2006, the environments delivered some solid scenery porn that holds up today. The story was also compelling enough to make me play to the end.
With Dreamfall Chapters in development, this is a must play. If you can overlook its shortcomings and focus on the story, you'll definitely enjoy Dreamfall: The Longest Journey.

While only about half as long as The Longest Journey (no pun intended) Dreamfall has a much different feel to it. The characters are likeable enough and the return of some fond favourites does still keep the series trademark sense of humour; I'm looking at you Crow! Even so, I wouldn't rate it as highly as The Longest Journey, but it still hits those important "life as a journey" ideas and questions.
***Potential Spoiler Alert***
Additionally, to those that might be put off by the rather abrupt abd confusing ending, Dreamfall was never meant to be a standalone game but part of a trilogy which, due to unforeseen circumstances, was cut a little short. Thankfully, Red Thread Games will (or have depending on when you read this review) be releasing Dreamfall Chapters which will not only finish the games stroyline. but also start new ones with new characters; and hopefully some old ones too(?).

Here's a quick summary of Pros and Cons:
+ New Gameplay and Control Style
+ Leveling up is challenging (aka no dumb AI)
+ Massive Exploration
- Unhelpful Community, and social is non-existent
- This recent MMO will have equipment durability
- Despite combat update, still few classes viable
This game offers you several ways to control characters, you can use Mouse (Point and Click), Keyboard (arrow key), and
even gamepad.
For some classes, such as Wizard and Archer, it's recommended using Mouse because it's easier to target.  For Swordsman and Cleric, it's recommended using gamepad or keyboard because of Melee.
I like how good this game it is on implementing these control scheme.  And it's the only MMO so far, that won't give me disadvantage for using gamepad -- you can assign up to 40 skills into a gamepad!
This is a grinding game, period.  If you don't like a heavy PvE content game, you won't like this game.
But the difference between this one and others is that, you WILL die while grinding and going through story mode.  It gives you challenge, and I like it.
Most of games I played gives players dumb AI on story mode until the endgame content.   But this game won't spoil you... oh no.  You better prepare.
To me, this is a plus.  And I hate fighting against dumb AI until endgame content, it bores me.
As you explore through story mode, you will notice many maps are not related to story.  They are here simply for you to discover and enjoy its gorgeous art.
Sometimes, I like the take time of the grinding and just to do exploration, side quest, and  collecting items.
It's like an single player game with a lot of extra content for you to do even you finish the story.
I am going to say it first and foremost.  In-game community sucks.  Try to ask a question, they tell you to google it!
I have also asked a question on other games too, and they answer me.
If you are expecting a nice and helpful community, you will be extremely disappointed because rarely did people will try to help you.
On top of that, due to the nature of class system.  If you want to make a guild, you NEED to pick a Swordsman class and specifically pick Templar when you can pick a new job.  This will severely limit your ability on dealing damage, because most of Templar skill is related to Guild function.
As a result, Guild is a lot less than other games, you rarely see Guild is recruiting.  If they are, they only recruit top of tops -- you must be close or near max level cap in order to be consider.  Otherwise, don't even bother.
This kind of social limitation strongly hurts a MMO games, a LOT.
Do I need to say more?  A equipment durability still exists these days.  It's extremely annoying.  It doesn't add anything to gameplay.
If you plan to play Fencer class, let me warn you that Rapier weapon (Fencer's weapon) has less durability than others.
One way to deal it, is to use player-open repair shop to "over-repair" it, so that you will have more durability than usual.
It's frustrating that I always need to go back to town while exploring maps and immersing myself in gameplay and quest.
It breaks the experience and atmosphere.
Although combat update is an attempt to make more class viable, the only class viable in Swordsman tree is Doppelsoeldner.  Hoplite and Cataphract is no longer viable.  Peltasta is rarely picked these days because you no longer need taunt and tank at all
At least for Swordsman, variety becomes less.
On top of that, nowadays general recommendation is less CON and ever before, and putting all of your point into either STR and INT.  It fails on one purpose game developers trying to achieve in the first place -- putting/encourage more variety in this game.
Overall, my recommendation to this game is neutral.  If you can look over bad community, equipment durability and monotone (lack diversity), this game may be for you.
It has great Gameplay and control scheme, massive exploration and challenge AI.
Otherwise, I suggest you to look elsewhere.

I think Dark Souls 2 is overall a bad game due to three main issues, being level design, enemy design and the core combat loop.
Level design is bad due to an over-reliance on cheesy traps, sudden un-telegraphed ambushes and other similar elements that effectively punishes the player for exploration in an otherwise exploration centric game, and also promotes a trial-and-error style of gameplay or the use of a guide.  This can work for certain games, but when the game actively punishes you for being bad at it (reduced HP every time you die) this becomes an issue, especially when it takes a while in some cases to get back to where you were.  These mechanics work in a precision/troll platformer with instant respawns (I wanna be the guy and super meatboy for example) but not very well in the context of Dark Souls 2 and simply makes the player feel unwelcome rather than challenged, like the game was designed by someone who hates you rather than someone who wants to challenge you and see you grow.
Enemy design is bad for many of the same reasons that level design is bad, but also because enemies feel unpolished.  With many weird animation faults such as lack of proper telegraphs on impactful attacks and unclear blocking animations along with the loss of the enemy combo canceling mechanic that existed in Dark Souls 1 (enemies will continue their combo only if the player is within range, otherwise they will stop and do something else like walk closer) and just a general feel of floatyness, where enemies just seem to flow between attacks rather than emphasizing each one which leads to the player often wondering how they were even damaged at all, and leaves enemies feeling more like a hostile cloud of hitboxes rather than a concrete creature which obeys the same rules you do.
Which segways in the poor combat loop, with many issues such as adaptability messing with player muscle memory as ENB mentions, as well as other issues such as floaty dodge rolls with no immediately clear beginning and end as well as a lack of distinguishing between the fast, medium and slow rolls apart from just the same animation slowed down each time.  The dreaded input buffering also rears it ugly head again, with players executing attacks they were attempting after being stunned or flinched without them actually wanting to.  Blocking also feels very sluggish, with it not being clear how soon after pressing the block button you will actually block.  Weapons that attack from behind a block also behave very strangely, with you being able to continue performing a block-attack without even having block pressed if you keep pressing attack after performing a block-attack, on top of that block-attacks are performed toward where your trying to move, rather than toward what you have locked on.
In general Dark Souls 2 feels like a very unfinished game that absolutely lacks the precision to make it's high challenge level enjoyable, feeling more like a constant struggle with the controls rather than a fluid combat experience.  As a standalone game, it is outshone by many other action RPGs, such as Nioh, and compared to other games from Fromsoftware, especially Dark Souls 1 and Bloodborne, it feels like a poor imitation, playing more like an unfinished mod of Dark Souls 1 designed by someone who wanted to troll players I Wanna Be The Guy style.  It lacks the former's charm, cohesive level design, tighter controls, vastly superior enemy design and general feeling of fairness that makes its high difficulty an invitation to challenge and improve yourself rather than an endless source of frustration directed primarily at the game itself.
TL;DR, Dark Souls 2 is an unfinished shell of a game, which when compared to Dark Souls 1, or other more recent ARPGs like Nioh, leaves a bad taste in your mouth.

Dark Souls 2 is a fantastic game in its own right that suffers from comparisons to the flawed masterpiece that is Dark Souls. I agree with many of the criticisms that have been thrown at this sequel, such as boss design that can't even compare to the first game (with a few exceptions), the world that seems rushed and nonsensical, and the enemy encounters that are trivialized by simply baiting them one by one.
Despite these flaws, I'd be hard pressed to call Dark Souls 2 a bad game. From my time with it totalling around 300 hours on console and pc combined, I've thoroughly enjoyed most of it. I love the gameplay that presented more viable options for builds than the first, I love the lore that the minimalistic story is built around, I love many of the individual environments (especially in the DLC), and I love the feelings of futility and hopelessness that permeate the entire experience.
While my favourite in the series remains the first Dark Souls by a considerably large margin, I still love the second entry in the franchise and I highly recommend you check it out and form your own opinion on it.
Also, if you do care about PvP and/or slightly better graphical fidelity, go with Scholar of the First Sin. Otherwise, I'd recommend this edition. The new enemy placements don't do much for the experience except artifically inflate the difficulty.

I never intended to review this game, but after beating it four times, I think I should. Somehow, I keep coming back to it. Time to dissect why.
The gameplay doesn't happen in the present; the protagonist, Silas Greaves, is telling stories of his past, and that's what you play through. As a direct result, the levels change in front of you as other characters jump in or Greaves does a bait-and-switch. This is something that I don't see many other games do, and it's a very good addition to this one.
Speaking of which, the characters listening to Silas in the bar all add something to the story in one way or another. Depending on what they're doing, the gameplay changes. In fact, in one of the stages, two of them tell their own version of what happened that day before Silas chimes in. That level is, I think, one of the best in this game. It's also very interesting to see how Silas catches up to his own past, so to speak. (I can't say more without spoiling the plot)
Lastly, the duels. This, I think, is the main draw (pun not intended) to this game. In almost every level, you engage in a quick-draw with one (or two, sometimes) of the Wild West's most famous outlaws. It's fun, it's engaging, and it's unique.
Also, I think this game is the reason for why I really like revolvers now.

This, in my opinion, is as close as a game can come to perfection. It's beautiful and artistic both in its aesthetic as well as its storytelling. It has a great story if you dig a bit to find it. It's got some comedic elements here and there, such as rating your jumps from jumppads later in the game. Its got a deep backstory and a beautiful sci-fi setting, with a bit of apocolypse thrown in. It has great characters, representing each and every ability or 'function' you find as a person who all have their own stories.
That's not even getting into the gameplay. This game has a very intruiging system that doesn't take much to get into and takes a lot of experimenting to master. Your functions all have 3 modes: active ability, upgrade, or passive, and you mix and match throughout the game to find the best combos. The health system is also inventive: When your health runs out, you lose your most valuable active ability along with all of its upgrade functions, and so on and so on until you die. This forces you to think with your placements of valuable functions, and not to rely too much on one super-function.
In conclusion, this game mixes story and gameplay to create an incredibly meaningful experience. I would highly reccomend playing this game for yourself, or at least watching it, though that's not quite the same experience.

Honestly, I was never crazy about Bastion.  I thought it was overhyped, so I held off on getting Transistor, since I figured it wasn't for me.  Despite getting good reviews, I imagined that the good reviews Transistor got were probably for the same reasons that Bastion was well reviewed.  So reasons I had not to like Bastion's awkwardly trying to do everything gameplay with an infantile aesthetic made me skeptical that I'd like what seemed like a similar game from the same developer.
I was terribly mistaken… Transistor is infinitely better than Bastion.  I picked up Transistor during a sale, after watching some tempting YouTube videos that showed the thematic elegance of the game (I have a softspot for cyberpunk) and the awesome tactical "pause" ability.
(gameplay) This game blew me away, the gameplay is phenomenal: action rpgs are in the long run mindless and repetitive, but despite being an arpg, Transistor doesn't fall prey to this problem because it continuously confronts you with intricate puzzles.
(customization) There's really cool rpg elements for *how* you customize your abilities by either equipping them to one of four ability slots or using some abilities to enhance other abilities (for example, you can equip an explode ability or you can use that ability to add some explosive aoe to another ability).
(aesthetics) Sometimes a game has good gameplay and rpg elements, but i'm not so crazy about the aesthetic.  However, Transistor pulls off the cyberpunk aesthetic with some unique genius.  It captures the thematic in every little intricacy, and it brings out the aesthetic with vibrant handdrawn art.  In almost all games, I rarely care for the music (and I mute music in those games and launch iTunes in the background), but here we actually get an amazing soundtrack that sounds like Radiohead + Portishead + some postrock mixed in.
Transistor is in a class of its own.  I don't think I've ever been more blown away by a game…

I will start by saying: its not as bad as people are saying it is.  And ill tell you why.
Sure this game is very different from Amnesia The Dark Decent.  But i wouldnt want it to be identical to TDD.  It does have less features and less gameplay and it doesnt offer really any type of survival elements to the game.  But what i did was went into this game as if i hadent played TDD before.
I will start with its cons.
CONS:
You have no inventory.  Makes the game feel and play weird.
Your latern has no oil meter so you can have it out for forever.  This is kinda a pro and a con because it makes lighting easier but also takes away that sense of anxiety about your oil level and the fight of trying to find more oil.  Kinda ruining survival.  Still good though regardless.
Puzzles are much more carry item orriented (since there is no inventory.)
Puzzles are much harder to figure out on your first try.  This is ok but its almost a unfair type of confusing.
Theres some fps stutters but thats only the game so its not too bad.
You can barely pick up anything.  In TDD you were able to pick up nearly every entity found inside of the game.  Like you could run around and pick up random rocks and throw the around.  Pick up books and pens and tables and so many more things. But in A Machine for Pigs you can almost exclusivly pick up puzzle items.  But oddly enough you can pick up every single chair found in the game which is strange.
Enemies feel a little underpowered.  It doesnt make them not scary just not too brutal if they actually do see you.
This game is based more around its fear factor and continual scares then the actual survival and hiding parts.
PROS:
The story is almost excelent.  Yes it copies nearly all aspects of its own story from TDD but its ok cause theyre both a part of the same series.
Voice acting is actually amazing.  Its kinda rough at first but then it gets very good in the more stressful moments of the game.
The visuals are good and dont really lack in any area.  It just looks like a reskinned TDD.
Enemies make good sounds.
Puzzles make you think (as i said above sometimes a little bit more then others.)
The game still being extremely linear, offers some variation when approaching paths.  It takes a little bit away from the full on exploration and puts more into the visuals of the map and what to see.  Because in TDD youre always looking around for tinderboxes and oil and stuff.
The overall story is a 8/10.  Its still sloppy in some areas but it still is intriguing.
Many more animations.  (Without telling any spoilers)  You do get to see actual other people move and run.  You only get to see them for a split second for most of the time, but still, it feels a little bit more complete on the animation side.  Overall every literal in game aspect feels slighly more polished than TDD.  But TDD offers more features and gameplay.
OVERALL:  AMFPigs isnt that bad of a game.  I reccomend grabbing this game when it goes on an extreme sale.  Cause i only have 4 hours on this game and it was all the time from playing it from start to finish.  So not too much gameplay and gametime.  Id give it around a 8/10 or 7/10 overall.  But in all honesty it still doesnt deserve that.  Going from TDD to AMFPigs is very dumb-downing. It makes TDD seem like it was the better and more inovative sequal instead of AMFPigs.  So i should give it a 6/10 but i dont think i can draw myself to say that.  So ill say it gets a 8/10 or a 7/10 but really im saying its more like a 6/10.  If you get what i mean.
BUT still, its worth to play this game if you can get it for under $5.  I got it on sale for $2.50.  Which in that case makes it totally worth it.
ALSO ONE MORE THING:  This is another con that i thought would be best to say last.  Ahem... I NEVER DIED ONCE DURING THE WHOLE GAME.
I never died once.  Somehow.  In TDD its nearly easy to die.  But even in the most stressful run away parts in the game i never died.  And id say that i myself (no pride meant to be implied) am pretty good at video games, but i still felt like i should have been pushed around or bullied by the difficuly of this game.  But i wasnt. It really is just a walking simulator with a good story and a good couple of scares.  So just make sure that you keep that in mind if you get the game.  Youll be doing a lot of holding down the 'w' key and moving your mouse around.
I hope that you can enjoy this game.  Cause i still did even tho TDD is light years better.

A walking simulator with a horror theme! What a world we live in.
Like the first Amnesia, you can die. Unlike the first Amnesia, it's not annoying at all and in fact you are often placed ahead of your obstacles when you do, so repetition is rare. The focus here is strongly on the walking and exploring.
The story is unsettling, but not overly scary or horror-filled. You'll see lots of pigs or pig-like things, and a machine. Really, the title isn't full of exaggeration or poetry: this is literally the backdrop for the game setting.
The story itself is interesting, and in true walking simulator form, has pretentious ruminations on life and death. There is also a (somewhat expected) plot twist. Given that the story is dripped out and the setting is creepy, there aren't too many surprises. Speaking of, there aren't really any jump scares either so don't go into this expecting to pee your pants.
Graphically, not too bad: it's dark and grim but it all works. If you love Victorian brickworks, this game has you covered.
Recommended: 3 out of 5. A tolerably good time but nothing extraordinary.

This is the sort of game that you either love it, hate it, or find yourself swinging suddenly from one to the other.
Its a sequel to the longest journey which was originally a point and click adventure/puzzle game with a very strong plot. This is sort of similar, except that its more adventure based and is only the beginning of the game with more chapters to come.
What you need to be aware of  however is that the creators added what is possibly one of the worst cameras ever and definately the worst combat feature ever. This, in my opinion as someone who loved its predecessor, ruined the game. There were times were I simply wanted to stop playing because the combat was messed up. It seemed very basic, as though they added it in as a feature which means that the controls are simple but clunky and the characters movements make it very hard to actually succeed. Combat occurs in the game often enough  for the creators to seriously put more effort in, but you get so drawn into the plot that it is easy to forget about until it appears again.
The camera is awful at first but you can get used to it after a while although the awkwardness rears its ugly head once combat begins. The plot however is fantastic, exactly what you would have expected as a sequel to the longest journey. So don't misunderstand me, I would totally recommend this game purely because of the plot alone. The camera and combat are just things that you need to be aware of before you start playing. Also that the game is unfinished but you can still get a few good hours of play from it, although it ends quite suddenly and abruptly at a major point in the plot.
Long story short, the game has many flaws but can stand alone on the strength of the plot.

+Excelente voice acting, efectos de sonido y musica tipica de un western.
+Los controles responden a lo que haces y la mayor parte del tiempo, tus muertes son por tu culpa, repito, la mayor parte del tiempo.

Super recomendado, vale los 15 dolares, si lo ves en sale por menos de eso, vale la pena comprarlo y jugarlo, el juego es corto y al estar dividido por capitulos es facil jugar un rato e irse a hacer otras cosas.

The Elder Scrolls Online : Tamriel Unlimited is basically RIFT the MMORPG (3rd person view). You can also play it like Skyrim by scrolling the mousewheel to first-person view. However, the gameplay is far worse compared to what is currently in the market. It is definitely below World of Warcraft and Guild Wars. The whole game is a generic MMO land where you go to a zone, do kill/fetch quests, rinse and repeat. The only good quests that they put effort into designing are the main quests levels. All other quests just follow the generic pattern. Oh, there's also no diving, so no underwater level in this game.
Gameplay-wise, it's like any other MMO. The only difference being how they input skills. Skills are similar in Skyrim where you have to use the skill in order to level it up. If you go around sucking energy from crystals, you will get Skill Points which you can spend to level up your Skill. If you level up, you get attribute points to pump into Magicka (Blue), Health (Red) or Stamina (Green). Depending on your build, you can choose to go down the path of a mage, fighter/tank, assassin/archer.
The Pay To Win is also really ridiculous. They literally lock players out of essential core mechanics like the Craft Bag, unless you pay cash. If you pay cash, you can even get a 42,700 gold Horse for free. I really don't understand whether Zenimax and Bethesda care that it will affect the gameplay.
Conclusion, just skip this game. It's another Pay To Win game using the RIFT MMO. It's so generic that I wonder whether they even bothered to make a game. It's like Zenimax and Bethesda have decided to insult their customers and playerbase instead of making good games.
1. Amazing Advertisement
The amount of money going into the Elder Scrolls ads must have been the bulk of where the money went.
1. Pay To Win
It's amazing how much core mechanics is locked behind a paywall. If you get an ESO Plus subscription, you get a horse, craft bags, access to Cyrodil,etc. The cash currency is called Crown Packs where you can get 750 CP for $10.80 or 21000 CP for $199.
2. It's RIFT
This is basically another MMORPG reskinned with The Elder Scrolls theme. It's the same idea where you have magical rifts/portals opening up at predetermined locations. In the Elder Scrolls, you have big iron rings floating in the sky instead.
3. Is Everything Humanoid?
Lizardmen
Catmen
Elves
Black Elves
Black-Skin Men (Redguard)
Blonde White-Skin Men (Nords)
Brunette White-Skin Men (Bretons)
4. No Diving
You can float/doggy paddle but there is no diving and not underwater level.
5. 80 Gigabytes
I don't know what you put it in there but it definitely didn't help your game.
6. Humongous Waste of Space
The maps are so huge with nothing interesting to do.
7. Dead Zones
Once you clear Zone A, you don't want to go back there again.
8. Repeated Quests
Go to Zone A, kill/fetch, go to Zone B, kill/fetch. Rinse and repeat.
9. Less Content Than What is On The Market
If you compare it to World of Warcraft, this game is so far behind on content that Zenimax is going to have massive catchup to do.
10. No Flying
I am not sure why they decided to use the RIFT MMO style of gameplay but it's so outdated that they have no flying even.
11. Lamp Post AI
As long as you are far enough from another AI, killing one within vision distance will never trigger the AI to attack you. They just stand there in one spot forever.
1. Bare Minimum
For an MMO, the minimum standard to refer to is World of Warcraft. If you are missing more content that a >10 year old game, you are really screwed.

I really feel bad for SGG on this. Several things that worked so right on Bastion just didn't work in this one. The music was several steps down from Korb's masterwork, relying far too much on turgid 4/4 downbeats and bare arpeggios and without the excellent tone and mixing of the previous. Logan Cunningham's dulcet tones goes off-aim with him talking endlessly to a mute PC who couldn't even respond via body language most of the time due to the camera being panned very far out instead of to us in a naturally one-way conversation. The story (and this isn't the last you'll hear of this critique), is nearly severed from the gameplay, almost as if it was to another game.
That out of the way, it is a BEAUTIFUL looking and playing title. The Function system is a revolutionarily brilliant little toolbox; whoever got that idea to allow skills be modifications on other skills is a goddamn genius. It's also very beautiful, with a lovingly utilized early Art Deco motif that feels and looks like part of a real place; a Bioshock without the negative connotations to the movement.
This is a Recommended, but with real caveats.

Transistor has shown that Supergiant Games can yet again make an amazing indie game after making the masterpiece known as Bastion and made this truely amazing masterpiece. Transistor is a beautiful combination of multiple genres from hack-and-slash to strategy to RPG.
The game starts in the middle of the story with you as Red finding the Transistor, figuring out what happened and what to do now building the curiousity and mystery of the world of Transistor and Red for the player.  The story shines wonderfully with an amazing narrative to help build a truely amazing story experience that ends up building to a truely beautiful ending.
The world opens  up in beautiful visuals that helps bring the character and the situation going on in the world of Transistor. With the same use of isometric gameview that Bastion had, the city is build on beautiful layers to make what seems like a flat world amazing. The designs of the Polarized Plastic white of the enemies in the game truely shows build up for the game as you see the city being covered and surrounded by them as you progress throughout the game.
What shines the most was the Soundtrack score by Darren Korb who provided a more punked  base soundtrack that compares to Bastion with the voice of Ashley Lynn Barrett humming and singing to bring the beauty and the character of Red out to the player. The soundtrack DLC was probaly the greatest DLC I have ever bought for any game.
The game lacked however with play through time of 6 hours , making you want more through the game. But the game is strongly replayable with the Postgame providing a more challenging storymode and also providing challenge modes that will challenge you hard.
In a nutshell, this is truely the greatest Indie Game ever made.

Editing from original not recommended.
Original:
It feels like an ok game so far.  But if you care what server you are on then this is not a good game to try to play.  They constantly have servers restricted from making new characters, even if you already have one on there.  It's a big guessing game as to when the server you WANT to play on is going to be unlocked.  So good luck picking a server with friends unless they happen to be on a server that is extremely low pop or are willing to start on a random one that you CAN find unlocked.
Added:
After getting on the right server.  (It took some planning and finding the forum post that does tell you when each server will be open.)  I've come to enjoy the game.  It has it's pro's and con's like anything else.  It has a story, but if you follow just the main story quests be prepared for a crapload of cutscenes.  (There is a handy settings option to skip cutscenes you've already seen.  Helpful for dungeons.)  There are spots that you HAVE to do solo, so between those and the cutscenes it makes it harder to level with friends like you would in any other game.  A nice thing tho is that you can still group up with people no matter what their level is because dungeons and fates will sync your level if you're too high.
The dungeons are great and annoying at the same time.  Mechanics do matter in them.  I've even had a friend that wiped a new raid because once she saw the boss and heard the music she just couldn't stop laughing enough to do her tankly duties.  They have a fun variety of things, heck there's even a boss that the dps do pretty much nothing.
The game is pretty, even on lower settings.  Sometimes there is a little too much 'flash' with abilities, making it hard to tell what the heck is going on.
Forget having a house of your own.  They are mostly if not all taken, and if you do find one it's got a pretty price tag.  You can buy a room in the house your free company owns (if they own one.)  Downside is you lose that room if you get kicked out of or leave that free company.
Overall I find it a good game to play by yourself.  You have lots of quests to get the story, mounts/minions to go collect, and a casino to gamble in.  When you're feeling social and want to deal with people, you have fates and easy to que for dungeons.

Dreamfall: The Longest Journey provides a truly immersive and memorable gaming experience.  This is the the second entry in the "Longest Journey" saga and continues to provide an intriguing story line, interesting characters and beautiful visuals.  Dreamfall is an adventure game akin to the point-and-click games of old, but also provides an optional control scheme to accomodate for the use of gamepads.  The game is not perfect, however, as I found the combat to be quite forgetable and seemingly unecessary.  Also, the character animations are rather stiff and some of the puzzles were not very challenging.  Of course, this is a game that released several years ago on the original Xbox as well as PC, so that is something to keep in mind when it comes to the graphics.
I would recommend Dreamfall: The Longest Journey to fans of adventure games and RPGs, as well as those who are looking for an imaginative and intriguing story in a game.  The first game in the series, "The Longest Journey," is also available here on Steam for those who wish to start with that one, which is an amazing old school adventure game.  Also, "Dreamfall Chapters" was recently announced for launch later this year and will be the next and final entry in the series.   Adventure fans and those of you who can appreciate a well told story, GIVE THIS SERIES A SHOT!  Happy gaming!

Ragnar Tornquist's storytelling power doubles the immersion in the sequel to The Longest Journey. This tale draws more people into the surreal, mind-bending world(s) portrayed in the original, adds a touch of horror to the narrative, and continues almost flawlessly to build on the story already constructed. The game is very playable, the victories very rewarding.
On the downside, there are some few holes in the plot between the two; nothing I found painfully glaring, but one or two things seemed to be missing. As well, not all the gameplay pieces make it through the storytelling process alive; once or twice you might feel like you're doing less exploring and more pacing down a one-lane alley to your ultimate doomstiny. A combat system was also worked into the game that might have been intended to be a prominent feature, but comes out shallow and just a touch broken.
Ultimately, an amazing story told in an amazing game with excellent for its time visuals that still manage to mostly draw the player in. Gameplay and puzzles that work well together; a beautiful set of environments to explore.
It's an addictive storyline, really worth it... only con with it is that it leaves you wanting more..

Wow, I can't believe that this game is already 8 years old...
I originally discovered this game in a very unique way. In 2008, I was homeschooled, and we bought a computer for me to use with the schooling program. As the studious little boy I was, I searched on the computer (which was not connected to the internet) for ways to procrastinate, and one item I found was a compilation of hundreds of game demos, which would allow a limited amount of times that you could open it, 2-3 times I think. While playing the many games that were offered, I eventually stumbled upon this one, and I was drawn to it. I did everything I could to be able to continue to play it, including keeping it open for days, on end, and even creating new profiles on the computer to open it again (loophole!). Eventually, I finished all I could with the demo, with all of the levels of Goo Filled Hills beaten with OCD, and the highest tower I could build completed, I set it away the game and forgot about it.
4 years later, in 2012, I was given a Nook tablet to use for school, and one day as I was browsing through the apps, I saw this game on the app store, and bought and downloaded it as fast as I could. I played the game for hours, working to build a higher tower, or just beat that next level with OCD, and I can safely say, this is a game that I will never become bored of. A few more years later, I became more interested in video games, I downloaded steam, and discovered and bought this game straight away, both for my personal enjoyment, and for the support of the developers of this amazing game.
Alright, enough about me, lets get to the review!
World of Goo is a game where you build towers and structures with goo balls to reach a pipe with a certain amount of goo balls left to be sucked up by it. The challenges begin simple, but as you progress you face more difficult and unique obstacles. This game also contains one of if not the most beautiful soundtrack in all video games, with fitting music for each level. The visuals and graphics of the game are very nice, and it runs very smoothly, even on lower end computers. Finally, the story is very interesting and creative, and it ties the game together beautifully. I highly recommend you play this game!

Call of Juarez: Gunslinger seems like one of those games which pops up in your Steam discovery queue that you mark as 'not interested.' But boy, oh, boy, are you in for a ride.
Gunslinger does something extremely well. I can't quite put my finger on what, though. Maybe it's the extremely satisfying gunplay, innovative narration of the campaign missions or just the tense dueling system.
The campaign relies a lot on a unreliable narrator - resulting in a memorable, unique experience single-player experience. The old main character tells a story, narrating events of the past and sometimes gets called out on suspicious or inconclusive parts of the story. Then, the entire sequence might change and you have to adapt tactics against entirely different enemies in a different environment.
It's a great mix of comedy and creates a sense of freedom in an otherwise linear level design.
The gunplay feels really good, something I can't believe Techland of all developers managed to excel at. The guns are relatively few: some revolvers, shotguns, a rifle and dynamite. That's it.
But it doesn't matter. Every single bullet, pellet and explosion just feels SO good, that you begin to wonder how almost no studio has been able to bring the same sense of adrenaline to your fingers during the past 3,5 years.
It can get pretty difficult at times. Some instances might require multiple tries, even from a skilled player.
Gunslinger is one of those games which truly deserve a sequel; if not a direct, then a spiritual one.

Can I just use my hours played as my review? No? Okay then.
My experiences:
Dark Souls 2 is, among fans of the franchise, one of the least liked games in the series. Is this because it is missing core game mechanics, or the story is lacking? Nope, the only reason that it is disliked is because it is "easier" and feels slower than the other games in the series.
This was my first game in the franchise, and for a long time, it was my only game. I played this game to the ground, learning enemy and item locations, minmaxing my builds, and doing fun challenges. I was never one of the "hardcore" players who beats bosses with a broken spoon, but I did dabble in challenges. Mostly, though, I just played PVP with strange builds.
Of my 1,414 hours played, at least 600 of them were spent in PVP. Dark Souls 2 has one of my favorite mechanics which was sadly removed in Dark Souls 3: weapon parries. Normally in a Souls game, you would parry an opponent's strike with your shield to knock them off balance and leave them open for a powerful riposte, but not quite so in Dark Souls 2. In Dark Souls 2, you can parry with any weapon, although it is more difficult. Let me tell you, there is nothing as satisfying as winning a duel because you randomly parried a dagger with a greataxe.
Pros and Cons:
Pros:
Learning: This game is great for learning the series. It is less punishing of individual mistakes than other games, and almost all builds are viable in PVE.
Roleplaying: Do you want to play as a mighty tank? A mobile archer? A master spellcaster? A monarch butterfly? In Dark Souls 2, you can build your character however you want to play through the crumbling world you find yourself in. You may make your character represent how you see yourself, or you may cosplay a character that you like. But let's be honest, you're just going to mash the "similar face" option until you have an inhuman monstrosity anyways.
Co-op: One of the main mechanics of any Souls game is the ability to summon other players into your world to help you progress. If you find yourself stuck on a boss, confused on how to progress, or just lonely, you can summon other players who usually know what they're doing.
PVP: There are two versions of PVP in Dark Souls 2: Invasions and Duels. An invader is a player who used an item to forcibly enter your world for the sake of killing you. Normally invaders aren't a major issue, and some of them are just there for laughs. However, if you don't like the idea of other people coming to your world to kill you, you can simply play offline. Duels are by far the more popular option for PVP. In a duel, the host of a world chooses to summon an invader for the purpose of fighting them. Duels are a great way to see new builds and master the core mechanics of the game.
Story: As with any Souls game, the lore in Dark Souls 2 runs deep. It is up to you to read item descriptions, listen to dialogue, and connect the dots to discover just what is going on in the crumbling kingdom of Drangleic. Learning the lore of the series provides new insight as to why a character behaves a certain way and gives you, the player, a sense of purpose in the world. If you find searching through item descriptions to be too daunting of a task, there are several YouTube channels dedicated to Dark Souls lore.
Atmosphere: In my opinion, Dark Souls 2 has the most pleasant atmosphere of any Souls game. The hub area, Majula, serves as a beacon to return to when the world seems dark, and as you progress there will be more and more NPCs populating the area.
Cons:
Speed: Dark Souls 2 is by far the slowest in terms of the pace of combat, and unexperienced players may find that their swings are being easily punished as they are trapped in the ending lag on their moves. This is the part of Dark Souls 2 that takes the most adjusting to, and will kill any new player at least once.
Difficulty: The difficulty curve in Dark Souls 2 feels steeper than most other Souls game, with a massive leap in challenge when you approach Drangleic Castle. Bonfires become scarce and enemies become plentiful.
Neutrals:
Death: You WILL die. Welcome to Dark Souls!
One last thing: Despite all my hours, I still haven't beaten New Game Plus.

Renowned for his tenuos grasp of things like the english language, directing, producing, writing and acting, Tommy has now turned to videogames as the medium in which to ply his craft. His first foray into this is a painstaking look at the nature of puzzles and how they effect us in life. After being betrayed and torn apart by his girlfriend Lisa, and discovering he is the fool, Tommy constructs an elaborate puzzle box to house his will and testement that names Denny, his mentally challenged neighbor/adopted son, the sole heir to his monumental fortune from working in at the Bank before commiting suicide. You play as Johnnies lawyer, charged with unlocking the box before Lisa and her evil cohorts can kill Denny. Their plan is to assassinate him while he's playing football in a tuxedo, something he does every day, so the time table is very tight on this thriller. Unlock box after box and throw spoons at the screen as puzzles refuse to relent. With exciting physics, massive interactability and a story that will have you saying, "What a story Mark" The Room: The Movie: The Game is a must own.

A very fascinating little game with puzzles spanning over several dimensions and combining several kinds of puzzles, both the kind you may or may not have seen before and some new ones, in one bundle. Some of the puzzles were rather straight forward instead of being an actual puzzle in my opinion, but it was still a good little brain exercise.
However, the amount of puzzles was a bit of a letdown. But to compensate, the puzzles were MUCH longer than what you see in average flashgame puzzles. For me it took almost 3 hours to complete the game. May not seem much, but you have to remember that there are "only" five chapters, then that puts my average time to roughly 32 minutes per chapter. I should also clarify that each chapter consists one big puzzle made of several smaller puzzles.
Aside from the puzzles themselves, despite the fact that there wasn't much aside the puzzles, the atmosphere made it somewhat thrilling. As the whispers began to show up, it first made me feel like I should stop as I felt like there's going to be something eating up my face. Then they started to resonated with the emotion of wanting to find out what's behind all the puzzles, a kinda of a "What's in the box?!" -feeling. A very interesting set of emotions. And as for the quality of the graphics, it was just beautiful. Only the hardest zooms were able to break the quality as it became too obvious that I was actually looking at a flat surface, but that's just because of the way how some of the textures are made.
TL;DR: Puzzles made of puzzles, quality over quantity, not for those don't like puzzles and gem for the rest.
Hoping to see more to this game, maybe new puzzles via updates or DLCs.

Well what can I say that hasn't already been said about FFXIV ARR, it's a really great game and done just about everything to make it so after what was a very disastrous situation from its first 1.0 release. With A Realm Reborn, Yoshi P and company at Square Enix do what seldom companies do for their players, listen and communicate with player base constantly through live letters, 3 convention events a year, and twitch broadcasts. They do what they can to make the game better with each "patch". I honestly hate the word patch when it comes to this game as in most games, they just mean bug fixes. In this case of FFXIV, it's been consistently more than just bug fixes, they add dungeons, raids, jobs. New quests and storyline additions with each patch! Not many games do that without making you wait a year or pack new features into an expansion.
This aside, the game is very story driven and single player focused as far as the story goes. Told through in game cutscenes and cinematic cutscenes, which helps makes the story come to life. Add in amazingly good graphics that can run on very low hardware and you truly have a great game. From good communities and a great development team to add.
The game is fast in it action, and made with a means that any casual or new player to MMO RPGs can jump right in and progress well enough. But that's not to say this game is easy and only for casuals, it definitely ups the difficulty with some of the toughest raids out there for the hardcore player (bahamut coils anyone?) to spend days on. So it's a nice mix of gameplay, from easy to the extreme. Tons of emotes and crafting abilities. Crafting in itself is its own game. Requiring you to earn skills in order to craft and build raw materials into something powerful and beautiful sold for millions of Gil if you're good enough. It's deep and enriching to craft or fish.
Lastly, the ability to just change jobs (class) with the swap of a weapon without having to make a whole new character is awesome. Need to tank, equip your weapon and your done. It's that simple.
All in all it's a great game and a rare one that is worth the subscription fee, with so many games going the F2P route in order to recoup their losses from having their own set of problems - generally leading F2P models as being end of life or last ditch efforts to make a buck with numerous micro transactions, it's great to see a game that hasn't had to do this to keep going. A game that legitimately entertains you and encourages you to want to support it wholeheartedly.
Yes, that to me is FFXIV in a nutshell and I suggest you try it out at the very least.

I honestly believe that this game would have made for a better book or movie than a video game, but that's not because it was lacking as a game. Instead, with the incredible language the game uses and how much of the game is told through writing, it sets itself up to flow incredibly well through multiple forms of media. The score is also incredible, with several moments being nothing shy of grand, thanks to the excellent music of Jessica Curry. Of course, the music also serves to enhance the atmosphere of the game, which is spectacular. It really feels as though you're an insect in the belly of this massive machine, snooping where you don't belong. There are moments, however, when it feels as though there is little gameplay. It's mostly creeping around mechanical environments while collecting pieces of the story, slowly putting it together. There are few moments that can even hardly be called puzzles and rather simple monster encounters. This is where this game falls short where its predecessor, The Dark Descent, succeeded. Very basic puzzles and less intimidating monster encounters. The game also won't make you jump out of your chair as much as The Dark Descent did. It is still very scary, don't worry, but in a different way. A Machine For Pigs doesn't rely soley on jump scares or chase scenes to scare the player. Instead, it makes the player really think about what's happening. I came out of The Dark Descent scared, but nothing more. After playing this game, I couldn't get it out of my head. I just kept thinking about those damn pigs. When you read Lovecraft or Poe, you don't scream in fear. Instead, you think about what you read, let it get to you, mess with you. If you're not a gamer who enjoys wondering about a game and piecing things together, this isn't the game for you. If you want to simply run away from mosters and have bloody figures go "boo," this isn't the game for you. If you want an experience that makes you think and take it further in your head long after you've finished the game, this is the game for you. If you want a story that haunts you as you pace steel corridors, wanting to uncover more of this horror, this is the game for you. The best tip I can give for someone playing this game is check the momentos whenever the book icon appears in the corner. This is your character writing down his thoughts. Just hit "m" to check them. It's a weird mechanic that you may like or dislike, but I personally loved it because if gave insight into your character and offered more information. It also played a bit more like how a book reads, which I also enjoyed. And no matter what, read everything you come across. Much of the fear comes from what you read. Now go play this beast of a game.

This is a pretty novel concept for a game.
You basically do paperwork for a 5 minute day in day out work shift, trying to accurately process as many immigrants as you can. You have to balance your speed and accurately precisely enough to make sure you remain stable in your job.
If you're too slow in processing paperwork, your paycheck will suffer, and hurt your family. The country you live in only rewards labor to citizens with a family to feed, so if you fail them you lose your job. If you're too fast and sloppy with your paperwork, you'll end up either wrongfully denying immigrants, or letting in people with false information, sometimes criminals, and terrorists. If you keep failing in your responsibility to properly check their information, you'll end up getting citations that can deduct from your paycheck and make you lose your job.
As you keep going forward into the game, the immigration process becomes more and more complex, making the game even harder.
It ends up being a pretty good game in time management, and an overall political commentary on the immigration process, and the harsh reality of the work place.

Right off the bat, the game doesn't present itself or play like other games. It's got branching paths and tough moral choices that impact the game later. image-and-info match style game that manages to engage you. Repetitive gameplay that you don't tire of. These familiar themes come together to create something different unpleasant to watch and play, and yet, so weirdly addicting and entertaining.
Some people cannot get into the mood Papers, Please forces onto you. This may make the game annoyingly repetitive for them. The thought of doing paperwork within a game seems to repel many. It may also be a very depressing topic for them, making this whole experience a bit of a downer.

This is the closest I'll ever get to the "games shouldn't always be fun" crowd. The game is engaging with a severe atmosphere that pushes down on you. The game is good, but it's not conventional. It's a successful art game, and should be looked upon jealously by those insistent that they had to sacrifice gameplay for their vision and message.

This game is strangely compelling. Shuffling around paperwork, looking up rules, seals, and district names and eventually stamping passports sounds boring, but I'm mentally adding this to the list (along with Euro Truck Sim 2) of games that look/sound boring but are actually very engaging. There is a surprising amount of little side stories in the game that is given to you just through interaction with people at your checkpoint window. I highly recommend it if you like checking other people's paperwork for errors, or if you find satisfaction in denying service to someone who has been waiting in line for many hours. I also recommend it if you like unique games; this game is extremely unique and can be thought-provoking as well.

The premise is fairly unique: you play the part of a customs agent reviewing people's papers, admitting people who have everything in order, denying people with missing or expired documents, and detaining people with the audacity to try to fool you with a forgery. Depending on how much you believe someone's story or if you are pleased with their offer of a bribe, you may choose to let through someone you aren't supposed to. Admit someone you shouldn't or deny access to someone who deserves it and you get nastygrams from your boss that shift into fines. There's also a plot to mess up the government you can assist or ruin and as many as twenty different ways to end the game.
There's just one problem: it gets boring. It actually reminded me quite a lot of a job reviewing documents that I quit because ... boring. The difficulty here is largely in your attention span to minute details - after a while, even when you know what all to to look for, your attention will drop off and you will make mistakes and start racking up nastygrams.
If you enjoy studying numerous documents for any appearance of a contradiction, forget playing this game - get a job as a policy services analyst for an insurance company and get paid to do it instead of just doing it here for pretend.
Final verdict: An excellent tedium simulator. If only that weren't what I'm trying to escape from.
