Dark Souls 1 was a hard, challenging game, but it was hard and challenging in a fair way and for a reason. Dark Souls 2 however, is a ♥♥♥♥ing♥♥♥♥♥♥to you for the sake of being a ♥♥♥♥ing♥♥♥♥♥♥ L'art pour l'art dickery. It feels tedious, frustrating and somehow manged to loose the charm the first game had, and in my opinion this has a lot to do with what they did to the parrying system.
Namely, they ♥♥♥♥ed it up.
They ♥♥♥♥ed it up big time. They ♥♥♥♥ed it up so hard, that parrying is now an entire scientific branch of its own. Seriously, in DS1 I spent a good hour or so to learn how to parry and then adapting to another weapon was a matter of minutes. Here? Here you can build up a 6 month long academic course solely about parrying, because it is not just about YOUR weapon anymore but the weapon of your ENEMY as well. In fact, it seems so overcomplicated that I can barely find anyone who does it in PvP. While in DS1 parrying was a choice of playstile, in DS2 it just does not worth the time to bother with it. The game is a god damned tumbling simulator now, and if you don't like it you can either move along or spend a few months learning this god forsaken parrying system.
Other than that, the level design somehow seems more primitive than in the first game. DS 1 featured a map design that was simply brilliant. The shortcuts, the fact that you had to traverse the maps in both directions mixed with phenomenal concepts and resulted in a unique experience. Here the maps are just... tubes. You move forward to the next bonefire, then you just fast travel everywhere. And the shortcuts, J. F. Christ! Just bring up Google, and type in "lost bastille shortcut"—seriously, what the♥♥♥♥♥♥! Also, I would like to bring up the fantastic experience of Heide's Tower of Flame here. Not because it was so hard, or challanging, no, simply because it was straight up BORING. I guess a lot of dimwits who failed utterly in grasping the fundamentals of the first game complained to the devs that "the game just throws you into the deep end, so unfair!" Well boo-♥♥♥♥idy-hoo! Speaking of which, the enemies seem lackluster which sometimes borders frustrating. There are hordes of those ♥♥♥♥ing dogs from the first game, there are hollows without end, and multitudes of god damned exploding mother♥♥♥♥ing undead. The boss mechanics are laughable, you just circle-strafe around the entire world, and you'll be okay, at least with the first half of the bosses. As the player starts nearing the endgame, however, the devs had a really ♥♥♥♥ing genius idea: since the boss mechanics are totally ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, they elected to make the encounters more exciting by giving you a bunch of boss TEAMS. This means that sometimes you fight bosses of 3. THREE. ♥♥♥♥ING. BOSSES. Yeah, sure, that works, because suddenly the quality of the mechanics just tumbles over from ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to infuriating. The patterns that were simply laughably primitive quickly become  laughbly primitive AND maddening... because, you know, just TRY to get near to 3 bosses, I dare you, I double dare you!

Let the downvotes come, I didn't like Transistor and I can't even tell precisely why. I just felt it to be overhyped, overpriced, overrated, and, in the end, disappointing.
It's pretty obvious to me that the producers tried to transfer the features that made Bastion great to Transistor, but they couldn't also transfer the feeling of novelty and originality that Bastion had, or its heart and immersiveness.
They used that narrator again, but while in Bastion the narrator was inspiring and emphatetic, the Transistor's narrator feels rather shallow and soulless. It often says the most, utterly useless things and feels cold and superficial. They tried to maintain the same story-unravelling-as-you-play approach, but while this approach made Bastion captivating and more interesting, it only manages to make Transistor confusing and unengaging. I played for 4 hours and got undeniably bored, hoping almost desperately for something special to happen and trying to lie myself into thinking it's worth keeping on playing. They tried to make the main character (Red) as mysterious as Bastion's kid, but it end up just being lackluster. And so on....
It's hard not to compare Bastion to Transistor, they even have the same difficulty level system and similar "challenges zone" systems, but Transistor just ends up feeling empty by comparison to me.

God. This game is incredible. A joy (so to speak, as this is a fairly bleak game) from start to finish. Others have already commented on the absolutely gorgeous art and music (which is more than worth buying), and I have nothing to add to that.
I loved the characters - Red and the voice in the Transistor, and the others that we meet both as functions and as living people, the little tidbits of life we see all over the city Cloudbank that slowly lose colour and personality as the story progresses. I loved how even though Red's voice was missing, her agency wasn't. The little ways she found to communicate and rebel and reassure, though unspoken, still spoke volumes.
The voice acting is excellent, especially Logan Cunningham in the role of the Transistor's voice, which is what tells us most of the story of the characters and Cloudbank. Nostalgic, angry, soothing, thoughtful, frightened, reassuring - all of these were delivered with an accuracy that's very rare to find.
One of the things that intrigued me the most was the
, which I liked very much - it's both turn-based and real-time at the same time, somewhat similar
and yet very different. Like COL, you can take a step back and plan your next course of action. Unlike COL, the game also allows the player to completely ignore the turn system and fight entirely in real time. Both strategies have their advantages and disadvantages, and I often found myself choosing one over the other depending on which enemies I faced and my proficiency at the abilities (functions) I had at the moment,
To my delight I discovered that the game also encourages the player to learn as much as possible about the functions and how they operated. Often enough in RPGs I'm used to getting comfortable in one way to battle, and set in my ways, and should that thing become unavailable for some reason my entire strategy is shot. Well, not in this one! It allows you (and sometimes even forces you) to experiment and become more and more proficient. I thought it worked very well.
Highly recommended.

Call of Juarez: Gunslinger is unfortunately exactly what I expected. On the outside it looks like a well polished game with unique high quality caroony graphics. Unfortunately though the reality is that certain gameplay mechanics will infuriate you about as much as a constantly jamming rusty old pistol.
Basically you play through gun-toting stories of a few folks sitting around a table at a saloon. The playstyle is quite unique in that you are playing through 'tales' which can both, change on-the-fly and also which of course contain some exaggerated circumstances.
Call of Juarez: Gunslinger doesn't take itself very seriously at all. You're pitted against hundreds of enemies and are tasked with killing them as a one-man-army. In order to do this you make use of a few abilities like being able to slow down time, literally dodge bullets and a skill upgrade system. Shoot dynamite out of the sky, kill 10 people within 10 seconds. It's all very over the top, and it would be fantastic fun if....
You weren't getting shot through solid objects and from areas where you can't even see your enemies.
The biggest fault of this game is the fact that enemies can see you through objects, and often can shoot you through objects. Shooting an enemy doesn't 'stun' them or cause them to 'recoil' allowing them to basically keep shooting you in the face continuously. However, every time that you are shot, you are hit with recoil that throws off your aim, making it almost entirely impossible to hit anyone until your aim recovers. It's a completely unfair and unbalanced mechanic considering that you are often facing tens of enemies all shooting you at the same time.
Add that to the fact that every couple of seconds whilst you're in the middle of a gun fight, even if you are at full health, you will have to randomly (and with absolutely no warning) dodge left or right, a bullet that WILL INSTANTLY KILL YOU. If you dodge the wrong way. It's called your 'sense of death'. Honestly I wish I could turn this stupid thing off, as all it does is break your concentration to instantly have to choose which side to dodge to, or be killed instantly.
And finally... As if things couldn't get ANY WORSE!
THE FREAKING DUELS ARE RIDICULOUS!
This is honestly perhaps the worst thing about the game. The duels that you do 1v1 with people are so unfair.
First you start off having to keep your mouse cursor (reticle) over the enemy in order to slowly gain focus before they draw their gun to shoot you. Sounds easy right? WRONG! Because the cursor handles like a pig and has some kind of random acceleration applied to it where a small move of the mouse will either send the cursor flying from one side of the screen to the other... or it will barely move. The person you are dueling will also move in a random pattern as well and you have to follow them with your mouse.
BUT WAIT!!! THERE'S MORE!!
Later on you ALSO have to use the freaking 'WSAD' keys to position your hand on top of your gun in order to slowly build up your draw speeds! So not only with one hand do you have to carefully follow the person you are dueling, you also have to f**king watch where your hand is and make sure you use the WSAD keys carefully to keep your hand there. This requires you to basically be 'cross-eyed' and focus on both the foreground and the background. It's such a stupid mechanic, that can probably only be explained by watching a Youtube video.
All in all, it's a good looking game with unique cartoony graphics that reminds me of a 'western' styled Borderlands game that performs pretty well I guess. Performance could be better but I had no real drops or issues on my machine. It's just a shame that there are 3 ridiculously unbalanced and badly thoughtout mechanics thrown into this game that make it a total pain to play. In the end I had to force myself to finish the game.
_______________________________________________
TL;DR
Pros:
- Great graphics
- Unique idea for a game
- Pretty 'okay' voice acting
Cons:
- Infuriating gun fight mechanics
- Completely bugged cover system
- Stupid dueling system
- Somewhat repetitive gameplay

Well what can I say that hasn't already been said about FFXIV ARR, it's a really great game and done just about everything to make it so after what was a very disastrous situation from its first 1.0 release. With A Realm Reborn, Yoshi P and company at Square Enix do what seldom companies do for their players, listen and communicate with player base constantly through live letters, 3 convention events a year, and twitch broadcasts. They do what they can to make the game better with each "patch". I honestly hate the word patch when it comes to this game as in most games, they just mean bug fixes. In this case of FFXIV, it's been consistently more than just bug fixes, they add dungeons, raids, jobs. New quests and storyline additions with each patch! Not many games do that without making you wait a year or pack new features into an expansion.
This aside, the game is very story driven and single player focused as far as the story goes. Told through in game cutscenes and cinematic cutscenes, which helps makes the story come to life. Add in amazingly good graphics that can run on very low hardware and you truly have a great game. From good communities and a great development team to add.
The game is fast in it action, and made with a means that any casual or new player to MMO RPGs can jump right in and progress well enough. But that's not to say this game is easy and only for casuals, it definitely ups the difficulty with some of the toughest raids out there for the hardcore player (bahamut coils anyone?) to spend days on. So it's a nice mix of gameplay, from easy to the extreme. Tons of emotes and crafting abilities. Crafting in itself is its own game. Requiring you to earn skills in order to craft and build raw materials into something powerful and beautiful sold for millions of Gil if you're good enough. It's deep and enriching to craft or fish.
Lastly, the ability to just change jobs (class) with the swap of a weapon without having to make a whole new character is awesome. Need to tank, equip your weapon and your done. It's that simple.
All in all it's a great game and a rare one that is worth the subscription fee, with so many games going the F2P route in order to recoup their losses from having their own set of problems - generally leading F2P models as being end of life or last ditch efforts to make a buck with numerous micro transactions, it's great to see a game that hasn't had to do this to keep going. A game that legitimately entertains you and encourages you to want to support it wholeheartedly.
Yes, that to me is FFXIV in a nutshell and I suggest you try it out at the very least.

This is a pretty novel concept for a game.
You basically do paperwork for a 5 minute day in day out work shift, trying to accurately process as many immigrants as you can. You have to balance your speed and accurately precisely enough to make sure you remain stable in your job.
If you're too slow in processing paperwork, your paycheck will suffer, and hurt your family. The country you live in only rewards labor to citizens with a family to feed, so if you fail them you lose your job. If you're too fast and sloppy with your paperwork, you'll end up either wrongfully denying immigrants, or letting in people with false information, sometimes criminals, and terrorists. If you keep failing in your responsibility to properly check their information, you'll end up getting citations that can deduct from your paycheck and make you lose your job.
As you keep going forward into the game, the immigration process becomes more and more complex, making the game even harder.
It ends up being a pretty good game in time management, and an overall political commentary on the immigration process, and the harsh reality of the work place.

Right off the bat, the game doesn't present itself or play like other games. It's got branching paths and tough moral choices that impact the game later. image-and-info match style game that manages to engage you. Repetitive gameplay that you don't tire of. These familiar themes come together to create something different unpleasant to watch and play, and yet, so weirdly addicting and entertaining.
Some people cannot get into the mood Papers, Please forces onto you. This may make the game annoyingly repetitive for them. The thought of doing paperwork within a game seems to repel many. It may also be a very depressing topic for them, making this whole experience a bit of a downer.
I got plenty of hours of gameplay out of this, so I find it to be worth full price. It's very fun and even a little relaxing despite the grim atmosphere. Still, it's discounted during every major sale.
This is the closest I'll ever get to the "games shouldn't always be fun" crowd. The game is engaging with a severe atmosphere that pushes down on you. The game is good, but it's not conventional. It's a successful art game, and should be looked upon jealously by those insistent that they had to sacrifice gameplay for their vision and message.

This game is strangely compelling. Shuffling around paperwork, looking up rules, seals, and district names and eventually stamping passports sounds boring, but I'm mentally adding this to the list (along with Euro Truck Sim 2) of games that look/sound boring but are actually very engaging. There is a surprising amount of little side stories in the game that is given to you just through interaction with people at your checkpoint window. I highly recommend it if you like checking other people's paperwork for errors, or if you find satisfaction in denying service to someone who has been waiting in line for many hours. I also recommend it if you like unique games; this game is extremely unique and can be thought-provoking as well.

The premise is fairly unique: you play the part of a customs agent reviewing people's papers, admitting people who have everything in order, denying people with missing or expired documents, and detaining people with the audacity to try to fool you with a forgery. Depending on how much you believe someone's story or if you are pleased with their offer of a bribe, you may choose to let through someone you aren't supposed to. Admit someone you shouldn't or deny access to someone who deserves it and you get nastygrams from your boss that shift into fines. There's also a plot to mess up the government you can assist or ruin and as many as twenty different ways to end the game.
There's just one problem: it gets boring. It actually reminded me quite a lot of a job reviewing documents that I quit because ... boring. The difficulty here is largely in your attention span to minute details - after a while, even when you know what all to to look for, your attention will drop off and you will make mistakes and start racking up nastygrams.
If you enjoy studying numerous documents for any appearance of a contradiction, forget playing this game - get a job as a policy services analyst for an insurance company and get paid to do it instead of just doing it here for pretend.
Final verdict: An excellent tedium simulator. If only that weren't what I'm trying to escape from.

It's your bog standed survival PvP game - you'll find the a******s who go around destroying and raiding bases, you'll get hackers, but slowly they've been weened out; you'll be minding your own business when someone just starts hacking at your shins. But that's your standard PvP game and doesn't that make it fun? Of course it does! And I personally hate PvP games because I'm sickly competitive sometimes!
The game has a lot of promise if all goes well with the developers continuing to update it in their own time. It's great fun, it's simple, can be frustrating and a little boring at times, but honestly it's great fun. The graphics aren't amazing, but they're dynamic. Animations are questionable, but the dancing animations would put any popstar to shame - just make sure you do it in the nude with a big grin on thy face. The fighting mechanics are good: it's always satisfying when you can hack off your enemy's (or friend's!) limbs off, or perhaps drag them to your dungeon. The building mechanics is highly reminiscent of Minecraft, since you get blocks, ramps, corner blocks, stairs - some people have built some amazing bases - I myself went a bit mental with making towers using Minecraft blueprints.
To conclude, with hopes that the devleopers will continue to update the game, it'll eventually be a lot smoother and have more content. If you want something a little simpler than Rust et al., this is a good start. If you've got Rust et al. and you want a change of scenery, get this game. It's plain simple fun.
The bottomline is, get this game on personal preference - I saw this game had mixed reviews, but I saw some gameplay from some Youtubers and thought I'd give it a go. Turns out it's pure simple fun and I love it.

In my entire first visit to Arcadia, the fantastical world that contributes half the setting of
,  I didn't make a single decision or solve a single puzzle. Instead, the game fed me a string of explicit or implicit instructions on what I should do next. When a puzzle finally bothered to turn up, the game practically leapt up and down in its efforts to show me the solution, reducing the act of solving it to yet another follow-the-instruction exercise. After tolerating this for over an hour, I shut the game down in disgust and looked it up on Metacritic. I felt that reading some of the critical drubbings handed out to it would soothe my frustration.
The Metacritic score for
is 75%. The ration of positive to negative reviews is 26:2.
Maybe I'm becoming a cranky old man who is increasingly out of touch, but...
??
Is following instructions good gameplay? Can I put together some IKEA shelves and then exclaim, “wow, that game was fun!”. Certainly I've had more head-scratching puzzles presented to me by flatpack furniture instructions than in the whole nine hours of
.
It's not as though the game is much better in its other sections. Throughout, the puzzles are almost offensively easy to solve. In one location, a mysterious set-up of statues and symbols taunted me with the half-promise that I would have to do some serious thinking to progress. And then I turned a corner and discovered... well... the
. Just sitting there, waiting for me to go back and do the busy work of implementing it.
Even these very easy puzzles are occasionally so badly implemented as to defy belief. One puzzle required me to recreate a tune I had previously heard, but the game had allowed me to
the source of the tune from the game. Unable to remember what the tune had been, and without any means of hearing the tune again, I was completely unable to progress. On two other occasions I realised the puzzle solution instantly, but the game was so pedantic about how I went about it that I had to trial-and-error my way to taking the correct action. It reminded me of early text-parser games where you needed to type in multiple different phrases before the game finally understood what you wanted to do.
And when the game isn't insulting you with non-puzzles, it asks you to slog through some typically dull and clunky fighting and stealth sections. I understand that when adventure games began falling out of mainstream favour, developers thought they needed to sex up their games with this stuff, but did it always have to be so badly implemented? The best fighting strategy turns out to be 'press forward and mash the quick-attack button until victory', and I found the best sneak strategy to be 'try not to die of boredom while watching your character inch like a lethargic snail towards their objective'.
So... why the good reviews?
Well, the passive elements of this game are generally very good. The plot is intriguing, and becomes genuinely gripping once it gets into gear. Budget limitations make the locations feel pretty sparse, but they're beautifully stylish and full of distinctive characters. Voice acting is good throughout, though I found the main character (Zoe)'s voice to be somewhat tepid and unconvincing during more emotional scenes. The dialogue is usually great, and skilfully conveys character in just a few lines. I can certainly see many people playing this game, falling in love with the characters, getting hooked on the plot, and coming away feeling they just played something wonderful.
But they didn't. They watched a lot of wonderful things, they heard a lot of wonderful things, but they didn't
much of any worth. Especially near the end where the developers once again stop bothering with this whole 'game' thing and go back to 'Talk to A, talk to B, talk to C...' interspersed with dramatic cutscenes.
And the sadder truth is that even the plotting and characters aren't good enough to warrant the skew towards positive reviews on Metacritic. I understand the game was scaled down from a more ambitious vision due to budget restrictions, but it has left some odd effects. One of the player characters undergoes a crucial and transformative change in perspective, but the reasons for this whoosh by without examination, which makes the change feel cheap and contrived. As the plot develops, you can see that the writers are aiming to explore a theme, but its all very muddy as to what they're trying to say, if anything. The end of the story is a huge 'To be continued...' with only one plot element resolved satisfactorily, though even that left me wishing for more detail.
Irritatingly, there are hints of something better here. Early in the game, I was given a set of choices in a dialogue tree that I saw would take the scene in different directions. I made what I felt was a smart choice, and was pleased to see the result. Suddenly, I was
: using my wits to make a decision and see what happened. Even now, I wonder what would have happened had I chosen the
option. These choices pop up later too, though they are unfortunately few, infrequent, and generally of little consequence. Having watched the developer introduction to
, I am hopeful that this avenue will be explored to its full extent in the sequel.
Play
if you're a sucker for reasonably well-told fantasy stories and you don't mind not having an active role to play in the experience. But if you think 'interactive entertainment' should encompass the whole spirit of the phrase: avoid, avoid, avoid. My personal score on this is 4/10. Your mileage may vary.

IMPORTANT: before you buy/play this game, be aware that this game is the 2nd part of a trilogy. Make sure you play part 1 (named "The Longest Journey") first, the story and the characters will be much more clear. And FYI the third part isn't finished, expect it in 2014.
Now my musings about the game:
It's okay generally. Visually it's satisfying considering it's age and it's way better looking than part 1 (TLJ). The story is good like in part 1, but I wouldn't call it a straight adventure like its predecessor. It's more streamlined, less puzzles, more cutscenes. That's not bad, but it's surely a change from part 1. Most of the puzzles are straightforward and I had to consult a walkthrough only once and I ain't an adventure guru by far. The characters are well defined, though the story elements sometimes feel rushed. Many of the characters reappear in part 2, which is welcome. If you have a soft spot for children, like probably most of us have, be warned. Nothing explicit, but I had trouble at some parts (or just me getting old). The game is in my opinion less epic than part 1, and shorter. Don't let my playtime fool you, I tend to leave game open while I'm away and I play at snail speed anyway.
In short, if you like adventure games with a good story, play The Longest Journey first. If you have a stomach for retro visuals. Then play Dreamfall and wait for part 3. Maybe the best idea would be to wait for part 3 and play them all in order at once.

I've gotta hand it to you IMC, you had a rough, rocky start and you're still not the best but you're learning and improving.
Full disclosure, I was hype for this game from the moment that it was announced- I'm a long-time ragnarok online player, I applied for every closed beta they had, and I even paid for the most expensive beta slot that was available. To me, this was set up to explode as the next big thing!- But then it wasn't. I didn't get terribly far in the beta so I didn't quite reach the point where the cracks in design became evident. I was also riding high off of a sense of nostalgia and longing for another game to fill the Ragnarok Online niche so I was pretty blinded.
Eventually it came out of beta and launched for real- I was a little less enthusiastic but I was going to rush into it headfirst and be one of the best, so I thought. I tolerated the fairly decent story and the seemingly on-rails quest lines, but reaching one of the big levelling curve dead zones that were prominent back then I finally gave up. I agreed with what others were saying- Skills didn't have scaling, which made all earlier choices completely pointless. The diversity of classes was seemingly an illusion, the grinding was fun but issues with spawn behaviors severely hampered it in all but a few scant zones. The lack of PVP made some more PVP-centric classes immensely underwhelming and further limited the amount of interesting things to play-... You see where I'm going. I quit, wrote it off as a huge mistake and thought I'd never look back.
Then comes the most recent patch, completely and utterly reworking stats, gear, and several skills in the game. I hemmed and hawed at the idea but I still really want a true Ragnarok successor so I gave it a shot- and I was completely blown away!
The game has changed so much for the better. Grinding feels fresh and rewarding, the addition of dozens of very very low drop chance niceties make it feel like no amount of grinding is ever a waste, when you have a chance to drop dungeon instant clear vouchers or dungeon exp multiplier tokens from enemies. Boss cards have more usage than just the three classes that used to use them, now. Gear feels rewarding and solid- they have a good amount of staying power and it's actually quite nice to boost, enchant, reforge, gem socket and otherwise trick out the pieces of gear that you really like.
The classes have so many interesting interactions and skills that play off of one another in strange and unique ways that every party you join up with feels different. Oh wow, this time we have a psychokino that can pull every enemy in the dungeon into a line that's just perfect for our monk to blast with energy beam- Oh fantastic we have a peltasta to pull mobs into my fully casted meteor- Oh look a that the identifier just gave our hoplite a baffling amount of crit so that her stabbing special move instantly murders this boss. The list goes on, and they're all fun to explore.
There's a ton more nuance to things and it seems like IMC are working hard to bring back an incredibly nostalgic, fun grinding game that caters to a lot of different playstyles. I applaud them for this, and can't wait to see where things go- Especially with the Klaipeda rennovation coming right around the corner.
As an answer to the negative nancies with completely unrealistic expectations here- Yes, the game isn't perfectly optimized. If you play on an AMD card expect sub-optimal performance. On the flip side, for Intel cards the game plays perfectly even on older computers while still looking great.
The game isn't perfect by any stretch- I'm not saying it is. What I can say is that it started badly but is quickly gaining ground. If you decide to play, keep in mind that it's come a long way and seems to continue trekking along towards being an extremely fun game. IMC isn't afraid to admit when they heck up, and they're overwhelmingly generous with compensation for the times that they do manage to heck up. If you've looked at this before, written it off, or even played in the beta and were left feeling like the game had potential but wasted it, I highly encourage you to give it another shot.

Honsetly, Transistor is the single most brilliant game I have ever played. Every aspect of both gameplay and the narrative is 100% on point. Combat first: Transistor is completely intelligence based. The combat system is remarkable in that you don't have to have amazing at aiming or have super fast reflexes, but you just have to use some common sense. The way your abilities work in tandem is unprecedented and the sheer amount of ways you can fight is brilliant. The turn function is amazing and it opens up worlds of possiblities, but I suggest that people not use it 100% of the time as fighting in real time is somewhat amazing and powerful. The combat only gets better when you start your recursions (or New Game+). The way you can modify the abilities you have as you receive copies of those abilities during the recursion is so powerful and opens up new doors into how you can approach combat. Transistor has the most innovative combat system I've seen to date and is completely enjoyable. The story is jawdropping in its scale and complexity. It may be hard to understand in the first half of your first game, however once you understand the world and how the transistor works and the motivation of the antagonists in the game, everything meshes wonderfully. The OVC terminals also add a lot to the game as you get glimpses into what Cloudbank was before the Process. And, of course, the ending is jaw-droppingly good. Combine the story and combat with the glorious soundtrack and beautiful art and you have yourselves what Transistor is: an 11/10 game. Years later, a playthrough of this game is still a beautiful work of art.

I had a lot of problems with this game, but overall I think the positives outweigh the negatives.
The primary positive for me in both Supergiant games is the sound direction, especially the music. Darren Korb is fast on his way to becoming one of my favorite composers and Ashley Barrett's vocals are amazing. The sound effects also stick out as appropriately digital, given the game's motif. Normally I would lead with sound direction and music as positives only if the rest of the game isn't up to snuff, but that isn't the case here: I just think that the auditory portions of this game are SO fantastic as to deserve top billing even among the other positives. Voice acting gets an additional nod, and while I don't think the "narrator" of this game reaches the grand standard set by Logan Cunningham (from Bastion) he does a great job nonetheless.
Graphically the game is gorgeous, and there are several different types of setpieces that break up the isometric perspective you see in most screenshots. I suppose it's more correct to say that the first 3/4 or so of the game is gorgeous; due to storyline reasons almost the entire last quarter of the game is nothing but white cityscape, and while it fits with both the story and the tone it doesn't change the fact that it loses a lot of the visual appeal of the earlier sections. A sea of grayscale isn't particularly visually engaging, but on the plus side Red sticks out that much more in the blankness.
Although the creators said during production that the gameplay isn't Bastion 2.0 (which would have been fine by me; I adored Bastion), fans of Bastion will notice one similar element: the "choose a deity to make the game harder" element of Bastion is matched in Transistor by the Limiter system, which functions almost identically. You are allowed to choose several limits for your character (less Memory, which is spent on moves, or more Cells to pick up after battle, etc.) which increase the experience gain for each combat session. Even taking every Limiter the game gave me, however, I was unable to reach max level on the first playthrough; you'll have to go through the game at least twice for those achievements, it seems.
Combat, however, is very different. At max level you'll have 4 move slots, 2 upgrade slots per move, and 4 passive slots. Functions go in all of these slots and have different effects based on where they're placed (the function Ping can be a low-damage spam move, or when used as an upgrade for another function it reduces the cost for that function during Turn(), or as a passive it increases the amount of distance Red can travel while in Turn()). There are no weapons (the Transistor is your one and only weapon), merely Functions that you can slot as you will to create the exact moveset and passive benefits to fit your combat style. Do you want to be a summoner who can charm enemies? Use Help() and slot it with Switch() and you can now summon a robo-dog whose bark turns other enemies to your side. Want to be sneaky and backstabby? Use Jaunt() to teleport behind enemies and surprise them with a Breach() to the♥♥♥♥♥ boosted for backstab damage with a Mask() helper function. Or maybe you want to use Void() slotted with Spark() to doubly weaken enemies before hitting them with Crash() slotted with BOTH Switch() and Purge() to stun them, charm them, AND put a DoT on them all in the same move. And that's just a small taste of all the options you're presented with. Transistor does a great job of giving you building blocks and allowing you to make your own fun.
While Bastion had a lot of reliance on timed hits and judgement of distance, the gameplay of Transistor is defined by its Turn() system. Using Turn() you plan out a set of moves for Red to perform, and when you end Turn() she performs all of those moves in hyper speed (not instantaneously, which is very important to note; she moves much faster but it still takes her time to perform all of the inputs). More powerful Functions require more of your planning time; when you run out of planning time, you can input no more commands. You can rewind your commands and see if a different set will give you the outcome you're looking for, however; your Turn() isn't set in stone until you actually end it. However, using Turn() means that you can't use ANY of your functions afterward until all of that planning is regenerated. Do you use up all your planning time at once for a big combo attack knowing that afterwards you'll be entirely helpless for a few seconds, or do you sacrifice on damage and utility during Turn() to use up less planning time so that your period of helpelessness is as short as possible?
While you CAN play Transistor without using the Turn() system and simply manually inputting commands in real-time, I feel the combat is built around the system to such a degree that realistically it's a necessity. And that's one of my sore points with the game; due to the Turn() system the combat functions like some weird combination of RTS and action, but it blends them in such a way that the deficiencies in both systems are readily apparent. If you use Turn() the only thing you can do afterwards (unless you use a particular helper function) is run around like a chicken with its head cut off, but the game throws so many enemies at you in most combats that playing Transistor like a straight action game WITHOUT Turn() is an exercise in futility since you'll just be overrun. It certainly doesn't help matters that almost every single enemy in the game is faster than Red, ensuring that even with a head start provided by Turn() they'll be sure to catch up while she's recovering.
As a programmer myself I got quite a bit of enjoyment out of the programming references in just about every facet of the game. The story is intentionally vague and cloudy in the beginning, which I found a bit annoying, but the game slowly fills you in as you go along and I eventually came to realize that it worked better by keeping you in the dark for so long. One interesting thing to note about the story is that, to get the most out of it, you'll have to keep mixing up your loadout; you can only get the backstory on all of the characters by using their related functions in each slot. Even if you find a very powerful Function combination, if you want that extra plot information you'll have to pass it up for at least a little while so you can use those Functions elsewhere. There are only 4 really important characters throughout the story (and only 3 of those are voiced) but there are plenty of background characters with interesting backstories that do relate to the ongoing plot.
For a quick story synopsis: you play as Red, a singer without a voice, wielding the titular Transistor, a talking dual-combination sword and memory chip, fighting against both the mysterious Camerata, an Illuminatiesque organization, and their destructive Process, whose sole goal seems to be the utter destruction of your city. Getting too much more into it would rob you of finding out the information for yourself. I did find myself losing interest in the story after about the halfway point (the game's relatively short length does it favors here, I think), but the ending makes up for it.
tl;dr Though I have some issues with how the combat plays out due to its odd mixture of RTS and action elements, they're relatively minor in the grand scheme of things and overall the gameplay is good. Music and voice are amazing just like in Bastion, and just like in Bastion they absolutely steal the show here. Graphics are good and art direction is (mostly) interesting. The plot becomes less interesting the more you learn about it (it starts off great and mysterious, but completely lost my interest about 3/5 of the way through) but pulled through in the end. Overall, I definitely recommend it.

Hmm, perhaps go for it with the sale but if you're thinking about it when it has returned to £14.99 then maybe give it a miss. It's a decent game with an interesting story, but it's nothing like Amnesia The Dark Descent. At first you're given the similar sense of fear that you encounter in the first game, but you later find that fear wearing off pretty early on.
GAMEPLAY:
The gameplay is the same as the first game, the only difference is, there are no pick ups or necessities like oil, health, etc. The only thing you'll be looking around for are notes that aren't really necessary either. This was a massive dissapointment for me because the thing that makes the first game so great is the need for certain items in order to survive. This massively reduces the feeling of danger. There are a very small number of "puzzles" if you want tocall them that but unfortunately they're super easy to figure out. Because of the small number and ease, you feel yourself doing nothing but walking through corridors with literally NO sense of fear or danger.
THE MONSTERS:
You very rarely come across them. You see them a lot in the beginning but they're mostly scripted events that won't harm you. For the short number of times you do encounter them, they're not really scary nor do they pose much of a threat as they're easy to avoid and evade. Their design isn't really great either. There was a point later on in the game where you see a few up close and, if I'm honest, they were more cute than scary. Just think of a pig with a more ape like body. Amnesia: TDD had very well designed monsters and they came in a small variety to spice things up. They were legitimately scary at times whereas these "Pigmen" are anything but.
THE STORY:
It's OKAY. Not great but okay. It does do a good job in making you curious but I never felt satisfied, especially when I completed it. I was more "Meh, not bad" and I came off. I wasn't blown away and, with such limiting gameplay, I don't think the story is worth the £14.99 price tag.
Overall, not a terrible game but I wouldn't say it deserves to be an Amnesia title. It took me 3 hours to complete but I was wasting time looking for notes that I wouldn't read just to fullfill my OCD so I'd say probably 2 hours. Not very long at all which surprised me greatly. As it's £2.99 then grab it. Have a go and see if you enjoy it but after the sale, I'd advise leaving it to rest. You wouldn't be missing out on much.

Oh man, World of Goo.
This game is a relic of fantastic game design.
To put things simply, this game puts you in a world requiring you to build builds and complex constructs to overcome obstacles and reach the end. The end result uses encompasses your construct allowing your "goos" to reach the end pipe, with plenty of spare and win.
While super simple, this game can be frustratingly hard to beat. But once you beat the level, you are overwhelmed with a feeling of accomplishment. On top of beating the level, you can do what is known as an "OCD" challenge. Typically these result in a time trial, overabundance of goos or the least amount of moves possible.
This game's physics constantly challenge you and require you to use your own intuition and reasoning to beat the level.
Overall, I HIGHLY recommend this game. It is cute, has an engaging storyline (which I won't spoil), and has the best engine for a physics-based puzzle game I've ever played.

At first glance you see a game with low resolution graphics with only one screen you ever play on. What you find when you dig a little deeper is an addictive and engrossing game. You get to learn about the lives of some of the characters. It is a dark and gritty experience into the lives of people in a war torn era. Checkpoints like the ones in this game actually existed. There is the pressure to get people through the checkpoints, but not get those awful citations of when you made a mistake. It is quite challenging to make it through each day without mistakes. The learning curve it not steep, but to master it can take quite a while. You will start and restart many games. It's like those old school Nintendo games that were punishing in how difficult they could be. Keep going and your perseverance will pay off.
You also need to be aware of those heart attack moments when someone climbs the wall. The game does a great job of gradually getting more difficult each day. You need to be aware of how the rules and regulations change and what to look for. What might be acceptable one day is grounds for denial through the checkpoint the next. You need to check and see if anyone is concealing anything. Do they have a passport or documentation if they are returning to their home country?
There are many endings and some hard to get achievements. These are the pros of the game. Oh, and I love Jorji. You not need passport. Right?

To any and all who have ever worked a boring desk job especially in retail or customer care, I highly recommend:
"Papers, Please" A document thriller.
You are a father, a husband, a son-in-law, and a brother. You are a provider for 4 mouths. Your budget consists of 2 checkboxes: Does your family eat? Does your family have Heating in Russian November?
Also the rent went up.
For a game that is essentially a desk job work-a-holic simulator where you only work 16 hour shifts because your son needs medicine, it is compelling. It is powerful, and at times, rewarding.
A woman is entering Arstotzka (in-game Russia) from Impor (another in-game country) to visit her son who she hasn't seen in 5 years. She ignores your request for her entry visa until asked because she is so enamored with her trip. Upon receiving the visa, you discover that it is expired. You have 3 mistakes on your belt already, and you've taken a $5 cut to your $55 salary.
Another mistake will be an additional $10.
Your son is sick.
Your family hasn't had food in 2 days.
The rent is $30 and food is $20.
You deny her passport and send her on her way.
Need to train mouse precision and concentration? This game is for you.

In my eyes; It's not the devs' fault that this game went to balls. It's the community's. I'll tell you why--
Hackers, DMers, trolls, and all sorts of other nasty ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s running up in your grille, just to mess with you.
You could be building the house that you spent two hours gathering resources for, guess what? Someone's gonna' run up, stab you in the back with the King's sword, and steal all your gear, because they got a band of friends together to take the throne, stab the first King in the throat, set the taxes to 100% and run around the server destroying everybody's♥♥♥♥♥♥
The devs can't counter that.
You could be running around as a new spawn, minding your own business, and somebody could fly across the map and hook you with a rope. They take you to their house and lock you up in stocks just to whip you and laugh about how you couldn't fight back.
The devs could probably counter that; but they haven't.
You could be squaring up to your friend, a stranger, or a hostile, and you could be evenly armed in every field-- except hit detection, it seems to go one way or the other in a completely unbalanced fashion. Either you kill the guy really badly, or you die really badly.
The devs could probably counter that too; but they haven't.
There are moments, though, where the community shines a diamond in the rough at you.
A hacker flew out of nowhere, offered me a lift to the castle-- I reluctantly agreed, and he picked me up with a rope. Off we went to the castle. Next thing I knew he was battling the King whilst I was settled on the throne, taking his crown. Slowly and mockingly, as the hacker spurted some RP nonesense about him being a tyrant ruler and how he's ushering in a better age in time. In reality the guy had taxes set to 5% and the hacker wanted them to go down.
Or when I was a lonely newspawn tossing about on the beach when a group of friendly fellows in full iron armor waltzed up and asked if I needed any help building a home. They chopped down trees, mined rocks and ores and did all of the work for me, to build me tools to help them get more. We eventually built me a small castle to live in, complete with furnishings, weapons for defence, and armor for survival.
It could still be worth a shot to buy this game, but... you'd best bring friends to combat the loneliness of empty servers, or the trolls.

I guess I am going to be one of the rare few people to say this but, I preferred this game to The Dark Descent.
While it was lacking on gameplay with fewer puzzles and less interaction for the player after the removal of the sanity meter, I felt this game to be a much better horror experience as a whole. One of my complaints about The Dark Descent was that the story was quite vague unless you read all the notes and books around the game but this game, was a lot more interesting story-wise in my opinion and it was told in a much better way. It was told in a way that actually added a lot more emotion and the world was really well made.
A few reasons why I felt this game was a lot better as a horror experience include the story. The story is a horror story alone and it hits hard as you near the climax of the game. On top of that, I read a couple of reviews of this game all saying that the game wasn't great in the horror aspect especially because
While you might think that reduces the scare factor, I felt it made me a lot more nervous as I ended up playing more recklessly near the beginning and when I did reach a scary moment, I was less prepared for it and from then on I was way more afraid of what could happen. On top of all this, the ambience and environment was perfectly created to add even more chills and a creepy factor that was also present in The Dark Descent.
The soundtrack of this game is also amazing. It suited the game perfectly and added a lot more emotion when it needed to and a lot more tension when it needed to.
Basically, all my complaints with The Dark Descent were removed and that, in my opinion, made for an amazing horror game.
My only warning for the game is that it is quite short being around 3 - 4 hours so I would suggest getting it on sale as the normal price can be considered to be quite high. Especially if you are going to end up being disappointed with the game like a few other people, specifically The Dark Descent fans.

What an awesome game, easily one of my all-time favorite shooters (and games) ever made. The worst thing about this game is how short it is, you just want more and more of it. Luckily there is a fair amount of replay value in the form of collectibles, a new game plus mode (I am on my second playthrough at the moment), and some duel/arcade modes that you can mess around with outside of the main story. It's just a damn good time.
The story itself is superbly narrated, with the main character telling bits and pieces of his adventures as you are going through levels. The graphics are colorful and eye-catching, the combat is an absolute blast, and there are even several skill trees for you to pour over. This is one of those games where the collectibles are actually fun to go after, as they provide you with little bits of history from the time period. Fittingly labeled "Nuggets of Truth" they give you a brief glimpse into the lives of famous chracters and places from old west. Some folks may not be that interested, but being something of a history nerd myself especially when it comes to the old west time period, I loved reading through them.
There are several weapons to play with, and your skill selections will impact not just how they operate but how they look as well. Combat is explosive and engaging, it makes you feel like you are in the middle of a shootout. There is a matrix-like slowdown mechanic that makes you feel pretty badass and though I will admit that it can be somewhat overpowered at times, it greatly adds to the fun factor.
I could go on about this game, but you should really just buy it. It is totally worth the price and you'll have tons of fun playing.

Honsetly, Transistor is the single most brilliant game I have ever played. Every aspect of both gameplay and the narrative is 100% on point. Combat first: Transistor is completely intelligence based. The combat system is remarkable in that you don't have to have amazing at aiming or have super fast reflexes, but you just have to use some common sense. The way your abilities work in tandem is unprecedented and the sheer amount of ways you can fight is brilliant. The turn function is amazing and it opens up worlds of possiblities, but I suggest that people not use it 100% of the time as fighting in real time is somewhat amazing and powerful. The combat only gets better when you start your recursions (or New Game+). The way you can modify the abilities you have as you receive copies of those abilities during the recursion is so powerful and opens up new doors into how you can approach combat. Transistor has the most innovative combat system I've seen to date and is completely enjoyable. The story is jawdropping in its scale and complexity. It may be hard to understand in the first half of your first game, however once you understand the world and how the transistor works and the motivation of the antagonists in the game, everything meshes wonderfully. The OVC terminals also add a lot to the game as you get glimpses into what Cloudbank was before the Process. And, of course, the ending is jaw-droppingly good. Combine the story and combat with the glorious soundtrack and beautiful art and you have yourselves what Transistor is: an 11/10 game. Years later, a playthrough of this game is still a beautiful work of art.

I had a lot of problems with this game, but overall I think the positives outweigh the negatives.
The primary positive for me in both Supergiant games is the sound direction, especially the music. Darren Korb is fast on his way to becoming one of my favorite composers and Ashley Barrett's vocals are amazing. The sound effects also stick out as appropriately digital, given the game's motif. Normally I would lead with sound direction and music as positives only if the rest of the game isn't up to snuff, but that isn't the case here: I just think that the auditory portions of this game are SO fantastic as to deserve top billing even among the other positives. Voice acting gets an additional nod, and while I don't think the "narrator" of this game reaches the grand standard set by Logan Cunningham (from Bastion) he does a great job nonetheless.
Graphically the game is gorgeous, and there are several different types of setpieces that break up the isometric perspective you see in most screenshots. I suppose it's more correct to say that the first 3/4 or so of the game is gorgeous; due to storyline reasons almost the entire last quarter of the game is nothing but white cityscape, and while it fits with both the story and the tone it doesn't change the fact that it loses a lot of the visual appeal of the earlier sections. A sea of grayscale isn't particularly visually engaging, but on the plus side Red sticks out that much more in the blankness.
Although the creators said during production that the gameplay isn't Bastion 2.0 (which would have been fine by me; I adored Bastion), fans of Bastion will notice one similar element: the "choose a deity to make the game harder" element of Bastion is matched in Transistor by the Limiter system, which functions almost identically. You are allowed to choose several limits for your character (less Memory, which is spent on moves, or more Cells to pick up after battle, etc.) which increase the experience gain for each combat session. Even taking every Limiter the game gave me, however, I was unable to reach max level on the first playthrough; you'll have to go through the game at least twice for those achievements, it seems.
Combat, however, is very different. At max level you'll have 4 move slots, 2 upgrade slots per move, and 4 passive slots. Functions go in all of these slots and have different effects based on where they're placed (the function Ping can be a low-damage spam move, or when used as an upgrade for another function it reduces the cost for that function during Turn(), or as a passive it increases the amount of distance Red can travel while in Turn()). There are no weapons (the Transistor is your one and only weapon), merely Functions that you can slot as you will to create the exact moveset and passive benefits to fit your combat style. Do you want to be a summoner who can charm enemies? Use Help() and slot it with Switch() and you can now summon a robo-dog whose bark turns other enemies to your side. Want to be sneaky and backstabby? Use Jaunt() to teleport behind enemies and surprise them with a Breach() to the♥♥♥♥♥ boosted for backstab damage with a Mask() helper function. Or maybe you want to use Void() slotted with Spark() to doubly weaken enemies before hitting them with Crash() slotted with BOTH Switch() and Purge() to stun them, charm them, AND put a DoT on them all in the same move. And that's just a small taste of all the options you're presented with. Transistor does a great job of giving you building blocks and allowing you to make your own fun.
While Bastion had a lot of reliance on timed hits and judgement of distance, the gameplay of Transistor is defined by its Turn() system. Using Turn() you plan out a set of moves for Red to perform, and when you end Turn() she performs all of those moves in hyper speed (not instantaneously, which is very important to note; she moves much faster but it still takes her time to perform all of the inputs). More powerful Functions require more of your planning time; when you run out of planning time, you can input no more commands. You can rewind your commands and see if a different set will give you the outcome you're looking for, however; your Turn() isn't set in stone until you actually end it. However, using Turn() means that you can't use ANY of your functions afterward until all of that planning is regenerated. Do you use up all your planning time at once for a big combo attack knowing that afterwards you'll be entirely helpless for a few seconds, or do you sacrifice on damage and utility during Turn() to use up less planning time so that your period of helpelessness is as short as possible?
While you CAN play Transistor without using the Turn() system and simply manually inputting commands in real-time, I feel the combat is built around the system to such a degree that realistically it's a necessity. And that's one of my sore points with the game; due to the Turn() system the combat functions like some weird combination of RTS and action, but it blends them in such a way that the deficiencies in both systems are readily apparent. If you use Turn() the only thing you can do afterwards (unless you use a particular helper function) is run around like a chicken with its head cut off, but the game throws so many enemies at you in most combats that playing Transistor like a straight action game WITHOUT Turn() is an exercise in futility since you'll just be overrun. It certainly doesn't help matters that almost every single enemy in the game is faster than Red, ensuring that even with a head start provided by Turn() they'll be sure to catch up while she's recovering.
As a programmer myself I got quite a bit of enjoyment out of the programming references in just about every facet of the game. The story is intentionally vague and cloudy in the beginning, which I found a bit annoying, but the game slowly fills you in as you go along and I eventually came to realize that it worked better by keeping you in the dark for so long. One interesting thing to note about the story is that, to get the most out of it, you'll have to keep mixing up your loadout; you can only get the backstory on all of the characters by using their related functions in each slot. Even if you find a very powerful Function combination, if you want that extra plot information you'll have to pass it up for at least a little while so you can use those Functions elsewhere. There are only 4 really important characters throughout the story (and only 3 of those are voiced) but there are plenty of background characters with interesting backstories that do relate to the ongoing plot.
For a quick story synopsis: you play as Red, a singer without a voice, wielding the titular Transistor, a talking dual-combination sword and memory chip, fighting against both the mysterious Camerata, an Illuminatiesque organization, and their destructive Process, whose sole goal seems to be the utter destruction of your city. Getting too much more into it would rob you of finding out the information for yourself. I did find myself losing interest in the story after about the halfway point (the game's relatively short length does it favors here, I think), but the ending makes up for it.
tl;dr Though I have some issues with how the combat plays out due to its odd mixture of RTS and action elements, they're relatively minor in the grand scheme of things and overall the gameplay is good. Music and voice are amazing just like in Bastion, and just like in Bastion they absolutely steal the show here. Graphics are good and art direction is (mostly) interesting. The plot becomes less interesting the more you learn about it (it starts off great and mysterious, but completely lost my interest about 3/5 of the way through) but pulled through in the end. Overall, I definitely recommend it.

This has been my go to game for the last couple of years  now. Its pretty good, but the fan boys will do all they can to ignore its flaws. I'm gonna talk about what's bad, while the number of hours I've spent playing this game should demonstrate the good.
1) Antisocial design. The focus is on instanced dungeons, accessed via an auto group making function called the "duty finder." This really kills the need for social interaction, making this feel less like an MMO and more like a single player dungeon crawler. The fact that everything is accessed through a menu in my eyes makes the world feel disconnected, ruins the immersion and is very un-rpg. Most of the content is trivially easy, and ammounts to simple time sink- the vernacular is that dungeons are "ran" ie; speed ran ie; no time to chat, and because it is so easy, no need to work together to develop strategies. The guilds in this game are called "Free companies" but there is no content that teams you up with your free company in a meaningful way. The free company is essentially just a chat room.
2) No character customization. You can change your aesthetics, and the visual design is very good, however the actual gameplay design is severely lacking. All gear forms a simple linear progression, there is no interesting gear with unique effects or procs whatsoever. Every Black mage is exactly the same as every other black mage.
3) In game economy. The in game economy is bad. Its not an economically focused game per se, but there is a fairly robust crafting system. Unfortunately, crafting is largely irrelevant, as it is too easy to get through the whole game without patronizing and crafters.
4) Lack of strategy elements in combat. The combat in this game is all about moving around to dodge enemy attacks. Each class has a set rotation of skills which are used against all enemies. These rotations do become complex for many / most classes by endgame, but it still ammounts to an endlessly repetitive recital, devoid of any strategic thought. When people speak of "Strategy" in this game, they are refering to mechanics that consist of "Don't attack x enemy or it will trigger an instakill or wait til x phase then max DPS"  DPS checks and Traps, thats it.
5) The dialogue...! Square enix and Final fantasy are known for having amazing stories. And some of the story arcs in this game are quite good. But the dialogue sequences are soooo long and not in an interesting way. The writing could be much more succinct. Its clear that some producers were walking around saying "Make this scene longer! Make this dialogue wordier! We need to have x minutes of cutscenes for this story arc!" Its all just drags out and it detracts from my abilitiy to care about the story. Also the voice acting is annoying, all the characters seem to have really contrived british accents. I think I'd like it better without voice acting.
6) They went overboard with combat animations. You can't see whats going on in fights 90% of the time.
7) PVP. The PVP in this game sucks. It has pvp technically, but it is not a pvp game. Don't get it if you like pvp. PVP is only in controlled battlegrounds, and everybody sucks at it, probably because they are used to mindlessly slaughtering helpless AI.
8) Treadmill progression. Ok, so to some extent this is what MMOS are all about. But in this game its really silly because every 3 months a new tier of item comes out that makes everything previous completely obsolete. And these items are just grinded for, no interesting quests, and the items are just more stat points, again, no interesting mechanical design in terms of gear.
So what's good about this game?
1) The community, despite being full of apologists and footsucking SE worshippers, is really one of the best out there. The game is relatively devoid of trolls and the toxic wasters that ruin so many other games, *cough archeage* *cough league of legends* *cough wow*  I just wish people would be more critical so that SE might actually try to improve on the game's shortcomings. Its probably because the game is subscription based and has no real pvp, but whatever it is this pretty much outweighs all the negative things about this game.
2) Character models. The characters have this universal type of appeal, the game isn't dark, it isn't gritty- its markedly Final fantasy. If you are a fan of Final Fantasy you will love this game, even if they slam you in the face with "subtle" references to classic titles every 5 minutes. Seriously square, you could be more subtle.
3) Crafting system. Crafting in this game is kind of a cool mini game, and crafting classes are nearly as involved as combat classes, which is cool. Its too bad crafted gear is useless.
4) Housing system. I'm not sure whetehr to make this a positive or negative factor, but it connects with point 3. The housing in this game is falls into identical instances which is lame. And you can't really design your own house, which is lame. However, there are a great many items you can place in and around your house to make it your own. And most of these items are crafted. Really, this is what crafting is about.
So the REAL metagame is Adventure > Earn money > Buy stuff for your house > Play FF "The Sims" Online

Dreamfall: TLJ is a 3-d third-person point and click adventure game. The game is a sequel to a classic adventure game released in 1998 called The Longest Journey. It is not necessary to play the original TLJ to play Dreamfall, but it helps a lot, since the game universe and many characters are the same. The game is very heavy on story, dialogue, and cinematics, and light on puzzles and gameplay.
Story: the story is both the best and the worst I have ever seen in an adventure game. In the last two years I have completed 12 adventure games including old classics and modern indies. Dreamfall has a very complex and compelling story involving several interesting characters, political movements, and the complex game universe. It includes elements of comedy, drama, and tragedy. The story really gathers steam toward the end, resolving one storyline while introducing several more. Then, in the middle of the gathering drama and revelations, the game suddenly ends with no resolution to the fate of a dozen major characters and a dozen major plotlines. This is perhaps the most unsatisfying ending I have ever seen in a game, movie, book etc. Even if they did plan on a sequel, this was just plain terrible. I know a lot of people hated The Empire Strikes Back because of the unresolved plot lines. This is 100x worse.
Gameplay: there are a few puzzles that require some thought, but overall the mental challenge of this game is on the light side for an adventure game. It is a little unfair to say that this is just an interactive movie, there are some clever puzzles. Unfortunately there are many times you are just sent on a mission to fetch a particular item and bring it to a particular place. The purpose of these brainless missions is to trigger cut-scenes that move the story along. A lot of the action takes place in small rooms and tunnels. This means the camera that follows you has to zoom in and out a lot. I suppose this is a problem with any 3-d third-person game, but it can make you a bit dizzy. The interface was tweaked to be more "console friendly". This makes it a little more clunky for the PC, but not terrible.
Fighting and stealth: the developers added a few fights and a few stealth sequences in the game. The fighting is flat out a waste of time. Just stand in front of your enemy and smash the mouse button and you win. Either that, or the enemy is so tough you always lose. The stealth sequences were much better, although they did not really fit in an adventure game. I like to play adventure games leisurely, with one hand on the mouse and the other hand holding a cup of coffee. I don't want action.
Graphics: the graphics are dated by 2013 standards, but they are nice, especially the Dreamcore sequence. The close-up shots of faces look the worst. Lots of cut-scenes, some of which are pretty cool.
Sound: there seems to be a lot of interesting music and sounds, much better than the typical adventure game.
Overall, from the quality of the story, to the quality of the sound and graphics, to the overall scope of the game, this had the potential to be EASILY the best adventure game of all time. Unfortunately the game was crippled by bizarre decisions by the developers: the mega-cliffhanger ending, the introduction of bad action elements, the clunky interface, the too-easy puzzles. What were they thinking?

Great game! A must buy for adventure fans who love a good story,
First, you should know that this is a sequel to the game The Longuest Journey, also available on Steam. You should play that game first for story continuity, and it is a good adventure game as well.
The story is what made me fall in love with this game. The well paced plot keeps you interested throughout, while well written dialogue and excellent voice acting made the characters believable, and even pretty darn likable. Zoe and Kian, two of the three characters you will play as, are particularly very charismatic.
The other staple of an adventure game are the puzzles. The worst scenario for a player is to be stuck on a puzzle they cannot solve, which is not a problem at all in this game, as puzzles are relatively easy, and consequently do not slow down story progression.
The scenery is simply breathtaking: varried, colorful, and beatiful. Don't just take my word for it, look at the screenshots above. Graphically, the game still looks good (current year 2013).
Around 4 or 5 times in the game, you are asked to fight. The game suddenly changes to an action game, the controls of which are awkward, and the experience felt unpolished. But it is only a small flaw with the game that you can get by easily enough.
Also of note, as the story focuses initially on the lives of two women and their relationships, it may be more appealing to a female audience.
The Longest Journey & Dreamfall are works of art. They sustained the Adventure genre when most publishers dared not touch it, before Tell Tale brought it back in full force.

*UPDATED*
So I just got this game last november for the 9euro pricetag while it was on sale and would like to give it a little bit of review.
TL;DR
Pros:
+Really immersive
+Really helpful and possitive community
+Beautiful tamriel landscape
+Plenty of quests to keep you busy (+750 quests), including dungeons and trials.
+The mechanic of the game which lets players to dodge and time their next attacks demand a more dynamic play style (which is the strongest point of this game for me)
Cons:
-it's quite confusing to comprehend the game
-there aren't any Asian dedicated server (only EU and NA)
-the inventory is limited for non-subscription players
FULL REVIEW:
First of all, this game offers you the experience of elder scrolls games with a touch of an mmorpg to it. The immersion that I get from this game is amazing, especially knowing that it is in the same universe of other elder scrolls online (only thousand years before Skyrim and Oblivion)
All the stories are well-driven and you get to choose a lot of possibilities for your character which becomes really helpful for you to get comfortable with your character from the get-go. Everytime you finish a quest and save a kingdom or a small village will benefit your future quests as people will know you from your previous deeds. Sometimes, your choice during the quest also affects the ending of such quest. The huge selection of quests and different mechanics of each quests and dungeons make this game even more interesting and challenging (although for normal quests sometimes it gets slightly repetitive).
Unlike the review videos that came out 3 years ago, which shows how killing a boss will only give you 2 gold or nothing at all, the current patch is really rewarding. Depending on which side of the RNG god are you, the final bosts will give you a high-end weapon for your current level. (on veteran dungeons the final bosts will gives a 100% chance of getting a particular type of epic headgear, with random traits on it.)
On the other hand, the mechanics and how to play this game get quite confusing at first, especially for the crafting system. Nonetheless, it will be really rewarding once you know how it works and I suggest that you need to start working on your crafting skill line since the beginning, as it will become really handy during the end-game. This is not a big problem, however, since there are quite plenty of guides and tutorial on how to master this game or get your perfect character, either on youtube or eso forums. So, you will not have a hard time understanding this game.
My biggest gripe about this game is that it doesn't have any Asian dedicated server which is really a shame since that means I cannot play this game when I come back to my country in ASEAN.
The conclusion is that although it has some minor downsides, for me, this game brings the things that I really want the most from an mmorpg game, especially with the 9euro pricetag. 10/10 would recommend it. (unless you live in Asian countries)

The first challenges are pretty much self explanatory and very easy. Others need planing ahead, and very intense knowledge of the game mechanics on Magic: The Gathering (for example that you can use Mana activated powers or others several times in just one combat round).
The game is fun to play, and it even doesn't get boring after you played the campaign mode. So if you have some friends who also might like to play magic - try to buy several copies of it, and gift it to them... or let them gift it to you.

I know this game is well over a year old but I felt that it was good enough after me finally completing it to come back and do a review. 'Papers Please' is a deeply immersive 2D simulation. It gives you the relatively boring and repeditive job of being an immegration control officer and makes it fun with it's rich narrative and complementary art style. The mechanics of the game also change based on the narrative and really make the communist and authoritarian world your playing in feel all that more real as the ruels to immegration change based on the will of your nation. The many multiple endings and the achievements for the game also add to the experience and don't just feel like last minute 'tack on's' to make the game look or feel like what many would conisder 'a real game should look like'. No instead each achievement and each ending earned is something unique and either gives you context to the world in which you find yourself or it makes you question things such as the value of freedom in our own world. While I was a tad dissapointed with the meer   4 - 5 hours of game time in the main story mode of the game, none of that 4 - 5 hours was in any was dissapointing. This game will definatly leave you with a yerning for more and while I am a tad upset to have heard that Lucas Pope does not plan to do anything further with this title, I would still STRONGLY RECOMMEND it to be part of any decent steam library.

This is quite a good game. True, it's terribly short - I didn't use any hint and was done in aprox. an hour, and for that length, it's rather expensive. It can feel a bit plain at first, maybe due to the fact that it doesn't use that fancy ornate cursor we're used from Hidden Object Games but the system cursor, and there's no talking, only sound and music (except for one situation where you have to dial a phone number). I had played previous games by this developer (not available on Steam), which were dense, athmospheric, had very good voice acting and a compelling story - and they were nice and long. Compared to them ("Margrave: Curse of the severed heart" and "Margrave: The Blacksimth's daughter"), "Escape from Darkmoor Manor" comes short, and I wonder if they run out off funding.
However, if you regard this game as a ghost story, it works, and for a ghost story, the length is just fine. This is not Lovecraftian horror, but if you like stories by M.R. James or E.F. Benson, this is the game for you. There's no hidden object scenes, and though there are some puzzles, you don't buy this game for the puzzles. Buy if for the story it tells. Diary pages scattererd around a derelict house are nothing new, but this time, the story is told well, and combined with the eerie atmosphere, subtle music and sound effects, it's spine-tingling. No jump scares, no moaning spirits, but when I played this game late at night and was ready to enter the last room, the one the diary said noises came from at night, I felt safer to quit the game and wait until morning.
Sometimes all it needs is a compelling story. What I liked about this one was that usually when you walk a house in a hidden cbject-style game, you'll find rooms barred and locked with puzzle locks and covered in cobwebs, allegedly not open in ages, but if you open them you find the room behind it inhabited, or Doctor Evil is already there, or stuff like this. In Darkmor Manor, not only is the house truely deserted - the diary also tells the story of how or why each door was locked, of why keys were hidden or doorknobs went missing, all without feelings forced. There's a palpabled connection between the story told in the diary and the visuals, making this game an interactive ghost story.
It's a short game, but I don't mind having paid almost 4 Euros for it. Just like re-reading a good story now and then to enjoying the spine-tingling sensation, I can imagine re-playing this game in a year or so.
