Magic: The Gathering, for those who aren't familiar with Nerd Culture, is the collectible card game in the vein of Pokemon or Yu-Gi-Oh where nerds take a break from reality and pretend to be powerful 'Planeswalkers' able to cast devastating spells and summon powerful creatures (not to be confused with Streetwalkers who have very different powers). They do this by buying lots and lots of cardboard cards with pretty pictures of (sometimes scantily clad) women in dramatic poses. There are cards of other fantasy-type things too but nobody cares about them. The winner is usually the nerd with the most expensive cards although there is some minor element of strategy and luck involved.
The creators of Magic (who may or may not have been sober at the time) once declared that they wanted Magic to become a classic game like Chess. Chess of course is a symmetric game of pure strategy with no element of luck whatsoever and rules that have remain unchanged for hundreds of years. Magic on the other hand is an asymmetric game of luck, ephemeral rules, endless erratas and sore losers who complain about top decking. Given the huge role luck plays in Magic, it has a pedigree more in common with Snakes and Ladders than Chess. Also, Chess doesn't make you buy new pieces every month (unless you really want to).
The computerised Magic 2012 is really Magic-Lite, offering only a subset of the Magic TCG and serving shamelessly as an enticement to lure unsuspecting nerds into playing Magic Online or the Magic TCG. For fans of the genre it's worth getting in a sale for the occasional Magic fix.

What I like about about Call of Juarez® Gunslinger ist that it focuses first and foremost on being an enjoyable FPS. Weapons feel meaty and powerful and the movement, while fast, still feels grounded for the lack of a better word.
This is aided by a bunch of unlockable skills that allow you things like bullet time, etc. depending which of the three "classes" you choose (though you are not restricted to any class or weapon and thanks to New Game Plus can unlock every skill becoming basically unstoppable with every weapon):
- The Ranger, focusing on long range shooting
- The Gunslinger built around rapid fire dual or single pistols and
- The Trapper, a close combat class using mainly shotguns
The game very much encourages an agressive playstyle using your skills to chain longer and longer combos together for more XP and, more importantly, the sheer fun of it.
It also has very good narration both when it comes to the voice actors and its structure.
CoJ Gunslinger comes with three modes:
1. Arcade, that allows you to compete for the Highscore by using your skills to hopefully complete sections of the Single Player maps without breaking your combo chain.
2.Duels Mode, which let's you either pratice or replay the duels found in the Single Player and of course
3. The Story Mode.
Aside from minor technical issues, i.e having to edit some files when you want to change the FOV or remove the stylised black borders around the screen, "I heartily endorse this event or product."
How to change FOV, etc.:
A true return to its roots! A bit short though, make you want to play over and over again... That's good honest fun!

Though I do agree that the first Amnesia had a lot more mechanics, such as an inventory, having to conserve your light source, more "roaming" enemies, etc., I think that a lot of people are uneccessarily hard on this game. Is it exactly like the first one? No. But really, would it be as interesting if it was? Gameplay may be a bit watered down from the previous game, yes, but in my opinion the story and psychological terror more than make up for it. I honestly enjoyed the storyline of this game more than Dark Descent, and the soundtrack is equally as excellent as the first game's.
It's kind of unfair to just tell people who've never played it to not even bother. I say play it for yourself or even watch a walkthrough/let's play and then judge. Is this game for everyone? No, probably not. However, if you enjoy a good horror story, I say this is definitely a game to look into.

You are a wealthy industrialist with two children. One day your children are playing with this gigantic machine you have built to kill off the entire world population, when the machine captures them and locks them deep below! Can you save your children before the machine kills them, along with everyone else in the world?
As a successor to Frictional Game's Amnesia: The Dark Descent, it's pretty mediocre. Most of what made that game so terrifying and immersive has been watered down here, or just taken out entirely. No need to carefully conserve your light sources, no more insanity mechanics, very little (if any) sneaking around monsters with no way to fight them, all of which made TDD such a unique experience. Overall, more of a walking simulator than a worthy successor to The Dark Descent.

This review is from someone who played the original Amnesia, the Penumbra games, and SOMA before playing AMFP. I played Dear Esther, and didn't partiularly enjoy it.
Many of the negative reviews are from people who were expecting a sequel to Dark Descent. Having read these negative reviews before playing, I did not go in with that expectation. I went in with very few preconceived notions of what to expect.  I think I enjoyed the game for that reason.
AMFP is not "scary" in the way that Dark Descent was. There are only a couple places where you need to sneak around and avoid enemies. Most of the game, you are free to explore and solve the puzzles without worrying about getting killed. In a way this is a good thing, because I was able to explore, instead of trying to take the most direct route possible.
AMFP is very atmospheric, and the sound design is excellent. The environments, sounds, and narrative go together very well. I enjoyed the concept of the game, and the story was interesting enough to keep me playing until the end (although it is somehwat predictable).
Bottom line: on sale, (I paid about $3), this game is worth your time. Do not treat it as an Amnesia game. Treat it as its own game, and you will enjoy it more IMO. At full price, the value becomes more debatable, as I completed it in 3-4 hours.

Surprisingly enticing game. Describing it as a border agent simulator is accurate, yet the game is a lot of fun! Set in a totalitarian country, you have to race the clock and work efficiently in order to be able to care for your family, with the difficulty and complexity of your tasks ramping up gradually. Your POV as a border agent becomes an observatory on this dystopian world and of its effect on people: you are presented a spectrum of characters and situations, and you can organically choose, among others, to be a heartless bureaucrat or to take part in the resistance. Your stamp and rulebook give you a good sense of power and purpose, yet you feel the pressure build up from your moral choices, from your need for income, and from greater powers.
Great game.

This game has NO right to be fun as it is. The game boils down to you scanning documents for inaccuracies, and approving or denying entry to various citizens of the futuristic world trying to enter your home country; Arkotsk. You were drafted into working there, and you and your family were forced to move to a new rent-controlled home. You are expected to pay for their food, heat, medicine, and other needs as well as a hefty rent on your measly salary as border/customs agent.
What's really cool about this game though, is that while at first you struggle with the simple basics of the "job", it soon becomes second nature. Once you become a jaded ♥♥♥♥ at the customs office you start to notice weird things happening around you; corrupt guards, terrorist attacks, ethical dilemnas relating to your post, bombs, murders, and of course forged documents.
It takes only a very short time to get into, and you'll likely want to play it more than one time since you'll fail the first time and recieve the 'worst; of the 20 DIFFERENT ENDINGS. One playthrough takes about 3 hours but checkpoints are created at every day, allowing you to explore all the alternate endings easily.
Don't trust your common sense, buy this game that is literally about fact-checking documents. You will love it,
Its hard to explain the joys of analysing paperwork, but that moment when you don't get a citation is some of the most gratifying I've ever felt in a game.

This has been my go to game for the last couple of years  now. Its pretty good, but the fan boys will do all they can to ignore its flaws. I'm gonna talk about what's bad, while the number of hours I've spent playing this game should demonstrate the good.
1) Antisocial design. The focus is on instanced dungeons, accessed via an auto group making function called the "duty finder." This really kills the need for social interaction, making this feel less like an MMO and more like a single player dungeon crawler. The fact that everything is accessed through a menu in my eyes makes the world feel disconnected, ruins the immersion and is very un-rpg. Most of the content is trivially easy, and ammounts to simple time sink- the vernacular is that dungeons are "ran" ie; speed ran ie; no time to chat, and because it is so easy, no need to work together to develop strategies. The guilds in this game are called "Free companies" but there is no content that teams you up with your free company in a meaningful way. The free company is essentially just a chat room.
2) No character customization. You can change your aesthetics, and the visual design is very good, however the actual gameplay design is severely lacking. All gear forms a simple linear progression, there is no interesting gear with unique effects or procs whatsoever. Every Black mage is exactly the same as every other black mage.
3) In game economy. The in game economy is bad. Its not an economically focused game per se, but there is a fairly robust crafting system. Unfortunately, crafting is largely irrelevant, as it is too easy to get through the whole game without patronizing and crafters.
4) Lack of strategy elements in combat. The combat in this game is all about moving around to dodge enemy attacks. Each class has a set rotation of skills which are used against all enemies. These rotations do become complex for many / most classes by endgame, but it still ammounts to an endlessly repetitive recital, devoid of any strategic thought. When people speak of "Strategy" in this game, they are refering to mechanics that consist of "Don't attack x enemy or it will trigger an instakill or wait til x phase then max DPS"  DPS checks and Traps, thats it.
5) The dialogue...! Square enix and Final fantasy are known for having amazing stories. And some of the story arcs in this game are quite good. But the dialogue sequences are soooo long and not in an interesting way. The writing could be much more succinct. Its clear that some producers were walking around saying "Make this scene longer! Make this dialogue wordier! We need to have x minutes of cutscenes for this story arc!" Its all just drags out and it detracts from my abilitiy to care about the story. Also the voice acting is annoying, all the characters seem to have really contrived british accents. I think I'd like it better without voice acting.
6) They went overboard with combat animations. You can't see whats going on in fights 90% of the time.
7) PVP. The PVP in this game sucks. It has pvp technically, but it is not a pvp game. Don't get it if you like pvp. PVP is only in controlled battlegrounds, and everybody sucks at it, probably because they are used to mindlessly slaughtering helpless AI.
8) Treadmill progression. Ok, so to some extent this is what MMOS are all about. But in this game its really silly because every 3 months a new tier of item comes out that makes everything previous completely obsolete. And these items are just grinded for, no interesting quests, and the items are just more stat points, again, no interesting mechanical design in terms of gear.
So what's good about this game?
1) The community, despite being full of apologists and footsucking SE worshippers, is really one of the best out there. The game is relatively devoid of trolls and the toxic wasters that ruin so many other games, *cough archeage* *cough league of legends* *cough wow*  I just wish people would be more critical so that SE might actually try to improve on the game's shortcomings. Its probably because the game is subscription based and has no real pvp, but whatever it is this pretty much outweighs all the negative things about this game.
2) Character models. The characters have this universal type of appeal, the game isn't dark, it isn't gritty- its markedly Final fantasy. If you are a fan of Final Fantasy you will love this game, even if they slam you in the face with "subtle" references to classic titles every 5 minutes. Seriously square, you could be more subtle.
3) Crafting system. Crafting in this game is kind of a cool mini game, and crafting classes are nearly as involved as combat classes, which is cool. Its too bad crafted gear is useless.
4) Housing system. I'm not sure whetehr to make this a positive or negative factor, but it connects with point 3. The housing in this game is falls into identical instances which is lame. And you can't really design your own house, which is lame. However, there are a great many items you can place in and around your house to make it your own. And most of these items are crafted. Really, this is what crafting is about.
So the REAL metagame is Adventure > Earn money > Buy stuff for your house > Play FF "The Sims" Online

I've given MTG 2012 quite a few tries, but ultimately cant recommend it. I want to like it, and when it works properly its even kinda fun, but the amount of things wrong with this game are staggering. Poor UI design AND clunky interface, slow animations, automatically progressing turn timers, dumbing down of well understood mechanics, card logic bugs, autotapping/instacast, lack of proper deck building.. Ultimately some of those design choices can be overlooked. And some card logic issues can be forgiven. But the thing that comes back and kicks you in the face time and time again is the fact that the user interface for this game is just garbage.
1: The interface is HORRIBLE. From the main menu design, to the way that cards are displayed in the game. The cards in your hand are nearly too small to read and overlap eachother despite having plenty of room to display. You have to zoom in on nearly every card to read it. You often cant see whats in your hand or on the battlefield due to something obscuring your ability to look at it. Many situations will ask you to make a decision before you've had a chance to either consult your hand or battlefield to figure out how you wish to respond. No key customization either. Mouse controls are pretty terrible too, although its hard to explain why.. everything is just crammed together in such a way that it obscures everything else and makes clicking on things difficult.
2: Deck building: You cant. You start with 60 cards in a deck, and you unlock 20 more cards. These cards get AUTOMATICALLY added to your deck after every time you unlock a card.. meaning that for an optimal deck you have to go and remove them from your deck after each and every game. You also cannot select how many land to put in. the deck builder automatically does that for you. Also, scrolling left/right through the deck of cards to remove them is time consuming and tedious. Cant remember if its 2012 or 2013, but if you are zoomed in on a card while trying to build a deck and go to switch cards, it zooms out and then back in for each and every card rather than just instantly flipping.
3: The turn and phase timers. (this -mainly- applies to multiplayer but to some degree single player too.) The timer is terrible. Yes its important to make timely decisions, but the timer in this game is frustrating. The turns pass automatically unless you pause them, rather than prompting you to pass priority. When you do 'pass' the turn, then theres still a ~4 second countdown that allows your opponent to interact, even when playing with the AI in multiplayer which chooses not to interact. If you are an MTGO player and try to play MTG2012 you will want to scream at how poor the system feels. Its designed to be newbie friendly as best i can tell.. As someone who was once a newbie to the 2012 planeswalker game, i found it frustrating. As someone was has 30+ hours into it, it still is. Sometimes i find that i cant seem to pause the game at the right time, other times i dont realize that its been paused and sit there like an idiot waiting.
4: Interacting with cards at the right times is nearly impossible, its very easy to miss opportunities due to an automatic pass timer rather than a 'finished' prompt as might be found in MTGO. To this day i've never once been able to figure out the proper time to regenerate a creature in MTG 2012. Logically you would regenerate it after it takes damage, does MTGO bring up a prompt and ask you if you'd like to regenerate it during/after combat damage is being assigned? Nope.
5: Triggered effects: Many cards give your entire team triggered effects. Such as any time a creature enters the battlefield, gain one life. Each time this effect triggers, theres a 3-5 second animation that plays. Each time a creature lifelinks, 3-5 second animation. Having 2-3 creatures that get +1/+1 counters each time you gain life, and multiple creature with lifelink, 3-5 second disruption per creature, per lifelink. I've literally had turns against the AI where i walk away for a minute or two at a time while waiting for trigger animations to resolve. I can understand why this kind of system is in place, however this can make a game that should take 15-20 minutes, take well over an hour, sometimes two. Theres no such thing as a fast turn, especially not against the AI.
6: Cards on the field which have enchantments or equipment on it are near impossible to sort through or to target and require pixel perfect accuracy, especially those that are stacked with multiple enchantments. Double that difficulty for cards with flying that bounce up and down as you try to click on the 2-3 pixel wide card just barely sticking out from the side of your other. If you dont get the target right the first time you dont get a second chance when targeting.
7: Selecting the right card in your hand (or from your deck/graveyard when searching) with the mouse can be very tricky. Theres a very narrow window of where the center of the card is Its about 1/3 the card's width. Its incredibly easy to bump the mouse and cast the wrong spell. The deck builder has the same problems. Theres enough room at the bottom of the screen for the cards to be bigger, and to not overlap so significantly. Considering that a click means autocast, you better get it right the first time.
8: Tapping land is done automatically and the auto-tapper can and will screw you. This not being a toggled option for players baffles me. Considering all the issues with the interface though.. maybe this is actually some sort of blessing in disguise. Typically im going to say no, its not.
9: The time between when one game ends and when the next one begins can be fairly lengthy with unnecessarily long pauses and loading screens. When you win or lose a game you are stuck at the 'game over' screen for what seems like 10-15 seconds before it sends you back to the menu. When trying to do the puzzle challenges this was exceptionally infuriating, one accidental click that you cant take back and there goes 30-45 seconds of restarting ontop of all the time you wasted with unskippable animations and such. There is nothing at all in this game that is fluid, fast, or free flowing.
10: The AI. In multiplayer the AI is fairly bad. Playing two headed giant with a friend where the enemy had literal unblockable creatures during a semi-stalemated board, it only attacked with them once or twice. Apparently if you get enough creatures on the board the AI will just stop attacking entirely even when it has the advantage. Having many creatures with two unblockables that could continue to do damage turn after turn and who wouldnt be viable defenders; the AI just sits there turn after turn. Perhaps it simply does not understand unblockable, Or perhaps its incapable of functioning properly in a multiplayer experience or with so many units on the board. As far as i can recall it seemed to be a decent opponent in single player, mostly.
11: Bugs: Bugs that cause the host of a multiplayer game to get disconnected from his own game. Bugs that cause you to be unable to cast spells on your own turn, bugs that break the interface in some regard and cause you to be incapable of continuing your match, bugs that stop you from being able to swap out of and into the game.
Couple all the bugs with the relatively awful UI, the dumbed down 'user friendly' systems, and slow and general clunkiness of the game and honestly the experience feels pretty unsatisfying overall. The only redeeming quality of this game is that its one of only a few modern MTG games that has a single player component to it. And i -believe- its the only modern magic release (2012-2014) that has the arch nemesis game mode, which is actually quite fun.

If Dreamfall was just a dream then I don't want to wake up..EVER. This chapter is set 10 years after the original (The Longest Journey), many things have changed that will engage the player's curiousity from the start. Ofcourse memorable characters and locations make a comeback and look better than ever with the leap in graphics. I caught myself warmly reminiscing the sights of Venice- the border house where April Ryan lived and the Fringe Cafe ahhh the memories! April and Crow do make an awesome return though much of the game focuses on a lovely new character named Zoe. When I started this game, I wanted to play as a familiar face but I grew quite fond of Zoe very early on. Partly because the developers have obvious talent for building characters but personally because of how quickly I identified with her and her decisions that many people make in their youth and stuggle through: dropping out of school, letting go of relationships, and trying to find a purpose in life. And just like in TLJ, destiny and curiousity turn her dull life into an otherworldly adventure that makes for an always unforgettable story. I absolutely cannot wait for the third installment and highly propose this series to anyone who seeks an emotional and enchanting game like none other!

Love this game. You can really tell that the people involved in making Bastion placed their talents here as well. From the moment we are dropped into this world, the gorgeous scenery and music draws us in. Then a voice speaks to us and I am brought back to that Narrator in Bastion.
The combat is different. You can try to hack and slash your way through but clever planning in Turn phases could save yourself much grief. Each enemy has their own unique abilities and a bunch of them will require you to use Turn phases to dispatch them. It makes combat more engaging instead of mindless work.
The music. The music is appropriately atmostpheric. I often find myself pausing just to hear Red sing. Her voice is haunting and beautiful. Her story is sad, along with the tone of the game, and the music reflects that.
I highly recommend getting this game. I bought mine with the original soundtrack and I have no regrets about it.

Beautiful art, great music, difficult to wrap my head around. When I first bought it, I played for a few hours and then dropped it for 9 months. When I picked it back up again, I was consumed so much by it that I blew through the game and got all the achievements in around 3 days.
The combat system and ability customization are definitely areas that I imagine most people would have a rough time approaching. Not to say that they are anything bad, but assigning and modifying functions allows so much freedom to the player it's almost jarring. Once you really get hang for customizing functions, making combos, and timing your Turn(), every fight is extremely satisfying.
The setting and story are fleshed out enough to maintain the mistique of a jazzy cyberpunk future. Every scene is dripping with style that I can totally dig. The game has just the right amount of detail in just the right places to make the city feel alive despite encountering very few actual characters. It invests hard in its universe and it pays off in the immersion that it creates.
I'm really glad this game ressurected itself in my library.

Okay. I played through this like three times to try and see if you can get any sort of different ending. I could only bear to play three times because the thing is: the game already makes it really hard for me to care about what ending to get, let alone the character I'm supposed to be "in love" with. That's the kind of game this is.
For a good few minutes, you're forced to play the role of some friendzoned Schmosby that can't seem to get over some girl that is obviously using him as an emotional crutch. For five years. Honestly, How I Met Your Mother at least had other characters to deepen the story, but this game only has the two.
As someone who's been there and done that, I tried to play it as I would act if I were in a similar situation now: someone who will be nice to a friend but won't drop everything for them if they haven't done the same for me, a.k.a. someone with some self-respect. However, you have absolutely no control over the outcome of the game, despite it advertising that you can. Even if you choose to be direct or try to pick options that seemingly try to work things out, your dialog option is deleted and replaced with some cringeworthy small talk. What kind of ♥♥♥♥ery is that?
You're basically just riding along to a simulation of your own high school nightmare; and for those who have yet to go through this kind of thing, then sure it'll be a sad but necessary lesson for you, which is pretty much what this game tries to shove down your throat. It lacks any other sort of merit or good content for it to be redeemable for those who were actually expecting to be able to change anything at all.
I don't get why this game has such a positive rating here. I kid you not, by my second playthrough, I didn't even care about getting with Emily and instead tried to get with this other girl I apparently met in college. Nope. Not possible. You barely get to know or have the chance to actually care about Emily, and here you are getting friendzoned. What the ♥♥♥♥.
Overall, it was just a disappointing waste of time. The game fails to deliver what it promised so you're left with a linear game with frustrating content. There's no satisfaction from playing it and it felt like I was just reading a really ♥♥♥♥♥♥ novel written by some teenager trying to be edgy and deep. The "lesson" it tries to give is just.....really poorly delivered, in my opinion. The only good thing I liked was the nostalgic feel it gives you through its interface.
If you want a linear game like this, just play Super Mario or something.

Like that title? You better do, because that’s the best part of the entire game! Amnesia: The Dark Descent was created by Frictional Games, who was known for making a survival horror series called Penumbra. Amnesia: A Machine For Pigs however, was created by The Chinese Room, And the only game they had created before this was Dear Esther, a  walking simulator. The reason why I’m telling you this, is because A Machine For Pigs is exactly that. A walking simulator. Now, I’m not saying walking simulators are bad. Some of them are actually really good! Is Amnesia: A Machine For Pigs one of the good ones? Let’s find out!
*STORY*
You play as Mandus, who suffers from amnesia. You’re spending the game descending into a nightmarish place, and the further you get, the more you’ll find out about what horrible things you have done in the past. Sounds familiar? It should, because the plot is basically the same as The Dark Descent! All of the twists in this game you’ll see coming if you’ve played the first one. Well, there are some changes. Where TDD was supernatural, this one is more of a sci-fi. Instead of going on a quest to kill an old man, you’re trying to find your children. Instead of being in a dark castle, you’re in a dark machine. There’s this man who will call you on a phone throughout the game, and tell you what you’re supposed to do. The story i pretty good, but while it does copy a lot of TDD's story, i find TDD's to be a bit more interesting that A Machine For Pigs's.
*VISUALS*
This game looks and feels like The Dark Descent. It does have a lot more variety though. for example, you start the game of in a mansion, and then you spend some time outside in the streets. Most of the game is spent in the machine itself, which looks pretty good if i might add, but there are some cool stuff in between. The heart of the machine looks awesome, and the last place you are in the game does too! The visuals is actually something i like more than in the original. The monster though, looks pretty silly. It is even less scary than TDD’s monster. But just like TDD, the build up is so ♥♥♥♥ing good! you’ll catch a glimpse of the monster here and there and it was truly terrifying! The first hour of this game was by far the creepiest, since you didn’t know when the monster would show up! sadly though, the last two hours aren’t nearly as scary as the first.
*GAMEPLAY*
Get ready for a LONG rant about this game’s missteps: This game has no gameplay at all! They took pretty much everything away from TDD! No longer do you have a sanity meter, so the darkness isn’t scary at all! Actually, the darkness is more like your friend in this game, since the monster can’t see you! There is no longer a punishment for looking directly at the monster, so you stare at it for as long as you want! No longer does your lantern need oil. Oil was rare in the original, so you spent a lot of time with your lantern turned off, because you didn’t want to run out of oil. In this game you can have the lantern up as long as you want without worrying about running out! That takes a lot of the stress out of the game, which is really bad for a horror game. Also, they removed tinderboxes, because there’s literally no use for them anymore. Your health will regenerate on it’s own, so taking damage doesn’t penalize you at all! They've taken away the inventory because there’s no need for it with all of these game mechanics gone. The monster is extremely slow! I only died once in my second playthrough, and it was not the monster that killed me! You can actually run right past the monster and be alright, because it’s to slow to to follow you, and any damage you might have taken will regenerate in ten seconds anyways! There is apparently only six times in the game where the monster can kill you! You can only pick up puzzle related items. (And chairs, for some reason) And to top that off, it took me three hours to finish it. THREE HOURS! For the price it’s at, it’s not worth it at all. definitely wait for a sale on this one. As you see, they’ve pretty much taken all the game out of amnesia. It is a walking simulator with a not very dangerous monster chasing you around.
I’ve taken a long time talking about how bad it is for an amnesia game, but let’s talk about how it hold up for a horror game. I find the first hour of the game to be really scary. there was this room you couldn’t enter, but you could see inside through a window in the room next to it. In the room, there was a bed with the monster crawled up in it. In the room I was in, there was a puzzle, and when I finished the puzzle, a loud sound played. On my way out of the room, I looked through the window again, and the monster was gone. At that moment I was horrified. I waited ten seconds, and then I moved out of the room. I quietly looked around, and then I saw it: The room with the bed was slammed open! Looking down the corridor by the door, I could see something walking behind the corner. I was scared out of my mind. There is something walking around in the mansion! I’m not safe anymore! the truth is, I was safe. When the monster got behind the corner, it disappeared. I didn’t know that though, so I was in crouch mode for the rest of the mansion, and opened doors as carefully as possible. That was just one of many similar moments. The game plays with you, making you think you’re in danger when you’re really not! It does this for an hour, until the monster finally appears for real. That is a good way to scare you, and while the other two hours might not be nearly as scary, I won’t forget the first hour anytime soon!
The second hour is more of the same, but with a monster walking around, which is not nearly as scary as it sounds. the third hour changes things up a bit. I won’t give away too much, but it’s a lot more action filled. There’s still no combat, so I wouldn’t really call it action filled, but once you play it, you’ll know what I mean. While not scary, it was a welcoming change!
*VERDICT*
Amnesia: A Machine For Pigs is a terrible sequel. It takes everything that made the original so great away from it, and what you’re left with is a mediocre walking simulator. I was thinking about giving it a five, or even a four, but I discovered a trick that makes this game a lot better. Just call it
A Machine For Pigs! When you take the Amnesia away, it goes from a disappointing sequel, to an okay horror game. With that, I’ll give this game a:
While the gameplay is non-existent, the scariness is! Most of the hate this game gets is that it is compared to TDD, which it shouldn’t, because they’re very different games! If you look away from the fact that it’s called Amnesia, you might actually enjoy yourself! The game is really short, but when I think about it, I actually kinda like it that way. It can be beaten in one session, and that’s fine.
And that wraps up my horror trilogy! I would say it would be nice to play something that is not scary, but the next game on the list is Bad Rats Show… yeah, the future's not looking bright for me.

Are you the kind of person that theorycrafts your world of warcraft character?  Do you create spreadsheets to help determine the optimal way of executing a task?  Do you find it fun picking apart mechanics of a game to optimize your playthroughs?  If any of these apply, you'll enjoy Factorio... If they only kind of applied, you'll also love Factorio.
Factorio is an incredibly well done, niche game that is quite possibly one of the most well done titles I've come across for a multitude of reasons.
On the surface, Factorio is a game about automation, logistics, and optimization.  It doesn't sound like it should be fun at all.  But when you get into the game itself, it ends up being more like a puzzle game, where you're trying to determine the best ways of maximizing yields from your machines.
It's easy to get complacient your first time playing the game through... Sure... One science facility is sufficient to unlock everything... you don't NEED more... but by the end, you'll be in a position where, why not build another couple hundred... a couple thousand.  Why?  Why not?  Each play through, you're astronomically faster at knowing the ideal logistics, you have the foresight for knowing problems that you've run into in the past to plan for the future, and you're more familiar with the game interface/hotkeys/etc to be able to execute your actions in a more timely fashion.
This game is also amazingly optimized as well on the actual programming side.  Multiplayer servers (still in beta), have been recorded, and videos are available to display the server supporting over 150 concurrent users with no lag.  Furthermore, the developers are incredibly engaged, and constantly trying to further develop the game.
It's weird to think of a game built around logistics, automation, factories, etc, would be so entertaining, and maybe that speaks more to me as a person than the game itself, but I recommend watching a video or two, and if it looks even marginally interesting, grabbing the game and giving it a shot.

Dreamfall: The Longest Journey is an adventure game released for the Windows and Xbox platforms in 2006 and is the sequel to Funcom's The Longest Journey, which itself was released in 1999. The roughly 13 hours long story takes place ten years after the events of the first game and focuses on three characters, Zoë Castillo, April Ryan, and Kian Alvane.
Graphically, this sequel is a step up above its predecessor showcasing a fully 3D world to explore. While the environment art is very nicely rendered, the 3D characters themselves look a little dated by today's standards. Music and sound are appropriately orchestral sounding and melodic and were a nice treat.
Storywise, while the first game emphasized on the grandness, mystery and majestic scope of the two worlds Stark and Arcadia, Dreamfall takes a much more up close and personal look at the lives of the inhabitants. Characters that you know from the first game do make their return and is especially nice to see how they have evolved. It was especially interesting to see how the first game's protagonist April Ryan had matured, even though some may not like the new direction she has taken. Because this is a sequel, it is advisable to have played the original game first to better appreciate some of the story elements.
The story is not without its faults however as I felt the pacing seemed to be slow at the earlier chapters. It does pick up pace right around Chapter 6 as the plot slowly unravels. Although It is an intriguing tale, some parts felt unfinished as there are some questions that remain unanswered even at the end of the game which itself ends at a cliffhanger. This is a tale in which the journey is definitely more rewarding then its destination. Hopefully the upcoming Dreamfall: Chapters due to be released in 2014 will provide more closure to the story.
Downsides, the game felt really linear even for an adventure game. You are never given multiple puzzles to solve at a time and can only progress in a very linear fashion. Focus field (which is the game's way of interacting with hotspots/objects) also felt very awkwardly implemented. It makes the protaganist look like a robot scanning for items.
Because this game was also made for the XBox, there are way too many loading screens even though certain areas looked like they could've been connected together. This really kills the immersion sometimes, and it would've been alot better if they just freeze the screen and have a little loading bar at the bottom instead of just completely blackout the screen and showing the game's title for the umpteenth time.
The game also introduced some combat and stealth elements which I felt was very shoddily designed and very tacky. (Eg: Winning a combat means to just spam the attack button. Sometimes the opponent just stupidly stands there without even doing anything!) Had they been designed and implemented well, I wouldn't have minded, but as they are now, they really felt out of place and unnecessary.
The game also did not have any ingame maps and there is alot of travelling back and forth between locations. There isn't any way to warp between them, and it is very painful to have to slowly jog all over the place. It really felt like a very cheap way to artificially lengthen the gameplay time. The ability to at least increase the character's movement speed would've been very welcome here.
Overall Rating: 6.0 / 10
In conclusion, this is a worthy sequel to the original game but is let down by its technical issues / questionable gameplay design which hinders the enjoyment somewhat. If you had enjoyed the first game, definitely pick this up and if you are willing to endure its flaws, you will experience a story that matches and sometimes even exceeds the quality of original.

I didn't particularly enjoy the original The Longest Journey, and all 3D adaptions of point 'n click adventures have been fairly terrible.
So when I first tried Dreamfall I went in with negative preconceptions. I got a few minutes in and found the start too slow for my liking, plus I didn't particularly enjoy the 3D camera control and I was generally critical of some of the lack of polish. I shelved Dreamfall for a number of weeks.
However, I'm very glad I picked Dreamfall up again. About an hour in, a gripping story begins to unravel. There are also some very likable characters and several genuinely funny parts later in the game. Dreamfall is also extremely beautiful.
This game is more of an interactive story than an adventure. There are barely any puzzles, and the few it has are very easy. However, this isn't necessarily a negative point because it's still enjoyable.
There's way too much unimaginative and redundant dialogue in Dreamfall, often to the point of frustration. Fortunately, you can skip over most of it without missing any story, and you can read back on previous conversations via in-game UI.
There are currently many good, cheap adventure games around, and I think although Dreamfall is absolutely worth the price (compared to other forms of entertainment), it is still overpriced in todays games market, so best to put it in the wishlist and play other games until the sequel nears towards 2015.

The gameplay in a nutshell and why i don't recomend it

Your class abilities consume the mana resource while your weapon specific consume fatigue (the weapon specific abilities are more like "fillers" or "cantrips" and are the same for every weapon even among different classes )
Some races are meant to use more MANA based abilities and others are meant to use more FATIGUE based abilities as on the former races the mana pool starts bigger and replenishes quicker and on the latters the same happens with the fatigue resource. So it becomes pretty obvious why so many high elves around...
It is because the class based MANA abilities are the stronger/more interesting.
The fatigue based are based on the specific weapon but you can't switch weapon when on battle and have your ability bar replaced by new specific weapon skills like in Guildwars2. So if you have set up the character bar with 3 mana consuming class abilities + 2 two hander weapon abilities you can't switch weapon style in battle (into staff for example) and at least have those 2 2-hander abilites  replaced by the new staff abilities. You are stuck with the 2 hander weapon abilities that will just grey.
So all in all out of the 5 abilities you have usually 3 class specific + 2weapon style ones  or on mana stronger races 4class+1 weapon style abilities. (You are supposed to get at some advanced point a 6th abiliy that is like superstrong and can be done only rarely but i haven't reached that point so...)  You need to share your abilities this way to be viable in combat, otherwise you will  consume your prefered resource too rapidly and end up with nothing left to use. Another problem is also the simple "white damage" attacks you do by swinging your weapon. (without activating any abilities) Initially that seems to work but as you advance you realize that not only it does very small damage but it also tricks you into thinking you are actually doing something useful but in fact the weapon swinging animations (elder scrolls style) takes away seconds out of actual useful abilities you should be using. I guess those simple attacks are only good if all your other resources are depleted and have nothing else to do. (but only then)
Anyway It was fun for a few hours  and i thank the company of the game for letting us try their game for free for a weekend but i can't imagine myself having to play this for weeks or months so i don't recomend it even if on sale.

Another gorgeous, fun and thoughtful game. The game definitely feels like Bastion, with the story unfolding around you, but the new mechanics mean combat is less reactionary and more thoughtful, while remaining intense.
The graphics and sound are coordinated beautifully, with Supergiant's signature narrative commentary and environmental touches. Like in Bastion, you pick from your powers, buffs, and challenges. However, the system is more flexible, allowing you to use any ability either as a primary power, a modifier for another power, or as a passive ability. This lets you experiment with power combinations and find a setup that's fun and effective. To prevent it from getting stale, the unlockable background information encourages (but doesn't force) you to keep mixing it up.
While I do keep drawing comparisons to Bastion, this game very much stands for istelf as a distinctive, worthwhile experience.

For anyone who's played and liked Bastion:
It's better than Bastion in every aspect; music, artstyle, story and with a way better combat system. Just buy it.
For everyone else:
Where do you start with this game? With a great soundtrack, a beautifull art style and a touching story, it surpases most "artsy" video games with its unique and interesting combat mechanics.
You can either fight freely, using your up-to-4 abilities, or pause time, to plan a set of abilities and execute them in lightning fast speed. Then you have to wait for the pause ability to recharge, unable to execute most of your abilities.
Additionaly, you might decide not to equip an ability, but to use it as an upgrade on another ability, or even a passive bonus for your character, opening up a massive ammount of possible loadouts to make and have fun with.
Only complaint I have, is the difficulty, which was rather easy, BUT, the game provides you with what it calls "limiters", allowing you to make the game as hard as you want.
Still, I found most of the limiters to be just an annoyance rather than making the enemies more challenging.
But when it comes to recommending the game or not, my answer is simple, "Buy it and buy it NOW, be it on sale or not. And get the soundtrack as well, if your pocket allows you to".
TL:DR BuyIt()

The staff of IMC have shown gross incompetence in the past, but as time goes on it only becomes worse:
-Bugs that render the game unplayable persist for months at a time
-All new content is only on Korean servers for a minimum of two months before being released to the International version
-Support tickets are answered by people who do not speak English and will not assist you
While this was all par for the course, recently a bug was introduced that caused monsters to drop more items than they were supposed to. The current response is to ban players who received multiple items as a "punishment" for "exploiting."
It's unfortunate because the game itself is normally fun to play. It's a great concept, the music is fantastic, the art style immersive. While you might enjoy playing it for a while, being a dedicated player only results in you being punished time and time again from a multitude of bugs.
While I was willing to forgive a lot of issues for feeling that the developers were at least trying their best despite a small staff, it's obvious now that they simply want to get as much money as possible out of the game before the population crumbles for good. Banning long time players for an issue that was not an exploit, but the fault of the developers themselves, was the final straw.
If you do play, do not support them with any money. It pains me to say it, but none of it will go towards improving the game.

For a sequel to Amnesia (and later game SOMA, speaking of which) to not include such a beloved and important feature is simply unacceptable.

So they (the publishers, IMC) have an event to invite old players back. And another to welcome new players to the game. And even a free daily respec event to go with it so people can try out different builds. YAY! Sounds great right? OK but a week in, we old returning players are given a sudden reminder of why a lot of us left in the first place...
IMC noticed a drop rate bug for some rare items. So they patch it to fix it, which leads to ALL droprates across ALL maps increasing drastically. Which leads to exploiters camping the places where high value items drop, while the rest of the playerbase goes about our own business grinding, questing, and doing dungeons. We wind up getting a lot more loot than usual - but nothing gamebreaking just the usual drops. IMC's solution to the bugged drop rate?
Lock the accounts of almost everyone who got multiples of just about ANY rare item, worthless or otherwise. Which pretty much meant anyone logged on and playing normally during the time the bug WHICH THEY CAUSED was happening. Oh and all this time from back to before i even left the game, AFK summoner-type characters are STILL blatantly parked at high spawn zones to make easy money letting their AI kill trash mobs, and bots are still roaming all over the place despite players asking the devs to fix both problems. Which of course they havent.
A buggy game who's patches and fixes cause even LARGER bugs + a publisher that swings from completely unresponsive lumps to panic-mode gestapo and back again at the drop of a hat? Yeah. Fun times. The game itself at it's core is VERY nice but these shenanigans are a pain. I'm just waiting to see if they get their act together after the current fiasco before i decide to keep playing or uninstall completely. Not gonna hold my breath though with their track record.
EDIT: well, the GMs unlocked most of the accounts that got accidentaly trampled in the recent drop rate fiasco, and gave very generous item compensations by way of apology. I'm willing to say that at least they recognized their mistake and want to make up for it. I have spent an ungodly amount of time with this game. And I've only just begun again, this time on the Steam version.
With the Steam version, I found myself asking, "Well how can I motivate myself to enjoy this game after I spent so much time playing it before?"
Then the answer dawned on me like the many suns I'd be shocked to see outside of my window after only playing for a few minutes.
"Mods," I whispered quitely. I amused myself thinking, "Oh how hard can the mods make it? It'll be a fun refresher and I'll enjoy seeing new life and challenge brought into a map!"
I was setting myself up for a long, grueling hell. And only about 20 hours into my map, and not having expanded my base out yet did I realize how well and truly ♥♥♥♥ed I made myself with the assortment of mods I added on.
A small CHUNK of mods choseable to enhance your game experience, or delay it. Or have it ream you time and time again.
Unfortunately, it's the latter for me. But I love every second of it.
Make no mistake, you SHOULD play this vanilla first. Or a few times, just to get the feel of its basic concepts. Just be prepared to throw your social life away.
Then, when you're ready to throw away everything else you enjoy about your life; other video games, TV, movies, anime, books, you name it, you can install mods and go in for the long haul.
Tl;dr: This game has a great amount of replayability, and game length just by itself. The mechanics fit smoothly, the logic is intuitive after a small amount of time, it has an EXTENSIVE community mod base behind it. And, as an added bonus, it will help you completely eliminate the need for a "social life". It's as if the developers read the memoir,
, and decided to make a spiritual follow-up in the form of a video game.

Dreamfall, the second TLJ game is, as far as sequels go, extremely well done.  Dreamfall takes the original Point-and-Click adventure theme and takes it to full 3D.  I was amazed at how true to the world this game is.  I had just finished TLJ and was so engrossed by it I immediately moved to Dreamfall, and there were numerous places that you explore in TLJ that are revisted to almost pixel-perfect replication of their 2D counterparts - or - recognizable, and yet changed by time.  The attention to detail is outstanding - I distinctly remember a point where a familiar character is writing in a book and narrating what he's writing and if you look closely you can see that the words he is writing are actually what the narrator is saying, not scribbles or obscured text.  I found that impressive for a game released in 2006.  To go with this 3D update, the player is given a much improved settings configuration, along with full controller support, which I found nice since Dreamfall really works well with one.  Also, while TLJ had beautiful backgrounds the character models were pretty dated; however, in Dreamfall, everything is quite beautiful.  The textures are good and the world is vibrant and alive.
One of my favorite things about TLJ was the voice acting.  While the VA is good in Dreamfall, I felt that TLJ had more outliers for the VAs.  In TLJ some people *really* nailed their part, but some really failed.  The median voice acting performance in Dreamfall is better than TLJ, but that also means these standout performances are unfortunately lacking.  Another major problem this game has is the combat.  It adds a sense of urgency to the game, unlike in TLJ you can actually lose and have to reload, and that's fine, but the combat is slow-paced, clunky, and just downright terrible.  I would have preferred removing it entirely.  There are also sneaking sections in the game and they could have been improved as well.  Coupled with these "failable" sections is an autosave feature, which is nice, as I usually find myself sucked into these games so much that I forget to save after awhile.  They're well placed and non-intrusive.
Gameplay wise I like the puzzles in Dreamfall much more than in TLJ.  In TLJ the puzzles were extremely convoluted at times.  In Dreamfall the puzzles make sense; for example, you need to make a torch, so you get a broken axe handle, a rag, dip it in petrol and light it - it makes sense and is easy to figure out through intuition.  There is also less backtracking than TLJ had, which is nice, keeping the storyline progressing and the pacing of the game better.
The main reason I love The Longest Journey is the plot and storyline and Dreamfall is a worthy successor in this regard.  There are recurring faces and familiar places, but since the game takes place ten years after the events of the previous all have changed, some good, some bad, but they are all well done.  The game also plays more on the creepy side TLJ had, setting up a sense of mystery and horror.  The developers also took advantage of their new engine, making the game extremely cinematic and utilizing four different points of view, granting the player control of different characters to explore the world and storyline.
Pros:
Story/Narrative/Pacing/Characterization
Nice Variations in Setting
Logical Puzzles
Attention to Detail
Cons:
Combat
No Map
Few Minor Bugs
Ending?
While it isn't *necessary* to play TLJ before Dreamfall I would highly recommend it, especially since the first game is so good.  I really appreciated the developers staying true to the world they created in the previous game.  That said, the combat was awful, and it's impossible to overlook it.  The ending also doesn't resolve everything in the game.  Had I played this when it was released I would be furious; however, now that Chapters has been kickstarted I can wait a few more months to see how Dreamfall wraps up.  I'd really like to rank this game in the As; however, with these issues cited, I'm going to have to keep it on the very upper edge of the B range.  B++

For anyone who's played and liked Bastion:
It's better than Bastion in every aspect; music, artstyle, story and with a way better combat system. Just buy it.
For everyone else:
Where do you start with this game? With a great soundtrack, a beautifull art style and a touching story, it surpases most "artsy" video games with its unique and interesting combat mechanics.
You can either fight freely, using your up-to-4 abilities, or pause time, to plan a set of abilities and execute them in lightning fast speed. Then you have to wait for the pause ability to recharge, unable to execute most of your abilities.
Additionaly, you might decide not to equip an ability, but to use it as an upgrade on another ability, or even a passive bonus for your character, opening up a massive ammount of possible loadouts to make and have fun with.
Only complaint I have, is the difficulty, which was rather easy, BUT, the game provides you with what it calls "limiters", allowing you to make the game as hard as you want.
Still, I found most of the limiters to be just an annoyance rather than making the enemies more challenging.
But when it comes to recommending the game or not, my answer is simple, "Buy it and buy it NOW, be it on sale or not. And get the soundtrack as well, if your pocket allows you to".
TL:DR BuyIt()

It's easy to tell that this game is a work of passion.

It's a fun game. It's got a lot of puzzle variety and a pretty good amount of content. But it's so bare bones in certain areas that I was absolutely convinced it was a poorly done mobile port until somebody corrected me.
What am I talking about? Dispite being a PC game first, it has no options menu of any kind, you can't correct the resolution, change the graphics (though I doubt you would need to) or even do something as simple as change the game volume. Distinguishing between the balls must be hell if you're colorblind, a menu option for that would have been really helpful for a lot of people. It does not lock the mouse to one screen if you have multiple monitors, but still requires that you move your mouse to the edge of the screen in order to pan the camera. It has no keyboard controls, even though it could have direly used some, such as the ablity to pan the camera with the arrow keys which would have delt with the mouse not locking issue, and a key for undo which would remove the need to click those stupid bugs (or more often, accidentally click one when you're trying to do a quick action).
Did I like it? I kept playing through the problems and beat it, so yeah I must have liked it dispite its problems. At the same time, would I recommend it? no, especially not at the normal $10 price tag. I found the missing features made it feel very unpolished and at the price point there are a lot of better games. Maybe on sale I'd recommend it, but that isn't an option.

My god, this game was one of the better experiences I have ever had on PC! I went in expecting something similar to Amnesia: The Dark Descent and it wasn't quite that, but was its own thing, and was just as genius. A Machine For Pigs didn't have the mechanics-derived horror of Dark Descent but this was dripping with terror and existential dread.
"Terror is usually described as the feeling of dread and anticipation that precedes the horrifying experience. By contrast, horror is the feeling of revulsion that usually occurs after something frightening is seen, heard, or otherwise experienced."
A Machine for Pigs revels in the terror side of the equation while Dark Descent settles into the horror side.
Dan Pinchbeck's and The Chinese Room's Dear Esther also left an equally powerful mark on my life during a time of sadness. A Machine for Pigs stands proudly next to that. The Chinese Room's games may not be as focused on mechanics as other titles, but for me that has allowed their superlative narratives, text, and dialogue to shine bright--unfettered and unburdened.  The ending of this is still living with me and racing through my mind.
I cannot wait to play Everybody's Gone to the Rapture now.
Thank you Chinese Room for giving me such powerful and memorable experiences. They have really impacted me.

To fix the installer bug that requires an additional 80GB on top of the initial requirements, browse to the folder:
C:\Users\["user"]\AppData\Local\Temp\[ "temp folder" ]\InstallerData\Disk1\InstData
Where "user" is your user name and "temp folder" is something like "lI1512253535" (the number is random).
If you're having trouble finding this folder, order the files by modification date. If it's not there try launching the game from Steam and leaving it open while you browse.
When you find it, open the "Resource1.zip" archive, browse to:
\$IA_PROJECT_DIR$\src_path\
Copy the whole "Launcher" folder into the Steam game folder in:
C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam\steamapps\common\Zenimax Online
The Steam folder can be in different places depending on your Windows version.
Once copied, execute the "Bethesda.net_Launcher.exe" inside.
Let it run and update the game files.
When it's done, quit the launcher and execute from Steam. It should work.

Gunslinger is a well-executed FPS that's becomes noteworthy based on its story, setting, and the "duel" mechanic it employs for boss fights. The bread and butter gameplay itself is good, with the shooting feeling smooth and responsive and the selection of weapons on offer striking a good balance between having variety without feeling too samey. There's also a slo-mo mechanic as well as various persistent skills you can unlock via an XP system, though both of those have been featured in other games before.
The duels stand out as the most novel gameplay mechanic. The player is challenged to split their attention between keeping their crosshairs aimed on the enemy and their hand near their six gun, so as to be the most prepared when the time comes to draw. For those who find the duels frustrating or boring, there is also the option to simply draw first, though you'll be considered "dishonorable" for doing so. The duelling system does, however, make "normal" human enemies challenging enough to be actual bosses without just making them unnaturally tough bags of HP. The duels even culminate by throwing a second opponent into the mix for the finale, in an obvious homage to the classic triple duel from The Good, The Bad, & The Ugly.
The game also earns points on account of how it tells its story. While it's not difficult to find games that aren't trying to be serious, Gunslinger's story is relayed by an obviously unreliable narrator who often is doubted even by his in-game audience. In short, even within the games' world the events the you play through likely didn't really happen, or if they did they did not occur the way the narrator claims. There are some bits of truth in this tall tale, however, and the game even uses this to make the collectibles that all games must have these days into something actually interesting. Finding the "nuggets of truth" will open up snippets of the actual history surrounding the settings and characters featured in the game. I found this to be a welcome change of pace from the bog-standard "in-universe diaries" or, even worse, collectibles for their own sake.
Finally, it is worth mentioning that once the main story is completed the game isn't out of content. Although there is no multiplayer there are challenege levels that may be played individually with one of three pre-set loadouts, and you can post your scores for these to the games' leaderboards. You may also play through the duels from the single player mode on their own, if you found them to be interesting and fun enough in the main game. All of this is rolled up into a package costing at present only 15 USD at full-price. Given the amount of content included I can't see calling this anything other than a good deal, providing any of the above sounds interesting to you.

Another gorgeous, fun and thoughtful game. The game definitely feels like Bastion, with the story unfolding around you, but the new mechanics mean combat is less reactionary and more thoughtful, while remaining intense.
The graphics and sound are coordinated beautifully, with Supergiant's signature narrative commentary and environmental touches. Like in Bastion, you pick from your powers, buffs, and challenges. However, the system is more flexible, allowing you to use any ability either as a primary power, a modifier for another power, or as a passive ability. This lets you experiment with power combinations and find a setup that's fun and effective. To prevent it from getting stale, the unlockable background information encourages (but doesn't force) you to keep mixing it up.
While I do keep drawing comparisons to Bastion, this game very much stands for istelf as a distinctive, worthwhile experience.

For anyone who's played and liked Bastion:
It's better than Bastion in every aspect; music, artstyle, story and with a way better combat system. Just buy it.
For everyone else:
Where do you start with this game? With a great soundtrack, a beautifull art style and a touching story, it surpases most "artsy" video games with its unique and interesting combat mechanics.
You can either fight freely, using your up-to-4 abilities, or pause time, to plan a set of abilities and execute them in lightning fast speed. Then you have to wait for the pause ability to recharge, unable to execute most of your abilities.
Additionaly, you might decide not to equip an ability, but to use it as an upgrade on another ability, or even a passive bonus for your character, opening up a massive ammount of possible loadouts to make and have fun with.
Only complaint I have, is the difficulty, which was rather easy, BUT, the game provides you with what it calls "limiters", allowing you to make the game as hard as you want.
Still, I found most of the limiters to be just an annoyance rather than making the enemies more challenging.
But when it comes to recommending the game or not, my answer is simple, "Buy it and buy it NOW, be it on sale or not. And get the soundtrack as well, if your pocket allows you to".
TL:DR BuyIt()

I was initially hesitant on buying this game; I had heard of this game when it was launched, seeing many ads in PC Gamer back in the day, but I wasn't really interested in playing it. I'm so glad I did. This game is truly one of the greatest adventure games I've ever played. It's not without faults, but you will find an experience that will keep you up for hours on end regardless.
The story is phenomenal! It's initially slow and is executed slightly cheezily (given the age of the game), but it quickly hooks you in once the atmosphere of the game has settled. After the first to second hour of this game, I found myself wondering why I've never played it before! It's intriguing, mysterious, and almost detective-esque. The story really picks up in the middle of the game-- to save you all from some major spoilers, I'm just going to say it's magical.
In addition, the music is fantastic: the composer puts subtle musical cues into the world's environment and professionaly crafts those into the score, creating several memorable and beautiful themes! I'd have to say that this is the greatest video game soundtrack that nobody has heard.
The voice acting is hit and miss; however, when it hits, it HITS. There are some fantastic voice actors in this game. The main character sounds great, but some of the minor characters that you run into are downright HILARIOUS! There are moments and lines in the script that are just joys to watch and listen to, some examples being the hilarious elevator scene, the spice trader, and a few others. A couple of the voice actors kinda suck.
Sure, the combat sucks and the animations could be better, but c'mon: this game was released in 2006! The Steam screenshots are touched up with effects and shaders to make the game look better than it actually is. Some of the puzzles are just rediculously hard and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. You'll definitely look those up online to save time.
If you can get past the minor setbacks (and trust me, you will), you will find yourself a well crafted, memorable adventure that will consume your thoughts! I mean, if I wrote this LONG review on STEAM, that has to mean that the game is fantastic, RIGHT?!

Modern Warfare 2 and its MP is full of the craziest BS as opposed to any other CoD, and yet it's the one that stands out as the definition of CoD. CoD4 revolutionized first person shooters, but (at least, for many fans) MW2 was the cherry on the top. Super fast-paced multiplayer gameplay, a wild, absurd (not to mention controversial) campaign, and one of the greatest video game soundtracks ever orchestrated make this CoD different from the rest. Some say Black Ops 2 takes the cake, other say Call of Duty 2. But MW2 (in my humble opinion) is where CoD reached its peak of originality. Now as for recommending this game, I will say yes. Not because of the hacked multiplayer lobbies and people calling it the "Ultimate Rage Simulator," but because of the nostalgia and good moments of the game. When the going gets good in MW2, nothing gets better than hearing Craig Fairbrass as Ghost saying "Tactical Nuke ready. Turn the key." As far as the price goes, it is worth half the price of 20$ on the market (excluding sales). Wait for a 50% sale and buy the game if you're a fan of CoD and will have nothing to do with the new, futuristic rip-offs of Titanfall and whatnot. Several hundred people play everyday, and chances are you'll run into a few nice people along the way (like I did). 1v1 with friends, go for nukes, and experience the sixth Call of Duty as it is - Absurd, unbalanced, yet downright incredible. And you don't like the BS of MW2, then play its predecessor, CoD4. But in the end, Modern Warfare 2 is the most memorable CoD to date. I can't very well describe the feeling of MW2. You just have to play it for yourself. And if you don't like CoD, go play Battlefield. Or Arma. Or Minecraft. Many dislike it, but for those who appreciate MW2, it's one of the greatest games in video game history.

Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs is as hollow as the product rolling off of its titular assembly line.
A Machine for Pigs is set in 1899, mere hours from the turn of the century.  Wealthy entrepreneur Oswald Mandus awakens from a deep sleep inside of a caged bed to the sound of his two boys, Edwin and Enoch, calling to him from the attic of his mansion.  Delerious and weakened, he stumbles out of bed to investigate, continually following the sound of their voices.  His memory seems to have a massive blind spot between now and when his wife died in child-birth.  His children turn out to be hallucinations, as a strange voice on the phone warns him his real boys are actually trapped in some sort of machine deep underground.  The machine is flooding with water, and if he is not quick to reach the bilges and drain them, he will never see them again.  This might have been an interesting objective if he didn't literally dream about someone speaking the words "Daddy.  Daddy, please don't kill me." before waking up at the very start.  Most games try to save their plot twists for the mid-game but A Machine for Pigs wants it right out in the open from the get go.  It doesn't work.  The boys are dead, and the game will spend half of its incredibly short length pretending you don't already know that.  Far more interesting is how they died, and what Mandus took to doing in the wake of their deaths.  Unfortunately, too much of the game's story goes completely unexplained.  A great deal of the far more interesting plot points are thrust in front of the player or whisked by them but never are they actually dug into.  A story of despair, anger, and ascension; A Machine for Pigs is ultimately underwritten, and while it has many neat and grotesque concepts, can't keep them in focus enough to really keep me hooked.
Set in the first person, A Machine For Pigs is a stone's throw away from being a full on walking simulator.  Mandus can move, run, jump, crouch, and pull up or stow an electric lantern.  Although the game has a robust physics engine for the player to interact with things like physically pulling doors open and closed or picking up and manipulating objects; the world is utterly devoid of things to grab.  Ninety-nine percent of interactable objects are progression necessary, and this makes the system feel completely moot.  Mandus has no inventory and his health regenerates automatically.  Monsters stalk some areas but are easily avoided and often lose sight of you within mere feet from where they spotted you.  The lantern and surrounding lights actually blink on and off in the presence of enemies, giving you some fore-warning, but even this is muddling by the fact that they often just blink for the sake of making the player tense.  Puzzles are almost non-existent.  If you're not pulling levers to progress, you're putting items into things.  These items are usually right beside the thing they need to be put into, or a room over.  Many levels merely block your progress until you turn a wheel, move forward, turn another wheel, and move forward again; as if the act of turn wheels somehow adds to the experience.  Collectible journal pages can be found that give insight into the world, especially Mandus' works, and he also keeps a journal of his own as he moves through the game.
Graphically the game fails to impress.  Which is a shame, because the opening dream is actually very artfully done and set my expectations high.  The lighting and color grading in general is impossibly washed out to the point where it can be hard to tell what you're even looking at in a room.  Monster designs don't look particularly spooky but they certainly are horrifying to listen too.  In fact sound and music in particular is a higher point than the visuals.  The soundtrack really starts to kick in during the latter half of the game and it manages to dredge up some emotion out of the story with its sometimes grand use of opera; assisted by some quality voice acting by Mandus himself.  But much of the game seems lazily put together.  Even your lantern can't aim the right way.  Built like a flash-light with a foward facing beam, it hangs in Mandus' hand by a swinging handle and thus, if the player looks down, it still points ahead, but the light beam will be shining bright at the ground as though the player is wearing a headlamp.  The Machine is made out to be this horrific devise but it is never truly portrayed in the game.  My own imagination conjured far worse things by reading the game's journal pages than anything the devs cared to show me.

I just left a pretty glowing review for Amnesia: The Dark Descent, and I wish I could say I were about to do the same here.  Alas, I only played through A Machine for Pigs once, and have not felt compelled to return to it.  After finishing The Dark Descent, I was chomping at the bit to play the sequel.  I wasn't sure what to expect from the sequel, but I came expecting the same quality horror experience I got in the original; I am sorry to say that I was disappointed.  To give credit where it's due, the plot and backstory of this game are intrigueing and a lot of themes are brought up and explored, if not given satisfying conclusion (nor, without giving away the ending, is the conclusion of the game satisfying).  The real problems come in the gameplay and overall experience.  Taken on its own, this is a fine game.  As a sequel to The Dark Descent, it falls short; the exclusion of major gameplay elements from the original, especially an inventory and sanity meter, subtantially cuts back on content and all but eliminates puzzle aspects, as well as reducing the fear and difficulty faced by the player, who now no longer need worry about losing control, who can now stare at monsters as long as they want with no repercussions or threat of being caught.  The first time I encountered a monster that was an actual threat and not a mere scripted event, I simply ducked into a shadow and watched it lumber past.  I stared at it for a solid 30 seconds as it hobbled past, then simply went on my way. In The Dark Descent, the player character would have descended into madness and given himself away, if not passed out in fear outright, or I would have huddled in the corner with my back turned to the monster hoping and praying it didn't see me and kill me.  Instead I sat and watched it pass and went "well, guess it's safe now," and off I went.  The first time I was actually spotted by a monster, I jumped up, ran around a pillar, ducked into a shadow, and turned- and he'd already given up the chase.  Any sense of danger melted away instantly.  These monsters were practically blind, deaf and dumb, and I could breeze past them with ease, watch them all day to find the gaps in their patrol patterns, then waltz right by.  No fear of the dark, no fear of the monsters, no management of environmental light with tinderboxes and fuel (the lantern is electric and never dies) and no inventory meant there was no horror, no strategy, no puzzles, nothing but the story- which I am sorry to say was not compelling enough to compel me to reccomend this game, even, or perhaps especially, to fans of The Dark Descent.  This sequel took everything you loved about The Dark Descent, stripped the meat off of it and fed it to the pigs, leaving you just the skeleton of the first game.

I have spent an ungodly amount of time with this game. And I've only just begun again, this time on the Steam version.
With the Steam version, I found myself asking, "Well how can I motivate myself to enjoy this game after I spent so much time playing it before?"
Then the answer dawned on me like the many suns I'd be shocked to see outside of my window after only playing for a few minutes.
"Mods," I whispered quitely. I amused myself thinking, "Oh how hard can the mods make it? It'll be a fun refresher and I'll enjoy seeing new life and challenge brought into a map!"
I was setting myself up for a long, grueling hell. And only about 20 hours into my map, and not having expanded my base out yet did I realize how well and truly ♥♥♥♥ed I made myself with the assortment of mods I added on.
A small CHUNK of mods choseable to enhance your game experience, or delay it. Or have it ream you time and time again.
Unfortunately, it's the latter for me. But I love every second of it.
Make no mistake, you SHOULD play this vanilla first. Or a few times, just to get the feel of its basic concepts. Just be prepared to throw your social life away.
Then, when you're ready to throw away everything else you enjoy about your life; other video games, TV, movies, anime, books, you name it, you can install mods and go in for the long haul.
Tl;dr: This game has a great amount of replayability, and game length just by itself. The mechanics fit smoothly, the logic is intuitive after a small amount of time, it has an EXTENSIVE community mod base behind it. And, as an added bonus, it will help you completely eliminate the need for a "social life". It's as if the developers read the memoir,
, and decided to make a spiritual follow-up in the form of a video game.
