Transistor is a different take on the action RPG set in an alternate reality with a heavy influence of computer programing.  The world which you explore is one giant programed city that is on the fritz and you play as Red, a singer who lost her speech and is rapidly losing her world.  As you try to fight against the forces at work you unlock many interesting abilities that are at their best when you are "programing" your turn.  These "programing" sessions allow you to plan out your moves ahead of time and then watch them be carried out to the dismay of your opponents.  It’s a fresh take on the action RPG formula, and with plenty of abilities to unlock, mix and match and power up it stays fresh till the end.
The visuals are solid and the music appropriate.  I did not find either the Narrator or Story to be nearly as interesting or impactful as that of Bastion, the spiritual predecessor of Transistor.  I mostly played thru the game to enjoy the combat hoping for a meaningful end to the story to make it all worthwhile, but the ending did not satisfy.  Overall a refreshingly different take on action RPG combat is offset by the week story and characters, still a worthwhile play, but a critically overrated one.
The soundtrack alone makes this game worth it. Don't expect any of the story to be told to you directly. Prepare for a game that is short, sweet, and indirect with its meaning.

I played Dreamfall back in 2006 when it first came out... and it blew me away.  The game played more like an interactive movie, with a stirring soundtrack, great voice acting, fantastic graphics/setting and a story that held my attention like no other before it.  Although it is a sequel to the "Longest Journey" you can still enjoy it if you have not played the original.  If you like science fiction adventure games you MUST play this... plan on losing track of time for about 15-20 hours.

Entirely opposite to the game that preceded it, Dreamfall begins strong and grows weaker as time passes. Unfortunately, this game comes from the era when every adventure game felt the need to include mandatory action sequences, almsot exclusively poorly implemented, with this as no exception.
Zoe is a lovely character though and the game is enoyable enough. It's a certain addition to the collection of any adventure game fan, but I doubt you'll pull it off the shelves too often.

A direct sequel to The Longest Journey.
I was really amazed playing The Longest Journey. Dreamfall, the sequel, fell slightly short of the bar set by the original, but having played the first title right before jumping into this one, there were a lot of little things I could appreciate quite a bit.
Things I felt were improvements over the first title:
- Better sense of direction
- No more ridiculously complex "we won't give you any hints, figure it out yourself" puzzles.
Areas where the first title felt superior to this sequel:
- Imaginative world, setting, and character designs
- Lack of facial animations in the original actually was an improvement, since Dreamfall's characters felt too stoic in their expressions.
I recommend this game, but only after having played and enjoying the original The Longest Journey, as Dreamfall really is a pretty direct sequel in many ways.
Here's hoping we get a 3rd entry in the series someday.
No idea why people didn't like this as much. The only thing I have against it, was that it's too short, and I want more. D:

This game will remain among my absolute favourites, together with the original TLJ. This is not in contradiction with admitting that the gameplay is often lacking, and the puzzles have not been very puzzling. It's been a run-through.
But this game has given me something that very few games seem to offer: first of all, immersion and identification with the characters, all very much "alive", recognizable, with strong personalities and different, clashing beliefs. But, most importantly, a rich, complex and simply wonderful plot and storytelling.
There are several themes, and no easy resolution; but the game dares facing things like scientific and technological development, the world of art, magic, creativity, religion, faith and its loss, dreams and their values, questioning of beliefs, the relationship of all these elements in the world and in the human mind.
Finally, the state of entertainment (therefore, games too) and the value of storytelling, and our risk of losing it.
Loved it.

This game is a fantastic little game about the monotony of life in a Soviet-Style republic.  The minutia that one has to pay attention to, which increases as the actual story goes on, is simply ridiculous.  You could be the guy who feels sorry for the refugees, but then, your family "gets it"-- if you know what I mean.  You could be absolutely sure that you checked everything, but NOOO-  the name of the person's country of origin was misspelled.
This game is addictive, and endless mode is infinitely replayable.  And at the end of the game, you get precisely what you expected-  the satisfaction of having completed your work for 30 days, with the promise of working for infinite more days at the same exact job.  Also-  you get VGA-era graphics and sound, which makes the experience that much more realistic.

After 117 hours I watched my rocket ascend to the heavens in a glorious triumph of automated industrial power.
I felt a real sense of achievment creating a huge complex system out of nothing, fighting off attacks from the natives and laying out my lines of production. But the key to success is sound logic, creativity and to remember that this is NOT a game about crafting, it is a game about automation. It was also amusing (but kinda sad and cruel?) to see the native fauna mindlessly throw themselves at my defenses, only to be butchered by bullets, lasers and flamethrowers, accomplishing nothing.
The other thing about the game is that it has a deep underlaying theme to it. There is a dismal and thought-provoking  parallel to the real world we live in; the consumption of natural resources and endless production at an ever increasing speed and scale, which results in more and more consumption of resources in the endless pursuit of efficiency.
My factory is like a living being that devour natural resources and defecates materials, machines and pollution, just like the real world.
Verdict: KOYAANISQATSI/10

Having now finished this title I’m torn on whether to recommend it or not. I think the deciding factor has to be on whether or not this works as a horror game and as a worthy ‘sequel’ to Amnesia: The Dark Descent, which is the method I judged it by in my first impressions video.
A Machine for Pigs is dripping with atmosphere thanks to its moody visuals, creepy setting, intriguing story and haunting music. The sound effects in general are pretty great, with the groans, clanks and hisses, coming from the titular machine and the piercing screams of the pig men.
This would seem to fulfil the criteria of a successful Amnesia sequel but AMFP lacks gameplay and tension. There are so few encounters with monsters in this brief game that you rarely feel tense and when they do appear they do not affect the player in the same way they did in Amnesia: TDD. You can brazenly stare at them which breaks the magic. Dying to them will also just drop you straight back into the game, removing any threat they possess and any feeling of panic.
The game also quickly becomes a series of linear walkways so you can listen to The Chinese Room tell their story, without being interrupted by irritating things like gameplay and pant wetting terror. It’s a shame, because for my first ‘walking simulator’ experience this wasn’t bad. It’s just not what I wanted from the franchise.

When you say "Amnesia"..
I am going to explain 3 different aspects now.
1. My own opinion based on what I do like,
2. What is Amnesia: The Dark Descent about and finally,
3. What is Machine For Pigs compared to its 1st episode.
__________________________________________
1. I have always preferred slower, darker atmosphere over killing and running.
It just seem much more scary when you basically can't attack monster, its even more realistic this way.  Just imagine yourself in damn gothic castle (Dark Descent) or god damn pig machinery!
Dark atmosphere is ruling over player and story of both episodes fulfill its potential 100%. (If you have played both)
2. The Dark Descent is really all about you and your pants. Its really scary, and that is why this game lays in ours steam libraries for few months before we play it. The fact, you are defenceless, makes game really scary. I like concept, story and the fact its available for Linux platform. I like game mechanics too.
3. What is Machine For Pigs then and what are the differences?
Machine For Pigs feels like different game placed in the very same universe. Main differences are:
a) Its not scary, its creepy. Which is not a bad thing because we wanted more from developers, we didn't want the exact same game but different textures, right?
b) puzzles are being solved within level(!) and game makes sure you know what to do. Compared to The Dark Descent, I appreciated this as I found my pants constantly wet during Dark Descent gameplay, thanks to 50000000 doors in total darkness with crazy noises, hiding from creepy monster(s) who smells when you r around, with just really not enough batteries for your torch (y) good luck.
c) Story. Story is very much better, overal acting is very well done. Music and so on.
d) Lets be honest, due to the facts mentioned above, the game is easier. Still can change your heart rhythm tho. Game is easier to play, but much harder to handle psychically. This episode is psychological horror.
Don't hesitate to try both of the games. Each episode has something the other hasn't got. Maybe you decide to play one or prefer another, I just hope you will enjoy the game.
If you asking me, YES I RECOMMEND

-It's free to play for a few more days at the time of this writing. Download and try it while its free! It may save you from what you consider a terrible waste of money. (It did for me.)
-The intro is true to other ES games, you start as a prisoner.
-It will offer plenty of things to do to keep you busy for some time if you're not greedy with your time.  If you have absolutely nothing else to do, this will amuse you (possibly).
-It sortof has an Elder Scrolls feel to it?  You start with an encounter to draemora (if you can call them that) and Hermaus Mora (by name only). They look/sound hardly anything like what we've previously encountered, which could be a good thing.
-Character creation is mediocre at best, you get some preset faces and sliders to change a few things like weight, similar to previous Edler Scrolls games, but those are also not really good.  I don't know why I listed this as a pro... I guess cause it wasn't as bad as it could have been?
Cons: Whoo boy, where to start.
- As you should already know, this is NOT Skyrim 2.0.  That in itself is not a bad thing, but this game was a solid 1-2 steps back on quality.  There was no improvement in the system, they tried to take some Morrowind mechanics and forcibly shove them into the game to give a certain "feel," while only minimally updating them.  Looting general items still requires a loot menu, butterfly wings no longer directly deposit into your inventory.
-Graphics are garbage.  Surrounding creatures are marginally better than Oblivion, and much worse than Skyrim.  Grass and flowers are similar as the creatures.  Textures are something from early 2000's at best.  Yes, this is an MMO, but it can't make use of anything more than a 5 year old budget gaming system.
-Khajiit look like some really bad ape/cat crossbreed and their voice acting is completely human with a hint of accent.  No gruff/growly cat noises anymore.
-Movement and combat are lackluster and generic at best.  It feels NOTHING like Oblivion/Skyrim, so if you like these combat mechanics, you will most likely not enjoy TESO playstyle.  It feels like a less polished Dragon Age 2 combat style, and that, to begin with, was pretty bad.
-Bethesda probably had little to no involvement in this development, it's all Zenimax, and from previous encounters with their products, this was a terrible decision on Bethesda's part.  Take that as you will.
Overall, for a pay game, I'd say this is a really bad start.  Neverwinter would be a good option I'd recommend before paying for this game, and that's even at a $10 sale price.  If you want things hidden behind a paywall and constant advertisements to buy things and upgrade, Neverwinter and KotOR are great options.  If you start this game you'll quickly hit your limit if you don't separately purchase also the Morrowind expansion, the guilds packages (thieves guild, mages guild, dark brotherhood, which should be included in the base game) and if you want to play as an Imperial, you also have to pay seperate for that.  Unless you pay their monthly subscription fees, you're looking at easily $50+ just to start playing this mediocre game.
For my final thoughts about the overall feel of this game (from what I experienced) it's a poorly done WoW-clone with Edler Scrolls slapped over the names and races.

You awake on the dock of a mysterious island. The air is clear and there's not a soul in sight. You find a few buildings and an assortment of levers, wheels, and buttons. You see a looming tower, overlooking a small, wood-paneled room. There is a shelf of books inside the room, but most of them have been charred and are unreadable. A few remain, still intact. You open one and begin reading. You soon realize there's much to uncover about this world on the isle of MYST.
(Before we go any further, you should know that this 15 year-old game doesn't like to cooperate on modern hardware, so you'll need to mess with some compatibility settings or other workarounds to get it running decently) I'd heard about MYST for years. People always complained about its difficulty or praised it as one of the classics. After toying around with some settings, I got the game running fairly smoothly and I felt...confused. MYST is infamous for its lack of instruction, so I didn't find myself off to the best start. Unfortunately, this was a somewhat common theme for me, as I had to look up a couple hints and solutions along the way. Aside from a couple short video clips and some writings, you're pretty much on your own. Despite my early troubles, I think MYST's puzzles are generally very fair. Yes, they can be difficult, but most are straightforward and very logical. Most of the challenge comes from figuring out how to put together what's directly in front of you. MYST doesn't give you a lot of tools to work with. All you can do is walk around, open doors, manipulate objects in the environment, climb ladders, and pick up a small handful of items. This isn't really a problem, however, since the puzzles are focused and the small number of elements are very efficiently used. Overall, the gameplay is simple and challenging, and the mechanics are sound.
Now MYST is already a great puzzle game, but the game's sound and visuals are what really makes it special. realMYST takes the original's pre-rendered static scenes and replaces them with a fully rendered and animated 3D world. Though this is a contentious decision, I think this change really suits the nature of the game and, from what I understand, it still preserves the original look and feel of the world. A movement speed setting would have been a nice addition, though. realMYST isn't exactly a pretty game by modern standards, but the graphics do convey a very desolate and eerie atmosphere. The textures, while dated, still make the world look fairly realistic. There are even day and night cycles in most of the environments, though their inclusion isn't exactly necessary. The sound design is top-notch, with howling wind, flowing and rippling water, chattering birds, creaky walkways, and more. The sound cues are even necessary for some puzzle solving, but they're used sparingly and expertly. An ambient soundtrack occasionally plays when suitable and it too greatly enhances the atmosphere of the game. Overall, the aesthetics combine to create moods of tranquility, fear, and melancholy, as well as a constant state of lonliness that really immerses you in the environment.
This was my first real experience with MYST and it will not be the last. While the game is relatively short and it's ending abrupt, I'm more excited than ever to experience the other titles in the franchise and hone my puzzle solving skills. If you're a fan of games with puzzles or a great atmosphere, you should definitely play MYST in some form. I can now clearly see how much MYST has impacted both classic and modern gaming. If you consider yourself a general fan of games or a games enthusiast, I highly recommend you play this treasured (rightly so) adventure of the past.

World of Goo is a masterpiece of design.  Everything about this physics-based puzzler fills you with that grand feeling you used to have, back when you were 10 years old, playing in the yard. That feeling of Adventure.
The game starts very simply. Here are a bunch of cute quirky goo balls, and there’s a pipe up above them.  They make little squeals and pops when you click and drag them.  As you experiment with the balls, you learn how to build a tower out of them, yearning to reach that pipe. Where does it go? That’s a secret. Soon you’re building bridges, and balancing on ropes.  You come across species of goo that behave slightly differently, and let you interact with and build crazy new goo-based architecture, all in an effort to reach a pipe that’s just over there.  For instance, green goo balls can be removed from the structure and replaced, letting your structure climb up trees or snake through tight spaces.  But the difficulty never gets overwhelming. The learning curve here is expertly controlled, to where each level builds on the last. You are never forced to learn something in a totally new situation, not without a little gentle guidance from the invisible Sign Painter. The game seems to say “OK, you understand the basic dynamics here, but what if we do this?” The game adds a simple wrinkle you can immediately understand.  And you will eagerly jump in trying to solve it.
That eagerness will be due in no small part to the music. You can get the whole soundtrack for free right here.  The combination of whimsy and epic just fills you with that sense of Adventure and, honestly, it will just make you happy.
The visuals here are top notch. The cartoony, Dr. Seussical aesthetic serves the game’s atmosphere well, and each level feels very distinct. One early level makes the entire foreground, goo balls and all, completely black, while the background is a brilliant fiery sunset.  Truly a work of art.  Everything is clear and responsive, and behaves as expected.  One minor complaint is that when there are many goo balls in one area, it is difficult to select exactly the one you want.  This is a minor problem in the later levels, when you have 3 or 4 different types of balls and you’re on a time limit to finish your move.
The game is divided into 4 distinct chapters, each focusing on one season of the goo balls’ journey.  There is plenty to do here, but if you think the game is too short then each level has an OCD criteria (Obsessive Completion Distinction) which challenges you to solve it with a certain number of rescued goos, or within a set time or moves limit.  Going after the OCD achievements was a really good challenge! They force you to take your skills and knowledge of the physics systems to their absolute limit.
World of Goo was one of the first mega-hit indie games when it came out in 2008, and its success laid the path to the golden age of gaming we are enjoying today.  When my daughter is old enough to start playing mouse-and-keyboard games, this will be one of her first.  I recommend this game to anyone, for it is an important piece of gaming history, and it’s an amazingly fun Adventure.

text: Very few games have made me cry like a ♥♥♥♥♥, and fewer still deserved that level of emotion. Transistor is one such game.

I almost didn't buy this game at first. The camera angle of Diablo, the combat of Final Fantasy, and the silent protagonist of any one of a million other games all turned me away. Then I got a good look at the visuals. I heard about the game's design that trusts its players to be intelligent human beings; allowing you to piece it together without handholding. I listened to the soundtrack. I bought it 12 hours later. What I found surprised me even more. The world-building is the best I've seen since Bioshock (One reviewer described the atmosphere as similar to Cowboy Bebop mixed with Bladerunner. Much more accurate than you think). The camera angle functions as a diorama, displaying everything you need to see easily in plain view. The combat is actually closer to Mass Effect, but more in-depth. Red's voice can be heard in the soundtrack, and with the Transistor itself as an engaging character narrator, I was drawn into the experience. On certain terminals, Red will type and delete comments in order to reword them, just like a real person would. She sometimes uses this to convey messages to the Transistor, which add a LOT to her character.
10/10
This is just... play it, soak in the art, the music. Enjoy the story and the combat, this is one of the best games I've played.  I don't think I can recommend this enough!

Write a story based on this line : "By evening, she was running a high fever ... "

Far up in the mountains of Canada, there is an old abandoned log cabin. Once it was occupied by a young couple who wanted to distance themselves from the chaos of this modern world. Here they were miles away from the nearest town. Bob, the husband, made the occasional trip into town to buy supplies whereas Jan, his wife, spent her free time by the fire, sewing. Their life was simply idyllic.
Then, one midwinter's day, Jan woke up from bed with a strange ache in her bones. Putting it down to overwork, Bob shooed her to bed and made sure she rested. Though Jan was impatient to get to her chores, Bob soothed her, "Relax, Sugar. You're overdoing things. All these chores will be here when you recover."
However, Jan seemed to be getting worse instead of recovering. By evening, she was running a high fever and in greater pain. In spite of his best efforts, Bob could not manage to ease her suffering. And then suddenly, she started to lapse into unconsciousness.
It was then obvious that she was seriously ill. What could Bob do? He had no experience in treating the sick and Jan was getting worse by the minute. He knew that there was an old doctor in town but he lived three miles away, downhill. Pot-bellied and obese, there was no way the doctor could make it up to their cabin.
Something had to be done quickly! Bob racked his brains but to no avail. The only thing left to do was to go to the doctor. In Jan's condition, she could never walk that far in the waist-deep snow. Bob would have to carry her!
Bob searched his mind for a way to move poor, sick Jan. Then, he remembered. He had once made a sledge so that they could ride together over the mountain. They never got around to using it though, because the whole mountain was thickly covered with rocks and trees. He had never found a safe way down, not even once.
"Well," he thought, "looks like I'm going to have to try it anyhow," as he dug out the sledge from the storeroom. "Jan may die unless I get her to the doctor, and life means nothing to me without her." With this thought in mind, Bob gently tucked Jan into the sledge, got in the front, and with a short prayer for safety, pushed off.
How they got through that ride alive, Bob has never figured out. As trees loomed up in front of him and just as quickly whizzed by his side, close enough to touch, he felt relieved that Jan was not awake to experience the ride. It was all he could do not to scream as collision seemed imminent, time and again, with only inches to spare.
At last, bursting from the mountainside, the town came into view. Barely slowing down, they sped through the icy streets, only losing speed as they neared the doctor's house. The sledge, battered through the journey, collapsed in the left ski as it came to a halt, spilling out its occupants. Bob picked up his Jan and made his way into the doctor's house.
After what seemed to be a long winter, Jan recovered fully from her illness but Bob never recovered from his fright. They moved into the little town so as to be near help in times of crisis, and have lived there ever since.

Very beautiful indie game made by Supergiant Games - the Makers of Bastion. In this, their 2nd game, which has already sold over 600K copies, you play as Red, a woman without a voice, and a man without a body. It really reminded me personally of the Nintendo DS game from Square Enix - The World Ends With You.

Ok time for criticism: the game may be stylish, but it is VERY short, each playthrough of the game might give you 10 hours. In short it's a border checkpoint simulator and it conveys it's message incredibly well. There are different aspects to take notice of like passport expiration dates and much more. It has it's replayability and is sort of based on roguelike money management

I can't express in words why this game is fun.  You would think that sitting at a border checkpoint examining papers all day would be boring...but....this game is addicting.  Basically, you start out just examing passsports for fraudilant information, but by the end of the game you are comparing passports, work permits, entry permits, and id supplements against each other, while checking for wanted criminals and contraband.  You can, if you so choose to be a disloyal Artstoskan, to help the Ezic agents overthrow the government too.

In Papers, Please you play as an immigration inspector working for the Ministry of Admission of Arstotzka in East Grestin. Your job is to check on people trying to enter Arstotzka and decide who can pass through the border and who has to be denied or even arrested.
Most of the time, your decisions will lead to a different ending (not always a good one!).
Choose wisely, the destiny of Arstotzka, your family and many other people is in your hands.
Pros:
-Well written dystopian settings
-20 different endings
-Lovely retro graphics
-Jorji Costava
-Great plot and sub-plots
-Shooting terrorists from your inspection booth since 1982
-Did I already mention Jorji Costava?
Cons:
-Maybe old school graphics are not everyone's cup of tea (I personally love it though)
-Stamping visas and check out papers will probably sound boring to someone
-There's no "Escape to Obristan with your newfound best friend Jorji" ending
Papers, Please is hands-down one of my favorite games. Be sure to give it a try, you definitely won't regret it.

After having played through this game three times, I figured it was about time to write a review! Seriously, the replay value is that good! Noticing certain bits of scenery and dialogue that you didn't before, along with using different weapons than what you'd usually use, is quite fun!
This game is an absolute gem that deserves a ton more recognition! The story, graphics, sound, voice acting, music, and of course the main character are all fantastic and come together to form a game that is simply unforgettable!
My favorite aspect of this game is how they go about telling the story. It's a brilliant and quite unexpected take on storytelling that is incredibly unique. You'll understand what I mean once you start playing the game, but for me this was a redefining moment in gaming that made me want to continue playing to see what might happen next! Then again, I'd have definitely kept playing anyway even if the story didn't have its unique way of being told! I was that hooked onto this game, in huge thanks to the main character: Silas Greaves. He is a bounty hunter and as he begins telling his story in a bar you immediately jump into action as the player.
This western style game is one for the books! The levels are designed beautifully, the backstories for all the villains are enticing as they each have affected Silas Greaves in their own ways, and the final level absolutely blew me away.
Delving into the mind of a bounty hunter may be a dangerous game, but hell if it isn't one to remember.
Buy this game and experience the thrilling life stories of Silas Greaves!
Support Techland, the company who developed the game, and thank them for creating this monumental game!

Normally, I'm not so much into puzzle games but this one was a great experience.
It really gets everything right: graphics, ambiance, story, difficulty and atmosphere.

The Room is a great game. There's no arguing about that.
First, the game looks amazing and the animations are fluid. It just feels satisfying to even look around the puzzle to figure out what to do next, and it's very responsive with very few problems of control.
And speaking of the puzzles, there are challenging but not excrusiating : the difficulty is well balanced with a healthy progression. They were also very well thought and put together, giving a good sense of progression and investment in it. It was enjoyable to bits.
The atmosphere of the game! Another great point. Great graphics added to great background music/noises gave a seriously enjoyable atmosphere. The more you progress, the more the room you're in (with the spot lights and walls) dissapear and you slowly seem to be drained into another world (well, before it becomes litteral of course).
Now, for the bad sides, I'd say it was a little short. Of course it can be long if you struggle with the puzzles, but I wouldn't have minded a few rooms in more. And here's just a minor, meaningless complaint : when a new hint is available, the hint symbol should at least blink or get highlighted, because sometimes the noises around make it hard to hear the faint sound of the new hint being unlocked. But again, just a minor complaint, nothing too bad.
If you like a good puzzle game, it's one to be bought without any hesitation.

I'll try keep the review brief, but I urge anyone to try the trial (which let's you level up to 20) so you can get a feel for the combat and see what the dungeons are like (not guildhests).
Combat -
The combat is smooth, and every class (especially towards the end game) is very distinct from each other. One is able to level every class with one character, and switch between classes on the fly. Many, many dungeons and trials. With Heavensward, more raids are on the way. FATES provide a good source of EXP, and can be especially fun to heal through.
Downsides:
My friends have told me that the game is much more simplistic than something like WoW, so this may or may not appeal to you.
(Heavensward edit: DPS queues got better with all the new tanks and healers. Increased story exp makes grinding unnecessary until post-50)
Everything else -
Community is great. You get the occasional elitist or ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, but that pretty much applies to most MMOs. There's plenty of side content in minigames, crafting (which may be main content to others), hunts, and other things.
The story is good enough, and gets much better later in the story when you aren't doing pointless fetch quests for exp. Hell, up until like 47, you could exclusively do story quests and be all set.
(Heavensward edit: they heavily increased story quest exp and added more high level loot, so it looks like Square Enix is doing their best to rush new players along; most likely grinding won't be necessary until past 50. )
The game is incredible, but it takes time get to the fun stuff (not to say that it isn't fun from the beginning). If you're looking for a good MMO, give this game a shot. At the very least, try the trial and see what the dungeons are like.

I have a confession to make. When I first played this game it just didn't grab me and I almost gave up the second time too but fortunately I stuck with it and was rewarded with a very enjoyable puzzle game that whilst not too taxing is hard enough to usually require several attempts to complete each level.
The game is actually quite difficult to describe but the best way I can describe it is to say you have a fixed number of goo balls that you can attach together to form a web like lattice that you can then use to transport the goo balls from one place to another. The idea is that you have enough goo balls left when you reach your destination to meet the level completion criteria.
There are different types of goo balls; the main ones can be attached together to form the web; some have no special function other than to count towards the count at the end of the level; some can only be shot into the air from the point you grab them; some float and can be used to lift the lattice into the air and others can catch fire etc.
The levels are relatively short; I generally finished each one in around 5-10 minutes (not counting re-attempts if I failed). There is a handy restart button to restart a level if you realise things are going pear shaped and you won't be able to complete a level. You can also click on the flies buzzing around to redo a move but top be honest I found this facility next to useless.
Hints are available by clicking on signs that also provide the game narrative. The hints tended to be pretty cryptic but occasionally very useful. The game narrative was a bit surreal for me ..
There is an excellent, unobstrusive soundtrack to the game.
There are 4 chapters & and epilogue to complete, each containing multiple levels. You have to finish one chapter to move onto the next but can replay any level you have previously completed.
It's possible replay value is in going back and redoing the levels faster or with more goo balls left over or to complete in OCD, which I think basically means you complete at maximum efficiency. I only managed this a handful of times

For those interested in a team-oriented action-packed game with a central focus on mythology, this would be a great choice, especially for those familiar with MOBA's. Its playstyle is centralized around taking control of a god of your choice to go into battle with, along with 4 other players on your team for its primary gamemode Conquest where you will be faced against 5 other gods in a battle using your gods abilities and your knowledge, skills, and tactics to come out victorious. It is heavily centralized around team-fighting strategy which means cooperation with others is essential in order to have a significantly improved chance of winning. Although there isn't much in game methods for communication other than its built in VGS (Voice Guided System) to act as team communication, there are other 3rd party services you could choose to use to allow for better communication like Curse (now called Twitch), Discord, Skype, etc. This game would be particularily great to play with friends, and offers tutorials, guides and AI matches to help newer players learn. The community is mostly positive, and toxicity is rather low. For the perhaps excessive time I've been playing the game, I've come across a low amount of unpleasant people, and have greatly enjoyed playing this game both with friends and by myself. I would definitely recommend having friends to play the game with, as it makes it far more enjoyable and entertaining. The game is free to play (Not pay to win) and in no way requires you to pay for anything, however buying gems allows you to support the developers and get great cosmetic items as well. I would absolutely recommend this game.

Let me preface this by saying it is not bad. For all intents and purposes, it's a decent game. Would I recommend it? No. I'll keep it simple and say it's a 5/10. Here's the pro/con of this thing.
Pros:
*Graphics and visuals (runs smooth, didn't experience any issues)
*Controls/interface (plays and controls like Amnesia)
*Journals/memos (pretty much the only reason to continue playing it and it explains alot more than what is being said aloud)
*The level design was very spacious and I took some time to look at the scattered art and scribbled notes in the environment
*The main story arch (it's really the only reason you play this type of game)
Cons:
* I didn't like the setting. Sue me. I enjoyed the medieval castles more than industrial factories of the early 1900's.
*Characters other than Oswald Mandus (his kids models are the friggin same and you don't actually meet other characters to interact with them)
*Overarching relation to amnesia lore felt weak (in my opinion).
*Monsters- few in number, weak, and their AI is stupid (I just ran past them, I never hid from them. Oh, and speaking of hiding...)
*The level design made no use of hiding spots and the usage light and dark was painfully under utilized
*Little to no replay value aside from collecting memos
*Autoregen health makes damage negligible and there is no sanity meter
*Infinite lantern
*Reduced interacton with objects (Dark Descent had more objects to pick up and throw)
*Linear story line, no player choice
To conclude, there is very little innovation to the formula and I might even say they're scaling back. I played the Penumbra series first and then went to the Amnesia series. They kept improving the visuals and story but they keep taking away the player interaction. I understand them taking away the combat but without any usable items, abilities, or player choices which affect the plot or gameplay, it turned into a walking simulator with little worry of dying. I don't want their games to turn into action adventure but they need to improve on gameplay and player interaction.
To end this on a positive note, Dark Descent and the Penumbra series have aged but hold up pretty well. These were the last games I completed. Go play them! Also, I'm currently working on Soma and I'm really enjoying it. There is hope for a brighter future for this company. They just need to talk more with their fan base and ask them what they want out of a game.
I was a huge MYST fan in the day (still have the books on my shelves and the think about the world) but the 3D remake loses something from the original.
You shouldn't buy this version of the game, unless you want a crash simulator.

I got this working on Windows 7 Pro SP1 64-bit. After installing the game, just make sure you find the RealMYST.exe program file, right-mouse click it, and troubleshoot compatibility first before launching the game for the first time. Running as if in Windows XP SP2 works for me. Due to rundll32.exe related issues, you may need to find the RealMYST.exe running process in the Windows Task Manager and end it before attempting to launch the game again. I can also choose any of the video graphics options on the RealMYSTSetup.exe; they all work as they should (I have two Titan Black cards in SLI). I didn't need to do any crazy hex mods (as purported elsewhere on the internet) and the game doesn't crash for me.
As for the game itself, this is probably my all-time favorite version of Myst. I had only briefly played the original at a friend's house a few times, but played and beat this version in the early '00s. I also like it better than the realMyst Masterpiece Edition as I think it does a better job of fully realizing and visually achieving the setting and mood of the game. Though the graphics are more dated looking in general, I think it still looks aesthetically pleasing and appropriate overall. Some of the textures, especially wood, can still hold their own more than a decade later.
In the original Myst they had a very limited color pallet and resolution to work with by today's standards, so objects and visual features needed to stand out more to be seen and identified in a scene. This was largely corrected in realMyst with textures that made more sense, making it more of a true update. realMyst Masterpiece Edition seems like more of a nostalgia motivated rerelease of the original, but doesn't really hold its own nor make sense by today's standards. Things like the flashlight/excessively dark areas, marker arrow indicators, "tower rotation" being displayed on the Myst island map in the library, and so on just seem out of place and don't really add anything to the game.
Even though I already own realMyst on disc, it was worth getting another copy of it on Steam for the current price.
Enjoy.

C:\Windows\System32\gameux.dll
C:\Windows\SysWOW64\gameux.dll
...and correspondingly renamed the files to...
C:\Windows\System32\gameux.old (dll)
C:\Windows\SysWOW64\gameux.old (dll)
...so hasplms.exe no longer needs internet access and I don't get the issues with rundll32.exe using available CPU resources.
This is a known issue with Windows Games Explorer – regardless of whether or not you actually want to use it or if you even have it disabled – that's apparently been around for several years.
I wouldn't recommend doing the above system file name changes unless you don't care to use Windows Games Explorer, which apparently downloads box art for your games that it lists and similar – I wouldn't have known, since I've never previously used it.
Hopefully Microsoft fix this issue sometime, but I have my doubts since it's been a known issue for several years now.

Papers, Please is a game that sounds incredibly boring in a nutshell.
You're a border patrol passpor inspector.  It's stylistically low-key (though quite pleasing), simple, and the rules are available to you on-screen at all times.
But somehow the game makes me feel anxious and alert the entire time you're playing it.
Did you check it all?  Did you get it right?  Every approval or denial leaves you with gritted teeth for the 5 seconds it takes the entree to walk away.  As soon as you hear the mechanical whirr of the fax machine printing your mistakes, you kick yourself for missing a detail and keep going.
Really engrossing.  Fun to get all the endings, and the way the game saves files makes it incredibly easy to correct previous mistakes allowing you to skip over the need to completely start a new file.  A very underrated feature.
Much enjoyed.

This is the kind of indie game that I really like... it's obviously low-budget, and the graphics, interface and sound are totally old school. Yet, it doesn't matter, as the game itself is pretty unique and interesting... maybe even addictive.
Basically, it's an exercise in concentration. Each day, your job as a passport-controller becomes more difficult. At first, there are like 2-3 things to watch out for. Each day, a new thing to observe and look out for is added, and so you need to remember more and more things to watch out for. Some of them don't come up for quite some time, but once you get too careless, you miss those things and fail.
Fortunately, you can mess up a few times each day without having to pay a fee from your measly pay. Then again, the more complaints you get, the worse it gets, as there also is some kind of inspector who will judge your efficiency every once in a while.
I recommend to write down the issueing cities from each region on a piece of paper... otherwise, you might lose quite some time checking every time.
I have played this for 5 hours so far, in two sessions, and I notice that it really can eat away at your ability to concentrate, so I think this is best played casually... do like half an hour at a time so you don't burn yourself out.
I really like the theme, as it DOES make you think a bit about how unfair the system in that country is, and you have to make some harsh decisions. There even are a few puzzles in there in the story-mode.
Kudos to the developer... this is a fun little game, and to me, the old school graphics don't matter at all, as the core of the game is very well thought out, and it's fun!

The design of this game is fantastic. Using the backdrop of an opressive country, the player takes on the role of a border guard checking documents, and the atmosphere is suitably bleak. Weaving an increasingly sinister storyline into what at first appears to be a simulation of probably the most mundane activity possible, the game becomes tense, interesting and ultimately intensely story-driven. The design decisions, in terms of music, graphics and presentation are spot on, the interface is extremely well designed, therefore making this a game I couldn't help but be drawn into. All the different types of people, dialogue and situations which present themselves help keep you on your toes. Lucas Pope did a fantastic job with his vision in this regard.
So, amazingly, the process of checking every migrant's documents, which would be a soul-crushingly mundane job in real life, actually becomes
, at least for a while. The game has a charming interface and top-notch presentation, and is just very polished. Definitely a quality product, at least for a small indie game.
But the pacing is painful. Make no mistake, this game definitely falls into the category of a slow burner. The decision to take the tedious task of border checks, making it into the entire substance of the game is both the game's greatest strength and it's biggest problem. Intriguing and surprising at first, eventually the checks, which are the main "gameplay" aspect, become more and more complicated and it becomes a chore rather than a challenge. The gap between meaningful plot points ends up feeling too large. The actual checks and "levels" really needed some tweaking to remain fun and remove any big lulls of interest, which is easier said than done considering the nature of the game: essentially, a "boring job" simulator.
The story drives the game, but ultimately it comes up empty. The plot ends up pretty cliché, and you can't help but lose interest towards the latter half of the game, at which point the problems with the gameplay itself become glaringly apparent, and you begin to question why the game stopped being fun, and why you should continue playing it. Most people click X at this point and never return.
Games can be artistic, games can be emotionally affective, and games can be basically novels like those 5 million Telltale games. There are no boundaries (and there shouldn't be) but games are just that - games. They exist to be played, and the gameplay will always be the most important part of any game. And purely from that perspective, playing this game loses its appeal too severely.
It was difficult to decide whether to recommend this game or not. On the one hand, I can recommend this game as a one time experience, at least until the gameplay rather quickly becomes boring. Lucas Pope created something special here, a truly unique, memorable game which even if one doesn't totally "enjoy", is crafted fantastically. Even though I didn't like the game much, I did think about it a lot after I left it. Considering the subject matter, maybe that's the way the game - and my recommendation - should be.

I knew that Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs had little in common with The Dark Descent going in (mostly just a couple of diary entries mentioning an uncle from Brennenburg, laudanum and vitae, etc.), and I had no problems with that. The most egregious faults, in my opinion, lie with the graphics, story, and presentation in general.
The game starts out well enough, you wake up in a mysterious mansion, with an intriguing setup for what promises to be an interesting story. Starting in the second level, while still in the mansion, the screen inexplicably gets a greenish/greyish filter applied to it, which sticks around for the remainder of the game and makes everything look bland and washed out, like someone rubbed dirt in your eyes. The story takes a nosedive as well and oscillates somewhere between predictable and nonsensical. Unlike the original Amnesia, nothing is really explained in the end and the ending itself makes little sense. I can only assume that at least part of the journey was metaphorical and should be interpreted in the Dear Esther vein.
All of the useless items from the original game are removed (like tinder and health potions) and the character no longer has night vision, making the lantern actually useful, but most of the levels have very little light and feel empty, with the only reward for exploration being the scattered diary pages that someone took great care to spread all over London. As a result, most of the game consists of walking through empty, grey/brown, dark corridors, with some of the more interesting locations like the mansion, London streets, and, my favorite, The Nest of the Wretched, being over in minutes. During one of the London levels, you see the only two NPCs in the game, and boy do they look out of place. I hope that it was just a bugged out scripted event rather than a conscious choice to place a weird tiny gentleman in the open doorway with nothing behind him. At least, the music is great throughout, even if it doesn't always quite mesh with what's going on.
Ironically, A Machine for Pigs is a strange split of Amnesia and Dear Esther that doesn't really work as a whole, with the same predicable formula as Amnesia and Penumbra and stretches of narration a la Dear Esther. Outside of the few expected chase sequences and jump scares, the scariest part of the game is seeing all of those lit candles on the attic floor of the mansion, and it is a shame, because it could have been a great game, with a great setting and premise.

A "document simulator." You review documents of an endless, dreary parade of people trying to enter your crappy country from one of its crappy neighbors, granting or denying entry as you see fit. Some sort of omnipotent oversight system penalizes you for technical mistakes. Or technical *cough*"mistakes," since that last guy slipped you a $20, causing your finger to slip and hit the wrong button, of course.
An excellent diversion from the usual videogame moral dichotomy of "to be or not be an (donkey is censored?)," where there's actual difficulty in making a decision. As you're usually some variant of The Chosen One, games have to find a way to let you keep playing even if you prove to be a total (censored, evidently) who no one would ever trust to do anything. As such, you're usually free to be as much of a (censored again) as you'd like, and some characters might scowl at you differently, but otherwise with little or no consequence. Or to chase the carrot-on-a-stick they included to try and get you to
do so. In Papers, Please, however, I feel they've done a much better job giving your choices positive
negative consequences. Do you help the rebels, knowing it could lead to your imprisonment or death? How about if it can lead to your
imprisonment? Do you let a probably-not-terrorist trying to escape an even worse country in, if it means you can pay rent? Or that it could result in a demerit? Do you let your boss violate the rules he continually berates you with? Do you turn in the guy with forged documents, knowing he's probably harmless? Or just turn him away? How about if the guard promises to pay you for each person you arrest, regardless of guilt?
Most of these are not necessarily
questionable, I suppose - it's still just a game, basically restricted to what the designers intended, but it is quite a refreshing change from choosing to kill or save the Little Sisters, or selecting the Paragon or Renegade responses (and usually receiving an obvious tangible benefit, regardless of what Peter Molyneux promised you this time around). It's just pleasant to have a game give you pause for thought, rather than pause to calculate reward. Or figure out which of the things is going to actually make Commander Shepard say what you want him to. But in Papers, Please: Does your family go cold tonight?
Or do they go hungry, instead?

Leonardo has always been an intriguing historical character & to see a puzzle heavy game inspired by this is an appealing combination. His creative machinations feature strongly in
as does the Renaissance era decal that fill each location. It’s a very beautiful & immersive game with some highly detailed artistry.
In search of your Master Da Vinci, who has mysteriously gone missing, you explore a number locations throughout his estate, navigating deeper to the inner sanctums as you solve more & more intricate puzzles. Each location generally has a one or two larger puzzles with numerous smaller brain benders interwoven with the larger solution. It works well giving you the feeling you are getting closer even with the larger puzzle still being unlocked.
Movement around the set areas/views is smooth, and rotating screen or performing mechanical actions in each area/view works fluidly 99% of the time. Occasionally, you will click or move something that doesn't work the way you expect & also had some clunkiness with circular movements. Some locations were very dimly lit as well, where I wish there was a gamma/brightness setting in the game to compensate to a degree.
The hint system offers multiple tiers of responses going from basic info to more in-depth which can be unlocked over time. Not an insta-win button, the hints tend not to give too much away initially, but they do minimise the stuck moments. I gave each puzzle a red hot go, but still used some hints to keep progressing sanely. With some hint use, a playthrough may be in the range of 7-10 hours.
With any such game, puzzles that I struggled with could be quite easy for you
, but general speaking the difficulty does vary considerably yet overall progress is fairly easy going. Many puzzles will be straightforward, but others while even using hints, can be infuriatingly vague, time consuming efforts. Sometimes you will be kicking yourself at how obvious a hidden object or solution was that got you stuck. My enjoyment of the puzzles, as a result varied too.
Ones like the Risk-eques domination game seemed a bit illogical, boiler room main puzzles were a bit convoluted & the shield wall which
had me completely confused & sick of moving those cranks around.
Then there were incredibly satisfying ones like the Luna Astro wheel which needed a range of skills to solve, unlocking the globe puzzle in the workshop through multiple different steps & the courtyard statue puzzle which had some well-hidden bits under the surface which I thought were well done. Can see a lot of effort went into their designs & overall they are masterfully done. I also liked using the time dilation device to uncover a puzzle solution from the past
.
has great artwork & puzzle designs, that employ changing combinations of mechanical movement, hidden objects, alternative vision modes & a swag of riddles/codes/sequences that will keep your mind active & thoroughly engaged.

I really wish I could recommend this game, but it doesn't really deliver anything particularly interesting. As almost all reviews, I'll do it in a pros and cons format.
Pros:
-No required subscription model, unlike most other MMORPGs.
-It's in the Elder Scrolls world
-It can be really pretty at times
Cons:
-It's in the Elder Scrolls world (It takes a dump over every single bit of established lore in the games. There is a reason for this in game, but it doesn't excuse the fact that it takes over a decade of lore and make it an uninteresting mess that feels like every other MMORPG lore out there)
-The art style is just uninteresting. Once you see a single set of a certain armor time, you've pretty much seen all of them.
-The combat is boring. It's a tab target MMO disguised as action combat, and it'd work better not lying about what it is. The fake action combat comes off as repetetive and clunky.
-The story is dull
-Microtransactions in this game which costs money to play in the first place. It also has a subscription model to give you items from the in-game store. It's ridiculous how microtransaction filled the game is. Oh yeah, can't forget, it's got lootboxes as well.
Conclusion:
It's not a horrible game. It's just *incredibly* boring. If you want to play another WoW clone, you'll probably enjoy this game. However, if you didn't enjoy games like Star Wars: The Old Republic, you will most likely not enjoy it. It doesn't offer anything new, and the microtransactions are absolutely awful.

Hands down the best PVP in the entire series. Period.
Dark Souls 1 PVP was only good, and had imagined depth because of all the bugs that were being exploited by the meta.
Dark Souls 2 PVP had depth from the start, by design not by chance like DS1. Great covenants and rewards, great invasions, great co-op system. Everything about the online option of this game just feels great.
Dark Souls 3. Well lets say that this game should have been a sequel to DS2 rather than being Bloodborne 1.5 lite. Dark Souls 3 and Bloodborne only served to prove that Hidetaka Miyazaki and the A Team have no clue how PVP should function, or what makes it fun. There is a reason these two games were dead as fūck only a few months with content creators trickling out content at best, meanwhile DS2 was strong all the way up until the release of DS3.
By choosing to use the Bloodborne over Dark Souls 2 for the Dark Souls 3 system they:
1. Stripped out everything that made the online covenants worth a fūck. The rewards are all garbage too.
2. Added the arena in as an afterthought within a cut-down short DLC (Andariel) with NO REWARDS, not even a fūcking glowing AURA. Whereas Dark Souls 2 had two arenas for Brotherhood of Blood and Blue Sentinels on launch day.
3. Poise in pvp, the A Team and Miyazaki chose not to add Poise to DS2, this is due to Bloodborne 100%, and then claimed it was "working as intented" when the fans backlashed against it. They added it in a patch (only during hyperarmor swings, and it only improves hyperarmor.) only after like a year after the game's release, and only after vitriol and memes made such a mockery of them they were forced to change it.This is an example to show that these developers don't know what the fūck they are doing, or what the fans want.
4. Like the Bloodborne system they absolutely destroyed invasions in DS3. You can invade almost anywhere unlike Bloodborne, but everything else that made this game bad stayed. (With the exception of passwords, which was a good quality of life change from the Nameless Ring.) You have an auto-summon covenant that summons two different covenants (Blue Sentinels and Darkmoon Blades.) Having two covenants do the exact same thing, only to congest both of them and make it take HOURS to get summoned (unless you are extremely low SL) was a brain-dead decision. They recently "fixed" it so that now every time you are invaded with way of blue equipped, you instantly get 2 blue phantoms, and infinite ones after that. This made invasions basically impossible unless you are a god with hundreds or almost thousands of hours in the game (like me) and are willing to try so hard to kill that host that you will be sweating on your gamepad trying to thread the needble between an endless torrent of R1 spammers. 2 Blues, up to 3 whites and oh yeah I forgot to mention your health is gimped by 30% while the host is buffed 30%. Thanks Myazaki, that's what makes invasions fun. Complete morons. This goes to show you that the greatness of Dark Souls 1 was purely by chance and not from real skill or insight from the "god" Miyazaki.
5. Weapons in the left hand were a staple of Dark Souls 2, and many of them were designed specifically to be used like this, whereas there’s only about 2 in DS3 to my knowledge (Rapier and Handmaid’s Dagger) which gave you and extremely high amount of variety and versatility to any build.
6.The variation of viable builds in this game also far exceeds Dark Souls 3 or Bloodborne for that matter. Even magic is far more useful in this game especially in pvp.at launch. DS3 had a few useful dark pyromancies.
Dark Souls 2 is the true Dark Souls experience, especially for everything online. The only reason that Dark Souls 3 is such a garbage game is because of the massive backlash of fanboys over Dark Souls 2 on it's release. It did have it’s problems, to be sure but because of this the publishers pressured From Software away from those design decisions and instead chose Bloodborne mechanics over Dark Souls 2. This made them steer clear of ANY designs from Dark Souls 2, including those that were carried over from Dark Souls 1, and is why we got a thoroughly disappointing third sequel.
A lot of those problems in Dark Souls 2 have also been hashed out with the SotFS release of the game, which most of these vitriolic fanboys never even finished one new game cycle, let alone the improved SotFS experience, and the online component is even better.
In Dark Souls 3 and Bloodborne, PVP is an afterthought, in Dark Souls 2 PVP is the main point and focus, and it’s obvious where the development priorities were in these games.

I never left a review because, well, everyone else who likes Dark Souls games disagrees with me so meh. I decided today to do it because it's been ages and the Souls series finally ended. Dark Souls 2 was my second game in the series but I played only a little Demon Souls first. I didn't like Demon Souls but thought the combat might have improved, so I picked up Dark Souls 2. I had no expectations excepting that I wanted it to be better than my experience in Demon Souls. Well, it was, and I ended up getting through the first quarter of the game in a few hours. I took the game slowly and instead of learning the game, reflexively dodged everything. Seemed to work. Found out about this neat stat called Adaptability, but leveled Strength and Dexterity instead so I could use that cool Drangleic Greatsword. Used it with a shield, but spent most of my time two handing. I didn't even know magic existed (that I could use) for the whole playthrough, but I did find this cool Moonlight Greatsword thingamagig. Anyways, beat the game in about four days, then looked up stuff about it. Found out I missed a bunch of NPC questlines.
Good to know.
That stat I thought was cool actually would have made my dodges better.
Good to know.
Magic exists and destroys the world.
Good to know.
Found out there's such thing as an item description beyond the little box you see normally.
Good to know.
Found out that stats had soft and hardcaps.
Good to know.
Found out that there was no DLC left, but that the game gets harder if I accept the new journey option at the end.
Good to know.
Then I beat the game 12 more times (which took about 300 more hours and a great deal more deaths than my first playthrough), discovered PvP, and discovered Co-op. Until Dark Souls 3, I played this game in PvP and Co-op with people over and over, and even hit the level cap. Once I'd finally put it down for good, I said to myself, "That was a good experience," and that was it.
Pros of the game:
+Combat is pretty fluid actually.
+Dodging can save you from basically anything if timed correctly.
+PvP is long but very engaging.
+Once you've mastered a boss, you can beat it with some rediculous challenges in effect (beat a giant hunk of demonic blue metal with a wooden ladle)
+Magic is varied and fun to use.
+The world is interesting.
+The story is told in small short stories for item descriptions, and you have to put it together yourself.
+Most of the NPCs aren't ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s.
+The DLC content available now contains some of the best fights I've had in any Souls game.
+A good variety of armor sets that can mix and match while still looking fantastic.
+Dual wielding weapons completely changes their movesets with the proper stat investment.
+Upgrade materials for weapons can be farmed indefinitely, meaning you can have as many fully upgraded weapons as you want.
Cons:
-Adaptability is a stat. Originally I liked the idea of being able to increase my rolling ability, but then I realized it probably made my life a lot harder than it should have. Plus for PvP, there's a meta level and Adaptability steals away precious damage, health, or stamina.
-Only a few rings are useful. In PvP, you're basically required to wear the stone ring and one health ring. In the main game, your rings are only useful in certain situations largely, with the exceptions of stat-buffing rings (like health, stamina, or chiefly equip load).
-Durability drains a bit too fast. In some areas it's very noticeable (for design of course, but still).
-Magic is too overpowered to play the game with fairly.
-Soul Memory makes matchmaking difficult(semi-impossible actually). At this time, the game's basically dead anyways, so that matters a lot more.
-Some hitboxes are a bit... meh. Certain enemies can hit you from behind them, or grab you from too far away. It's not that bad compared to some other souls games, but still.
-There isn't much replay value. The most you have to incentivise you to replay is NG+, but after that it doesn't change excepting in difficulty. Once you hit NG+7, the game is unchanging.
-There wasn't much you could do to multiclass and still do effective damage like purely specialized builds could.
-Damaging miracles are largely a joke with a few exceptions. Always inferior to other spells.
-Respeccing was mostly limited. You could farm a special item to advance a particular area to the next NG to respawn items, but that was it and it was really tedious.
-The softban system (I don't know if it's still the same) goes crazy and bans people in waves. Since launch it was improved, but while it does get the cheaters, it can take other people down with them if certain items exist in your game because they were dropped, or sometimes just being in the world with a cheater.
-Soul Memory again. The only way to stop this from going up is to not gain souls with a special ring (this was made available with the re-release updates). Other than that, it's way too easy to completely leave the area of playability with friends or just people your level in general. Especially if you die carrying a lot of souls.
-The DLCs are not scaled at all with the rest of the game. They are designed on about NG+2 stats for the normal game, so they're past end game difficult. I like a challenging game, but some enemies basically one shot you if you make any mistake, which sucked.
That's about it. I probably missed some stuff, and I tried not to spoil, but I think I can honestly recommend the game to people who like action RPGs. There's a lot of hate for this game, but I think it was designed very well and I enjoyed all 3000+ hours I have on it.

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

I heard that this game was like The Room, and yeah, it pretty much is.  It's a 3D puzzler, and if you've played The Room games, you pretty much know exactly what you're getting:   You have an open area with things that aren't explained, and you play with them until inventory items pop out that help you make the next thing (or the next function of the current thing) work.  Sometimes there are hidden inventory items or things to find.   Repeat until you open up the way to the next area.
It took me ~8 hours to complete the game, although I had some AFK moments in there, and I found the puzzles mostly entertaining, with only a few instances of "hunt the hotspot".  (But be aware, there are a few of those places.)
There were only three things that really frustrated me about this game.  The first was a lack of a mouse invert option, which got patched in literally as I was writing this review.   The second was a lack of gamma slider.  The game is way too dark in places that it shouldn't be.  The last is this genre's obsession with limited mobility.  I know there's supposed to be an "on rails" feel, but the sheer arbitrariness of when I could look around and when I couldn't, and the degree of that mobility... let's just say I might have said more a few non-family-friendly words.
Overall, I'd recommend this game for puzzle enthusiasts.  $20 might be a little steep, depending on your budget, but I probably got at least a solid 7 hours of pretty decent fun out of it, which is OK for what I'll spend on a game.  If money is tight for you, wait for a sale.

DotP 2012 is a huge step up from the previous failure "Duel of the Planeswalkers" (2009) which was a terrible direct port from XBL. While much has been fixed from 2009's release, with improved graphics, UI, and controls, DotP 2012 still struggles to properly emulate the actual Magic: The Gathering card game. The devs are so bent on keeping the players from editing their own decks that they purposefully include simplistic and poorly designed decks. Many decks are binary with boring win conditions and are missing their color's most basic traits, with unlocks only adding bigger numbers and not wider options. However, compared to DotP 2013 and 2014, I think overall this has the best decks. Besides the boring deck design, the real problem with the decks is the unlock system: although you only have to unlock 20 cards total and multiple can be unlocked at once, they lock you out of all the best cards. As you get deeper into the campaign, you are basically forced to continue using one deck, backtrack (or play MP) to "grind" to unlock more, or pay to unlock a deck. This problem is most visible in the Revenge campaign, where your opponents have every card unlocked in every duel.
So what makes DotP 2012 worth picking up? It has the best game modes out of the three numbered releases; Archenemy is great fun because of the wildly powerful effects of the Archenemy's deck, even just with (or against!) AI. With all the expansion decks, 2012 also has the most decks available at 19 total. My favorite are Dark Heavens (B/W angels & tokens) and Ancient Depths (G/U mana ramp & eldrazi). Despite the multiplayer bugs and lag issues, I think this is the best DotP game available and is the best intro to MTG for new players.

I waited awhile to get this game but I am glad I did get it. I was absolutely enamored with Bastion and heard good things about this one by the same people.
Straight into the game you are greeted by a fantastic soundtrack, the one thing you always hear about when someone mentions the game. The audio is a good mood setter for the current level and generally keeps pace with what is going on.
The art is as beautiful as the soundtrack. I've never been that picky with graphics but this still looked really good with smooth animations.
The gameplay, being the most important factor usually, is something I didn't expect to love as much as I did. The combat is done through a mix of real time fighting and time frozen turn planning. You get a special ability that lets you use a certain number of moves based on point values and then you have to wait for the cooldown. You could probably make your way through the game without ever using the special turn planning, or you could make your custom build based on getting that special ability to recover faster. That brings me to the custom build part I just mentioned, it doesn't force you to use set skills or even restrict you with classes. You are able to mix and match a variety of functions to make your own way of fighting, and I rarely kept the same combination for more than a few fights because in order to get more of the lore you have to try out all the combinations. Even without that incentive I found it much more fun to mix things up than stick with the combination I found to be the best.
Overall I put somewhere around 20 hours into a game that costs 20 dollars when not on sale. Definitely worth the price whether on sale or not and a fun game to play. I look forward to what the developers come up with next.

Review for "Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs" (PC):------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------I don't really think that this game was all that bad. For most people who dissagree with me, fell free to click the not helpful button right now, but this is just my appinion, alright?
Anyways, on to the review:
So please note that this is almost NOTHING at all like "Amnesia: The Dark Descent".
Missing features that I've noticed:
-Tinder Boxes
-Oil (witch obviously means that you're lantern will NEVER run out)
-Sanity
-You're freaking inventory!
-Hiding spots
I think it would still be recognized as an Amnesia game, but I really would've liked to see those things from TDD in this game.
I've played thru the game for start to finish, and hear are the pros and cons (and pro-cons) about this game that I would like to put down on the table:
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------PROS::
-Some suspenful and creepy survival parts in the game
-Neat story
-Atmosphere is decent
-Smooth controls
-Sountrack and voice acting is pretty good!
-I didn't need to look up any walkthroughs at all, but the game's puzzles are still okay
-Temporary sale (85% off!)
PRO-CONS::
-No hiding spots, but I haven't really needed any in the game for the most part
-Lantern doesn't run out
-Kinda few monster encounters
-Graphics are alittle bit dated
CONS::
-Some glitches here and there (and a game breaking one) encountered in my playthrough
-No sanity level
-Some of the paintings in the game are just plain un-nessesary
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
So, over all, a pretty good survival horror experience. Like I said before, I don't really think it was all that bad. Surely not the best horror/puzzle game I've ever played, and definitly not as good as TDD, but I think it was still worth my time and money. Try getting it when it's on sale, though.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Final verdict for "Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs" (PC):

describes itself as a horror game, but rarely provoked more than a minor sense of unease.  And I'm generally quite easy to scare, so that's a bad thing.  But even if I ignore that and treat the game as an environmental interactive narrative, it still has some serious problems.
Most damning of all is that I basically spent the last hour of the game wishing it would
.  Too many moments when the game thinks it is being profound when it isn't.  Too much purple prose.  A main character who was irritatingly stupid; I figured out that we
very early on, and there are plenty of documents you can find that all but confirm it, but it's only about 10 minutes before the end that the protagonist manages to see the obvious.  Too many points in the game where I completed puzzles without understanding what I was doing.  Too many other puzzles that were just too easy.  And, at the end, too many points where you are forced to move slowly or the environment suddenly drastically changes.  It's not a long game, but it felt it by the end.
There were a few things I liked.  The music was good, and well-used.  The environment in the first two-thirds of the game were well-designed, doing an excellent job to maintain suspension of disbelief and make the factory seem real.  It's part of why I was so disappointed when the internal consistency seemed to disappear late on.  Also, the nature of the primary antagonist was kind of clever, though I actually had to look this up as it was poorly presented in-game.
But these good points aren't enough.  I just can't recommend any game that bored me as much as this one.
