First off, let me clear the air. Yes, there are performance issues with RealMyst on Windows 7/8. When I first ran it, it was very choppy in certain parts, and crashed every 5 minutes or so. I tried a few solutions online, but none of them seemed to work. However, after setting the game to run as an Administrator and in Windows XP Compatibility mode it runs smoothly, and without any crashes. There is no guarantee that this will work, but it seems to solve the issue for most people.
As for the game itself, it is the same old Myst that you know and love, only taking the time to add a small (but cool) age at the end of the game, and to update the graphics. The new graphics on highest settings look similar to the screenshots, though it is worth noting that you can add anti-aliasing and resolutions at least up to 1366x768. They add a refreshing coat of paint to the outdated visuals of the original, making it more than playable even in this day and age. Also, the new control scheme is pretty nice, allowing you to mouse and keyboard, though I preferred using just the mouse. Granted, the controls aren't perfect, but they aren't horrendous either.
Now would I recommend this over RealMyst Masterpiece Edition? I only own this edition, so take my opinion with a grain of salt. However, it seems to me that the Masterpiece Edition's graphics jumble and confuse things more than they ought to. Watching videos of the Masterpiece Edition makes it seem like certain elements are harder to see, but that of course is up to personal taste and perception. It seems to me that this version is a fine version of Myst, and it's price is hard to beat. I don't know that the Masterpiece Edition's graphics are worth the extra $12.
Bottom Line: If you feel like replaying Myst, or want to experience it for the first time, I think this game is the one for you.

I don't understand this game. From what I can gather it follows a man called Mandus who writes notes like he's Dr Suess or something and scatters them everywhere. Anyways, Mandus at some point sees the two world wars in his sons future and decides to kill his sons to save them from it (and possibly his wife? not sure but she's dead anyway). Then he hatches a big plan to build a machine that will turn humans into pig hybrids (or pigs into human hybrids?) so on the last night of the century they can go out kill everyone thus saving the world from the world wars? But at some point he has a change of heart and decides to sabotage his own diety-like machine. Then he gets Amnesia? (not sure how that happened but it did, I don't think it's ever explained) and the machine tricks him into hatching his own plan anyway. Also, why are there kids toys scattered everywhere if they died years previously? And are we expected to believe that Mandus built this machine himself? Maybe there is something I missed?
Anyway. This game seems to take itself very seriously and the solid production shows it. I found no bugs and the graphics and audio work shone. Regretfully, when compared to Amnesia Dark Descent, this game isn't as good. The scares aren't really there, the pig monsters aren't that scary. Later in the game you encounter some electricity being which freaked me a bit but the encounters were too short and too close to the end. The puzzles are very simple. In fact, they shouldn't really be called puzzles. And the plot is just.... meh. There's too many questions in my head. Like such.
Why was the water splashing monster there out of The Dark Descent? In the sewer levels when you're not even meant to go in the water, it's down there splashing away. Or is that a drowning pig monster? I read something about Mandus being able to keep things in a constant state of dying or something, but either way, it made no sense.
Why were there screams and moans down there? In the Dark Descent, you're in a giant castle, people are getting tortured, it's grim times. Other than the pigs, there was nothing but machines in the Mandus complex. Using those sounds made no sense in my mind.
WHY THE HELL WERE THERE KIDS TOYS EVERYWHERE? For foreshadowing? Bit weak if you ask me.
Why and how did Mandus get amnesia? Who was closing the door upon the game's start if it was all the machine's doing? Who was in that coffin in the end? (possibly his wife at a guess?) I got more sense out of Bioshock upon my first play and that has a much more complex plot. What am I missing?
Anyway, I do recommend this game. It was a fun play and deffo not a bad game. Just when pitted against Amnesia: The Dark Descent, it doesn't favour well. The Dark Descent has a better plot, better scares and better puzzles.

I recommend this game on sale. I feel like $20 is a little steep for what it actually is. I'd prefer a $14.99 price point.
Is this game good? Yes! Absolutely I enjoyed it and even cried a little at the end.
Is it as good as Dark Descent? Meh, not really.
There were some things that I immediately noticed were very different from the first title:
1. There were a LOT less interactable objects/rooms to explore. I appreciate that it saves a bit of time by not having to check every single chair or cabinet in a room, but I really enjoy exploring. The mansion is gorgeous and detailed, but I really would have liked to have more places to snoop around.
2. There was this terrible blue fog everywhere I went. Some folks were able to get used to it and some even preferred it(scandalous!). I hated it because I felt like it took a lot of the horror away since it was really distracting. I couldn't see much through it and it gave me a horrible headache. Like the insanity effects that made me batty in the first game, this also has a toggle(color grading)!! I promptly shut it off and the game was leaps and bounds more scary.
3.
4. There is no more inventory. So there are no matches, health potions, or keys/items to collect. That made me a little sad. For the same reason as I stated in #1-- I love to explore and if there is nothing to collect(besides notes), then there is no reason to look anywhere.
As far as the story is concerned, I really didn't like it as much as I liked the first story. It was nice that they mentioned the orbs and had a couple letters from Daniel, but I was hoping for more of a connection to the first story(especially since they mentioed the orbs). That being said, it was still a good story. I just liked the other better. :P
The puzzled were all incredibly easy and the only time I had a hard time was when I go a little lost in a big room where everything looked the same. I ended up walking in frustrated circles for about 15 minutes before I noticed that there was a little red light pointing to a path(haha).
I wasn't a fan of how slowly I seemed to walk everywhere. It felt like it was needlessly padding my play time. You can run in several parts of the game, but there are a lot of places where it forces you to go so slow that you think that your shift kep is broken. I don't mind being slowed down for audio recordings or memories. Those are fine. There were actual areas where it made no sense to walk so slow and yet something was still slowing me down. Maybe it was a bug?
All in all, this is a solid game that deserves at least a once through. The first one is definitely better as it was so amazing that it is simply a tough act to follow.

This review is for the realMYST version and not the game Myst in general, that game is recommended many times over for any fan of adventure games.
Graphics:
This game is a full 3D remake of the original, with much better graphics that the original and I had it running in full 1080p resolution.  Some people have complained about some texture issues, but I haven't noticed it, but it is possible that there is more graphics quality inconsistency than the original, but everything is still better than the original.  I found that having fluid movement helped my immersion of the game.
Controls:
Some people have complained about the game's controls, personally I found them better than the original.  You can adjust several control settings such as mouse speed and dead zone size in the options to suit your needs.  I found the game easier to play when using just the mouse and ignoring the keyboard, left clicking to move forwards.
Compatibility:
Be aware that some people have had some compatibility issues with the game; you should be able to get the game running, except maybe with some bugs.  Expect more issues if you have a 64bit system.  I personally ran the game with Windows XP SP3 32bit and the game ran perfectly for me, so if you can fall back to an XP system, that will work for you. I will update the review when I upgrade to Windows 10 64bit.
Recommendation:
I would recommend this version of Myst to any newcomer of the series.  The only issue is that it doesn't cater to nostalgia as much as the original version, so if you are playing the game purely for a nostalgia trip; you might prefer the Myst Masterpiece Edition.

I ran realMyst on:
- Win 8.1 64bit
- Intel Core i7-4710HQ CPU @ 2.50GHz
- GeForce GTX 980M
- 16.0 GB RAM
- compatibility mode set to Win XP SP3
- running as an administrator
The original Myst came out when I was a teenager. I loved it then and devoured not only the game and its sequels but also the novels and the soundtracks.
Now, many years later, I've revisited the island. realMyst ran well for me: no crashes or other issues on my modern hardware. Sometimes I saw some artifacting around the edge of the screen but this was minor. Navigation and clicking was a bit wonky at times but not too bad for what I expected. My only real complaints are that the Steam overlay never worked, I couldn't take any screenshots with either the Steam function nor the Print Screen key, and alt-tabbing was a bit finnicky.
The game shows its age texture-wise (I will probably buy realMyst: Masterpiece Edition for the updated textures later) but content-wise it still held together well. It's been long enough that I didn't really remember the puzzles (was even stumped a few times despite knowing I should know the answer) and even the content of the remaining journals in the library was only partially familiar.
The two sons evoke the right kind of emotional response—Achenar especially. For a game that isn't violent or frightening, it nevertheless has its disturbing moments, and this is perhaps made more potent because of the extra freedom of movement to get up close. There's a curtain in one room, and given the other paraphranalia present...I couldn't help but wonder...what's hidden behind that curtain...? Certainly not a window. And then I decided I didn't want to know.
I enjoyed what to me seems to be enhancements from the original. Stumbling across the grave marker for Ti'ana in particular was an "oh wow" moment that has me wanting to reach for the books again. The bats in one of the underground tunnels were a nice touch too. Discovering the additional content after the original "desired" ending was a real surprise and quite satisfying.
Definitely recommended.

For the years I've owned this game and neglected to do a review of it, I finally have made up my mind on this game.
Let's start at the strongest, the gameplay. Gameplay consists of looting for currency and weaponry to improve in combat in order to level up to use stronger weaponry, of which there are more than 17.75 million guns, the world record set by the original borderlands. As astounding as that sounds, I must first clarify that there are multiple rarities of guns. In order from lowest to highest, common, uncommon, rare, very rare, E-tech, and legendary. With each tier the guns get stronger but also lose uniqueness. A common rarity shotgun from a manufacturer could have 0.5 million different variations, but a legendary shotgun of the same manufacturer might only 12 or 20. On top of all these weapons, you have shields, class mods, relics, and grenade mods and a cast of 4 characters, 6 with DLC each with unique and arguably fun abilities from cloaking, to locking down an enemy in the air, to going full berserk, and with so many skill trees, a total of 18 with 2 being able to be utilised by any one character, it is pretty much impossible to not find a playstyle that suits you. Gunplay is extremely satisfying. Bullets feel like they impact and critical hits are extremely satisfying with bright red text displaying the wonderful shot. Only issue is that enemy AI is fairly basic and that enemies only become bullet sponges with few added traits or abilities as difficulty increases.
Of the manufacturers, there's Bandit, Dahl, Hyperion, Maliwan, Jakobs, Vladof, Torgue, and Tediore, each with their unique strengths and weaknesses, and of the elements there's incendiary, shock, corrosive, explosive, and the unique slag which when inflicted will mark enemies for death, increasing damage taken from non-slag weapons by double.
The variety in weaponry aswell as unique pieces of equipment makes for a game that promotes usage of multiple different weapons and playstyles. In theory this works wonders as to have many playstyles each based on unique skill trees and equipment, but in execution the first 2 playthroughs of the story slowly getting more difficult over time leads you to use specific variants of unique weapons acquired from endless farming in order to be powerful enough to progress. At some point you may find yourself in a tough spot, and unless you're particularly good at combat or got lucky with loot drops, you may find youself needing to farm a boss for up to an hour for loot that will help you progress.
The story is decent with some intrigue here and there mostly found in side-quests. There's a good bit of exposition with even the second NPC you meet apologizing for running his mouth on. Characters have their moments especially when interacting with eachother, but I rarely found them interesting. Most characters just don't feel like their personality, instead feeling like personality traits mashed together with nothing to show of it. Admittedly, I haven't played the previous game to completion so I know I'm missing integral parts of their character there, but if you're coming into the franchise on this game like I did, you may feel the same. Side quests will explore little tid-bits of information such as character relationships. Something that you somewhat suspected before could be opened in a whole new light for you. Unfortunately there's a lot of waiting for the story. Cutscenes are unskippable and there are many points where you simply cannot move on without watching something happen first. On subsequent playthroughs it starts to become a trudge.
It also doesn't help that the visuals are boring. While unique due to the incorporation of cel-shading, most environments have muddy color schemes. From endless deserts, to endless tundras, as nice as it is for the landscapes to be as big as they are, they simply do not look visually appealing. It's worth noting that one thing in particular, the rakk hive, (both Roscoe from the Scarlett DLC and the one I managed to find buried in Torgues DLC) made me want to spew into a bucket.
I nearly forgot music. Most of it is forgetable, and the only bit I can remember is a bit of guitar strumming in one of the tracks. I have absolutely no idea which track either. I wanna say it's the desert track, but I also wanna say it's the tundra track. I feel as engaged without any music as I do with it.
I do have 7 of the DLC's which only one I find more satisfying than the main campaign, that being Tiny Tina's Assault on Dragon Keep. The other three campaign DLC's are boring just like the normal game and the Ultimate Vault Hunter pack is simply an extension of the main game being another 11 levels and a new increased difficulty. The final 2 DLC's are characters which only the Mechromancer I deem fun enough to do an entirely new playthrough of. The other DLC's I cannot speak for as I have not experienced them.
As much as I love the game just for the combat and funny moments, it has too much going against it for me to consider it a good game. Story gets boring quick, visuals are muddy and may rarely disgust, music had nothing going for it, and eventually it all just slows down becoming a grind towards the end of the second playthrough.

After Dark Souls changed my life in June of 2016, my room mate, seeing me bored and broke, bought me Dark Souls II: Scholar of the First Sin for Xbox One. Much of my feelings about that game are laid out in this review, but this is specifically a review for the vanilla version.
I bought this very much on purpose. Scholar of the First Sin is, I found out after starting it, a sort of "ROM hack" version of Dark Souls II. Enemy placement and in some cases level structure had been rearranged (and the graphics cranked up to 11) in response to fan concerns about it being too easy. Thing is, in Scholar, a lot of that game was almost too hard. At least the opening hours. DSII has some weird design choices that really punish the early-game player, and Scholar amplified those with more and harsher enemies. That said, once you clear the hurdle and your stats start to get more in-step with where you want them (I still resent having to put points into Adaptability and Vitality), things start to open up and, if you haven't abandoned the game yet and run off to join the legion of "DSII sucks" players, you'll find a game that is very fun and special in its own right.
Sort of how The Legend of Zelda: Link's Awakening was an acid trip of experimentation in storytelling and game design in a mostly predictable series, Dark Souls II does something similar in a dreamlike, bizarre new kingdom. I really grew to appreciate that, even if the game didn't have the oppressive majesty and foreboding of its predecessor. There are some good design ideas here too that were not in DS1 and some of those were even backpedaled on for DSIII, which is kind of insane...
But if you like Dark Souls, you should play DSII, either Vanilla or Scholar. Vanilla's a touch too easy, Scholar is difficult but not always in smart ways...but they're both good, valuable experiences that deserve to be played. No, it's not Dark Souls 1. But yes, it is still a great game. Don't skip it just because some curmudgeons want each Dark Souls game to be the same as the last. Give it a shot.

realMYST is a remake of the original game Myst, re-rendering the entire environment in 3D and allowing for more normal FPS controls. For a game originally released in 1993, it actually looks and plays quite well - it will require a little bit of work (including one patch) in order to play properly on modern machines (the QT plugin isn't correct) so don't assume it will be plug-and-play.
Controls are a little floaty, and the puzzles are not changed at all from the original game, so people who have played Myst before won't find anything all that compelling about playing through again. For people who are on their first play through but don't want to pay for the Masterpiece edition, this may be more to their liking (Channelwood, in particular, is a lot less obtuse when you're actually walking around).
Beyond that....it's Myst. It's a very good point and click adventure game that manages to balance being obtuse without being unfair. Worth a playthrough in some form, at the very least.

I'm a real hardcore Myst fan. Have read all the books, got the OST CDs and played all the games mulitple times (Except Uru.. hated that one), so I'm coming at RealMyst as someone very passionate about the games as well as the genre.  It had been a while since I last tackled Myst, so the puzzles were vaguely familiar, but not easy to solve: e.g. I knew the way to solve the generator puzzle on Myst, but not the specific response.
The translation to full 3D brings this game back to absolutely fresh. It was great to be able to experience this all over again from a completely new perspective.    I'd say that many of the puzzles were a lot easier thanks to the ability to spin around and see the status of switches and pipes without having to step-move-turn-step-etc  to see.
The graphics are all quite rudimentary for a 3d game - polygons as well as shading and fogging artefacts show up a lot, reminding you that this is quite an old game.   Saying that, the translation to full 3D has been done in a really sympathetic way:  the ages all feel the way they used to, and the addition of atmospheric effects, variable lighting, day/night cycles and so on really adds that "well loved" feel to this remake.  The world feels exactly the same, basically, which is a remarkable achievement considering the time span between the original and remake, the different teams and technologies.
The new team has added in some new content as well, including a new "Age" which helps to link to the next game, Riven.  There's a nod to "Ti'Ana" from one of the books, and other small additions here and there.  Very nicely done.
The music and sounds have been lovingly ported over.  The music is exactly as I remember it, and the videos in the books look to be direct copies of the original video files: No upscaling or re-taping has been done, so the grainy feel of the books is perfect.
The game plays through virtually seamlessly (see Crashing notes below).  The ability to only move forwards and backwards and spin is probably some way to make it 'feel' more like the original, so you gently slide into the "myst groove" as you move through the world.
OK, so the game itself has clearly been remade by a team dedicated to the faithfulness of the original.. But how did they do technology-wise? Well if you're playing this on a modern PC (windows Vista or above) you're gonna run into problems.     The game really needs to run as administrator in XP compatibility mode to reduce the number of CTDs.  Secondly, the format of the videos in the books is the exact same "Indeo v5" that was used in the original game, so I'm guessing the video files are the self-same video files!   Unfortunately Steam doesn't install Indeo.  I had to hunt about to find an appropriate install. The "official" ones didn't install properly, so ended up going to cucusoft to get theirs... Once that was done, the book videos started to play, and I didn't get the wierd "1FPS" bug when I was facing towards the "library".
Once that was all sorted, the game crashed on me about 5 times during the playthrough, so I advise saving every 10 minutes or so.  Set an alarm clock or something to remind you... Once I played for about an hour and it crashed.. not too pleased.
Getting to the end was a real joy.  Totally enjoyed the addition of "Rime", but it confused the heck out of me when the game didn't "End", I was just left at (basically) a dead end.  This is intentional, and Even Atrus says that's what I should do, so I can't be too gripey, but it was a bit "hunh?".
This is a fantastic remake. Anyone who enjoyed the original should get this and re-enjoy it all over again.  It doesn't take long to finish.  Just remember: save often!  Two-thumbs-up!

Magic: The Gathering is a super complex card game that is not for the faint of heart. On the surface it seems intuitive enough because the cards tell you exactly what they do, but once you start playing, the myriad of microscopic details start unraveling and it ends up becoming an exponential learning tree. Not only do the obvious abilities seem overwhelming, but there are so many hidden caveats of what you can play and when you can play them. The game continuously makes me feel like a novice by making me say "I didn't know it worked like that." Things just aren't obvious enough plus the weak tutorial isn't much help.
And don't get me started on the impossible puzzles they throw at you with zero explanation on new card usage or expecting you to know how the AI is going to respond to gift card selections. There is one puzzle I still don't get where you block three attackers that get sacrificed before the block occurs, yet the attackers are still blocked? WTF is that?
I seriously don't know how people can play this game in real life with real cards because of the massive amount of minute details that need to be tracked and managed. You seriously have to combine a geekish life of masturbation and blow up dolls with the organization skills of a librarian. Hopefully the computer version has saved some lost souls from that path.
Is it hard? Yes. Is it fun? Yes. Is it my type of game? No, but I do like the fact that it feels like a challenging puzzle game and it keeps me on my toes. There's lots of experimentation, but I expect after achieving some level of proficiency, it will be time to move on to the next game.

It's as good an adaptation of Magic as you can get without unrestricted deckbuilding. Much cheaper than the real thing too.  All of the decks are well-designed and fun to play, with Kiora Atua's (Ancient Depths) being my standout favorite.  Archenemy mode is overwhelming at first, but it grew on me after a while—keep in mind your AI allies use your personalized versions of the decks, so it's a great incentive to play them all to unlock cards.
It's definitely nowhere near the same as playing MTG in the old days, but if you want to ressurect a bit of the thrill, it's worth the dough.

After Dark Souls changed my life in June of 2016, my room mate, seeing me bored and broke, bought me Dark Souls II: Scholar of the First Sin for Xbox One. Much of my feelings about that game are laid out in this review, but this is specifically a review for the vanilla version.
I bought this very much on purpose. Scholar of the First Sin is, I found out after starting it, a sort of "ROM hack" version of Dark Souls II. Enemy placement and in some cases level structure had been rearranged (and the graphics cranked up to 11) in response to fan concerns about it being too easy. Thing is, in Scholar, a lot of that game was almost too hard. At least the opening hours. DSII has some weird design choices that really punish the early-game player, and Scholar amplified those with more and harsher enemies. That said, once you clear the hurdle and your stats start to get more in-step with where you want them (I still resent having to put points into Adaptability and Vitality), things start to open up and, if you haven't abandoned the game yet and run off to join the legion of "DSII sucks" players, you'll find a game that is very fun and special in its own right.
Sort of how The Legend of Zelda: Link's Awakening was an acid trip of experimentation in storytelling and game design in a mostly predictable series, Dark Souls II does something similar in a dreamlike, bizarre new kingdom. I really grew to appreciate that, even if the game didn't have the oppressive majesty and foreboding of its predecessor. There are some good design ideas here too that were not in DS1 and some of those were even backpedaled on for DSIII, which is kind of insane...
But if you like Dark Souls, you should play DSII, either Vanilla or Scholar. Vanilla's a touch too easy, Scholar is difficult but not always in smart ways...but they're both good, valuable experiences that deserve to be played. No, it's not Dark Souls 1. But yes, it is still a great game. Don't skip it just because some curmudgeons want each Dark Souls game to be the same as the last. Give it a shot.

Let's go back, Jack, and do it again!  If you liked Amnesia:  The Dark Descent, then, well, it sucks to be you, because most of the things to really like about it were removed or watered down in Amnesia, Part II, "That's a lot of machine, all right!"  Yes, I know, I'm giving this a thumbs up, because that's what my numbers say, but I promise you, it's just barely.  And, really, you should play this game, but just barely, so I think it all works out.  OK, so, first, the good.  The sound is fantastic.  While it's a little obvious that they were limited in the sound content they were able to make, we have to give a shout out for outstanding implimentation.  The sound really helps to set the mood, drive the immersion, and it is, quite frankly, more important to the player than what you see, in most cases, and this is something really nice to see in a game, where the expectation is that graphics is at the forefront.  OK, so, yeah, the graphics.  Well, they are ok, and the first few levels are pretty interesting, but it becomes quickly obvious that they only created so many graphical assets and just reused them over and over and over to the point that it becomes distracting from the game.  Yes, we all know how this works, but we need to put SOME limits on it, or it really does start to hamper enjoyment.  Also, the machine parts (where you'll be spending most of the game), become boring quick and just, well, stay that way.  That said, there are some decent effects here and there, but they aren't quite enough to really immerse the player as they should.  This game just isn't scary, and the weak effort on visuals is a big part of why.  "The Dark Decent" did much, much better at this.  But, this is a game that pins itself on the plot, right?  Well, I've got more disappointing news, because the hollow, shallow plot will be fully understood in less than an hour of play, and all of the further reveals will just dully confirm what the player already knows.  The plot's ok, though...certainly better than the vast majority of popular games, but still, you just, well, expect more.  So, well, how does it play?  The challenge just isn't there enough to maintain the tension.  The puzzles are so easy a cave man could solve them, and the monsters just don't harass you or threaten you enough to keep the pressure on.  The player feels as though they are just waltzing through, looking at dark scenary, and solving obvious puzzles among a plot that you already know.  Altogether, this experience just isn't what it should be overall, kind of making me wonder if Chinese Room isn't another one-hit-wonder of the gaming world.  I hope not, though, because there's definitely some major inspiration behind all of this.  They CAN do better;  let's just hope that, in the future, they do.  Then there's a heaping helping of blah, blah, blah, we're British and we like Socialism, blah, blah, blah.  You'll get bored of that pretty quick as well :\  Now, don't get me wrong; it's impressive and interesting any time developers attempt to tackle philosophical issues, but the game goes out of its way to referrence the upcoming horrors of the 20th century, then seems to embrace the ideological force that murdered around 300 million people in the 20th century (where are these peoples' history teachers?).  Then it asks the question, left open ended, sort of, of whether humanity should be able to exist at all (which is great for a horror game, if inconsistent).  That last part (ie, the intellectual absurdity and confusion) is all totally cool with me, though, as crazy artists often create good art, especially when designing works wrapped around insanity and horror.  Thus, again, here's to forgetting this game just like Highlander 2 and a brighter future for Chinese Room:)

Amnesia: A Machine for pigs isn't a bad game, and offers some stunning visuals and nice jump scares, but it suffers heavily from being the follow-up to an excellent game sharing the Amnesia name.
Like its predecessor, A Machine for Pigs focuses around exploring an (almost) abandoned abode of a madman, and dealing with said madman hellish plans. Like the first game, this one is all about solving riddles, avoiding enemies, and thereby advancing through the game.
However, Amnesia: A Machine for pigs abandons several of the important elements that made the first game such a hit, namely the sanity, the inventory and the ressource management. Sadly, the game is poorer for this. The first game always  presents a sadistic choice: do you use your lantern and tinderboxes to light the way, thus reducing sanity loss and making navigation easier, but also risking discovery and running out at crucial points, or do you conserve your items and make the game harder for yourself? In addition to that, hiding requires darkness, and darkness drains your sanity,
Amnesia: A Machine for pigs, give you an electric torch that never runs out, and no torches can be lit. That takes away the effect of exploring. Amnesia: The Dark Descent always rewarded careful exploration, and sometimes it was worth sneaking by a monster to get some additional stuff. In AMfP, there's just no reason to look around safe for maybe one or two additional notes.
Also, the enemies in AMfP aren't all that dangerous or numerous. Since you don't lose sanity, you can keep them in your sight always, and if ned be simply outrun them, in the few areas they actually pose any dangers.
It's still a good game, and maybe I would have viewed it more favourably, but it just pales in comparison to the first game. It certainly has its moments, and the game really nails the creepy vibe that some of these Victorian factories can give of, but it had the pontential for more.

I must note some key features that aren't outright stated:
-Biggest problem is the lack ot total deck construction. Instead you are given an extra 30-card sideboard that is specific to each deck. On the bright side, this forces you to try out decks you might not have considered to begin with, and aren't inclined to make the same deck over and over.
-Be wary of the DLCs and other optional junk. Most just unlock stuff you could already earn in-game. In fact, this was a major problem I had -- once unlocked, you cannot re-lock them. I *wanted* to earn my cards at the end of battle, but that was not available to me since they were all already unlocked.
Overall, I enjoyed it. For the price of a $10 starter deck of cards, you get a reasonable  digital Magic experience. I actually prefer the 1997 Microprose Magic though. I give this an 8/10

Here the TL;DR premptively: This is a decent horror game, but I recommend it largely as an interesting take on your standard Lovecraftian narrative. It's not for everyone, but if you enjoy horror, it's certainly worth a look.
It's easy to be of two minds about Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs; on one hand, it's a densely atmospheric game with a few decent scares and a uniquely Victorian narrative, but on the other hand, it suffers from all of the problems that are so characteristic of its developer, The Chinese Room. In short, I DO recommend playing this title, but opt for purchasing it during a sale.
The plot is intially straightforward enough. English industrialist Mandus has awoken with amnesia (hence the title), and he, at the bequest of a mysterious voice over the telephone, must descend into the depths of an enormous machine situated beneath the streets of London to rescue his questionably absent children. Oh, and pigs are a recurring motif. There are many pigs. Narratively, the plot is LARGELY predictable, treading many of the same beats as Amnesia: The Dark Descent; that is, until the third act. It's impossible to describe several of the narrative beats in the third act that make the game so interesting, so to keep vague,
. It's a shame the game is as short as it is, but I do suppose that means the game doesn't outstay its welcome.
On that note, despite somewhat aged graphics, A Machine for Pigs is a brilliant example of what cohesive art direction and sound design can accomplish. The depths of Mandus's machine are positively oozing with an oppressive atmosphere, and crawling along the steampunk gears and rusty grates can be a chilling experience. HOWEVER, it's worth noting that the game does suffer from a choppy framerate at times, even on a decent PC. I've heard that there's an easy work around for this issue, though I myself I haven't attempted it.
Gameplaywise, A Machine for Pigs is what can be
called a stealth-horror title. The gameplay mostly consists of inventory puzzles interspersed with occassional stealth and chase sequences. However, in typical Chinese Room fashion, interactivity is light. Very little in the environment can be interacted with, and most of the game takes place along a specific, linear path. The experience is enjoyable, but this means that replay value is low and that the more genre-savvy player will be able to anticipate MOST of the narrative beats before they occur.
There's a lot to like about A Machine for Pigs. The third act plays with the cosmic horror genre in a number of interesting ways, the art is lovingly designed (if a tad dark), and the sound design is superb. The game has many problems (In fact, the game has many,
problems.), but in spite of them, this is an journey that fans of the horror genre should consider experiencing.

So let me first state that of the two Amnesia games, this one is, by far, definitely my favorite.  That being said, the arguments made against it are completely understandable.
This game is more of a walking simulator than a horror survival like the first one was.  It doesn't have many puzzles as the first one, the insanity and health mechanics have been pretty much been done away with, and the game doesn't have many scary moments (as in jump-scares and trying to sneak past enemies).  If you're looking for more survival gameplay and puzzles, you won't really find them here.
What it does have, for me at least, is a very disturbing atmosphere/theme, creepy soundtrack, and enticing story.  I find the industrial atmosphere and haunting music of this game more horrifying than the dark castle from the previous game and the story overall just feels like it has a bit more grit and to it.  It's scary, but scary as in an uncomfortable feeling that lingers with you after you quit.  But again, that's my opinion, and most would probably disagree.
If you're a die-hard fan of the first game, want to be scared crazy, and/or don't care for walking simulators, I'd probably advise against getting this one.  If you're not really sure if you want it or not, I'd say wait till it's on sale and then try it.  But if you're not opposed to the different game style, and like the idea of the industrial setting, I'd say go for it.

I've played the 1st and 3rd installment and reviewed the first souls game. I went with melee builds and tested both strenth and dexterity builds. I 100%-ed the achievements. For DS2, I first played a strength character 90% through the game and then - almost at the end - just stopped. It did not really challenge me enough and felt too generic and trying too hard with some BS-moments to create some rage-inducing passages. And there are always other games. ;)
Now I have picked it up again for the sole purpose of 100%-ing it and trying out a hex build. I prefer PvE and detest the circumstance that I can be invaded even if hollowed, unless I burn a human effigy. There is still some online play going on (lol wtf, go do it in DS3 ^^), but it felt rather scarce, both invasions and friendly summon signs.
And FYI: I played it with an XBox 360 Controller, never even tried this stuff with M&KB....especially after the debacle of the first Souls port. xD
Still the solid combat system you know and appreciate. The only feeling I could never quite shake was that there is a slight recuperation phase after you strike or cast a spell before you can dogde again. Maybe I remember it wrong, but it felt like that was not the case in Dark Souls 1. Anyhow, this slight delay freaked me out tremendously and it took some time getting used to it....and quite some deaths, to be honest.
So you have your different strategies: Oneshotting or staggering your enemies before they can jump on you, blocking and waiting for an opening to strike, or nimbly dodging and then doing the attack of your joice.
Also, you now have the option to jump by clicking down your left analog stick instead of pressing b, which made some platforming passages feel smoother for me.
OOOOOOH, and lock-on distance, almost forgot that one: Totally♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off repeatedly! I understand that you don't want to have people in PvP locking on a mile away and blasting the still unwary opponent.....but come on, let me lock onto my enemies from far away on a sunny day at the dragon shrine! Casters beware! This was a recurring frustration for me. Died many times because my camera centered the wrong way while I was circling an enemy and wanted to lock onto said enemy. I don't think git gud applies here, that was just plain PvP-balance bullcrap messing up my PvE-experience. >.<
I guess the graphics are absolutely ok considering the release date of the game and the size of the developer. The game ran well on my machine (better mid-range),
The presenation is nice, FromSoftware/NamcoBandai has definitely not lost their touch for aesthetics and ambience. You will see what I mean once you leave the tutorial area. The different areas are diverse and I really enjoyed the many open areas the 2nd Souls game has.
Most of the times, I liked the level design. The length from bonfire to bonfire is often adequate and there are our beloved shortcuts. But every so often, there are just some passages that reek of tryhard. It felt like a designer was trying to make a point by throwing an almost certain death in your direction. Yes, we get it: Welcome to Dark Souls! ;)
This component gets a little life draining if it happens on your way to a boss. I know the game is supposed to be challenging, but I don't see the fun in running to the boss over and over again - and I mean the sheer distance you have to travel, no matter if there are enemies or not - when, instead, you could let me just take a gander at the boss without making me a marathon runner... But that's just me being demanding.
As you start the game, you can choose different areas to visit first, and in my opinion, this time around, they are all manageable with a fresh character. And for more proficient players, there is even the possibility of skipping a huge portion of the game, which is very handy as I will point out in the OAC section.
In my first playthrough, when the game was just released, I went through the game like a hot knife through butter. I either chose a very powerful build, played very well, or the game was not that challenging. In my second playthrough (new character because I lost my savefile -.-) I played a caster, and that comes with the price of struggle early on in the game. So I can say your experience with this game may vary depending on the build you are going for. If I had to objectively judge the enemy and boss design, I'd say they have a decent variety of attacks and their AI is ok. After some time, you can outplay or outmaneuver almost everything, but there are some a-hole attacks that are hard to dodge. I played a glasscannon up to SL 270 with no point in health, so I should know. ;)
Just like in the first part of the souls series, the bosses are hard and not hard at the same time. By that I mean that they will easily kill you if you are foolish or greedy or slow. If you don't act on their behavior and moveset, you will struggle. But if you are quick on the uptake and are capable of analysing them, then you will be able to run certain areas up to difficulties of NG+20, as I did for certain farming purposes). So rarely, you get hit in the face by RNGesus, but otherwise, it can be a cakewalk, if you chose and/or are able to make it so.

Transistor is a short--approximately six hours if you take your time and do all the challenges, it does however, have a new game plus mechanic--linear RPG, that takes place in a computer simulated city. I won't go into details on the plot, and neither will Transistor. It has a very well developed world, and a fascinating plot, but it will leave it up to the player to deduct the context by studying the environment, and piecing together implications of the dialogue. As such, it's not a good game for casual play, and demands your full attention and immersion. Something it obtains rather well with its flexible, surprisingly complex combat system, amazing soundtrack, beautiful hand-drawn environments, and incredible voice acting. Transistor manages to be intelligent without being pretencious, but that said, the vast majority of your audio will be the monologuing of one character and the background music. While both are stellar, if you prefer two way conversations, or silence, it's something to keep in mind.
However, if plot, music, and writing isn't enough to sell you on a game, Transistor has an interesting skill system where a skill can either be equipped as an active ability, attached as a modifier to another ability, or slotted into your character as a passive effect. This allows for a wide variety of playstyles that can be changed on a whim, and opens up a lot of opporunities to attempt to power-game, or develop specialized gimmicks.
Another interesting aspect is the 'Turn()' command, which allows you to pause the game and queue up chains of movement and abilities, which will be executed at extreme, superhuman speed. However, doing so will lock your skills for a duration based off of the degree of which you used your turn. This allows you to dynamically play Transistor as a real time and turn based game, based off of prefence and situation.
Transistor is a lovely, humble, artistic game that excels at everything it attempts. It has a reasonable asking price, a lovely soundtrack, and equally interesting gameplay. However, if you like sandboxy RPG's with a large cast of characters, this isn't the game for you. Otherwise, I have no quams recommending this lovely game.

I really wanted to get more time on this game before this review but here is what i think of the game so far:
Personally i Used to play Ragnarok Online back in the day, it was my first mmo ever and i had a ton of fun in it, so how this is the spiritual sucessor to RO i had extreme high hopes like everyone who plays or has played this game. I expected it to be so similar to RO, but it was extremly diferent, and not in a bad way. I was impresed on how good this game is, its story line is just so good it will get you atached to it. So here it goes:
Pros:
1-Huge Class Tree:
there are 4 main classes, swordman, mage, priest and archer, then there are diferent class roads you can take wich make your gameplay change a lot, here you can see the class tree so you can get an idea:
2-Its really simple to know what your skills do and how to use them wich make the game really simple to get into for new players, however this does not mean they will be easy to use, only to learn.
3-The quest sistem is really good, it indicates where to go and what you need to do wich makes a really comfortable gameplay.
4-The map is huge including the amount of quests there are and monsters, there really is a lot to do!
5-Economy system is pretty simple and easy to get used to so any player can get into it.
6-New Classes are coming out (called Ranks) wich keeps the game updated and constantly changing.
7-There is a well made pvp system, however i would change it because a level 200 can get mached with level 300+ so it can be unfair some times.
8-Loot system is great as well as crafting system, it gives players the chance to grind for better gear for pvp and pve.
9-People are nice and friendly, however the game feels empty sometimes.
10-The max level is currently 600 (possibly has changed) so yeah you will allways have something to do.
11- On the beggining the game is fairly easy so you can get used to how it works, once you get to level 30+ it becomes harder and harder (keep in mind that there are a ton of levels +500)
12- its not pay to win.
13-You can see how developing team actually listents to their community, sometimes its slow but changes do happen when players dont like something or want something new.
Cons:
1-The game feels left out, a lot of the players that came hype left and there are about usually 7k-10k on a daily basis and sometimes up to 15k-20k on weekends, the game is not empty but it feels like its dying, however the player base is going up a lot lately specially with the new updates that come out.
2-It can get boring if you play alone. The whole idea of an mmo is basically meeting people and playing with them so you shouldnt have much trouble if you are social, however you can get lonesome some times and it can get boring when you are alone, however with friends it is really fun and enjoyable.
3-You can see some times a lot of bot spam, however they are almost immediately banned as long as players report them or an admin is nearby.
4-Mobs feel repetitive in some maps; i say some maps because there are actually a huge amount of monsters, but some maps lack monster changes and sometimes really bad quests.
5-As much as the game is not pay to win, it does feel like its a pay to convenience, for example before recent updates you could not trade with other players unless you had at least 1 token (tokens are paid) however this has changed and it shows how the developing team actually hear their community.
Thats about it so far, i wish i had more to say but sadly i dont have enough time to invest, however i will continue to play this game because i find it really good and entertaining. I recomend you do try this game, it may not be a masterpiece or anywhere near that but this game has so much potential and so much future i think everyone should try it and make an opinion for themselves, dont listen to other opinions, dont be another sheep in the herd, try the game yourself.
Best of luck!

For the years I've owned this game and neglected to do a review of it, I finally have made up my mind on this game.
Let's start at the strongest, the gameplay. Gameplay consists of looting for currency and weaponry to improve in combat in order to level up to use stronger weaponry, of which there are more than 17.75 million guns, the world record set by the original borderlands. As astounding as that sounds, I must first clarify that there are multiple rarities of guns. In order from lowest to highest, common, uncommon, rare, very rare, E-tech, and legendary. With each tier the guns get stronger but also lose uniqueness. A common rarity shotgun from a manufacturer could have 0.5 million different variations, but a legendary shotgun of the same manufacturer might only 12 or 20. On top of all these weapons, you have shields, class mods, relics, and grenade mods and a cast of 4 characters, 6 with DLC each with unique and arguably fun abilities from cloaking, to locking down an enemy in the air, to going full berserk, and with so many skill trees, a total of 18 with 2 being able to be utilised by any one character, it is pretty much impossible to not find a playstyle that suits you. Gunplay is extremely satisfying. Bullets feel like they impact and critical hits are extremely satisfying with bright red text displaying the wonderful shot. Only issue is that enemy AI is fairly basic and that enemies only become bullet sponges with few added traits or abilities as difficulty increases.
Of the manufacturers, there's Bandit, Dahl, Hyperion, Maliwan, Jakobs, Vladof, Torgue, and Tediore, each with their unique strengths and weaknesses, and of the elements there's incendiary, shock, corrosive, explosive, and the unique slag which when inflicted will mark enemies for death, increasing damage taken from non-slag weapons by double.
The variety in weaponry aswell as unique pieces of equipment makes for a game that promotes usage of multiple different weapons and playstyles. In theory this works wonders as to have many playstyles each based on unique skill trees and equipment, but in execution the first 2 playthroughs of the story slowly getting more difficult over time leads you to use specific variants of unique weapons acquired from endless farming in order to be powerful enough to progress. At some point you may find yourself in a tough spot, and unless you're particularly good at combat or got lucky with loot drops, you may find youself needing to farm a boss for up to an hour for loot that will help you progress.
The story is decent with some intrigue here and there mostly found in side-quests. There's a good bit of exposition with even the second NPC you meet apologizing for running his mouth on. Characters have their moments especially when interacting with eachother, but I rarely found them interesting. Most characters just don't feel like their personality, instead feeling like personality traits mashed together with nothing to show of it. Admittedly, I haven't played the previous game to completion so I know I'm missing integral parts of their character there, but if you're coming into the franchise on this game like I did, you may feel the same. Side quests will explore little tid-bits of information such as character relationships. Something that you somewhat suspected before could be opened in a whole new light for you. Unfortunately there's a lot of waiting for the story. Cutscenes are unskippable and there are many points where you simply cannot move on without watching something happen first. On subsequent playthroughs it starts to become a trudge.
It also doesn't help that the visuals are boring. While unique due to the incorporation of cel-shading, most environments have muddy color schemes. From endless deserts, to endless tundras, as nice as it is for the landscapes to be as big as they are, they simply do not look visually appealing. It's worth noting that one thing in particular, the rakk hive, (both Roscoe from the Scarlett DLC and the one I managed to find buried in Torgues DLC) made me want to spew into a bucket.
I nearly forgot music. Most of it is forgetable, and the only bit I can remember is a bit of guitar strumming in one of the tracks. I have absolutely no idea which track either. I wanna say it's the desert track, but I also wanna say it's the tundra track. I feel as engaged without any music as I do with it.
I do have 7 of the DLC's which only one I find more satisfying than the main campaign, that being Tiny Tina's Assault on Dragon Keep. The other three campaign DLC's are boring just like the normal game and the Ultimate Vault Hunter pack is simply an extension of the main game being another 11 levels and a new increased difficulty. The final 2 DLC's are characters which only the Mechromancer I deem fun enough to do an entirely new playthrough of. The other DLC's I cannot speak for as I have not experienced them.
As much as I love the game just for the combat and funny moments, it has too much going against it for me to consider it a good game. Story gets boring quick, visuals are muddy and may rarely disgust, music had nothing going for it, and eventually it all just slows down becoming a grind towards the end of the second playthrough.

Papers, Please is an indie game developed by Lucas Pope, in which you play an immigration inspector whom is working at a border checkpoint in a country named Arstotzka . The goal of the player is to inspect documents using a set of tools and in some occasions to inspect the individual per se, in order to keep criminals out of the country . Everything is a bit unknown, until it will be disclosed , the more you play .
Every work day, you receive a document with informations about particular things you have to notice about, the arrival of important people and/or if you have to take some measures if a specific occasion happens, like having to do body scanning to all civilians who belong to the country of Kolechia . We also have a rule book all the time, so we can know what is allowed in the documents we inspect and if there are any discrepancys, you have to reject the entry to the person and later on, if you want, arrest them . A situation with a spy, terrorists and smugglers with not be uncommon, and you will decide if you will let them pass, because you can bribed and even threaten .
After a day of work, you receive a wage, which depends on how well you did your job, and you will have to decide where your wage will go, some option include 'food', 'medicine' and 'heat', also as you progress in the story you will be able to choose to move to a better house, but it will also have bigger expenses . You also have freedom of will in basically everything since the game changes with your decisions .
Be careful too, this game will play your emotion and will play mind games with you, sometimes you must choose between doing your job or doing the right thing sometimes, there will be families slip apart because of you, but if you decide to let someone passe the border without the correct documents so he or she can be with her/his family, you will face the consequences . Your gaming experience with this game could end in 20 different ways, each occur depending on what decisions did you take in a certain way because you actually have a lot of choices throughout the story, some of them may include, being part of a conspiration group named EZIC against the government of Arstotzka, accepting bribes and even saving money on medicine or food, which will let to the starvation of members of your family .
This game is worth all your attention, since its incredibly addicting, has a great plot and the gameplay its really original, you will not regret it .

This game is heavy. The atmosphere is heavy, with the only music being the deep march of the starting screen. Meanwhile, the graphics, reminiscent of NES graphics and earlier, combine well with the garbled speech that only ever seems to sound like "gestaht" (gestalt? get out? pretty authoritative and germanic sounding) or "hayaku" (japanese for faster?). Even the core action is heavy, forcing you to focus on the tedium of finding discrepancies in the paperwork of immigrants lest you return home with less pay for food and heating.
Yet just because it isn't strictly fun in the "Saints Row" sense of reckless abandon and indulgence, doesn't mean "Papers, Please" isn't engaging. The stress of living out each day, pulled between the attention of your family, your country, and the enigmatic Order of the EZIC Star. Loyalty has its rewards, but any inkling of seditiouis activity may lead to a most miserable end. Thus, it is up to you who to help, both on an individual level and on society at large.
Personally, I was intrigued by the procedurally generated people interspersed between the scheduled characters. Jorji Costava was undoubtedly the one glimmer of comic relief amongst the procession of separated families and sly smugglers. Right when I saw that passport from "Cobrastan" I knew he'd be my number one source of warnings, though I thankfully managed to never have pay taken away via excessive citations.
While I generally took pride in getting no citations and returning with plenty for my family, I took exception with truly momentous events, especially since I wanted to get all the foreign coins in one playthrough. In particular, reuniting Sergiu with his love was sweet, and there was a grim satisfaction in going along with the vengeful fathers plan to murder Simon Wens, the man who killed his daughter.
Nonetheless, this is definitely a melancholy game as a whole, and is all the better for it. Rather than the shiny, happy veneer one might find in free to play or corporate games, "Papers, Please" confronts the anxiety of being an unassuming, yet critical, cog in the machine. Feeling powerless, yet potentially influencing the development of these shifting nations, with you being the decider of who permeates the membrane between them. It's an interesting position to be in, even if the mechanics aren't as exhilirating as one typically expects from a game.

Papers Please is one of those indie games that are quite difficult to categorize. It is considered a puzzle game but more specifically it is a work simulator with adventure elements. The story follows an immigration officer working at a border checkpoint of a fictitious dystopian country named Arstotzka somewhere around the 80s.
The game play is pretty simple. You inspect documents of arrivals, checking if everything is in right order, looking for discrepancies, forgeries etc. If something out of order is found you can interrogate the applicants, do further inspection, like taking fingerprints or body scans and go as far as detain them in a bid to keep out smugglers, criminals and terrorists.
What makes this thing actually a game, rather than actual work is the progression of the story. At the end of each day you earn money based on the number of entrants that have been processed. This money you have to spend wisely on your family’s needs, which include food, rent, heat etc. As your economical situation aggravates you have to consider giving in to various dilemmas, like taking bribes or do certain crime activities in order to make it through, always under the fear of being revealed and consequently be sent to prison. The game despite its dark and emotional theme provides several humorous segments which try to break the monotony.
The art style with plain and retro-like graphics is pretty satisfying. The same can be said about the audio. The nice crisp paperclip sounds and the occasional music segments, combined with the art design provide a cold war era feeling.
Overall, I would say that Papers Please is a nice innovating game which transforms the boring paperwork task into a fun and engaging experience. But it is an experience that should be kept short, otherwise it will end up being actual paperwork.

An excellent MMORPG with all the polish and shine you expect from a Final Fantasy title. Squeenix took all the lessons learned from FFXI and the failed initial launch of FFXIV and put them to good use. The story is fun, the leveling experience is fun, the job system is fun, and character creation is fun. Although inventory management is still a time-sink, it is much less of a headache than other games. I will give FFXIV all the credit it is due. There is no real pay-to-win. The world is constantly evolving and growing. The end game is vibrant.
Grinding, unsurprisingly, sucks. I feel that there is more grinding in this game than other MMORPG's, but far less than there was in FFXI. There is little gear customization, as well. You can change the colors and even the look of your gear, but there is always clearly a "best" gear set depending on your level and job. Once you hit a certain level in a certain job, you must dedicate your time to get the gear that is best for that level, especially in end game. There is no ability to use unconventional gear to enable an unconventional play style that achieves satisfactory results. You gotta get gear set X, or you're not going to be able to survive.
Eventually you will hit a point where you will wonder why you should continue paying the monthly fee, and then you may quit the game, or you may find the community and the end game interesting enough to continue playing. Nevertheless, the experience is worth it, at least for a few months, at least until you get 1 character into end game and satisfactorily geared.

No character customization.
Well, appearance... yes... what class you are... sure.
Stats and what skills you get?  Well, that's all automatic.
That's right.  FFXIV took a progression option that was available since the days of Ragnarok Online and tore it from our hands.  Even in the single player FF games, such as FFVI, FFT, FFX, etc, etc, you got to select skills and build your characters as needed.  No, you didn't choose your stats individually, but they each had a bevvy of skills you could browse around and choose when you leveled up.
Not in this.
What skills you get at what level are pre-determined from the moment you select your class.
Yes, the story is... neat.  The graphics are... on par with what you'd expect FF to have.  The voice-overs are absolutely abhorrant though.
Yeah, you can change classes as easily as changing equipment. (Remember FFX-2?)
You even have individual levels for each class, and get to use skills from your other classes.  One of these is a shot in the foot and the other is a gift-wrapped shoe box.
However, take into account that every level 50 character is basically the same.  There's 5 different races, (all of them are variations of human... really...)  The only thing that'll differ is equipment, which I'm sure is a situation you'll have to grind for.
As someone who enjoys the journey more than the destination, (I hate end-game emphasis...) I cannot recommend a game that cookie-cutters each character into the same underlying thing.
Also, I bet I could recommend the game if it gave your character more options than to follow this "new adventurer & one of the chosen" path.
Geez, Squeenix, you're so worried about making sure everything is always balanced for everyone in your MMORPG, you left me sad for my nostalgia and what the series has become.
As of my second day of playing I have already logged over 24 hours. I can tell I will be here a while.

Myst is a remake of an old point-and-click puzzle game from many years ago. I came into the game knowing it age, and realizing that I would be dealing with compatibility issues because of it. So, after a bit of tweaking- thanks to the Steam forums for help on discovering that disabling scaling on high-DPI in the compatibility issues would keep it from freezing- I was able to dive right in.
With no death or real failure- mostly- in the game, it is a nice change of pace from most games in one's library to explore and investigate the ages, or worlds, bridged into by the linking books found on the island of Myst.
The worlds were beautiful, the sound was excellent- though repetitive in some areas, and the atmosphere of the game was excellent down to the very end. While the interface took some getting used to, and remained a little clunky even after I got used to it, Myst is enjoyable when you play it for what it is. The puzzles may be easy to some, boggling to others, but its a fine little game if you come to appreciate it for what it is. If anything, I am a little saddened that the game was limited in its scope by the technology of the time.

I've played the 1st and 3rd installment and reviewed the first souls game. I went with melee builds and tested both strenth and dexterity builds. I 100%-ed the achievements. For DS2, I first played a strength character 90% through the game and then - almost at the end - just stopped. It did not really challenge me enough and felt too generic and trying too hard with some BS-moments to create some rage-inducing passages. And there are always other games. ;)
Now I have picked it up again for the sole purpose of 100%-ing it and trying out a hex build. I prefer PvE and detest the circumstance that I can be invaded even if hollowed, unless I burn a human effigy. There is still some online play going on (lol wtf, go do it in DS3 ^^), but it felt rather scarce, both invasions and friendly summon signs.
And FYI: I played it with an XBox 360 Controller, never even tried this stuff with M&KB....especially after the debacle of the first Souls port. xD
Still the solid combat system you know and appreciate. The only feeling I could never quite shake was that there is a slight recuperation phase after you strike or cast a spell before you can dogde again. Maybe I remember it wrong, but it felt like that was not the case in Dark Souls 1. Anyhow, this slight delay freaked me out tremendously and it took some time getting used to it....and quite some deaths, to be honest.
So you have your different strategies: Oneshotting or staggering your enemies before they can jump on you, blocking and waiting for an opening to strike, or nimbly dodging and then doing the attack of your joice.
Also, you now have the option to jump by clicking down your left analog stick instead of pressing b, which made some platforming passages feel smoother for me.
OOOOOOH, and lock-on distance, almost forgot that one: Totally♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off repeatedly! I understand that you don't want to have people in PvP locking on a mile away and blasting the still unwary opponent.....but come on, let me lock onto my enemies from far away on a sunny day at the dragon shrine! Casters beware! This was a recurring frustration for me. Died many times because my camera centered the wrong way while I was circling an enemy and wanted to lock onto said enemy. I don't think git gud applies here, that was just plain PvP-balance bullcrap messing up my PvE-experience. >.<
I guess the graphics are absolutely ok considering the release date of the game and the size of the developer. The game ran well on my machine (better mid-range),
The presenation is nice, FromSoftware/NamcoBandai has definitely not lost their touch for aesthetics and ambience. You will see what I mean once you leave the tutorial area. The different areas are diverse and I really enjoyed the many open areas the 2nd Souls game has.
Most of the times, I liked the level design. The length from bonfire to bonfire is often adequate and there are our beloved shortcuts. But every so often, there are just some passages that reek of tryhard. It felt like a designer was trying to make a point by throwing an almost certain death in your direction. Yes, we get it: Welcome to Dark Souls! ;)
This component gets a little life draining if it happens on your way to a boss. I know the game is supposed to be challenging, but I don't see the fun in running to the boss over and over again - and I mean the sheer distance you have to travel, no matter if there are enemies or not - when, instead, you could let me just take a gander at the boss without making me a marathon runner... But that's just me being demanding.
As you start the game, you can choose different areas to visit first, and in my opinion, this time around, they are all manageable with a fresh character. And for more proficient players, there is even the possibility of skipping a huge portion of the game, which is very handy as I will point out in the OAC section.
In my first playthrough, when the game was just released, I went through the game like a hot knife through butter. I either chose a very powerful build, played very well, or the game was not that challenging. In my second playthrough (new character because I lost my savefile -.-) I played a caster, and that comes with the price of struggle early on in the game. So I can say your experience with this game may vary depending on the build you are going for. If I had to objectively judge the enemy and boss design, I'd say they have a decent variety of attacks and their AI is ok. After some time, you can outplay or outmaneuver almost everything, but there are some a-hole attacks that are hard to dodge. I played a glasscannon up to SL 270 with no point in health, so I should know. ;)
Just like in the first part of the souls series, the bosses are hard and not hard at the same time. By that I mean that they will easily kill you if you are foolish or greedy or slow. If you don't act on their behavior and moveset, you will struggle. But if you are quick on the uptake and are capable of analysing them, then you will be able to run certain areas up to difficulties of NG+20, as I did for certain farming purposes). So rarely, you get hit in the face by RNGesus, but otherwise, it can be a cakewalk, if you chose and/or are able to make it so.
This was a big middlefinger in my face. Let me elaborate on that: When I first played DS2, I got r.aped - and I mean
with a capital R -  by certain builds with certain spells and/or weapons. So naturally, when I come back to the game to find my character gone, I decide to go for something that is OP and aim for a hexer. We got rid of the "upgrade every possible weapon" achievements, instead we get spells that will only be available for certain rank 3 online covenants (good one, that will be an even bigger laugh in a few years!) or in NG++. This game rides Bastion's coattails without really understanding why it was good. Bastion got a lot of mileage out of a good soundtrack, excellent visual design, good narration, a decent story and actually fun gameplay.
Transistor manages a decent soundtrack(though, ironically, the worst parts are the ones featuring the protagonist's singing, when she's supposedly an amazing artist), decent visual design(cues mostly lifted wholly from Bastion), terrible narration(literally 500 variations on ellipses or obtuse statements that feel like the ♥♥♥♥♥iest outtakes from a manga or anime, "It's THAT THING...!"), a story that never actually goes anywhere and just plain bad gameplay.
The gameplay can't decide if it wants to be a turn-based tactical game or a fast-pased bullet-dodger/brawler like Bastion, so it awkwardly jams the two together and makes neither of them particularly satisfying. The turn-based part is too easily broken and the brawler part really only lets you dodge the occasional projectile and... really isn't too great at that.
The story starts out seeming interesting enough, but the only way I can really describe is that it seems like it was "written" for fanfiction enthusiasts. That is to say, it's obtuse and opaque simply for the sake of being obtuse and opaque, when what little it obscures with that is painfully obvious to anyone who's even the slightest bit educated, and so much more could have been done with the thing if they had just kicked the obtuseness to the curb and answered some questions.
For that matter, it might also have helped us understand what the actual things at risk were.
Most of the game simply involves Red and her terrible White Knight of a sword(chuck that thing and fisticuffs up the badguys, and the game would have been much more satisfying) wandering from place to place, staring dully at things, and then proceeding along the only available path. You really just "adventure" to find the next name or address, head towards that, find nothing... except another name or address, rinse, repeat, until the very goddamn end.

This game...wow. At first, I wasn't sure what to make of it; it was confusing and hard to grasp at best. But once I hit the first "cutscene", the game took flight. I've read previous reviews complaining about the length of the game, the lackluster story, and the repetitiveness  of the controls, among other things, but I have to say, all those reviews are horribly, horribly wrong. The game is short, sure (I'm not sure how many hours it took me to complete it, as the game stopped working through Steam 3 hours in and I had to finish it via the separate .exe file), but it's still the perfect length - the story would've felt dragged out if it was longer and cut off if it was shorter.
Not only is the game addicting, its story is 100% one of the best I've ever had the priveledge of finishing. The plot of Transistor isn't written out clearly from start to finish for you to comprehend; it's scattered throughout the story, giving you tantalizing and heartbreaking bits of history and explanation for you to piece together yourself. That being said, it seems extremely difficult to not come to most of the conclusions you're meant to, so even if you don't get the full picture, you'll certainly get the key points of it. It's also impossible to not get emotionally attached to Red and the voice of the Transistor, which, despite not having a body, is one of the most deep and fleshed-out personalities I've ever met in a video game. The story is well worth any tedium the gameplay offers (although it never did feel tedious to me), and the OST is, of course, fantastic. Just remember to press TAB every once in a while to make Red hum along to the background music.

Transistor, a game which totally blew my expectations away. Having heard of this game I decided to give this game a go at 2am one fateful morning. After passing out early in the evening. Lets just say the hours flew by quickly as i finished the game at 11am. Short, but very memorable and entertaining game.
The game thrusts you into the world of Red. A very popular singer at a crime scene. No explainations. No background story. You are sort of left feeling your way through the dark. A little off putting, but i gave it a chance, as you should too. Things in the story begin to explain itself as you venture out into this wonderfully rendered environment. You'll forget you're playing in something of a 2D game. The combat is fun but can also be intense. The functions() you learn, skills if you will, are interesting and can be very entertaining. Mixing and matching combinations and using functions to upgrade other functions to modify the result. The sound track of this game, even though i heard much about it definitely is well done, adding to the mood of the game and sounding great at the same time. The voice acting is great and being someone who is hard of hearing I must add that the speech was very clearly recorded.
I'd recommend this game to anyone who likes RPGs with turn based/action based fights. Transistor is a wonderful, enjoyable assault on your mind and senses. Perhaps the only complaint i can find is that it is not a long game, Reclusion mode after beating the game certainly adds some fun to replay as opponents are tougher and one is more seasoned in Transistor battle.
For me i'd give this game a 9/10. Give it a chance. You wont regret it. Perhaps you'll thank me. Happy gaming!

This, together with a huge class tree, made the game really interesting and promising. When the beta was launched, I got a key and I play since then. So, I have about 2.5 thousand hour played. This whole time I had to deal with lag, bugs, crashs and an unbelievable incompetent company (IMC), who made the most basic and stupid mistakes managing it. But, despite those problems, I always had hope that the game would get better and good friends and guildmates helped me deal with the frustration of the IMC's incompetence.
In some points, IMC did a good job, like to avoid the game to turn play-to-win, and kept it to the mininum. For a long time, the influence of real money in the game was limited to buy tokens (that give some benefits, like a 30% experience bônus and access to the team storage), cute hats and customes. However, the presence of silver sellers was always there, but didn't play a great role in the game economy.
Although, the company seems to don't care about the game economy. It always organize some events that would give for free, and with no effort, many important items and loots, that have a key role in the game. This always destroyed part of the game economy and made many players who struggled to get theirs to have huge losses, because those goods would get a ridiculous devaluation.
Today, IMC (together with Nexon, who bought part of the IMC) is launching a cube that promises to make the pay-to-win mechanics to have a huge role in the game and that probably will, once again, destroy the game economy, making the old player to have a huge loss. This cube will give some end game loots that are essencial to craft the best gems and weapons in the game. By buying some of theses boxes, you can get, for instance, a item that can give you a lvl 8 gem, what is a important asset of any equipament and weapon, and demanded about one week of work to get it. In an instant, the struggle of the whole community to get such itens is dismissed and considered irrelevant. Another example, is practonium, a core craft item that is necessary to craft the best weapons in the game, and cost around 20 and 30 millions, now can be obtained by this box.
I'm finally leaving this game, and I don't recommend you to play it. The company doesn't hear the community, doesn't care about the players efforts and economy, and don't provide a good server service, since the players deal daily with lag, bugs and crashs.
