Papers, please. A dystopian document thriller.
Nothing would sound more boring right? Well, you are right. It does sound boring.
But dont let the graphics, the minimalistic gameplay and repetetive music fool you. This game is one of the greatest out there, and easily beats AAA titles. I peaked you interest yet? Good.
You play as a border inspector in the fictional communist country of Arstotzka, just having finished a war against the neighbor country Kolechia that lasted 6 long years. Your job is paperwork. All you do is stamp passports and look through papers. Fisrt day, only citizens of Arstotzka are allowed entry. Next up, foreingers with valid passports are allowed to enter. Same day terrorists attack the border. Next day all foreingers must present a valid entry ticket. It all goes on and on and on. Eventually you will be dealing with a lot of papers. Still, you are expected too keep the same amount of presicion and speed as you had before. Why? At the end of each day you manage your expenses: Heat, food and rent. On top of this, we have your family: Son, wife, mother in law and your uncle. Not paying for food or heat will result in them being sick, which will result in them needing medicine. If you cant pay for medicine, one of your family members die. But on top of that, if you make a mistake at work, you get a citation. First two are warnings, after that you have to pay 5 credits per mistake. Incedentlly, every entrant you procces correctly will give you 5 credits.
Now, with that out of the way, this game has a lot of choices. There is no black and white, there is only gray. This women does not have the right papers, but she will be killed if she returns to her home country. Do you let her in at the expense of your family, or do you deny here and move on? This man carries what he calls 'harmless medicine' and pays you 10 credits to let him pass. Do you detain him, or do you give a stamp?
Do you help a secret group overthrow the proclaimed corrupt goverment? Do you do your thing as a upstanding citizen?
Papers, Please is a work of art. Amazing and fitting gameplay, awesome story and sub stories.
Also, you might wonder what happens when your family dies or you run out of money. You will be replaced and put either into forced labor or ported back to your village.
Glory to Arstotzka.

+Animal behaviour is well modelled
+loads of missions to and competitions running every day in which you can earn ingame currency. (Free players can enter comps too)
+The RPG elements of your skills works really well as you increase your spotting, tracking and shooting skill you get real benefits from the not just higher numbers on a stats page.
+Really nice and helpful community especially on the official forums.
So what are you waiting for?, get started hunting now and keep in your mind that's it's free to try but to get a fuller game experience you will need a membership costing a few quid (£3-£4) a month.

An MMO with gameplay that is immersive and requires more than just mindless button-mashing, with an online community that's almost unusually friendly and helpful. This review will mostly be comparing FFXIV to WoW.
Whereas WoW has more complicated raid gimmics, FFXIV's 2.5 second global cool down it is much less forgiving of mistakes. Due to this fact, FFXIV is a lot less about button-mashing than WoW can feel at times.
A single death from any player, regardless of class, can cause a wipe in FFXIV whereas in WoW losing a few players is not the end of the world.
WoW has more content overall and much better PVP. Even though PVP in FFXIV can be enjoyable it feels like it was added in as an afterthought.
Healing is more proactive than reactive in FFXIV. Towards the harder level content reactive healing isn't enough and you have to know the fight well enough to be a "good" healer. If you're quick on the draw in WoW, and you can manage your mana/threat, that's it: you're a good healer. In contrast, FFXIV requires study, memorization, practice, multitasking ability and flexibility. Being quick is not enough.
Regardless of how difficult you find the gameplay to be, since most people will be using practically the same gear (give or take a bit adjusting for 1-3% from BiS options etc), player skill accounts for most fluctuation in DPS/healing ability/tanking ability. That, and a bit of luck. Most combat classes will do almost the same DPS in a majority of fights, so skill really shows. In my opinion if you are average with your rotation in WoW you're good to go without much thought put in to what you're doing outside of keeping your rotation going, but that isn't quite the case in FFXIV.
FFXIV has a much much more casual player base than WoW. While FFXIV players overall can be more sensitive about being crtiqued, they are extremely friendly and far less likely to be verbally abusive. You'd be hard pressed to find FFXIV players that act as though dedication to or familiarity with a game entitle them to be complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s.

Transistor is like candy, in that it gives you a rush but ultimately leaves you feeling a bit empty.
Initial impressions are fantastic - the first few minutes of the game has genuine emotional punch, voice acting is great, graphics are vibrant and evocative, and the game’s soundtrack is arguably one of the best ever released for a computer game (I’ve purchased it). The game is set in a unique and engaging world, and a range of intriguing characters are regularly hinted at.
Disappointingly, the story remains surprisingly lightweight given the cracker start, and the game finishes with both the world and the characters remaining enigmatic and unexplored.
Gameplay is primarily combat in a modified “real time with pause” style, which suits me great and has a ton of potential. You have the ability to combine a large number of different powers and effects, creating some genuinely interesting combinations. Unfortunately there is little variety in enemies, and consequently, combat lacks depth and replayability.
I feel bad being critical about a game this good, but for a game only a few steps away from having been a genuine classic I can’t help but reflect on what might have been. If only the developers had explored the intriguing world and characters they have created in a little more detail.
Regardless, Transistor is undeniably a top-shelf game by any measure, and a worthy (though not essential) addition to anyone’s game catalogue.

Having only recently discovered the Myst series I have to say it is an aquired taste. Compared to modern games, the Myst series can be merciless in how vague it can be about what to do next. I'm not joking when I say I'd suggest playing this game with a pen and paper available on your desk is almost mandatory. Essential clues are dotted about which can be visual or aureal and sometimes you won't need the clue until much further into the game, so taking notes about every significant sound or unusual symbols or every scrawled peice of text you is a very good idea. The Myst storyline is somewhat light so don't do expecting much but if you enjoy good brain teasers and solving mysteries I'd highly recommend this. Patience WILL be required though.

Though the graphics are a bit outdated today, they were relatively great for the time they came from.  On computers with lower memory and graphics capabilities, Myst has a tendancy to crash.  On machines with higher graphics capabilities and newer opperating systems and more memory, Myst runs smoothly.  It is the mother of all 'escape' games. By that I mean the user must complete various and seemingly unrelated puzzles to move around between 'ages.'  I wish more of the story were told through a short video or pictures or even a vocal narration.  Most of the story is in books, and although books are the basis of travel between 'ages' it is tiresome to read book after book to get all the details.
Overall, Myst is a great puzzle/logic/thinking game where everything you do has a consequence.  It is challenging, and addicting.

Huge fan of the total war series of Rome 2 is by far the title I go back to the most- despite the undeniable genius of Rome 1 and Medieval 2, Rome 2 combines excellent graphics and fun gameplay- and above all quite fulfilling in my case. Attila is a personal fave game that surpasses Rome in many aspects but I would say the time period is just marginally better in Rome 2. Some quick opinions on pros and cons:
PROS
- fantastic unit design, and the modding community is incredible
- the new power and politics update, despite breaking several huge mods (Radious...), does introduce an much greater political interest in your faction: it is now fun to follow the successes and failures of each general and how they use their influence, especially on 4 turns or 12 turns per year mods
- incredible era to play in- the rise of Rome, Carthage, Egypt, the Seleucids, Sparta, Athens, PArthia...
- addicting as hell with the turn per year basis- you'll always want to conquer the next settlement.
CONS
- A somewhat lack of unit variety for some cultures, with germanic or eastern tribes often having the exact same roster, BUT this is fixed easily with every mod existing that you could hope for.
- A lack of challenging late game opponent: few factions other than yours get really big and dangerous quickly, which means that by the end its really easy to just snowball down on every faction as they are too weak to oppose you and lack the capacity to form meaningful alliances against you. Big challenging factions do come up in some playthroughs, and the civil war system is now more interesting, but I don't think I have ever felt under threat in the mid to late game. Ever.
those would be my outstanding impressions, but I love this game overall and always have fun playing it- theres nothing quite like it in the gaming world. If you love ancient history, big battles and streamlined but still interesting empire-management, then Rome 2 is for you.

It's Magic, baby! Magic: The Gathering - Duels of the Planeswalkers 2012 is a very competent port of the titular trading card game, despite some limitations.
Players will quickly discover that they are only able to make mild changes to pre-constructed decks, only being able to remove cards from decks or add one or more cards from a set of unlockable cards tied to each deck.
That being said, the pre-built decks are fun to use, and there is quite a diverse selection of these decks to satisfy most tastes.
The game contains worthwhile single-player modes and a bunch of multi-player modes. You'll be able to duel strangers online, play co-op against stupidly lucky AI, play free-for-alls and the like.
If you already play Magic, you will be instantly familiar with the gameplay. If not, the game does well enough to teach you the basics, as this game is meant to introduce newcomers to Magic: The Gathering.
Recommended for fans of, and newcomers to Magic: The Gathering. It's good stuff.

'Papers, Please' is a point and click, puzzle game developed by 3909.
There isn't much story in the game. You basically play as a immigration inspector who manages who get into the country of Azoska (as well as look after your family). Certain events are detailed via text boxes or in the newspaper. There a over ten endings in the game, which occur based on player action.
Gameplay is exceptional. You need to check the credentials of people who are entering the country and only let in people who meet the laws. This includes checking height, photo, passports, work visa etc. to find any discrepencies. If there are no problems you let them through, else you have to deny access into the country.  At each level, you only have a limited amount of time to work and earn money. Therefore you have to arrange where each piece of document you are given goes (either on the desk or counter) so you can efficiently check and hand those papers back as quickly as possible in order get the next visitor and hence more money. Each person you let in earns you ten dollars, while at the same time any mistakes you make (after the first one) will deduct money from you. Money is used at the end of the level to pay for your family's needs e.g. food and rent. Failure to earn enough money will mean that your family members start dieing off. Your moraility will also be tested in the game with various decisions such as whether to accept bribes, detain people to get more money, whether to let a grieving mother through etc. Basically you have to manage your job, family and morales during the game.
There is minimal audio in the game. Alarms and paper sound as they should. People speak via text boxes and some of their dialogue are quite humorous.
Graphics aren't that detaile, but they do a good job at setting a surpressive atmosphere.
If you want to have unique, somewhat-funny point and click game, this game won't dissapoint.

A truly unique and very fun indie game that combines elements from city builders, management games, and a little bit of survival. Put simply, you crash land alone on an alien planet, then work your way all the way up from steam technology to your escape rocket. The true enjoyment of the game is processing coal, iron, copper, and other raw materials through an increasingly advanced automated factory that you design, piece by piece. You also have to manage electricty, research, and defense while you progress. The game's only major shortcoming is the enemy AI; while the aliens pose a great threat in the early game, they can be fairly easily subdued and pretty much ignored in later stages.
TLDR: Excellent game, buy it and surrender yourself to the machine.

This game surprised me.
I first played it back in 2014 and almost immediately didn't like it. I think I was one of those players who wanted a Skyrim like experience and this game does not really fulfill that. There were a lot of issues with the mega servers and connections and the dungeon system. If you look at the negative reviews most of them are unhelpful as they are short and vague or super outdated or have to do with technical issues not being able to run the game. The game does take up a lot of space (massive amounts of content) and it can be intense to run, I will give them that. But if your computer is technically up for it, it's hard to come up with a good reason to not play based on the game's merit.
I came back to the game after the One Tamriel update. It was a new game. I won't go into all of the details but they changed everything, for the better. You can adventure all over with your friends no matter what your level or faction. The quests aren't just stupid and grindy, they have interesting stories and some variations on the things you do. The crafting system is involved enough to be a meaningful addition to the game without being so complex that it's difficulty creates a barrier to entry. The voice acting is still superb. New content seems to be on a steady release pattern, with events and stuff in between. I am 550 hours into the game and still unlocking new things and having new adventures. Housing system is fun and gives a lot of options for decorating.
You can quickly play through the main storylines and have an Elder Scroll style adventure to hold you over until ES6 (whenever that may be) or, if you're like me, this could be your new digital home. When I hear the calm music right after logging in, I instantly feel at ease. I've put the game down for a couple months at a time to focus on other games or things in life but when I come back it really does feel like being back in your digital fantasy world. You get to know Tamriel and the characters and the whole experience is really excellent.
The combat is fun and action oriented and so you're not just standing around clicking skills like in many MMOs, although it isn't as visceral as something like BDO or a single player action game. There are dungeons, world bosses, an entire zone with dedicated group content, PVP, raids, basically something for everyone.
The game is not perfect, and if you break down the features of this game you'll probably find specific MMOs that do it better but when you look at what they have created overall as an entire game it's truly amazing. One thing that impressed me is that I was part of a survey/focus group for the game and essentially every piece of feedback I gave them is something they have fixed/changed/improved upon since then. Not that I'm in any way important to them, but the fact that they listened to their community says good things about the direction they are going in.

This game has some interesting ideas, but has a long way to go. Most importantly, wipes prevent me from wanting to invest any time in creating a character. While this game has very interesting features, I feel that there are too many barriers to creating a long term community.  The building system is amazing but not worth investing in as it will most likely be deleted by the developers before anyone has a chance to siege your castle.  The combat is fun but there is no long term reward for stealing that coveted piece of treasure. This game has a lot to learn from the others of the survival genre, especially "Ark Survival Evolved" which has implemented far more features in less time without the need to constantly wipe characters and structures regularly. From the Medieval genre it should learn from the new release " Gloria Victis" which has made its characters free of server limitations. The ability to roam servers and maintain your character when your current server is down has  prevented so much frustration and reign of Kings should implement a similar system. The developers may have technical limitations for saving character content, so I propose this: Character saves can be set to a paper doll, preserving the core attributes and features of a character. When a milestone in game development occurs for the devs, this data is saved and transferred to the new format of the game. while characters are not necessarily their original form, some of the progress players have worked on will be saved, thus encouraging long term play. I sincerely hope that the developers listen to the playerbase including myself as there are some simple fixes that could make this game enjoyable for long term play. Untill that time, I would discourage others from spending money on a time sink that maintains none of your progression.

Transistor is like candy, in that it gives you a rush but ultimately leaves you feeling a bit empty.
Initial impressions are fantastic - the first few minutes of the game has genuine emotional punch, voice acting is great, graphics are vibrant and evocative, and the game’s soundtrack is arguably one of the best ever released for a computer game (I’ve purchased it). The game is set in a unique and engaging world, and a range of intriguing characters are regularly hinted at.
Disappointingly, the story remains surprisingly lightweight given the cracker start, and the game finishes with both the world and the characters remaining enigmatic and unexplored.
Gameplay is primarily combat in a modified “real time with pause” style, which suits me great and has a ton of potential. You have the ability to combine a large number of different powers and effects, creating some genuinely interesting combinations. Unfortunately there is little variety in enemies, and consequently, combat lacks depth and replayability.
I feel bad being critical about a game this good, but for a game only a few steps away from having been a genuine classic I can’t help but reflect on what might have been. If only the developers had explored the intriguing world and characters they have created in a little more detail.
Regardless, Transistor is undeniably a top-shelf game by any measure, and a worthy (though not essential) addition to anyone’s game catalogue.

I only played a half hour of this game, and I can't bring myself to play any more. I enjoyed Amnesia: The Dark Descent, although I didn't love it as much as many other people seem to do. I enjoyed TDD for its tense atmosphere and excellent mechanics, even though I didn't enjoy how the plot was resolved. A Machine for Pigs, however, just left me angry and confused after a mere half hour of playing. Here are my thoughts after my brief foray into this letdown:
Pros:
- Beautiful graphics. The textures, colors, and overall scenery are very nicely rendered.
- I don't want to have only one pro here, so I'll say the voice acting was nice (what little I heard of it).
Cons:
- This game has entirely gotten rid of the survival mechanics, which are what made TDD enjoyable for me to play, despite my qualms with its storyline. There's no inventory in this game, no health or sanity. Your lantern never runs out, so there's no tense moments where you have to choose between letting your sanity suffer and staying in the dark or using up your precious oil. Omitting these mechanics was a very poor decision in my opinion.
- In both games, you start out not knowing where or who you are or what you've meant to do. What TDD does right, however, is give you small breadcrumbs through the letters you find in the very beginning that give you enough information to pinpoint a basic objective and give you a strong desire to delve into the storyline and figure out what is going on in Brennenberg. AMFP, however, gives you no such guidance. The only information you encounter (or at least, that I encountered) can best be described as nonsensical and even downright insane. It's fine to have little information right when the game begins, but I need *something* pretty soon after beginning to give me a sense of direction and make me want to care about the plot. I couldn't care less about this game's plot, which is why I ultimately abandoned it.
- In the limited time I played, there was very little challenge. By contrast, there were many moments in TDD that had me scratching my head as to how to proceed. It seems that with the omission of the inventory system, AMFP has also gotten rid of the puzzles that made TDD challenging and intriguing.
Admittedly, I do not plan to finish this game, so it's entirely possible this review could be wholly wrong and the game could turn out to be great. I don't think I'll ever find out, though, because the first half hour put me off from it so much. Don't waste your time. 4/10

is literally a puzzle box, a fantastic mechanical device that you open by solving the puzzles built into its surfaces.
The incredible mystery of this absolutely incredible box.
pure puzzlers.
Often puzzle games will wrap their puzzles around some artifice, some premise that explains why you are solving puzzles.  A whole sub-genre of video game logic deals with how preposterous and improbable it is that, for instance, an ancient civilisation designed its temple such that only by rolling sixteen balls into position and solving a maths equation could they enter.  The puzzles might be solid and entertaining and challenging, but the premise requires a hefty suspension of disbelief.
Never in my life have I played a game whose puzzles are so cohesive, so plausible, so absolutely real as they are in the Room.  Fantastic, sure; impossible, absolutely, but impossible in a completely consistent, believable way that draws you into the magic of this puzzle box.  Couple this with some of the most gorgeously detailed visuals I have seen in a game and you have without question the most immersive, engaging puzzler.  Rather than a series of brain teasers connected weakly by narrative, literally the entire game is just you peeling back layer after layer of this mysterious, mystical box, very occasionally reading a cryptic note by your predecessor that answers nothing but raises more questions and drags you further into the labyrinthine structure that seems to get bigger the more you delve into it.
I cannot help but say this: the science-mysticism, the mood, the puzzles, the box itself - I couldn't stop thinking this is what Hellraiser would have been like if it were made by Rand and Robyn Miller.
A word about the puzzles: despite the impossibility of these mechanisms all fitting within the box, the puzzles all feel solidly mechanical, they all make perfect sense as a set of puzzles you could actually use as a sophisticated locking mechanism for a box.  Many of the puzzles involve you poking at nooks and crannies to find hidden buttons or activators or concealed drawers containing cogs or codes, and the puzzles on a layer often feed into each other, one puzzle releasing the mechanism of another.  You are given almost no clues (unless you use the hint system, which, honestly, don't - this is one game where perseverance is its own reward, and I say this as an habitual user of walkthroughs), so it really feels like you are exploring and fiddling with this incredible device, moving around it, examining its finely-crafted detail, touching it and testing for a reaction.  It feels very real.  Even in the later stages when the mystical elements start to take over - a perfectly natural evolution of the box as you delve deeper - it still feels so scientific and so physical.
On the puzzles themselves: they are not very challenging, for the most part.  Figuring out what you need to do is harder than figuring out how to do it.  There are just enough hidden activators that you can overlook that it drives home that realism and that mechanical feel, but not so many that it turns into a frustrating hidden object game.  If you know roughly what you are trying to do - for instance, activate all the levers on one side of the box - you can generally work backwards to figure out which panel you should solve first to unlock that final side, and this process of deduction and experimentation is really the core of the puzzle gameplay.  Codes don't need to be deduced, they just need to be found, but recognising that what you've found is in fact a code is the challenge.  It makes for a very deductive, exploratory experience, rather than intellectual brute force trying to calculate permutations as is common in many pure puzzlers.
There is one single puzzle towards the end of the game that I think is poorly designed.  Without spoiling it, at one point in the penultimate stage you need to interact with a music box in a way that makes no sense, cannot be predicted, cannot really be witnessed or tested, and, even after reading a walkthrough for this one roadblock, I still didn't understand the puzzle.  When you get to this bit, if you can solve it, kudos to you; I couldn't, and not because it was hard but because it was so utterly random in a game that otherwise makes perfect sense from start to finish.
This single puzzle aside, the game runs for a couple of hours, and those hours are absolutely gorgeous and engrossing.  I want to say again how stunning the detailed art for the box actually is.  I, and especially my partner with whom I played this, have a love of antique furniture, and this game won us over from the very first sight of the box.  I cannot oversell this box: mechanisms aside, if you had a piece that simply had the visual detail of any layer of this thing you would treasure it as art.  With less attention to detail, the game would still be good, but because of the incredible work they did on the appearance and fidelity of the box itself, and the way the puzzles felt so mechanical and so cohesive, the whole process of solving this game felt real in a way that puzzle games never do.
If you like puzzle games, play The Room.  It does not get any better than this.

Don't let my current play time fool you. I originally bought this game for my tablet, and I've played through it on there at least five or more times. I absolutely loved it from the start. Even when I got stuck ("I SWEAR TO GOD I HAVE POKED EVERY SIDE OF THIS STUPID THING
") I flat-out refused to look at the hints. The answer was there. I knew it was. I just had to find it. If I were really in this strange room, trying to find the secrets of this strange box, I wouldn't have
magical hints to help me.
The puzzles are clever and "logical", so to speak. Everything here makes sense within the world of the game.
And the world is actually a huge part of the game, for all that you're trapped in the eponymous room: the atmosphere in this game is amazing. Overall:
-First third of the game is a bit boring.
-Good B-movieish writing with believable and sometimes even interesting characters.
-Plot follows suit with appropriately over the top missions, cutscenes and totally not foreseeable twists.
Combat and movement:
-A solid meh. It feels like every time you start to get in the fun stuff the game throttles you right back to it's own pace.
-No sprinting combined with Rico's granpa-jog make grappling around mandatory, yes, even on flat ground.
-No dodgeroll forces you to do some more grappling.
-Overzealous animations for absolutely everything make you wait a lot.
Grappled onto a ledge? Enjoy seeing Rico's beautifully animated jump which takes almost a second and doesn't for some godforsaken reason allow you to shoot during it even if Rico's not doing anything with his hands.
Grappled to not die of old age due to Rico's "run" "speed"? Enjoy that second of sliding to slow down. Etc.
Complaining about things that take less of a second might seem petty but the fact is every little thing you do seems to come with these speedbumps really throttles the overall experience down to a fast uneven slog.
Vehicles:
-Everything explodes way too easily. Trying to land anything flying is almost quaranteed suicide.
-Ground vehicles go from "it turns like a tank without steering wheel" to "a light touch of steering wheel will make you spin with enough speed to counter gravity".
-Boats go from "this doesn't hurt too much" to "it doesn't turn at all and hurts way too much".
-Planes don't. They just don't.
-Helicopters sort of work though for some reason they turn reaaaaally slowly. Sort of a theme with the vehicles really.
Character upgrades:
-Third of the early upgrades should have been default. Like aiming down sights, shooting while reeling in, etc.
-They're acquired trough doing challenges (side content) which is terrible. Challenge rewards should be extra. Then again seeing how creatively devoid the upgrading system is I'm not too surprised there's no extra.
Graphics & audio:
-Overall very good looking visuals, especially some of the explosions and smoke effects.
-Looks decent even on lowest settings which is nice.
-SFX and music are well made and feel fitting for the most part.
-Both SFX and music is really finicky when it wants to work. Often it's in a bad mood and doesn't want to.
Performance:
-So badly optimized I seriously doubt the game runs on the listed minimum requirements.
-Has a habit of crashing randomly.

Grating combat, repetitive duels, barely any weapon options.. That's Call of Jaurez for you.
EDIT: To be fair, I decided to start a New Game+ on the True West Difficulty, to give a more accurate review.
This only revealed the flaws in level design that you wouldn't notice in the easier difficulties.
The levels all lack intuitive, and often any, cover at all. Many of the levels leave you in an "ambush" environement, where you're surrounded by all sides with an attacking force, and you have to deal with them to survive.
However, you're a sitting duck, surrounded on all sides with dead-eye accurate NPCs, no cover whatsoever, and you even are supposed to run out of ammo. I was met with frustration after frustration, when I just repeatedly died over and over again trying to survive. Worse still, in the stage directly after this, you're attempting to escape pursuit while with no ammo, and no cover system, while enemies constantly spawn almost directly behind you, and shoot you. I also had an issue with enemies turning a corner and instantly getting a killshot on me, with no chance to react. The duels are a major irritant to me, every single one is the same thing, over and over again until the last one, where you're forced to try and focus on three things at once.
I'd like to see more weapon choices, more options in duelling, more diverse enemies, more diverse situations, I'd like for the modified guns to not be unlocked with perk points, rather a reward for the Nuggets of truth perhaps? I felt very constricted with my perk choices as well, you can choose only two paths per perk "cylinder", and often you need to useless perk to get a good one. Also having the dynamite perks so spread out was odd, especially when the "Splitting Dynamite" perk was in the Sharpshooter tree? This is just a poorly planned out game, with poor level design, almost no diversity in enemies and locations. 3/10

A good base game that is, unfortunately, brought low by boneheaded design decisions.
Tree of Savior is, as a whole, genuinely fun to play. I like the gameplay, and the class system works very well, allowing a variety of builds in a way that few MMOs really let you get away with. ANd the art, the art is gorgeous. Sure, it has the usual neckbeard appeal - pantyshots, etc, but normal people can ignore these. And if they do, there's really good stuff there- Cute animations, nice enemy designs, pretty maps, the works.
But the more you play, the more problems emerge.
-The Localization is absolutely terrible. Entire plotlines can only be understood by guesswork, with grammatical mistakes, text overflows and broken English all over the place.
-The loot system is one of the worst I have ever seen. The game uses "DPK", which essentially gives many loot drops a 0.1% chance to drop, or worse. For various items, you need 40+ of these. THere's a way to increase the drop rate - every kill improves it a little bit. Map wide. Meaning you can farm for hours, then another player wanders into the map, gets a kill, and the drop. Then the drop rate resets, and you get nothing. Sounds like a nightmare system by crazy people, but it's actually how it works, confirmed by the devs themselves.
-The latest patches unfortunately introduced massive pay to win, coupled with making gear far more important than it was before. The worst offender here is Leticia's Cube, which essentially gives some items that take months to acquire just like that.
I joined the game recently. Early on, it was really fun, but as I got near the high end, these problems really converged. A single item to improve my character suddenly required months of farming (since I have a job, and can't just play 5+ hours a day), with, of course, the pay to win cube as an alternative.
And well, nah. There's better games out there. I can't recommend it until you want to feel nickel and dimed or have tremendous amounts of free time. I've now uninstalled it, as my time is respected more elsewhere, by games that don't give me only two options: Either farm for months, hoping for that 0.1% drop chance, or pay out of my nose.
Ain't got the time for that.
That said, the overall time was fun, and I enjoyed wasting some of my free time in it. Just don't expect more than the usual Korean P2W in the end. Sadly :(

PC Compatibility 4/10 (You dont really need a good pc because that wont help, they shouldnt have rushed this game's release) - Bad lag spikes when there's many players around, but 90% of the time its over 60fps for good PCs.

Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs (AKA MFP) is a loose sequel to the original castle crawler, The Dark Descent (AKA TDD). This game was not developed by Frictional Games, but rather The Chinese Room.  The setting is late 1890s Steampunk London and starts in a very cool looking mansion. A newer engine was used for this game and the visuals are definitely a step up. Overall I was very pleased with how the game looked, although some of the levels are super dark. Sound design was excellent and the soundtrack superb. Unlike TDD, there is no inventory and your lantern has unlimited power. I can see where this made some folks not very happy. No inventory meant simpler puzzles and that's very much the case here.  Some of the puzzles felt more like busy work. Most of the time you'll be running through the samey environments pulling levers, hitting switches and turning cranks. Also the unlimited lantern took some of the mood away but on the other hand I can appreciate not looking under every nook and cranny for tinderboxes or oil so that can be seen as a plus. The story was pretty cool and helps when you read the notes. The biggest problem with MFP is easy:  It just wasn't scary. Some of the levels like the mansion and factory were nice and creepy but the looming sense of dread wasn't there. The pigmen monsters weren't all That made the four hour running time just perfect to me because you can only crawl through labs, climb ladders and go across catwalks so many times. Overall Amnesia: MFP gets a 7/10 from me.  It's not a bad game by any means but I was hoping for some scares and didn't get that many.

This game has some issues that no one seems to address. I will be making direct comparisons to WoW, which has its own problems nowadays, but was the perfect mmo and pretty much set the unreachable bar for all MMO's to come.
The classes are based around the weapon you are currently using, each class can only use ONE kind of weapon. All classes are bound to a single role and there is no changing that. For instance, the 2-handed axe wielding class can only be assigned the role of tank. You want to be a 2-handed damage wielding class? Gotta play a Lancer, Lancers do damage, Marauders tank. Don't like it? Too bad. Want to be a 2 handed sword wielding Gladiator? Too bad, 2 handed swords don't exist. How about crossbows for Archers? They don't exist. Its amazing how these limitations exist in this game, compared to WoW which gives some classes up to 3 options for what role they want to fulfill based on a talent system. Where it is a cool idea that you can simply change your class to whatever you want for a single character, you are limited to specifics for each one. To go even further into this issue, FFXI did not have this limitation. I was able to use a large array of weapons as a Warrior, and i was able to fulfill 2 roles, tank and DPS. Obviously FFXI had a lack of abilities for all non-caster classes but there's no excuse for this kind of limitation in a current, popular and thriving MMO. There is only one class that can become 2 different roles. A level 30 Arcanist can learn to be a Summoner focuses on Damage, and a Scholar which supports and Heals. Why can't tank classes have that option and why can't some damage classes be tanks as well? Paladin tank sword and board, Crusader damage 2 handed sword/mace, your tank abilties switch to damage abilities when you equip said weapon. Wouldn't be hard to make new abilities considering every melee class is the same 3 button combo with some self buffs, some aoes and CC on cooldowns.
Lets talk about the party system. The light party is a group of /4/ players. A tank, a healer and 2 dps. The early game dungeons are sluggish and boring after the first few times, maybe even the first. What the ♥♥♥♥ is with a 4 person party? Why not 5? 5 is the perfect number. Just throw another add onto group pulls or give them a little more health, 4 is a pathetic number for a party. With 5 people there would be less DPS queue lock up. DPS queues are always a problem in MMO's with a party finder system. You are playing a role that 6 other classes share, where there are 2 tank classes and 2 healing classes. FFXI had a party size of 6, which was a bit much at times when you needed so many people just to do ANYTHING in that game, but 6 would work in this game just as well. Its just being lazy to set up for the Full Party.
A Full party consists of 8 players. 2 tanks 2 healers 4 dps. This is okay, but it would just be better as 10. Optional healer and damage or just 2 damage dealers. Raids would be 3 parties of 10. Your game isn't dead yet, you can still find 30 people that want to do Raid content easily.
This game is great as it is for many reasons but it has some terrible/lazy design choices. It has the ability to be so much better and not limit the players to specifics. I don't need to go over the good parts, i just want to mention problems that NO ONE ELSE MENTIONS.

When Supergiant released Bastion, they had created a really amazing piece of art. The gameplay was excellent. The story was interesting. The music was amazing. In Transistor, they replicated the level of quality that Bastion had, and then amplified it.
If you've played Bastion, you know exactly why you should buy this game. If you haven't, let me explain what makes Transistor so enthralling (without spoiling the story).
The main focus of the game is the blade known as the Transistor. The Transistor allows you to actually stop time and plan your attacks against every wave of enemies from the pesky little bots to the huge bosses. This additional function turns Transistor into a hybrid of turn based strategy and action, which adds a little something that you didn't see in Bastion (hence why it's worth playing both games).
The Transistor is also a more customisable weapon. In Bastion, you had individual weapons which each gave their own play style. In Transistor, you only get the one sword (because of how important it is in the story). So to make up for that, you get the ability to customise it. The more you play, the more you unlock unique abilities that can be loaded into the Transistor for use in combat. However, you only have so many slots, so you need to choose carefully. Not only that, but the ways in which you can use each ability varies. Each ability can be used as a passive power, an active power, or a support for an active power. In addition, each combination is different, providing a massive array of different effects that you can use to give yourself the edge in battle. If you find you keep losing to a certain enemy, just swap the abilities around and you suddenly have a brand new setup that's massively different to your old one.
This unique mechanic gives Transistor tons of replay value, since you can keep experimenting with every possible combination of abilities. Would definitely play again. Hopefully Supergiant release another game. I'd love to see them top this.

With an art style reminiscent of Klimt paintings, excellent voice acting and an otherworldly, atmospheric soundtrack, Transistor provides a memorable gaming experience. It drops you right into the middle of the action and never lets up - it is by turns, creepy, terrifying and fascinating. You want to know more, about the city, the people, Red, and the disembodied voice inhabiting the Transistor itself. The fighting system is simultaneously complex and easy to understand; you can easily get sucked into the many combinations of active and passive powers, limiters and more. Or you can cruise by, choosing the more obviously powerful powers and smashing your way through with far less finesse.
In many games there is the struggle between the dynamic of a voiceless playable character and the companion that usually functions as a guide, giving exposition and providing help - hopefully in a more entertaining matter than drop-down menus. In some cases it can work well (think Midna and Link in LOZ Twilight Princess) and in other cases it can be very annoying (think Fi and Link in LOZ Skyward Sword). Transistor fulfills both rolls beautifully, even providing reasons for both characters being as they are. Red has lost her voice. She can communicate only by humming and typing messages in the half-broken terminals they come across. Her sword, a sexy disembodied voice that sounds like it has smoked a generous amount of cigarettes, provides the perfect balance of letting you know what's going on and where you should go without ever making you feel like he's just a bit of recording. He talks a lot because he feels helpless; he has no body, after all and is entirely dependent on Red. The two make a great pair and their interaction really makes the game worthwhile.
Where the game falls short, however, is in two areas. The actual world itself is very limited. At a glance it looks huge and you think you're about to explore this massive, post-apocalyptic city, empty of inhabitants. However, in reality, you are basically being carted along a tunnel, with very limited choice in where you can go and what you can do. For the most part, you walk along a prescripted path, fight the monsters you are supposed to face, leveling up enough to beat the boss, then it's off to the next part. Rinse and repeat. There are very limited  options for exploring and none for backtracking that I could find. No side quests, except for the 'Beach' area which is a series of challenges, or tests.
Now, to give the game credit, because of the excellent atmosphere and voice acting, this did not really bother me as much as it might have. I enjoyed the voice in the sword leading me along this strange and mysterious world. However, I would have enjoyed it more if I could have broken into buildings, maybe met a few people, discover secrets, go down secret alleyways, unlock new things and have multiple endings and/or methods to traverse and ultimately beat the game.
The other area where the game let me down is in the ultimate unraveling of the story. There is a lot of build-up, and world-building going on. Every power you collect has information on a colorful variety of characters with very interesting histories. I looked forward to reading each one. The 'terminals' where you can answer polls, even change the weather are fascinating, provide Red a chance to 'speak' as she types out responses and further flesh out the world and story. All of this is great because it gives you information about the world without dumping exposition on you. But in the end, very little is resolved. I don't want the story force-fed to me and I don't mind some ambiguity, but it seems such a shame that so much time was spent on build-up and very little on explaining what exactly happened, how, why and so on. I ended the game feeling quite unsatisfied and wanting to know a lot more. However, the ending is VERY good, perhaps a perfect ending, and a great boss battle.
Transistor is very much worth buying. It is fun, interesting and has a great battling system. It has its flaws, but so does any game. If the premise sounds interesting to you than I'm sure you won't regret playing it!

I've actually logged more hours in the Android version of the game than the PC version, but I believe the two versions are identical.
You start every level with a lot of black goo balls. You have to connect them into a grid-like structure, expanding that structure until it's able to touch the exit point. You also need to have at least several goo balls remain unused (each level specifies the minimum) so that they can "escape" into the exit.
This game can really make you rage at times (please do not smash your phone/tablet if you are playing on a mobile device). You can have a seemingly perfect, elegant structure that suddenly collapses because you didn't keep track of the weight on the upper portions. However, it is easy to revert your mistakes, and when you do fail you never feel that it was unfair - it's a great learning experience for your next attempt.
I highly recommend this game as a casual time killer at the train station or the airport lounge. If you're like me and don't really touch these games very much on the PC, support the devs via Google Play, the Humble Android Bundle, the Apple App Store, etc.

Gonna try to keep this short...
I've played MMORPGs since EverQuest in 1999.
I'm only level 230 at the time of writing.
There hasn't been an MMO in quite some time that gave me the feeling of exploration that this one does.
The initial progression is fairly linear, but once you reach a high enough level and start learning farming spots and dungeons, you can go out and farm where ever.  Most of the non-instanced dungeons are pretty awesome too, multiple levels, quite huge like you'd see in older MMORPGs.
The PVE starts out very easy, but once you get to a certain point, the difficulty gets much harder. The game tries to ease you into this and does a good job. Point here is, the PVE isn't a snoozefest. It requires thought and skill, like old MMOs.
There are also very few quests that you /have/ to do, you could technically just grind to cap if you wanted, though it will take A LOT longer because quests reward xp cards.
The drop rates are low but not so low that you don't feel progression. The same thing goes with XP.
The theorycrafting that goes into creating your build is pretty much unmatched in the genre at the moment. This is something I very much enjoy as an oldschool MMO player. The closest to it would be Grim Dawn or Path of Exile (those aren't MMORPGs, though).
There's not really any useless gear, either. And chances are there will always be an upgrade for you somewhere.
Something else I really enjoy about this game are some of the more drawn out/cryptic quests. An example would be the Shinobi quest line. I had to camp a spawn for an item for ~20 hours before getting it. I am now in the process of farming a lot of rare materials to finish up the quest line to unlock the hidden class. It feels /very/ similar to epic weapon quests from EverQuest if you're familiar with them. If I understand correctly, there are other quests in the game that are somewhat similar in difficulty. There also aren't markers for every quest, there are quite a few hidden ones. I personally enjoy this immensely.
While I'm on the topic of quests, a lot of them are run of the mill. However, there are some I've come across that are more complex than your standard MMO stuff. They actually require a bit of thought or puzzle solving, much like quests from the days of old.
I haven't touched the PVP yet, but I hear it is incredibly fun.
Another small detail I enjoy, you actually have to prepare before going into far off zones or dungeons. Stock up on potions (ideally player crafted), buy buffs, over repair your gear from a player smith, enhance your weapon from a player smith. Oh yeah. Players can set up their own "shops" in town or in the wild, too. It requires you to pick specific classes, but it's a neat feature.
Another big plus for me... the GMs actually interact with the community and do events. Not enough MMORPGs do this any more.
All of that said, some of the things that might be downsides for some people:
Token users get 30% more xp and one more instance run per day than non-token users.
The monster card system is pretty grindy. So is the gem system.
You can buy XP tomes off the cash shop. Not necessary but it helps to get over some "XP walls". Also think you can buy them for silver from the in game market. Boosted xp rate essentially.
You get 4 free character slots iirc. You have to pay for more. I think it's around a dollar each. The only catch here is that companions (pets basically, not pets for classes but combat pets that can help your character) also take up a character slot. Somewhat blatant cash grab, but luckily slots are cheap.
I don't have much experience with it yet, but items have so much "potential" in them. Basically, after you start putting gem sockets in your gear or enhance it past a certain point, the item's potential goes away. When it reaches zero, if you try to go further, it can break the item unless you use event items that come from a cash shop item which is only available for a limited time.
There are cosmetic items called "hair accessories". These can be upgraded using enchant scrolls from the cash shop (these scrolls can also be bought from the in game market for silver). The potential thing also applies to these I believe. Only really necessary for min/maxing for super endgame stuff, but it does give an advantage. You can buy pre-enchanted ones off the market or do it yourself with silver instead of spending RL money though.
Due to the game being somewhat niche, information isn't as readily available for EVERYTHING like it would be for a game like WoW. It takes some real digging to find information sometimes. Personally, I enjoy this. Google has ruined a lot of things that made MMOs difficult/fun in my opinion.
It also still has some minor bugs.
The good news about all of this: Most of these systems are pay for convenience and not entirely necessary except for super end game stuff. Most (if not all) of them can also be done without spending a dime. Silver is pretty easy to get once you learn the farming spots and find holes in the market that need to be filled.
The only other downside is that the game could use more players. Don't get me wrong, there are no shortage of people to do your dailies with or farm with, but it can take a minute to get a group set up.
I tried to explain everything to the best of my ability, and if I got anything wrong, feel free to correct me.
I can honestly say that I've enjoyed VERY few MMOs as much as I have enjoyed this one.
Absolutely in my top 5 of all time. Maybe even top 2.
Basically, if you enjoy old school MMO mechanics, theory crafting, anime art style, deep dungeons, good loot actually being rare (in a good way), you'll probably love ToS.
The game also has an event going on at the moment for new players, so if you've been on the fence about trying it, now is a good time.
PS: Do your research before wildly spending stat points (int dex str spr con) as reset items for them are paid / timed items.
Same for deciding on your class build.
You can reset skills at any time if you're willing to shell out 10 bucks though.

Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs is an great game. Well done, visually stunning, amazing storyline. The environment isn't as interactive as the first game but it works in this context, giving you access to what you need so the player isn't being sidetracked. They also did away with the sanity bar which is a godsend in its own right. I would recommend people check it out.
On that note though, there were two cons that made it difficult for me to really get into it.
The first being that it doesn't really feel like an Amnesia game. It doesn't give that same vibe of absolute terror and almost helplessness the way Amnesia: The Dark Descent did. The fear vibe is much more subtle and more like dread than terror.
The second is the monsters, pigmen, whatever you want to call them. Unlike the Brutes and Grunts from A:TDD, pigmen are seen quite often and there isn't anything stopping you from getting a good look at them. By doing that, it takes away quite a bit of the terror feel. It's much more scary if you don't know exactly what's coming after you.
Honestly, I think if you play A:MFP for what it is and don't think of it as a sequel, you'll find it really is a great game and definitely worth checking out.

I got this way back when it was first released, excited to play the sequel to Amnesia. However, upon realizing that there was no inventory, no light system, the inability to pick up everything, or even open everything...I was rather disappointed. I meant to keep playing, but as it seemed to be strictly a walking simulator without the physics based puzzles of the original, I could never motivate myself to keep going. (And that was just from like, the first half hour or so, before you even realized how much of a walking simulator it was.)
But now, fastforward a few years, and I've played a few walking simulator spectrum games that I've enjoyed (namely the free game Fingerbones, and the other two adventure games by the same dev). They were all short (under an hour) but really entertaining experiences.
I even went and played Soma since, so it's been a while. So, I've finally found myself back to this game. And frankly, I'm pleasantly surprised. Without the expectations I had from Amnesia (which is fair really, given the name lol), it was an excellent journey. The music, the atmosphere, the story and the way it developed...
You get a reasonably diverse range of environments, lots of nice scares, and an unsettling feel throughout, which increasingly intensifies over the course of the game as things get weirder (there's a few design and aesthetic choices that I thought were excellent) and you learn a bit more about what the protagonist has forgotten.
I do recommend it; I think it's an excellent game as long as you realize what it's going for. This isn't quite Amnesia 2.0, and as long as you're not expecting crazy puzzles or neverending cat+mouse situations in the latter half of the game, I think you'll find it to be a fun and engaging experience.

With an art style reminiscent of Klimt paintings, excellent voice acting and an otherworldly, atmospheric soundtrack, Transistor provides a memorable gaming experience. It drops you right into the middle of the action and never lets up - it is by turns, creepy, terrifying and fascinating. You want to know more, about the city, the people, Red, and the disembodied voice inhabiting the Transistor itself. The fighting system is simultaneously complex and easy to understand; you can easily get sucked into the many combinations of active and passive powers, limiters and more. Or you can cruise by, choosing the more obviously powerful powers and smashing your way through with far less finesse.
In many games there is the struggle between the dynamic of a voiceless playable character and the companion that usually functions as a guide, giving exposition and providing help - hopefully in a more entertaining matter than drop-down menus. In some cases it can work well (think Midna and Link in LOZ Twilight Princess) and in other cases it can be very annoying (think Fi and Link in LOZ Skyward Sword). Transistor fulfills both rolls beautifully, even providing reasons for both characters being as they are. Red has lost her voice. She can communicate only by humming and typing messages in the half-broken terminals they come across. Her sword, a sexy disembodied voice that sounds like it has smoked a generous amount of cigarettes, provides the perfect balance of letting you know what's going on and where you should go without ever making you feel like he's just a bit of recording. He talks a lot because he feels helpless; he has no body, after all and is entirely dependent on Red. The two make a great pair and their interaction really makes the game worthwhile.
Where the game falls short, however, is in two areas. The actual world itself is very limited. At a glance it looks huge and you think you're about to explore this massive, post-apocalyptic city, empty of inhabitants. However, in reality, you are basically being carted along a tunnel, with very limited choice in where you can go and what you can do. For the most part, you walk along a prescripted path, fight the monsters you are supposed to face, leveling up enough to beat the boss, then it's off to the next part. Rinse and repeat. There are very limited  options for exploring and none for backtracking that I could find. No side quests, except for the 'Beach' area which is a series of challenges, or tests.
Now, to give the game credit, because of the excellent atmosphere and voice acting, this did not really bother me as much as it might have. I enjoyed the voice in the sword leading me along this strange and mysterious world. However, I would have enjoyed it more if I could have broken into buildings, maybe met a few people, discover secrets, go down secret alleyways, unlock new things and have multiple endings and/or methods to traverse and ultimately beat the game.
The other area where the game let me down is in the ultimate unraveling of the story. There is a lot of build-up, and world-building going on. Every power you collect has information on a colorful variety of characters with very interesting histories. I looked forward to reading each one. The 'terminals' where you can answer polls, even change the weather are fascinating, provide Red a chance to 'speak' as she types out responses and further flesh out the world and story. All of this is great because it gives you information about the world without dumping exposition on you. But in the end, very little is resolved. I don't want the story force-fed to me and I don't mind some ambiguity, but it seems such a shame that so much time was spent on build-up and very little on explaining what exactly happened, how, why and so on. I ended the game feeling quite unsatisfied and wanting to know a lot more. However, the ending is VERY good, perhaps a perfect ending, and a great boss battle.
Transistor is very much worth buying. It is fun, interesting and has a great battling system. It has its flaws, but so does any game. If the premise sounds interesting to you than I'm sure you won't regret playing it!

The soulsborne series of games is known to harbor some of the most innovative and exciting action-rpg games of the past decade. Whilst Dark Souls 2 (DS2) is part of this illustrious collection, it is the weakest of the Souls games, but this does not make it a bad game…not by a long shot. DS2 builds on many of the strengths of the first Souls game; it has strong combat, challenging encounters, the most diverse array of spells in a Souls game, an enthralling musical score, and for me, oh so important, it is rich in lore.
Yet, it stumbles in places such as the many lackluster boss fights and uninteresting locations to explore. In general, the game’s design suffers from repetition and reskinning. Many boss fights feel as if they are the same boss just reskinned to look different; and the same applies to the locations you will spend approximately 30+ hours exploring. Also, it is by far the most conservatively designed outing in the Souls series, never really hitting that “OMG…what the ♥♥♥♥ is that?” factor that the first and third games do so well. However, a major redeeming factor are the dlc expansions that add much variety in terms of enemies, locations, and expanding the story and lore vaguely explained in the initial release. 8/10

After all the negative reviews when this title came out, I never bothered to get Rome 2.
Recently I got it on sale, so last week I decided to give it a try. I launched and saw the most ugly intro.
It ends with a bit of morale lesson, but the characters facial animations and textures are so bad it failed to convey.
In the menu I select the campaign as the Roman Empire in its early days and apparently I'm at war with the Etrusken League, my Northern neighbors. The map looks georgeous like they always do in TW. My first battle is a bit disappointing though, my red dressed melee infantry look like they have wooden cutting boards attached to their chests and back. Fortunately even these troops get visual armor upgrades later on in the game, looking more like something roman.
After capturing the two northern cities I turn my attention to Corsica and Sardinia to the West, the last of the Etrusken cities. When my army sails around the island to kick in the backdoor, their general starts to reqruit like crazy. So I sent my spy to set fire to their barracks. But when my spy arrived I found out there were no barracks at all.
Cheating ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ mofo AI...
After putting the league to sleep I decided all of Italy belongs to Rome and set out to conquer Northern Italy.
I made some vital mistakes during this campaign which halted my advance in the long run.
During this campaign I ended up in war with 3 tribes to the North, the Nori, the Helvetii and the Raeti, so it seemed like a good idea to form an alliance with Massilia - the tribe located between Rome and Spain - also with the invasion of Hannibal in mind.
I ended up being stuck in the North defending my new territory against 2 bar-experience armies, while the idea was to conquer Carthage next. But I lacked resources for campaigns on multiple fronts.
Cheating ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ mofo AI...
After resisting the northern tribes for some time they offered me a peace treaty. Great! just the brake I needed to start my campaign against Carthage. But soon my northern territories were flooded by spies and champions, harrassing the crap out of my generals and towns. When I tried to subverge one of them I was notified I have to declare war first, but apparently the AI did not have to.
Cheating ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ mofo AI...
I ended up razing two of the three northern towns and almost got run over by the Nori.
Heavily outnumbered and outclassed I managed to subjugate the Nori, make my way South towards Greece and conquer Carthage at the same time. This resulted in some truely amazing battles. I loved balancing my armies and experimenting with testudo in 3 line checker board formations. I love how the front line of melee infantry automatically shifted from testudo into a toothed line to hold the storming madmen. Great job, nice detail! I love historical accuracy. Together with the cinematic views the battles can be quite a spectacle.
On the downside, when your units charge, they just run straight to their target and forget to look militairy. They all end up in the same spot and it seems collision between friendly units is lacking.
And maybe I'm just doing something right but the battles don't last very long. Average about 5 minutes. It's also a hassle to adopt your armies to the coming threat as troops can only move with generals. And somehow it always feels like an army is a few slots short.
On with the campaign, when I finally got rid of those pesky Asterix and Obelix tribes, my ally Massillia was whiping them all out and was well on his way to Romania. I checked his ally and he conquered all the land West of Carthage, so I was pretty much surrounded by an ally that got dangerously powerfull. It didn't take long before Masillia started to demand military access or else... So I desperately started looking for an alliance to counter the new threat, but none of the other cultures liked me anymore. In the end my empire fell to Pesky Spain!
What a bloody mess with the blood & gore DLC (which should have been included in the 1st place)

Number 2: Servers - Servers can be largely different, some with Roleplay and Player vs. Player, just building, no roleplay and night pvp, most with very specific rules, and the rest with completely different specific rules. The biggest problem would be lack of players with to many servers, which spreads the player base. Finally for the servers, if you find a server just right for you, it's probaly on the opposite side of the world... Number 3: Lack of Content - Many people would argue, but in large open world games, theres always a lack of content. While many fans of 'The Dark Descent' will undoubtedly want to crack open my skull and paint 'The Last Supper' with the grey matter inside for saying this, I actually think that I prefer 'Amnesia: A Machine For Pigs' to it's predecessor.  Don't get me wrong. This is not just a deliberate attempt to disparage 'Amnesia: The Dark Descent' which is a brilliant game in it's own right. I just feel that 'A Machine For Pigs' has been given a very bad rep as of late and I believe unfairly so.
My reasoning is primarily that the story feels so much more relevent to this day and age than the story for 'The Dark Descent'. With it's anti-hero, industrialist-turned-luddite Mandus, the far more rigid and story-driven plot of 'A Machine For Pigs' dissects the self-destructive nature of capitalism which so often becomes exposed when the shiny surface veneer has been stripped away. Thus, the game is best experienced when regarded as a piece of Gothic revisionism instead of the usual mix of haunted house cliches featured in other games.
Also enjoyable is the more effective use of lighting. Other reviewers have complained about the lack of hiding places in comparison to 'The Dark Descent' but I for one applaud the move. Make no mistake, I enjoy stealth-horror gaming as much as the next genre fan. However, when playing a first-person adventure, there are few things that I find more stunting than being forced to cower in a cupboard like a frightened child. In 'A Machine For Pigs' this feature has been adapted to suit the improved transform and lighting effects. No longer simply an atmospheric tool, the innovative use of light and shadow once more becomes the main tool for the game's stealth element, which in my opinion works just as well.
Ultimately, the emotional power of 'Amnesia: A Machine For Pigs' is the same emotional power apparent in late 19th Century Gothic literature. It is a world where the monstrocity of the modern urban metropolos far surpasses the monsters that lurk within. A maddening network of claustrophobic corridors and miles of endless pipelines left to rust at the behest of condensed steam and personal neglect. Above all, much like Daniel in 'The Dark Descent', the Horror of Mandus' story comes not so much from the fact that he is being hunted by monsters but from the sheer bleakness and solitude of being so profoundly alone in such a harsh world. A world built by monsters where monsters dwell. Sound familiar?
Story, impressive visuals and fitting atmosphere aside, 'A Machine For Pigs' does have the one glaring draw back of mainly being an exploration based game. Like 'The Dark Descent' and 'Layers of Fear', this game can only truly be enjoyed if you do everything in your power to soak in the experience and immerse yourself in the grim, hopless setting (something which some gamers will have trouble doing). Also, comparison to 'Amnesia: The Dark Descent' WILL compromise the playing experience. No ifs. No buts. It just will. Instead, 'Amnesia: A Machine For Pigs' should be approached as naively as possible. As with SH series fans who are playing 'Silent Hill: Downpour' for the first time, this game should be regarded solely as a stand-alone title with no similarity to the previous games. If you can achieve this, then 'Amnesia: A Machine For Pigs' becomes far more pallatable, and dare I say even a little enjoyable too.

First of all, let say thanks to Frictional Games again for creating such type of games that gave us hours of fear and psychological trauma while lying in bed...
Amnesia: A machine for pigs... The game came out after the successfull and terrifying Amnesia TDD (The Dark Descent). But what about it you would ask ? In the same way as Penumbra, Amnesia will take you within a world of anguish, fear and psychological pressure where your two only weapons... Are hiding and running. Yes you are weak, yes you will experienced fear, yes you will have to hide. The games strongly rely on atmoshpere and it is important to immerse yourself as much as possible for an increased gaming experience.
Within the beginning of an industrialized London, you are Oswald Mandus, owner of a meat processing company, on the lookout for your children who strangely disappeared... Or maybe something else. Through the shady and smelly streets of London to the deepest corridors of your factory, you will look for them and make some terrific discovery about your business... And about yourself.
As mentioned, the gameplay follows the same one as the previous games such as Penumbra, Amnesia TDD (or later ones sch as SOMA): You will solve puzzles, and your two only weapons in this game will be to run and hide. No weapons, only a light and your brain to survive. Nothing else !
Time now for some pros and cons...
First of all the atmoshpere and ambiance of the game... Clearly, we can see a important difference with Amnesia TDD: Not as terrifying. This particular point mainly come from the facts that your euipment for example and especially the light is no longer limited with fuel as it was in TDD. Consequenly you do not have really this particular feeling of emergency or need for light which was omnipresent in TDD and could drive you insane, without seeing any potential thing that could come to you in a room or corridor.
Nonetheless rest assured that thanks to its storyline, it will guarantee you a much more sordid atmoshpere and feeling of deep malaise than TDD.
Regarding the gameplay... We will unfortunately quite regret as I mentioned the insanity system, the unlimited light, the night-vision effect also (You would see slightly better in the dark while crouching...)... And the interactions with the environment. Indeed, where it was almost possible to throw or move any chair, box and books in TDD; A Machine for pigs will restrict your movements to the minimum. Choice of the creators or just screw up ? I would tend to say that the game design is responsible as the game appears much more linear and "corridor" made than TDD where you could visit in any order the different places of the castle (To some point).
Conclusion ?
Despite having been made in a much more "simple" way than TDD, with less interactions with the world and less oppressive gameplay, Amnesia A Machine for Pigs will still be able to guarantee you some nice gaming hours, with an increasing sordid atmosphere the further you complete the game. You will definitively find it different as its predecessor but should like it at least for its story. Nice to have in your library if you like this kind of game !

After trying this game a fourth time, I still can't recommend this at all. Tree of Savior, like any Korean MMO, has a LOT of grinding, but little to no purpose for grinding. At the start of my fourth attempt, I made it a point to talk to some of the community, and get some information about things in the later stages of the game. First, I'd asked when the game starts to pick up, which is apparently at level 100. I didn't quite make it there, only managed 74, but I jumped in with a bunch of friends this time that made it way farther than I did, two of them going past level 200 even. To start with, I'll be talking about the early game.
The early game is easily one of this game's weakest points. Right off the bat, you have a half-baked story questline shoved down your throat, which doesn't bode well. All the quests in this game are exactly the same, that being the interchangeable "Kill five two-legged onion people and get thier nipple piercings for me to assemble into a chain to shove into my ear and pull out of the other ear so I can floss my brain." Plug in whatever scenario you wish, it's probably better than whatever the writers came up with.
So, the story and quests are a bust. They aren't the main way to level up, however. Most of your levels will come from killing sixteen quadrillion monsters over and over, which would be fine if they didn't become progressively more tanky, making it take SEVEN hits per enemy in the level 70 area. Crowd control skills would come in handy, if using them didn't eat through your MP like a seven hundred pound man at an all-you-can-eat-buffet. I only managed to get to 74 because I had a Canadian Cleric giving me an OP buff, which we will call, "The Good", that causes attacks to just one shot everything.
So if you don't have a cleric friend, or unlimited silver to buy The Good from (yes, you can sell buffs to people) the various clerics in the starting town, grinding is also a bust. And did I mention MP potions have a long cooldown? Once you get to 50, though, you can start doing dungeons. The level 50 dungeon will get you to 75 in no time, if it weren't for only being able to enter a dungeon two times a day. Three times if you pay real money. And you absolutely need to do dungeons to get anywhere after 50. But not only are you limited in how many dungeons you can do a day, there's also an item that just CLEARS THE DUNGEON FOR YOU. I wish I was making this up. They're only obtained from monster drops however, so I'll let that one slide.
At this point, I threw in the towel and deemed the game unworthy of my time. From there, I talked to my buddies that were still playing the game, and they confirmed for me that the game DOES NOT get better after level 100. You just get higher level dungeons to do. And after your daily runs, you literally just log out until the next day. You could go do some PvP in the meantime, if the system wasn't horrendously unbalanced. There are multiple attacks that can kill players outside PvP, for example. The attack doesn't stop after a duel has ended, and health doesn't go back up to full after a duel. So with one HP left, the onslaught doesn't end and simply kills you. And when you die, you lose EXP and gems you're carrying. And when you lose EXP, you can actually DE-LEVEL. So all the time spent getting that level is wasted. Need I remind you, it can take HOURS to get a level. And those gems? Those also take hours upon hours to improve.
PvP isn't just a bust; it's flat out broken. That leaves the PvE situation. Endgame PvE consists of, you guessed it, more dungeons. There's also this tower thing, but that's just a glorified dungeon. The game literally has nothing to keep players playing. The only ones remaining are just there because they've already dumped too much time and money into this game.
Sidenotes:
You need to pay real money to transfer ingame money to other characters on the same account. Yuck.
Basic functions such as trading are behind unreasonable restrictions. Level 40 to unlock trading doesn't sound bad, but as mentioned before, grinding is fundamentally broken.
Customization is nonexistant. Expect to look like everyone else.
Early game doesn't have any real content; just pointless repetetive quests.
Marketplace tax is unreasonable for a new player. Silver is very slow to get early on.
Cash shop sells a lot of stuff that gives ingame functionality, just as EXP boosts that wreck everyone that doesn't have them. Can argue pay for convenience, but I label it pay to win as the entire game is inconvenient.

The game follows the exploits he tells on a saloon over several beers, and its gimmick is that things happen as Greaves tells them, sometimes backing up on his claims, interrupted by his listeners, or sometimes just plain making♥♥♥♥♥♥up to get their attention, complete with duels and garish stories that most certainly didn't ever happen.
So why did I buy the game again when I have it already on Platinum in CD-ROM? Well, because it's a very enjoyable game, it's rather replayable, the graphics hold up very well, mustic's great, it's got Steam achievements, and it's a great product of Ubisoft's pre-Uplay era. Simple, well done, and its Arcade mode is great for a quick get-your-rocks-off play session. It's a great shooter that I absolutely recommend to everyone who hasn't played it yet. 8/10.

Call of Juarez Gunslinger stands out from today's shooters (besides its setting) by focusing on making the shooting an enjoyable experience. There is a score system in place giving you bonus points for chaining up kills in a relatively fast time window, getting headshots, killing people who just ran into sight, etc.
The time period itself is a pleasant setting to play such a game in. The graphics are nice and colourful. The story is great background noise. It gets told through voiceover during gameplay, since the main character is retelling his life in a bar. This means there are only a handful cutscenes that keep you from the action.
It however starts to drag along a bit, not freshening up its formula after a while. You will simply start approach every encounter the same way. It's a good thing the game ended when it did.
