World of Goo is a physics-based puzzle game where we get to mess around with silly sentient spheres of ooze. The object of any level is pretty simple—move as many gooballs from point A to point B as quickly as you can. You can build towers and bridges, break down your towers or bridges, or hoist gooey-pink balloons on top of other, denser oozing inkblots to lift your structures into the air.
Though most of the levels are fairly simple, World of Goo offers some refreshingly quirky, downright silly art, with highly addictive gameplay. It's been a long time since I've been so engrossed in playing a game that I lose track of time, so when I looked up from my screen to see three hours passed since I first clicked on the icon, I realized I was playing a classic.
World of Goo is an utterly charming adventure that any gamer, or lover-of-fun would be severely remiss in avoiding. It's not quite perfect, but it manages to capture an element not-often seen in more modern games: it's a helluva lot of fun.

Alrighty, so after playing for a few days I've decided to write a review for all that wish to purchase this game.
I got this on sale During Christmas and got everything for around 80ish USD. Though, I can't say it was worth it.
The Game itself is enjoyable with friends and can lead to a lot of fun and the co-op campaign is great when your armies meet. But, It's not a good game. So here's a quick Pro/Con list
Pros
-Expansive Grand Campaign Map
-Nice Looking Maps
-The design of the Seige maps and Port Battles are Amazingly fun
-Good Free DLC
Mehs
-Graphics, They're kind of in the middle, nothing outstanding but nothing outright garbage.
Cons
-Horrid AI, I cannot stress this enough
-AI Skirmish Mode, The fact that 3 Slinger units can outrun and kill around 15 Units of Hoplites is absolutley disgusting. It's not an issue when you have Cavalry but that takes awhile to get for some nations.
-Around 95% of the DLC that costs money is Garbage, Horribly un-fleshed out nations and generally not worth the cash
-Friendly AI (And I quote, Defensive Allies) WILL RAID YOU, BREAK YOUR BARRICADES AND SET OFF YOUR DEPLOYABLES DURING DEFENSIVE SEIGE BATTLES, AND GENERALLY BETRAY YOU AT EVERY TURN. I've even had defensive allies declaring war on "Vassal States" of mine.
-Randomly Being Kicked from Games while Hosting (It's a serious issue when I'm Hosting and get Kicked mid-battle)
-The UI is honestly Garbage but you can work around
-The Advisor tells you nothing useful and only serves to give you relatively basic information
-Arideai (One of the Pirate Pack Nations) Gets absolutely nothing in terms of good melee infantry, It's hard to win fights without sneaking half your force behind the enemy and none of your 18 Billion Spear Units can use Phalanx formation.
-There are 3 General Trees for most Nations with a few getting a special tree (I.E Rome). Honestly, only one of them is useful which is the Commander tree because Rally is byfar the greatest help to any army.
-The Custom Battle Units do not match the units you can receive in Campaign, For Example, Roxolani can only use Cavalry in custom battle but you get an amount of infantry and archers in campaign.
I won't lie, there are more but frankly while writing this list I forgot some of them, I'm sure i'll remember once I boot the game up again but as far as this is, While the game is fun for a bit, It's a FAR shot from a good game.
Overall the game is a 3/10

The scariest part of A Machine for Pigs for me was the beginning; not because it was actually scary, but because I was all psyched out thinking about TDD. After playing for a bit, I realized nothing was really happening, so I calmed down and stayed calm. I don't really remember much of the story any more, just that it read like someone took the "scary" creative writing assignment of a sixteen year old and turned it into a game. The "reveal" in the story was ridiculously obvious from the beginning, and I wouldn't have thought about it as a "reveal" except that I remember them making a big deal about it. You can't attempt a "soylent green is people" moment when every bit of narrative you provide is as heavy handed as opening a freezer and seeing a box labeled "totally not people parts". AMFP was such a disappointment.
Even if it wasn't a let down, $20 for a game that has less than 5 hours of playability (and I actually explored as much as this walking simulator lets you), isn't really worth it.

I'm going to start this review a bit from the middle.
There are way too many freaking notes from the main character. He writes a note after every single thing he does. "I solved this puzzle! I must now move onwards into this madness!", "I opened this door! My epic struggle continues!", "I farted into an oven! When will my nightmare end?!". There is no point to most of them, they provide no worthwhile insight into the mind of the protagonist. Unless you consider him repeating the same god-damn thing in 10 different ways as insight. Other notes are very frequent too. There's a note in every other room. In addition, the game has one of the cringiest lines I have ever had the displeasure to read:
I have no idea how the writer decided "yep, that's an exceptional piece of work, nothing cringeworthy to see here". Also, I'm not even going to write down the note where a character apparently
. What's more, the game drowns you in needless metaphors and analogies: nearly every note uses elaborate manners of describing the simplest of things. The pretentiousness is palpable at times, which is a shame, since the game's story is overall thought-provoking and worth exploring further. It takes a while to get going, but the ending is pretty intense and I loved the ending monologue from
.
The music is really good and stands out.
Enemy encounters very few and far between and are easily avoided by just running past. They lose interest surprisingly fast and are not persistent like the ones in The Dark Descent - just shut a door in their face and they'll leave. This makes the game almost a walking simulator: almost, because you can die... if you stand still and let yourself get hit.
As an Amnesia game, is this scary? Nope. Is it worth buying? 4 hours of a good story and soundtrack and notes every 30 seconds: buy for $5 or less.

What I am saying is: I have no problem with it sharing the Amnesia name,  however with all of the features that were changed or removed e.g. infinite lantern, no inventory, no insanity meter; etc, they (The Chinese Room) could have crafted a new style of story telling without the documents.  Something that matched the pace of the game.  Really, the story seems epic, but I understood nothing of it due to such awful pacing.

To put it simply: It's alright. It was made by the same people involved in Dear Esther - and the influence takes over the original Amnesia feel. The original Amnesia was a great game, especially considering it wasn't a triple A publisher. A lot of what made the original game so great is not at the forefront this time around.
*potential spoilers*
The game starts with the same scary vibe, but after a few minutes that completely diminishes. You have an infinite supply of light, something that was scarce and added to the tension of the first game. That on its own isn't a game breaker, BUT - there is now a system in place that WARNS YOU when an enemy is nearby. Not only does it warn you when an enemy is nearby, but there are barely any enemies to speak of. I spent a good majority of the first half of the game with anticipation, just waiting to be scared. Go into a new room "oh god, I hope there isn't anything spooky in here" nothing. Next room, nothing. By the time the game actually starts to pick up place, that feeling of dread is completely replaced with a feeling of boredom. There were a few moments of being scary, but for the most part it feels more just like you're playing an interactive story like Dear Esther rather than ever actually feeling the need to survive.
The game isn't horrible. On its own, I think it is a decent enough game - but as an Amnesia successor, and judging it as so - the game isn't that great.
If you can get it for a decent price, and are a diehard fan of the first game - it's worth it just to experience, but it isn't anything quite as memorable.

If you liked Myst at all (or if you like puzzle games in general) this one is fantastic.  It's exactly like the original Myst, but it has normal first person controls and operates fluidly (unlike the original which simply a series of images and quicktime videos).
Myst is simple enough that you never really feel stumped, but it's tricky enough in most cases to make you feel accomplished when you solve something.  The upgrade to a "live" world totally transforms too, and makes it much more fun to play.

realMyst is the classic point-and-click exploration puzzle game Myst, recreated with a proper 3D engine now that computers can render its visuals in real time.
Unfortunately, the game has a dependency that it neglects to install, so you'll have to do so manually.  The game will run without it, but not without massive framerate issues and crashing, and the videos in the linking books won't show up.  You'll need to install the Ligos Indeo Video 5 codec, which can be found on
, and reportedly on Windows 7, you'll need to set Windows XP SP3 compatibility mode.
Anyway, doesn't a 3D, real time rendered version of Myst sound awesome?  Well, yes.  Yes, it is.  It's still the classic game you know and love, but updated with a healthy dose of modern technology.  In addition, once you beat the game, you get clues on how to access a 5th age that's exclusive to this version of Myst, called Rime.  There's not much to Rime, but it's neat regardless.

Myst is one of the best games out there. A stunning, challenging, and intersting adventure game, it has captured the hearts of many gamers (myself included) since 1993. And now, we have realMYST, the best copy of Myst in all of existence. Conclusion: BUY IT XD.

The first of a five part series, Myst was released back in 1993, and was one of the few true Puzzle games with a RPG element: Story.  While I didn't appreciate it when I first played it back in '94, it was one of the few games available on the elementry school's library computer back then, and it's puzzles were difficult (at least, to my 6th grade self it was).
realMYST, is a step forward... literally.  The original Myst was point and click to move or to manipulate the environment of the current "room" you were in.  realMYST is redone with full 3d movement, with all puzzles and textures intact.
Although the whole series aren't available to the PC market; Myst, Riven, and End of Ages are available, and are a must-have for any true puzzle fan.

You only use your mouse when playing (no keyboard input) so you can kick you feet up and play.
The biggest downside to this game is that it's short; 5 chapters of different puzzle boxes. But if you can pick this game up for cheap (again, I only spent a dollar), it's worth your money.
LASTLY, the only bug I found was if you play on a monitor above 60Hz, the sliding blue gem puzzle near the end will be unsolvable. You need to lower your Hz setting on your monitor OR switch your game to windowed mode and move your window to a monitor that IS on 60Hz, and then you can solve the puzzle.

EDIT: After playing Scholar of the First Sin, and then this, I have an actual opinion now.
This game is really a mixed bag. It does a lot of things right, but also does a lot of things wrong.
It is fun though, and I guess that's okay, but you have to go through so much crap to actually HAVE fun.

Here's some of the crap you have to put up with:
The beginning of the game is REALLY confusing and can easily scare off new players. There are 2 areas to go to from the start; Heide's Tower of Flame and Forest of Fallen Giants. If you go to Heide's Tower of Flame, enemies there will tank a lot damage you deal to them and in turn DEAL a lot of damage. Yet despite the enemies in this area, the bosses in this area are EXTREMELY easy. Forest of the Fallen Giants is clearly the way to go, with enemies more scaled to a starting player. Both of these areas end up at the Lost Bastille at some point.

Another flaw in DS2's design philosophy was more enemies=difficulty, and while that may be the case, it's not FAIR difficulty. There's a big difference.

Some people also complain about the world not making sense and while that may be an issue to some, in this specific case it's not too big of a problem.

And personally, I feel that DS2 has really clunky movement and combat, reminiscent of Demon's Souls, but that might just be me.
Here's the fun stuff:
The game immediately picks up after the Lost Bastille, because by that time you'll have decent armor and weapons, so you can actually start making progress.
The game looks and runs really good at high graphics, running a solid 60fps with little to no frame drops, and even if you have a potato computer you could still play this game at a decent framerate.
The bosses are really fun, with the exception of a select few.
Pvp is actually kind of fun, unlike DS1 and DS3, where it's an R1 spamming♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥
TL;DR, Dark Souls II is actually a pretty decent game, and I'd recommend getting it if you're patient and willing to put up with the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.

This game certainly has improved quite a lot since CBT.
I've played the game for quite a while and can say that a lot of issues encountered earlier on were fixed. Though, there are still some problems remaining, it's so much better than what it was a few months ago.
What the game is:
- Choose between four base classes; Swordsman, Cleric, Wizard, and Archer. Experience gained is split onto Base and Class level, after every 15 class levels, you get to advance your character to a different class, or upgrading a class you've taken already. You get new skills or upgrades to your older ones for advancing.
- You have two starting cities to choose from: Orsha and Klaipeda. Both cities have different storylines, but you can do both upon reaching level 100.
- Combat system is similar to Ragnarok Online, moving your character over the map, attacking and killing enemies for XP/Drops.
- Dungeons are available to be ran starting level 50. They are short(or long for a certain dungeon) instances where you can solo for silver, or queue up with a party(preferred) for high XP gains. You can run twice(thrice with Token). Upon reaching level 100, Missions become available, similar to dungeons, but giving you tasks to complete.
- Gears and such are often buyable from Auction House, or by farming them. Most often recipes are obtained, requiring you to craft them using the recipe + the materials needed according to the recipe.
What you should expect:
Graphics-wise:
- ToS has graphics similar to old-school RPG's, with sprites reminding you of the 1990's JRPG's made in 3D.
- NPC portraits, on the other hand, are works of art done by Maggi. My personal favourite is the Rune Caster Master Shelly Pennington's portrait.
Sound-wise:
- Beautiful is an understatement, ToS offers quite a large selection of BGM's that fit well with the map's scheme. It's honestly amazing and well-done.
Gameplay-wise:
- If you're into grinding/farming types of MMO's ToS will appeal quite well to you, having large amounts of gears on varying level ranges means that if you're a min-maxer/grinder at heart, you're going to have a field day.
Pros:
- Old-school style gameplay, with graphics reminding you of Ragnarok Online, or Final Fantasy Tactics.
- 'VIP' access via Tokens can be bought on the Market/Auction House, along with some costumes, meaning you don't have to spend $$$ to buy premium content, unless you're planning on buying hairstyles/eye lenses.
- Large amount of character builds to choose from, allowing you to mix and match classes and ranks to your preferred playstyle. With combat revamp more builds become viable to choose from.
Cons:
- Game is very lag-sensitive, and will disconnect you very often if your internet is the slightest bit intermittent.
- The game has been optimized a few months ago, but it still runs kind of crap compared to other more CPU-intensive games.
- Lack of a way to test out character skills before commiting to a class means that you'll go in blindly to your preferred build, or need to base off off Youtube/other players.
- Endgame gear takes weeks, if not months, to farm. Mitigated by the new hunting grounds giving rather great gear.
- The recent change of DPK to %tage for droprates caused some items to drop at a horrendously lower rate.
- Rather small playerbase means you'll be soloing for a bit.
Neutral:
- Not Pay 2 Win, unless you're planning on whaling via RMT with other people. Release of Leticia's Cube made me want to reconsider the non-p2w part of the game. It's something I didn't expect would even be released.
The best way to play the game is get a group of friends to play with you, or join a guild early on to help you with things. There's a new player event right now that helps you on reaching level 100 easier, along with Goddess' Lada's present giving out some neat items, namely a costume, hair colour dye, headgear, and lenses, along with a Token.
Also to note is that the game is free to play, you're free to try it out if it's your type or not.

Oblivion, Skyrim and now ESO -- I like this game a lot more than I thought I would, tbh.  After playing WoW for 10+ years, and then trying other MMOs, (and deleting them), I was more than happy to discover a MMO that can compete directly with Blizzard's juggernaught.
Like the early days of Vanilla WoW, ESO dumps you into a world with minimal preparation and a tutorial that covers base movement and combat.  Everything else is pretty much up to you in terms of discovery and depth.   Unlike what WoW has evolved into, ESO requires some thought, planning and coordination - it's not an MMO "button masher" even if you are limited to six spells/actions on your action bar.  Seven if you include potions.
Like most Bethesda games, the open-world is done exceptionally well.  You can spend hours playing how you want, for whatever your current mood is, without penalty.
There are some significant game-play changes from the Skyrim so don't expect a 1<->1 experience - it's very, very different.  I do enjoy the level of character customization with skill-point allocation, the crafting, and the combat play.  As alluded to previously, I do wish there were more action-buttons on-screen so that I can have more of an option range, but it works as-is.  I suppose this "feature" is a limitation driven by console play.
I have no problems subscribing -- $15/month is a pretty decent ROI for a game of this caliber.  I have a long way to go before I figure out all the class/character combinations.  The racial divides don't make a lot of sense to me other than establishing different starting points on the world map -- I suppose it's more important if you PvP which is an aspect of the game I intentionally avoid.
All-in-all, it's a great experience, great game play, and a lot of fun.

There are far better MMORPGs out there in terms of both game mechanics and atmosphere and immersion - I would recommend WoW, Neverwinter and Age of Conan any day over ESO. I guess the only gamers who would really love ESO are only die hard Elder Scrolls fans who have been dreaming since forever to see the whole of Tamriel in an open-world game.
However, I wouldn't keep their hopes up too much. The game just doesn't achieve a good enough level of immersion in the world compared to other MMORPGs. It has boring maps and levels with very little to do apart from going through the story.
Also - there are some ridicilous things that you have to pay additional money for through the online game store -  like expanding your inventory slots, and buying the Imperial race. Yes, your inventory has very limited slots and yes, after FIVE Elder Scrolls games where we could play as Imperials, now we have to pay for them. So you either pay additional cash or you just play a half-baked game that constantly forces you to manage your inventory.
Now, it's possible that the end-game phase is very different, but the game still needs to keep the player interested enough to reach it. The story itself is nothing new and original. It takes place in the distant past (Second Age) and guess what - a daedric prince wants to conquer the world. Wait... What?! Didn't we play this already in a game called Oblivion?! Oh, and guess what - we were allowed to play as an Imperial there without paying additional money!
Not worth.

Alright, I love the total war series, and I can gladly say that this is indeed a good game. But even with all the updates and patches since the first release of this game, it still has some glaring issues that I'd like to point out.
So let's start with the positives of this game. The games campaign is pretty fun, but the fun was doubled when I played this game with my friend. Playing as parthia and baktria and becoming a powerful conjoined empire was massive fun.
I also think the diplomacy in this game is for the most part good, your allies generally won't attack you out of the blue. The inner politics update also added another layer to this game, albeit a thin one, but still one you must engage in.
The battles are okay. They can feel like a chore sometimes, but the battles are servicable. As someone who's first total war game was the first rome total war, the battle system does not feel nearly as fluid as they did for Rome I, but it was done well enough that it is not always painful to fight battles out.
The biggest proble I have with this game comes mostly from the ai's stupidity. The game feels too easy on the normal difficulty. I have united 4 gallic tribes including myself via confederation by turn 38 on normal difficulty. And Rome is nowhere near us. Also, generally the ai spam bottom tier units. I expected this might happen in the early game, but when me and my friend betrayed a bunch of our four allies for land, I expected it to be a hard fight, and while sagartia was a huge pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ I beat a 20 unit army with a seven unit garrison and a general. It was ridiculous.
Also, one very ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t buisness practice that I cannot support is having many playable factions put behind a paywall. If you were hoping to play sparta or athens, well I am sorry to disapoint you but you have to pay 8$ and if you paid 60$ for this game you're going to feel so ripped off. Without the "paywall factions" the game is playable, but to some who really like the factions locked behind the paywall, this game is going to feel like a skeleton of what it could be.
I am not absolutely against the idea of additional campaigns that you have to pay for like for example, Caesar in Gaul, though just the idea that have to pay for additional factions already in the grand campaign.
They also have a dlc for blood in the game. What a ♥♥♥♥ing joke.
So what do I think overall? Despite my adoring of this game's time period, and the amount of fun I have had with this game thus far, it's still 7/10 material. If someone asked me what was a better game between this and shogun 2, I'd say buy shogun two. If you really like the time period in which this takes place though, as I do, then you will probably enjoy it more than shogun two though.
But, my only reccomendation I can give you is please, but this while it is on sale.

I have played several MMOs but A Realm Reborn (ARR) is one of the few that has maintained my interest. Maybe it's the franchise name. Maybe it was simply timing. All I know is I enjoy it.
Now I know there are people who dislike it, so I'm trying to keep this level-headed. ARR offers similar gameplay to current popular MMOs. It borrows a little from World of Warcraft and Guild Wars 2, but it feels unique in that it still IS Final Fantasy. By that I mean, you get a lengthy story with with occasional cutscenes, sometimes voiced. It might not be the greatest story, but it's a feature that I felt was missing from other MMOs I have played.
Luckily, I had a few friends already playing the game so it wasn't hard to find people to help get me started. I have found in my experiences though that even the regular community is helpful and cordial. Of course, there are people who aren't so friendly, but for the most part the people are well-humored and fun.
Another cool feature is your character is never limited to a single class. If you reach max level with one class, you can easily take up other classes after. So while each class/job(think prestige class) has their specific roles, your character is never limited to just one.
ARR is a massive time sink, however. What game isn't though especially an MMO? At the time of this writing, I am pretty sure ARR tops my list for longest played game. If you can't dedicate to the time or the monthly subscription fees, I wouldn't suggest the game. But if you are looking for a solid MMO, look no further.
Also, it's always worth playing through Hildibrand. Trust me.

Short version: This art-house action-RPG comes with an unconventional/semi-turn based battle system, gorgeous music and visuals, a somewhat thin but wonderfully told narrative, and remarkable integration of gameplay and storytelling.  It's a gem of a game with a decent amount of content and is absolutely worth cherishing.
--------
Long version: Transistor begins gently and without a lot of explanation, giving the player just enough information to know what's going on and where to go.  In short, you're on the run from your would-be assassins, fighting enemies along the way.  You have a sword that talks (voiced by Logan Cunningham, the narrator from Supergiant Games' own Bastion), and the game doesn't bog you down with needless explanations of how a lot of the setting's pieces work.  You quickly acquire abilities as you go, and these skills make Transistor special in several ways:
1) Battles in Transistor work somewhat like Diablo's where you can button-mash if you want, but you can also queue up and instantly execute a limited number of attack commands or move a certain distance without enemy reprisal.  The catch is that until your Turn() meter refills over a few seconds, you can't use most of your attacks, so you have to be careful to play conservatively.  At the same time, you'll eventually become strong enough to where you can and should try to stay in real time more often, which works out well since your time-stop ability can leave YOU vulnerable if you're not careful.
You can only equip a few of your skills as hotkey actives at once, and dying restores your health but disables one of your remaining skills until either you have none left, or you win the battle and make a certain amount of forward progress in the game.  This arguably leaves you even worse off than if you'd simply been forced to restart the fight, which you can also choose to do from the pause menu.  (Note that a few areas place you in big battles right after long interactive cutscenes without giving you a save point first; since battles can sometimes be immediately repeated, try not to hit "Retry" on impulse if circumstances turn against you.)  Enemies usually don't have a lot of defensive immunities, though, which is great about keeping you from feeling penalized for using a certain play style.  They're also smart enough to be aware of one another and to know how to protect and even heal each other.
More importantly, skills never feel redundant, and they're designed to play off of each other, not to exist in isolation or to be used at random.  Your abilities have their own slots where they can plug into one another and change each other's properties.  One skill fires long-ranged arrows when put on a hotkey, but it can also be plugged into other skills, which usually increases their range.  You can later do the same thing with your own character, which grants additional benefits like a deflector shield or a health recharge--one of the few you'll get, so don't take it for granted.
There are no character classes in Transistor, but the wonderful skill system allows you to customize and change up your play style throughout the game.  If you want to play a stealthy assassin, a somewhat tanky gunner, or a manipulator who turns enemies against each other, you have quite a few options to choose from.  The variety of different animations and graphical effects for the huge number of potential skill combinations is simply stunning--these aren't just throwaway stat boosts here--and it makes your abilities feel almost like they physically affect one another rather than simply doing whatever the game tells them to do.  I might have overlooked a way to do this, but it would be nice to be able to simply click an upgrade slot and see my various effect options at a glance, instead of just clicking on a skill itself and seeing the various places it could go.  In other words, "I know what ability I want to augment, but not specifically how I want to do so."
2) This is one of my favorite parts.  Skills are connected to different characters and their individual stories, and while I sometimes don't like when a game presents a lot of its story through text, this method is genius--your abilities' text logs are divided up into parts that must be uncovered by equipping your skills in different ways.  Use one ability in its active mode to get one piece of text, then use that ability to upgrade another and get the next piece of text, and so on.  Hence, the game rewards and demands experimentation if you want to read all of the background info.  You can't get too comfortable with a certain battle strategy you like, since you have to constantly rearrange your skills and try new things with them in order to get the most out of the story, let alone the battles and their fairly sharp challenge curve.  It feels a lot more involving than simply having info dumps thrown at you because you discovered an unfamiliar character or area.
Speaking of difficulty, you can customize it to some extent by turning on various options you earn called Limiters, which increase your rate of experience gain but also help your enemies out in some way.  Have fun turning them all on at once, achievement-lovers!
When you're not battling, you navigate the deserted but absolutely beautiful streets and alleys of the city of Cloudbank, and I can't tell you how refreshing it is to play an adventure that takes you by multicolored, modern-looking restaurants, residential areas, and concert halls as opposed to yet another fantasy forest/desert/cave.  The city feels lived-in and familiar while still maintaining its own distinctive touches, such as weather and sky color being up to a popular vote, which you can take part in.  You'll be taking gorgeous, probably wallpaper-quality screenshots almost constantly--I have almost as many screenshots saved from 20 hours of Transistor as I do from 150 hours of Dota 2.  Even in the few cases where the game's tendency to not always explain itself makes for some genuinely weird encounters, the journey never stops being compelling and never overstays its welcome.
The main story isn't that long, and while you'll fly through it on New Game Plus (especially if you turn off all the limiters after finishing the character-level achievements like I did), the various "challenge room"-style quests will keep you up at night.  My favorites were the planning tests, where you're given a specific loadout and tasked with clearing an area in one turn, which implicitly teaches you new strategy ideas and lets you play around with skills you don't always have immediate access to.  Woe be to those who forget to take notes.
The soundtrack, which Supergiant was wonderful enough to post on YouTube --
-- is for the most part spectacular, even though some of the more intense songs sound better while in the context of the game, like when you're busy running from something dangerous.  Ashley Barrett's vocals are indescribably wonderful, and the game even gives you a dedicated button for humming along to the background music, which gets put to genuinely awesome use at times.
------
Transistor, despite perhaps having room for more detail in the main plot, crams more visual and musical identity into its small but thoroughly memorable scale than I can recall from a lot of much bigger games, and even without the wonderfully fun Turn() system, the skill combinations and the wonderful production values make the combat more special than any number of hotkey bars ever will.  As of this writing, the game is currently on sale for $7, but I'd say it's easily worth its $20 asking price if you don't mind a product that exchanges length for sheer specialness.  Pick this up right away!

I am almost speechless. I just completed Amnesia: A Machine For Pigs and I am beyond lost for words. Overall, I played AAMFP for approximately 9 hours and I loved every minute of it.
In A Machine For Pigs, you take on the role of Mandus who invests all his savings into a meat processing factory years after his wife died of childbirth complications. You wake up in a room with no memory of what occurred, besides the fact that your children are missing. Throughout the story, you discover notes and have flashbacks as to what happened before waking. I have to say, AAMFP is utterly immersive and you can sense the feelings ejected from the characters. For a more detailed explanation visit this link
.
Gameplay was fantastic - it really brang back memories of the previous Amnesia game, The Dark Descent. I experienced very minimal bugs and those which I did happen to come across were minor and did not affect anything. The textures, in my opinion, improved from ATDD and were much more polished and clean. Each area had textures which suited them, and overall, it gave off a steampunk, 19th-century vibe.
The voice acting was incredibly well done. It only helped in getting more insight into the characters regrets, thoughts, personalities and experiences. I loved it, brilliant job. All models were beautifully created too. But what got me the most was the atmosphere. Throughout, you get a feeling of being watched and followed and there are multiple scenes which give you sudden jumps when you least expect it.
However, the only aspect which I disliked was the fact that some features which made ATDD original were removed in AAMFP. In ATDD, oil was a huge part of surviving. If you lingered in darkness for too long, you began to lose sanity. This rocketed the atmosphere and gave you that survival feeling. You also had to search for tinderboxes to light up light sources around you. This was unique. There are pros and cons to this - Having to find oil in order to recharge your lantern often proved difficult and oil was rare. In AAMFP, this is not necessary. This did erase that realistic feeling but it is also helpful as you can use your lantern whenever you please without having to worry about your oil depleting.
As I mentioned, you also don't lose sanity when in darkness. Again, this removed that realistic vibe but was also beneficial as the majority of AAMFP is quite dark.
Regardless, the team did an absolutely astounding job with the atmosphere, tension, climax, gameplay and everything in-between. The ending really hits you and was a huge improvement from the ending in ATDD, as it was led up to well and ended flawlessly. The manpigs roaming every inch of the factory and streets is also nerve wracking. I would recommend Amnesia: A Machine For Pigs to anyone considering buy it. You will not regret it. <3

I have mixed feelings about this game, you could play it but you will probably be dissappointed because it was a huge step back for a title with "Amnesia" in it
Pros:
-The music and sound effects are great and terrifying
-Story is interesting
-Locations and environment are good
-Gives chills
After playing Amnesia: the Dark Descent those are the things i couldnt ignore, it feels that the game lacks so many things, I immediately felt being cocblocked because i couldnt open all the doors and search all the drawers
Cons:
-No inventory
this kills the purpose of exploration and collecting and risking to enter side rooms, which leads to
-Point A to point B gameplay
with no side areas, therefore the only doors which are open are the ones you have to enter to get further into the game
-No sanity meter
Stay in the dark, stare at monsters, do whatever you want: your actions are not punished, you dont have to be careful and balance being in light with a risk of being seen or sitting in the dark, raising insanity meter.
-Infinite lantern
You dont have to manage the oil and use lantern only when needed, just leave it on. I understand they wanted to imply that pigmen cause electric lamp to freak out but it wasnt worth it.
-No tinderboxes
Everything is lighted up already, you dont have to light anything up or manage tinderboxes: no more thrill of limited view
-No places to hide
If in the first Amnesia you didnt have the means to defend yourself, in this game you dont have means to hide! You dont need it because there are no enemies! and if there are you just outrun them, so no more closing doors and sitting in the dark, no more closet hiding
-Cannot interract with many objects
No more stacking boxes on top of each other, no more throwing barrels or books. Thats how you know that if you finally found something you can interact with, you will need it for puzzle
-No puzzles
You could, of course, call pulling levers or spinning wheels a puzzle, but it as dumb as it gets: walk in the room, you see there is a lever, you pull it, you go further.
-Little environmental jumpscares
Yes, there are such things as shaking ground and loud roars, but very little and game mostly scares you through audio, not visuals
-No enemies
There are enemies, of course, but 80% of the game youre so lonely you actually get happy when you are finally being chased
-No stress, no fear
There is no tension throughout the game, it gets very predictable and dull as you progress.
-No immersion
Main Hero doesnt behave like Daniel in ATDD, he fails to express fear
Conclusion: this is my opinion and although i was very dissappointed with the game and completed it just for the sake of the story, you could still play it, go ahead and do so, but dont expect it to be like ATDD. This game doesnt live up to standards set by the first Amnesia, either, as a standalone it is more like a interactive story than a horror stealth game

It's hard to describe exactly what MYST is.  Calling it a "puzzle game" is like calling the graceful albatross "a bird."
People who played it (long ago) nod to each other and sigh, remembering simpler times.
The 3D version retains all of the 2D version's gameplay, and adds some nice environmental features; time of day lighting, dynamic insect life and water.  The graphics are far below modern standards, but it does run at resoultions far higher than the original, with the added bonus of actually being able to move and look around seamlessly.

No really, hear me out.  Myst is a game that came out in the dawn of CD based games, and was hailed as a masterpiece of technology with it's (holy crap) pre-rendered static 3D environments!  This was a game which in 1993 was squarely levelled at the thinking audience, not those playing Super Mario Bros 3.  Adults who never played another computer game in their life could become completely engrossed in this game and its mythology.  In these spoilt brat days of Unreal 3 based gaming, an interactive slideshow is frustrating and unlikely to hold your attention for more than the time it takes you to make one complete circuit of Myst island itself.  Your spatial awareness was so hampered that even the relatively simple puzzles could make you dizzy.  Enter, realMyst.  Yes, it's a DirectX9 engine, but when compared to the technology used to prerender the original game, it's like handing Plato your PSP, and he probably wouldn't have minded Myst.  (Aristotle would've sneered at it.)

I can’t quite articulate the feeling I had when I first awoke deep in the dark haunted depths of Drangleic. The haunting shadows, the sense of isolation, the fear mixed with wonder as I set out to explore.  If you allow yourself to get drawn into this world you will never forget it.
Dark Souls 2 is quite simply one of the greatest games of all time. The game may have its faults, but I cannot see how any rational sane lover of games could give this masterpiece a bad review. You will notice that nearly all the negative are written by people that are either unfairly comparing this to Dark Souls 1 [arguably THE greatest game of all time], or by people that don’t enjoy a challenge in their video games.  Yes, these days most games are designed to be so effortlessly easy to appeal to as large an audience as possible, and to all ages.
For those who are intimidated by the games difficult reputation… yes the game is difficult. [I found it to be far harder than DS3]. But it isn’t difficult for the sake of masochistic punishment. This is not a bullet hell or super meat boy type of difficultly. You can’t beat the game through boring memorisation. You will need skills to beat this game. I'm not sure if this game was supposed to make me feel something or not but it ended up being really, really... dumb. I honestly have no idea what even happened between me and Emily. Apparently something happened, but because the exposition is entirely through dialogue I never found out. The dialogue eventually becomes so limited and clunky that the only emotion I felt was frustration with the writer. I'm not sure whether or not this game is trying to sell me some sort of social message or something but the only lessons I got out of it were:
1) Capitalization is important and you look like an idiot without it.
2) Social skills are important and you look like an idiot without them.
3) Exposition in storytelling is important and you look like an idiot without it.
Emily seems to suffer from what I call "High School Sophomore Syndrome" where not only is she unable to express her emotions, but she is also unable to express if she even has an emotion. But don't worry this can be easily treated by actually being able to talk to someone. See most people are under the illusion that you are the socially awkward character in this game. They're wrong. You AND Emily are the socially awkward ones. Now past this point I'll be talking about spoilers for whatever it is you call this.
Alright spoiler time.
"NONE OF YOUR CHOICES MATTER AND YOU ARE A TERRIBLE PERSON NO MATTER WHAT YOU SAY" is what this game politely screams in your ear. The problem this story throws at you is that you apparently have sex with Emily. No matter what you choose this happens. But the probem is that the very minimalist gameplay is used as a means of exposition. So afterwards you have no idea if the problem is that there was consent involved  or that she is just very confused about how she should feel about it. So I'm going to guess that it was the former of these two (since this game is trying to give a message). The problem is it wants you to feel bad for Emiy after this. So you do. The problem is that you are the defendant in this situation and you honestly end up having no idea what's going on if you choose to feel sorry the dialogue is so extremly wishy-washy that you have no idea what actually happened at all. It doesn't help that Emily also has no idea what happened either. Which in any other situation would convey that she herself is emotionally vulnerable and confused. But somehow this game just made it seem like she instead didn't know how to feel about hooking up with one of her friends. Which is an understandable and justifiable feeling. Except when one of the main characters has no idea what happened and the other one has the emotional comprehension of a sixth grader--and you are completely unable to tell which one of the characters is which. And when dealing with a topic like this its good to make the player attached to at least one of the main characters. Except by the time a game would have normally done that, you've already finished where the emotional confrontation was supposed to be.
Overall, the game's minimalistic gameplay just make the story dance around the subject in a situation where it needs to take a definitive point of view. The dialogue becomes so extremely limiting eventually, where instead of it becoming a hopeless situation in which you (the player/main character) tries as hard as they can to fix an unfixable situation, it instead becomes a hopeless situation in which you (the player) becomes so frustrated with how idiotic you (the main character) are acting that the situation becomes unfixable only because there is literally nothing you (the player) can do to stop yourself (the main character) from acting like the aforementioned sixth grader.

Reign of Kings had an infinite amount of potential attached to it upon release, an exciting and innovative PvP system that utilized similarities to Chivalry provided fun fighting, accompanied by interesting building and siege mechanics offered Reign of Kings players a fresh new perspective on survival oriented games. I honestly believe this game still has the potential to be a contender with the likes of Ark and Rust. If I am being candid, the two aforementioned games have stale, dull, and mundane features, but offer certain gameplay aspects and mechanics that make them more attractive to players than Reign of Kings currently is, for a multitude of reasons.
Reign of Kings short comings include:
A: Official servers are virtually unplayable because of the ubiquitous and pervasive Chinese hackers and dupers that flood the servers with colossal citadels of bases that are made out of the best quality building blocks, and encompass the Kings mountain and various proximal areas, which make contesting the King's throne impossible, because you either get killed by one of them hacking, or can not penetrate their duped walls. These official servers are rarely wiped and have no admins moderating play either.
B: Community servers are mostly run by middle aged men who are incredibly self-aggrandizing, and who exhibit astronomical amounts of bias towards their friends/guildmates that lead to spawned in bases and ill-gotten resources/items that individuals playing the game normally would not have access to as readily. The owner bias also leads to individuals being wrongfully banned as well.
C: Developers seem to have jumped the proverbial ship sometime within the past year for reasons unknown, and stopped providing updates to this game to deal with the tremendous optimization and lag issues. Item and weapon balance changes would be nice as well, considering the only viable weapon in PvP are the halberds and the iron-star mace.
D: The amount of hacking that occurs regularly on this game has gotten so out of hand it is becoming patently ridiculous, by now, one would assume that any respectable game whereby the developers give even minutia amounts of cadence to would have already installed a better anti cheat system that would be more difficult to circumvent than the one currently in place.
All in all, Reign of Kings is an amazing game with untold amounts of potential, but that potential in itself is not nearly enough to excuse it's short comings.
~Earl Hooker

Dark Souls 2 is not a good Dark Souls game, i would hesitate to even call it a good game, it's more of a bench test for frustration. I'm going to make a lot of comparisons to the other games. Becaue it's part of the same goddamn series and thus, must be held to their standard.
I've played and beaten Dark Souls 1, Dark Souls 3, Demon's Souls, and Bloodborne, but i cannot for the life of me beat this one. Don't you dare tell me to 'git gud'. Because i already have.
And the entire reason is simply because of the way the character handles.
The other games have their share of awkwardness, especially Dark Souls 1, being rushed through development. Dark Souls 3 has trouble with weapon viability, magic and poise, but at least the parts that work are fun.
Everything about the controls in this game feel stiff and clumsy.
For one you're locked into animations for longer, on average there is a .75 or 1 second delay after a swing, and a longer delay when you run out of stamina, even on high levels swinging an average straight sword 2 or 3 times will drain your stamina. Don't even bother rolling. You have almost no iframes by default and have to invest in an otherwise useless stat to get more. Or else you'll get hit in the middle of your roll. AT LEAST the poise works unlike in Dark Souls 3, but you take so much damage it's not worth it.
If you run out of stamina while blocking your character will stand there for a moment and slowly flail around like a drunkard trying really hard not to fall over.
Enemies do unreasonable amounts of damage for the speed and accuracy their attacks have. You'll lose 50 to 80 percent of your health from most hits. If you could dodge properly this wouldn't be an issue.
Enemies can turn on a dime even in the middle of swinging a weapon that weighs more than they do, and they can also go into fast combos.
In comparison, the player attacks like they can barely lift their weapons, even the ♥♥♥♥ing daggers feel slow and clumsy.
It's almost like you're in slow motion sometimes.
The sound effects for the weapons and magic are awful too, they sound like a budget PS2 game. The music is forgettable, though the DLC's have some good tracks.
The maps feel bleak and hollow, and not in a thematic way like they do in the other games, it just looks like someone made a model set and never bothered to finish it, most of the areas are just a series of dull cubic rooms. There's no sense of them having any sort of history or purpose besides being a slightly run down room.
Enemies and bosses are boring, i can barely remember most of them. Just the ones that had awful gimmicks that make you want to commit Seppuku.
There are some improvements, some of the attack animations look quick good, they just need to be a bit faster and have better sound effects, the duel weild system is good too, but mostly useless. There's a lot of weapons and spells and armors sets, but most of them are just redundant reskins with different stats, and you'll get beaten to death trying to use the spells.
As you may expect from the series, the story is ambiguous and largely told through item descriptions. In this case, there isn't much of one, the previous game may as well have never happened considering how sparse the references are.
(Though Dark Souls 3 went a bit overboard with them at times.)  Sometime about the curse and there being a magic throne that can grant wishes, this is never given the usual hints at it's origins or even really mentioned.
And the HD version adds a talking pile of burning wood, he dribbles on pretentiously about the nature of the soul and what could lie beyond fire and dark. This never actually goes anywhere as far as i can tell, and has the same depth as conversing with an idiot on an LSD trip.
Maybe the game explains some of this stuff later, but i can't be bothered to try and beat it, i'm stuck at the penultimate bossfight with Throne Dickweed and Throne Shitwad. They have some stupid gimmick where if you don't kill them at roughly the same time the one that's already down revives with full health, INFINITELY. Apparently the Super Londo Bros weren't cheap and gimmicky enough. (I actually love the O n' S bossfight.)
The final boss is just some skeleton lady with a scythe anyway, and the final-final boss in the HD version is the semi-sentient smouldering pile of wood anyway, so i'm not missing much.
Apparently the DLC bosses are good, but i can't be bothered to fight them either, because regardless of the quality of the boss itself, handling the character will still feel like moving a brick through molasses, and have the same reward as grinding my balls against sandpaper.
3/10, buy DS1 or literally any of the other games in the series, Dark Souls 3 basically retcons most of this one anyway. Not like it matters much since nothing interesting or important happens anyway. Kind of fitting since the faint thread of a story here is about futility and forgetting.

If you're looking for a puzzle game that packs both charm and challenge, then you've come to the right place. World of Goo is almost instantly addictive for players of all skill levels, with simple controls and play mechanics that are easily grasped.
Click and drag the adorable goo balls into position to construct towers, bridges, and other structures to reach your goal. You only have a limited number of goo balls, and since some of them need to exit the level safely, you'll have to avoid hasty decisions and start planning ahead. You must carefully consider where to place the next goo ball--and (when later goo balls with different abilities are introduced) WHICH goo ball to place. It may take a few tries (and retries...and maybe even MORE retries), but you'll feel a sense of accomplishment once you've nailed the goal. Even after you've beaten the level, you can replay it again later to see if you can figure out method of achieving the goal with less moves and faster times (the "OCD" goals in the menu beckon you to try this).
The art style is clean and colorful. All of the characters and interactive elements are distinctive on the screen, so you can easily focus on the task at hand. The sound effects are simple and cute, and the musical soundtrack is very well done. A large number of levels and a progressively increasing challenge means that you'll be coming back for more for a very long time.
This highly enjoyable game will put your logic skills to the test and bring a smile to your face. I highly recommend it!

This game is a rollercoaster of emotions.
At first I was amazed by the great graphics, the very detailed world, beautiful locations and huge selection of weapons, vehicles and ways to destroy stuff.
Freeing every single town got a bit repetitive sometimes. But this part is highly optional, so I can't really blame the game for it. The main story is funny and entertaining enough, while offering impressive cinematics and sometimes a feeling as if I was playing a powered-up James Bond.
There are some random encounters and sidemissions like assassinations, liberation of allies and all kinds of assist and delivery tasks. Nice variety.
Some of them you can't finish for a very funny reason: Accidents. You try to open a gate to help a villager and accidently smash him with the gate, instantly killing him. Or someone asks you for help with his car but gets run over by another car shortly thereafter.
Of you just stand idle next to the road while there's a single object on the roadway and try not to die from laughter as you see villagers and rebel soldiers crashing into each other while the AI tries to figure a "save" way, creating even more of a mess and leaving corpses and destruction everywhere.
There's lot to do in the world of Just Cause 3. And if you ever get the feeling that something starts to get boring you can take a break and do something competely different. For me, when I felt that I needed to relax a bit, it was nice to take a speedboat and send it flying over the waves.
Truth be told, my first review was negative. Partially for the already mentioned reasons like repetitive, frustrating or simply boring moments that may occur. Another reason were some random crashes to desktop I experienced during play. They weren't that rare. About one every 5 hours or so.
But the game saves the progress frequently, so even if you die or the game crashes, usually you won't lose much - if at all. So at the bottom line the positive aspects of the game outweight the negative ones.
Other notable issues are:
- long loading times. Occur when you start/continue your game and on every death
- enemies spawning near you and at the most impossible places to pursuit you
- they use any gun with sniper accuracy. Even a machine gun mounted on a motorboat 1km away will hit you with 9 out of 10 shots.

Amnesia: A Machine for pigs a loosely based sequal to Amnesia: The Dark Descent. Most of the vital gameplay elements found in Dark Descent were completely removed in Machine, such as tinderbox collection, lantern oil, health, and "sanity". These elements played a vital role in making the player feel truly vulnerable and hapless, essential to this genre of game. In Machine, I never felt challened to complete the few puzzles, and the enemies were never more than a nuisance and could simply be ran past. I would say get it on sale if you enjoy mild spoops and spooks and easy achemevents. Good atmosphere and an interesting steampunk setting, but other than that it doesn't offer much else.

I actually don't mind this game that much. Yes I am disappointed in a few things such as: not losing sanity and never needing to replenish supplies, but I personally don't mind it being a walking simulator. The game isn't as scary, but the story and music are very interesting. I came in open minded and thus more accepting of the big differences between this game and TDD. I think this game would have gotten higher ratings if it wasn't branded as an Amnesia game, but personally I'm not bothered by it at all. Highly recommend this game but only on sale as there isn't much replay value and it is a short experience.

It's like Amnesia: TDD except if it was 200% less scary, involved less puzzles, had less monsters, had no sanity mechanic, and was overall worse save for a slightly better story. If you desperately crave something vaguely akin to Amnesia...
Get the Penumbra collection instead. You'll get spooked more often even though you can actually fight back in the first game.

I hesitantly recommend this game, but im going to lean on the side of, "this was a let-down comparing it to the first amnesia game." I played the first amnesia game and really, absolutely loved that game. I truly never felt safe in that game. Never. It was everything a horror game should be, with long periods of nothing but yourself to scare you, mild puzzles, horrible storyline in that the story was good, but it was about horrible things, and even mild choice selection that changed the endings. Buuuut. This is NOT THAT GAME.
This felt to me like a short horror story brought to life via a video game. because, if you dont treat it like an amnesia game and be all hesitant, like i was, you'll easily complete this game in less time than i did it in (less than 7 hours, and half of that i was AFK helping someone move but forgot to log outta the game). once i realized how simple and not at all dangerous this game was, yeah, i sailed right through it because, really, you're safe 90% of the time in this game. truly a let down. it had nice music and overall ambiance. I mean, it's a giant machine dug deep into the earth - that's a crazy setting! And they could have done SO MUCH with such a setting!...but they didnt. They just gave us really bad light.
All in all, if i had never played this game knowing what i know about it now that ive completed it, i can say that i would not have missed out on anything. If you find it on sale for a few bucks and want to waste a day away with a story about a dude who did horrible things, go ahead and pick this up. but, otherwise, you're really not missing out on anything. I end this game being quite disappointed.

Short but sweet, the game mechanics are vastly different from The Dark Descent, which can be for the better or worse depending on your opinion and playstyle. No collectibles allows you to run through the game quickly and focus on the story instead of searching every corner of the game looking for a tinder box or lamp oil like in the last game. I do wish there were more enemies or varients to spice things up more every now and again though. True, like many have stated, there aren't very many jump scares, but this game is based on a good morbidly twisted story and atmosphere instead of just plain ol' horror game jump scares. The game did feel a lot easier, especially not having to manage health or sanitylike in TDD.
TL;DR - If you are looking just for jump scares, look somewhere else, it is more of a psychological horror game with a morbid and symbolic story. Overall, I honestly have to say I enjoyed this one a lot better than Dark Descent.

The Room isn't actually about a room, it is about a mechanical puzzle box within a puzzle box within a puzzle box, with some ethereal but no less mechanical elements thrown in.  Unlike other puzzle games, you're never doing "levels" in this one; your current box always teases you with several obvious locks to open, but it depends on you, your skills of logic and observation, to figure out which one and how. It is a very quiet, patient occupation: you're turning the box this way and that, examine it here and there, until something clicks (sometimes literally) and you are one step further to the solution.
The puzzles are, for the most part, novel; Steam says I played 3 hours, but it sure feels longer, and it was worth every second. I had turned hints off in the options, which means you still get some basic feedback when you're attempting the impossible; with hints on, you get a question mark icon you can click on when you're stuck.
Of course a game such as this has little replayability unless you have forgotten how everything works and where the hidden bits are -- you can just rejoice in the beauty of it (it is a mobile port, but it sure doesn't feel like one, it looks positively amazing on 24"), and wait for "The Room 2" (and 3) to come to the PC. at the Halloween sale, but I will be getting the sequels at full price, because it's well worth 5€.

The Room is is an atmospheric puzzler with beautiful graphics and
haunting music that draws you into the mood of the game.  On the surface, the
goal of this game is to solve a puzzle, but there are many deeper levels that
make up this game.
The level design is 3d, with each level drawing you deeper into the
game, which leads into further puzzles and mysteries.   Each puzzle is unique,
and  solving them gives a sense of accomplishment.
The story is told through notes that you discover as you progress through
the puzzles, with each one urging you forward to the end.  The supernatural,
spooky atmosphere ties everything together beautifully pulling off a feeling of
unease as you go further into the experience.
I would recommend this for puzzle enthusiasts, and for those who are
on the fence about whether or not they enjoy puzzleers.  This game can change
your mind

There are some interesting puzzles along the way, which make you think about the order of things, rather than simply going through motions.  Not overly difficult, but definitely makes you think a little differently, which is refreshing!
The puzzles and mechanics develop over time, therefore giving you fresh and new ways to explore new puzzles as you progress.  I think it is a great use of applying tools to puzzles with having your hand help too much ;)
I think the controls are where this game is a little weak and lacking.  The game has turbo jump, which I think gets in the way of your own precision.  Also changing weapons is a little cumbersome, especially if you are trying to cycle in a hurry.

You're a damaged TV, miraculously revived, trying to escape a rubbish processing facility. This is largely done by puzzling your way though rooms, frequently by triggering switches to (de)activate lasers, moving platforms, barriers, etc. And careful jumping.
Amass an arsenal of conventional weapons and heavy munitions! Soon realise you won't get to use them in a proper fight against enemies. I think this is meant to be ironic. They're mainly tools for solving puzzles. Like, by spraying bullets for clearing away trash, or exploding to let you jump further.
The dumb automaton enemies aren't proper opponents. Because they don't seem to actually, y'know, oppose you. They're fine for what they are, placed as obstacles, as elements in the puzzles. Their contact with you has an interesting effect which was a cool touch: you temporarily lose control and behave like a walking drone, like them. Plus analogue TV-style visual distortions. Throughout the game, glitchy, static-like visual and sound effects abound.
The best parts are the time-limited action sequences, which can feel quite tense. It's a modern action game, so you've got instant restarts. You 'die' a lot. (Does that still trick gamers into thinking a game is hard?) This isn't a hard game, and rightly so. How much time do you want to spend in a dump? Fortunately it isn't like a huge sprawling castle, so it's not too long! It's about the right length, at under 2 hours.
3/5

If you're looking for a puzzle game that packs both charm and challenge, then you've come to the right place. World of Goo is almost instantly addictive for players of all skill levels, with simple controls and play mechanics that are easily grasped.
Click and drag the adorable goo balls into position to construct towers, bridges, and other structures to reach your goal. You only have a limited number of goo balls, and since some of them need to exit the level safely, you'll have to avoid hasty decisions and start planning ahead. You must carefully consider where to place the next goo ball--and (when later goo balls with different abilities are introduced) WHICH goo ball to place. It may take a few tries (and retries...and maybe even MORE retries), but you'll feel a sense of accomplishment once you've nailed the goal. Even after you've beaten the level, you can replay it again later to see if you can figure out method of achieving the goal with less moves and faster times (the "OCD" goals in the menu beckon you to try this).
The art style is clean and colorful. All of the characters and interactive elements are distinctive on the screen, so you can easily focus on the task at hand. The sound effects are simple and cute, and the musical soundtrack is very well done. A large number of levels and a progressively increasing challenge means that you'll be coming back for more for a very long time.
This highly enjoyable game will put your logic skills to the test and bring a smile to your face. I highly recommend it!

Excellent game let down by an absurd "Politics" system.
I have sunk over 80 hours into this game and played several different factions, each time I took a different approach to the Politics system, and each time I got absolutely identical results. On one run-through I ignored Politics completely. On another I sunk a fortune into concilliatory strategies. On another I spent heavily on aggressive strategies. On more than one I tried to balance the two.
And each time, the outcome was the same... at some point between capturing 40 and 45 settlements, a family/clan within my faction will always secede and reduce my armies, fleets, agents and settlements by roughly 15-20%. Every time. Without fail. No matter what I do.
Of course, it's usually possible to overcome this seccession within 5-7 turns, and then you have to spend another 4 or 5 turns recovering and rebuilding.
So ultimately it feels like the game designers just chucked in a cheat code for the AI. The Politics system appears to provide player control but actually just functions as an arbitrary speedbump when you hit a certain point in the game... like when your character gets captured two thirds way through an RPG and has all their gear and upgrades stripped away, simply to prolong things.
I'd love to recoomend this game. It's the perfect Total War game in every other way. But having just played a lengthy campaign only to have it happen again -- like clockwork -- when I captured my 42nd settlement... despite following every single hint and tip provided on the TW Wiki to maintain "balance"... I've once again decided to abandon a game unfinished.
And that's not something I can recommend.

One of the best Western games ever made. It even vies with Red Dead Redemption for me. There is nothing like this out there for one. A first person shooter, with a stylized look to it, with terrific narration that unfolds over the course of many of the greatest Western myths and tales out there? Yes please. The COJ team outdid themselves here.
Bound in Blood was a decent game, marred by a pretty crappy engine that detracted from its decent gameplay and narration. The game they made after that I cannot remember and do not care to. But Techland hit one out of the park here and you can tell a lot of love and devotion was put into this 20 dollar title. The locales are done with accuracy and aplomb; the dusty deserts and mountainsides will have you in awe of the old West. And the engine has been redone and refocused. Gone is the hideous pop-in. There is more detail to this world. Better sound. And you can also use Nvidia AA codes for SGSSAA and HBAO to make the game look extra special, and far above the console versions' image quality.
The guns are great, if not too different from what you had before. The upgrade paths seem decent, and you do have to pick one or the other style if you are only doing one playthrough of the game. I picked rifles for the main path and then decided to do a bit of my pistols near the end. You will be rewarded with various skins and upgrades to your main guns throughout the game. On hard difficulty I had a decent challenge playing with my DS4 through Input Mapper. Controls were all around very good.
What is most appealing about this game is definitely the very solid narration and script. I loved every moment of the storytelling here, and it never takes itself too seriously at all. There are many facts you can read about the West when you find the secrets, and I heartily enjoyed the pictures and tidbits of info about the various real life stories. There is also an arcade mode and a duel mode if that is your cup of tea, But even so, the main game is a worthy send-up to the Western genre. In many ways it goes above and beyond the call of duty to give you an interesting take on the legends of the West. And all for a very fair price. Not to be missed.

Gave myself a good chuckle after I finished it since I was below the 2 hour mark. Basically went and put in a refund request for a game about greed,  just found it ironic. Not that I don't mind supporting the devs but a part of me just couldn't help but find it humorous to do this. All in all, a good game gameplay-wise, the puzzles were pretty simple and some fell down to straight up guess and check rather than having to actually use your head, but for the most part they were enjoyable little puzzle things. This game in my opinion has some serious topics it centers it's themes around (some would ever say overdone in this genre) but overall I couldn't say that it was really scary or anything or emotionally impactful, also some rather trite jumpscares although there was ONE instance where it was used in a moderately decent way. The story did finish on a bit of a high note though (didn't mean that in a bad way for anyone who has played it already lmao) and tied everything together nicely which left me content despite my previous greivances. The themes of this game didn't really interest me which may be altering my interpretation of the game so it's really up to you to decide what you think of it when you play it, it is a good game however a bit overpriced for what you get. I did get this on sale for like $1-2 (can't really remember, and makes the fact I refunded it even more petty but as I said it wasn't really about the money that caused me to submit a request) which I feel is a good price to spend on this game. Also the sound design could've been better, the constant creepy atmosphere generic sounds made the game feel even more tropish for lack of a better term, even if that isn't a word. A better executed sound design could've made this game much more effective.

SPOILERS: DONT VIEW THIS REVIEW IF YOU ARE LOOKING TO START PLAYING THE GAME
story:
A story of greed and greed hungry companys and the fact that we play as one of those people who work for them is a great idea. The only thing I had with the game is its lack of story to Price. I would like to know more about his family before he died and what caused him to get the job. I would be suprised if the sequel will be a prequel where we see Price getting his job. That would be great. And the fact that everything repeats from start to end amazes me. Makes me question if it was all fake. Whos the real Price. Would the other Price go through the same thing now? who knows. I kinda had a few feels of fear going down my back while playing but I was never scared. I noticed that the monster looked the exact same to the body at the start. And the fact that the monsters like the elephant are mentioned again further in the story. Great detail to the story I must say.
gameplay: I ain't a fan of walking sim like games or VNs but for some reason this game makes it stand out. The fact that you can use anything to your avantage is great. The only issue I had was the fact that at one point I could not find a generator until looking forward and back several times. Stupid of me, I know.
Graphics and Visuals: What can I say about it. Its bad.... Oh wait I misspelled "amazing" wrong. The games 16 bit like graphics stuns me with its lighting and film grain like filter (cranked it up all the way for the whole game) game feels like a horror film I would watch when I had nothing to do. Sadly the issue I had with the game is the fact that when its done, thats it. I lost my money I spent on it and I only get an hour of a great experience.
Pretty much I would like a bit more. Like 5 hours or 6 hours of gameplay would be great. The game has great ideas and great out come. But its a bit short. Not too short. But just short enough to feel like a short film. Even for its shortness I would recommend this game to anyone and I am excited to see what the sequel will show us in May.

A charmingly cute little gem of a physics-based puzzler! What's particularly brilliant is that the levels feel distinctly unique. For a straightforward idea, the puzzles are exceptionally diverse and really challenge you to think. Some are fast-paced, others are ponderous and require meticulous planning. Most are just plain fun. Solving it is also only half of the challenge... executing it is where it gets tricky; as you helplessly watch your lovingly crafted structure teeter and crumple into a pile of oblivious-looking blobs
New goo ball species are also introduced often, and really add their own distinct flavour to the game
My only gripe are the OCD flags. Level completion jumps between 'barely scraped by' to 'completed perfectly'. There's no half-way point to encourage players, so I didn't feel motivated to get them half of the time. You either have to do it perfectly or you might as well have not bothered (and the global highest tower isn't something I care for either). But that's a small gripe: The OCD flags are entirely optional (and hidden away) so doesn't detract from the casual element of the game if you want to just play it to enjoy

World of Goo is an Indie-Physics-Puzzle Game developed in 2008 by 2D BOY. World of Goo is one of those quaint games that you would probably prefer to play on a mobile or smaller electronic device (with touch screen capabilities); in World of Goo you create bizarre contraptions with Goo to get to the end of the level.
You progress through the game being guided by "Signs"
, you'll want to read every single sign in the game because they are quite humorous. The game is broken down into Five chapters, and each chapter would usually have 10-12 levels within the chapter.
Being a puzzle game, you need to spend a fair amount of time thinking, and once you get into the farther difficult levels, at times you'll need to restart the whole level because of one mistake. There is a requirement of how many "Goo Balls" you need to save at the end of each level to pass. So that means you can't use all your Goo on construction, you need to be as minimalistic as possible in your building.
The game starts out very easily and simple, but quickly gets complex and difficult. To construct, you click and drag a Goo Ball to a certain location near the starting structure to "add" to that structure. Generally after using that Goo you cannot reuse it... but some Goo has special properties that lets you reuse them, or have other special effects.
World of Goo has 8 Steam Achievements, all of which are pretty rough to obtain.
I only have 2 of those achievements at this time, most of them require perfect scores on each level... Getting all of the achievements will require a great deal of determination.
World of Goo is priced at $9.99, I spent 6 hours playing through the game once. So for me that's not a fair price.... However, I picked up the game on a 90% off sale, so I've actually gotten my monies worth, and then some.
I recommend this game to people who enjoy puzzle and/or indie games, World of Goo was a very fun play through, and it only took one afternoon to get through it, so it's a nice quaint little play through. Depending on how good you are at puzzle games World of Goo does get pretty tough at times.

This game actually does something I've never seen done before, and that's change the layout of a level depending on what the narrator is saying. The game is brought to life by a gunslinger in a bar who is telling a crowd about his deeds, and sometimes it can become a tall tale. Sometimes, someone will call the narrator out on that, and he quickly "fixes" his story, which leads to the level you are playing to be recreated, or have a path open up. My favorite example of this is when the narrator is talking about a virtual suicide charge into a gold mine filled with enemies, and then, realizing he can't talk his way out of it, quickly changes his story by saying "That's what I would have done if I was a complete idiot." Then he proceeds to retell the level, and you go through the level again, but in an entirely different way.
Overall, this game is tons of fun to play, has great voice acting, an engaging story, and some good replay value. Definitely give this one a try!
