​It seems as though linear first-person shooters have gotten a bad rap in recent years, perhaps because of the stagnant carbon-copies that triple-A publishers like Activision and EA push out annually like clockwork. Consequently,
comes as somewhat of a pleasant surprise. Set in 1910 in the the wild West, the game from
developer Techland is a story-rich corridor shooter with a twist - the entire story is told by a man in a bar who becomes progressively more inebriated throughout the game's brief playtime. It makes for some fantastically entertaining gunfights in which more elements are introduced as he recalls them. This story element goes a long way to spruce up an otherwise fairly standard shooter.
opens with our hero - famous bounty hunter Silas Greaves - arriving in Abilene, Kansas. Silas sits down at a bar and almost immediately begins telling the lengthy tale of his quest for vengeance to a group of strangers, including a boy rather obviously named Dwight (I wonder what he'll be when he grows up). Some of
's best scenes are those with an irreverent disregard for the story itself, including a section which repeats the same room multiple times because Silas has gone to the bathroom and is unavailable to explain what happened next. Supplemented by a superior voice cast with some pretty top-notch Texan drawls, it's a unique, subversive way of telling a fairly bog-standard plot that is literally sparked by a "you killed my brother" cliché.
The gameplay itself is a blisteringly bloody dash through small towns, gold mines and sawmills, all while popping bullets in the heads of a seemingly endless number of bandits and otherwise no-good folk. It's fast and precise, making kills highly satisfying and making it easy to go on a perfect 28-man killing spree. Besides the regular, arcadey gameplay, each level ends in a good old standoff straight from
. Winning these 'duels' honourably requires that you draw your gun last but fire it first, turning the entire showdown into a lengthy period of silent concentration followed by a split-second of twitch-reflexes. It's highly enjoyable, and although it felt somewhat frustrating at times, it doesn't detract from the flow of the gameplay.
Although it won't keep you going for very long,
is a fantastically polished shooter that perfectly encapsulates the raw, untamed nature of the spaghetti Western film genre in a game that doesn't take itself even remotely seriously - a view that it greatly benefits from.

First off: I actually was pleasantly suprised by the game, I like it.
So I have played and absolutely love the Penumbra series and Amnesia the Dark Decent.
I knew this was made by a different developer and that it was received with less enthousiasm.
So when I played it I curbed my expectations but that seemed in the end to be unneeded.
Gameplay:
Well....there isn't much of that in this game, less then a handful meaningful encounters with enemies and I dont think the game ever actually threw a puzzle my way that took more then half a second to figure out.
In fact most things that could have been a puzzle, the answer to it was given by the game (character) anyway.
Story:
Ah now this is were the game shines.....ok well partly.
This is what the game is pretty much all about, figuring out what happened, who you are, what is going on.
The game does a good job with the pacing and giving little bits of story along the way.
Where imo it falls a little flat is that in the end its still not clear what is actually going on, the game drops hints, then drops hints that is not really like that, then drops hints that it is again or something totally different.
In the end its hard to make heads or tails from what is going on.
But the journey imo is a good one, and the writing is really good.
Thats actually a major...if not the biggest part of the game, reading.
You do a LOT of reading in this game, but its not a bad thing imo as again, the writing is really good.
Its poetic and emotional, its understandable and vague in other areas, its just all very interesting.
If you go into this game and expect a game like the previous, you will be kinda dissapointed.
But if you go into this and see it as a novel in game format, very much like Gone Home, I think you will appreciate it.
I think this is an experience worth having if you care about story telling and dont mind reading and can immerse yourself.

On an objective level, the components of this game aren't great. As an adventure game, the puzzles are easy, but a few still have some moon logic silliness to them. As a horror game, there's lots of psychological horror tropes and moments of tense ambiance, but there's nothing truly scary. As a story, it's very focused on trying to tell a morality tale and uses horror symbolically to that end, but the script's tonal inconsistencies often makes the presentation feel goofy, and the moral is a bit hamfisted, especially by the end.
But this game has heart. It's difficult to describe, but there's a sense of ambition here that's admirable, and there are genuinely touching moments that resonated deeply. I don't really know how to convey this in a review where it seems like my negatives are more than my positives, but for a buck and two hours, I still think this is an experience worth having.

It seems a little bit unfair to me to call this game a "First Person Shooter." The term "FPS" just leaves you without much to go on; compare it to the word "rocket." If I say the word "rocket", you don't know if I am talking about Elon Musk's SpaceX vehicle or a Fourth of July bottle rocket.  I found that there is a lot more to "Borderlands 2" than the shooting. It is a trip into a fascinating world that is full of surprises, and it just so happens that to explore it you have to do a lot of shooting and rack up a huge body count. I'll warn you about one thing, and I don't know if it is a spoiler or not; early on you figure out that the native inhabitants of Pandora are a little bit on the uneducated side.  They misspell stuff. Their conversation is of the most rudimentary kind, largely limited to ungrammatical death threats; but I was rocking along and noticed one dude was ranting longer than usual and his raucous bellowing seemed to be real familiar; he was doing one of Hamlet's soliloquys - no, not the famous "to be or not to be" speech but one that gave a clue to some of the terminology in the game. Good luck trying to find the one bad guy in the game that paid attention in English class... If that spoiled anything for you, I am sorry; it hasn't spoiled anything for me, because I don't yet know whether this literary quote hidden in plain sight is a big clue to more and greater adventures, or whether it was just a gag the game developers decided to throw in. And there is a lot of interesting stuff like that in itf. Anyway, I am having a lot of fun with it. One bit of advice: don't go near the water. You might fall in. Anyway, that's what I keep doing.

Going into Papers Please I didn't expect much, and what I got was a very well thought out game. Which, in my opinion, is one of the best games I have ever played.
The game is set in a fictional country called Arstotska, and you have the job of being border control. You let immigrants into the country and if they don't have valid paperwork you send them on their way (later in the game you get the option to detain them). This is what I saw in the trailer, so I figured this was one of the boring of the dozens of simulators that are out on the market. So I started the game up, and realized that it was 3 in the morning.
I wouldn't say that this is a fun game, but rather I very entertaining and tense game that gets you very well intrigued with the other countless stories of other immigrants that come into your country. The stress that comes with making enough money each day to keep your family healthy is something that not even Dark Souls could replicate with it's teeth grinding difficulty. Your job becomes more and more difficult as the rules constantly change and you have to check more paperwork until your desk is flooded with it. The last couple of hours were the tense I've had in gaming for a long time. For the cons of this game, well, I can't really think of any. The only thing that comes to mind is the paperwork does become a bit less interesting by the end of the game, and becomes more of a task.
Overall I very much recommend this game, and if you haven't already, buy this game. You will be amazed at how good a paperwork simulator actually is.

I would recommend the game since it feels like a polished game that runs well and looks great. Also, I enjoy playing it, regardless of the things I'm about to mention.
Cons:
I wish the quests gave more useful rewards, since at this point I don't even complete quests anymore, I simply run dungeons as they reward you with better gear and more experience.
Since I also really like support like characters, it would have been nice to see roles that are dedicated buff/debuffers rather than just tank, melee-dps, ranged dps and healer. Sure, some skills have CC and do buff party members, but to be of use to your team you need more than just one or two possible buffs. The same goes for debuffs.
Another issue I had was the fact that pretty much everyone is running the same builds. You don't feel unique or special in any way. There aren't THAT many skills to choose from. A mage will use a destruction staff, a healer a healing staff and melee will use two-handed, dual or one handed and shield. Each of these has about 6 skills you can unlock of which you'd use at least 4. You only have 6 slots on each action bar. So that leaves just a few slots for your class skills which ultimately means that if you run a dungeon with another mage, both of you are probably going to use the exact same skills. Same with two-handed, dual and one handed / shield. You do get a stamina sorcerer which is basically a mage that uses dual blades and stamina instead of magica, but that's probably the most unique character I've seen.
If you take for example a game like Rift (which sucks right now), you'd have 3 skill trees, each with a LARGE number of skills to choose from. You can then combine these in any way you'd like, thus ending up with quite possibly a very different mage, tank, or ranged-dps than the next guy.
NO CHESTS IN YOUR HOUSE???
I also hate that dps can queue as healers or tanks. Again using Rift as an example, but they detect your skills or skill lines and based on that determine whether you can queue as a healer or tank. So a mage with dps abilities can't queue as a healer, but only as a dps or support. Here you may very well end up with a dps queued as a tank or a healer, thus making your dungeon experience horrible as you're running away from monsters more than you are fighting them.
Suggestions:
I'd think about offering a 5-man dungeon where you'd have a dedicated tank, healer, 2 dps and then a support role which can be filled either by a dps or an off-healer/tank.
Prevent people from queuing for roles in dungeons that they are not able to fulfill.
Balance quest rewards with dungeon rewards to avoid people forgetting about the quests and the story.
Introduce more skills to differentiate characters and classes more. Even in Skyrim you have more freedom to build your own character. Here you can build a mage using any of the classes and STILL end up with a character that uses almost identical skills.
Allow players to pay for housing AND INCLUDE A CHEST WHERE THEY CAN STORE THEIR ITEMS. You're already getting money from them, so at least add a bit of incentive to getting a house.
Chinese people can pay using Alipay on Steam - so open up an Asian server or at least ensure a better connection so people living here don't need to use a VPN. Get them off WoW and onto ESO! More money = more resources to spend on making this game truly great.

I've been playing this one for some time now so I figured best time to finally write this.
The easiest way to sum this title up is "Good for an MMO, not a traditional an ElderScrolls".
Essentially this is an MMO set in the ES world.
The game has some nice qualities as well as some flaws.
COMBAT & CONTROLS
The game hybrids the forms of most MMOs with that of TES, so spells and special attacks have quick bars and hot keys but only 5 can be equiped at a time meaning quick bars wont be cluttering your screen while the main controls are mostly the same as Skyrim.
The combat can be a bit dodgy at times.
For some reason enemy projectile spells can go through walls and even floors, as can other projectile attacks...
Also going through doors or activating objects is disabled when engaged or being attacked, as such fleeing can be a joke and timed challenges can be a complete irritation from this.
Although other enemy attacks can be blocked or avoided well enough that it can otherwise be enjoyable.
UI
The Interface is decent for an MMO, fairly strait forward but lots on it.
Its easily navigated and could be considered cleaner than Skyrim's vanilla Interfaces.
QUESTS
Likely one of the best parts of the game.
There are a staggering number of quests accross the game that have a huge variety, from helping a farmer put out fires to helping plan a city festival to traveling through a daedric portal and saving a noble family from cultists to even playing diplomat between alliance leaders!
With just how many there are these alone would keep a player busy for a good long while, not including any of the DLCs!
MAPS
These are also very expansive and varied, plus the shear number of terrains is great!
The game takes almost 85GB and this is a very large reason why, they just have so many details and nooks that make the land so complex.
Icons are also spread pretty well across the maps.
However beware with Mounts as they cannot go up the mountain sides (Sorry but Skyrim Horses are special) and they dismount you in deep water which is almost all water...
GRAPHICS
These are quite nice for the most part, human meshes and textures have definately had an upgrade from vanilla Skyrim.
Although this doesn't exactly extend to all other mobs, the main horse textures have definately suffered compared to vanilla Skyrim with low resolution drawn on harnesses and even drawn on eyes...
There are other non-humanoid mobs that share this issue as well... Even some purchasable pets...
As for the enviornments they have fairly nice textures and effects, water and lighting are as nice as SSE and lava glows.
PAYWALL
In this case the game is more pay-4-convenience than pay-2-win with most purchasable items being non-combat pets, mounts, and cosmetics.
DLC is also something that requires real money but unlike the rest it can be rather expensive in comparison...
Overall I would rate this game a 7/10 on its own.

I wanted a fun little puzzle game that I could pick up and put down easily, but honestly this one is kind of annoying.  I would give it a 5/10 if there was a side-thumb button, but since there isn't I just can't see myself recommending this to anyone.
The game is a very simple concept that, like any good game formula, has a lot of depth to it when properly explored (something I think the developers were on the right track with).  After a short time in the game, though, I found myself kind of disappointed with the PC options: resolution doesn't scale (as far as I can see from the UI, and frankly I'm not interested enough in the game to even look for the config files), config options are pretty much non-existant, no windowed mode option, and if you have multiple monitors your mouse can still go off-screen (despite the fact that this is a single-monitor full screen game) and if you accidentally click your game will be minimized (this causes issues when you're trying to edge-scroll from right to left, for example).  If these options exist they were not clearly visible in the main menu as far as I can tell, and with a pick-up-and-put-down game like this I shouldn't have to be spending much time configuring things anyway...Binding of Isaac is a good example of how to do a simplistic PC port.
Put aside my gripes with the port (the reason I decided to not continue playing the game in the first place) the game just isn't that fun and there are some slightly clunky mechanics that get in the way.  The goo balls are constantly moving along your little wired network so you have to be rather precise with your mouse if you want to pick up a particular one in a crowded area, something that can be a major annoyance with the levels that require you to act quickly.  On top of this it was kind of annoying to discover that when you actually pick up a ball its hitbox is still present in the world, so if you accidentally drag your mouse over a harmful object you destroy the thing.  This turns the game in to one of those stupid games where you drag the mouse pointer through the maze and it detracts from the overall experience I was hoping to get.
TL;DR  it's not a bad game, but when a simple game can't deliver on simple and expected concepts I have no desire to play it.  Hell, if I could play the game in windowed mode I'd probably give it another try because shrinking it down would make it not look like♥♥♥♥♥♥

Looking back, I can understand why this game got a lot of hate.  Obviously, it had huge shoes to fill, seeing as how Amnesia: The Dark Descent is one of the most well known and critcally acclaimed pc-horror games of all time.  But if you take a step back, take a chance to look at all the intricacies that are in the game and the world it takes place in, it really does shine.
The Victorian-era theming, the imagery for machines and swine, even the voice acting; it all has an incredible effect on the player if you let the story tell itself.  Not to mention that the game has plenty of twists throught it, so it'll keep you guessing till the very end.
Some may argue that the enemy AI is weak, predictable or bad, but being a lover of these games, I can say that the game gives you plenty of warning and even tosses in a couple of enemies as "teasers" (ones that are scripted and can't actually harm the player) to prepare you to deal with them.
As a successor to the first game in the series, A Machine for Pigs may be stuck in the shadow of its predecessor, but as it's own game, it stands out in a dark, terrifying way.
If you enjoy horror games, or if you have been reluctant to try this game because of the negative reviews, give it a chance by going into the game with a clean slate.  I promise it'll be worth you while.

Are there any reasons to live if the future is dark and harsh, if it's full of blood and suffering? If every human being has to die, why do we live? These and other questions are treated in "Amnesia: a machine for pigs". The plot is deep and can be compared with a book story. The begining is proper for "Amnesia". Main character, Mandus, industrialist obsessed with his multiple ideas, wakes up in his mansion and discovers that he doesn't remember some episodes of his life, especially considering his last inventions and researches. His children are gone, the voice in the telephone says, that they are trapped somewhere in the depth of the area, where is situated a machine for pigs. Mandus has to launch a machine for an unknown to save his two children, but he should face his greatest fears on the way, of course. During this journey you'll be supposed to collect the notes  to restore your memory and to see the whole picture wich may shock you and make you think over it many years after playing the game. So, i recommend you to set off for the travel into the industrial buildings in London of 1899, wich can turn out to be  the real maze, as well as Mandus consciousness.

While being very different from Amnesia: The Dark Descent, which created most expectations people have of a game like this, A Machine For Pigs was an amazing game for me in its own way. Short but very powerful in its theming and storytelling, which really immersed me into its world. I consider this game its own little masterpiece which, while being pretty spooky, should be viewed as its own experimental game instead of a game that should bring the same feelings and scariness as The Dark Descent. The soundtrack is also definitely worth mentioning, as it's very fitting and gorgeous.

While this game lacks backstory, which I felt was detrimental to the story as a whole, as the game goes, along with the character encounters, Transistor continually builds upon itself. With great voice acting, powerful hymns, and a beautiful soundtrack to accompany the rest, Transistor sets itself apart from larger titles as Bastion had before.
Transistor starts off easy. As you become used to your abilities, the enemies, and the unique hack-and-slash turn-based combat system, the game evolves further. Delving deeper into Red’s story, you find stronger enemies, unlock upgrades and must learn to re-evaluate everything once more. With the ability to combine powers with each other to create new, deadlier abilities, this game offers many combinations for the player to try out. Add the tests in with occasionally preset ability combinations and limited MEM, you will be finding exciting new ways to use those old obsolete abilities.
Help Red and the Transistor fight their way through the gorgeous city as it gets ripped apart by the Process and shredded by the Spine. This title truly knows how to make destruction look appealing. Get ready for those screenshots and snap away as you complete Supergiant’s second title and whatever you do, don’t forget to buy the soundtrack!

Absolutely loved this game.
While you simply cannot beat Bastion's soundtrack or narrator, Transistor's soundtrack does not disappoint, and the Hum feature is really cool. I enjoyed the world and storyline, though both can be confusing at times.
The battle/customization system is awesome, based on Functions used in Active, Upgrade, or Passive slots, in addition to the given Turn() Function which allows you to pause battle and plan out your next few moves. Trying out different combinations is encouraged through optional tests the player can complete for experience at various points throughout the game, as well as receiving information on a Function's associated character as you use it in different slots, but the game allows you to use your tried-and-true combos enough that you don't feel you're constantly having to switch things around (though I found it fun to).
Once you beat the game, you have the option to start Recursive Play, where you keep your User Level and all Functions/Upgrades and start the game anew, earning the same Functions as before allowing their use in more than one slot. I enjoyed this second playthrough, though I really wish that you could continue the original story instead of restarting.
COMPLETELY, 100% worth the money if you pick it up on sale, and I highly recommend you do.

This game is probably the second biggest love/hate relationships with a game i've had. Maybe third, if you count WoW - but I can safely say I'd recommend it.
First of all, the game is free. You can, without putting a dime in, play the game to a very wide extent. Like other mobas except Dota, you have to pay for the characters with an ingame currency "favour" (favor for you
non-UK readers).
This can be alleviated if you're willing to spend a little, though, as the God Pack is ~£20 and provides every single God in the game.
The game, replayability wise, excels in it's class. Due to the nature of the aiming etc, you can outplay people a huge amount of the time and the macro game is always a fresh challenge for any competitive people who may want to play it with friends - with a lot of resources available.
The wide array of characters to play with also increases replayability, as they are all "viable" at some level, and if you put time into a particular character.
A major thing for eSports titles is that there is a discrepancy between what the top level play, and what you play. In some games, there is a completely different meta - with Smite that isn't the same. The picks that pros pick, can be picked up - and the patch they play on is the same as the patch played on in live clients.
The first two intertwine. Because it's a MOBA, regardless on the kind of player you are - you will find ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s in the community. MOBAs especially draw this crowd in, and you will see stereotypical "moba etiquette" a lot of the time. Happily, HiRez have allowed you to mute people as other games so you can significantly reduce the amount of rude individuals you have to put up with.
The third point is balance. Honestly, it's not BAD. It's just NOT GOOD. HiRez balance teams do try to upkeep balance so the effort is there, and obviously since balance is largely subjective it depends on how you are as a person. If your attitude is to try improve and learn, you'll be fine. If your idea is to win and that you are God, just like other MOBAs - the balance will drive you off.
I'd give the game a 7.5/10. It's not perfect, but it's definitely better than a large amount of mobas on the market and due to it being free, you'll have not wasted any money trying the game out.

Reign of Kings is definitely a game with a lot of potential, but it is not very well made, and has a lot of issues.
First of all, I'll talk about the good things about the game. It's very easy to understand how to do the various necessary things in this game like gathering, crafting, and fighting, among others, with simple controls that make it much less difficult to become accustomed to than some other games. The map is small enough that you will run into other players occassionally, but not so large that you feel isolated and have to actively go hunting for other players to find any. Overall, this is definitely a solid game, other than the few bad things that I'll talk about now.
Glitchy animations are definitely a problem. There are a few harmless ones, but there are others that make the game overly difficult and unfair. This appears primarily in fighting. Sometimes an animation can fail to play correctly and result in you being hit without even knowing that they were attacking.
Another thing that I've found wrong with the game (this may not be a "problem" because I see why it was added to the game, but it's just something I don't like personally) is the amount of health on building blocks. If the block is claimed, it can take hundreds of strikes on it to destroy it, depending on the material and your weapon. This makes attacking bases almost impossible without siege equipment, even when attacking building make out of leaves and sticks.
I do not recommend buying it unless the price is lowered, 20 dollars is too much for a fairly broken game.

It's good for what it is...
...which means it's really not very good. The root issue I have found with this game is that CA simply can't program AI to save their lives -- or they can't be arsed to. Which leads to problems ranging from a barebones diplomacy system that lacks basic features such as demanding or gifting regions because the AI couldn't handle anything more complex, as evidenced by its systematic stupid decisions such as not accepting becoming a client state only to request to become one itself in its turn, demanding payments from ME as a condition to peace when I'm besieging their last cities, etc. to completely random army compositions (8 cav, 3 inf as ♥♥♥♥ing Carthage, that'll work for sure), complete economic mismanagement that results in armies starving because the AI can't comprehend the need for food, nonsensical research priorities, abandoning cities and taking to the seas instead of trying to mount a defense, etc. The CA approach to higher difficulty levels is cranking AI cheats up to 11, as the AI is still dumb as a bag of hammers.
The game is also marred by plain bad design decisions. You can generally put two stacks next to any one city and autoresolve the assault to take it with few casualties which will be replenished automagically in one or two turns, after which you can just take out another city; there is no point in besieging when assaulting is faster and results in less casualties taken. GG. It takes literal years to cover distances by sea with armies because 1TPY means that otherwise people could launch "surprise" attacks with armies from across the sea, and fleets would be powerless to stop them. You can only upgrade units as Rome because they couldn't bother establishing retraining paths for other factions. Etc.
I got this game dirt cheap, and still it's not worth it because I feel that I mostly wasted my time trying to enjoy it. It's not that it's a really bad game, it's that there's so many little things that get in the way of fun that it ends up being tiresome. There are many mods that solve some of these problems, but I don't want to encourage the Bethesda design paradigm, and frankly, it's a hassle to have to look for mods to make up for stupid or lazy dev decisions.
Oh and the whole sequential turn thing where you have to twiddle your thumbs for the duration of the other player's turn? It's like PBEM, only you don't get to do other things meanwhile because they still need you to sign off on their battles. I ended up alt-tabbing and doing work stuff while they played, asking that they message me through Steam if they needed me to click on "OK" when they engaged.
Just... don't bother.

A game entirely based on being a paper pushing border guard? How on earth could that be any fun? Well it is, it sort of hits that spot most "addictive" mobile games might but in a much more in depth and profound way.
You work at a border checkpoint  into a Soviet totalitarian state and you have to let people in or turn them away based  the criteria your bosses leave you as you start your day. So you kindly ask "Papers, please" all day, make sure the documents check out, let people in or turn them away, then head home...
But the thing you have a family to support behind all this, that are hungry and sickly gits that cost money, if you don't make enough -they'll die on you. So you better make sure you make enough money to support them until the end of the story! Oh and watch out for terrorists, they'll dampen your mood too.
The game has multiple endings depending on how long you survive/keep your job too.
Absolutely brilliant game, a must buy for the price. It combines a really fun set of mechanics with a bleak and depressing world, with some really hard choices to make that have consequences on the people you let in or turn away.

SOMA only strengthened my resolve a couple of years later.
And that, my friends, is the highest praise I can possibly give to Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs.

This game is probably the second biggest love/hate relationships with a game i've had. Maybe third, if you count WoW - but I can safely say I'd recommend it.
First of all, the game is free. You can, without putting a dime in, play the game to a very wide extent. Like other mobas except Dota, you have to pay for the characters with an ingame currency "favour" (favor for you
non-UK readers).
This can be alleviated if you're willing to spend a little, though, as the God Pack is ~£20 and provides every single God in the game.
The game, replayability wise, excels in it's class. Due to the nature of the aiming etc, you can outplay people a huge amount of the time and the macro game is always a fresh challenge for any competitive people who may want to play it with friends - with a lot of resources available.
The wide array of characters to play with also increases replayability, as they are all "viable" at some level, and if you put time into a particular character.
A major thing for eSports titles is that there is a discrepancy between what the top level play, and what you play. In some games, there is a completely different meta - with Smite that isn't the same. The picks that pros pick, can be picked up - and the patch they play on is the same as the patch played on in live clients.
The first two intertwine. Because it's a MOBA, regardless on the kind of player you are - you will find ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s in the community. MOBAs especially draw this crowd in, and you will see stereotypical "moba etiquette" a lot of the time. Happily, HiRez have allowed you to mute people as other games so you can significantly reduce the amount of rude individuals you have to put up with.

Distraint is a short psychological horror game that is only mildly disturbing at best. If you’re looking for a horror game, maybe look somewhere else. The game is pretty short on spooks -- and I’m saying that as someone who was traumatised by Snow White as a kid. But if you want a game with an interesting story that’s mostly overshadowed by tedious game mechanics and heavy-handed storytelling, then that’s probably all Distraint will offer you.
Don’t get me wrong, I’d really like to recommend this game. On a superficial level, the art is so beautifully unique in a world with too many goddamn copy-paste pixel games, and the music is moody and fitting -- not only the creepy-as-all-hell ambient strings and sounds, but also the more melodic songs that play, including my favourite jam, the bourgeoisie accordion. Beyond that, the atmosphere is consistently unsettling, but as far as the “horror” part of the game is concerned, there isn’t much. A few almost-jumpscares, and a few moments of, “Hey, that’s messed up.” That’s not bad on its own, especially for a psychological horror game, but that means the game relies heavily on its story. And the story seems interesting enough: a modern-day cautionary tale about greed. Where it falters is in its execution.
Most obviously, the game is short. You can finish it in under two hours even if you’re absolutely terrible at sussing out the really simple puzzles. And trust me, puzzles are my Achilles heel. But Distraint being a short game is not necessarily an issue – some of my favourites (Gunpoint, Brothers) are about the same length. For horror, though, this becomes a problem.
There’s no nuance, no unknowns. You have a solid understanding of everyone you meet within moments. Even your three bosses have a scene where they go from a mysterious watchful presence to clear-cut villains in a flash. The game leaves very little to the imagination, and there’s nothing gripping about knowing what to expect, which in Distraint means some ‘scary’ blood on a door, or something. At one point, there’s even a room with a television and static. That’s it – that’s the whole room. There’s not even a purpose to the room beyond that, or any gameplay mechanic that furthers the plot, the message. It’s just there to be ‘creepy’. And it fails at that.
That problem of heavy-handedness affects other aspects of the story, too. The emotional parts of the game, like the ending sequence, are almost completely ruined by how rushed they are. Even the character progression of the protagonist goes from 0 to 100 in an instant, and it makes it hard to truly love the game, or for the message to have a lasting impression. Or for the ending to even seem reasonable, at that.
The most disappointing part about it is that the premise is so promising. But rather than fleshing out the story or horror, the game focusses on absolutely mind-numbing gameplay. Other horror games do this quite often. “This door is locked. Find a key. The power is down. Turn it back on.” The difference is that most other games ‘reward’ you with jumpscares or tie it into the plot – Distraint rarely does either of these things. For the most part, the gameplay only exists to drag out the game. The horror aspects could have been so much more engaging if the gameplay served it; instead, it seems like an add-on, undermining both the game’s story and horror elements.
Distraint has a lot going for it, and I’ll definitely be checking out the sequel when it’s available. But while I can see the appeal, I can’t quite recommend it as a horror game, or for its story, and definitely not for the fetch-and-get gameplay. However, it all comes together in a polished and unique package with a good message, and for that alone, I wish I could at least give it a neutral recommendation.

Final Fantasy XIV: A Realm Reborn (2.0) is a reboot of the failure that was Final Fantasy XIV 1.0.
FF14: ARR is said to be a fairly casual MMO, and I can't deny it. I don't have a lot of MMO experience, but I can tell the game is slow-paced. That being said, this game is very easy to pick up and there is no built-in DPS meter, so no one can say you're bad without letting everyone know they're using a third party program (Illegal, oh no! But Square Enix doesn't care if you use a third party program, as long as you don't call other people out on doing subpar damage. How nice.) The game does cater to the casual crowd more often than not, and as a result some people seem to be absolutely clueless when it comes to playing their class. I sometimes wish Square could throw in a DPS meter so DPS would be encouraged to not be dumpster-tier when they see that a healer or tank is doing more DEEPS than they are.
The races in this game are very similar: human (Hyur), human with cat ears and a tail (Miqo'te), giraffe humans (Elezen), big human (Roegadyn), and potato/little human (Lalafell) and with the upcoming expansion, demon/dragon human (Au'ra). There are differences between the races of course, but there is nothing too drastic between them. Square played it safe and decided not to include actual beast races, as cool as that would be. Maybe in the second expansion Square will realize they're making bank and that people actually want a beast race (see Au'ra concept art that got dropped. Jesus, why'd you do it Yoshi-P?). Expect a lot of c@girls running around, often half naked, coolcool. Character creation isn't the game's strong point, there are no sliders unfortunately, so you can't make a monster like you could in Oblivion or Skyrim or anything of the like (as fun as that would be). A lot of characters do look similar and that leads to people trying to make special snowflake characters that look atrocious.
The game is by no means perfect; there are good aspects of it in the middle of all the bad. It's a fun game with a lot of content to do. The story is pretty good in my opinion, nowhere near the caliber of FF6. That being said, there are a lot of references to previous FF games. Off the top of my head, there's a Crystal/Sycrus Tower raid (FF3), an Ultros & Typhon Fight (FF6), a FF13 event which had Lightning appear in Eorzea. And I'm sure there's a multitude of other references I've missed or forgotten.
The sound was one of the first things I took note of when I started playing the game. I was captured by the ambient noise, the music (the music in the game is especially great), the sound effects, everything; everything sound-related is great. What I love the most is the weather sound effects, my personal favourite being the stormy weather, it really does sound great with the lightning and rain sfx. The game is very pretty and quite colourful (minus some select areas), if you're starting out I suggest choosing a class that starts in Gridania. Gridania is super comfy with its music and environment and has the most simplistic layout of the 3 starting areas. The graphics aren't as good as FF14 1.0, but that game required a supercomputer to run smoothly. My game runs fine on medium settings with a computer built in 2009.
The community in this game is very friendly except for a small minority. Most will go out of their way to help other people and it really does encourage people (someone like me who's turned into an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ because of LoL & DotA 2) to be as helpful as I can be. I'm guessing that the community is so nice is because a good portion of it is from FF11, so don't be surprised to see married people, or even parents playing the game.
As I've said before, the FF14 we have now is a reboot of its 1.0 iteration, after the failure of 1.0, Square had to play it safe, which pretty much explains the casualness of the game, alongside the seemingly similar races.
It's definitely not the best game out there. Updates are plentiful & full of content; the game is easy to get into, a lot of throwbacks to previous FF games, half naked c@girl waifus if you're into that, good sound and a friendly community.

Awezome mmo! One of the best i played!
World of Warcraft used to be my favorite untill they started with daily ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t and garrisons, making their game feel like a chore. Another thing that made me switch was the use of alts, spending countless of hours atempting to level each character up because their classes were separated to new characters, in Final Fantasy your free to switch to any job just by equipping a weapon or tool.
+ So for Final Fantasy, expect to spend alot of time on a enjoyable story line for all jobs and quests you come across, something thats been missing in many mmo's. The depth of the story makes this game truly unique, even your job weapons and tools have their own stories!
+ The world is gigantic, so theres alot to explore, though don't forget to attune to every crystal you come across as they will all serve as a teleportation method troughout the zones.
+ The bosses you come across on your travels feel challanging and tactics will be needed ranging from basic to the most  advanced nerve wrecking ones.
+ The economy is well made within the game, allowing players to forge the economy. As you come across certain materias within your main quest you will be able to sell them for over 100.000 gil which will be enough for any gear or items your going for.
+ The graphics look amazing, though a better anti-alising method is needed, edges do look jagged even in 1080p with high desktop settings.
+ The soundtracks are great! though i preffered certain tracks in v1.0 compared to the new ones.
+ Rapid patches are thrown out with ever month or so, giving you even more to enjoy!
+ The pricings are quite on the cheap side, monthly subscription is not all that expencive compared to other mmo's as you can choose between multiple or a single character for each server.
+ PC gamers and Console players can play togheter! The community is friendly and supportive, something rarely seen in most free to play games.
- Farming bots are present in the game, though they are harmless to players, they are capable of damaging the economy. But such bots are present in most mmo's, so Final Fantasy are not alone on this.
And as for the conclusion of my review, if your looking for a deep and well thought out mmo, this one is most certainly recommended!

Bad for immersion.
The game itself isn't bad, visuals are good, areas so far look to be varied which is good. There's a lot of good things in there.
But it falls down for me on the massive grindfest, microtransactions (pay to win) and due to the way it handles multiplayer, very obviously immersion breaking.
First the grind. I expect this from ES titles, especially after Skyrim and how you progressed up levels and such, but this does it in a bad way. I can only craft a single weapon/armour part after finding my 'style' material. Raw ore? Easy. But that style stuff (in my case star metal), well I've only found 1 in many hours of playing and hit level 10.
Of course you can buy some, but it's massively expensive, the same with most things. All of it seems centered around putting in massive amounts of hours grinding, or paying to get them via real money (since you'd quickly run out of game currency due to the high cost).
But borderline game breaking is the way it handles enemies, I mean come on. Enemies have very very obvious spawn points, and CONSTANTLY spawn. Like, right in front of your face. Including bosses.
I get #why# they did it, since there is obviously other players online doing the same thing.
And of course the other players. Have to say, the community so far seems better than most I've seen, helpful people and not too much trash talk. But....and this is a very personal preference...it looks silly.
Personally I think seeing people run around with huge, garish coloured panther/weird/dead horse mounts along with even weirder familiars everywhere makes it feel a lot less epic.
I'm sure the above isn't a problem for most people, and I'm guessing the developers listened to the calls of the majority when making these decisions.
But for me, it's so far very unenjoyable and has moved from being Eldar Scrolls to World of Warcraft.
I'll stress again these are personal points, so read over it rather than just looking at the 'not recommended' vote.

This is a fairly early review granted not seen the full extent of the game, such as end game dungeons and pvp.
So far the games got a lot of ups and downs  on the basis that it becomes lost in translation  between an mmo and of course a standaloen elders scrolls game.
Granted this is their first try and its not a bad attempt,  exploration and visuals  go on par with an in depth feel to the games audio which helps envelope you into the mood perfectly for the game.
Lore is pretty rich and ties in a lot of questions an avid fan of the elder series would enjoy, personally i couldnt get into much of the story or the characters.
Game mechanics such as  creation ie. blacksmithing , woodworking, provisioning.   some work well where others feel a bit -shrug-     favorably i enjoyed the enchanting and oddly enough cooking ,   crafting armor and weapons can seem a bit of a grind followed by a feeling of dissapointment as most gear you can farm with relative ease with the  oblivion games opening up in a city , swarm farm and you have blue gear for your level quicker then it takes to farm materials and cross your fingers.
Classes roles,  most  have got it down fairly well to a degree, theres more immersion of choice with a role you choose   such as templar's  and rouges , so on an mmo perspective this is great. However theres a few features sadly removed i would of loved to of seen to give more emphasis on  magic casters, such as  alteration, mysticism, illusion     which does not really seem to be put into this game, which is a bit of a shame  so fingers crossed  they will add this in the future.
Another nit picky thing for me  which is kinda bit of a marmite subject, but  it would be nice if they added teh feature to be able to swim -under- the water and explore aquatic areas  , sunken ships . so more places for treasure out of interest would be a nice touch.
The quests are great solo,  but with other players it didnt feel like i was playing the quests with party members, you tend to feel you are just in a different phase from them so it can make you feel a tad frustrated at times when you want to immerse into the games story and quests with other players more closely,
This is all i got for now, but aside some ups and downs  its still a worthwhile game to play at a more relaxed pace compared to other mmo games.

If you choose to grind it gets rather dull and boring, if you do wanna get a fast xp grind i suggest teaming up with a friend or guilde and doing a few dungeons, they can provide a lot of xp

Some of the world and gameplay is locked, unless you buy the DLCs, or pay for ESO+ although I don't have an issue with it, some people might turn away from it.
Requires time, if you are tied up for time, then I wouldn't suggest this or many other MMOs, this needs time to both get used to and to do quests, the issue is not with struggling but locating the areas, if you haven't all ready
Overall this game although I haven't touched on a lot both Pro and Con A lot of it is personal preference, and thus I didn't see a reason to add. Is a really strong game and I probably give it 9 Crowns out of 10.

Have you ever fancied being a border inspector? Me neither. Papers, Please grants you a chance to try it anyway.
The background is grim: you only got the job because of a lottery. Arstotzkan border is a busy place, all kinds of shady people trying to get into the country that gives out a communist vibe. You make sure their papers are in order by meticulously checking each bit of information for the smallest mistakes. You do this manually by eye. It doesn't help that each day the ministry announces new, subsequently more bizarre rules for you to follow.
At first the user interface is confusing and it takes a while to get used to and see the logic behind. All the tutorial you'll get is in the instructions you're given each day. Interestingly, this adds to the all-encompassing dystopian feel that is well delivered by the pixelated graphics and ominous music.
The story elements are brilliantly woven into the protagonist's role, served with dark humour: you often have to make moral choices by either admitting or denying desperate immigrants or whether you'll help the insurgents. You generally can't do everything because the salary comes from admitting immigrants and you are fined for mistakes.
Keeping your family alive provides the motivation to keep doing a good job. Money is always tight and you have to manage your expenses after each day. Fortunately, being a border inspector in a corrupt country, you can make additional profit by accepting bribes and striking deals with the honest people you meet in your job.
Each playthrough, one month of game time, lasts approximately 4 hours but to complete everything will require several playthroughs: there are three different "winning" endings and 20 different endings in total that depend on your choices and performance. Afterwards, there's the endless mode to pour hours into.
Striking into a niche as small as it gets, Papers, Please does a tremendous job at providing an interesting and even amusing experience as a border inspector. If you have an eye for detail and fancy scrutiny and perfection, you'll probably love this game. Otherwise you might want to check some gameplay videos first - it is a niche game after all.

This game has a lot of negative connotations, and it's understandable why.
Being the official follow-up to what some claim to be the 'scariest game of all time', Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs simplified the core gameplay of its predecessor. It has an interesting narrative, absolutely fantastic voice acting and it's hard to put the game down. But there's something that every apprehensive buyer wants to know - is it scary/scarier than The Dark Descent?
...Yes, it's scary.
No, it's not as scary as The Dark Descent.
But that doesn't mean it's not worth your time. MFP excels in constructing a believable environment
in atmosphere, and although it strips a lot of features off from the original, it was The Chinese Room's take on a fantastic horror gem. Could it have been better? Yeah. If it wasn't hailed as the direct sequel to The Double D, then no one would be comparing it to the original, and there would be less negative connotations associated to the game.
Overall, it's got solid writing, atmosphere and scares, and it's an experience that shouldn't be overlooked.

It seems a little bit unfair to me to call this game a "First Person Shooter." The term "FPS" just leaves you without much to go on; compare it to the word "rocket." If I say the word "rocket", you don't know if I am talking about Elon Musk's SpaceX vehicle or a Fourth of July bottle rocket.  I found that there is a lot more to "Borderlands 2" than the shooting. It is a trip into a fascinating world that is full of surprises, and it just so happens that to explore it you have to do a lot of shooting and rack up a huge body count. I'll warn you about one thing, and I don't know if it is a spoiler or not; early on you figure out that the native inhabitants of Pandora are a little bit on the uneducated side.  They misspell stuff. Their conversation is of the most rudimentary kind, largely limited to ungrammatical death threats; but I was rocking along and noticed one dude was ranting longer than usual and his raucous bellowing seemed to be real familiar; he was doing one of Hamlet's soliloquys - no, not the famous "to be or not to be" speech but one that gave a clue to some of the terminology in the game. Good luck trying to find the one bad guy in the game that paid attention in English class... If that spoiled anything for you, I am sorry; it hasn't spoiled anything for me, because I don't yet know whether this literary quote hidden in plain sight is a big clue to more and greater adventures, or whether it was just a gag the game developers decided to throw in. And there is a lot of interesting stuff like that in itf. Anyway, I am having a lot of fun with it. One bit of advice: don't go near the water. You might fall in. Anyway, that's what I keep doing.

DISTRAINT is a 2D adventure game about a man named Price who is working for a company that seizes people’s property. If he wants to earn a coveted partnership with the firm, he must take on some of their most difficult assignments: kicking an elderly woman, a recluse in the woods, and a drug addict out of their homes.Though DISTRAINT is described as a psychological horror game, it’s not in your face enough to terrify you or inspire nightmares. Instead, it uses horror elements to represent his guilty conscience. Sure, blood dripping and television static are on the cheesy side, but they’re also effective within the context of their scenes.
The sound design in DISTRAINT is brilliant and builds a tense, haunting atmosphere. Disturbing noises, dramatic music, and other small cues construct Price’s world, underscoring the moral bind he’s found himself in. The artwork is pretty standard fare, and the story presents a common dilemma, but it’s the sound that pulls this game together and makes it shine.
puuzles...Some of the puzzles are even quite clever and enjoyable to solve. I really liked using a mysterious green substance to shift between dimensions at the druggie’s place. It required a certain amount of skill at timing to weave through the maze of boarded up doors and holes in the walls before the drug’s effects could wear off.
Distraint makes you realize what it is to be a human, to have a soul, conscience and be responsible for your own actions and choices in life. Restro-styled pixelated graphics, little bit of a good soundtrack with decent light effects..and The ending was gripping, holding a dark twist I didn’t see coming at all..

In the past, the MOBA genre has never really sucked me in. The standard for these games is a mostly top-down camera angle that takes you right out of the action and makes you feel like you're ordering just one character in an RTS game rather than actually playing the character. Smite gives you a third-person camera and direct control, and it feels so much better as a result. It's still a very flat game, even with verticality involved in leaps, knockups, various ultimates and more. There is no aiming up or down, jumping is purely aesthetic, but I find these things to be a nice way to simplify what could otherwise be a very chaotic game.
Smite's roster of characters is what initially piqued my interest about the game, and it's only gotten better since I first took an interest. Ratatoskr still stands as my favorite character design in any multiplayer game, bar none, but they've come out with quite a nice variety of gods, in terms of visual design. Goddesses, unfortunately, have a lot of catching up to do. But at least in terms of gameplay, there's a fairly even ground here. Every character of the nearly 90 in the game is pretty unique and stands out on their own, each with interesting little elements that make them a totally new challenge to play, and they're coming out with new ones every month or so. There's a nice, consistent drip feed of updates to add in new characters and skins and balance existing content.
As with most MOBAs, the Big Deal Mode in this game is a 3 lane map with your standard assortment of defensive turrets and minions, with jungles in between. Smite doesn't really seem to fight the status quo there. But the other game modes get a lot of play as well, with 6 maps to choose from, each hosting their own unique spin on pushing minions into the other team's no-no zones. There's something here for whatever you happen to be interested in, if it's playing on a smaller team, going for kills in teamfights, highly objective-based play, the variety is quite welcome.
Where Smite absolutely blows its main competition, League of Legends, out of the water is in how it manages locking away playable content. By which I mean, it basically doesn't. The free rotation standard to MOBAs is here as expected, along with unlocking characters via in-game currency. What's not here is anything like the 'rune' system which lets you build stat bonuses onto your characters before a match is even started. Smite ain't about that life. What really makes it awesome, though, is the God Pack. $30 ($20 on sale) gets you everything, forever. All gods, past and future, are unlocked at that reasonable rate, and you're refunded any points spent on unlocking them beforehand. Once you have the god pack, you are denied access to nothing but cosmetics. If you want to look pretty, it's going to really cost you, but that's the only remaining carrot they dangle in front of your nose.
But if cosmetics are important to you, you may find that this game burns you pretty often. Without going into too much detail, the game has set prices for various 'tiers' of skins, many of which you can buy outright, but the vast majority of which are either permanently unavailable (you weren't there for the event, too bad~) or only obtainable via 'gachapon' style chests. Those chests are consistently awful, offering almost no additional value other than exclusivity of their contents. You pay 400 gems to get a random 400 gem skin, or maybe just a 200 gem waste of time, or rarely a 600 gem nice thing. Given the randomness involved and the likelihood of getting less than you paid for, the value proposition is awful and there's no system in place to make chests feel worthwhile. For most players, it will forever remain a way for the developer, HiRez, to taunt you with skins you'll never get. At least, not while the prospect of paying up to $100 for a model swap is unreasonable to you.
But all negativity aside, that's just cosmetics. They're still putting out good content, and even nice skins that you can just outright buy. You'll never find your free login gems stacking up too much with nowhere to spend them, and you might even find a reason to spend some money on gems, too. It's just a shame that almost all the skins I'm really interested in getting my hands on are locked away behind an awful chest system.
Overall, I recommend Smite. I wasn't a fan of any MOBA before this one, but Smite is honestly a lot of fun, and it's a good deal. Free to play, reasonable to play for free, and cheap to unlock everything. The action is good, the community is at least a step up from LoL, and there's plenty to enjoy.

This game is fantastic.
I avoided this game for years, and it was an absolute mistake. I heard like many others it was a skyrim knock-off cash grab and believed it. Until on a whim my wife and I were craving a fantasy game we could play together. We were both burned out on WOW, so I decided to take a look at r/elderscrollsonline. They claimed it was actually a fun game and to not believe the rumors circulating, so I figured why not, it looks fun.
We spent about 3 days searching out every nook and cranny in Auridon. Holy smokes, this game is gorgeous. Every nook, every cranny has something new to discover. Chests, books, secrets, delves, podunk towns with actual interesting quests to do. The amount of content and love ZOS has poured into this game is apparent. The writing is hilarious, yet serious. The combat is exhilirating, the best in any MMO I've ever tried. You feel like you're actually in a populated Tamriel, not some demi-god thrown into a story book.
The crowning moment of this game that led me to write a review was the Wrothgar questline. The writers of that story need to write TES6 in it's entirety. I was more attached to the characters by the end of it than I ever came close to being in Skyrim. The consequences felt real, the ending was bittersweet, and by the end I felt like I had accomplished more in this orcish political struggle than defeating Alduin. I was blown away.
All in all, I'd give this game a solid 9/10. There are small little things like fishing, mounts, and various other QOL improvements that could be done, but I'm still having a blast every time I fire it up, and I've barely explored anything yet. I highly reccomend this game.

Final Fantasy XIV: A Realm Reborn (2.0) is a reboot of the failure that was Final Fantasy XIV 1.0.
FF14: ARR is said to be a fairly casual MMO, and I can't deny it. I don't have a lot of MMO experience, but I can tell the game is slow-paced. That being said, this game is very easy to pick up and there is no built-in DPS meter, so no one can say you're bad without letting everyone know they're using a third party program (Illegal, oh no! But Square Enix doesn't care if you use a third party program, as long as you don't call other people out on doing subpar damage. How nice.) The game does cater to the casual crowd more often than not, and as a result some people seem to be absolutely clueless when it comes to playing their class. I sometimes wish Square could throw in a DPS meter so DPS would be encouraged to not be dumpster-tier when they see that a healer or tank is doing more DEEPS than they are.
The races in this game are very similar: human (Hyur), human with cat ears and a tail (Miqo'te), giraffe humans (Elezen), big human (Roegadyn), and potato/little human (Lalafell) and with the upcoming expansion, demon/dragon human (Au'ra). There are differences between the races of course, but there is nothing too drastic between them. Square played it safe and decided not to include actual beast races, as cool as that would be. Maybe in the second expansion Square will realize they're making bank and that people actually want a beast race (see Au'ra concept art that got dropped. Jesus, why'd you do it Yoshi-P?). Expect a lot of c@girls running around, often half naked, coolcool. Character creation isn't the game's strong point, there are no sliders unfortunately, so you can't make a monster like you could in Oblivion or Skyrim or anything of the like (as fun as that would be). A lot of characters do look similar and that leads to people trying to make special snowflake characters that look atrocious.
The game is by no means perfect; there are good aspects of it in the middle of all the bad. It's a fun game with a lot of content to do. The story is pretty good in my opinion, nowhere near the caliber of FF6. That being said, there are a lot of references to previous FF games. Off the top of my head, there's a Crystal/Sycrus Tower raid (FF3), an Ultros & Typhon Fight (FF6), a FF13 event which had Lightning appear in Eorzea. And I'm sure there's a multitude of other references I've missed or forgotten.
The sound was one of the first things I took note of when I started playing the game. I was captured by the ambient noise, the music (the music in the game is especially great), the sound effects, everything; everything sound-related is great. What I love the most is the weather sound effects, my personal favourite being the stormy weather, it really does sound great with the lightning and rain sfx. The game is very pretty and quite colourful (minus some select areas), if you're starting out I suggest choosing a class that starts in Gridania. Gridania is super comfy with its music and environment and has the most simplistic layout of the 3 starting areas. The graphics aren't as good as FF14 1.0, but that game required a supercomputer to run smoothly. My game runs fine on medium settings with a computer built in 2009.
The community in this game is very friendly except for a small minority. Most will go out of their way to help other people and it really does encourage people (someone like me who's turned into an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ because of LoL & DotA 2) to be as helpful as I can be. I'm guessing that the community is so nice is because a good portion of it is from FF11, so don't be surprised to see married people, or even parents playing the game.
As I've said before, the FF14 we have now is a reboot of its 1.0 iteration, after the failure of 1.0, Square had to play it safe, which pretty much explains the casualness of the game, alongside the seemingly similar races.
It's definitely not the best game out there. Updates are plentiful & full of content; the game is easy to get into, a lot of throwbacks to previous FF games, half naked c@girl waifus if you're into that, good sound and a friendly community.

Tree of Saviour is one of the biggest letdowns I've come across my 15 years of playing MMORPGs.
Although it's only ~1 year since the start of the Open Beta, the game managed to lose over 10k players in the first half year and another 2-3k until now.
The reason for this are the neverending bugs, FPS issues with a mediocre graphic card [the minimum requirement stated on Steam won't even enable you to play the game], the horrible stat-balance [most stats are useless] and the non-existing Class balance [some Classes are so bad that you won't be able to take them to level 280+ content].
The graphics look nice on the first view, but they are also the reason why this game has so many issues in the first place.
They use up a lot of the graphic cards RAM because of the generated "particles" that form by movements,attacks,skills and environmental effects like dust clouds/candles/etc. This causes your FPS to drop a lot if your character is moving/taking some action, making it impossible to play with a low-standard graphic card. Once your FPS drop to a certain point [below 1], you have a high chance that the game client crashes on you.
There are also many skills [mainly Cryomancer/Psychokino] which cause a similar effect by dropping your FPS below 1.
The gameplay is getting incredibly boring once you've caught the gist of it.
That's mainly because the monsters have an A.I. of a bath sponge. They will run beside you and start hitting you with normal attacks or try casting skills, which you can evade by simply moving backwards and/or to the sides.
Even the bosses don't have any challenging tricks upon their sleeves; instead, their try to wear you down with their high damage magic and knockback/-down combos[which are quite frustrating once you get caught in them].
The worst thing is that you can easily make them deal only 1 damage by slotting two five-star yellow gems into your armor and 2 five-star blue gems into your shoes, because every damage is reduced by your defence by a flat amount.
This allows you to actively skip all trouble until you hit around level 280+...
One of the worst things is the daily restriction on dungeon entries/daily mercenary post missions/Saalus convent, which are the most convenient way to level up and strenghen your equipment.
It basically urges you to either grind&quest or wait for another day to run again.
It gets boring very quickly because those dungeons&missions are extremely linear and don't have any great gains except for some RNG-bosscubes + a few silver per run.
There are also many more restrictions, and if you don't pay for the premium service (i.e. "Token"), you'll be even more limited with daily dungeon runs, market place useage and even personal trades. You're also unable to use the Team Storage, which allows all your characters to share their silver&equipment, if you run without a Token.
It's also rather discriminating that you have to pay more $$$ for the same amount of TP (the ingame cash currency) if you come from Europe or North America than you have to pay if you come from a 2nd/3rd world country, regardless of which server you're actually playing on.
About the general gameplay:
It's fun while you're still leveling below level 270, although it's not really challenging.
However, this game has way too many restrictions and too many silver sinks (to counter inflation I guess) for a casual player to enjoy the game. You're practically forced to farm tons of silver to buy attributes to make your skills stronger, to upgrade your equipment (which is quite expensive at higher levels, even at the lower stages/grades of upgrade), repeat daily Practonium quest until you get your Practonium to craft a ridiculously strong weapon for level 315+, repeat daily Saalus runs to get Blessed Shards to craft Blessed Gems which can be used to transcend your equipment to make it extraordinarily strong [a stage 10 transcended weapon is 6,5 times stronger than the basic weapon is] and farm tons of cards to upgrade your card/tons of gems/loot to upgrade your gems.
So much grind just for one character. And because of the restrictions and RNGs involved, people are basically forced to run several characters at once just to build up one character. The 4 basic character slots are nowhere enough to become a decent player in less than one year with daily 3-5 hours dedication, so you better buy TP to increase your team slots.
And, if you get a pet, it also counts as a character, so it uses up a slot,too, even if it's just a useless leg drag because the A.I. of the pets is even worse than the monsters A.I., causing a lot of bugs/errors.
You just have to visit the forums of the game to get the gist of the terror the game is going to unleash onto you, so better get informed and prepared first if you want to play it. This is not Ragnarok Online, even if it looks similar.
My advice: wait at least another year till you try the game. The developers have recently begun to tackle a few issues the game has, but they're nowhere near the point where this game is enjoyable. The rebalancing of basically everything seems to be planned [at least according to the recent player-developer discussion session in February 2017], so until then  it's better to stay away for your own good.

If you're expecting it to be a sequel to Amnesia, with its gimmicky fear mechanics and try-try again difficulty, as the origonal advertising campaign for the game might have lead you to expect, then keep clear.

If you've played the original Amnesia, 'Machine for Pigs' will leave you disappointed. Just about everything that can be defined as 'gameplay' was gutted from this successor, turning it into a spooky walking simulator with little to no intricate reaction with the world around your digital character. However, if you're just a simple onlooker passing by whose curiosity has been piqued by that title artwork, who's seeking an intriguing story experience of a tragic tale with weird Bioshock-esque sci-fi properties and a light spook here or there, don't hesitate to grab this game for a look-see. You'll enjoy it.
Also, as one would guess, 'Machine for Pigs' uses the titular farm animal in quite the iterative way that complements the game world and its themes seamlessly, which is why it should win the nomination for "Best Use Of A Farm Animal" in the Steam awards. So nominate it up, folks. This award's not about quality gameplay.

This is a true masterpiece, and a revelation for the Survival Horror genre. I had played the game's predecessor, and completed it years ago, and it was the first truly good horror game I had played, in-fact it had set the bar for any future experiences with the horror gaming genre. I first heard about the game a few months before it's initial release and had brought it soon after it came out for Mac, however it wasn't until a long time later that I began to play the game.
I recently started playing this and I wasn't too sure about how it would be, as overall the reactions from people who had played the predecessor were generally negative. Nonetheless, I started this game and noticed a lot of differences straight away. First of all, I noted that the graphics were a fair part better than the graphics in 'The Dark Descent'. Secondly, I realised that, unlike in Amnesia:The Dark Descent, you cannot move objects around anywhere near as much in this game. In-fact only a few objects, such as chairs, can be moved around in this game. As I walked around, I noted the suprisingly good level of attention to detail in the level design and I began gathering all the notes I could find, as I did in the previous game. The grammar, of course, was perfect, something that a suprisingly large amount of games miss out on.
As I walked around the first area in the game, upon entering various rooms, I had recieved telling flashbacks from the mind of Oswald Mandus, the character you play as. From the start of the game, I knew that Oswald had two twin boys, Edwin and Enoch, aswell as a wife that died giving birth to the latter twin. I progressed through the first part of the game fairly quickly and witnessed the story unravel as I played through. Please note that a good portion of the story is revealed in notes and other found documents, it is important to read a few of these notes as they can help in puzzles and often give interesting information to the backstory of the game's characters. The story to Amnesia:The Dark Descent was, in my opinion, absoloutely brilliant. As I played through the first portion of the game, I still kept my opinion of the predecessor's story being far better, however as I got closer and closer toward the end, I found myself preferring the story of A Machine for Pigs.
Now, of course, this isn't just a game for the story. This is a horror game. I thoroughly enjoyed the scares of The Dark Descent, not at the time of course, but I did find the scare sequences in this game somewhat lacking. The AI of the Manpigs is still lacking, but is a definite improvement from the enemies of The Dark Descent. To give a balanced review of the scares, let's look at what makes monsters in games scary. First of all, the appearence. The Manpigs are not scary based on appearence alone, I mean don't get me wrong, if one was chasing me in real life I would be absoloutely terrified, but in a horror game, especially the sequel to such an amazing horror, they were definitely lacking in scare-factor. Secondly, the buildup. The buildup tells a different story, apart from one or two encounters, the buildup was equally as great as The Dark Descent. Overall, however, The Dark Descent was definitely more scary. There are definitely a few encounters, and not just with the Manpigs, that were incredibly tense. How tense, you ask? Remember the first time you saw the Water Lurker in The Dark Descent? THAT tense.
Overall, the story in this game is absoloutely amazing and, based on story alone, I would give this game a solid 9/10. This is a horror game, and the scares were definitely lacking overall, but some encounters were extremely tense and I could feel my heart race afterwards. On the scare-factor alone, I would rate this game 7.8/10. Other than those two aspects, you have to bear in mind the puzzles, the graphics and the atmosphere. Firstly, the puzzles in this game are definitely easier than in The Dark Descent, but are still good. I would rate the puzzle factor 6.5/10. The graphics, for the year it was made, are not brilliant. But this is no Elder Scrolls game, and so long as the graphics are good enough to get immersed, then that is all that is necessary. For the graphics alone, bearing in mind what I just said, I would give it an 8/10. The atmosphere in this game was a lot better than I expected it to be, the soundtrack was fantasic, the attention to detail in the level design was brilliant and the other aspects, such as lighting was awesome. In fact, I would go as far to say that the atmosphere in this game was better than the one in The Dark Descent, which was not far from perfection itself. For atmosphere, I would rate this game a 9.2/10. So using maths to figure out the score average...
Ladies and gentlemen, this masterpiece of a game scores a well deserved:
8.1
With great atmosphere, good puzzles, amazing story, and some extremely tense monster encounters, this is a true masterpiece.
If you liked Amnesia:The Dark Descent, or any horror game in general, then I highly recommend that you order this game.
