Compared to the first game -
the second "Amnesia" game hasn't gotten such an extremely positive reception. This is probably more due to people constantly comparing it to the first game than to it being the lesser of the two. Comparisons with the original Amnesia game are of course to be expected - after all, that game has obtained a cult-like status as one of the scariest horror games EVER - but are not really fair in my opinion.
Of course, the two games share part of their title and there is also a fairly strong connection between both games' storyline (although more in the background, subtle referred to in the documents that are to be found everywhere). But the developers clearly had a different goal in mind with
, and the deserves to be rated on its own merits. These are very strong and pronounced indeed: the all important story is told in a brilliant way, with lots of documents being interlaced with revealing diary fragments and mysterious phonecalls. Although the story is certainly not straightforward and demands some thinking and re-reading to become completely clear, The Chinese Room has done an awesome job in this department.
Equally well done is the setting of the game: there is a very pervasive sense of darkness, gloom and horror during the game, helped by excellent use of the (fairly limited) graphical engine and, especially, by anothr gorgeous soundscape and musical score. Especially the music - freshly composed for the game by Jessica Cury - shines: it jumps between styles with astonishing ease, sometimes sounding as classical as Bach, and then all of a sudden going very dissonant and most unsettling. In fact "unsettling" in perhaps the single word that defines this game best: the unfolding story, the entire setting, the slow realisation of the unimaginable horrors that wait to be discovered, turned this game in a true horrific experience.
But that is not the same as a truly frightening experience: I didn't feel the same sense of utter fear as when playing the original game, when I often had to stop after some time in order to recompose myself. The horror in
is of a different sort: it is the horror of discovering the extreme, unhuman cruelty which lies beneath it all, combined with the slow but dreadful realisation of one's own part in this. Quite often I found myself reluctant to progress as I didn't want to discover more of the story, however intriguing it was. I simply refused to believe this was actually happening - which testifies to the complete feeling of immersion this game manages to achieve.
As with all true horror games, it is of course very highly recommended to play this one in a very dark environment, preferably using headphones in order to absord the amazing sound world of this game. Recently some sort of "sound mod" for the game was released, offering players using stereo headphones the opportunity to experience the sounds and music in a true threedimensional, positional fashion. I didn't try this out myself yet, but I can imagine that it even adds to the atmosphere. Please refer to the guides in the community section for the game.
Not everything is perfect though: the amount of actual gameplay has been reduced, not by a lot, but at least in one very important way. In the first game, you had to collect tinderboxes to be able to light candles, and lamp oil for the lantern you could carry with you (and which proved to be utterly necessary in the many pitch dark passages). Collecting tinderboxes and oil, adn keeping an eye on your oil level and the amount of tinderboxes left, made me play that game in a cautious, very slow manner, trying to keep at least something in reserve. In this game, however, the entire inventory has disappeared, and so have the light sources which needed to be managed. The lantern you are carrying with you stays "on" all the time, and the only thing you have to worry about, is not to attract the attention of "the enemy". It seems like a minor quibble, but it is not: the game changed from an interactive horror game into an almost exclusively story- and atmosphere-driven experience, although an extremely strong one.
But in the end, both the story and superb soundtrack manage to overcome any shortcomings, and make this game an essential one for anybody not being deterred by the horrors to be found within.

If you say this is the best souls game to my face I will resort to physical violence. This game plays more like a Dark Souls Ripoff than a Dark Souls Sequel.
From's B Team knew exactly one thing about Dark Souls, that people said it was difficult. They didn't know why, or in what ways but they had to do better. How? By making it harder than the first game of course. Apparently the combat system in the first game was too polished, satisfying and worst of all, TOO EASY.
Here's a list of the biggest and best things the B Team changed and fixed:
- Most hits that can take 80% of your health are now very quiet and have awkward hit reactions
- Hitting an enemy with a Greatsword (read: Ultra Greatsword) heavy attack can frequently stun you more than the enemy you hit, ensuring they can also do big damage to you.
- Rolling? PFFFFFF TOO EASY, they fixed it by removing all of the I-frames and forcing you to waste money on leveling a stat to get them back.
- Backstabbing? That's not nice, why should you get a couple of seconds to assess threats anyway? Now you will take damage from other enemies while in the backstab animation.
- When using health items or picking items up, there is an honorary 1-2 second delay after the animation has finished before you can do things like use another item or raise your shield
- 5 health items? That's 4 too many to start the game with! No! You start with ONE and be grateful!
- Much more linear and restrictive level design and for all you cheeky kids trying to outsmart the monkey level designers, they jacked up the fall damage! Take THAT enjoyable gameplay!
- NPC dialogue is now very straight forward and any implications are presented with a *wink* just so you don't miss the details, but don't worry! They left the laughter-as-end-of-sentence writing that you remember.
- The game world is now so huge that all the levels have to blatantly lie about where and how far you've travelled. That's pretty big!
- Did someone say texture tiling? Many levels are now easier on the eyes and by that I mean less distractingly beautiful. In fact, the whole game has a much lower level of polish in every way to keep it consistent.
- More realistic Medieval Zombie A.I.
- All explosives do Real LifeTM amounts of damage
- Bonfires and merchants are made exciting now that they're in enemy lines of sight
- The Dark Souls 2 HD Remix moves and rearranges enemies with a level of finesse only seen from the finest weekend modders, for only the full price of the game, again!
Did they do anything that I won't insult? There are a couple of things:
- Raised amount of equippable items in all categories
- An O.K. PC port. Not great but a step in the right direction.
- O.K. Mouse and keyboard support but then they left all the controller prompts in.
- Being able to eat multiple cheques at once.
The best part about Dark Souls 2 is the playerbase who started with it and then claim the others aren't as good because you can't perform that post-it note's worth of actions. I'm sure there are people who said the same thing about Insect Armageddon, which is a game I'd rather play than Dark Souls 2. Pre-order now for an exclusive sword you won't use.
At least we did finally get a real sequel.

Rome 2-
So I had not played this series in a long, long time.  I played a lot, I mean A LOT, of the original Rome and Barbarian Invasion back in the day.  I was on YouTube and stumbled across a couple of battles and got intrigued.  The game was still 60 bucks, so I had to put that on hold.  Luckily, Cyber Monday (or thereabouts) the game was finally under 20 bucks.  Voila!
There are some issues in getting this game set up.  It took me a fair amount of time (and new hardware) to get the game to run correctly.  Even then, the hardware alone isn't enough without playing with lots of settings, testing, benchmarking, and re-testing.  Glad to say, after much effort the game runs smoothly even with large armies, etc. it runs smooth and looks like a milllion bucks.
The campaign is fine but its lots and lots of effort to build up to great battles.  If that is your thing, great.  It's there and I played a bit but I haven't finished a campaign game and honestly I don't think I ever will.
To me, the custom battles are way more fun.  There are tons of maps and cities and multiple size setting on settlements so there is lots of replay value.  Also, you can click on any place on the campaign map and fight there.  Kinda cool to have pretty much unlimited settings for battles.  The city seiges are unlike any RTS I have ever played.  Deep, layered city defenses can be just as effective as a staunch wall stand in winning the day for the defender.  There is a great depth into what determines a good fight for your units.  Morale, fatigue, unti type, terrain, local force superiority, posiition of attacker relative to front of unit, etc.  Lots of fun figuring ways to flank you foes or to work a company of archers in the rear of those annoying enemy swordsman to give them a taste of heavy shot a point blank range.  Very satisfying, indeed.
The online gaming community is still very much alive, too.
The game has way overpriced DLC so be smart and wait for sales to get it for less than 8 bucks for culture packs and the $15+ they charge for the campaign packs.  There is some good stuff there for sure, just don't any of you go paying full price for any of it.  As Marcus Antony says, "Be patient till the last."

I don’t usually write reviews, but when I do, they are about Factorio. ;) Factorio has to be one of my top 10 all-time games. I almost didn’t get past the first five minutes as the controls were frustrating for me (though they won’t be if you play a lot of FPS), but I have VERY glad I did. It is a wonderfully deep and complex game, that will have you wishing there were 48 hours in a day.
I tried to figure out how to do everything on my own without Googling things, and I am glad I did as each factory I made evolved and look unique. If I look back at my first few I think ‘ugh!!!’ how could I have made such a mess! But each factory was better and more efficient and more organized, and it was a fascinating and fun journey.
This is not a passive game. If you don’t like to think, you will likely not enjoy it. It isn’t something you can zone out with like watching a movie. The graphics could use an update too, as on large monitors if you zoom they are lacking. But the programming is so top notch that it just makes up for any flaws. Seeing a massive factory in full swing without a hint of stutter or slowdown is amazing. Yeah, it is that good.

In Factorio you build an automized factory on a foreign planet.
If you like games with economic systems and production chains, this one is for you! It also has aspects of RTS, RPG, and crafting games, like Minecraft.
To sum it up just now: It is one of the best games i've played in the last years and I dfinately recommend it!
Gameplay
The gameplay is really innovative and i've never seen anything like it before:
As you start the game, you find yourself as a tiny dude walking around on a foreign planet. You gather first ressources and craft the first basic assets for your upcoming factory yourself. As you place them somewhere, things are starting to get automated. As you continue to build your factory, you automize more and more. Ressources are mined automatically and shipped to refinement buildings via conveyor belts. There, they can be grabbed, refined and shipped along. Not only do you start to dive into new areas of research and production, but you also constantly try to optimize and make things work more efficiently. In later stages of the game, you can even start to compute stuff with intelligent electronics, if you want to.
So long so easy – but that's not all. As you work on your planet, the planet's native aliens are not so happy about your fresh factory, since it pollutes their home. They will attack you from their bases in troops, requiring you to protect your factory with automated gun towers or even shoot them yourself with some guns or vehincles you can craft.
Resume
I always starve for new innovative games that aren't just a lame 1000th remake of the same genres with just 1 or 2 tiny new features.
Factorio is just that! It offers such deep gameplay, so much space to optimize stuff and just have fun with blasting the Hippie aliens! If you have some spare Dollars to spend, put them in Factorio's dev's pockets! You will not be disappointed!

Where to start with this...
I originally played this on a Powermac G5 when it first came out around the end of 2008, I remember that I originally got it sometime around the 2008 election. My attention was focused on this game the whole time.
It's one of those games where it seems extremely simple at first, but then the complexities and depth of it gradually shine through. The puzzles are neat, and I never had to use any skips until the last part (and I normally sucka t puzzles) but they don't feel easy, they feel satisfying regardless.
The visuals are nice, and they're crisp and good looking, and most importantly they do NOT resort to trying to look like pixel art. However, the game does run at a low resolution and there is no way to change it.
The soundtrack... Well, let's just say it's one of the best soundtracks in an Indie game ever produced. It is well performed, it is entirely originally composed, and it doesn't resort to sounding like chiptune or 16-bit stuff to try and manipulate nostalgic nerves. One of the best parts of the game for certain, and even better is that all of the soundtrack (the full versions, not the shortened versions in the game) can be found right on Youtube. Very memorable soundtrack, I can say that about very very few games.
Buy it? YES! It's on sale frequently anyways.

The grind to the endgame may seem annoying at first, but once ya get there it's worth it. Can pretty much play as any class all on one character, and the community varies but mostly it's all good. Plus, would recommend finding a good group of people or join an FC with some experienced players if you're really struggling; they'll help you get to the end content and it makes the game more exciting to play knowing you don't have to face the dungeons, trials and raids alone. I haven't played any other MMOs that are out there but this is a really excellent one to get into. And bonus: the DLC that is coming will only add more amazing content. And avid FF fan or not, the game just sucks you in. There's a lot of positives from this game, maybe with a few downsides here and there.
You always have the trial version to test out the game - whether you can run it smoothly on your computer, or to test out and see if you'll like it. If you don't, then it's no risk. Just keep in mind that if you do want the full version, you're going to have to pay that monthly subscription (cheapest being $15 a month).
Is this game worth it? In my opinion, hell yeah it is.
